articles.title: FBI leads action to shut down Virtualine bulletproof service linked to major cybercrime activity
articles.text:
FBI leads action to shut down Virtualine bulletproof service linked to major cybercrime activity
Virtualine was hosting multiple illegal forums
- FBI and international partners seized infrastructure tied to Virtualine, a hosting provider allegedly serving cybercriminals
- Authorities say the service facilitated phishing, ransomware operations, illicit crypto activity, and other crimes
- Investigators seized servers and customer data, though no arrests have been announced so far
The FBI has announced it seized the website of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service that allegedly allowed child pornography, laundered stolen and extorted crypto, and facilitated a wide range of other criminal activities.
The operation was carried out in partnership with German and Dutch authorities, as well as multiple private companies, with police raiding a data center in Limburg to seize “dozens of physical servers” that also hosted “hundreds” of virtual servers. As a result, they gained access to information about more than 3,000 of Virtualine’s customers, it was said.
“The police are currently taking follow-up actions towards these users,” the Dutch police said, although it’s difficult to say how valuable the information will be, since most bulletproof hosting providers don’t ask for private data, and criminals are good at hiding it, as well.
Bulletproof hosting
Every website, including hacking forums, criminal service providers, even fraudulent landing pages, needs a server that hosts it. Hosting providers renting out these servers are generally compliant with law enforcement agencies, so when the police requests a takedown or files a complaint, most of them comply. However, there is a subset of hosting providers, colloquially called “bulletproof hosting”, which are unusually resistant to pressure from the authorities.
It doesn’t mean all of them are inherently illegal or malicious. There are cases where such services are necessary - in countries with strong censorship, or where website owners want to protect their identities.
In this case, however, Virtualine was openly criminal, with the US Department of Justice (DOJ) saying it advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums saying, on at least one occasion, “You can use Virtualine for all illegal/black hat activities (including phis[h]ing, carding, email spam, port scanning and all others) except for child contents and terrorism activities.”
The company took it a step further. In March 2026, it introduced an “additional protection plan” that offers customers who receive takedown requests “another shell company not affiliated with Virtualine, after which the server is reactivated.”

Interestingly enough, Virtualine said it did not accept child porn or terrorism content, but according to the DOJ - did exactly the opposite.
One of its clients created a forum that allowed users to post and sell access to “nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults,” while also promoting a hack-for-hire service that broke into people’s accounts and stole their explicit photos and videos. Virtualine was even notified about it by law enforcement agencies from Germany, Canada, and Australia, but decided to ignore the warnings and continue hosting the client.
At the same time, Virtualine’s customers were allowed to pay in Bitcoin, offering an unhosted bitcoin address that allowed customers “to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit”. Citing Chainalysis data, BleepingComputer said the company’s wallet was seen receiving funds from ransomware operations, infostealers, Russian-language cybercrime forums, and more.
“Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added.
Piercing the kevlar
Besides confiscating the servers and the data, the main website - virtualine.net - was defaced and now shows the usual FBI “this website has been seized” message. Unfortunately, no arrests have been made, which means the service will most likely continue operating.
According to BleepingComputer, it is “partially online” but its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, which could mean that much of its infrastructure was pulled offline.
Usually, disruptions such as this one are only temporary, and it won’t take long before they are remedied and the service becomes fully operational again.

articles.title: La FIA mise à fond sur l'IA d'Amazon pour imaginer la F1 de demain
articles.text:
La FIA a officialisé, mercredi, un partenariat mondial avec Amazon Web Services. Le géant du cloud mettra son intelligence artificielle au service des règlements des futures Formule 1, mais aussi de la pratique amateur.
Déjà partenaires de longue date sur la data notamment, la Fédération automobile internationale (FIA) et Amazon Web Services (AWS) ont annoncé, mercredi, avoir scellé une nouvelle union, plus globale encore, sur l'intelligence artificielle, le cloud, le machine learning et l'infrastructure cloud. Le groupe américain devient le partenaire officiel de l'instance sur toutes ces composantes. Le géant du cloud connaissait déjà bien les paddocks, mais le voilà désormais officiellement associé à ceux qui écrivent les règles. Qu'il s'agisse des souffleries virtuelles, des ingénieurs épaulés par l'IA ou des licences dématérialisées, l'accord va de la F1 aux courses de club, pour concerner autant la monoplace de demain que le pilote amateur du dimanche.
Pourquoi la FIA mise désormais sur l’IA et le cloud d’AWS pour la Formule 1
On sait que la FIA fait déjà tourner ses simulations aérodynamiques sur les capacités de calcul haute performance d'AWS. Le principe s'appelle d'ailleurs la simulation numérique des fluides. On découpe l'air qui entoure une monoplace en une multitude de petites cellules, puis on calcule comment chacune se comporte. Il n'y a ni pièce à fabriquer, ni maquette à souffler. Du coup, on innove plus vite, pour moins cher, avec un impact environnemental réduit. La directrice mondiale événements, sport et divertissement d'AWS, Kristin Shaff, rappelle que le sport automobile est l'un des environnements les plus exigeants et les plus riches en données au monde.
Pourquoi la FIA s'y intéresse-t-elle autant ? Tout simplement parce que c'est elle qui fixe le cadre technique dans lequel les écuries devront ensuite rivaliser d'ingéniosité. Avant d'imposer une contrainte à dix ou onze équipes, autant savoir comment l'air réagira autour de la voiture, quitte à faire chauffer les serveurs. AWS jouera ainsi un rôle déterminant dans l'élaboration des règles techniques de la prochaine génération de Formule 1.
L'accord concerne aussi les équipes techniques et d'ingénierie de la FIA, qui recevront des outils d'intelligence artificielle. L'objectif est de renforcer leur capacité à concevoir des règlements qui font progresser la sécurité, la performance et la durabilité. Le communiqué présente bien l'IA comme un outil mis entre les mains des ingénieurs, pas comme un législateur autonome.
Au-delà de la F1, l'IA d'AWS veut ouvrir les portes du sport auto
L'autre volet du partenariat fait moins de bruit qu'un V6 turbo hybride, mais il touche bien plus de monde. Il s'agit de la plateforme de licences numériques lancée l'an dernier par les deux partenaires. Elle simplifie les démarches des pilotes, officiels et bénévoles. Elle offre aussi aux autorités sportives nationales, l'équivalent de la FFSA en France, un outil unifié pour administrer et faire grandir leur discipline. La plateforme s'étend désormais à davantage de pays, en plus de devenir multilingue, de gérer les renouvellements de licence et de se connecter à la FIA University.
Cette hyper modernisation pourrait aider à doubler le nombre de pratiquants du sport automobile dans le monde, l'ambition assumée de la FIA. La fédération prévoit d'ajouter des outils de gestion d'événements pour les bénévoles et les officiels. D'autres applications et services internes basculeront vers AWS dans les années à venir. Le chantier figurait en tout cas parmi les engagements de campagne de Mohammed Ben Sulayem, son président. Ce dernier a conscience que la technologie transforme chaque facette du sport, et la fédération doit mener ce changement. Le dirigeant compte aussi sur ce partenariat pour aider les clubs membres à travailler plus efficacement. L'instance réunit déjà 246 organisations membres sur cinq continents et encadre six championnats du monde.
Mais attention toutefois : mieux vaut ne pas confondre les casquettes, et l'embrouille peut vite arriver. AWS accompagne déjà Formula 1, le détenteur des droits commerciaux, depuis 2018, notamment pour les statistiques affichées pendant les retransmissions. Ce nouveau contrat le place cette fois aux côtés de l'arbitre. AWS rejoint le programme de partenaires mondiaux de la FIA, où il retrouve notamment Rolex, DHL et Hankook. Il s'affichera aussi aux FIA Awards, la soirée annuelle qui célèbre les champions du monde. Enfin, il soutiendra la Sustainable Innovation Series, une plateforme d'événements tournée, comme son nom l'indique, vers l'innovation durable, et menée en étroite coopération avec les championnats du monde FIA.

articles.title: The next Hitman elusive target has Agent 47 taking down a podcaster 'completely obsessed with content'
articles.text:
The next Hitman elusive target has Agent 47 taking down a podcaster who is 'loud, paranoid, and completely obsessed with content' — and played by a real-life influencer
👨🦲
- The next Hitman Elusive Target has been revealed
- The limited-time mission will see Agent 47 taking down an annoying podcaster
- The target will be played by real-world content creator Seán McLoughlin
The next Hitman Elusive Target has been revealed, and it's something that could happen in 2026.
As of October 29, players will be able to take out Finn Colton – a controversial millionaire content creator who goes by the online handle 'Finnvictus'. The mission will see the flashy mansion of the existing Hawke's Bay map turned into an even more elaborate space for content creation, with its own underground studio and cameras that live-stream everything 24/7.
Bald assassin protagonist Agent 47 has managed to gain entry thanks to an invite to appear on the content creator's flagship podcast and will have to contend with an environment that has eyes almost everywhere.
That's not all, however, as Colton is played by Seán McLoughlin, better known as 'Jacksepticeye', with the popular streamer lending both his likeness and voice to the character.
"I’ve been playing Hitman with my community for years, so getting to actually step into the World of Assassination is unreal," shared McLoughlin.
"Finn is loud, paranoid, and completely obsessed with content, and playing him was an absolute blast. I can’t wait to see all the creative ways you take him down."
The mission will be available for free for a limited time, though die-hard Hitman fans can pick up a themed DLC pack as well. It costs $7.99 / £6.99 and includes permanent access to the mission via the Elusive Target Arcade mode plus a new suit and some unique equipment to try.

articles.title: La Fnac écope de 7 millions d’euros d’amende pour avoir pisté les utilisateurs de son appli
articles.text:
La CNIL a infligé une amende de 7 millions d’euros à la Fnac pour un traceur intégré à son application mobile. Celui-ci collectait l’historique de navigation des utilisateurs, y compris lorsqu’ils avaient refusé de donner leur consentement.
La Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL) a sanctionné deux sociétés du groupe Fnac Darty d’une amende totale de 7 millions d’euros pour non-respect des règles sur les cookies et autres traceurs dans l’application mobile de la Fnac. Le gendarme des données a rendu publique sa décision ce jeudi 29 octobre 2026. En cause, on retrouve un dispositif qui transmettait à un domaine tiers les produits consultés par les utilisateurs, afin d’alimenter des recommandations personnalisées, sans leur consentement. Le régulateur exige désormais une mise en conformité rapide, sous peine d’astreinte.
Dans l'application Fnac, un traceur qui prenait des notes
Tout a commencé avec une plainte de l'association None Of Your Business (NOYB), fondée par le militant autrichien Max Schrems, rompue aux bras de fer avec les géants du numérique. La CNIL a ensuite longuement étudié l'application en mars 2024. Elle a constaté que pendant son utilisation, celle-ci envoyait des requêtes vers un domaine tiers, contenant un identifiant attribué par la Fnac à chaque utilisateur et des informations sur son activité, à commencer par les produits consultés. Le tout sans que l'intéressé ait donné son accord.
Ces informations partaient via une API, un peu le guichet automatique par lequel deux logiciels s'échangent des données sans intervention humaine. Elles servaient ensuite à remplir les rayons virtuels de l'application avec des suggestions taillées pour vous, comme des produits choisis d'après votre historique de navigation, des articles semblables à ceux que vous aviez consultés, ou encore des accessoires, consommables et services liés à un produit regardé, voire déjà acheté. Ces mêmes données servaient aussi à entraîner l'algorithme de recommandations, c'est-à-dire à lui apprendre, exemple après exemple, quels produits mettre sous vos yeux.
Le cookie n'est qu'un traceur parmi d'autres. Aux yeux de la loi, il concerne tout dispositif qui lit ou dépose des informations sur votre téléphone ou votre ordinateur, qu'il s'agisse d'un petit fichier logé dans un navigateur ou, comme ici, d'un identifiant transmis par une application. Dans ce cas, l'article 82 de la loi Informatique et Libertés impose de vous demander votre accord avant toute chose. Il n'existe que deux exceptions, à savoir les traceurs qui servent à faire fonctionner la communication elle-même, et ceux sans lesquels le service que vous avez demandé ne pourrait tout simplement pas marcher, comme un panier d'achat. Pour la CNIL, des recommandations commerciales n'entrent dans aucune de ces cases. Comme l'appli fonctionne très bien, sans vous suggérer une housse pour votre téléphone, il fallait donc demander la permission.
La Fnac a un mois pour rentrer dans le rang
La sanction, prononcée le 22 octobre 2026 par la CNIL, est partagée entre deux sociétés du groupe. Il y a une sanction de 6 millions d'euros pour Fnac Darty Participations et Services, et une autre d'1 million pour Fnac Direct. La formation restreinte, l'organe de la CNIL chargé des sanctions, justifie ce montant d'abord par le refus des utilisateurs passé à la trappe, ensuite par le large public de l'application.
L'addition pourrait être encore plus importante. Les deux entités sont visées par une injonction, c'est-à-dire qu'elles doivent prouver, dans le mois suivant la notification de la décision, que leur nouvel outil recueille bien le consentement quand c'est nécessaire. Sinon, elles s'exposent à une astreinte de 10 000 euros par jour de retard.
Sur les traceurs qui servent à personnaliser ce que vous voyez ou à vous cibler commercialement, la CNIL fait savoir qu'elle applique la même ligne sévère, sanction après sanction. Autrement dit, les règles étaient connues de tous ici, et la Fnac pouvait difficilement plaider la surprise devant elle. Compte tenu de la gravité du manquement, de l'ampleur de la collecte et du nombre d'utilisateurs concernés, la CNIL a donc choisi de rendre sa décision publique, sous la référence SAN-2026-015, plutôt que de la garder confidentielle. Avis aux éditeurs d'applis : un refus de consentement n'est pas une suggestion.

articles.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon Leads Benchmarks for Finding, Exploiting, and Patching Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.
"It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said.
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55).
One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon.
Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection.
The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program.
Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing.
The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks."
"GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said.
"GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task."
Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software.
This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft.
"These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said.
"These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

articles.title: Ofcom reveals age-check methods for UK social media ban — facial scans and photo ID spark privacy pushback as 40% of teens plan workarounds
articles.text:
'The risks aren’t hypothetical': Ofcom reveals age-check plans for UK social media ban — but privacy experts aren't convinced
Take your pick
- Ofcom has assessed the best ways of enforcing age checks online
- The regulator also identifies methods that aren't effective
- Around 4 in 10 under-16s plan to try to get around the ban in the UK
Back in June, the UK government ruled that under-16s should be banned from social media platforms, with enforcement scheduled to start during the first half of 2027. Now the communications regulator Ofcom has set out the ways it expects tech companies to abide by the law.
In its new announcement (via the BBC), Ofcom highlights four "highly effective" methods for keeping under-16s out of apps and off sites they shouldn't be accessing — and they're all going to be familiar to anyone who's used age-gated services online in recent times.
The four methods are photo ID matching (using something like a passport or driving license), bank-based checks (Ofcom says 90% of UK 16-17 year-olds have a bank account), digital ID services (a third-party service like EasyID or Yoti), and facial age estimation via a webcam (which Ofcom says is best deployed as a secondary check).
This is a "rapid assessment" from Ofcom, and none of these approaches are confirmed yet — UK lawmakers will take the suggestions on board, and decide the best way to enforce the rules at a later date, most probably before the end of the year. All of these methods can be delivered "in a way that protects users' privacy" according to Ofcom.
Ultimately though, it will be down to tech companies to decide how to implement age checks that fulfil the requirements set down by the government. "Here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you," Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes told the BBC.
Challenges ahead
Ofcom also lists checks that it thinks are ineffective: self-declaration, general contractual agreements, and verifiable parental consent. The regulator also acknowledges that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", but says that correctly implemented safeguards should "significantly reduce the likelihood" of unauthorized access.
In its rapid assessment announcement, Ofcom also encourages app stores to take more responsibility over age checks. Right now, self-declarations are most commonly used to unlock downloads for age-restricted content.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
These are going to be tough rules to enforce, whatever the approach is: recent research from EE suggests that 42% of 11-15 year-olds are planning to try and get around whatever restrictions are put in place. This could be by switching to apps or platforms not covered by the new laws, including messaging services and gaming sites.
Last week Ofcom also admitted that the Online Safety Act introduced in July 2025 had so far made "no significant change" to the harmful content children had been exposed to online. The act was intended to ensure protection from content involving pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny, and bullying.
"This finding is concerning and shows that further progress is needed to protect children online," says Ofcom. The regulator also recommended adding material around body stigma and depression to the primary content categories that children should be protected from online.
Analysis: What do privacy experts think?
Ofcom's proposals are likely to spark some familiar privacy concerns — and security experts told us they aren't without foundation.
“The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check," said Pieter Arntz, Senior Malware Intelligence Analyst at Malwarebytes. "Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, potentially creating another attractive target for criminals. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year, a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users," he said.
Even if facial estimation techniques are more secure, there are are still downsides. "Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction," Pieter Arntz added. "Ofcom itself acknowledges that some technologies have a margin of error of a few years at 16, meaning people near the threshold may face an additional verification check," he said.
"My preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement but doesn’t learn which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you are old enough should not mean revealing who you are," he said.
Others feel the risks are more around teenagers finding workarounds.“The challenge for social media platforms is that teenagers don’t like to be told ‘no’. Many will conform, but tech-savvy young people are going to search for an open window on the ground floor," said Olli Krebs, SVP EMEA at the identity verification software provider Incode. "If the process is clunky, users of all ages will actively seek ways around it," he added.
Those workarounds could unintentionally make the problem worse. "The experience of countries such as Australia is that there will be a real risk of an increasingly technologically sophisticated population of young people will resort to a variety of circumvention techniques (primarily, but not exclusively VPNs) to access content hosted outside of the UK," said Will Richmond-Coggan, Partner specialising in Data and Privacy Disputes at Freeths.
"Such content is liable to be less well regulated generally, and to pose further risks of users gaining unsupervised access to progressively more dangerous and problematic content in relation to which the UK online safety legislation is largely powerless to take action," he added.
“None of this will be perfect. Young people will always push boundaries, and anyone promising a hundred per cent online safety is being unrealistic," concluded Olli Krebs from Incode. Exactly how successful it is depends very much on how the social media giants implement Ofcom's suggested age-check methods.

articles.title: Sabotage de câbles sous-marins : pourquoi la Chine inquiète Washington au plus haut point
articles.text:
Un nouveau rapport commandé par le Congrès des États-Unis décrit comment Pékin pourrait couper, discrètement, les câbles sous-marins qui relient les États-Unis à l’Asie. Nouvelle preuve de la nécessité de protéger ces infrastructures critiques.
Ancres traînées sur le fond, filets de chalutiers, glissements de terrain sous-marins… La grande majorité des coupures de câbles sont accidentelles. Mais depuis quelques années, des incidents troublants en mer Baltique comme près de Taïwan, impliquant des navires russes ou chinois, soulèvent de sérieuses questions.
Dans ce contexte, la commission américano-chinoise sur l’économie et la sécurité (USCC), un organe indépendant qui conseille le Congrès américain, a ordonné un rapport visant à réellement évaluer ce dont la Chine serait capable. Sa conclusion : le pays cherche à s’imposer comme la puissance dominante des fonds marins.
Une arme parfaite pour exploiter la « zone grise »
Ainsi, Pékin serait en train de mettre au point des technologies à double usage : un submersible capable de plonger à 10 000 mètres, baptisé Striver, des essaims de drones sous-marins interconnectés et, à l’étude, des coupeurs de câbles « hibernants ». Posés à l’avance sur l’infrastructure d’un adversaire, ils pourraient être activés le moment venu.
Car les câbles sous-marins sont des cibles idéales : l’attaque est discrète, difficile à attribuer et peu susceptible de provoquer une escalade. C’est, d’ailleurs, toute la logique de la « zone grise » : frapper sous le seuil politique et juridique d’une agression militaire, tout en obtenant un avantage stratégique. Concrètement, comme rien ne prouve que l’attaque est volontaire, la victime ne peut ni accuser ouvertement son adversaire ni riposter sans risquer de passer elle-même pour l’agresseur.
Mais certaines liaisons sont plus exposées que d’autres. Car les câbles qui relient les États-Unis à Taïwan, au Japon et aux Philippines traversent des eaux peu profondes, très fréquentées, et en partie revendiquées par Pékin. De même, Hawaï et Guam dépendent de très peu de routes alternatives.
Pour s’y retrouver, les auteurs ont donc créé un indice de vulnérabilité qui classe les câbles transpacifiques selon leur exposition. Parmi les dix infrastructures les plus à risque, on retrouve TPU de Google, ORCA de Meta, et E2A, codétenu par Verizon et des groupes japonais, sud-coréens et taïwanais.
Des conséquences en cascade
L’enjeu dépasse largement le monde des télécoms. Couper un seul câble pourrait saturer les capacités directes entre les États-Unis et leurs partenaires asiatiques, et renvoyer les données vers des routes plus longues et plus lentes. Si plusieurs câbles tombaient en même temps, lors d’une crise autour de Taïwan par exemple, c’est l’ensemble de la capacité transpacifique qui pourrait être submergée, avec des communications contraintes de faire le tour du globe.
Même un simple ralentissement coûterait cher : le trading haute fréquence et les services d’intelligence artificielle dépendent de connexions ultra-rapides. Une perturbation plus large toucherait la finance, le cloud et les communications du quotidien. D’autant que réparer après coup ne suffira pas, préviennent les auteurs.
Ils appellent d’abord Washington à renforcer la surveillance avec ses alliés : outils communs de suivi maritime, patrouilles plus fréquentes, protocoles partagés en cas d’incident, sanctions durcies et zones d’exclusion près des secteurs sensibles. Ils recommandent aussi de reconstituer les flottes de réparation, vieillissantes et sous tension, et de prépositionner le matériel critique.
Enfin, ils plaident pour des investissements massifs dans les capacités sous-marines, civiles comme militaires, afin de rattraper une Chine qui en a fait une priorité depuis 2014.

articles.title: Webinar: How to Build AI Threat Readiness Into Your Security Operations
articles.text:
Security teams have spent years trying to detect threats faster. AI is changing the harder part: how much time defenders have left to act.
Advanced AI models can now help attackers discover vulnerabilities, generate exploit code, and move through weaknesses faster than traditional security processes were built to handle.
The challenge is no longer just finding another vulnerability or generating another alert. It is knowing which exposures matter, what an attacker can reach, and which issues need to be fixed first.
That is the focus of next week's webinar, How to Build AI Threat Readiness Across Your Security Operations, featuring an expert from Wiz. The session will show how security teams can improve visibility, prioritize real risk, and shorten the path from detection to remediation.
Most security teams already have plenty of data. They have vulnerability findings, cloud alerts, identity signals, application telemetry, and threat detections. The harder problem is connecting those signals quickly enough to answer the questions that drive action.
Is this vulnerability reachable? Does the exposed asset contain sensitive data? Can an attacker move from it to something more important? Who owns the affected system? What should be fixed first?
When those answers live across different tools and teams, investigations slow down. That delay matters more when attackers can automate parts of the discovery and exploitation process.
📅 Save Your Spot Today: Register for the Webinar Here.
The webinar focuses on two practical needs: broad visibility and faster action.
Security teams need enough context to understand risk across cloud infrastructure, code, identities, SaaS, AI services, and the software supply chain. They also need a way to identify exploitable paths, investigate suspicious activity, and deliver remediation to the right owner without having to rebuild the same context every time.
A Wiz expert will explain how organizations can use unified security context to separate urgent exposure from background noise, understand attack paths, and bring security agents into investigation and remediation workflows.
For SOC teams, that can mean less time spent manually assembling context. For vulnerability management, it means knowing which findings deserve immediate attention. For cloud and security engineering teams, it means connecting risk to the people and systems that can actually fix it.
The goal is not to automate every security decision. It is to remove delays caused by fragmented tools, repetitive investigation, and unclear ownership.
Attendees will leave with a framework for assessing whether their current security operations are ready for faster, AI-assisted attacks. The key questions are practical: Can you see enough of the environment to understand an attack path? Can you quickly determine whether a new issue affects something attackers can reach? Can you move a validated risk from detection to remediation fast enough?
AI is increasing the speed at which weaknesses can be found and used. Security teams need to respond with better context and less delay.

articles.title: Data breach at Sony ISP subsidiary exposes 2.5 million customer records as Japan hit with another major cyberattack
articles.text:
Data breach at Sony ISP subsidiary exposes 2.5 million customer records as Japan hit with another major cyberattack
Hackers are gunning for Japan's ISPs
- Sony Network Communications discloses breach affecting roughly 2.5 million ISP customers and former users
- Exposed data included personal details, while some email service users also lost email passwords
- Company contained the intrusion, notified authorities, and warned customers about phishing and fraud risks
A subsidiary of Sony Network Communications, the Japanese tech giant’s Internet Service Provider (ISP) arm, has confirmed suffering a data breach which saw it lose sensitive data on roughly 2.5 million people.
Among the stolen files were people’s phone numbers, email addresses, and in some cases - email passwords.
The company confirmed the news in an apology and notice letter in which it said threat actors accessed So-net, the company’s consumer-facing ISP service brand. The identity of the attackers was not disclosed, and nor was the method they used to break in. The breach happened on Monday, October 19 2026, and was spotted four days later, on October 23.
“Immediately after confirming the incident, we shut down the affected server and blocked communications from the source of the unauthorized access,” the machine-translated letter reads. A day later, the investigation determined that the attackers exfiltrated a total of 2,141,986 sensitive records belonging to both current and former members.
Trickling down to NTT Docomo
Of that number, roughly 1.8 million belong to current members, who had their names, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, dates of birth, genders, and internet connection IDs exposed to the hackers. Passwords were not leaked, Sony said.
There were also more than 440,000 records taken from plala (S Course), and this part also affects NTT Docomo, a separate internet service provider that uses Sony Network Communications’ underlying infrastructure as part of its service.
NTT Docomo issued a separate statement, notifying its customers of the incident, and urging them to stay vigilant with incoming emails and other communications:
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“There is a risk of suspicious communications from those who misuse potentially leaked information in the future,” the machine-translated notice reads. “Please pay attention to the following points:
・Do not respond to emails, SMS, or phone calls
・Do not open links in the body
・Do not open attached files.”
The company added that the incident affects all Hikari service clients, as well as those that cancelled from May 2026, onwards.
Some So-net members’ email addresses and email passwords were, indeed, taken. A separate set of data affecting Email Service (G), A-Box (an additional mailbox service), So-net VAIO Mail, and PostPet Mail Account Service was nabbed, and the company reported 24,655 affected addresses for Email Service (G), 17,672 for A-Box, 7,005 for So-net VAIO Mail, and 5,069 for PostPet Mail Account Service. The breach affects both current So-net customers, and those that cancelled their subscriptions in March 2026 or later. Those that cancelled by the end of February were not affected, according to the announcement.
Banking data struck, too
Some customers also had their banking data exposed - but not many. “We confirmed the leakage of 16 records containing bank account information, including financial institution name, bank code, branch name, branch code, deposit account type, account number, and account holder's name,” the company said.
It stressed that it does not hold bank account PINs and therefore, they could not have been compromised. “We will individually contact the affected customers to apologize,” the notice reads.
Sony Network Communications said it notified the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission and other relevant government and law enforcement organizations and is currently investigating the attack.
So far, no hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the attack, and the data has not yet appeared anywhere on the dark web. There is also no word of this being an extortion attempt.
The attack comes less than a week after Japanese internet giant GMO Group told its customers to scan their computers for viruses, back up all of their data, disconnect the devices from the internet and then shut them down.

articles.title: Volkswagen perd 5,8 milliards en trois mois : le constructeur prépare un séisme social historique
articles.text:
Le constructeur allemand a essuyé une perte nette de 5,82 milliards d’euros au troisième trimestre 2026. Porsche et le recul des ventes chinoises pèsent lourd, tandis que le succès des voitures électriques en Europe ne rapporte pas encore assez pour soulager les comptes.
Vendre davantage de voitures électriques en Europe ne suffit pas à remettre Volkswagen sur la bonne voie. Les résultats publiés ce jeudi 29 octobre font apparaître une perte nette de 2,72 milliards d’euros sur les neuf premiers mois de l’année. Le dernier trimestre se solde par sa plus lourde perte opérationnelle depuis le Dieselgate, en 2015, et la direction veut accélérer les économies.
Selon Reuters, la restructuration pourrait porter à 100 000 le nombre total de postes supprimés dans le groupe, en incluant les 50 000 suppressions déjà actées en Allemagne. Ce scénario était déjà évoqué en septembre.
Porsche fait déraper les comptes
Volkswagen a revu à la baisse la valeur comptable attribuée à Porsche, ce qui se traduit par une charge de 6,4 milliards d’euros. Cette dépréciation ne correspond pas à une sortie de trésorerie, mais elle traduit des perspectives moins favorables pour la marque, confrontée aux difficultés du marché chinois et aux droits de douane américains.
En ajoutant notamment un milliard d’euros de dépréciations sur des actifs chinois et les frais liés à la vente prévue du site d’Osnabrück, les charges exceptionnelles atteignent 7,8 milliards sur le trimestre. Sur neuf mois, elles s’élèvent à 8,7 milliards. Sans elles, le groupe aurait dégagé 8,8 milliards d’euros de résultat opérationnel, avec une marge de 3,8%, que son directeur financier Arno Antlitz juge insuffisante.
Les électriques séduisent, mais rapportent moins
Les difficultés dépassent donc les seules écritures comptables. Volkswagen a livré 1,89 million de véhicules entre juillet et septembre, soit 14,3% de moins qu’un an auparavant. En Chine, le recul atteint 38,5%, avec environ 406 000 voitures écoulées.
L’Europe offre un tableau plus encourageant pour l’électrique, avec quelque 150 000 commandes pour la famille de petites voitures comprenant l’ID. Polo. Mais Arno Antlitz rappelle que les voitures électriques dégagent encore des marges inférieures à celles des modèles thermiques. Leur part croissante dans les ventes pèse donc sur la rentabilité du groupe au moment où il doit financer sa transformation.
L’emploi de nouveau sous pression
Oliver Blume mise sur une gamme resserrée, des usines plus efficaces et des structures simplifiées, dans le cadre d’un programme de réduction des coûts d’environ 31 milliards d’euros. Comme nous vous l’avions expliqué le 7 septembre dernier, le patron de VW prépare 100 000 suppressions de postes dans le groupe, ce qui porterait les réductions bien au-delà des 50 000 déjà actées.
L’objectif annuel a lui aussi été revu à la baisse en septembre. Volkswagen vise désormais une marge opérationnelle d’au plus 1% pour environ 315 milliards d’euros de chiffre d’affaires. Il prévoit près de 10 milliards d’euros de charges exceptionnelles sur l’exercice.
Le succès des petites électriques montre que Volkswagen sait encore trouver des clients. Il doit maintenant parvenir à les séduire avec des prix compétitifs tout en gagnant suffisamment d’argent pour financer les modèles suivants. Cette équation concerne toute l’industrie européenne qui doit rendre l’électrique aussi convaincante dans ses comptes que sur la route.

articles.title: Telegram Android Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code When Users Answer Voice Calls
articles.text:
A flaw in Telegram for Android allowed an attacker to run code on a victim's phone via a voice call once the victim answered, according to security startup NebuSec.
The attacker needed only an ordinary Telegram account. Telegram fixed the flaw in version 12.10.4 of the app, released in late September, and NebuSec disclosed it on October 29.
The flaw can be triggered in every version from 8.6.2 through 12.10.3, NebuSec's co-founder and chief executive said in an email to The Hacker News. Those versions came out between March 2022 and September 2026.
The company confirmed it in private phone calls on ARM64-based phones and has no evidence so far that it directly affects Telegram's iOS and desktop apps or group calls.
Anyone using Telegram for Android should make sure the app is on version 12.10.4 or later. The version number appears at the bottom of the app's Settings page. The flaw had no CVE identifier as of October 29.
The Hacker News has asked NebuSec and Telegram whether the flaw was used in real attacks, and asked NebuSec what an attacker's code could reach on a phone.
During a Telegram call, the two apps send each other short messages to set up the call and report its state. One type, called MediaState, reports whether the microphone is muted, whether the camera is on, and how the video is rotated.
The flaw was in the code that reads MediaState messages. That code did not handle missing fields correctly and accessed memory it should not, according to NebuSec.
Telegram's published source code for version 12.10.3 contains a flaw that matches that description, a review by The Hacker News found. When a MediaState message included a rotation value, the code checked that value. It then read a different field, the video state, even if the message had no such field.
Version 12.10.4 reads the rotation value from the right field. The calling code that uses this message was switched on in version 8.6.2, the first version NebuSec names.
Telegram's Android, iOS, and desktop apps use one shared library, called tgcalls, for calls. A change labeled "Fix camera rotation" made the same correction in tgcalls on April 21, 2026.
Telegram's iOS source code included that change from version 12.7, released in May, and the desktop app's code from version 7.0.1, released in July. Telegram for Android received it in version 12.10.4 in September.
Whether the earlier code could be exploited in those apps has not been shown.
NebuSec's video shows two phones, one marked as the attacker and one as the victim. The victim accepts a Telegram call. About half a minute into the call, the victim's phone switches to its home screen, the app icons fall down the screen, and a "HACKED BY NEBUSEC" logo appears.
The video does not show which Telegram or Android version the victim's phone was running. No technical write-up of the flaw was on NebuSec's website as of October 29, so the step from the flaw to running code depends on the video and on what the company says.
NebuSec, a startup backed by Y Combinator, says its Code Security product, which runs on OpenAI's GPT-5.4 model, found the flaw. In July, the company described an Android exploit chain that started with a Firefox flaw and reached the kernel of an ARM64 device running Android 17.
Separately, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) published an advisory on October 15 about an unpatched flaw in rlottie, the library Telegram apps have used to draw animated stickers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111105 (CVSS score: 7.0), can let an attacker run code if a user opens a malicious file or page, ZDI said.
Telegram had told ZDI in March that checks on its servers mitigated the flaw, and in April asked ZDI for a full remote code execution chain.
Those checks could be bypassed, researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says in the abstract for his OffensiveCon talk in Tokyo. The research used AI-guided fuzzing, which feeds code with large amounts of broken or unexpected input, to find memory-corruption bugs in rlottie across Telegram's iOS, Android, and desktop apps. It then chained those bugs, which stem from flaws in how stickers are delivered and checked, to run code on Telegram for iOS.
The Android app replaced rlottie with tlottie, a library written in Rust, between versions 12.8.1 in June and 12.10.0 in August, according to Telegram's published source code. The desktop app's code made the same switch in September, and the iOS code added tlottie in version 13.0 in October while still including rlottie.

articles.title: Cómo ha cambiado el valor de la criptomoneda bitcoin en las últimas 24 horas
articles.text:
El bitcoin, la primera moneda virtual lanzada al mercado, fue creado por Satoshi Nakamoto (pseudónimo) en 2008 tras la crisis financiera que afectó al mundo; esta divisa digital tenía como base un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales.
Conocido en el mundo de los mercados bajo las siglas BTC, el bitcoin utiliza la criptografía para garantizar que su gestión sea descentralizada, es decir, que no pueda ser regulado por ninguna institución u organismo bancario, lo que a su vez hace que las criptomonedas sean volátiles.
Pese al avance y alcance que ha tenido el Bitcoin y otros activos digitales de gran talla como Ethereum, organismos como el Banco Mundial, el Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI) y el Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo (BID) aún se muestran dudosos sobre los "pros" de este tipo de criptomonedas.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Valor de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
La cotización de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 80011.3 dólares, lo que significa que la criptomoneda sufrió un cambio de -0.72% en las últimas 24 horas.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0% con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #1.
El flujo histórico de inversiones impulsa a bitcoin a máximos nunca antes vistos
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: ‘The most entertaining durability test video I've ever seen’: this Trump phone teardown proves it’s American in name only
articles.text:
Teardown reveals the Trump phone to be an HTC U24 Pro in almost all but name — but at least it’s fairly durable
Proudly American, but mostly Taiwanese
- JerryRigEverything has performed a teardown and durability test on the Trump phone
- This revealed that it's so similar to an HTC phone you can even swap their motherboards
- The Trump phone did at least survive the durability tests
It was starting to feel like we wouldn’t have to hear any more about the Trump Mobile T1, but a new durability test has confirmed what we already largely knew — namely that it's little more than a rebranded HTC.
A previous teardown from iFixit revealed that the Trump phone had essentially identical specs and components to the HTC U24 Pro — a mid-range Taiwanese phone from 2024. The design is ever so slightly different, with the Trump phone having a different camera housing and a gold paint job, but the dimensions are the same too.
Now, though, JerryRigEverything has gone a step further, revealing that not only is the internal layout the same, right down to the number of screws, but if you swap the Trump phone’s motherboard with the HTC U24 Pro’s, both phones still work.
So the Trump phone really is almost a carbon copy of that HTC handset — rather calling into question its claims of being “proudly American.”
Passes the durability test
The only upside to all this is that, by essentially being an HTC U24 Pro, the Trump phone matches that device for durability. It survived being bent in multiple directions, seemingly has effective water resistance, and has a screen that’s just as scratch-resistant as most modern smartphones.
So if you have bought one of these devices, then at least it might last you a while — but that’s likely more down to designers and engineers in Taiwan than anyone in the US.
And even if you haven’t bought one, the video is worth a watch, targeting as it does not just the phone but the entire Trump administration, to the point where one Reddit commenter described it as “the most entertaining durability test video I've ever seen”.

GravaStar Introduces the Mercury Edge Series of Wireless Gaming Headsets
GravaStar, the design-driven gaming hardware brand known for its sci-fi aesthetic, today announced the Mercury Edge Series. Led by Mercury Edge Pro, the lineup pairs GravaStar's distinctive design language with 53 mm dynamic drivers and spatial gaming audio. Mercury Edge adds versatile wireless connectivity and extended battery life, while Mercury Edge Lite offers a direct, battery-free USB-C experience.
Sculpted Design with a Distinct Gaming Identity
Inspired by skeletal architecture, the series combines flowing contours, polished transitions and layered earcup geometry with seven-color RGB lighting. Memory foam cushions, 90-degree rotating earcups and a sliding headband provide an adaptable over-ear fit.Mercury Edge Pro Brings Flagship Audio into Focus

Active Noise Cancellation reduces up to 34dB of environmental noise, while a detachable unidirectional microphone with ENC call noise reduction supports clearer team communication.

articles.title: Claude a réussi à pirater Chrome, Safari et Android en combinant plusieurs failles, pour le meilleur et pour le pire
articles.text:
Une version expérimentale de Claude a réussi à découvrir et à combiner plusieurs vulnérabilités pour construire des attaques fonctionnelles contre Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows et Linux. Une avancée qui pourrait transformer la recherche en cybersécurité, et pas uniquement au profit de ceux qui protègent les systèmes.
Pour mener une cyberattaque jusqu'au bout, il faut parfois identifier plusieurs vulnérabilités complémentaires, comprendre comment elles interagissent et déterminer dans quel ordre les exploiter. Un travail ardu, longtemps réservé à des équipes de recherche particulièrement expérimentées, qu'Anthropic affirme désormais pouvoir confier à l'intelligence artificielle. Dans un rapport publié le 27 octobre, l'entreprise a détaillé les résultats obtenus par un modèle expérimental de Claude, capable de découvrir des failles et de les combiner lui-même pour compromettre des navigateurs et des systèmes d'exploitation parmi les plus utilisés au monde.
De la faille isolée à l'attaque complète, Claude franchit une nouvelle étape
Pour mettre Claude à l'épreuve, Anthropic a mobilisé sa Frontier Red Team, l'équipe chargée d'évaluer les capacités et les risques de ses modèles les plus avancés. Pendant plusieurs mois, les chercheurs ont fait travailler l'IA sur des logiciels complexes, à l'aide d'une plateforme qui lançait de nombreux agents en parallèle. Certains inspectaient le code, d'autres cherchaient comment accéder à des données protégées ou contourner les restrictions d'un programme. Le modèle disposait aussi d'outils de rétro-ingénierie pour analyser les logiciels dont le code source n'était pas disponible.
Sur Chrome, ce travail a débouché sur une chaîne de quatre vulnérabilités. Les deux premières permettaient de corrompre la mémoire du moteur JavaScript et de prendre le contrôle du processus d'affichage, les deux autres de franchir l'isolation du navigateur pour exécuter du code sur l'ordinateur. Lors des tests, l'exploit conçu par Claude a ainsi réussi à lancer la Calculatrice sur un Mac quelques secondes après l'ouverture d'une page web piégée, sans autre action de l'utilisateur.
Les attaques contre Safari et Android ont, elles, donné accès à des données normalement protégées, qu'il s'agisse d'informations appartenant à d'autres sites web ou de photos stockées sur un téléphone verrouillé. Sur Windows, une faille a permis de provoquer le plantage d'un serveur à distance. Sur Linux, enfin, l'exploitation d'une même vulnérabilité du noyau pour découvrir l'organisation de sa mémoire puis détourner son exécution a permis de lancer des commandes avec les privilèges root sur un serveur distant vulnérable, sans authentification ni intervention de la victime.
Une nouvelle course entre chercheurs et attaquants
Au total, Anthropic a signalé à Google 62 vulnérabilités dans Chrome, toutes classées critiques ou de gravité élevée, dont 13 permettant de s'échapper d'une sandbox. Google les a corrigées dans Chrome 156 et crédite les chercheurs de l'entreprise, assistés de Claude, pour plusieurs de ces découvertes. La possibilité de produire des exploits fonctionnels donne aux éditeurs un moyen de mesurer les conséquences des failles identifiées et de déterminer lesquelles corriger en priorité.
Anthropic préconise désormais d'étendre cette recherche à chaque modification du code, afin de détecter les vulnérabilités avant qu'elles n'atteignent les utilisateurs. L'entreprise a également élargi l'accès à ses modèles les plus puissants pour les professionnels de la cybersécurité sélectionnés, dans l'espoir d'accélérer la découverte et la correction des failles.
Mais les compétences acquises par ces modèles ne sont pas réservées à la défense. Si des capacités comparables deviennent accessibles à des acteurs malveillants, elles pourraient leur permettre d'explorer davantage de logiciels, de multiplier les tentatives et de raccourcir le délai entre la découverte d'une vulnérabilité et la mise au point d'une attaque. Des opérations qui mobilisent aujourd'hui des équipes très spécialisées pourraient ainsi être menées par des groupes disposant de moyens plus modestes.
Le modèle utilisé par Anthropic n'est toutefois pas accessible au public. L'entreprise affirme avoir obtenu ces résultats après quelques instructions initiales, moyennant peu d'interventions humaines, mais ne détaille pas la contribution exacte des chercheurs aux différentes étapes. Les exploits ont été réalisés en laboratoire, les vulnérabilités présentées ont toutes été corrigées et aucune exploitation malveillante de ces attaques n'a été signalée.

articles.title: The LG C6 is our TV of the year — and this five-star OLED is now at a record-low price in the early Black Friday sales.
articles.text:
The five-star and TechRadar award-winning LG C6 OLED TV drops to a record-low price ahead of Black Friday — the ideal upgrade for GTA 6
A new best-ever price for our TV of the year
Are you waiting for Black Friday before picking up a brand new TV this year? Well, you might not need to, as this five-star-rated model — and our pick for the best TV you can buy this year in the TechRadar awards – is already down to a record-low price before the sales are even fully underway. Yep, the LG C6 65-inch OLED TV is now at Amazon for £1,699 (was £1,899).
• See all LG OLED TV deals at Amazon
If the 65-inch model is too large for your room or outside of your budget, several other sizes of this top-rated TV are also reduced to record-low prices right now. Amazon has the 42-inch LG C6 for £899 (was £999), the 48-inch LG C6 for £999 (was £1,099), and the 55-inch LG C6 for £1,199 (was £1,399).
Whichever one you choose, you can be confident that you're getting the strongest all-around display for most people, according to our testing. The C6 is a top-tier OLED TV for streaming your favourite shows, watching 4K movies, enjoying fast-paced sports, or playing the latest games — especially something like GTA 6.
One big question remains: will the price go lower as we get closer to Black Friday? Of course, we can never know for sure, but I would be surprised if the C6 gets any cheaper than this over the next few weeks. Maybe by a small amount of about £50 tops, but Black Friday deals usually stick around the same price for a longer time these days, so personally, I would be happy to buy now if you don't want to wait.
LG C6 record-low price at Amazon
LG reclaimed the top spot on our best TV guide with the C6, as it boasts fantastic overall picture quality and excellent all-around performance, making it the number one pick for most. Contrast is top-tier, with vivid colours and rich blacks, while motion is handled expertly. No matter if you're watching films, streaming TV shows, playing games, or watching sports, it's up to the job. This is a record-low price for the top-tier TV and an early standout deal from this year's Black Friday sales. Smaller models from 42 inches also now start at £899.
Want to read up more on this TV before hitting the buy button? Then you can check out our five-star review of the LG C6. The brand has been leading the way in the world of OLED TVs for many years, and we concluded that this latest model is "a worthy successor to, and upgrade over, the LG C5."
Our expert tester has praise for basically every part of the C6, saying that it offers fantastic picture quality, with superior brightness and excellent contrast, a modern processor to refine images, brilliant motion smoothing that makes fast-paced sports and games great to watch, and surprisingly strong built-in sound. It'll be worth investing in a soundbar eventually, though, for the best experience.
The C6 is also one of the best options if you're hunting for a new gaming TV to prepare for GTA 6. It sports four HDMI 2.1 ports and a full suite of premium gaming features, such as support for 4K resolution at 165Hz, giving you a smooth and responsive experience when playing the latest games on current-gen consoles.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
James Pickard is a Deals Editor at TechRadar. After many years of scouring the net for the cheapest games and tech for his personal use, he decided to make it his job to share all the best bargains and coupon codes with you. James also has almost a decade of experience covering some of the biggest sales events of the year at Eurogamer and VG247, including Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Amazon Prime Day. When not deals hunting or stacking coupon codes to get the biggest savings, James can be found on the PS5, watching a classic film noir or cheering on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

articles.title: The Rise of the Threat Operator: How AI Will Redefine Security Operations and Careers
articles.text:
AI is beginning to take over much of the work that has traditionally defined the security analyst's job. Investigating alerts, collecting evidence, correlating activity across tools, and executing response actions are becoming tasks that AI systems can perform on their own. As these capabilities mature, security operations centers (SOCs) will see major changes in how work is organized, how decisions are made, and what is expected of the people responsible for defending organizations.
For security professionals, this is a chance to take on a much broader role. As AI assumes more of the operational workload, analysts can move beyond individual alerts and investigations to direct the defense across the entire security lifecycle. We call this emerging role the Threat Operator: an AI-native security professional who translates business risk into defensive priorities, directs AI-driven operations, and exercises judgment over the decisions and actions taken by those systems.
The impact reaches beyond day-to-day SOC work. It will change the skills organizations need, how security professionals develop expertise, and the career paths open to people entering the field.
From Individual Tasks to Overall Defense
The traditional SOC developed around specialized functions, each supported by its own tools and workflows. Threat intelligence teams study adversaries, detection engineers create rules, threat hunters search for activity that existing controls may have missed, analysts investigate alerts, and incident responders contain confirmed threats. These functions are closely related, yet the work often moves between teams through separate systems, tickets, and manual handoffs. AI is starting to tie these activities together. For example, intelligence about a new threat can lead to a hunting hypothesis, which can reveal a detection gap and produce a new detection. That detection may identify suspicious activity requiring investigation, followed by containment and further improvements to the organization's defenses. AI agents can coordinate and execute these workflows, carrying context and findings from one stage to the next.
That changes where security professionals add the most value. A Threat Operator works across the defensive lifecycle, setting priorities based on the organization's exposure, business operations, and threat landscape. They determine which risks deserve attention, what the defense should accomplish, how much autonomy AI should have, and when a decision requires human intervention. They are also responsible for judging whether the operation is actually improving security.
Consider a financial institution facing a newly identified threat targeting identity infrastructure. AI agents could assess the institution's exposure, hunt for relevant activity, identify gaps in existing detections, and recommend defensive actions. The Threat Operator would provide the institutional context needed to guide that work, including which systems support critical business processes, what constitutes unacceptable risk, and which actions require authorization.
The result is a gradual shift from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop, with security professionals supervising and governing AI-driven operations. The level of autonomy will depend on the maturity of the technology, the consequences of particular actions, and the organization's tolerance for risk, but a human remains accountable throughout.
Rethinking How Security Professionals Gain Experience
Junior security analysts will feel some of the biggest effects. For decades, the SOC has provided an entry point into cybersecurity, with analysts developing their skills through alert triage, evidence collection, investigations, documentation, and escalation. Although much of this work is repetitive, it has also served as an apprenticeship. Over time, analysts learn how systems behave, how attackers operate, and how experienced practitioners distinguish genuine threats from benign activity. As AI absorbs more of these responsibilities, organizations will need to rethink how that experience is acquired. The traditional progression from handling simple alerts to managing complex investigations may become less relevant as AI takes on more sophisticated work. Without a deliberate approach to training, security teams may struggle to develop the experienced professionals they will need in the future.
AI can also open up a different path for professional development. Junior Threat Operators can gain supervised exposure to a much wider range of security activities, examining how intelligence informs hunting, how detections are developed, how investigations reach conclusions, and how response decisions affect the business. They can review the evidence behind AI-generated findings, challenge assumptions, identify missing context, and learn from the decisions made by more experienced colleagues. This only works if organizations invest in technical fundamentals and structured mentorship. Analysts still need to understand networks, operating systems, attacker techniques, and the security technologies underlying AI-driven workflows. Experienced practitioners will need to teach younger colleagues how to evaluate conclusions, recognize uncertainty, and exercise judgment when the available evidence is incomplete.
The Skills Needed
For the current generation of security analysts, technical proficiency has often been measured through familiarity with security tools and the ability to extract useful information from them. Query languages, detection logic, endpoint telemetry, and investigation techniques have been central to the profession. Those skills still matter. AI adds new demands on top of them: orchestration, governance, and interpreting automated decisions.
Threat Operators will need to translate business security risks into clear defensive objectives that AI systems can execute. They must understand the organization's architecture, critical assets, operational dependencies, and relevant adversaries, and know how to communicate that context to AI agents. Their work will involve evaluating hypotheses, validating evidence, setting escalation criteria, and determining whether an automated action has achieved its intended outcome.
For example, an AI system investigating a compromised server may recommend immediate isolation. That call could be technically sound. But the server may support a critical business process where disruption carries significant consequences. A Threat Operator must understand those dependencies and determine how the response should proceed, balancing containment requirements with operational risk. This need for defined oversight and accountability is also reflected in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.
The role will combine four areas of expertise:
- Business security risk: Understanding organizational priorities, critical assets, and the consequences of security decisions.
- Threat and adversary understanding: Interpreting intelligence and anticipating how attackers may target the environment.
- Defensive operations: Understanding detection, hunting, investigation, and response across the security lifecycle.
- AI orchestration and judgment: Directing AI workflows, evaluating their conclusions, and governing automated actions.
Building a Career Path Around Defensive Outcomes
The Threat Operator role should become a career path with increasing levels of responsibility. Early-career operators can focus on validating evidence, reviewing AI conclusions, adding environmental context, and understanding how decisions connect across the defensive lifecycle. As they gain experience, they can begin translating business risks into defensive objectives, directing agent workflows, identifying coverage gaps, and determining when operations should escalate or act.
Senior Threat Operators will take responsibility for defining autonomy boundaries, governing consequential actions, evaluating the reliability of AI-driven decisions, and measuring whether security operations are reducing organizational risk. Professionals may enter this career path from investigations, threat intelligence, detection engineering, incident response, security architecture, or risk management, bringing different areas of expertise to a role that spans the entire defensive operation.
Security leaders should start building the training, governance, and progression frameworks needed to support these responsibilities. That includes establishing which decisions require human approval, how operators validate AI-generated evidence, how autonomy expands as systems demonstrate reliability, and how individual performance is evaluated. Measures such as the quality of defensive decisions, the closure of detection gaps, and improvements in threat coverage will matter more alongside traditional operational metrics.
This will happen at different speeds in different organizations. Security professionals will have more say in how their organizations defend themselves. The old SOC trained people to operate tools. The AI-native SOC has to train them to operate the defense.
