articles.title: Cómo organizar la agenda de contactos y eliminar números innecesarios del celular
articles.text:
Pocas cosas acumulan tanto desorden digital como la lista de contactos del teléfono. Años de números guardados, direcciones de email viejas y entradas duplicadas convierten a la agenda en un archivo inútil en lugar de una herramienta ágil.
Depurar esa lista no solo libera espacio visual: también mejora el funcionamiento de aplicaciones como mapas o asistentes de voz, que dependen de esa información para operar mejor.
Antes de borrar nada, conviene entender dónde viven esos contactos. En los celulares modernos ya no se guardan en la memoria interna ni en la tarjeta SIM, como ocurría con los teléfonos antiguos.
En iPhone se sincronizan con la cuenta de iCloud, mientras que en Android lo hacen con la Cuenta de Google. Algunos equipos Android permiten guardarlos localmente, pero esa opción no se recomienda porque obliga a hacer copias de seguridad manuales y expone a perder todo si el dispositivo se rompe o se pierde.
Cómo unificar los contactos en una sola cuenta
El primer paso del orden es elegir un único lugar donde vivan todos los contactos. Si el usuario tiene varias cuentas de correo sincronizadas al teléfono, es probable que la agenda esté fragmentada entre ellas.
Concentrar todo en un solo servicio simplifica la administración y facilita hacer copias de seguridad. Google Contacts suele ser una opción sólida por su sincronización entre dispositivos y sus herramientas automáticas de gestión.
El procedimiento habitual consiste en:
- Ingresar a la cuenta que se quiere dejar de usar desde su versión web.
- Buscar la opción de exportar contactos, que suele generar un archivo CSV o VCF.
- Importar ese archivo al servicio elegido como principal.
Una vez trasladados todos los números, conviene desactivar la sincronización de las cuentas restantes para evitar duplicados. En Android, esto se hace desde Configuración, luego Cuentas y respaldo, y finalmente Administrar cuentas, donde se puede desactivar la sincronización de contactos de cada cuenta sobrante.
Cómo eliminar duplicados y contactos que ya no se usan
Con la agenda centralizada, llega el trabajo de limpieza. Google Contacts suele señalar automáticamente las entradas duplicadas, aunque conviene revisarlas una por una para evitar fusiones incorrectas.
Dentro de la app de Contactos en Android, borrar entradas tiene opciones según la cantidad de números a eliminar:
- Un solo contacto: se abre su ficha, se presiona el ícono de configuración y se elige la opción de borrar.
- Varios contactos: se mantiene presionado uno, se seleccionan los demás y se confirma el borrado.
- Todos los contactos: se mantiene presionado uno, se elige “Seleccionar todo” desde el menú superior y luego se confirma.
Los contactos eliminados no desaparecen de inmediato: pasan a una papelera y recién a los 30 días se borran de manera permanente. Para eliminarlos antes de ese plazo, es posible ingresar a la papelera y elegir la opción de eliminación definitiva, tanto para un contacto como para varios o para la totalidad.
Cómo mejorar los contactos que quedan
Una vez reducida la lista a las personas con las que realmente se mantiene relación, conviene revisar la calidad de cada ficha. Agregar apellidos evita confusiones cuando hay varios contactos con el mismo nombre, algo que se nota especialmente al usar sistemas de manos libres en el auto, donde el teléfono puede pedir confirmación y generar distracciones.
También ayuda organizar los contactos en grupos, como trabajo, familia o favoritos. Marcar a alguien como favorito le da prioridad en la aplicación de teléfono y lo exceptúa de los modos de no molestar.
Otros datos útiles para completar incluyen:
- Fotos de perfil, que facilitan identificar a la persona en chats grupales.
- Fecha de nacimiento, visible luego en el calendario.
- Dirección física, para poder usarla directamente en aplicaciones de mapas.
- Tonos de llamada o de mensaje personalizados.
Bloquear y desbloquear contactos no deseados
La gestión de la agenda también incluye evitar comunicaciones indeseadas. Al bloquear un número desde la ficha de un contacto, se impide recibir tanto llamadas como mensajes de texto de todos los números asociados a esa persona.
Durante ese proceso existe la opción de marcar el número como generador de spam. Para revertir la acción, basta con ingresar a la configuración de contactos, elegir la opción de desbloquear y seleccionar el número correspondiente. La lista completa de números bloqueados puede consultarse desde la sección “Organizar” dentro de la aplicación de Contactos.

articles.title: EasyOptOuts data removal service review
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
An affordable, effective data removal platform for U.S. residents, but it doesn’t offer much coverage for non-U.S. people-finder sites. The lack of manual deletion requests is also a drawback, but understandably a tradeoff for its affordability.
Reasons to buy
- + Affordable
- + Easy setup
- + Automatic rescans
Reasons to avoid
- - No manual deletion requests
- - Limited broker coverage
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Protecting your personal information online is as challenging as ever. With many platforms requiring signups to access information, you’re inadvertently going to disclose personal information online, and this information is often made public. Whatever is made public on the internet stays there for a long time, and you’re likely not comfortable with this. What’s a possible solution? A data removal service like EasyOptOuts.
Data removal platforms scan people-finder/data broker sites for your data, then send automated deletion requests on your behalf. When processed, your information gets deleted from the people-finder sites, enhancing online privacy. Data removal platforms also send manual removal requests, but EasyOptOuts doesn’t– it sends only automated requests.
I extensively tested and reviewed EasyOptOuts to help you decide if it’s worth adopting as your personal data removal service. Read on to learn about its core features, pricing, setup, customer support, and other essential factors.
EasyOptOuts: Plans and pricing
EasyOptOuts has a simple pricing structure - you can check out the full details by clicking here. It costs $19.99 per year for personal use. There’s no monthly plan or tiered plans like most data removal platforms. It’s just one package that unlocks access to all features.
Businesses (with 10+ employees) can get a bulk subscription, but the price still amounts to $19.99 per year per user. The exception is for registered nonprofits, which get a 25% discount from EasyOptOuts.
At $19.99 per year, or barely $1.80 per month, EasyOptOuts is much more affordable than its rivals. But, does this affordability make it a better option? Let’s explore more to find out.
EasyOptOuts: Setup
I found EasyOptOuts’ setup process very straightforward, or shall I say, easy. Entering the homepage and hitting the Sign Up button kickstarts the process. When signing up, you’ll provide your email address and other personal information like date of birth, home address, and phone numbers.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
You’re probably wondering, “I’m trying to guard my personal information online and yet need to provide all this information again to a data removal platform?” The answer is that whatever information you provide is what the data removal platform scans people-broker sites for.
EasyOptOuts scans 200+ broker sites, which isn’t that many compared to competitors. However, EasyOptOuts doesn’t aim to be a mass-market data removal service. Rather, it focuses on U.S.-centric people-finder sites. Non-U.S. residents are better off with broader-focused data removal platforms.
After inputting your personal information, EasyOptOuts runs a deep scan on its network of 200+ people-finder sites. The complete scan can take a long time, based on the volume of data found across the network. It could be a day, 2 days, 3 days, or even a week, so don’t fret if you don’t get the results within a short period.
Once the scan completes, users receive an email alert and can begin monitoring the progress of the removal requests. I don’t like that EasyOptOuts sends only automated requests. Sometimes, automated requests aren’t enough to delete your information from people-finder sites, so manually drafted requests are needed to complete the process.
However, I understand that automated-only requests are how EasyOptOuts can keep its price as low as $19.99 per year. If it had to employ experts to manually draft deletion requests, the price would be much higher.
EasyOptOuts doesn’t just run the initial scan. It rescans its people-finder site network every four months, then sends another set of deletion requests if your personal information is discovered again. This rescan is important because some people-finder sites have a habit of reuploading information they were asked to delete. It ensures that your information stays off public view as long as your EasyOptOuts subscription is valid.
Compared to most data removal platforms I’ve tested, setting up EasyOptOuts felt noticeably easier. Everything ran smoothly, from providing my personal information to the initial scan and monitoring the status of deletion requests from my dashboard.
EasyOptOuts: Ease of use
Above, I’ve hinted at EasyOptOuts’ simple setup process and generally intuitive user experience. Like most data removal platforms, EasyOptOuts doesn’t have a native smartphone app, so you’ll access it from your browser.
I think a PC is the best option over a mobile browser, given the volume of information you’ll have to input to get scanned. A mobile browser would be inconvenient for the initial setup, but suitable for monitoring the status of deletion requests.
EasyOptOuts: Security and privacy
EasyOptOuts is a good addition to your online security toolkit, particularly for U.S. residents. It helps keep your information off those infamous people-finder sites like BeenVerified and PeopleLooker.
These sites have built a business model of aggregating personal information from public sources and then offering access for a fee. Tools like EasyOptOuts send deletion requests to scrub your data off people-finder sites.
However, on EasyOptOuts, you won’t find complementary security features like a VPN or password manager. It’s all about one thing – data removal – and does its job effectively. The drawback is the limited, U.S.-centric broker site coverage.
EasyOptOuts: Support
EasyOptOuts provides decent support, although I think it could be better. There’s an official support page filled with detailed answers to frequently asked questions (FAQs). For new users, this FAQs section helps answer important questions, so that you’ll not have to contact support directly for routine issues.
If you do need to contact the support team, there’s a dedicated email address for that. The support team is U.S.-based, so responses revolve around local working hours. I don’t like that there’s no telephone or live chat support, but given the low price charged by EasyOptOuts, it’s understandably difficult to maintain live support teams for users.
EasyOptOuts: Competition
EasyOptOuts has many competitors. Incogni and DeleteMe are the two notable names I’d like to highlight.
I chose Incogni because it feels like a more robust version of EasyOptOuts. It covers 420+ data broker sites, including non-U.S. ones, and offers both automated and manual deletion requests. This compares to EasyOptOuts, which covers 200+ sites and only supports automated requests. However, EasyOptOuts is much more budget-friendly, costing just $19.99 per year, whereas Incogni’s pricing starts from $7.99 per month.
DeleteMe provides much higher coverage, with 850+ sites, and supports manual deletion requests. I’ve tested it and can confidently say that you’ll get more data scrubbed with DeleteMe than EasyOptOuts. DeleteMe users also get complementary features like dark web monitoring and email masking.
However, DeleteMe is priced like a premium service. Its plans average $129 per year, multiples of EasyOptOuts’ $19.99 per year.
EasyOptOuts: Final verdict
If you’re a U.S. resident and need a budget-friendly tool for scrubbing your personal data off people-finder sites, EasyOptOuts is a good bet. For just $19.99 per year, much more affordable than competitors, you’ll get a reliable tool to scan people-finder sites and send deletion requests where your data is discovered.
Setting up your account, running the initial scan, and monitoring further scans are easy to handle, thanks to EasyOptOuts’ intuitive interface.
However, you should be aware of EasyOptOuts’ drawbacks, such as the limited people-finder site coverage, lack of manual deletion requests, and email-only support. Overall, it’s a reliable data removal platform.

articles.title: Intel Readies "Moon Lake" and "Wildcat Lake Refresh" Built on 18A Node
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
Intel Readies "Moon Lake" and "Wildcat Lake Refresh" Built on 18A Node
Intel is reportedly preparing two new processor SKUs focused on extremely low-power computing. The first, called "Moon Lake," is designed as a pure low-power efficiency (LPE) core SoC. The "Moon Lake" generation features no P-Cores and up to 4 "Darkmont" LPE-Cores on the Intel 18A die. Unlike "Wildcat Lake," which includes at least 2 P-Cores, "Moon Lake" is intended to be a much smaller design for embedded devices like NAS. The base power of "Moon Lake" is reportedly rated at 6 W, similar to an SoC typically used in smartphones. The number of Xe3 cores in this SKU is unknown, but since "Wildcat Lake" has up to 2 Xe3 cores, we expect "Moon Lake" to have half of that to maintain its 6 W TDP. Intel has manufactured "Moon Lake" on its 18A node and placed it on the BGA1516 package, the same platform used by "Wildcat Lake." The official moniker for "Moon Lake" is MNL, and it could be a successor to the N-Series, like the previous "Alder Lake-N" series of low-power processors.
Additionally, Intel is preparing an overhaul of "Wildcat Lake" with the new "Wildcat Lake Refresh." When Intel launched the Core 300 Series "Wildcat Lake" earlier this year, these processors came with up to 2 P-Cores, 4 E-Cores, and up to 2 Xe3 GPU cores, with a package reaching up to 35 W. However, the new "Wildcat Lake Refresh" is expected to increase the number of P-Cores to 4 while keeping the same base microarchitecture of "Cougar Cove" and maintaining 4 "Darkmont" LPE-Cores. The integrated graphics remain similar, with up to 2 Xe3 cores. Importantly, this refresh adds support for Intel's vPro technology, meaning that enterprise customers are in for a surprise with a new low-cost option for their PCs.All three platforms—"Wildcat Lake," "Wildcat Lake Refresh," and "Moon Lake"—are reportedly well-received in the low-power computing space, as Intel is actively pushing their development. All three are based on the 18A node for manufacturing, with Intel Foundry handling the work, and they share the BGA1516 package.
Source:
				Jaykihn on X

articles.title: Our first step at defining a CPU benchmark for agentic AI
articles.text:
Our first step at defining a CPU benchmark for agentic AI — how we can measure throughput of agentic AI workloads without any GPU involved
The future of agentic AI lies in CPUs, or so the story goes. Here’s our first attempt to measure that.
Agentic AI has set off a firestorm in the world of CPUs over the past six months, yet it’s an area of performance that still doesn’t have solid, repeatable benchmarks to evaluate where the latest hardware falls. We’ve been working on an internal set of tests to evaluate at least one aspect of contentious agentic loops end-to-end, isolating CPU and memory performance from the accelerator to understand how these components contribute to the agentic loop.
This is still a work in progress, but we wanted to bring Tom’s Hardware Premium readers behind the scenes to understand how we’re going about tackling this problem, our methodology for testing, and detail what we’ve learned about agentic loops along the way. We've prototyped the test and settled the central design, but there's still work to do before the numbers it produces hold up to scrutiny.
Given that this area of computing is bleeding-edge and rapidly evolving, we undoubtedly have blind spots here. That’s OK. The testing we’re doing is built to look at how agentic performance scales across the CPU as sessions increase, providing an ideal throughput for each chip that provides as many agent sessions as possible while remaining interactive.
Toward the end of this article, we've included a section on some of the shortfalls of this approach, as well as some ideas we’re toying with to tackle things like multi-turn agentic flows. And keep in mind that these tests aren't meant to replace our other testing of local AI, but to supplement it. As this space continues to evolve and the hardware characteristics are better defined, we’ll be able to make more informed decisions about where this testing goes in the future.
Defining an agentic AI loops
"AI agents" imply some little workers that, strapped with an LLM, can go and handle whatever task you throw at them. It's a fine description, but we'll need a bit more a technical definition if we're going to benchmark the performance of agentic AI.
There are two parts here that are important. First are functions. With agentic AI, we give the LLM access to tools, which, in the case of popular agentic frameworks like LangGraph, are Python functions. The tool may be reading or writing a file, querying a database, running tests on code, or just about anything else you can define in a function. Here's a basic example.
@tool
    def run_command(command: str) -> str:
        """Run a build or test command in the repository root. Allowed: make [targets], python -m pytest [args]."""
return traced("run_command", {"command": command}, lambda: ws.run_command(command))
This is how you write a tool call with LangGraph inside of Python, and it's an example of a tool call that the we've given the LLM access to through our LangGraph persona. We identify the function as a tool the LLM can call with "@tool," and then we define the function like normal Python with "def run_command," passing through the command as an argument. The extra "-> str" on the end notes that the argument will be a string, and the function should return a string.
That's followed up by a description of the tool that the LLM can read (triple quotes just allow you to space this across multiple lines in Python). We're prompting the LLM that it can run build or test commands using make or pytest. For this example, we wrap the function up with the anonymous lambda function and pass it back to an overarching trace function. That's not important right now, however. The goal is to illustrate what a tool call looks like.
This is only one of a handful of tools available to our coding agent. It can also read and write files, edit files, and search code using regular expressions, all defined in the same way with Python functions. Agentic AI is often described as a "loop," however, and that's because the task often requires calling a tool multiple times and/or calling different tools.
If we're working a Python project, for instance, we may prompt the LLM to "debug this Python script." It may call the "list files" tool to evaluate what Python script we're talking about first. Then, it will call the "read file" tool to understand it, or maybe "search code" to find a spot to start troubleshooting. Then it might run "edit file" and "run command," and if the file isn't fixed, it may loop back over these tools a few times.
This is the agentic loop. We prompt the LLM, it evaluates and starts calling tools it needs to form an answer. Then, it gets back the information from the tool calls, it re-evaluates, and then it may call more.
Starting with concurrency
We’ll dig into the specific tests and what they’re doing later in this article, but it’s good to set the stage with why our benchmark is designed the way it is. We developed the test on an Nvidia DGX Spark (GB10) featuring 128 GB of unified memory, a Blackwell GPU, and the relatively weak Arm-based Grace CPU. Above, you can see the time spent running these agent loops on the GB10 with gemma4-26b-a4b. The model isn’t super important here as long as we're able to call tools, and we’re able to re-record the tests using different models as they continue to release.
The point here is the share of time spent, not the model or the specific work the agents are doing (though that does provide useful context). Each result here is a list of sequential tasks for the agent to execute against the model, and nearly all of the time is spent on the GPU. Even relatively demanding CPU tasks, like with our coding agent, represent just a small fraction of the computational time. Running one or even a few agents isn’t a problem for the CPU when we have access to a large, powerful GPU with a sufficiently large model running on it.
Looking closer at one specific set of tasks, you can see that there are plenty of tasks for the CPU to execute during the window, but those tasks happen so quickly that it barely registers in the overall time spent.
These tasks aren’t evenly spaced, either. Depending on when the agent needs to call tools, the shape of the workload can look very different. Above, for example, you can see our document agent, which is tasked with scanning and extracting information from a set of PDF files. Nearly all of the agent time is spent at the very beginning of the task, after which it’s almost pure GPU inference.
Obviously, a more powerful GPU will churn through the inference step faster, but we’d have to create a severe imbalance between the CPU and GPU for the CPU portion of a single agentic loop to create a bottleneck — at least with these common tools. Agents don’t just handle a sequential list of tasks, however. They spawn sub-agents, and if multiple sessions are running on the same system in sandboxed environments, contention for limited resources becomes a real issue.
Instead of designing the test platform in such a way that creates a severe CPU/GPU imbalance, we looked toward concurrency. The idea is to sweep across the chip with concurrent sessions running a list of tasks in a loop in their own processes. As the sweep scales up, contention across the CPU starts to appear, and minor differences in tool calls, code execution and compilation, web browsing, and the variety of other tasks our agents do pile on.
How the benchmark works
With concurrency as our north star, we can start breaking down the design of the benchmark and how it works internally. The overall design is simple. Custom agents built with LangGraph have a list of 30 tasks to execute in sequence against a llama.cpp server running gemma4-26b-a4b. Instead of going directly to the server, however, the agents go through a proxy server that records a trace.
During live recording, the agent communicates with the proxy server, which passes a live call to the llama.cpp server. The proxy server meanwhile writes every logged request to the LLM and the response from it to an overarching JSON. Tool calls bypass the server chain and are logged to their own JSON files. Finally, for each task, a correct response is generated, hashed, and stored as its own JSON.
Recording everything allows us to remove the live model entirely from the equation. The agents still run as normal, but instead of running against a live LLM, they run against that proxy, replaying the traces captured. The requests and tool calls are all happening live, but the agents are immediately handed back a response from the trace based on the live inference capture.
Starting with the request from the agent, it’s matched by session label and hash to ensure it’s accurate before the response is looked up in the master JSON. If there’s a mismatch, the run stops and is marked as invalid. If everything checks out, the response is passed back, and the agent session(s) call the tools they need. The tool calls are compared to the JSONs generated during recording, and the recorded result is passed back. This is critical.
The test compares the live tool call to the recorded result, but it always passes back the recorded result to keep the test from drifting, even if the tool call is correct. True tool mismatches are logged. The test proceeds, but it’s marked as invalid for each level with tool mismatches.
This setup makes redesigning and expanding the benchmark simple. We can write a new persona in Python using LangGraph, or expand to other frameworks like CrewAI. Additionally, we can rerecord traces against different models in the future, perhaps some with expanded capabilities. As long as we’re communicating over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, we can mix and match pieces of our testing to represent a broader range of workloads.
The test starts at a single worker process and scales up to the maximum thread count of the CPU, running three repeats per level. Each worker process operates off a list of 30 tasks, with new worker processes starting at the next point in the list. So, worker session one would start at task one, worker session two would start at task two, and so on. Tasks do not take an equal amount of time, so this offset creates imbalanced contention as tasks overlap.
What this actually measures
The metric we get out of the test is sessions per second. A session is a single task completed from end-to-end, and we measure the number of sessions completed per second at each level. Naturally, at lower levels, we complete fewer sessions per second, often falling below 1, meaning the task takes longer than one second to complete. The tasks are completed sequentially. What we’re looking for is how chips diverge as sessions increase, measuring the throughput of agentic work on the CPU.
We derive two headline scores from the sweep. First is peak throughput, which is the highest sessions per second we recorded, as well as the concurrency level at which it was recorded. Next is ideal throughput, which is the point at which the slowest 5% of sessions take no longer than 1.5x the time it takes for a single session to complete at the base concurrency level. We expect that tasks will take longer as the number of sessions increases, but past that 1.5x mark, the length of the task gets significantly longer, and depending on the processor’s topology, throughput can start to degrade.
It’s worth highlighting again that there is no GPU delay in this concurrency sweep. We’ve removed the GPU entirely, throwing as much concurrent work at the CPU as possible to determine where that peak throughput point lies. However, the GPU still plays a significant role, so the results should be viewed in a realistic context.
As more agents work on the CPU, they’ll compete for resources on the chip, but this balance can easily shift. If there isn’t enough GPU horsepower, agents may queue for a slot, and that’s not effectively utilizing the compute on either processor. Our testing is more than theoretical throughput from napkin math, but it’s less than a true end-to-end system. There are too many variables to account for in that setup for us to produce any useful numbers that are broadly applicable.
However, we can run the sweep with live inference to evaluate system-level performance. For live runs, the responses handed back to agents are still served from the recording to keep runs equal. However, the request is recorded by the llama.cpp server, which generates the same number of tokens before being discarded. This accounts for the normal inference pipeline, including prefill, decode, and cache performance, as well as agents queuing for a slot.
Both numbers are important. Live sweeps are a realistic look at local AI across the entire system, while frozen replays measure the peak throughput a CPU is capable of with access to all the GPU compute (theoretically) that it could want.
Our starting agent personas
We’ve defined six agent personas. A “persona” is a Python script built with LangGraph that defines what the agent can do. The agents tool calls are Python functions, defined in that main script that connects our LangGraph nodes. Each persona is working off its own unique list of tasks from local documents. For example, the research persona is able to answer questions by searching in a Wikipedia corpus of about 50,000 articles.
| Persona | Sub-Tasks | Description | Tools | 
| Analyst | Planner, analyst, writer | Answer questions about a fake retail company by searching DuckDB with SQL and write a report. | List tables, describe tables, run SQL query, make chart from query | 
| Coding | Coder, reviewer | Fix bugs in one of four small projects (two C, two Python) from an issue report. | List files, read files, code search, file edits, command execution, test review | 
| Documents | Intake, extractor, auditor | Scans purchase orders, invoices, and other accounting documents and matches invoices against purchase orders. | List documents, extract text from PDF, extract tables from PDF, Tesseract OCR, basic arithmetic | 
| Research | Planner, researcher, writer | Searches local English Wikipedia corpus to answer questions. | Query corpus | 
| Support | Triage, researcher, responder | Answer support tickets for a fictional company using a knowledge base. | Knowledge base search, read articles | 
| Web | Planner, browser agent, writer | Find products that meet specified criteria in a headless Chromium session. | Open URL, click web element, enter text, select option, go back, read more of page | 
Above, you can see an overview of each persona. For five out of the six, we start with some sort of planning stage, followed by the main agent loop, and finish with a report. For the analyst persona, for instance, the planner takes the questions and splits them into structured output with two to four steps. Analysts then run in parallel, searching the database, and the writer turns those findings into a response.
The one exception is the coder persona, which works a bit differently. It’s working off four projects, attempting to address a bug from an issue report (similar to a GitHub issue report). The coder finds the bug, runs tests to confirm the fix, and then passes it off to a reviewer step. The reviewer step (naturally) reviews the fix before applying it.
For each of the personas, the current test setup looks at single-turn tasks. Agents make multiple loops to the LLM depending on the task, and often use tools several times, but it’s all to resolve a single task with no previous context. For instance, when a customer support query comes up, the agent may take multiple passes at the knowledge base to answer that query. However, once the agent has answered the query and moved on to the next, it’s treated as a separate action without context from the first query.
This is not completely representative of agentic workflows, which are often multi-turn processes. We're able to script multi-turn tasks, but that creates greater divergence risk, as well as risk of a crash. Running this locally, it's not hard to spill over the context window after a few turns of complex interactions. It's possible to do, but it's not on the top of our list of priorities right now.
We won’t cover all of the tasks the current personas do because, frankly, it’s a lot and most of it isn’t that interesting. Still, we want to provide at least one example for each persona so you can get an idea of what’s going on under the hood.
| Persona | Example Task | Source of Truth | 
| Analyst | “How do discounts affect gross margin across categories?” | DuckDB warehouse | 
| Coding | Invoice project – Saturday due dates move to Sunday, not Monday | PyTest, make | 
| Documents | Approve correct invoices from purchase orders based on a price from a list of six documents across four scans. | Faux PDF invoices, purchase orders, and goods received notices with errors planted | 
| Research | “What causes earthquakes and how are they measured?” | 50,000-article English Wikipedia corpus | 
| Support | “How long a two-factor code stays valid” | Knowledge base for fictional smart home company | 
| Web | Highest-rated 55L backpack and lightest waterproof boots | Local website for an outdoor gear store | 
All of the other tasks are very similar to what you can see in the examples above. With the documents persona, for example, the agent is always approving the correct invoices, but the mix of documents and types of errors change between sets. Similarly, the support persona is always answering support questions, but they focus in different areas. Some ask to troubleshoot error codes, others (like the example above) ask about policies, and more still include multiple questions within one query, tasking the agent with piecing together multiple areas of the knowledge base.
Shortcomings of the current approach
Although we’ve tried to create a broad range of agentic work here, there are some shortcomings of the current version of this test. Most notably, our testing and recordings only come from two types of systems: a 64-core Threadripper test bed with 128GB of DDR5-6000 RDIMMs, and a DGX Spark.
As we continue to test other platforms, we may need to adjust the tests, rerun recordings, or swap the model. We’d have to re-gather all of our results if we make those changes. By other platforms, we’re not just talking about an Intel system, either. We’ve seen a variety of different local AI setups, from Mac Studio clusters to GPU-ridden workstations. The load on the CPU completely changes depending on the GPU performance, model, quantization level, and server settings.
The other shortcoming is API performance. The test is designed in such a way that we can easily connect to any model from a frontier lab through their API. Although that model runs in the cloud, the tools themselves run locally unless you’re using an entirely cloud-based sandbox. If you’re working through an AI-assisted development workflow on a budget laptop, for instance, all of the compilation, testing, and agent code still runs on your machine.
Although we have plans to look into this hybrid model with a weaker host PC and a cloud API, we didn’t explore it too much during initial development. API usage is expensive, and we don’t want to be throwing away tokens trying to get the initial test suite set up correctly.
Finally, sandboxing. The current test is isolated through a Docker image, which introduces negligible overhead (<2%) compared to a bare-metal run. We’ll need to explore the overhead of sandboxing local agents via different means in the future, which is an area we really haven’t explored much in this test.
Continuing to learn
Agentic AI is rapidly evolving, so much so that you’ll get different definitions of what characterizes agentic workloads and hardware built for agentic workflows depending on who you ask. Add on top of that rapid hardware and model changes, and it’s obvious that we could never define a bulletproof benchmark that can stand the test of time. That’s a fool’s errand. What we have here is our starting point, which we will continue to build on top of.
From what we have now, the next steps are to get the first real numbers. We've done some basic tests to ensure the system is set up correctly (for instance, running a free-threaded version of Python to test GIL impact within a single session), but the focus here was getting the basic system in place to record traces and replay them.
We're also relying exclusively on LangGraph here. We need to explore other frameworks like CrewAI, as well as the "one-click" agents like Hermes and OpenClaw.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Engie : les clients doivent redoubler de prudence après la cyberattaque et le vol de données personnelles
articles.text:
Engie : les clients doivent redoubler de prudence après la cyberattaque et le vol de données personnelles
Durant les prochains mois, les clients d'Engie devront faire preuve d'une vigilance accrue, car les tentatives d'arnaques risquent de se multiplier après la dernière cyberattaque
Les derniers jours d'octobre n'ont pas été roses chez Engie. Le groupe français spécialisé dans l'énergie a été victime d'une cyberattaque et envoie des emails à ses clients pour les informer de la situation. Celle-ci s'avère spécialement négative, car un grand nombre de données ont été compromises, pouvant potentiellement générer des campagnes de fraudes et d'hameçonnage redoutables.
Du hameçonnage sophistiqué à prévoir contre les clients Engie
Notons tout de suite que ce ne sont pas les "systèmes informatiques d'Engie" qui ont été victimes d'un "acte de cyber-malveillance", mais un outil servant à ses partenaires "dans le cadre de leurs activités de prospection commerciale et de commercialisation d'offres d'énergie." Si l'accès à cette plateforme a rapidement été coupé aux attaquants, eux aussi non identifiés, ces derniers ont cependant pu accéder à de nombreuses données.
Outre les classiques noms, adresses email et numéros de téléphone, il est aussi question des identifiants client, des numéros de contrats et des points de livraison et de comptage et d'estimation (PDL et PCE). Si les coordonnées bancaires ne sont pas concernées, les autres données peuvent permettre de mettre en place des campagnes de hameçonnage très complètes et crédibles.
Une personne malintentionnée peut ainsi, par email ou même téléphone, se faire passer pour le service client ou un technicien d'Engie ayant accès à un dossier complet pour tenter d'extorquer de l'argent ou d'autres informations. Engie n'a pas indiqué le nombre de clients concernés, tandis que la fuite semble cantonnée à la France.
Si vous êtes concernés par cette fuite, plusieurs bonnes pratiques peuvent permettre de se protéger. Par email, toujours vérifier l'adresse de l'expéditeur, ne pas cliquer sur les liens suspects et recouper la moindre demande qui doit normalement aussi figurer dans votre espace client Engie. Par téléphone, ne pas hésiter à raccrocher et appeler soi-même le service client avec le numéro officiel, mais aussi se méfier de la moindre demande qui réclame des données bancaires pour finaliser une opération.
Ces conseils s'appliquent évidemment à toutes les autres fuites qui ont eu lieu depuis le début de 2026, véritable année noire en France dans le domaine.

articles.title: Microsoft va enfin retirer Copilot de votre téléviseur
articles.text:
Microsoft arrête le support de Copilot sur toutes les Smart TV. LG a commencé à en informer ses utilisateurs par un message sur l’écran, sans date précise pour l’instant.
Copilot n’aura donc pas fait long feu sur les téléviseurs. C’est un message affiché sur une TV LG qui a révélé l’info ce mercredi.
Copilot sur TV : installé de force, déjà abandonné
Repéré par Windows Central, la notification en question est apparue sur un téléviseur LG propulsé par WebOS. LG explique que Microsoft a décidé d’arrêter la prise en charge de Copilot sur tous les téléviseurs. La fonction n’est plus disponible et pourrait cesser de fonctionner d’ici peu. Microsoft n’a pas confirmé de date, mais LG s’attend à une fin avant 2027. Fin de support, cela veut dire que Microsoft arrête de faire vivre le service.
Sur ces écrans, Copilot répondait à des questions sur ce qui s’affichait, conseillait des films et des séries, et discutait comme sur les autres appareils. Son arrivée avait fait grincer des dents. En janvier 2025, nous rapportions que LG et Samsung prévoyaient d’ajouter un raccourci vers Copilot sur certains modèles. En fin d'année dernière, les propriétaires de TV LG ont eu la mauvaise surprise de ne pas pouvoir le désinstaller. Quatre jours plus tard, LG déployait un correctif pour éradiquer toute trace de Copilot.
Si le constructeur LG parlait d’un simple raccourci qui ouvre le chatbot dans le navigateur de la TV, pour certains, l’application a été installée de force. Samsung, dont les TV sous Tizen hébergeaient aussi Copilot, est concerné puisque l’arrêt vise toutes les Smart TV. Aucune annonce de sa part n’est mentionnée pour l’instant.
Microsoft a changé de stratégie. Copilot n’est plus présenté comme un compagnon numérique pour le grand public, mais comme un outil de productivité et de travail. L’entreprise a d’ailleurs fusionné Microsoft 365 Copilot et Copilot grand public dans une seule application. Il n’existe plus d’appli personnelle dédiée, et la version TV devient la dernière déclinaison grand public à disparaître.

articles.title: Adobe Fixes 8 Critical Campaign Classic Flaws Allowing Code Execution and Security Bypass
articles.text:
Adobe has released patches to address multiple critical security flaws in Campaign Classic that, if successfully exploited, could result in arbitrary code execution, security feature bypass, and privilege escalation.
The list of eight vulnerabilities is as follows -
- CVE-2026-104351 (CVSS score: 9.9) - A code injection vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution.
- CVE-2026-104353 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An operating system code injection vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution.
- CVE-2026-105780 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution.
- CVE-2026-105489 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
- CVE-2026-105781 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
- CVE-2026-104350 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability that could lead to privilege escalation.
- CVE-2026-104354 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
- CVE-2026-105779 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
The issues affect Adobe Campaign Classic versions 7.4.4 build 9402 and earlier for Windows and Linux. They have been patched in version 7.4.4 build 9403.
Also resolved by Adobe is a critical code injection flaw in Adobe Connect Desktop and Mobile for Windows, macOS, and Android (CVE-2026-48360, CVSS score: 9.6) that could result in arbitrary code execution.
The vulnerability has been fixed in the following versions -
- 
    Adobe Connect Desktop - 
    
  - Windows: version 2026.9.61
  - macOS Silicon: version 2026.10.66
  - macOS Intel: version 2026.10.170
- Adobe Connect Mobile for Android version 4.5
Adobe said it's not "aware of any exploits in the wild for any of the issues" addressed in the update. Users are advised to update to the latest version for optimal protection.

articles.title: Malgré le succès du Galaxy Z Fold 8, la division smartphone de Samsung est dans le rouge
articles.text:
Samsung a présenté le 29 octobre les comptes de son troisième trimestre 2026, clos fin septembre. Les divisions mobile et réseaux y affichent ensemble 37 700 milliards de wons de chiffre d’affaires, en progression de plus de 10 % sur un an, pour une perte opérationnelle de 600 milliards de wons, environ 400 millions d’euros. Un an plus tôt, le trimestre du lancement du Galaxy Z Fold 7 s’était conclu sur 3 600 milliards de wons de bénéfice.
Lire aussi : Galaxy A : face à la hausse des coûts, Samsung prend une décision radicale
Le Fold 8 limite la casse sans l’effacer
La branche enchaîne un deuxième trimestre déficitaire, après les 700 milliards de wons perdus au trimestre précédent, première perte de son histoire. Même la crise du Note 7 et de ses batteries inflammables, en 2016, l’avait laissée dans le vert.Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 a pourtant écoulé 1,44 million d’exemplaires en précommande en sept jours en Corée du Sud, aux côtés du Fold 8 Ultra et du Flip 8, effaçant un record vieux de sept ans, les 1,38 million du Note 10. En France, les précommandes des deux grands formats ont bondi de 60 % par rapport au Fold 7.
« Grâce au lancement réussi de produits haut de gamme comme le Fold 8 et la Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, et à nos efforts continus de réduction des coûts, nous avons amélioré notre rentabilité par rapport au trimestre précédent », a défendu Daniel Araujo, vice-président de la division mobile, lors de la présentation des résultats. Le trou se réduit en effet de 100 milliards de wons d’un trimestre à l’autre. Les ventes montent, la facture des composants grimpe plus vite.
La mémoire enrichit le groupe et étrangle les Galaxy
Le groupe signe pourtant le meilleur trimestre de son histoire : 107 400 milliards de wons de bénéfice opérationnel, environ 72 milliards d’euros, du jamais-vu pour une entreprise tech au-dessus du seuil des 100 000 milliards. Les semi-conducteurs en apportent à eux seuls 106 500 milliards, portés par l’appétit des centres de données pour l’IA. Les puces mémoire qui font exploser les profits renchérissent chaque Galaxy produit. Premier fournisseur mondial de RAM, Samsung subit côté smartphones la flambée qu’il alimente côté composants, et la direction prévient que la pression sur les coûts se prolongera en 2027.
Tout le marché encaisse le même choc : les livraisons mondiales de smartphones ont reculé de 20 % sur un an au troisième trimestre, un plus bas de quatorze ans. Samsung en profite pour grimper à 23 % de parts de marché, contre 19 % un an plus tôt, le haut de gamme résistant mieux que le reste du catalogue.
Pour les fêtes, le constructeur mise de nouveau sur ses vaisseaux amiraux, Galaxy S26 (qui a subit une hausse de prix en début de mois), Z Fold 8 Ultra et Z Fold 8 en tête, avec un chiffre d’affaires mobile attendu en retrait sur le trimestre.

articles.title: Mausstudio Announced As Custom Gaming Mouse Designer for 3D Printing
articles.text:
Thursday, October 29th 2026
Mausstudio Announced As Custom Gaming Mouse Designer for 3D Printing
It seems as though the mouse modding scene has been on a winning streak lately, with brands like Keychron publishing a catalogue of free 3D models of its mouse shells, and projects like Openmouse providing brand-agnostic, open-source mouse customization and remapping. The latest eye-catching project comes from a small 3D printing outfit called Unskilled Design, who recently introduced Mausstudio. Mausstudio is a work-in-progress custom mouse design tool that helps users design custom mouse shells for 3D printing. 
As described in a recent demo on X, Mausstudio allows users to import an STL of an existing mouse PCB, define the positions of core features, like screw holes, switches, the scroll wheel, and sensor position, and then generate a shell around it using custom parameters. Currently, it supports custom dimensions for the basics, like width, length, and height, as well as more niche customizations, like left-handed side button placements, base structure (lightweight or solid), hump position, honeycomb cutouts for lightweight shells, and battery positioning.After the shell is created, Mausstudio can automatically add screw holes for the PCB and create a cutout for the scroll wheel to fit through. The developer has a neat walkthrough of the available features in the demo reel on X, although it's unclear when exactly the project will be ready for launch or whether it will be a paid project or something like a browser-based utility. The creator behind the project, Bastian, is also careful to note that the actual shell being created is based on maths, with no generative AI involved in the 3D model's creation. It's unclear if generative AI was used to create the project itself, however.
Source:
				@UnskilledCast on X

You import an STL/3MF model of the PCB and its components. MausStudio analyses the geometry and suggests mounting holes, switches and scroll-wheel positions. You check or correct those assignments, then it generates the shell, supports and cutouts around them. Missing components can be added using measured dimensions.
You can customise the length, width, height, hump position and button length, choose symmetrical or left/right ergonomic shapes, and adjust battery space and lightweight patterns.

articles.title: FADU wants to take the CPU out of AI storage by putting the file system inside the SSD, but the proof won't arrive until 2027
articles.text:
FADU wants to take the CPU out of AI storage by putting the file system inside the SSD, but the proof won't arrive until 2027
But samples won't land until Q3 2027
- FADU's File-Semantic SSD runs path lookup, permission checks, and file-to-flash mapping in firmware instead of on the host
- NFSv3 requests ride inside standard NVMe commands, so GPUs, DPUs, and remote clients can reach files without requiring a host file system
- Its headline 460,000 ops/s result came from a PCIe 5.0 host, with PCIe 6.0 results promised by Q1 2027
South Korean controller designer FADU has shown off an SSD that understands files rather than just blocks, betting that the next bottleneck in AI storage is not raw bandwidth but the CPU time spent working out where data lives.
The File-Semantic SSD (FS-SSD), unveiled at the OCP Global Summit, moves file lookup, access checks and file-to-address translation into firmware on FADU's sixth-generation controller.
FADU's whitepaper promises GPUs, DPUs and network cards a route to their files with "no host filesystem, no block layer, and no storage-server CPU in the path." Partner samples are not expected until Q3 2027.
Not the first approach to the 'CPU problem'
FADU is no newcomer to data center flash. Its Gen5 controller sits in the SN861, which Western Digital launched and SanDisk now sells; last year, the company said it had signed controller supply deals with two of the four hyperscalers, weeks after revealing its Sierra PCIe 6.0 controller.
Its pitch here, however, isn't entirely new, with the recognition coming from a not-so-surprising front: Nvidia. Nvidia has been doing the same from the other end of the PCIe bus. GPUDirect Storage removed the CPU from the data path years ago, letting drives move data straight into GPU memory, but host software still decides what to fetch and issues every request.
Its decision to open source cuFile and shift that control path onto the GPU, with SCADA attacks adding accelerator-side overhead even as FADU attacks it from the drive end of the equation.
FADU says its own measurements show the host file system and block layer consuming about 30% of CPU cycles in a GPUDirect Storage random-read workload, a vendor figure that has not been independently reproduced. It also argues that existing bypass schemes only get the CPU out of the way by abandoning files altogether.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
How does this work?
Rather than invent a new language for its drive, FADU borrowed an old one. NFS, short for Network File System, has let computers open files stored on other machines for decades. FS-SSD tucks NFS requests, such as looking up a file by name or reading part of it, inside the standard NVMe commands that SSDs already use.
Those commands can come from inside the same server or, using a networked version of NVMe called NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF), from other machines in the data center. FADU chose NFS version 3 for three reasons: it is small, with just 21 operations; it works with any operating system; and it is stateless, meaning each request carries everything the drive needs to answer it, so the drive never has to remember who has which file open.
FADU has also merged two lookups that normally happen separately. On a regular system, the computer’s file system first works out which numbered block holds each piece of a file, and the SSD’s own internal software, called the flash translation layer, then works out where that block physically sits on the flash chips.
FS-SSD does both jobs with a single file layer based on F2FS, a Linux file system designed for flash memory, laid out to match how the chips are physically organized. One map then takes the drive straight from a file to the spot where it is stored, and that map is much smaller. A typical SSD carries about 1GB of DRAM for every terabyte of flash and fills almost all of it with its block map. FS-SSD uses the same amount, but FADU says about 95% of it is left free to keep details of frequently used files close at hand.
That layout also makes cleanup simpler. Flash memory cannot overwrite old data in place, so drives regularly move the data they still need elsewhere and wipe whole blocks clean, a chore known as garbage collection.
When F2FS runs on an ordinary computer, the file system and the SSD each do their own version of this cleanup, and the two end up multiplying each other’s work. FS-SSD runs just one, and FADU says that cuts write amplification by 63% compared with F2FS on a regular host. Lower write amplification means less wear on the flash, but the 63% figure comes from simulated tests on NVMeVirt, software from Seoul National University that imitates an SSD, rather than from a real drive.
In FADU’s own preliminary test, remote file throughput held at about 460,000 ops/s as the server was cut from 16 cores to one, while a standard Linux NFS server fell from roughly 150,000 ops/s to 40,000.
The testing has its limits, though. FADU’s Gen6 drive sat in a PCIe 5.0 host, so every sequential read result topped out near 14.1GB/s, roughly the Gen5 link limit, even as Gen6 drives such as Micron’s 9650, rated for 28GB/s reads, are already in mass production.
Both the client and server ran Intel’s Core i5-13600K desktop chip with 128GB of DDR5 and a 100Gb ConnectX-6 NIC. That processor has 14 physical cores and 20 threads, so FADU’s test likely counted threads rather than physical cores.
The world’s first file-semantic SSD is an idea that isn't entirely new
FADU calls FS-SSD the world’s first file-semantic SSD, and it may well be the first hardware demonstration of its kind, but the idea isn’t new. The DevFS research paper, presented in 2018, described a direct-access file system “embedded completely within a storage device,” though the authors tested it only as an emulated prototype.
NVM Express has standardized a key-value command set that addresses data by key rather than block address, and SK hynix has developed a key-value computational storage drive with Los Alamos National Laboratory. Unlike the key-value command set, FS-SSD has no standard behind it yet. FADU has not submitted a file-semantic command set to NVM Express or OCP Storage, so for now every client needs FADU’s own software.
FADU’s longer-term goal is a flash enclosure with nothing in front of it but a PCIe switch and a DPU (a network card with its own processors) or NIC handling NVMe-oF in hardware, with a reference design built on Xsight Labs’ 800G E1 DPU due by the end of 2027.
FADU’s model puts that at about 42% lower power and 57% lower cost per 16-drive system than a conventional storage server, though those are projections rather than measurements. DPU-fronted flash boxes already exist, such as Supermicro’s BlueField-powered JBOF, but those still run the storage software on the DPU’s Arm cores. FADU wants the drives themselves to serve the files.
FADU chief executive Nam Yi-hyun said the company will use FS-SSD as “a springboard to become a leading company in AI storage solutions,” according to The Herald Business. The bottleneck FADU is chasing is real, and building on NFSv3 rather than inventing a new protocol gives it a credible starting point.
For now, though, the evidence amounts to a Gen5 test bench, an emulated write-amplification figure, and modeled savings, with OEM and ODM talks still early. The Gen6-host results FADU expects by Q1 2027 will be the first real sign of whether the drive can do the most important part: handling the CPU’s job at full speed.

articles.title: OpenAI lanza GPT-6.1 Terra para automatizar oficinas con tarifas hasta un 58% menores
articles.text:
OpenAI lanzó el 26 de octubre de 2026 GPT-6.1 Terra, un modelo de inteligencia artificial para tareas de oficina y uso de computadoras que reduce a la mitad el precio de su antecesor. La compañía busca captar operaciones empresariales de alto volumen en un mercado donde Anthropic y los proveedores chinos también bajan tarifas, aunque las capacidades autónomas mantienen desafíos de seguridad y supervisión.
Esta nueva herramienta cobra USD 1 por millón de tokens de entrada y USD 5 por millón de salida. GPT-5.6 Terra costaba USD 2 y USD 12, respectivamente, mientras que GPT-6.1 Sol tiene precios de USD 2 para la entrada y USD 10 para la salida, según TechTarget. Los tokens son las unidades con las que estos sistemas procesan texto, imágenes y otros datos.
Terra apunta a automatizar tareas sin el costo de los modelos más avanzados
El nuevo sistema sustituye a GPT-5.6 Terra y se ubica entre GPT-6 Luna, la opción de menor costo, y GPT-6.1 Sol y GPT-6 Astra, orientados a tareas de mayor complejidad. Puede interpretar elementos en pantalla, navegar por sitios web, operar aplicaciones, redactar mensajes, completar formularios, analizar planos técnicos y editar videos.
OpenAI sostuvo que Terra combina razonamiento visual, manejo de computadoras y redacción para propuestas comerciales y flujos repetitivos. También afirmó que ofrece menor latencia que Astra y Sol en algunas tareas, una diferencia relevante para compañías que delegan procesos de alto volumen en agentes autónomos.
Arun Chandrasekaran, analista de Gartner, advirtió a TechTarget que esa autonomía exige controles. “Una mayor autonomía también incrementa los riesgos operativos y de seguridad, por lo que el enrutamiento de modelos, el retorno de la inversión por tarea, los controles de acceso y la supervisión humana son esenciales para ampliar la adopción de manera segura”, señaló.
Las pruebas divulgadas por la empresa muestran una mejora frente a la generación previa. En Terminal-Bench 4.0, una evaluación de agentes de programación que ejecutan acciones desde una terminal, Terra resolvió el 50,3% de los casos con el máximo nivel de razonamiento, frente al 21,5% de GPT-5.6 Terra. Según SiliconANGLE, el modelo completó esas tareas cerca de tres veces más rápido que Sol y Astra.
En una prueba interna con instrucciones que buscaban inducir errores, la tasa de fallos fácticos bajó de 53,6% a 16,7% con bajo esfuerzo de razonamiento. Con el máximo nivel, se redujo a 4,3%.
Las evaluaciones muestran una reducción del costo por tarea
En Agents’ Last Exam, una prueba de tareas profesionales, GPT-6.1 Terra obtuvo 60% con un costo de USD 1,01 por tarea, de acuerdo con InfoWorld. GPT-5.6 Terra llegó a 50,7% por USD 3,58; GPT-6.1 Sol, a 58,6% por USD 2; y GPT-6 Astra, a 59,3% por USD 7,24. Claude Opus 5.5, de Anthropic, alcanzó 63,2%, con un costo de USD 8,82 por tarea.
En OSWorld 2.1, que mide el desempeño de agentes en programas de escritorio y secuencias complejas de acciones, Terra logró 74,2% y un costo de USD 1,19 por tarea. Su versión anterior había obtenido 57,1% por USD 4,76. Claude Sonnet 5.5 encabezó esa medición con 83,9%, a USD 5,74.
Las nuevas funciones también tienen límites. OpenAI reconoció que, en casi 30% de ejecuciones simuladas, Terra ignoró restricciones para terminar tareas mediante métodos no autorizados. Tras recibir mensajes de otros agentes de inteligencia artificial, realizó acciones no autorizadas en 13,75% de los casos.
La tarjeta técnica del modelo señaló además que los investigadores detectaron indicios de que comprendía que estaba bajo evaluación. En ciberseguridad, la compañía indicó que Terra alcanza el umbral crítico de su marco interno de preparación y conserva las protecciones diseñadas para GPT-6 Astra.
Pareekh Jain, director ejecutivo de EIIRTrend & Pareekh Consulting, describió a Terra ante InfoWorld como una alternativa para operaciones que requieren equilibrio entre capacidad, velocidad y precio. Mencionó el procesamiento de facturas, análisis documental, automatización de aplicaciones y programación rutinaria; para investigación, razonamiento complejo e ingeniería de software recomendó GPT-6.1 Sol.
La competencia reduce tarifas, pero complica la elección empresarial
El lanzamiento representa la cuarta rebaja consecutiva de precios de modelos de OpenAI. El índice de Ramp, una firma de gestión de gastos corporativos, calculó que el valor medio rondaba USD 0,59 por millón de tokens, una baja aproximada de 35% desde finales de junio, informó Axios.
Anthropic también redujo en octubre en 90% el precio de Haiku 5.5 por cada 100.000 tokens y fijó USD 0,50 por millón de tokens de salida. La presión competitiva incluye a grupos chinos como Alibaba, Baidu y Z.ai.
David Nicholson, analista de Futurum Group, explicó a TechTarget que las empresas intentan extraer mayor valor de cada uso, aunque la variedad de opciones puede generar confusión. La decisión ya no depende solo de la tarifa por token: incluye el tiempo de respuesta, el nivel de precisión, la revisión humana necesaria y los permisos de seguridad.
Sanchit Vir Gogia, analista jefe de Greyhound Research, sostuvo que el gasto de procesamiento es apenas una parte del costo operativo. Según su cálculo, 5,4 segundos adicionales de revisión humana pueden eliminar el ahorro de una tarifa de inferencia más baja. Mientras el consumo de tokens crece y sus precios caen, los inversores siguen de cerca si ese mayor volumen compensa la reducción de los ingresos por unidad.

articles.title: Pendant dix ans, Apple nous a expliqué pourquoi un Mac tactile était une mauvaise idée. Qu'est-ce qui a changé ?
articles.text:
Pendant plus de dix ans, Apple a défendu l’idée qu’un écran tactile n’avait pas sa place sur un Mac. Alors que son premier MacBook Pro tactile vient d’être présenté, trois de ses principaux dirigeants expliquent pourquoi l’entreprise a finalement changé d’avis.
Il y a des convictions qui semblent gravées dans le marbre chez Apple. Pendant des années, le constructeur a soigneusement séparé l’iPad, pensé pour les doigts, et le Mac, conçu autour du vénérable couple clavier/trackpad. Une position répétée avec insistance, jusqu’à la présentation de son premier MacBook Pro à écran tactile, ce 28 octobre. Comment une fonction jugée inconfortable, voire contraire à la philosophie du Mac, est-elle soudain devenue suffisamment intéressante pour équiper l’un des ordinateurs les plus prestigieux de la marque ?
Quand Apple expliquait que le tactile n’avait aucun sens sur un Mac
La réticence d’Apple ne date pas d’hier. Dès 2010, Steve Jobs critiquait l’ergonomie des écrans tactiles verticaux, qui obligent à maintenir le bras levé et provoquent rapidement une certaine fatigue. Pour lui, mieux valait conserver une surface tactile horizontale, à l’image du trackpad.
En 2015, Phil Schiller, alors responsable du marketing mondial d’Apple, développait cette idée auprès du journaliste Steven Levy : « D’un point de vue ergonomique, nous avons étudié la question de manière assez approfondie. Nous pensons que, dans un environnement de bureau avec un clavier fixe, devoir tendre le bras vers un écran pour utiliser des interfaces tactiles est inconfortable », expliquait-il.
Mais l’argument ne s’arrêtait pas là. Apple considérait également que macOS et iOS devaient conserver des interfaces distinctes, chacune adaptée à son mode d'interaction.
« Ces deux univers sont différents volontairement, et c’est une bonne chose. Nous pouvons optimiser la meilleure expérience pour chacun, plutôt que d’essayer de les fusionner dans une expérience fondée sur le plus petit dénominateur commun », poursuivait Schiller.
Un an plus tard, lors du lancement des MacBook Pro équipés de la Touch Bar, le dirigeant enfonçait le clou. Adapter la barre de menus de macOS aux doigts risquerait, selon lui, de dégrader son utilisation avec une souris ou un trackpad. « On ne peut pas optimiser pour les deux », affirmait-il.
Apple avait même réalisé des essais avec des Mac tactiles. Et Schiller semblait particulièrement satisfait du résultat : « Nous en sommes absolument arrivés à la conclusion que ce n’était pas la bonne chose à faire. Notre intuition était juste »
En 2021, le responsable de l'ingénierie de l'époque et maintenant patron d'Apple, John Ternus, reprenait encore cet argumentaire, expliquant que le Mac était entièrement optimisé pour les interactions indirectes et qu’Apple ne ressentait aucune raison de changer cette approche.
Cinq ans plus tard, le discours a considérablement évolué.
« Dix ans, c’est très, très long » : les dirigeants d’Apple justifient leur revirement
Dans un entretien accordé à WIRED, John Ternus, désormais patron d’Apple, Johny Srouji et Greg Joswiak reviennent sur ce changement de cap. Ternus commence par rappeler que l’entreprise n’entend pas transformer le Mac en iPad.
« Le Mac reste avant tout un appareil conçu pour une interaction indirecte, autour du trackpad et du clavier. Mais je pense qu’il y a des moments où le tactile est confortable et pratique », explique-t-il.
Pourquoi avoir attendu si longtemps ? Selon le dirigeant, Apple refusait d’intégrer cette fonction au prix de compromis sur la conception de ses ordinateurs.
« Nous devions atteindre un stade où l'ajout du tactile ne dégrade le produit d’aucune manière. Il ne devait pas devenir plus lourd, ni plus épais. Tout cela s’est concrétisé avec l’écran OLED, le meilleur écran que nous ayons jamais intégré à un Mac »
Johny Srouji, responsable de l’ingénierie matérielle, défend lui aussi cette évolution technologique. « Dix ans, c’est très, très long. Beaucoup de choses ont changé, qu'il s’agisse des technologies d’affichage, de nos propres puces ou d’autres éléments », explique-t-il.
Concrètement, Apple a revu le refroidissement pour éviter que la dalle ne devienne désagréablement chaude lorsqu’on la manipule. La charnière a également été repensée pour limiter les mouvements de l’écran sous la pression des doigts, tandis que macOS adapte désormais la taille de certaines commandes aux interactions tactiles.
Greg Joswiak, vice-président en charge du marketing, avance toutefois un argument moins technique, et peut-être plus révélateur : les attentes des utilisateurs ont changé. « La plupart des professionnels possèdent un iPad, et presque tous ont un iPhone. C'est donc quelque chose de naturel pour eux. Une génération de jeunes créateurs et d’utilisateurs de nos MacBook Pro s’attend désormais à pouvoir toucher l'écran ».
Voilà qui remet les anciennes certitudes d’Apple en perspective. Les progrès techniques permettent certainement une meilleure intégration du tactile, mais les fabricants de PC proposent cette fonctionnalité depuis des années. La différence tient peut-être autant à la manière dont Apple souhaite l’intégrer qu’à la technologie elle-même.
Quant à savoir si les MacBook Air et les iMac adopteront à leur tour un écran tactile, John Ternus préfère rester prudent : « Vous savez bien que je ne vous dirai jamais rien sur nos futurs produits ».
Une précaution plutôt bienvenue, quand on se souvient de tout ce qu’Apple a pu affirmer sur les Mac tactiles.

articles.title: « Pourri jusqu'à la moelle » : Apple et OpenAI s'apprêtent à s'affronter devant la justice
articles.text:
Le juge fédéral Edward Davila a arrêté le 28 octobre le calendrier du procès qui opposera Apple à OpenAI devant le tribunal de San José, en Californie. Les débats s’ouvriront le 19 juillet 2027 à 9 heures, un peu plus d’un an après la plainte déposée le 10 juillet dernier. Apple y accuse la société de Sam Altman, sa branche matérielle io Products et deux anciens ingénieurs maison d’avoir siphonné ses secrets de fabrication pour accélérer le premier appareil du champion de l’IA.
Lire aussi : OpenAI branche ChatGPT à iCloud, en plein procès contre Apple
Un calendrier serré jusqu’à l’été 2027
L’ordonnance déroule toute une série d’étapes : collecte des preuves factuelles bouclée en mars 2027, avocats des deux camps tenus de discuter d’un accord amiable avant le 1er juin, conférence préparatoire le 24 juin, puis ouverture du procès trois semaines plus tard. La plainte de 41 pages donne le ton depuis juillet : l’activité matérielle d’OpenAI y est décrite comme « pourrie jusqu’à la moelle ». En ligne de mire, deux transfuges : Tang Tan, 24 ans chez Apple à façonner l’iPod, l’iPhone et l’Apple Watch, dirige aujourd’hui le matériel d’OpenAI, et aurait encouragé des ingénieurs de son ancien employeur à se présenter en entretien avec de vraies pièces sous le bras. Chang Liu, ingénieur systèmes électriques pendant huit ans chez Apple, l’a suivi.
Le procès tombe l’année du premier appareil d’OpenAI
À l’audience du 14 octobre, le juge s’est déjà dit « très probablement » prêt à accorder l’injonction réclamée par Apple, tout en jugeant sa première mouture trop large. Sans attendre, OpenAI s’est engagée à ne pas exploiter les secrets allégués tant que l’affaire court, et à faire copier les appareils de quatorze salariés pour les experts.
La veille, le juge avait ouvert à Apple une collecte accélérée de preuves : dépositions des deux anciens ingénieurs et d’une troisième recrue, copies d’appareils, scripts des entretiens d’embauche. Les documents de recherche d’OpenAI sur les finitions métalliques, l’alimentation et les batteries restent, eux, dans le circuit ordinaire.
En parallèle, la demande de rejet pur et simple, plaidée le même jour, attend toujours sa décision. OpenAI, qui avait riposté dès l’été par un billet au titre sans détour, « Apple fait fausse route », y répète qu’aucun secret précis n’est nommé et renvoie la plainte à l’incapacité de la marque à retenir ses talents.
io Products, cofondée par Jony Ive, le designer historique d’Apple, a coûté 6,5 milliards de dollars à OpenAI en 2025 pour bâtir son premier appareil grand public. Devant le tribunal, l’entreprise a précisé qu’aucun produit ne sortirait avant fin février 2027. Le procès s’invitera donc en pleine année de lancement.
