articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing shows most of its compute goes to R&D, not serving customers
articles.text:
Anthropic’s IPO filing shows most of its compute goes to R&D, not serving customers — company details massive $800 billion in TPU and GPU contracts
Claude covers what it costs to serve, but the racks on order are another matter.
Anthropic spent less than a third of its $8.9 billion first-half compute bill on serving customers, with most of the rest going into training, research, and running Claude internally, its S-1 filing shows. It has meanwhile signed up for hundreds of billions of dollars more in TPU and GPU capacity. By our math, it has meanwhile signed up for roughly $800 billion more in TPU and GPU capacity, and revenue per compute dollar jumped from $0.40 in Q1 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026, which the company links to capacity purchased 12–18 months ahead.
Anthropic’s IPO is likely to beat that of rival OpenAI, which filed confidentially before CEO Sam Altman said its own won’t come this year, amid widespread doubts about an AI bubble. Whether AI labs can cover what it costs to serve their models is an open question.
Anthropic appears to do so easily: it spent $2.4 billion serving customers in the first half of the year, versus $16.3 billion in revenue. Paying for what it has on order is more difficult. Its five compute deals with the biggest stated amounts would cost an estimated $103 billion a year on average once delivered, more than twice its revenue at Q2’s pace of about $46 billion a year. The company also warns that margins may compress as new hardware lands ahead of the revenue it will support.
The company has three main costs: the cost of revenue, which is the inference cost of running Claude for paying customers; R&D, which is mostly compute for training and research into new models plus any internal use; and sales and marketing, which covers the cut taken by channel partners and cloud platform resellers.
Comparing the first half of last year to this year’s, cost of revenue is up about 2.3x, but with revenue up 14x, that means Anthropic keeps an estimated 85 cents for every dollar after serving costs, up from just 12 cents. R&D is up about 5 times, with 66% or more of the compute going to it, and that’s the main source of its operating loss. Sales and marketing is up 16x, and doesn’t show up in cost of revenue, but its partner fees and marketing would lower what it keeps to 66 cents a dollar. The trend here is that serving Claude now more than covers its costs.
| Where Anthropic’s Compute Goes |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | First half of 2025 | First half of 2026 | 
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $1.16 billion | $16.29 billion | 
| Compute and infrastructure, all workloads | $2.33 billion | $8.95 billion | 
| Serving customers (cost of revenue) | $1.02 billion | $2.38 billion | 
| Free access to Claude, at most (est.) | $119 million | $640 million | 
| Training, research and internal use, at least (est.) | $1.20 billion | $5.93 billion | 
| Serving share of compute, at most | 44% | 27% | 
| Revenue left after serving costs | 12% | 85% | 
| Revenue left after serving costs, partner fees and marketing | 2% | 66% | 
Serving has kept getting cheaper for customers since June: in September, Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 model cut costs per task by about 40% versus Opus 5, says the company, and Fable 5.1 cut the cost of typical workloads by about 25% against Fable 5; each came from “a combination of a lower price and improved efficiency,” made “while preserving our margins.”
As for compute, which runs through all three costs, Anthropic runs it as “a single, shared resource across all workloads” and doesn’t disclose how it decides the split between training, research, and serving. Serving was limited, as the company has “consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute,” which suggests serving costs were muted by a lack of supply, not just efficiency.
Anthropic runs a “multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs,” without giving any percentage splits or GW measurements. For TPUs, it has five-year equipment leases with Broadcom for “TPU-based compute capacity,” with rent of “approximately $161.2 billion excluding interest”; some of that capacity came online this year, with more from 2027. Another $114.5 billion or more is with Google “between April 2026 and July 2033,” with more from Google and other TPU providers from 2028 to 2031, estimated to be in the $125–$150 billion range.
Trainium comes through Amazon, with a deal for “at least $110.0 billion between May 2026 and April 2036,” though the filing doesn’t split AWS spend by chip. Nvidia GPUs come through a series of deals, including “up to $120.5 billion … extending into 2029” with SpaceXAI, “at least $44.9 billion” extending into 2033 with Microsoft, “up to approximately $44.6 billion” also into 2033 with Nscale, and about $41.3 billion into 2034 with Lambda. There is also an AMD hardware supply agreement which, in aggregate, may “exceed $20.0 billion” if Anthropic takes the full initial capacity. These deals each have their own conditions for termination.
| Anthropic’s Compute Contracts |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Partner | Hardware | Amount | Term | Can Anthropic walk away? | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Broadcom | Google TPUs (equipment leases) | About $161.2 billion in rent | Five-year leases; some capacity online in 2026, more from 2027 | No, except on default | 
|  | Google TPUs | At least $114.5 billion | April 2026–July 2033 | No, except on Google’s uncured material breach; minimum owed regardless of use | 
| TPU providers, including Google | Google TPUs | $125–150 billion (estimated) | Delivered 2028–2031 | Not stated; payments depend on capacity made available and deployment conditions | 
| Amazon | AWS (Trainium among its chips) | At least $110 billion | May 2026–April 2036 | No, except on Amazon’s uncured material breach; minimum owed regardless of use | 
| SpaceXAI | Nvidia GPUs | Up to $120.5 billion; about $3.1 billion a month at full delivery | Into 2029; full capacity expected December 2026 | Yes, on 90 days’ notice once the initial periods end in January and March 2027 | 
| Microsoft | Azure (Nvidia GPUs) | At least $44.9 billion | November 2026–May 2033 | No, except on Microsoft’s uncured material breach or for undelivered tranches | 
| Nscale | Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 | Up to $44.6 billion | Into 2033 | No, except in limited cases (missed delivery or availability targets, uncured material breach); billed only as capacity is delivered and accepted | 
| Lambda | Nvidia GPUs | About $41.3 billion | Into 2034 | Partly: either side can end $34.9 billion of it if Lambda doesn’t secure the facility lease in time; otherwise only on Lambda’s uncured material breach or missed delivery milestones | 
| AMD | Instinct MI450 (Helios) | Expected to exceed $20 billion; no fixed dollar commitment | First capacity in 2027 | No, except on AMD’s uncured material breach | 
| Total, deals named in the S-1 (our sum) | All of the above | About $782–807 billion | 2026–2036 | Mix of minimums, caps and estimates; the S-1 leaves its own total blank and mentions other deals it doesn’t describe | 
Anthropic’s minimum purchase commitments, which exclude equipment leases such as Broadcom’s, have gone from about $55 billion at the end of last year to about $265.6 billion by the end of Q2 this year. Since then, it has signed about $245 billion in new minimums, leases included, and TPUs are the biggest line overall. The Nvidia capacity, Microsoft’s aside, is also the easiest for Anthropic to walk away from.
With all these multi-year commitments, bought well ahead of delivery, expenses are paid and recognized “as compute becomes available to us,” the company says. That compute base “did not fluctuate with in-period demand,” so revenue per compute dollar increased as demand surged. When demand outruns that capacity, Anthropic buys short-term compute, which “typically carries a higher cost per unit.”
Our $103 billion estimate is straight-line, spreading each deal evenly over its term except SpaceXAI, which is at its full monthly rate, while payments ramp up as capacity is delivered. Also not included in the estimate is interest on the Broadcom leases. Compute also does not necessarily have to earn revenue, especially in R&D.
The filing has many blanks, such as the total commitment figure, the contractual obligations table, Q3 revenue, and Run-Rate Revenue, which an amended S-1 would normally fill in before pricing. No date for that has been given. Microsoft’s minimum starts in November, and SpaceXAI’s full delivery is expected in December, with non-cancelable periods ending in January and March 2027, after which either side can cancel on 90 days’ notice. More Broadcom TPU capacity and AMD’s first tranche follow next year, by which point most of these deals will be billing.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: FBI Seizes Virtualine Domain Over Alleged Criminal Hosting and Bitcoin Money Laundering
articles.text:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine.
The move was in response to the service being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct," the DoJ said.
Visitors to the "virtualine[.]net" domain are now greeted by a message that states it has been seized by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation as part of a coordinated operation between international law enforcement agencies and private sector entities, including the Hessen State Police, the National Police Corps of the Netherlands, the U.K. National Crime Agency, OverRIPE, and Lumen Technologies.
According to court documents, Virtualine, which also operated as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums, claiming that they can be used for phishing, carding, email spam, and port scanning, with the exception of child content and terrorism activities.
In June 2025 on HackForums, the provider is alleged to have boasted that "Virtualine ignored more abuse than your last three therapists." Earlier this March, it also began marketing an "additional protection plan" that promised its customers to move their criminal infrastructure to a shell company unaffiliated with Virtualine when receiving official requests from law enforcement agencies.
Snapshots captured by the Internet Archive show that standard plans cost anywhere between $19.99 per month for one virtual CPU, 2GB memory, and 30 GB storage to $179.99 per month for 24 vCPUs, 64 GB memory, and 130 GB memory. Virtualine also offered plans optimized by CPU, memory, and storage, starting from $21.99 per month to $379.99 per month.
"Despite advertising that it does not allow 'child contents' on its server, Virtualine knowingly hosted a website that did so, identified in court records as Vendor 1," DoJ said. "Vendor 1 is a criminal online forum that allows users to post and sell access to nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults."
"Vendor 1 also promotes a hack-for-hire service in which users can pay hackers to access victims’ online accounts without their consent and illicitly obtain explicit images and videos. In January 2026, about one month after Virtualine assigned an IP address to Vendor 1, Virtualine began receiving notifications about sexually explicit images and videos of minors on that server."
The Justice Department said Virtualine continued to host Vendor 1's services despite receiving numerous notices from law enforcement in Germany, Canada, and Australia; the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in the United States; and a victim's attorney.
Virtualine has also been accused of working closely with Vendor 1 to create a new website where its clients could upload their illicit content and download it upon completing a purchase. The website continues to be hosted by Virtualine to this day, the department added.
"Virtualine.net included a number of payment options for Virtualine's customers, including Vendor 1," the DoJ said. "Virtualine accepted payment through BTC [NO-AML], specific unhosted bitcoin addresses that allowed customers to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit."
"The funds Virtualine's criminal customers paid to Virtualine, some of which can be traced directly to various criminal groups, were received by Virtualine and then further laundered to conceal the origin of the funds."
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, in its own analysis, said Virtualine accepted direct Bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without triggering compliance checks at hosted exchanges.
"Virtualine's on-chain footprint has direct exposure to a broad cross-section of the cybercrime ecosystem, including ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses," it said.
Following the site seizure, the operator of Virtualine has published an open letter, refuting allegations that the service knowingly hosted child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The operator also claimed they have taken action on requests for cooperation concerning CSAM within 24 hours. In a post shared on their Telegram channel, they insisted that customer data was safe.
"When we identified prohibited material associated with the customer described as 'Vendor 1,' we ended our relationship with that customer," the individual added, claiming "Virtualine has been part of my life for five years."
"Please do not cast suspicion on me and the tens of thousands of customers who have trusted Virtualine because of the actions attributed to a single customer. I want you to know that I am prepared to respond to your requests concerning 'Vendor 1.'"
In September 2025, the Spamhaus Project revealed that Virtualine had expanded their operations to AS209800. "Thanks to Turkey- and U.S.-based IP address brokers with poor customer vetting procedures, Virtualine keeps obtaining new IPv4 prefixes for enabling internet abuse. AS209800 is currently routed via aurologic GmbH, a hosting provider proliferating several other bulletproof hosting operations."
"A lost ASN does not by itself mean the BPH has stopped," Silent Push said. "The speed of acquiring a new ASN is a crucial part of the problem, and we believe the process for registering an ASN should be tougher."
Update
According to an analysis published by TRM Labs, Virtualine received more illicit-attributed cryptocurrency than any other labeled bulletproof host in 2026, surpassing SecureHost, vpsbg, F0XYF0X BPH (aka Bearhost), and Gerry, despite lower total inflows.
A Russian drug marketplace accounted for nearly 44% of direct inflows, while a large sextortion scheme, a mixer, and ransomware groups were responsible for about 17%, 13%, and 5%, respectively. Direct payers include Coinbase Cartel, The Gentlemen, INC, DragonForce, and Qilin, alongside malware operators such as the StealC infostealer and the Matanbuchus loader.
Other counterparties that have transacted with Virtualine are darknet markets, illicit goods and services operators, bot and malware-distribution services, and sites linked to child sexual abuse material.
"Virtualine is another example of Russia's illicit economy at work: darknet markets, ransomware groups, non-compliant exchanges, and brokers all feeding the same ecosystem," Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.
"Bulletproof hosting is the connective tissue. Seizing a domain matters, but the blockchain record doesn't disappear with it. It shows who is paying, who is getting paid, and where they go next."
A press release from the Dutch police has revealed that dozens of physical servers located in a data center in Limburg were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline.
"Through the seizure, the police are in possession of data and information relating to more than 3,000 customers who used the servers for criminal activities," the Politie said. "The secured data will be used for further police investigation regarding customers who used these servers for criminal purposes."
As of October 29, 2026, virtualine[.]org, the domain that hosted the open letter, and the Telegram channel are no longer accessible.

articles.title: Smartphones Samsung : cette application disparaîtra de votre écran d'accueil le 21 décembre 2026
articles.text:
Le grand ménage continue dans l’écosystème logiciel de Samsung. Après avoir récemment supprimé Samsung Daily Plus et revu des plateformes comme Samsung Community, le constructeur coréen s’attaque cette fois à son application d’actualités. Lancée en 2023 pour succéder à Samsung Free (lui-même héritier de Samsung Daily et Bixby Home), Samsung News tentait de s’imposer face à Google Discover et Apple News grâce à des résumés quotidiens et des partenariats avec la presse. Malgré ces efforts, la plateforme n’a pas réussi à s’imposer durablement sur les tablettes et smartphones Samsung.
Ce qui change sur l’écran d’accueil de votre Samsung
Le panneau situé tout à gauche sur l’écran d’accueil de One UI, qui affichait jusqu’à présent Samsung News en complément de Google Discover, basculera vraisemblablement vers un affichage exclusif de Google Discover. Aucun service de remplacement n’a pour l’instant été annoncé par la marque.
Le widget dédié ne recevra plus aucune mise à jour, ce qui pousse l’entreprise à recommander directement aux utilisateurs de le supprimer de leur interface. Les données personnelles récoltées par l’application seront quant à elles supprimées à la date de fermeture, le 21 décembre 2026, à l’exception des éléments que la législation locale impose de conserver.
Clap de fin pour Samsung News
La décision de tuer Samsung News marque un tournant dans la stratégie du géant coréen dans la mesure où aucun nouveau portail d’actualités maison n’est prévu pour prendre le relais, ce qui confirme que la marque préfère se retirer de ce genre de service pour laisser la place à d’autres, plus populaires.

articles.title: Raquel Ayllón, controladora ferroviaria y portavoz de SCF: "El CRC de Atocha tiene una cantidad de trabajo inhumana. No se podía ni ir al baño"
articles.text:
8:53 de la mañana del 28 de octubre. El AVE 2080 embiste al Iryo 6076 a la altura de Urda (Toledo) en la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla. El choque por alcance es definido horas más tarde por el ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, como "inexplicable" y pone el foco de la responsabilidad en el operario de Adif que dio la orden al tren de Renfe de continuar la marcha "con normalidad", una vez el sistema de seguridad LZB se había caído y no había respaldo de seguridad.
Los trabajadores, sin embargo, apuntan a motivos que sí son mucho más explicables.
"El CRC de Atocha tiene una cantidad de trabajo inhumana", resume Raquel Ayllón, responsable de circulación y portavoz del Sindicato de Circulación Ferroviario (SCF), el estado en el que se trabaja dentro del centro de control desde el que se dio la orden equivocada de circular "con normalidad" en lugar de "marcha a la vista", como ordenaba el protocolo.
Los CRC son centros de control desde los que se supervisan las líneas ferroviarias españolas. Allí, los responsables de circulación tienen asignada una línea o un tramo de la misma. Por ejemplo, en el Madrid-Sevilla, la responsabilidad del CRC de Atocha llega hasta Córdoba.
Hay 16 CRC que controlan las líneas convencionales y de media distancia y cuatro que controlan el la alta velocidad española. Por encima, el H24 es "el peldaño superior en la pirámide de control del tráfico ferroviario. Desde aquí se supervisa de forma permanente el estado de la infraestructura así como el desarrollo de la circulación ferroviaria", describe la propia Adif.
Ayllón recalca que esta descentralización está muy descompensada. "Cobras lo mismo en cualquier otro sitio que no sea Madrid. Sí, hay una pequeña compensación por volumen de tráfico pero no llega a 1.000 euros al año", explica. Y eso, asegura, no es sostenible para un trabajador que tiene que gestionar una línea como la Madrid-Sevilla.
El doble de viajeros, los mismos trabajadores
En tres años, la línea ha duplicado su volumen de tráfico. En 2022, último año antes de que empezara a circular el primer Iryo por las vías, se contabilizaron 2,8 millones de pasajeros. En 2025 se rozaron los seis millones. El número de responsables de circulación en el tramo madrileño se ha mantenido invariable: uno.
En un CRC, un responsable de circulación tiene acotado su trabajo a un tramo de línea concreto, independientemente del número de circulaciones que tenga que gestionar. Es decir, para el tramo Madrid-Córdoba, el que más tráfico tiene de España en la alta velocidad, hay un solo responsable de circulación. El mismo número que para el Madrid-Badajoz, una de las líneas con menos trenes en la vía.
Ayllón pone un ejemplo del estrés que puede suponer. "Imagina una vía de Cercanías, con trenes cada tres minutos. Es parecido pero con trenes que viajan a 300 km/h", explica. Por encima de ese responsable de circulación, un supervisor controla lo que pasa en varias de esas mesas al mismo tiempo. Y de fondo, el problema de falta de personal.
Su sindicato lleva años reclamando más trabajadores y menos carga de trabajo para los que acuden día a día al CRC con mayor carga de trabajo de toda España. Señalan en El Mundo que SSCF envió una carta a la Agencia Estatal de Seguridad Ferroviaria (AESF), organismo adscrito al ministerio de Transportes, reclamando garantías para que "el personal de regulación y control de tráfico no supere límites que comprometan la seguridad ferroviaria debido a la fatiga". Esta carta es de 2025 pero en 2021 ya elevaron la misma queja. Según el sindicato, no se dio respuesta a ninguna de las dos cartas.
Ayllón refuerza el relato asegurando que "en el CRC de Atocha han estado sin poder siquiera levantarse para ir al baño. Necesitas que alguien te reemplace en ese caso, pues créeme que no había gente. No podían tener ni un descanso. Tenían que apañarse entre ellos para ir al baño".
La responsable de circulación y portavoz del sindicato denuncia que la situación a principios de año fue "crítica". "A veces, sólo había un regulador en la sala (la persona que supervisa varias líneas al mismo tiempo). Tiene que haber regulador del norte y del sur (el CRC de Atocha hace esta división entre líneas), pues a veces sólo había uno.
Estos, nos cuenta, son sólo algunos de los problemas que enfrentan. La falta de experiencia es otro. Y es que "antes tenías que tener 10 años para llegar a un CRC como el de Atocha, hoy entra directamente gente de fuera". Personal que, nos aseguran desde el sindicato, recibe una formación teórica y práctica de 10 meses.
Durante ese periodo, además, la persona en práctica puede estar recibiendo formación por más de un responsable de circulación. Es decir, al mismo tiempo recibe formación de líneas que trabajan con sistemas de seguridad y protocolos diferentes. "Desde el sindicato pedimos que haya seis horas de trabajo y dos de formación. En la alta velocidad constantemente están saliendo nuevas consignas, nueva documentación. Tendríamos que tener una formación continua. Ahora te dejan el libro en la mesa y tú te lo lees cuando puedes", concluye

articles.title: Cloudflare finds the largest DDoS attacks fell 69% as total attacks rose 208% - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cloudflare finds the largest DDoS attacks fell 69% as total attacks rose 208%
A new report out today from Cloudflare Inc.’s Cloudforce One threat intelligence unit finds that the largest distributed denial-of-service attacks fell nearly 69% in the third quarter, and network-layer attacks overall more than tripled from a year earlier, to 18.2 million.
The “Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3” details 251 attacks above 1 terabit per second between July and September. The second quarter produced 805, after a sixfold rise from the first three months of the year. Cloudflare ties the drop, tentatively, to law enforcement action earlier this year against four of the largest botnets built from compromised internet of things devices.
The Justice Department announced the disruption of Aisuru, Kimwolf, JackSkid and Mossad in March, when authorities in Canada and Germany also moved against people allegedly behind them. Internet of things botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat in Cloudflare’s assessment, with new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot already circulating.
August was the heaviest month for Mirai-classified traffic, at 57.23 petabytes. The quarter’s longest Mirai attack began Aug. 19 and kept going for 49.7 hours.
Small attacks made up most of the quarter’s 18.2 million, which work out to about 8,226 an hour. Nearly all were over quickly, 96% of them inside 10 minutes, and bandwidth stayed under 1 gigabit per second in 98% of cases.
The report points out that a flood that size is still more than enough to overwhelm a server or website. Cloudflare reads the overall profile as the signature of DDoS-for-hire “booter” services.
Attackers also switched methods. Floods abusing the Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol grew 580% in the first half of the year, according to the report. In the third quarter CLDAP made up just 0.05% of attacks, down 99.5% on the second quarter.
Other connectionless protocols filled the gap. Amplification attacks using the Domain Name System rose 215% from the second quarter to 3.4% of the network-layer total. The bigger beneficiary was the generic User Datagram Protocol flood, which went from 14.1% of attacks to 31.3%. Plain DNS floods held steady as the most common method, at 39.3%.
Media, production and publishing kept the top spot among industries with only about a fourth of the share it held from April to June, as attackers spread their aim more widely. The internet sector climbed to sixth from 12th. Further down the table, consumer services rose nine places to eighth and adult entertainment entered the top 10 in ninth after ranking 21st three months earlier.
Geographically, the U.S. was the most-attacked country in the third quarter after finishing second to China in the first half. Indonesia rose to third with 2.93% of attacks.
Canada and Israel made the sharpest climbs. Canada went from 16th to sixth on attacks against retail, telecommunications and marketing companies, during what the report called “an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes.” Israel moved up seven places to 10th on sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. That stretch brought contentious decisions ahead of parliamentary elections as well as the Rosh Hashanah holiday, the report noted, against a wider surge in hostile cyber warfare targeting Israel this year.
Cloudflare’s systems detect and mitigate attacks without human intervention. The report says they have to, since most attacks in the quarter “end long before a human analyst could see the alert.”

articles.title: Japan's GMO Offers $1 Million Bounty to Catch Hackers Behind FX Trading Cloud Breach
articles.text:
Japan's GMO Internet Group is offering up to $1 million in total for tips that help catch the attackers who breached its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service, after refusing to pay an extortion demand.
The reward program opened on October 28 and pays only if a tip helps lead to an arrest or an international wanted notice. The service hosts Windows desktops used for FX trading, and a broker has linked unauthorized trades on some of its customers' accounts to logins leaked from the service.
GMO says the attackers took customer information. It received a demand for about $50 million (about ¥8 billion) on October 21 from people it believes carried out the attack. They have also threatened its customers' trading accounts and data.
On October 27, the attackers posted material on their website that they say is information about GMO and its customers. The site's domain, including its mirror sites, was shut down at about 4 a.m. Japan time on October 28, and GMO plans to act against any new site.
How the Reward Works
GMO Internet Group runs and pays for the program, called GMO Cybercrime Bounty. Tips are sent by email to an address listed on a dedicated website, in Japanese, English, or Chinese, and can be anonymous. The program is open until an arrest, an international wanted notice, or October 27, 2027, whichever comes first.
GMO wants information linking people, servers, domains, IP addresses, accounts, or cryptocurrency addresses to the attack, extortion, or movement of money, along with evidence of how the crimes were carried out. Guesses, unsupported accusations and reposts of public information generally do not qualify.
A tip earns money only if it leads to an arrest, including one by police outside Japan, or to an international wanted notice, such as an Interpol Red Notice. GMO decides how much each tip helped, and one tipster can receive the full $1 million or the total can be split. Tipsters must prove their identity before payment, and if no tip qualifies, no payment is made.
Some people cannot be paid, including anyone involved in the crime, anyone who got information illegally, such as by buying leaked data, and GMO staff. GMO tells tipsters not to break into systems, negotiate with or pay the attackers, or send leaked data, credentials, or malware.
Tips are shared with police and other authorities in Japan and abroad as needed. GMO has already given police all its evidence on the threats, including communication records.
GMO will never ask tipsters for passwords, authentication codes or fees, and it writes to them only from addresses ending in @cybercrimebounty.gmo.
The Breach and the Trading Accounts
GMO Internet, the subsidiary that runs the service, found on October 20 that a third party had installed malicious programs on some customers' servers. It shut down the servers on every plan from October 21. It counts 26,739 servers as potentially affected, which is not the number of confirmed break-ins or data thefts.
On October 24, GMO said it had confirmed a security problem in the service's systems, unauthorized access to the service, and the exfiltration of customer information from the company.
Anything customers stored on the servers may have been viewed, including login credentials saved in trading software such as MetaTrader 4 and 5 (MT4/MT5). GMO does not keep customers' payment card data on the servers.
Customers began reporting trades they did not recognize on October 21. A broker, OANDA Japan, has confirmed that a third party logged in to and traded on some of its customers' accounts using ID and password pairs it believes were leaked from the GMO servers. It has restricted trading on accounts that may be affected, and as of October 26 it had not found a break-in or leak in its own core systems.
Another broker, FXTF, warned on October 22 that third parties may have stolen the logins of some customers who use VPS servers, in an attack it believes hit another company's VPS servers. They may also have used the logins to log in and trade. It told customers who had connected to Desktop Cloud to change their FXTF passwords from a device that had never connected to it.
GMO Internet Group said in a stock exchange filing on October 28 that it had not yet confirmed how many customers its payments will cover, how much information was published, or which trades qualify for compensation. It had not confirmed any impact from the breach on its other services.
The Threats and the Leak
GMO says the attackers threatened to keep manipulating customers' accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms, to publish information about the service and about customers' PCs, to hit those PCs with ransomware, and to publish details of GMO's systems.
They set noon on October 27 for publishing customer information and launching the ransomware attack. No ransomware attack had been confirmed as of 1:55 p.m. Japan time that day.
The material posted on October 27 was what the attackers called one customer's personal information, ITmedia NEWS reported that afternoon. GMO was checking it that day.
The attackers collected information about anyone who visited their site, according to GMO, which tells visitors to run a full antivirus scan. It asks people not to visit the site or any new one, and not to repost or link to the material.
How the Attackers Got In
As of October 28, GMO had not said how the attackers got in.
Masatoshi Kumagai, who heads GMO Internet Group, wrote in an October 25 blog post that the group's own white-hat hackers had warned the team running the service about problems in advance.
The response was neither fast nor thorough enough, he wrote, and the attackers took advantage of the gap.
On their website, the attackers claimed that one administrator account was shared across all the servers and that customers' PC drives were visible from the servers by default when they connected, ITmedia NEWS reported.
They also claimed they used a flaw in the service to reach customers' own PCs. GMO had not publicly confirmed these claims either.
By October 26, GMO had collected PCs from customers who offered them for analysis, as of 11:59 a.m. Japan time on October 27, it had found no malware, including ransomware, on the PCs it had finished checking. That does not confirm that every customer's device is safe, and the analysis is still ongoing.
What Customers Should Do
GMO has told Desktop Cloud customers to take these steps:
- Change trading-account and trading-software passwords from a device not used for FX trading, such as a phone.
- End every logged-in session, through the broker if needed, even after changing the password.
- Check trading history and balances, and report unrecognized trades to the broker first.
- Turn on two-factor authentication where the broker offers it.
- Change passwords reused on other services or saved in the browser.
- Run a full antivirus scan on devices used to connect, and back up data.
- Do not reply to messages from anyone claiming to be behind the attack, or open their links or files.
- Ignore offers to recover lost money for a fee. GMO will never ask for a password or authentication code.
GMO Internet will pay every current user ¥5,000 and cover actual trading losses and fees from trades it confirms were unauthorized and caused by the breach. Customers whose information it confirms was published will also get ¥10,000 to ¥25,000 for each type of information exposed.
GMO will not restart the service on the breached systems as they are. Customers who want a Windows desktop will be offered a move to a separate service, free for six months and only with their consent, with details due by October 30.

articles.title: xTool X1 review: The most versatile laser engraver I’ve ever tested
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The xTool X1 combines excellent CO₂ cutting performance with fast galvo engraving, plus optional specialist laser modules. It features hybrid motion, automated focusing, and the refined xTool Studio software. Add in the accessories and even in a professional workshop, you will need to allow for some considerable space. Build quality and software integration are, as ever, outstanding, but its weight, space requirements, and time-consuming module changes are frustrating. Additional modules are also incredibly expensive, all increasing the overall investment, but this doesn't detract from just how good this is..
Reasons to buy
- + Incredibly versatile
- + Fast engraving speed
- + Excellent workflow
Reasons to avoid
- - Substantial workshop space needed
- - Time-consuming module changes
- - Expensive additional laser modules
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
The xTool X1 might initially look like another large, enclosed laser engraver, but it wasn't long into my months-long test of the X1, to realise it's something far more ambitious.
Essentially, xTool has brought years of laser engraving development together into a single, expandable manufacturing platform, making the X1 one of the most versatile machines I’ve ever reviewed. This is not the first machine that I’ve looked at recently to do the modular laser approach, with the superb Creality Falcon T1 doing something similar on a far smaller scale.
At the X1’s heart is a 55W CO₂ laser, similar to that seen in the excellent Bambu Lab R1 although now the larger X1 has arrived at the same price and with far more potential it will be interesting to see how the R1 fares.
Once again, the 55W CO₂ laser proves to be a powerful option for cutting and engraving wood, acrylic, and a wide variety of other materials. On its own, this one laser option would already make the X1 a superb option for anyone looking for a professional laser cutter.
But then again, xTool already has the xTool P2. To differentiate this as something new, xTool has thrown all their technologies at the design and added an optional 20W diode galvo module, which sits alongside the CO₂ head inside the machine, and this forms the foundation of what this machine then develops into.
One of the key features to the dual head system is that rather than relying on a conventional moving-head laser for every cut, engrave, and score, the X1 can use the galvo system for intricate, high-speed engraving before switching to the CO₂ laser for cutting. What I like is that both are controlled through xTool Studio, and switching between the installed lasers just takes a selection option in the software.
Throughout testing, this combination of laser options with backpack modules also highlighted the potential and the direction these laser machines are moving. Multiple laser options mean projects like wooden placemats and detailed pencil boxes, which would ordinarily take considerable time to engrave and cut, can be completed much faster, with the galvo speeding through the detail while the CO₂ handles the cutting. In one test, a placemat project that took the xTool S1 around two hours was completed on the X1 in approximately half an hour.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
One of the X1's big features is its support for additional laser-source modules mounted on the rear of the machine. For this review, I used the 5W UV and 60W MOPA modules, which enabled me to engrave glass and emboss brass coins. I also used the MOPA for its accuracy to create precision apertures in thin metal for pinhole cameras.
Having previously used dedicated MOPA machines such as the xTool F2 Ultra, I was interested to see how a machine this size could perform similar metal engraving. The results were impressive, but as I found at every step of this review, there were a series of considerations due to the size, weight and complexity of the machine.
That first consideration is size. The X1 arrived in a substantial crate, and as it was dropped off in the driveway, I had to call on assistance from a neighbour to lift and manoeuvre it into position. Although the main machine can sit on a conventional workshop bench, the additional modules, extraction systems and accessories quickly highlighted that the space I had allocated was about half of what it should have been.
The second point to make is the modular system. While the additional laser sources proved excellent, swapping them isn't quick, unlike some of the small multi-laser modular systems I have looked at recently.
With the X1 positioned against a wall, accessing the rear of the machine, changing the hardware, and recalibrating could take about an hour. Some of this was down to the restricted space in my workshop, but the swap of modules required the recalibration of the lasers, it’s worth considering if you intend to switch between different laser technologies regularly.
Price is another consideration although I'm actually surprised how cheap it is on balance. The base machine is listed at $3,699 / £2554, but adding the diode laser, specialist modules and accessories can take the complete system well beyond $10,000, depending on configuration.
Even so, there’s no getting away from how capable this machine is, and if you were looking for the equivalent in separate machines, say the P2 and F2 Ultra, you’d be looking at much the same costs. For general cutting, detailed engraving and small-batch production, the X1 is one of the most refined laser engravers I’ve used.
If you have an established workshop or small business handling a wide range of materials, the X1 offers huge potential. Just make sure you have the space, budget and patience to make the most of it.
xTool X1: Price & availability
The xTool X1 starts at $3,699 / £2,553 and includes the 55W CO₂ laser. The base price is in line with other machines that I have looked at recently. It's worth knowing that the costs rise quickly with optional modules.
The 20W diode galvo at $899 / approx. £674 is an optional, but essential upgrade, as it first enables faster engraving but is also needed to support the installation of the additional UV, fibre and MOPA lasers.
A fully equipped system comes in at just under $10,000 if you buy the components separately as upgrades, however, the bundle offer prices bring the cost right down. The X1’s integrated workflow, versatility and all-in-one design do keep things neat. You can find out more at xTool.
X1 Single CO2 (55W CO2): $3,399 / £2,554
X1 CO2 + Diode Galvo (55W CO2 + 20W Diode Galvo Module): $3,999 / £3,005
X1 CO2 + Diode Galvo + Fiber (Includes 30W Fiber Laser Source): $5,799 / £4,358
X1 CO2 + Diode Galvo + UV (Includes 5W UV Laser Source): $6,499 / £4,884
X1 CO2 + Diode Galvo + MOPA (Includes 60W MOPA Laser Source): $6,679 / £5,019
xTool X1: Design
Machine type: Modular laser cutting and engraving platform
Primary laser: 55W CO₂, 10,600nm
Optional lasers: 20W diode galvo, 5W UV, 30W fibre, 60W MOPA
Laser technologies: Hybrid Motion and Laser Swap
Working area: 615 × 320 mm x 150 maximum
Dimensions: 
Weight: 
Camera and focusing: Dual cameras with image stitching, automatic focusing and height-adjustable bed
Connectivity: USB and Wi-Fi
Software: xTool Studio
There’s nothing particularly small or understated about the xTool X1. In fact, the first indication of what I was dealing with came when the machine arrived in a substantial wooden crate. I can usually handle these large machines with the help of a sack trolley and boxes.
However, this time I called on the help of a neighbor. It’s not quite the size of the P3, but you will still need two people to lift the X1 free of its packaging and to get it into position in the workshop. By the time we stripped away the protective materials and set it onto the work surface, it was obvious this wasn’t a typical desktop laser engraver.
The machine itself follows the same design direction as xTool’s recent P2S and P3 models, with a fully enclosed chassis and a level of refinement that feels far removed from the open-frame laser engravers that dominated the enthusiast market only a few years ago. When it comes to the size, it measures 1000×580×420 mm.
Having tested numerous xTool machines, I’ve consistently been impressed by the company’s build quality. While xTool and GlowForge used to be the two major players in this part of the market, rivals such as Bambu Lab, LaserPecker, and WeCreat have recently upped the game as well.
Everything from the large hinged lid to the internal processing bed feels solid and is exactly as I’d want in the workshop. The lid opens easily and is supported by pneumatic arms; on some machines of this size that I’ve looked at in the past, this can be a weak point, but here it all feels good and solid.
Compared with other machines of this type and size, the height of the machine is considerably taller; this is due to the adjustable bed inside that rises and lowers to position materials correctly beneath the laser. This is a far more sophisticated setup than the fixed-height beds on many smaller machines that require risers for larger objects. On the front of the machine, there are a couple of buttons that enable you to raise and lower the bed manually if needed.
Testing showed the bed adjustment was essentially fully automated, with the software handling most positioning. The work area is big, with a maximum of 615 × 320 mm, and offers plenty of room to lay out multiple parts, which is especially useful for small batches of products such as placemats.
What I quickly realised is that depending on the laser and type of work you’re doing, those work area dimensions change. For instance, with the CO2 laser the max height of anything placed into the machine is 150mm; however, with the other lasers that reduces to 140mm. Essentially, as you lay out your designs and select the lasers, the on-screen layout changes so visually that from the outset you know exactly where you are.
Inside, the materials are supported on the supplied slats, though as with other manufacturers, I would have liked a few more. I also had the optional honeycomb panel, which, as ever, became my preferred choice for almost everything I processed.
A honeycomb just provides a decent surface for supporting materials and makes it easier to remove completed work, and while small pieces of debris from the cuts will still fall through to the base, there’s less chance of scorching of cut pieces falling and accidentally getting re-lasered.
Unfortunately, one surprise was that there isn’t a simple removable waste tray at the base, so cleaning out smaller pieces requires a little more effort. I have a handheld Dyson for this exact job, and with the depth and space, it’s easy enough to get that into cleanup quickly after a few cuts.
In this review, alongside the 55W CO2, I have also installed the 20W diode galvo module. This sits alongside the CO₂ laser inside the main enclosure and takes a couple of minutes to fit; once installed, it can stay as a permanent part of the machine. After installation, the rest of the setup is completed in xTool Studio.
The software walks you through the calibration process, although some manual adjustment is needed to ensure that the laser paths are correctly aligned. I’ve encountered this with previous xTool machines, including the P2 and P3, and while it can take a little time to understand, the process is reasonably straightforward once you’ve done it a few times.
My first test didn’t produce the result I expected because the alignment wasn’t quite right, mainly due to me rushing part of the process. After repeating the calibration more carefully, the results vastly improved, and once everything was configured, the two installed laser systems are remarkably easy to use.
To switch between the two in the xTool Studio software, you simply assign the right laser to the right operation, and the machine handles the transition. There’s no need to remove one laser head and install another manually as you would have had to do with multi-laser machines in the past.
For everyday cutting and engraving, this combination of lasers works incredibly well and vastly speeds up the process of engraving and cutting, which is the bulk of what I personally do with these machines.
However, these two lasers are just the start of the story, and things do become a little more complicated when I started to install and use the rear-mounted laser-source modules.
xTool supplied the 5W UV and 60W MOPA modules; these are relatively compact, just larger than a shoebox and are solidly built. Before use, they need to be installed into the back of the X1, which takes time, especially when I needed two people to move the machine into the initial position. Essentially, I should have left a little more space to access the rear.
Installation of the modules involves removing covers, connecting power and communication cables, securing the module and checking the optical path. Depending on the configuration, you’ll also need to install the appropriate optics before calibrating the system.
I installed the combined UV/Fiber/MOPA field lens, which supports the different laser sources, and found that straightforward, it essentially just screwed in. The more involved part was mounting the modules and completing the optical alignment.
Initially, I was probably a little too enthusiastic with the manual adjustments, but thankfully xTool provide a small alignment target and tape which makes the entire process relatively easy. Once I realised that small adjustments were all that was needed, the process became much easier.
The software guides you through calibration using the supplied cards, and once the source has been registered, the machine recognises it automatically. My main issue here was the physical access to the back of the machine due to space.
My workshop already has several 3D printers, laser engravers, and other equipment, so I’d originally positioned the X1 against a wall on a fixed workbench. Every time I wanted to change the rear-mounted module, I needed to move other equipment, pull out the workbench and get behind the machine. Given the X1’s size and weight, I didn’t want to attempt this alone.
As a result, what might eventually become a 15 or 20-minute module change took me closer to an hour, including moving the machine, changing the source and checking calibration, the calibration is the part that takes the time. This issue would explain why xTool also provided the optional mobile work stand, which is where this machine will be moved to once I have had a bit of a reorganisation of the space.
Being able to wheel the machine away from the wall would make installation, maintenance and module changes substantially easier. I’d also recommend planning considerably more space than the official machine footprint suggests. In my workshop, allowing roughly half a machine depth more provided the clearance needed to work comfortably behind it, mainly due to the length of the tool you need to use to screw in the bolts through each of the modules.
As I got into using the machine, a few of the safety design features are also worth noting. First, as ever, the machine came with the Air extraction unit and, in addition, the fire safety 2 unit, which was attached, but again space was limited, so it sat on a lower shelf behind the machine.
The X1 is serious workshop equipment, though far nicer-looking than the machines from a few years ago. Its size and weight are balanced by its features, and after a month of use, I highly recommend the optional workbench, which, while not essential, it will ensure you can make full use of this machine's potential.
xTool X1: Features
The xTool X1 is unusual because many of its headline features aren’t immediately obvious. At its core, it’s a powerful 55w CO₂ laser cutter, but its modular design means that it has far more potential, and that potential can only be fully unlocked with the investment in the other modules and accessories, of which there are quite a few.
In total, the X1 supports five laser technologies, with the 55w CO2 being the only one that is provided wth the base machine. The 55W CO₂ laser can be used for cutting and engraving materials such as wood, acrylic, leather, cardboard and fabric.
Alongside the CO₂ laser, there’s the 20W diode galvo laser, which adds high-speed engraving and surface marking, particularly on wood and many other compatible materials. This module sits inside the machine alongside the CO₂ and is quick to fit; it’s also essential if you want to use any of the other three backpack laser modules.
These other models include the 5W UV laser, which can be used for engraving on glass, crystal and other delicate materials. Then there’s the 30W fibre and 60W MOPA options, which enable you to mark and engrave into metal. The MOPA adds the ability to use colour effects and deep engraving and is similar to the fibre option, but is more expensive. In this review, I’ve been supplied with four of the five available laser technologies: CO₂, diode, UV, and MOPA.
As I started the testing, the instant highlight of the features was the Hybrid Motion, as this is the one feature alongside the dual mount lasers that will make a noticeable difference to everyday project work.
Essentially, what this looks like with the lasers is that alongside the traditional gantry-based laser toolheads that move physically through the X and Y across the material, you also have the Galvo, which uses rapidly moving mirrors to direct the beam across the surface.
This means that for larger designs, Hybrid Motion moves the galvo system between regions, enabling detailed engraving over a much wider area than a conventional fixed galvo arrangement, as I tested in the F2 Ultra. When combined, you not only cover a far larger area, but the Glavo focuses on detailed engraving while the CO₂ does the cutting.
The dual tool head laser system inside is just the start of the multi-laser set, and a Laser Swap system is used to enable different styles of laser to be fitted for different projects and materials. These Laser Swap modules fit to the back with the UV, Fibre and MOPA options.
The idea here is that instead of buying additional machines, you just buy the module and fit it, cutting down on the space needed and ideally cost. Although looking at the cost of the modules, they’re almost as much as the dedicated machines.
The process of swapping the modules isn’t tool-free, and it requires access to the rear of the machine, alongside physical hardware changes and calibration checks. I personally think that this is a great feature.
However, I would have liked to see a faster change system. In this review, for instance, I swapped the modules multiple times, and it was a hassle. But then most people will inevitably settle on their laser selection rather than approaching the machine in the way that I have in this review.
Some of the other features that really impressed during use were the close-up cameras that just help position artwork against materials, with the image appearing in the XTool software. Compared with the laser outline that we used for the full image, this is such an improvement; however, you can still click the framing preview if you prefer that way of working.
The camera system is really quite advanced, and you have the option through the xTool Studio software to change from capturing one wide-angle image, to capturing multiple sections of the workspace which are then stitched together, which helps with the accuracy of the positioning.
Although the software documentation describes automatic image capture when closing the lid, I generally triggered the capture manually during testing. Image quality from the cameras was excellent overall, although some reflective materials and darker areas could still make positioning slightly more difficult; a boost in the workshop's lighting also helped with these previews.
Another of the big features that really stood out through the use of the machine was the automated bed adjustment. Rather than requiring constant manual focusing, the machine measures the material and adjusts the bed height as needed.
Through the test, I added a range of material thicknesses and found the process just worked; compared with the often convoluted focusing process of some other machines and the physical effort of adding a riser base, this system is just simple.
Even with slightly irregular or curved materials, the positioning system generally handled setup well, and I didn’t need to override the measurements manually.
Alongside the core accessories and in line with the xTools other machines, the X1 supports a wide range of accessories, including an automatic conveyor feeder, RA3 rotary attachment, honeycomb panel, mobile work stand, filtration, and fire safety equipment.
Throughout testing, I used xTool’s extraction and filtration setup, which is a little on the noisy side but does the job. For jobs that produce more smoke, particularly when cutting wood, I increased the extraction setting to keep the working chamber clear.
The optional Fire Safety Set Pro adds another level of protection. Installation was more involved than I’d expected, requiring the CO₂ cylinder, tubing and communication connections to be fitted before enabling the system in the software. Once configured, however, it didn’t actually require me to do anything else other than find somewhere for it to sit.
As a final point on the features, and an essential for any professional workshop, is that the machine also has an emergency stop button for quickly shutting down if needed.
xTool X1: Performance
After a month testing the xTool X1, what I realised was, that the way that I work with laser engravers normally would change with this dual laser setup. The mix of laser technologies in one machine isn’t just convenient; it means that you can select the laser technology that is best suited for the job, and often two lasers will enable a better and faster result. Most notably for me, that was the combination of the 55W CO₂ and 20W diode galvo lasers.
For most of my work, producing models, wooden components, boxes, camera accessories, and other workshop projects, these two laser systems provide an ideal combination.
The X1’s 55W CO₂ laser is excellent for all-round cutting, while the 20 diode galvo is better for detail.
To start the test, I ran through the supplied test projects before moving on to my own designs, including wooden boxes, placemats and model-making components.
Most of my work involved 3mm basswood plywood, although I also tested thicker materials up to 10mm. Across these tests, the CO₂ laser produced exceptionally clean cuts, with minimal scorching and very little need for additional finishing. The air-assist system kept the cutting path clear, while the extraction system removed smoke.
One of the most useful tests involved creating a series of 3mm plywood boxes. The accuracy was excellent, with the individual pieces fitting together cleanly without sanding or manual adjustment to the size. I could simply assemble and glue the components.
This accuracy and repeatability is something that is so important when producing models or small-batch products, where even small dimensional errors create extra work; even sanding takes time when it comes to getting the right fit. As this is a pre-production model, the usually excellent xTool Studio seemed to take most laser options down to 1, so initial models showed some scorching, however
I also tested acrylic sheets up to 10mm thick, including cutting a 3D-scanning calibration cube in half. Again, the results were impressive, with clean cuts and accurate positioning.
The machine also handled lighter materials such as paper, card, fabric, and leather without difficulty, though these need careful securing to prevent movement from airflow of the air assist and extractor.
For general cutting work, along the lines of what I use laser cutters for, the X1 matched the abilities that I have seen from other recent releases; the one point that made this slightly more exciting is that added height, which gives out-of-the-box flexibility without the need for a riser base.
The CO₂ laser provides the X1’s cutting power; the addition of the 20W diode galvo by its side for detailed engraving and speed is definitely an interesting development in the technology.
Essentially, rather than watching a conventional laser head mechanically move across every section of an image, the galvo rapidly sweeps the beam over the surface, completing relatively intricate artwork in a fraction of the time.
I tested it on wood, plywood, bamboo, acrylic, and coated metal samples, essentially everything in the samples box. Fine lettering was sharp and well-defined, intricate designs retained plenty of detail, and scorching was generally minimal, unless the piece that I was working on fell through the slats.
Initially, I worried the edges of the engraving might lose definition, or designs wouldn't join up perfectly as the galvo system moved from one area to another, however the meeting of the design and the quality remained consistent.
This, however, wasn’t quite the case at the outset, and initial testing showed a few issues, but after software updates and far more accurate calibration on my part, the joins between engraving regions became almost seamless.
Photographic engraving onto wood was also impressive, although as with most laser engravers, image selection makes the biggest difference to the success.
High-contrast photographs generally produced better results than flat, low-contrast images, and I used xTool Studio’s editing tools to adjust backgrounds and improve the final output.
Personally, I still prefer the look of detailed illustrations, lettering and line-based graphics when engraved into wood rather than photo imagery.
Taking a look at one of the main test projects highlights the workflow and speed. Normally, when creating a wooden box or placemat with decorative engraving, I’ll use a single laser head that handles both engraving and cutting.
The problem is that detailed engraving can take considerably longer than cutting the outline. With the X1, I was able to assign the intricate engraving to the 20W galvo and the cutting operations to the 55W CO₂ laser.
Once configured, the software handled the transition between the installed lasers without requiring me to reposition the material or swap heads; this made a dramatic difference to processing time.
For example, I created a series of wooden placemats with detailed artwork. A comparable project on the xTool S1 took around two hours, while the X1 completed it in half an hour.
That’s an enormous improvement in speed, particularly for small businesses producing multiple products. The same was true when creating detailed pencil boxes.
Projects that would normally take 20 to 30 minutes could be completed in minutes, with the galvo handling the engraving before the CO₂ laser cut the components.
Having both lasers permanently installed makes everyday projects straightforward, and once you’ve experienced the speed of the combined workflow, returning to a conventional single-head engraver feels a little archaic.
Hybrid Motion also changes what’s practical for larger designs. In the past, I’ve avoided elaborate engraving projects at scale because the processing time was too long and I’m hopeless at lining up materials when sheets need to be matched.
With the X1, I was able to start thinking about this type of project, as the speed of the galvo would vastly reduce the time involved, especially when used alongside the conveyor accessory.
After carrying out the majority of the review using the 55W CO₂ and 20W diode galvo lasers, I then moved on to the 5w UV and 60W MOPA.
The 5W UV module opens up a very different range of possibilities, particularly for glass, crystal and delicate materials. I ran a few tests on the glass samples, along with experiments on plastic components produced on a 3D printer.
The ability to add fine surface texture to printed plastic objects is interesting, as it creates new opportunities for finishing functional parts and decorative products. I’ll admit I’m still on the experimental side of this, but will update in the near future.
The glass side of the engraving process is also something that I have struggled with in the past, and again, I wasn’t entirely successful in achieving the results I wanted.
Based on the partial results, I suspect this was more about my initial setup and approach than a fundamental limitation of the machine. Still, it’s an area that needs further investigation.
The UV module adds even more felxibility, although I’ll explore its more advanced functions in a separate addition to th ereview once I’ve reorganised my workshop to give the interchangeable modules better access.
Of the two rear-mounted laser modules, I found the 60W MOPA the most interesting. I’ve previously used MOPA machines, including the xTool F2 Ultra, so I’m familiar with their capabilities for metal engraving, embossing and colour marking.
What makes the X1 different is the ability to use similar technology within a much larger enclosed working area. I tested the MOPA on brass, stainless steel and aluminium, producing detailed markings and experimenting with relief engraving.
One of the most interesting applications involved creating apertures in thin brass sheet for pinhole cameras. I produced holes ranging from approximately 0.25mm to 0.5mm with exceptionally good results.
This is the sort of precision work I’ve previously done with dedicated MOPA systems, and it was great to see the X1 handle it so well, as it’s such a large machine I did wonder if it could handle the intricate work that I have used the F2 Ultra for.
I also experimented with engraving the aperture dimensions into the metal and cutting individual pieces from the sheet, although these more complicated processes still need further refinement.
Another highlight was engraving brass coins. While the F2 Ultra can do similar work, the X1’s larger processing area let me arrange several coins for engraving in one batch. Again, this is not a quick process; think days rather than hours.
Colour marking is another capability of the MOPA laser, though I’ve consistently found it requires considerable experimentation to get reliable results. The X1 was no exception.
I could create colour effects, but producing exactly the result I wanted across more complicated designs wasn’t always straightforward.
The take-home from the modules is that they expand the use of the machine, but those more specialist lasers require practice and experience to get the results that you would expect.
The other major part of the machine is the xTool Studio software. I’ve used the software across several generations of machines, and it's improved substantially over time and has really become the benchmark for all others to follow.
That said if you're new to the software then working out what type of cut and what laser is being used on what path can still be a little confusing, even with the colour coding. A text summery would be a nice quick reference before cutting.
The latest workflow is much the same as I looked at with the superb xTool M2 recently, and once you’ve completed calibration and connected the machine, preparing a project is straightforward.
Import or create the design, select the material, assign the appropriate processing operation and laser source, then send the job to the machine; after that, you generally just press the start button and wait.
As ever, the xTool Studio software offers a huge range of material presets, and unusually the material presets for the CO2 and 20w diode were way off. Especially the power and air assist, which the software set to 1 for both, easy to rectify, but possibly something to do with the pre-release software as ususally the material presets from xTool are spot on.
Adding custom materials and modifying processing parameters is also relatively straightforward once you’re familiar with the interface.
USB and Wi-Fi connectivity were both simple to set up and reliable throughout testing. Despite using pre-release software, I didn’t experience any major crashes or application-caused job failures other than a little tweaking of presets, and it all seemed pretty final, really a reflection of what I have experienced before with the addition of being able to select the laser sources.
xTool X1: Final verdict
After a month of testing, the xTool X1 is one of the most versatile laser engravers I’ve ever used, but it isn’t without its faults, although those are mostly overcome by being organised and having plenty of space.
Essentially, the base machine is an impressive 55W CO₂ laser engraver and cutter, and once you invest in the 20W diode galvo laser, you have one of the most competent machines for any small to medium-sized business on the market. The point is that with these two lasers you have the base machine that you can then build on depending on what you need to do.
Through the test, I found that that simple combination was all I really needed, and the fact that I could then attach the UV and MOPA for more specialised work all added to the versatility. However, with the 55W CO₂ and 20W diode galvo lasers installed, the machine was able to sit on the workbench without issue; it’s large but containable.
As soon as I installed the MOPA, I not only needed the additional space to mount the laser module, but it also added to the depth of the machine and for me, having the F2 for the more intricate work still made sense. While I could do the work on the X1, it didn’t necessarily mean that I would.
That aside, the pure build quality, size of the work area and depth, along with all the upgrade options, all make this one of the most substantial and complete laser engravers on the market. It is expensive, but it’s been designed in such a way that you can upgrade as and when you need.
Should you buy the xTool X1?
| Value: | The base 55W CO₂ machine is well priced, specialist laser modules and accessories raise the total cost | 5 | 
| Design: | Exceptional build quality for a machine of this size. Rear-mounted module changes could be easier. | 4.5 | 
| Features | Support for five laser technologies, the new Hybrid Motion system offer one of the most feature packed lasers on the market | 5 | 
| Performance | The combination of galvo engraving and CO₂ cutting give it an edge even before adding the other laser options | 5 | 
| Total | The X1 is the most capable laser platforms I’ve reviewed, even considering its size and modular upgrade costs it's exceptionally well balanced. | 5 | 
Buy it if...
You need versatility
The X1 combines cutting, engraving and specialist material processing within one platform, making it ideal for workshops handling varied projects.
You produce products
Its powerful CO₂ laser and fast galvo engraving system can dramatically reduce production times for personalised products and small-batch manufacturing.
Don't buy it if...
You lack space
The substantial machine, rear-mounted laser modules and optional accessories require significantly more workshop room than the main unit’s dimensions suggest.
You need affordability
Although the base machine offers good value, specialist laser modules and accessories can quickly push up the total.
For more crafting tech, I've tested and reviewed all the best 3D printers and the best laser engravers.
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.
