articles.title: SK Hynix esgota estoques e prevê escassez de memória até 2030 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
SK Hynix esgota estoques e prevê escassez de memória até 2030
Falta de componentes pressiona os preços de eletrônicos de consumo.
Resumo
- A SK Hynix tem toda a sua produção de memórias DRAM e HBM prevista para os próximos três anos já comprometida.
- A oferta de memórias deve continuar abaixo da demanda até 2030, impulsionada principalmente pelos investimentos em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial.
- A escassez de componentes deve continuar elevando os preços de eletrônicos de consumo, afetando produtos como computadores, smartphones e TVs.
A SK Hynix anunciou que praticamente toda a sua produção de memórias DRAM e HBM prevista para os próximos três anos está comprometida. A fabricante também prevê que a oferta continue abaixo da demanda até 2030, impulsionada principalmente pelos investimentos em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial.
As projeções foram apresentadas nesta quarta-feira (28/10), durante a divulgação dos resultados financeiros do terceiro trimestre, e sugam a pouca esperança aberta pela concorrente Micron, em janeiro, de que os preços dos componentes pudessem se estabilizar até 2028.
Segundo a companhia, contratos de longo prazo já assinados e encomendas em negociação deixam pouco espaço disponível para atender a novos pedidos nos próximos anos.
Além da sul-coreana, Samsung, que adiantou o possível aumento de demanda no começo do ano, e Micron já tinham vendido a quantidade total de chips de memória projetada para o ano que vem. As três concentram grande parte da produção global desses componentes.
Contratos já cobrem maior parte da produção
Em comunicado, a SK Hynix alega que fechou acordou de fornecimento de longo prazo com 14 grandes clientes, incluindo algumas das principais provedoras globais de computação em nuvem. Os contratos já garantidos correspondem a mais de 50% da capacidade total de produção prevista para 2027 e 2028.
A situação fica ainda mais apertada quando entram na conta pedidos que ainda estão em negociação. Segundo a empresa, a soma dos contratos assinados com demandas baseadas em planos concretos de compra faz com que os volumes de DRAM e HBM estejam “efetivamente esgotados” até 2029.
A fabricante também já concluiu as negociações de volume e preços de HBM para 2027 e espera crescimento tanto nas vendas quanto na rentabilidade do segmento. Após o crescimento do setor, a empresa conseguiu superar a Samsung pela primeira vez em valor de mercado, em junho, e bateu recorde na estreia na bolsa estadunidense.
Memória para IA encarece produtos eletrônicos
A principal pressão vem da expensão de datacenters e servidores dedicados à IA. A memória HBM é usada em aceleradores para permitir a transferência de grandes volumes de dados em alta velocidade. Segundo a SK Hynix, os pedidos feitos por clientes para esse tipo de componente já chegam a mais que o dobro da oferta disponível.
A companhia está aumentando os investimentos na ampliação da capacidade de fabricação com novas instalação. No entanto, seguindo o padrão da indústria, a empresa afirma que leva anos até que a operação de uma nova fábrica se inicie, e a demanda deve continuar acima da oferta até 2030.
Até lá, o consumidor final de produtos eletrônicos deve continuar sentindo o peso desse foco em IA no bolso. Memórias DRAM e NAND, também fabricadas pelas três, são usadas em computadores, smartphones, TVs, eletrodomésticos “inteligentes” e até carros com sistemas digitais mais avançados.
No mercado de smartphones, por exemplo, vimos recentemente aumentos em linhas da Samsung e Apple, que pode subir ainda mais no ano que vem. As companhias já vêm se preparando desde o ano passado e não há uma previsão certa de que os preços voltem ao patamar dos anos anteriores, segundo a Lenovo.

articles.title: Hackers leak details of 41,000 Homeland Security employees, exposing undercover operations and surveillance tools
articles.text:
What we know so far: Hackers have leaked login records for more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors, revealing not only who works at the agency but also which surveillance and investigative tools they are cleared to use. Taken together, the files offer a rare inside look at the technology behind the department's investigations and the chain of command that directs them. The release also sharpens the debate over whether exposing the people behind federal immigration enforcement serves accountability or creates a security threat.
The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets published the archive, which it calls "Icepick," on Wednesday. It spans DHS and seven of its component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection.
The files include email addresses, phone numbers and office addresses, along with more than 55,000 permission groups that control access to internal systems. Some group names reference Palantir's Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Others point to tools for pulling data from seized phones, systems for reaching immigration court records, a "Title III Intercept Program" for wiretaps, a "Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program" and an "Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP)."
The records were last updated in August. DDoSecrets says they came from DHS' Okta login system, which Okta disputes. "We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised," a company spokesperson told WIRED.
Nearly everyone in the leak belongs to at least one of these groups, and the membership lists show who holds which capabilities. At Homeland Security Investigations, ICE's investigative arm, 39 employees in more than a dozen field offices sit in groups named "CUC," which government court filings say stands for "certified undercover operation." A group that appears tied to HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations references "Keyhole." Federal court filings describe Keyhole as a certified undercover operation that funded HSI's undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year.
More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, the face-recognition app immigration agents use to identify people. Members include field supervisors, special response team operators and tactical and intelligence agents. More than 700 accounts, nearly all of them CBP, link to a group that appears to reference the encrypted messaging app Signal.
Other groups reference AI tools, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Microsoft's Copilot. One, labeled "Grok.com," includes eight DHS technology officials, among them the department's former chief information officer and chief data officer.
Two more, "Executive Leadership" and "AI Access," appear to list people exempted from the DHS web filter that blocks some sites for employees. Both list the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed CIO who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, a senior adviser to the secretary and younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and policy adviser Jayce Krachenfels. None of the four responded to requests for comment.
Most records also name a supervisor, so the data can be used to rebuild reporting lines across the department. More than 300 records belong to senior headquarters officials, including those overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics and privacy.
Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at threat intelligence company Recorded Future, says that if the data is real and up to date, it is an extremely valuable intelligence resource for anyone trying to get inside DHS. He adds that its value grows when combined with previously stolen information, commercial data and other intelligence. He says an adversary could spend months using these connections to find vulnerable employees, convincingly impersonate staff, or compromise ongoing investigations.
A WIRED analysis found CBP staff make up more than half the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third in HSI. US Citizenship and Immigration Services has 6,200, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Together, they make up about a seventh of the DHS workforce.
The account data also tracks the buildup of enforcement. About 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts were created after July 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which paid for 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to Defense Department personnel, eight in a group titled "ICE Tip Line DOW Surge." About 170 accounts provide "military processing support" at ICE facilities, and 35 identify National Guard members.
DDoSecrets and the researcher and journalist Maia Arson Crimew say the files came from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," the hackers wrote. Crimew built a website that makes the records searchable. "I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them," she told WIRED.
The release comes as DHS works to keep its staff out of public view. The department has sought to unmask anonymous online critics and broadened its definition of doxing to include publishing employees' names and titles. In June, 15 Minnesota residents faced stalking- and threat-related charges that prosecutors linked to activities opposing ICE.
Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the civil liberties group FIRE, says the administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119, which bars sharing "restricted personal information" about federal officers with intent to threaten them. "This is information that would be on a business card," he says. "That's not something the government can criminalize."
DHS and the Justice Department did not respond to WIRED. The FBI referred questions to DHS.

articles.title: Cómo conectar un pendrive a tu móvil Android y ahorrarte la nube de pago
articles.text:
Las cámaras de los teléfonos actuales graban en 4K y hasta en 8K, lo que genera archivos cada vez más pesados. A esto se suma que los modelos de gama alta ya no incluyen ranura para tarjetas microSD, así que el almacenamiento interno se llena con rapidez.
La alternativa que suelen ofrecer los fabricantes es la nube, pero existe una opción local, económica y sin cuotas mensuales: conectar una memoria USB al teléfono mediante la tecnología OTG.
Este método permite mover fotos, videos y documentos directamente desde el móvil a un pendrive o a una unidad SSD externa, liberando espacio sin depender de ningún servicio de pago.
Por qué los móviles se quedan sin espacio de almacenamiento
El problema de espacio no es casual. Los sensores de cámara mejoran cada año y producen imágenes de mayor calidad, lo que implica archivos más grandes. Los vídeos en resolución 4K o 8K agravan la situación, ya que ocupan bastante más que los formatos tradicionales.
La ausencia de ranura microSD en la gama alta termina de complicar el panorama: no existe forma de ampliar la memoria física del teléfono.
Frente a esto, la industria propone el almacenamiento en la nube como solución principal. Es cómodo y funciona de forma automática, pero suele requerir una suscripción mensual o anual para acceder a espacio suficiente.
Quien prefiera no sumar otro gasto recurrente puede optar por un respaldo local. Una memoria USB conectada al móvil permite guardar archivos pesados fuera del almacenamiento interno sin pagar ninguna cuota, usando una sola compra que se amortiza con el tiempo.
Qué es el USB OTG y cómo comprobar si tu móvil es compatible
El requisito técnico para usar un pendrive en un smartphone se llama USB OTG (On-The-Go), un estándar que habilita el puerto del dispositivo para recibir unidades de almacenamiento externas, como si fuera un ordenador.
La mayoría de los móviles Android fabricados en los últimos años cuenta con esta función de manera nativa, sin necesidad de configuraciones adicionales.
Para quienes tengan dudas sobre su propio equipo, existe una aplicación llamada OTG Checker, disponible en Google Play Store, que verifica en segundos si el puerto admite esta conexión.
Cómo conectar un pendrive o una unidad SSD al móvil Android
Una vez confirmada la compatibilidad, el siguiente paso es la conexión física. La mayoría de los teléfonos Android actuales utiliza puerto USB-C, lo que determina dos escenarios posibles según el tipo de memoria que se tenga.
Si el pendrive o la unidad SSD ya cuenta con conector USB-C, la conexión es directa: basta con enchufarlo al móvil sin accesorios adicionales.
Si, en cambio, la memoria tiene conector USB-A, hace falta un adaptador OTG de USB-A a USB-C. Este tipo de adaptadores es económico y se consigue con facilidad en el mercado.
Al conectar cualquiera de estas opciones, el sistema Android muestra una notificación que confirma el reconocimiento del dispositivo, con un mensaje similar a “Almacenamiento externo agregado”.
Pasos para transferir archivos del móvil al pendrive
Con la memoria ya conectada, el traspaso de archivos se realiza desde cualquier gestor de archivos, como Files de Google, siguiendo un procedimiento sencillo.
Primero hay que explorar las carpetas del teléfono y seleccionar los archivos que se quieran mover, ya sean fotos, vídeos, documentos u otros elementos de gran tamaño.
Después, se debe pulsar el icono de tres puntos o el botón de compartir, según la aplicación utilizada, y elegir la opción “Mover a”. El último paso consiste en seleccionar la memoria USB como destino final de los archivos.
Al terminar la transferencia, solo resta desconectar el pendrive. En ese momento, los archivos quedan respaldados de forma local y el espacio correspondiente se libera en el almacenamiento interno del móvil.
Este proceso puede repetirse tantas veces como sea necesario, y su límite depende exclusivamente de la capacidad de la memoria USB utilizada. Se recomienda optar por un pendrive de al menos 128 GB, aunque cualquier capacidad mayor ofrece más margen para almacenar fotos, vídeos y documentos sin tener que repetir el proceso con frecuencia.

articles.title: ShinyHunters-Exploited Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day Turns Out to Be Three Chained Flaws
articles.text:
The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week.
Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login.
The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle.
In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record.
CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time.
In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide.
ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts.
The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach.
PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside.
From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account.
The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.
The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them.
In the September wave, Mandiant found ShinyHunters slipping past web application firewall (WAF) rules that blocked the /PSEMHUB/ path by url-encoding a single character, requesting /%50SEMHUB/ instead. Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.
What to Do
The fix and the guidance here come from Oracle and Mandiant, not from ZDI's analysis, which covers the flaw rather than the response.
- Apply the patch. Install Oracle's security alert fix for CVE-2026-35273 and stay on a supported PeopleTools release. Mandiant is explicit that path-based WAF blocking is not a substitute for patching.
- If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub service in multi-server setups, or remove the PSEMHUB application in single-server setups, as Oracle's alert advises. Restricting these admin endpoints does not break normal user sessions.
- If you may already be hit, Mandiant recommends treating any host with a web shell as compromised, preserving evidence, and rotating every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. ShinyHunters steals data and then demands payment, so affected organizations should prepare for extortion.
One thing the sources do not settle is whether applying the patch removes access an attacker already gained. Oracle's alert does not address it, and Mandiant's guidance to rotate credentials and hunt for web shells assumes it does not. Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

articles.title: Man granted first-of-its-kind religious exemption against mandatory AI use at work — Humanist argues that offloading his thinking to LLMs violates his beliefs, Title VII accommodation protects employee
articles.text:
Man granted first-of-its-kind religious exemption against mandatory AI use at work — Humanist argues that offloading his thinking to LLMs violates his beliefs, Title VII accommodation protects employee
David Durman says that he's unwilling to outsource his thinking to AI tools.
David Durman, a research administrator at the University of Kentucky (UK), has successfully argued that using AI violates his beliefs as a humanist and has received Title VII religious accommodation from university officials not to use the technology. According to the Religion News Service (RNS), Durman believes in "the human part of life," which includes making his own decisions. However, he says that when the UK asked its employees to use AI, he felt that doing so would mean outsourcing his thinking to tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, thus violating his deeply held beliefs.
“The process and work involved in thinking through situations, through my work, through my ethics, through the way I handle other people, is a key component in being able to develop myself as a moral person,” Durman told RNS in an interview. “And offloading that labor, regardless of whether it’s taxing or not, is undercutting my ability to be a moral actor.” Because of this, the research administrator was granted a Title VII exemption under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibited employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. While humanism is often a non-religious philosophy or a worldview, federal courts have ruled that it qualifies as a religion.
The American Humanist Association (AHA) assisted Durman with his request for the accommodation. “This is the first of its kind at the AHA and for humanism generally to exempt those who see AI use as flying in the face of their freedom of conscience,” AHA staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens said to RNS. She also added, “For us, humanism is a comprehensive way of life. It’s built on inherent worth and dignity, and everyone should have room to exercise this comprehensive way of life at work the same way Christians do, or Muslims do.”
It should be noted that while anyone can request a Title VII exemption, it will only be granted if the applicant has a deep moral conviction that could count as an article of faith. Aside from that, the law also states that the request should not place an “undue hardship on the employer’s business.” So, even though Durman is no longer personally required to use AI tools for his tasks, he is still expected to attend meetings and cooperate with colleagues who use AI or to submit materials to AI tools, as needed.
AI use in corporate settings has been one of the biggest questions ever since LLMs exploded in popularity with ChatGPT. While AI proponents have said that the technology would increase productivity multiple times, reports say that corporate America, except for Big Tech, is not seeing any financial returns. Even so, about half of all U.S. employees now use AI one way or another at work, even as many executives remain uncertain about AI’s return on investment. But as for Durman, he says that the fact that Americans are already thinking about the impact of AI is a good thing, and that he hopes that his story would help others who’d rather not be forced to use the technology.

articles.title: How AI Redefines Semiconductor Manufacturing, From Materials Up - EE Times
articles.text:
Demand for more powerful AI chips is pushing semiconductor design forward, but commercializing those designs depends on whether chip manufacturing and packaging technologies can keep up.
A far less visible part of the semiconductor ecosystem is therefore coming into focus: the equipment, components, and materials used to manufacture and package advanced chips. As semiconductor processes become more precise and performance requirements rise, materials must operate reliably under more demanding conditions. Materials engineering helps bridge the gap between advanced chip designs and what manufacturers can produce reliably at scale.
Advanced chips raise the bar for materials
Semiconductor manufacturing already requires materials that perform in highly specialized environments. Components used in semiconductor processing equipment must withstand extreme operating conditions, resist mechanical wear, and maintain process stability and precision.
Producing higher-performance devices requires even greater precision in all phases of manufacturing. Even small changes in a component’s dimensions, surface condition, or performance can impair precise semiconductor manufacturing processes. Advanced ceramics can help equipment maintain tight tolerances and consistent performance.
Importantly, materials selection involves more than choosing the material with the greatest strength or heat resistance. Depending on the application, engineers must consider chemical resistance, plasma resistance, wear resistance, and thermal stability, among other characteristics. The relative priority of each property can vary significantly depending on where and how a component is used.
Materials engineering is a balancing act
No single material can maximize every characteristic required by every semiconductor manufacturing application.
Instead, engineers determine which combination of properties is most important for a particular operating environment. A component designed to withstand plasma exposure will have different material priorities than one intended to withstand mechanical wear or significant thermal demands. Performance must also be considered alongside practical factors such as manufacturability, geometry, and cost.
Advanced ceramics illustrate how materials can be engineered to meet these increasingly complex requirements. Unlike traditional ceramics, advanced ceramics are formulated using specialized raw material powders, additives, and binders to optimize a specific set of mechanical, thermal, electrical, or optical characteristics. Their properties can therefore be tailored to provide chemical resistance, plasma resistance, wear resistance, and thermal stability.
Advances in manufacturing methods also expand the role ceramic materials can fulfill. Beyond traditional pressing and injection molding, newer ceramic forming approaches can enable more complex geometries while addressing manufacturing considerations such as cost. As semiconductor equipment becomes more specialized, the ability to pair material properties with complex component designs is an increasingly important part of the engineering equation.
Packaging as a performance driver
The same development can be seen further along the semiconductor manufacturing chain. Semiconductor packaging was historically viewed as a means of protecting an integrated circuit. Today, packaging plays a key role in optimizing performance.
Higher-performing devices now integrate multiple ICs, chiplets, and functions within a single package. Each component can introduce different requirements for heat dissipation, protection, isolation, and electrical connectivity. Rather than simply fitting an IC inside a package, engineers have to consider the interactions among multiple ICs, the package, and the board to maximize the performance of the complete device.
This represents a significant change from earlier generations of semiconductor technology. As recently as 10 to 15 years ago, package design could be driven largely by the mechanical requirements of fitting and protecting a device. As functions have become more integrated and IC architectures more complex, connections among components have become increasingly consequential to overall performance. Packaging is therefore becoming part of the system-level design challenge rather than a consideration that begins after the chip has been designed.
AI infrastructure makes those pressures particularly visible. In optical communications, for example, signal speeds at the device level have risen from approximately 10 Gbps two decades ago to around 200 Gbps per lane today. This requires packages capable of transmitting signals faster while minimizing loss, even as package structures and signal routing become more miniaturized and complex.
At the same time, greater integration creates additional thermal and structural challenges. Ceramic materials can provide advantages in areas such as heat dissipation, design flexibility, and rigidity, but the broader engineering challenge remains the same: Package materials and designs must evolve alongside the semiconductor devices they support.
AI innovation extends beyond the chip
These challenges will intensify as AI infrastructure evolves. Higher semiconductor processing speeds and greater functionality are expected to continue increasing demand for heat dissipation, while the integration of additional functions can result in larger and more complex packages. Engineers may increasingly need to achieve high-speed performance, thermal management, and low warpage simultaneously as package dimensions and complexity grow.
The same principle applies upstream in semiconductor production equipment. As semiconductor features become smaller and more precise, the equipment used to manufacture and inspect them must likewise support rising levels of performance. Materials that were adequate for previous generations of semiconductor manufacturing may not provide the combination of characteristics required by future processes.
For the semiconductor industry, this points to a broader lesson about the AI era. Progress will not depend exclusively on designing faster or more efficient chips. Every improvement at the chip level creates new requirements elsewhere in the manufacturing ecosystem, from semiconductor fabrication and processing equipment to the materials and packages enabling chips to reach previously unattainable levels of performance.
As AI chip designs become more capable, advances across the manufacturing chain will be essential to turning those designs into reliable, scalable devices.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft va moderniser son application Windows Sécurité
articles.text:
L’application Sécurité Windows, qui intègre entre autres Windows Defender, le Pare-feu Windows ou encore Smart App Control, a pour objectif d’assurer toute la sécurité de votre PC. Mais jusqu’à présent, son interface utilisateur reposait sur les codes graphiques hérités d’anciennes versions de Windows. C’est sans doute l’une des raisons pour laquelle vous évitez soigneusement de l’utiliser quotidiennement. La bonne nouvelle, c’est que son interface devrait rapidement évoluer. Microsoft vient d’annoncer une refonte complète de son application.
Une interface modernisée en accord avec le design de Windows 11
Microsoft ayant récemment fait la promesse d’améliorer son système d’exploitation, une refonte globale de l’application Sécurité Windows était donc inévitable. Et la prochaine mise à jour du module, qui est pour l’heure testé auprès des Insiders, devrait s’articuler autour de quatre évolutions majeures.
La firme de Redmond explique ainsi s’être penchée sur la navigation de celle-ci. Les différentes pages de l’application vont être revues pour adopter une structure et une navigation plus cohérentes avec une meilleure adaptation visuelle lorsque la fenêtre est maximisée.
Les différentes commandes et éléments visuels vont par ailleurs être modernisés. Microsoft explique que les commandes, l’indicateur d’état, les typographies utilisées, mais aussi les espacements et les couleurs vont profiter d’une remise à niveau pour que l’expérience utilisateur soit enfin harmonisée avec le reste de Windows 11.
L’interface devrait également proposer une meilleure lisibilité des différents statuts et actions à prendre. La présentation des différentes informations de sécurité va ainsi être entièrement revue dans l’ensemble de l’application.
Microsoft a également indiqué qu’elle planchait sur un chargement optimisé des informations sur les appareils gérés. Concrètement, sur les machines professionnelles ou gérées au sein d’un parc informatique, les détails de sécurité vont se charger progressivement pour que les données soient affichées plus rapidement.
Le déploiement de cette nouvelle interface est pour l’heure testé dans la version 1000.29680.0.1000 de l’application auprès des membres du programme Insider. Il faudra donc patienter encore quelques semaines avant que cette nouvelle interface soit déployée à grande échelle auprès du public, sans doute dans une prochaine mise à jour du système d’exploitation.

articles.title: Los Mossos piden ayuda al Ministerio del Interior para que cierre todas las cuentas de Blocus, mientras detienen al creador de "Blocus VLC"
articles.text:
Blocus, el movimiento que usa sus redes sociales como herramienta de movilización, sigue creciendo mientras ya llegan las primeras detenciones. Así ha sido con el joven de 17 años detenido en Valencia, creador de "Blocus VLC" y presunto instigador de saqueos y pillajes previstos para el 31 de octubre.
Entender este movimiento sin rostro que ya ha provocado graves altercados en Barcelona exige mirar más allá de los disturbios (y seguir el rastro digital), pero ahora mismo lo que pide la policía es paralizar su red de distribución de vídeos, montajes y mensajes virales para que no acaben trasladados en violencia al mundo real.
Qué pasó. El sábado 24, unos 600 jóvenes se concentraron en la plaza de Cataluña de Barcelona. La cita era a las 17:00 y la violencia arrancó hacia las 18:30. Hubo saqueos, barricadas y mobiliario quemado. El saldo: 23 comercios dañados y 15 policías heridos, y más de 130 detenidos, 89 de ellos menores, según la Fiscalía. Entre los primeros 128 arrestados, solo dos tenían antecedentes por desórdenes públicos.
Cómo se montó. Todo arrancó en TikTok. Cuentas anónimas con la etiqueta Blocus (“bloqueo” en francés) copiaban las protestas de los institutos franceses, aunque con inversa orientación política. El reclamo, a priori, era la calidad educativa. Un código QR llevaba a grupos de Telegram y WhatsApp, y allí las instrucciones cambiaban: ropa negra, cara tapada, material pirotécnico.
Un informe de Golden Owl, empresa alicantina de inteligencia de fuentes abiertas, analizó más de 10.000 elementos en siete plataformas. Su cronología: el 8 de octubre, un perfil convoca en Sol los días 10 y 11. Fracasó, por suerte. El 19, reactivaron cuentas en Barcelona y montaron la cita del 24 en un solo día. Un puñado de carteles hechos con IA, cuentas que se renombran y un lenguaje en clave que aparece cuando los chats se hacen públicos. El canal Blocus-BCN pasó de 690 a 1.376 miembros en unas 20 horas. La red ya opera en 18 localidades.
Telegram, el CITCO y la ley. El lunes 26, la Comisaría General de Información de los Mossos pidió al CITCO el cierre de un canal (el CITCO depende de Interior). Su unidad UNECI retiró propaganda terrorista y extremista de internet. Es la primera vez que la policía catalana usa esta vía.
Telegram cerró Blocus-BCN el martes. Los organizadores abrieron Blocus-BCN-2, que superó los 2.000 miembros en horas, y también cayó. Luego llegó Blocus 4 Bcn, con el vídeo de un supuesto líder que pide un “movimiento más radical”.
La base jurídica es el Reglamento (UE) 2021/784. Vigente desde 2022, permite a cada Estado ordenar a una plataforma retirar contenido terrorista, o bloquearlo en toda la UE, en una hora como máximo. España fue la primera en usarlo, en abril de 2023, y emitió 134 órdenes en 2023 y 2024. El 65 % iba contra propaganda yihadista.
¿Terrorismo? Sobre el papel, Blocus no es terrorismo, y los Mossos lo asumen: pidieron el cierre por incitar a delitos, dentro de una estrategia para frenar réplicas. No hay orden vinculante del reglamento, sino una petición. Telegram cierra porque incumple sus propias normas. La vía judicial, que permite identificar usuarios o clausurar canales, va aparte: la Generalitat pidió autorización a un juez para cerrar los chats.
Madrid, Halloween y una desconvocatoria sospechosa. Hay dos citas en Madrid el sábado 31: Puerta del Sol a las 17:00 y plaza de España a las 18:00. La cuenta BlocusMadrid anunció la suspensión por la presión policial. La Policía recela y desplegará 200 antidisturbios. Los administradores bloquearon las altas en sus grupos para frenar infiltrados. Los Mossos dan por hecho otro episodio en Barcelona. Golden Owl cita además el 2 de noviembre en Terrassa y el 30 en 12 ciudades, un día después de las elecciones del 29-N.
¿Solo chavales? Aquí hay varias capas. La comisaria jefa de los Mossos, Sílvia Catà, dijo que detrás no hay grupos criminales, sino gente (joven) que acude a una llamada. La consellera Núria Parlon habla de “delincuencia”.
La capa que convoca es otra cosa, aunque detrás no se ha encontrado a un gran magnate sionista ni a un genio creador. Cuentas desechables, códigos QR y carteles con IA los monta cualquier adolescente espabilado. Lo que desconcierta es el calendario: ensayo en Madrid, Barcelona en un día, réplica nacional. Golden Owl no identifica a nadie y advierte de que no hay pruebas de dirección extranjera.
Las hipótesis, que conviene separar de los hechos. La ultraderecha es la primera. Moncloa apunta a su entorno, sin atribuirlo a ninguna formación. Hay contexto, desde luego: el 3 de octubre unos 400 ultras se concentraron contra la acampada de Sol y tres fueron detenidos al intentar llegar. No consta ningún vínculo público entre Blocus y esos grupos.
¿La extrema izquierda?. Es la tesis del PP, que acusa a Sánchez de “incendiar” la calle. Vox acusa al Gobierno, como siempre. Otra apunta a Israel: el ministro Pablo Bustinduy señaló a ACOM, lobby proisraelí, como “brazo híbrido de Netanyahu” tras un mensaje suyo celebrando los saqueos. La Policía Nacional no ve injerencia de ningún país. Parlon, por su parte, no descarta nada.
Ahora mismo, lo que sabemos es que una red de cuentas efímeras van y vienen por Instagram, TikTok y Telegram, que no hay ningún responsable identificado (y que las plataformas cierran más lento de lo que otras reabren). Y todo esto en el marco de la precampaña del 29N. No todo lo que circula es real: la propia policía localizó un perfil con unos cien seguidores difundiendo el cartel del 24, así que conviene mantener la cautela. Esa es la fuerza de Blocus: nadie sabe cuánto hay detrás.

articles.title: SecurityScorecard benchmark tests AI on third-party risk work and resistance to attack - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SecurityScorecard benchmark tests AI on third-party risk work and resistance to attack
Security ratings company SecurityScorecard Inc. today released an open benchmark for testing whether artificial intelligence models can handle third-party risk management work without being turned against the companies using them.
The TPRM Benchmark is built for vendor risk programs, where a model may need to interpret security telemetry and decide which exposures matter. A lot of what the model reads comes from questionnaires and documents that vendors filled out themselves, and parts of that may be incomplete or manipulated on purpose. SecurityScorecard says generic benchmarks built around static or academic tasks were not designed with that in mind.
On the capability side, tasks cover disciplines such as exposure triage and fourth-party technology risk, and each one starts as a snapshot of SecurityScorecard’s own vendor-risk telemetry that domain experts check before any model is scored. The answer keys are protected. Inputs rotate too, so a model that memorizes the test has less to gain.
Scores are measured against a baseline with confidence intervals attached, and each model gets an autonomy readiness level from L0 to L4 based on its performance across repeated trials. SecurityScorecard says the rating is meant to show how far a model can be trusted to work without human oversight.
Attack resistance is tested separately in the Model Security suite, which hits each model with prompt injection, jailbreaks and other techniques. Grades run from A to F. Some of the capability tasks are also seeded with deceptive vendor self-attestations that contradict the underlying telemetry, and scoring on those tasks shows how far the false claims pull down a model’s accuracy.
Performance in the early runs, which covered closed frontier, open-weight and international models, depended heavily on the discipline being tested. Open-weight models are closing the gap with leading frontier models on supply chain security tasks, according to Mike Mylrea, chief information security officer and chief AI officer at SecurityScorecard. Several of the open-weight models are “highly susceptible to adversarial attacks,” he said. The announcement did not identify the models tested or give their scores.
Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at developer security company Snyk Ltd., said the benchmark gives security teams “a shared, transparent way to evaluate models on capability and attack resistance together.” Snyk’s own research across 3,000 enterprise environments found that 74.5% of those with a detected model reference at least one that scores “high” on an attacker goal under adversarial testing.
Aleksandr Yampolskiy, co-founder and chief executive of SecurityScorecard, likened putting an untested AI agent into a vendor risk program to “giving a new employee privileged access on day one and hoping for the best.” A company that can’t say whether its model can do the work, or whether the model can be turned against it, has “a new attack surface,” he said.
SecurityScorecard has open-sourced the framework. Participants who download it can run their own models or agents and submit the results to a public leaderboard. A limited group of AI labs, security vendors and researchers is also being invited to help decide what the benchmark tests and how.
Version 2026.09 of the public release is available now with documentation, the Model Security suite and registration for the leaderboard. Official expert-verified scores come from SecurityScorecard’s live internal tier. A security team running its own tests on the public tier will get results marked synthetic-calibrated, which the company says are directly comparable for research and self-assessment. For a certified evaluation of a candidate model or agent, enterprises have to go to SecurityScorecard directly.

articles.title: System76 Unveils Thelio Prime 11-Liter Linux Desktop PC
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
System76 Unveils Thelio Prime 11-Liter Linux Desktop PC
System76 has announced the Thelio Prime, a compact 11-liter (288 x 148.9 x 281.9 mm) desktop built at the company's Denver facility. The chassis is made from milled stainless steel and aluminium parts. To add a bit of finesse, there's a smoked-glass front panel and tool-free magnetic side panels. The interior is designed with two thermal chambers, separating the CPU and GPU. As for performance, System76 describes it as "An 11-liter Linux desktop that fits almost anywhere, without giving up on performance." Users can choose from an AMD Ryzen 9000 processor (up to Ryzen 7 9850X3D) with integrated Radeon graphics or go for a discrete AMD or NVIDIA GPU (up to RTX 5070), depending on configuration. The system can have up to 96 GB of dual-channel DDR5 and up to 8 TB of storage across its M.2 slots (one PCIe 5.0 and one PCIe 4.0).
Front I/O offers a USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-C, a USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A, and the audio jack. The rear adds two USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 1, four USB 2.0 ports, a BIOS Flashback button, and audio line-out. Networking covers 2.5 GbE, Wi-Fi 6E, and Bluetooth 5.2. Display outputs depend on the GPU. Integrated graphics get HDMI 2.1 and USB-C with DisplayPort 1.4. A discrete GPU option typically adds three DisplayPort outputs and one HDMI. Power comes from a 600 W 80 Plus certified supply with at least 90% efficiency. The system comes preinstalled with Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS with COSMIC Desktop Environment or with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. The Thelio Prime is expected to launch November 18, starting at $1,599.

articles.title: I tested the Hisense XR10 4K projector, and it has the best image quality I've seen that works in both bright living rooms and dark home theater setups, thanks to its 'adjustable iris'
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Hisense XR10 offers an amazing picture that can work in bright and dark rooms alike, and its flexible optics can adapt to all sorts of different placements. But it’s very pricy, and it has to face some newcomers with competitive capabilities.
Reasons to buy
- + Wonderfully bright and colorful
- + Incredibly flexible optics
- + Gorgeous looks and classy carrying case
- + Punchy speaker
- + Adaptable for bright and dark rooms
Reasons to avoid
- - Missed out on VRR and 4K/120Hz modes
- - VidaaOS could be better
- - Pricey
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Hisense XR10: One-minute review
The Hisense XR10 offers powerful projection that you can put all over the room and still get squared away. That’s thanks to extensive optical adjustments that include incredible zoom range and lens shift. Hisense definitely cranked up the elegance this year.
The Hisense XR10 is loaded up with blazing RGB lasers that give it stunning brightness and color, while an adjustable iris can help it clamp down black levels for dark room viewing with enhanced contrast. It’s all packed into a stylish box that’s much smaller and more portable than high-end theater projectors like the Sony Bravia Projector 7, and Hisense’s included carrying case will let you take it places in style.
All of this comes at a high price, though. The Hisense XR10 is $5,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999 after falling from the original $6,999 price tag in the US. Though it has decent speakers for a projector and a serviceable operating system in VidaaOS, these don’t lend a ton of extra value. It also jumped the gun a bit and missed out on the VRR and 4K/120Hz support that a newer wave of projectors are offering. At its price, it’s not going to lead the charge for value, but you do get a lot for the money. It’s still probably worth waiting to see if the XGIMI Horizon 30 Ultra Max, JMGO Iris Ultra Max, and Hisense C3 Ultra Max leave the XR10 any room to breathe.
Hisense XR10 review: Price and release date
- Release date: mid 2026
- MSRP: $5,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999
The Hisense XR10 made its debut at CES 2026 and started shipping in May. It came with an initial price of $6,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999 but that US price has generally fallen to $5,999. In the time it’s been out, some deals have even brought it as low as $4,499, but it hasn’t been a sticky price drop and prices elsewhere seem to be much more static.
For the money, Hisense does include a special carrying case that’s far and away the highest quality one I’ve seen included with a projector like this. But even then it’s not adding thousands of dollars in value.
Hisense XR10 review: specs
| Supported screen sizes | 65-300 inches | 
| Optical technology | 3 Laser DLP | 
| Brightness (specified) | 6,000 Lumens | 
| Audio | 2x8-watt + 15-watt speakers | 
| Ports | 2x HDMI 2.1 (1x eARC), 1x HDMI 2.0, 2x USB-A, 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm audio | 
| Smart TV | VidaaOS | 
| Dimensions | 11.5 x 10.7 x 8.4 inches | 
| Weight | 23.4 pounds | 
Hisense XR10 review: design and features
- Stylish, compact design and serious carrying case
- Highly adjustable optics
- VidaaOS is quick but may be limiting
Hisense has built something particularly gorgeous with the XR10. It simply looks like a work of serious engineering with its brown metal casing, stylish venting and machined accents, knurled lens cover, oversize lens cover, and dark color scheme. The front's sensor array also looks highly technical. The top is a little plain, but Hisense has included a volume dial, power button, ambient light sensor, and a little aesthetic nod to the RGB laser system inside.
The Hisense XR10 is a modestly sized box at 11.5 x 10.7 x 8.4 inches / 292.1 x 271.8 x 213.4 mm, yet with all its packing in it ends up weighing a considerable 23.4 pounds / 10.6kg. To help you lug it around, Hisense includes a fashionable carrying case that looks more like a piece of luggage than the styrofoam cases many projectors come with. It's complete with straps, zippers, padded slots for each component, and it even has wheels and an extendable handle for rolling.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The projector has everything it needs to help you get it set up for perfect alignment with your screen. It stands on four height-adjustable feet, so you can get it level and squared away with the wall. And it offers extensive zoom and lens shift capabilities. It can shift from a short throw ratio of 0.84:1 all the way to a 2:1 throw ratio, this means you can set it close to a wall or screen and still get a big picture or set it far from that screen and shrink it down to fit without having to use digital cropping. Plenty of competitors are offering zoom now, but the XR10 has a far wider range than most.
The XR10 goes well beyond that, too, adding on 130% vertical lens shift and 46% horizontal lens shift. This makes it much easier to set the projector wherever is convenient for you and still be able to dial in a crisp, perfectly aligned projection where you want it.
Hisense has also built in some automatic picture correction, like screen fitting and obstacle avoidance, but the projector tends to try zooming all the way out to make those corrections. So it's very easy to end up in a situation where the projection is simply too large for the projector to figure out what to do to fit it onto a small screen. Some features also get locked out if lens shift is used, like automatic keystone correction (something you should skip anyway) and eye protection (something it’s also great to have because these are some bright lasers).
Around back, the Hisense XR10 is pretty well geared up for serious home theater use. It includes a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports one of which supports eARC as well as one HDMI 2.0 port. It also includes a set of two USB 3.0 ports, a gigabit ethernet port, and both optical and 3.5mm analog audio outputs.
That ethernet port could be useful, but the XR10 actually has Wi-Fi 7 on board, so you can get pretty fast networking wirelessly as well. With that wireless connection, you can easily access streaming services using the built-in operating system, which is unfortunately not Google TV.
Instead it’s Hisense's own VidaaOS. It has most of the major streaming apps and some extras like Xbox Cloud Gaming but there's plenty that's missing. On the bright side, navigating the software is fairly quick and Hisense's included remote has a dedicated input button so you don't have to spend much time in VidaaOS if you want to use an external source for video.
The XR10 offers serious brightness for a small box, so there’s a bit of fan whir in operation to keep the insides cool. It’s noticeable in a quiet room when sitting close to the projector, but it’s easily drowned out by the 2.1-channel sound system.
The remote control included with the XR10 is a fairly simple one, offering directional navigation and direct access to input selection, autofocus, voice input, the settings menu, the home screen, volume and brightness controls, a mute button, and shortcuts to Netflix, YouTube, Prime Video, and Disney+. It also has backlighting, but it's only activated after you press a button, not motion activated.
- Design & features score: 4.5 / 5
Hisense XR10 review: picture quality and performance
- Brilliantly colorful, stunningly bright, and capable of deep black levels
- Good gaming chops
- Punchy sound, but not cinematic
One of the greatest aspects of the Hisense XR10 is its color, coming by way of its RGB laser light source. For most content, it can look perfectly natural, but when it really comes time to jazz things up, it’s simply amazing. The attack on Rosalina’s home in the beginning of The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is a stunning showcase of its capabilities, with dazzling magical effects, so many colorful stars, and plenty of opportunity for the XR10 to demonstrate its vibrant color.
As the convoy heads out at the beginning of Mad Max: Fury Road, the subtle reds of the sand against the blues of the sky are simply gorgeous, and the deeper reds of the flamethrowers are all the more vibrant. The inside of the sandstorm is simply wondrous, with the chaotic flashing of lightning playing against the deep shadows.
All that color comes alongside serious brightness. In my testing with the projector in its Vivid picture settings, with the iris open and brightness set to maximum, I measured it outputting 6,841 lumens. It has the potential to go higher with a cooler white point and a Brightness Enhanced mode, reaching 7,757 lumens, but this tints the whole picture green.
In practice, the high brightness means the XR10 is strong enough to use in a room even if you’re not doing much to shut out ambient light. I found watching a lot of content even with some of my room lights on more than comfortable, and depending on what I was watching, I could even get away with leaving the windows open in the middle of the day and still see well enough.
The Hisense XR10 offers potent contrast as well. It’s exhibited splendidly in Dune 2 during the black-and-white Harkkonen coliseum fight. Even without color, there’s splendid detail and rich shadows. This contrast comes by way of the low black levels that the projector is capable of by shutting down its iris. In all but the darkest scenes I find that the letterboxes around some videos appear almost completely black.
The projector gets dark enough that light control in the room actually becomes rather important. Light hitting the screen can bounce around the room and end up back on the screen where it should be dark, and this raises the black level. Using a VESA test pattern with two bright boxes in the corners of an otherwise black screen, I measured a contrast of 362:1 without controlling for room reflections. By blocking out the white boxes with black velvet, I could simulate a light-controlled room and measured a 3,251:1 contrast ratio. That was with the optical iris open. Cranking the iris down to its lowest level, I measured a 11,194:1 contrast ratio.
The XR10 uses motion interpolation by default, and this tends to introduce a lot of motion artifacts, though it can be a benefit to panning shots. I’ve found the visuals look smooth enough and avoid issues with the motion interpolation set to Film or disabled outright.
Gaming on the XR10 is a joy. It supports both 4K/60Hz and 1080p/240Hz modes with very low latency in both, even without enabling Game Mode. I dashed through levels in Hades 2, easily keeping up with the pace of combat and played through 007: First Light while enjoying the deep cinematic shadows the projector enabled. The XR10 misses out on VRR, though, and a new crop of projectors are bringing in 4K/120Hz capabilities as well, leaving the XR10 a little bit behind on those fronts.
The audio of the XR10 is quite something for a box as small as it is. It features a 2.1-speaker setup with two main drivers and a subwoofer. There’s a bit of low-end brunt to it, though I found the volume drops off a cliff below about 70Hz, leaving the deepest rumble out of the picture. The speakers do a good job with most content and get plenty loud without distorting, but they don’t have much stereo separation to help along with the stunning cinematic quality of the projection.
For what it’s worth, the XR10 still comes with the DLP rainbow effect. It’s not as bad as I’ve seen on some DLP projectors, tending only to be noticeable with white on black visuals, but it may be distracting to those who are particularly susceptible to it.
- Picture quality & performance score: 4.5 / 5
Hisense XR10 review: value
- Premium price
- Capable and flexible projection
There’s no getting around the fact that, at $5,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999, the Hisense XR10 is a very expensive projector, even next to a lot of its competition. It outprices models like the XGIMI Titan Noir Pro, XGIMI Horizon 30 Ultra Max, JMGO Iris Ultra Max, and even Hisense’s own C3 Ultra Max, and by a considerable amount. It is on the bright side of these projectors, though not the brightest. What it does have is a greater zoom range than any of these with its ability to go to a 2:1 throw ratio. For anyone who critically needs flexibility in positioning, that could be a big advantage.
The inclusion of decent speakers for a projector and a streaming operating system are nice to see, but not something that sets the XR10 far apart from its competition.
Ultimately the XR10 ends up with a sizable premium that might be hard to justify for everyone who’s seeking the most value. But if you’re after high-powered projection and serious capabilities, there are really only a few options that effectively undercut this one, and we're yet to see how well they hold up to their promises.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Hisense XR10?
| Hisense XR10 Scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Design and features | The Hisense XR10 is a complete package with advanced and highly flexible optics, powerful projection, punchy speakers, a competent operating system, plenty of ports, and strong wireless connectivity, all packed into an elegant box. | 4.5/5 | 
| Picture quality and performance | The XR10’s RGB laser light source offers stunning brightness and looks wonderfully crisp through the optical system. The projector can get plenty dark using its iris, making it great for viewing in both bright and dark rooms. It has solid gaming chops as well, though VRR would have been a bonus. The speakers also leave a little bit to be desired but are still pretty solid for a projector like this. | 4.5/5 | 
| Value | The XR10 brings a lot to the table, all in one package. But, it asks a high price, and a new fleet of projectors are offering a lot of its capabilities for much lower prices. Most don’t match its optical adjustments, but for many people, that may not be so critical. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You want both bright and dark room viewing chops
The magic of the Hisense XR10 is that it can both get extremely bright and dial things down for excellent darkroom viewing. If you just wanted one or the other, you could find a cheaper projector that was capable enough.
You don’t like the gimbal stand aesthetic
Many of the high-end projectors that the XR10 would compete with have all jumped on the gimbal stand train. The XR10, meanwhile, sticks to a standard box format that might be a little bit easier to find space for and is much easier to level horizontally.
You need the lumens
Brighter projectors simply cost more, and the XR10 is terrifically bright. If you know you’re going to constantly be battling ambient light or are going to take advantage of its maximum projection size, it may be worth it.
Don't buy it if...
You’re not going to put it to work
If you don’t plan on using the full brightness, engaging the iris, or adjusting the optics from time to time, you won’t be getting the most out of the XR10 and could be just as well served by a cheaper model. 
Gaming is your main use
The XR10 is good at gaming, but the latest wave of projectors steps it up with VRR and 4K/120Hz support. Many are nearly as bright and cheaper. 
You can wait a few months
The new wave of projectors from Hisense, Xgimi, and JMGO promise a lot of what the XR10 is delivering at a much lower price. If their performance pans out, they could be a real bargain next to the XR10. 
Hisense XR10 review: Also consider
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Hisense XR10 | Valerion VisionMaster Max | JMGO N3 Ultimate | Xgimi Horizon 20 Max | 
| Price: | $5,999 | $3,999 | $2,999 | $2,999 | 
| Screen sizes supported: | 65 to 300 inches | 40 to 300 inches | 40 to 300 inches | 40-300 inches | 
| Brightness (specified): | 6,000 lumens | 3,500 lumens | 5,800 lumens | 5,700 ISO lumens | 
| HDR support | HDR10+, HLG, Dolby Vision | HDR10+, HLG, Dolby Vision | HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision | Dolby Vision, HDR10+, HDR10, HLG, IMAX Enhanced | 
| Optical technology: | 3 Laser DLP | 3 Laser DLP | 3 Laser DLP | Triple laser DLP | 
| Smart TV: | VidaaOS | Google TV | Google TV | Google TV | 
| Connections: | 2x HDMI 2.1 (1x eARC), 1x HDMI 2.0, 2x USB-A, 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm audio | 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x HDMI 2.0 (with eARC), 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm | 2x HDMI 2.1 (1 with eARC), 1x HDMI 2.0 , 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm | 2x HDMI (x1 eARC), 1x USB 3.0, 1x USB 2.0, 1x 3.5mm, 1x optical audio out | 
Valerion VisionMaster Max 
If you don’t need all the brightness the XR10 offers, the VisionMaster Max offers a wonderful picture and exceptional black levels to rival the XR10 while including optical adjustments of its own, costing less, and bringing Google TV to the table. Read our full Valerion VisionMaster Max review.
JMGO N3 Ultimate
The JMGO N3 Ultimate isn’t quite as flexible, and it doesn’t adapt as well to dark rooms, but it comes at a fraction of the price, supports VRR, and is competitively bright. 
Xgimi Horizon 20 Max
Xgimi’s Horizon 20 Max also provides an alternative with competitive brightness, Google TV, and admirable performance. It also won’t quite win in a dark room battle, but that may not matter for everyone. Read our full Xgimi Horizon 20 Max review.
How I tested the Hisense XR10
- Tested at home in multiple, real-world viewing conditions
- Presented the display with a variety of media and formats
- I have tested numerous projectors and displays over the last half-decade
I tested the Hisense XR10 at home, in real-world conditions. This saw it faced with ambient light coming in from numerous windows, in-room lighting, as well as ambient noise that both the projector and speaker systems had to overcome. The projector was tested both against a bare, white wall and an Akia Screens CineWhite screen. It was presented with streamed content, HDR and non-HDR, and console gameplay.
My testing evaluates the projector’s performance with respect to its price and competition from other models I and colleagues at TechRadar have tested.
I have been testing projectors since 2021 and displays for even longer.

articles.title: Un joueur sur trois pourrait craquer pour GTA 6, tout simplement du jamais vu pour un jeu vidéo !
articles.text:
GTA 6 n'est pas encore en rayon, et il est déjà entré dans l'histoire. Selon le cabinet Circana, 29 % des joueurs américains sur console et PC comptent acheter le titre de Rockstar Games, un niveau jamais mesuré pour un jeu vidéo.
À quelques semaines de sa sortie officielle, prévue le 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, GTA 6 décroche un record d'intention d'achat aux États-Unis. Après treize ans d'attente, un GTA V qui n'a jamais quitté les classements après avoir lui-même battu des records à son époque notamment en France, et des précommandes qui se comptent en millions, il faut vivre sur Mars, pour qui s'intéresse même de loin aux jeux vidéo, pour ne pas voir l'engouement. Le jeu de Rockstar s'annonce ainsi comme l'une des plus grosses sorties de l'histoire du divertissement, et comme un moteur des ventes de consoles pour les fêtes, selon une étude publiée ce 28 octobre par le cabinet américain Circana.
Un niveau d'attente record pour GTA 6
Le cabinet d'études Circana fournit des données de marché aux fabricants et aux distributeurs. Son outil PlayerPulse suit notamment l'intention d’achat des joueurs américains sur console et sur PC, c'est-à-dire la part d'entre eux qui déclarent vouloir acheter un jeu donné. Pour GTA 6, elle atteint 29 %, soit près d’un joueur sur trois. Jamais un jeu vidéo n'avait obtenu un tel score dans les relevés du cabinet. Mat Piscatella, son analyste spécialiste du jeu vidéo, parle d'un moment rare pour l'industrie, aussi culturel que commercial.
Cet appétit doit aussi beaucoup à GTA V. Le jeu reste le titre premium le plus vendu de l'historique américain de Circana, en nombre d'exemplaires, comme en dollars. Il a figuré dans le top 20 des ventes américaines chaque année, sans exception, de 2013 à 2025. L'an dernier, pour sa treizième année sur le marché, il était encore troisième en nombre de joueurs actifs sur PlayStation et Xbox. Peu d'œuvres de divertissement gardent leur public aussi longtemps.
En France, GTA 5 s'est vendu à plus de 6 millions d'exemplaires, s'imposant comme un succès historique et l'un des produits culturels les plus rentables du pays grâce à sa longévité exceptionnelle sur trois générations de consoles. Sa première semaine de lancement avait permis à Rockstar Games de vendre 1,1 million de jeux dans l'Hexagone, un record à l'époque, avec une présence dans le top 10 des meilleures ventes annuelles quasiment chaque année dans le pays.
GTA 6 va profiter à tout l'écosystème du jeu vidéo
Pour Mat Piscatella, l’effet GTA 6 ira bien au-delà des ventes du jeu. Aux États-Unis et ailleurs, comme en France, sa sortie tombe juste avant le Black Friday, fin novembre, et les enseignes se préparent déjà à une forte demande pour les fêtes. L’analyste prévoit donc une hausse des ventes de consoles, mais aussi d’accessoires (manettes, casques…) et d’abonnements liés au jeu vidéo.
GTA 6 ne tournera que sur les consoles actuelles, la PS5 et la Xbox Series. Les joueurs encore équipés d’une PS4 ou d’une Xbox One devront changer de machine pour y jouer, et beaucoup pourraient en profiter pour s’offrir une PS5. Selon lui, cet engouement montre aussi le poids croissant du jeu vidéo dans le divertissement et la tech grand public.
On retrouve d'ailleurs cette impatience dans les précommandes. D’après Sensor Tower, qui suit les ventes sur les boutiques en ligne de Sony et de Microsoft, GTA 6 cumule 6,45 millions de précommandes numériques dans le monde, dont 74 % sur PS5. Et ce score est atteint malgré un prix élevé on rappelle 79,99 euros pour l’édition standard, et 99,99 euros pour l’Ultime, plus riche en bonus. Les amateurs de support physique devront aussi s’adapter, car la boîte vendue en magasin ne contient qu’un code de téléchargement, sans disque.
Dans tous les cas, mieux vaut prévoir de la place sur sa machine, puisqu'une fuite, que Rockstar n’a pas confirmée, évoque 210 Go d'espace nécessaire sur PS5. Les versions numériques pourront être préchargées dès le 12 novembre, pour jouer dès le jour de la sortie. Une intention d’achat ne garantit pas une vente, mais tous les indicateurs pointent dans la même direction.

articles.title: TVs da LG perdem acesso à IA da Microsoft • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
TVs da LG perdem acesso à IA da Microsoft
Integração com o Copilot acaba até o final do ano, mas ainda não tem dia certo para acontecer. Decisão impacta o Brasil.
A LG não terá mais o Copilot em suas smart TVs. A integração com a inteligência artificial da Microsoft será encerrada até o fim de 2026, conforme aponta notificação enviada para o sistema webOS dos modelos da marca. O recurso estava presente desde 2025 como IA nativa das TVs, permitindo tirar dúvidas e receber recomendações com base nas suas atividades.
Segundo a mensagem enviada aos televisores, a decisão pelo fim do suporte veio da Microsoft e atinge tanto o app de chat do Copilot quanto suas atividades no sistema operacional. O Tecnoblog realizou testes e confirmou o fim da integração em aparelho vendido no Brasil.
De acordo com o Windows Central, o movimento teria a ver com uma mudança de estratégia adotada pela gigante americana. A Microsoft anunciou mudanças nos serviços de IA em setembro e voltou suas operações para produtividade.
A Microsoft unificou os dois apps disponíveis até então, o Copilot padrão e o Microsoft 365 Copilot. A partir disso, a ideia é que o serviço funcione menos como um chat e mais como um recurso de produtividade, seja para atuar junto ao pacote Office ou realizar trabalhos mais aprofundados de programação.
Com a mudança de estratégia, a presença do modelo nas TVs da LG parou de fazer sentido. Vale lembrar que televisores da Samsung também receberam a integração com o Copilot, mas o app também já não aparece mais nos sistemas Tizen.
A presença do Copilot nas smart TVs da LG foi curta e cercada de polêmica. Apesar do anúncio feito durante a CES 2025, em janeiro, a integração começou de fato em dezembro, com um aplicativo web que não podia ser deletado. Além disso, a chegada do app se deu por meio de um download “forçado” nas TVs da marca.
Na época, muitos usuários foram pegos de surpresa e reclamaram da presença do app. Apesar de “nativo”, o recurso contava basicamente com uma versão web na IA, sem integração total com o televisor. Pouco mais de 10 meses depois, usuários recebem a notificação do fim da parceria.

articles.title: Canadian Startup Aims to Be Quantum’s ‘Picks’ and ‘Shovels’ - EE Times
articles.text:
There’s no shortage of hurdles that need to be overcome to scale quantum computing into a commercial reality. Canadian startup Meissner Technologies has focused on a critical bottleneck: superconducting materials used in single-photon detectors.
Founded in September 2025 by University of Toronto materials science graduate Olivia Leng, Meissner Technologies uses AI, machine-learning simulations, chemical and electrical simulations, and laboratory testing to discover new superconducting materials in quantum computing. The company is also exploring materials that could reduce cooling requirements for photonic quantum systems.
The Meissner team is largely drawn from the University of Toronto. The company has completed the Creative Destruction Lab program, a nonprofit objectives-based mentorship program for pre-seed and seed-stage deep-tech startups building massively scalable products and services.
Meissner also recently closed its first financing round, anchored by the BDC Thrive Venture Fund, with backing from founders, operators, and investors including Christian Weedbrook, founder and CEO of Xanadu.
Leng’s path to entrepreneurship began during her studies, when she worked extensively with superconducting materials in both research labs and simulation environments. “I spent a lot of time in the lab, ran a bunch of simulation work on them, and noticed that there has been a lot of momentum going into the AI for drug discovery space,” she said.
Leng realized that a similar framework and approach could be applied to finding new superconducting materials.
Although photonic systems operate largely at room temperature, they still rely on single-photon detectors that must be cooled to extremely low temperatures.
Current detectors typically use niobium titanium nitride or niobium nitride. According to Leng, those materials impose an unavoidable tradeoff between operating temperature and detector performance.
Meissner said it believes better materials could significantly change the economics of quantum computing infrastructure.
The company is searching for alternatives capable of operating a few degrees warmer than current options without compromising performance. While that may sound like a marginal improvement, Leng argued that the impact could be dramatic.
“If we’re able to remove the dilution refrigerators, we’d be able to replace them with closed-loop helium-4 cryostats, saving them up to 95% of their cooling costs,” she said.
The challenge is becoming increasingly urgent because of the industry’s dependence on helium-3. Leng noted that limited global supplies could eventually constrain scaling across multiple quantum computing platforms.
That focus immediately resonated with investors and industry participants, she said. “We want to be the picks and shovels to quantum computing. That’s where we think a large part of the value chain can be captured.”
With fresh funding secured, Meissner is moving from computational discovery into experimental validation. For several months, the company concentrated on refining its simulation stack. It is now advancing promising material candidates into fabrication and testing.
“We’re actually depositing them into thin films, etching them into nanowires, and packaging them into photon detectors and running actual lab tests,” Leng said. “Then we take that lab data and feed that back into our model, creating this circular materials discovery pipeline.”
The next major milestone is to deliver a minimum viable photon detector that can be piloted with a photonic quantum computing customer. A seed financing round is expected next year, with future investment directed toward detector manufacturing scale-up.
Beyond that, the company has a more ambitious vision: autonomous materials research.
“Our largest bottleneck right now is experimental validation,” Leng said. “We’re able to pump out so many candidates computationally, but we only have so much manpower.” Meissner ultimately aims to build self-driving laboratories capable of automating much of the materials discovery workflow, she added.
Leng also sees Canada as an increasingly attractive place to build a quantum technology company. She pointed to support from ecosystems in Toronto, Waterloo, and Sherbrooke, along with a growing base of talent and investors.
“I think our ecosystem has advanced to the point where it’s far more viable to build a company here in Canada, and we intend to stay Canadian,” she said.
Internationally, Meissner faces established detector suppliers such as ID Quantique and Single Quantum. However, Leng argued that those firms are primarily improving detector performance through engineering refinements, while Meissner is focused on discovering entirely new materials.
“Our hypothesis is [that] niobium titanium nitride has been around for decades in academia,” she said. “Every sort of variation has been exhausted. The only way to really improve detector performance meaningfully is to actually go in and investigate the materials science.”
The company’s technology roadmap could also reach beyond quantum computing. Leng cited opportunities in quantum communications, aerospace sensing applications, and nuclear fusion, all of which depend on advanced superconducting materials.
“Ultimately, we’re a materials discovery company,” she said. “We’re not going to just be bounded by quantum computing.”

articles.title: New York Knicks tricked employees with fake email in cyber test
articles.text:
New York Knicks slammed after offering employees NBA championship rings in what turned out to be a phishing test
New York Knicks face backlash after tricking employees with fake gifts
- Knicks employees expecting free championship rings received mandatory cybersecurity training instead
- A fake championship ring offer exposed employees to an internal phishing test
- Madison Square Garden admitted that using championship jewellery as bait was inappropriate
The New York Knicks have faced criticism after sending employees an email promising complimentary NBA championship rings that turned out to be a cybersecurity exercise.
Staff members who accepted the invitation were reportedly required to complete cybersecurity training instead of receiving jewellery commemorating the franchise's historic victory.
The incident involved workers at Madison Square Garden, where expectations of receiving championship memorabilia had already grown following the team's successful season.
Fake championship ring offer triggers mandatory training
The deceptive message circulated in late September, offering recipients personalized jewellery supposedly manufactured by the same company responsible for producing players' rings.
Employees could select between two advertised designs, Championship Gold and Garden Classic, before following a link to register their preferred choice.
However, the invitation was actually part of an internal security assessment intended to identify workers susceptible to fraudulent messages and credential theft.
Those who followed the instructions were reportedly assigned compulsory cybersecurity lessons, although the organization has not disclosed how many employees were affected.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Joe Vardon, a senior NBA journalist at The Athletic, reported that several individuals familiar with the situation verified the exercise's purpose.
The report also raised questions about whether the invitation contained recognizable warning signs that might have helped employees identify the deception.
Such exercises commonly use suspicious addresses or misleading website links, although the specific indicators included in this particular message remain unknown.
The controversy followed the Knicks' first NBA championship since 1973, making the promised jewellery particularly significant for employees celebrating the achievement.
Receiving commemorative jewellery was also a reasonable expectation because NBA organizations commonly distribute less expensive versions to personnel outside their playing squads.
Madison Square Garden acknowledges its mistake
Madison Square Garden Sports subsequently acknowledged the incident, describing its decision to exploit employees' expectations as inappropriate.
“Using the rings as a lure to gain employees’ attention was an unfortunate mistake,” it said in an official statement.
The organization explained that its security concerns stemmed from an earlier cyberattack in which employee credentials were compromised through a similar fraudulent communication.
Hackers had reportedly used those credentials to access company systems and subsequently extort the organization, prompting additional efforts to improve employee awareness.
The company also disclosed plans to distribute more than 275 commemorative items among players, coaches, employees and other individuals associated with the franchise.
According to the organization, those gifts, comprising championship rings and other jewellery, carry a combined estimated value exceeding $3.7 million.
However, the distribution arrangements have attracted attention because several assistant coaches initially received empty presentation boxes during the championship celebration.
The assistants are expected to obtain their rings later, although numerous long-time arena employees and business personnel reportedly remain excluded entirely.
The organization has not specified exactly how many workers will receive individual rings rather than alternative jewellery under its announced distribution arrangements.
Via Arstechnica
