articles.title: Check Point is turning network firewalls into cloud-based subscriptions
articles.text:
WTF?! AI agents are increasingly becoming a driving force behind large-scale cyber-swatting campaigns and dangerous security incidents. Israeli cybersecurity company Check Point believes an AI-powered firewall could be the answer to this emerging agentic threat – and hopes customers will keep paying for it indefinitely.
Check Point recently introduced its new Firewall-as-a-Subscription offering, giving organizations access to comprehensive network protection designed for the AI era. The Israeli cybersecurity company says customers no longer need to purchase expensive hardware appliances before getting started with the new platform. However, they'll be locked into monthly or annual payments for at least three years before they can switch to something else.
Put simply, Check Point has turned one of the most basic networking services into a cloud-based subscription – and expects customers to be grateful for it, too. The Firewall-as-a-Subscription service is based on R82.20, Check Point's latest firewall platform, which is designed to provide enhanced protection and management capabilities for bots, chatbots, and AI agents.
The R82.20 platform includes an "agentic console" for managing firewall devices and services. Check Point is using AI-powered technology to fend off AI-powered attacks, a strategy that's becoming a common refrain among organizations facing increasingly aggressive AI agents and bots.
The Firewall-as-a-Subscription package also includes additional features, such as Check Point Force hardware firewalls tailored to an organization's needs, SandBlast's AI-powered threat prevention, and security updates that can be applied on the fly. The company also promises "premium" support, which should mean having a (competent) human employee available to respond to customer support tickets.
Check Point's pitch for subscription-based firewalls revolves around the rising cost of hardware. Organizations are seeing their budgets shrink, while security appliances often go for long periods without significant upgrades. If an up-to-date AI firewall can be bundled into a single subscription with predictable monthly expenses, Check Point suggests, companies will be more inclined to upgrade and take advantage of the latest capabilities offered by its all-in-one R82.20 platform.
Avi Rembaum, Check Point's president of global technical sales, said that "with Firewall-as-a-Subscription, we are making our most advanced AI security, threat prevention and agentic management available through one simple subscription, so organizations can secure their AI transformation today."
According to the company, customers must commit to the firewall subscription for at least 36 months. In return, they can expect significant feature upgrades – and potentially hardware upgrades – throughout the same period.
Check Point's subscription-based approach to network security might sound bonkers, but AI agents are becoming a real threat that internet services must address one way or another. Big tech companies such as Amazon and Meta are clashing over agents' ability to shop online freely, while Nvidia is proposing a safety platform to keep rogue AI agents in check.
AI agents are hammering servers at some of the internet's most popular services, including Wikipedia. Meanwhile, someone in Delaware thinks letting AI agents run entire companies sounds like the best idea in the world.

articles.title: Meeting Room Tech Mistakes That Make Every Video Call Start Late - Tech Guide
articles.text:
In today’s fast-paced business environment, video calls have become indispensable for communication and collaboration. Whether connecting with remote teams, clients, or partners, organisations rely heavily on video conferencing to maintain productivity and foster relationships. However, despite widespread adoption, many companies face persistent challenges causing video calls to start late. These delays waste valuable time, disrupt workflow, reduce employee morale, and create poor impressions on clients and colleagues.
Understanding common pitfalls in meeting room technology is crucial for businesses aiming to streamline their video conferencing experiences and ensure punctuality. From technical glitches to user errors, various factors contribute to late call starts. Addressing these issues proactively leads to smoother meetings, better collaboration, and improved business outcomes. This article explores the most frequent meeting room tech mistakes that cause video calls to begin behind schedule and offers practical solutions to overcome them.
Common Causes of Video Call Delays
One frequent reason video calls start late is technical issues with the meeting room setup. These problems range from faulty hardware connections to software incompatibilities. For example, cables may be loose or incorrectly connected, the wrong input source might be selected on displays, or devices may fail to pair properly. Such issues often result in frustrating delays as users scramble to identify and fix problems before the meeting can proceed.
In some cases, video conferencing software may not be correctly configured or updated, leading to unexpected errors when attempting to connect. Compatibility issues between different platforms or outdated software versions can cause crashes or connectivity failures. These technical challenges highlight the importance of having a well-maintained and properly configured meeting room environment.
A surprising number of companies underestimate the importance of professional support for their IT infrastructure within meeting rooms. Leveraging the expertise of managed IT experts at Edgeworx can significantly reduce these technical hiccups by ensuring all equipment is installed correctly, updated regularly, and maintained proactively. Managed IT providers typically monitor systems remotely to address problems before they impact meetings, allowing video calls to start as scheduled. Their proactive approach includes routine health checks, timely software updates, and rapid troubleshooting, collectively minimizing downtime and disruptions.
Equipment and Setup Issues
Inadequate or outdated equipment is another common culprit behind late video call starts. Many organisations attempt to save costs by using consumer-grade webcams, microphones, or speakers, which often lead to poor audio and video quality. This results in repeated adjustments and retests before the meeting can begin, frustrating participants and consuming valuable time.
Moreover, insufficient bandwidth or network issues can cause lag, jitter, or disconnections, further prolonging video call start times. Network congestion, limited Wi-Fi coverage, or outdated routers can all negatively affect the quality and reliability of video conferencing sessions. Without a robust and optimised network infrastructure, even the best hardware cannot perform to its full potential.
A well-planned meeting room setup incorporates reliable, business-grade hardware and a network environment optimised for video conferencing. For instance, using dedicated video conferencing endpoints instead of relying solely on laptops can enhance stability and ease of use. These endpoints are designed specifically for video calls and typically offer better audio and video quality, simplified user interfaces, and seamless integration with conferencing platforms.
Organisations that invest in such solutions usually experience fewer delays and smoother call initiations. Additionally, ensuring that the network supports Quality of Service (QoS) prioritisation for video traffic can help reduce latency and packet loss, making calls more stable and responsive.
The Role of User Training and Support
Even with the best technology in place, user error remains a significant factor in late starts. Many employees are not fully trained on how to operate meeting room systems, leading to confusion and last-minute troubleshooting. This issue is especially prevalent when multiple platforms or devices are involved, requiring users to navigate different interfaces, sign-in procedures, and settings.
For example, users may struggle with starting the call, sharing their screens, or adjusting audio and video settings. In some cases, they may not know how to troubleshoot common issues such as muted microphones or disconnected cameras, which can delay meetings further.
Providing comprehensive training and ongoing support can drastically improve meeting punctuality. Companies that engage with Foresight IT’s technical expertise benefit from tailored training programs that empower employees to use video conferencing tools confidently and efficiently. These programs often include hands-on workshops, quick reference guides, and video tutorials that cater to varying levels of technical proficiency. Additionally, having IT support readily available to assist during meetings ensures that any issues are resolved quickly without causing lengthy delays.
Beyond initial training, fostering a culture that encourages employees to familiarise themselves with meeting room technology and report issues promptly contributes to smoother operations. Regular refresher sessions and updates on new features or changes in software also help maintain user competence and reduce errors.
Importance of Regular Maintenance and Updates
Neglecting routine maintenance and software updates is another factor causing video calls to start late. Outdated software may be incompatible with the latest video conferencing platforms or contain bugs that hinder connectivity. Similarly, hardware that is not regularly checked may fail unexpectedly during calls, causing interruptions and delays.
Firmware updates for cameras, microphones, and other peripherals often include performance improvements and security patches. Skipping these updates can leave devices vulnerable to malfunctions or cyber threats. Likewise, failing to update video conferencing applications can result in missing critical compatibility fixes or new features designed to enhance user experience.
Scheduling regular maintenance and updates as part of IT management helps prevent these problems. Managed service providers often include these tasks in their offerings, ensuring that both hardware and software remain in optimal condition. This proactive approach reduces downtime and supports timely video call starts.
Routine maintenance also involves checking physical components such as cables, connectors, and power supplies for wear and tear. Environmental factors like dust accumulation or temperature fluctuations can impact equipment longevity and performance, making regular inspections vital.
Environmental and Room Design Factors
The physical environment of a meeting room can influence how quickly video calls commence. Poor lighting, background noise, or inadequate acoustics can necessitate adjustments or relocation before a meeting can proceed. For instance, harsh backlighting may make participants’ faces difficult to see, while excessive ambient noise can interfere with audio clarity.
Additionally, rooms not ergonomically designed for video conferencing may require repositioning of cameras and microphones or rearranging furniture to ensure all participants are visible and audible. Such last-minute changes can delay call starts and reduce overall meeting efficiency.
Investing in meeting room design that considers these factors can enhance overall efficiency. For example, installing sound-absorbing materials and adjustable lighting can create a conducive environment for video calls. Dedicated meeting rooms with properly placed cameras, microphones, and displays allow participants to join calls quickly without needing constant adjustments.
Moreover, incorporating features like automatic camera framing and noise-cancelling microphones can further streamline meeting setups. These technologies reduce the need for manual intervention and help meetings begin promptly.
Data-Driven Benefits of Optimising Meeting Room Technology
Statistics underline the significant impact these issues have on business productivity and employee satisfaction. According to a report by ZK Research, 70% of employees say they lose time due to meeting technology problems, with an average of 20 minutes wasted per meeting setup failure. This lost time accumulates rapidly across organisations, leading to decreased efficiency and increased frustration.
Another study from Wainhouse Research found that poor audio and video quality is the top reason for video conference dissatisfaction, affecting 35% of users. Such dissatisfaction can reduce engagement, hinder communication, and ultimately impact decision-making during meetings.
Furthermore, a Microsoft report highlights that organisations with optimised meeting room technology see a 15% increase in meeting efficiency. This improvement translates to faster decision cycles, better collaboration, and a more positive workplace culture.
These statistics demonstrate that investing in the right technology, training, and support not only prevents delays but also enhances overall organisational performance.
Conclusion
Delays at the start of video calls can be frustrating and costly, but they are largely preventable. By addressing common meeting room technology mistakes-such as inadequate equipment, lack of user training, poor maintenance, and suboptimal room design-businesses can ensure their video calls begin promptly and run smoothly.
Engaging professional IT support, like the , and benefiting from can provide the expertise needed for seamless video conferencing experiences. These partnerships help organisations implement best practices, maintain systems proactively, and empower users with the knowledge to operate technology confidently.
Investing in the right technology, training, and environment not only saves time but also enhances communication and collaboration in today’s digital workplace. As remote and hybrid work models continue to evolve, optimising meeting room technology is essential for maintaining productivity and fostering strong professional relationships.

articles.title: Amazon tells engineers to stop ‘tokenmaxxing’ to look productive — says AI will be central to software development, but usage is not the goal, new guidelines claim
articles.text:
Amazon tells engineers to stop ‘tokenmaxxing’ to look productive — says AI will be central to software development, but usage is not the goal, new guidelines claim
Amazon still expects AI to sit at the center of software engineering, but says usage alone is not proof of productivity
Amazon wants its engineers to quit chasing token counts, warning that heavy AI usage does not automatically mean better work. In updated engineering guidelines published on October 27, the company laid out how developers and managers should gauge AI’s real impact — and the takeaway is blunt: consuming more tokens is not the same as delivering more value. Amazon is not backing away from the technology, though. “We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice,” the company wrote.
The guidance targets ‘tokenmaxxing,’ a practice where employees deliberately inflate their AI usage to look productive on internal dashboards. According to the memo, metrics such as AI adoption rates, token consumption, code changes, and code reviews become ‘deeply flawed’ when they are disconnected from actual results. Turning them into targets, Amazon says, encourages wasteful behavior that clashes with its emphasis on ‘frugality and simplicity’ and can raise both compute bills and software complexity.
The company’s preferred yardstick is long-term results. “We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes,” Amazon wrote. That does not mean managers should ignore usage data altogether, as input metrics remain useful when examined ‘with care and judgment’ alongside other indicators. Amazon suggests looking at both the teams using AI the least and those using it the most to determine whether adoption is translating into better delivery.
The push comes as Amazon, under CEO Andy Jassy, has been weaving AI deeply into its sprawling operations. Jassy said earlier this year that the technology will ‘change the scope and speed’ of everyday work, and he has suggested that automation could shrink the company’s corporate workforce over the next few years — though he also expects it to create ‘other jobs.’
The memo also pushes back on the idea that every task needs an AI tool. If current tooling does not benefit someone’s work, Amazon says, that is ‘a finding, not a failing.’ Engineers who can explain where today’s tools fall short are demonstrating judgment rather than reluctance to adopt AI.
In May, it emerged that Amazon employees were using AI unnecessarily to boost internal usage scores, amid pressure to use the company's tools. Workers reportedly used MeshClaw, an internal AI agent capable of handling tasks such as deploying code and interacting with Slack, to inflate their token counts.
Notably, Amazon is not the only company rethinking how it spends on AI. Uber president and COO Andrew Macdonald said in May that higher token usage has yet to translate into useful consumer features. “That link is not there yet,” he said. The remark stands out because Uber’s CTO previously revealed that the company had burned through its entire 2026 Claude Code budget by April.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Accenture appears to also be wrestling with the same problem on behalf of its clients. Leaked audio obtained by 404 Media in June captures executives acknowledging that token spending is climbing fast as companies move from simple chatbots to agentic workflows, and that nobody can reliably predict what a given task will cost or whether it was worth the money. Accenture’s agentic AI strategy lead described it as ‘not a niche problem,’ and the firm is reportedly building an advisory tool called ‘Token IQ’ to help customers manage the bill. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has previously acknowledged that AI token costs had become 'a huge issue', as companies faced mounting bills from heavy AI use.
Amazon, however, says it has not imposed token caps on its employees. According to CNBC, however, it shut down an internal leaderboard in May after workers were found gaming it to climb the rankings — an early example of the behavior the new guidelines are meant to discourage.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Newton Gitonga is a tech journalist covering gadgets, PC hardware, AI, data centers, and the wider tech industry. His interest in technology started early, taking apart things around the house to see how they worked, often to his dad’s frustration. His curiosity sometimes got the better of him, including a few failed attempts to fix laptops, one of them a gifted Dell XPS. He has previously written for Notebookcheck, ZyCrypto, CoinCentral, and Crypto News Flash.

articles.title: El iPad ha pasado diez años intentando convertirse en un Mac. Al final es el Mac quien se ha quedado con lo único que tenía el iPad
articles.text:
En noviembre de 2017, Apple emitió uno de los anuncios más recordados de su historia reciente. Una niña se estaba pasando el día entero con un iPad Pro. Con él hacía los deberes, sacaba fotos, chateaba con sus amigos y dibujaba tumbada en el césped. Al final, una vecina le pregunta qué hacía con el ordenador. Ella respondía con otra pregunta: "¿Qué es un ordenador?".
El anuncio no era una ocurrencia publicitaria sino una tesis de empresa. Dos años antes, en una entrevista con The Telegraph, Tim Cook se preguntaba por qué alguien seguiría comprando un PC. Apple estaba convencida de que el ordenador del futuro sería una pantalla que se pudiese tocar, y de que ese futuro se llamaba iPad. Ayer Apple presentó en Los Ángeles su primer MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil.
Casi todo lo que se ha escrito desde entonces ha girado en torno a Steve Jobs y a aquella keynote de 2010 en la que aseguró que un portátil táctil era, ergonómicamente, un error. Es la contradicción más llamativa, pero no es la más importante.
La contradicción que de verdad cuenta no es con Jobs. Es con la propia Apple de los últimos diez años. Durante todo este tiempo, la empresa ha defendido que no iba a fusionar el iPad y el Mac porque cumplían funciones distintas.
- El Mac era el ordenador de teclado y trackpad.
- El iPad era el ordenador que se podía tocar.
Y la apuesta de Apple era que, con el tiempo, el segundo se comería al primero.
No ha ocurrido. De hecho, Apple ha resuelto la pregunta de si el iPad podía sustituir al portátil de la forma más inesperada: dándole al portátil lo único que el iPad tenía en exclusiva.
Cada gran novedad del iPad Pro le ha dado algo que el Mac ya tenía: el teclado en 2015, el cursor en 2020, un chip de la serie M en 2021, las ventanas en 2022 y la barra de menús en 2025. La convergencia solo avanzaba en un sentido. Al iPad le quedaban dos exclusivas, la pantalla táctil y el Apple Pencil. Ahora solo conserva la segunda. El Pencil necesita una superficie horizontal donde apoyar la mano, y seguramente por eso Apple no lo ha llevado al Mac.
Greg Joswiak lo ha explicado en Wired: casi todos los profesionales tienen un iPad, y los creadores jóvenes, que han crecido rodeado de pantallas táctiles, esperan poder tocar la pantalla de su MacBook Pro. El iPad es uno de los dispositivos que han educado a millones de personas en el tacto, y ese hábito lo aprovecha ahora el producto al que pretendía sustituir.
Por abajo aprieta el iPhone Duo: 7,6 pulgadas desplegado, multitarea heredada de iPadOS y compatibilidad con el Pencil. A 2.339 euros no amenaza al iPad de entrada, pero un iPhone 18 Pro Max (1.619 euros) y el nuevo iPad mini (749) suman 2.368. Para quien compraba ambos, el plegable cuesta lo mismo y ocupa un solo bolsillo.
Nada de esto pone en peligro al iPad. Entre enero y marzo, más de la mitad de sus compradores eran nuevos. Lo que pierde es la promesa. Si quieres un ordenador que se pueda tocar, Apple ya tiene uno y también se llama Mac.
Quien vio aquel anuncio con doce años tiene hoy veintiuno. Es la generación que cita Joswiak. El iPad la educó en el tacto, pero ahora que llega a la edad de trabajar, Apple no le ofrece un iPad mejor, sino un Mac que se deja tocar. La niña del anuncio ya tiene su respuesta. Y no es el iPad.

articles.title: Un hacker filtró datos de más de 40.000 empleados de Seguridad Nacional de Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Un hacker que se identifica como Department of Peace robó y publicó datos personales de más de 40.000 empleados del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional de Estados Unidos, entre ellos agentes de inmigración y de fronteras. TechCrunch informó que la brecha no se había divulgado y que ocurrió a mediados de este año.
Los registros incluyen nombres, cargos, correos electrónicos, números de celular y ubicación de las oficinas. Según el medio citado, más de la mitad, unos 21.000, corresponden a la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP). Otros 10.000 pertenecen al Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) y a su unidad de investigaciones.
Casi 1.000 registros son de la agencia de ciberseguridad CISA. El resto incluye personal de la sede del departamento y de otras agencias, como el Servicio de Ciudadanía e Inmigración y el Servicio de Protección Federal.
El hacker afirmó que obtuvo la información de un sistema de Okta, una plataforma que permite a los empleados y contratistas iniciar sesión una sola vez para acceder a la red central. Okta respondió que no tiene pruebas de que sus sistemas o datos hayan sido comprometidos.
Wired, que también accedió a los archivos, contó más de 41.000 empleados o contratistas y señaló que los registros se actualizaron por última vez el 19 de agosto. Según su análisis, entre los datos hay referencias a programas encubiertos y de vigilancia.
Cómo salieron a la luz los datos
La información llegó a la periodista e investigadora maia arson crimew, que la compartió con Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), un colectivo sin fines de lucro que aloja datos filtrados de interés público. Según Wired, DDoSecrets publicó el archivo, al que llamó “Icepick”.
“Ellos tienen nuestra información, así que es justo que nosotros tengamos la de ellos”, escribió el hacker en una nota que acompaña los archivos. NBC News informó que activistas contrarios al gobierno de Donald Trump se atribuyen la acción.
TechCrunch comprobó una parte de los datos al cotejar los nombres de varios empleados conocidos con una copia del archivo. Según el medio, la cifra equivale a una quinta parte de los 220.000 empleados del departamento. Wired calcula una séptima parte.
Herramientas de vigilancia que usan los agentes
Los datos incluyen la pertenencia de cada empleado a grupos de acceso a programas internos. Cerca de 4.500 usuarios, incluidos agentes y oficiales de deportación, figuran en un grupo llamado “Headspace_users”. Un portavoz de Headspace dijo a TechCrunch que la empresa no presta servicios al departamento ni a ICE desde 2023.
Decenas de grupos mencionan a Penlink, una empresa de vigilancia en internet con contrato con ICE desde hace años. Uno de ellos reúne a más de 2.000 usuarios de la unidad de investigaciones. Más de 200 empleados de CBP aparecen asociados a Mobile Fortify, una aplicación de reconocimiento facial que usan CBP e ICE para identificar personas y verificar su estatus migratorio.
También hay empleados con acceso a ChatGPT, entre ellos altos funcionarios, y grupos vinculados a investigaciones sobre Salt Typhoon y Volt Typhoon, grupos de hackers respaldados por China. Penlink no respondió a la consulta de TechCrunch.
Ryan Shapiro, director ejecutivo de la organización Property of the People, dijo que los correos y teléfonos son herramientas indispensables para quienes investigan mediante solicitudes de acceso a la información pública. Emma Best, cofundadora de DDoSecrets, afirmó que los datos serán un “catalizador” de investigaciones.
Es la segunda brecha del departamento este año atribuida al mismo hacker, que antes dijo haber tomado miles de contratos entre la dependencia y empresas privadas.

articles.title: Galaxy A57 despenca 58% para quem busca custo-benefício • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy A57 despenca 58% para quem busca custo-benefício
Galaxy A57 (128 GB) tem tela Super AMOLED+ e câmera wide de 50 MP; celular acessível da Samsung sai muito mais em conta no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy A57 de 128 GB está saindo por R$ 1.583 no Pix com cupom VALETECH no Mercado Livre. O smartphone acessível da Samsung, equipado com câmera de 50 MP e tela Super AMOLED+ de 120 Hz, recebe desconto de 58% sobre o atual preço base de R$ 3.799, recentemente reajustado pela fabricante.
O Galaxy A57 possui uma tela de 6,7″ Super AMOLED+, evolução sutil da Super AMOLED que oferece melhor qualidade de imagem. A taxa de 120 Hz e o brilho de até 1.900 nits entregam imagens com cores vibrantes e alta fluidez nas transições em apps e games, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer lugar.
Seu chip Exynos 1680 e os 8 GB de RAM dão conta de apps em multitarefa e games, além de algumas funções da suíte Galaxy AI. Os 128 GB de espaço interno podem ser expandidos com planos de armazenamento na nuvem.
O kit principal de câmeras do celular custo-benefício da Samsung inclui wide de 50 MP com OIS e uma ultrawide de 12 MP, que captam belas imagens ao ar livre, e uma macro de 5 MP para aproximações de elementos pequenos. A frontal de 12 MP tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
O corpo de alumínio do A57 é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+, resistente a arranhões e pancadas. A certificação IP68 confere proteção extra em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh resiste por até dois dias de uso, segundo a fabricante. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 45 W via cabo USB-C permite receber uma carga de 60% em 30 minutos, evitando que o usuário fique na mão com um celular sem energia durante o corre-corre diário.
O Galaxy A57 de 128 GB (R$ 1.583 no Pix com cupom VALETECH) está sendo atualizado para o Android 17 e é elegível a mais cinco updates do sistema operacional. O celular custo-benefício da Samsung conversa com redes 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0 e NFC.

articles.title: Écran OLED à 120 Hz et 32 Go de RAM : le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7a baisse de 100 €
articles.text:
Le PC portable Lenovo Yoga Slim 7a OLED de 14 pouces avec 32 Go et 1 To est à 1 799,99 € (-5 %)
Avec son écran OLED à 120 Hz et ses 32 Go de RAM, le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7a vise le travail en mobilité. Amazon le propose avec 100 € de réduction.
Le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7a est proposé à 1 799,99 €, contre un plus bas prix des 30 derniers jours de 1 899,99 €. L’économie atteint 100 €, soit environ 5 %. Le PC est vendu et expédié par Amazon, avec la livraison gratuite proposée. Attention, le chargeur secteur n’est pas inclus.
Un écran OLED de 14 pouces à 120 Hz
Le PC portable Lenovo Yoga Slim 7a dispose d’un écran OLED de 14 pouces en définition 2,8K, avec un rafraîchissement jusqu’à 120 Hz. Son format 16:10 offre davantage de hauteur pour afficher des documents et des pages web qu’un écran 16:9 de même largeur.
La description de cette configuration indique un processeur AMD Ryzen AI 7 445, accompagné de 32 Go de mémoire vive et d’un SSD de 1 To. La mémoire est soudée : sa capacité doit donc être choisie dès l’achat.
Une connectique centrée sur l’USB-C
Le portable intègre le Wi-Fi 7 et trois ports USB-C, dont deux USB4. Des adaptateurs peuvent être nécessaires pour brancher des périphériques USB-A ou un écran HDMI.
Le chargeur est à prévoir séparément. Lenovo recommande un modèle USB-C de 65 W pour cette configuration. Ce coût supplémentaire est à prendre en compte si vous ne possédez pas déjà un adaptateur compatible.

articles.title: Alphabet's stock sinks after shocking investors with top-and-bottom line miss - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Alphabet’s stock sinks after shocking investors with top-and-bottom line miss
Shares of Alphabet Inc. fell more than 9% in after-hours trading after the Google parent reported a stunning earnings miss and a substantial drop in free cash flow at the end of its third quarter.
The search engine and cloud computing giant reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of just $2.67 per share, some way behind Wall Street’s target of $3.02 per share in earnings. Revenue for the period also came up short. Though it rose 25% from a year earlier to $127.58 billion, analysts had been targeting even bigger sales of $128.22 billion, and were sorely disappointed to see that the company couldn’t top that number.
The company’s first top-and-bottom line miss in almost four years meant that it also suffered an overall drop in net income, which came to $26.17 billion, down from $34.98 billion in the same period one year ago.
Alphabet also reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, which was far lower than the $2.7 billion number expected by analysts. Even more puzzling is that executives cannot just blame the shortfall on artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. That’s because Alphabet’s capital expenditures in the quarter totaled $51.36 billion, falling short of the $55.09 billion expected by analysts.
Going forward, Alphabet Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi said, the company is maintaining its full-year capital spending forecast of between $195 billion and $205 billion. She also reiterated the company’s plans for this figure to exceed $300 billion in fiscal 2027.
Some investors have become increasingly concerned over the runaway spending plans of so-called hyperscaler cloud providers such as Alphabet and are looking for signs that they will be able to generate a return on those multibillion-dollar investments, but that doesn’t seem likely to happen anytime soon.
Alphabet continued to borrow heavily during the quarter, with its long-term debt rising to $125.1 billion, up from just $21.6 billion a year ago. That’s an increase of around 479% year-over-year. Alphabet also missed on operating income during the quarter, with its total of $40.58 billion falling short of the $43.19 billion targeted by analysts.
The company did enjoy a $99.03 billion revenue windfall through its equity holdings in AI firms such as Anthropic PBC and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. But that category also weighed on its bottom line, with net losses relating to those investments coming to $8.66 billion in the quarter.
The headline earnings miss looks worse than Alphabet’s underlying business is performing because it was driven mainly by financial rather than operating losses, stressed Investing.com analyst Thomas Monteiro. “But operating profit also came up short and that matters more,” he said. “Until now, AI spending only hit Alphabet’s cash flow, but this quarter it started showing up in profits too, and the pressure will only grow from here as depreciation rises and the cost of capital is repriced upward.”
Most of the money Alphabet is spending on AI infrastructure directly benefits its cloud computing division, which houses most of the AI services it offers, and the impact can at least be seen in its growing revenue. During the quarter, Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, surpassing the $28.7 billion analyst target. Google Cloud Chief Executive Thomas Kurian, appearing in a conference call with analysts for the first time, said the company is seeing “extraordinary demand and strong growth from AI labs, capital markets, financial service institutions and enterprises.”
Monteiro said investors will be pleased to see the growth in Google Cloud, but warned that this is also helping many of its rivals in the AI industry, which are tapping into its cloud infrastructure resources to power AI assistants and agents that compete with Alphabet’s own offerings. “Right now, Alphabet earns more selling AI to its rivals than using it itself, and that gap should keep growing over the next few quarters unless its models change drastically,” he said.
This has become a source of growing tension within the cloud infrastructure market, said Forrester Research analyst Tracey Woo. Though demand appears strong, there are questions about how much of that demand reflects broader enterprise adoption versus the concentrated spending of a handful of AI firms, she explained.
At least consumer adoption of Google’s AI seems to be growing. Chief Executive Sundar Pichai (pictured) told analysts that the Gemini app reached more than 1 billion users globally for the first time during the quarter, making it the fastest-growing product in the company’s history. He added that the company is also seeing strong demand for new models such as Gemini Argon. It announced two other new models this week as well.
Valoir analyst Rebecca Wettemann told SiliconANGLE that the big question for Google Cloud is capacity. The company is seeing enormous demand for its cloud services, she said, more than it can cater to, but in order to fulfill that demand it has to keep on spending. “But can Alphabet build fast enough to meet that demand, and at what cost as its free cash flow drops?” she asked.
Alphabet continues to fuel much of its AI infrastructure buildout using the revenue derived from its traditional search engine business, but investors are likely disappointed to see the company came up short there, too. Search revenue rose 12% in the quarter, to $63.35 billion, trailing the Street’s $64.96 billion forecast. However, Pichai said the company’s investments in AI helped drive the highest search query growth rate in the last five years.
“The softer search performance is significant because it highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses,” Woo said. “As hyperscalers continue to expand infrastructure at an unprecedented pace, enterprises will benefit from greater choice, increased competition and more pressure on providers to demonstrate value. The next phase of the market will be defined less by who can build the most AI capacity and more by who can help customers generate sustainable business outcomes from it.”

articles.title: The Sony Bravia Theater Trio ‘matches the cinematic scale of even the very biggest TVs’ — I was blown away by how well this three-bar system creates huge, spatial sound
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Although it’s tricky to say exactly which home audio pigeonhole Sony’s Trio speaker package belongs in, we can at least confidently file it under ‘brilliant’.
Reasons to buy
- + Exceptional sound quality for both films and music
- + Excellent adaptation to any room layout
- + It’s a perfect partner for really big TVs
- + Good expansion options
Reasons to avoid
- - It’s… reassuringly expensive
- - Needs optional rear speakers for a proper surround sound effect
- - Rather limited listening ‘sweet spot’
- - Limited physical connectivity
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8) review
The Sony Bravia Theater Trio is hard to define, but easy to love. Hard to define because its three-speaker (Trio, geddit?) package doesn’t feel quite like either a soundbar or a home theatre separates system; easy to love because it sounds amazing.
Sony’s own story of how the Trio came to be states that it was borne from frustration in its audio department about the inability of regular soundbar solutions — even high-end ones — to deliver sound with enough power and scale to convincingly partner with really big TVs. It was deemed that rather than creating a mammoth uber-long single soundbar to solve this problem, a much more practical solution would be to create a three-piece centre, left, right speaker package instead.
While the left and right speakers of the Trio system are larger and heavier than the sort of satellite speakers usually sold with or as options for regular soundbar systems, the package overall still looks startlingly compact overall for a system designed for king-sized TVs. The center speaker only measures in at 23.19 x 2.52 x 6.5 inches / 589 x 64 x 165mm, in fact. But you can, of course, place the wireless left and right speakers pretty much as far apart as your room allows, to help create a soundstage commensurate in scale with a monster TV.
I would quickly add at this point, though, that I personally don’t see the Trio as only worth getting if you have a huge TV. It’s actually so good and, as I’ll explain, so flexible with its sound that it’s worth considering by really any home theater fan who’s able to afford it.
Just throwing a trio of speakers at the big TV audio problem won’t in itself guarantee a satisfying home theater audio solution, of course. Especially when those three speakers only deliver dedicated left, right, centre and up-firing channels, rather than the many more channels that even some single bar soundbars can manage these days. The thing is, though, the Bravia Theater Trio’s channel count isn’t actually restricted to the the handful we’ve just mentioned. The brand’s revolutionary 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system is capable of adding up to 24 ‘virtual’ (created by psychoacoustic processing) extra channels of sound to the system’s ‘physical’ ones.
The 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system’s calculation process for figuring out where to place the sound from these extra virtual speakers uses a supplied, high-quality mic dongle that plugs into your phone to tailor the sound to your room layout. This works so well that you’ll be able to still enjoy a totally coherent, balanced, symmetrical soundstage from your Trio system no matter how awkward your room layout might be.
This room adaptation part of the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system becomes even more useful if you add a pair of Sony’s new Rear 9 optional surround sound speakers. Even when I deliberately set the the two front and Rear 9 speakers in the most unhelpful positions I could manage, the processing still somehow manages to put me at the heart of a colossal 360-degree soundstage.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I’ve let the Trio’s cleverest trick, though, lead me into discussing the system’s performance before I’ve finished going through every feature it has to offer. So let’s quickly get back to that.
While the Trio’s centre speaker’s long, slim design suits simple placement on a desktop under your TV, the left and right speakers sneak a narrow straight bit into their otherwise cylindrical shape to allow them to be wall mounted if that suits your set up.
Connectivity is passable. The highlight is an HDMI loop through that supports 4K/120Hz gaming feeds — as you’d hope with a sound system from the brand responsible for the PlayStation 5 — as well as the HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision HDR formats, but not HDR10+. And the HDMI output also supports the eARC system for taking in sound from your TV.
Unfortunately, the only other port is a USB slot that’s apparently only for software updates. A second HDMI input and an optical digital audio input would have been nice on a £1,999 home cinema system these days perhaps, but the Trio’s support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth (6.0) alongside the HDMIs will likely deliver everything most modern households will need.
These wireless options support direct streaming from Spotify Connect and Apple Airplay 2. On top of this, the system can also utilize Hi-Res Audio files and carries Sony’s redoubtable DSEE Ultimate AI upscaling system for making compressed audio sound better.
The latest Bravia Connect app for iOS and Android helps you set the system up, as well as providing an attractive and useful visual interface as a back up to the fairly basic remote control the system ships with. And it's particularly handy, given the Trio doesn’t carry an LED display.
Finally in the feature department, the Trio can play both the Dolby Atmos and DTS:X surround sound formats. In fact, it doesn’t just play them; it eats them for breakfast.
Any doubts about the Trio’s $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999 price evaporate in an irresistible bombardment of almost impossibly massive sound staging, levels of power, detail and impact that seem to go far beyond the system’s claimed 405W of confirmed power. It also serves up mesmerizing detailing and precision, and an immaculate tone that has more in common with a premium full separates system than a minimalistic three-speaker package.
The system’s remarkable drivers and even more remarkable 360 Spatial Sound Mapping processing create a soundstage that fills at least the front half of even very large rooms, with the physical existence of the Trio’s three speakers essentially completely disappearing. As well as being capable of creating an epic sense of space for big movie locations, the size of sound the Trio can produce means it's effortlessly able to ‘fill’ the screen area and match the cinematic scale of even the very biggest TVs.
Despite its immense and immersive size, though, the Trio’s sound doesn’t forget the small things in home cinema and music life. It can pull in the boundaries of its sound superbly when a soundtrack wants to portray a tight space, for starters. Also, every detail in a movie sound mix is beautifully rendered, no matter how small, and produced with exactly the correct weight relative to other mix elements.
There’s no hint of harshness or brittleness to any sound the Trio makes, no matter how high pitched or deep it might be. In fact, despite the center speaker’s small size, the system gives the impression of having no ceiling for treble sounds to butt up against and turn harsh, and no low-frequency floor for bass sounds to flatten off against.
The relatively hefty left and right speakers do most of the heavy low-frequency lifting without making deep sounds feel trapped in, hard edged or distorted. They’re reactive enough to serve sudden bass hits with impeccable timing, too, and have enough range in the low frequencies they can produce to stop rumbles becoming overwhelming or coarse.
This excellent bass performance is particularly welcome, given that bass has been a weakness of some of Sony’s current soundbars, and that the system is quite compact. Perhaps an even bigger worry is that Sony sells Sub 8 and Sub 9 external wireless subwoofer upgrades for the package, which always makes me wonder if there’s a weakness in the core system that such an add-on is required to fix.
The Trio can deliver hard, sudden impact sounds with proper venom and propulsion, while the soundstage remains balanced and authoritative even at high volumes, no matter how dense the content might be.
Sound systems that go as big and dynamic with film soundtracks as the Trio can aren’t always able to turn their hands effectively to music. The Trio, though, is at least as engaging with music as it is movies.
Even in native stereo mode, without any of Sony’s remarkable virtual surround processing in play, the trio of speakers deliver excellent stereo separation and vocal placement. Nothing sounds at all strained, no matter what type of music you’re playing or how dense a track gets. It retains its genuinely hi-fi feel, too, at higher volumes than you’ve probably ever heard your favorite albums before. And yet, at the same time, people with neighbors will be pleased to hear that its speakers are sensitive enough to deliver music compellingly even at low volumes, something many soundbars struggle with.
Dolby Atmos music sounds similarly refined. It's detailed without being forensic, but also enjoys a more three-dimensional presentation that includes height elements. And if you’re happy to take off your purist music hat, I’d also recommend you try stereo tracks — or, at least, relatively poppy or ambient stereo tracks — through its 360 Spatial Sound Mapping processing, which gives it a more spacious and surround sound feel. Certainly Sony’s ‘upmixing’ with this effect is much superior to similar modes attempted by most other home audio packages.
It’s a tough ask to find things I don’t love about Sony’s Trio system. But I’m paid to try, so here goes. First, for all its virtual speaker creating talents, it only creates a quite limited sense of sound coming from behind your seating position. This can be solved extremely well by adding Sony’s new Rear 9 extra wireless surround speakers — though, at $749.99 / £699 / $ 1,299 a pair, this upgrade isn’t cheap.
The left/right spread of stereo music strangely narrows slightly when playing music through the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping despite expanding in every other way. And finally — and possibly most frustratingly depending on how big your household is — the area you need to sit in after calibrating the Trio for the optimal 360 Spatial Sound Mapping effect is quite small. Though even outside of this sweet spot, it’s still gloriously easy to appreciate just how good the Trio’s overall sound is.
Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8) review: Price and release date
- Released: July 2026 (UK and Australia), May 2026 (US)
- $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999
At first glance the Trio’s $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999 price looks substantial for a three-piece speaker package. Samsung gives you a full surround soundbar package, the HW-Q990H, for just $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$1,499, after all. Once you’ve placed the Trio’s speakers wherever you want them to go, though, and run the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping system setup, the system reveals itself to be a pretty much separates-grade performer capable of partnering with a huge screen and even filling a big room.
Hitting almost $2,750 / £2,700 / AU$4,300 if you add the admittedly impressive Rear 9 speakers starts to look a bit of a stretch, but you could always add the rears later as funds allow. The out-of-the-box Trio won’t let you down in the mean time.
Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8): Specs
| Dimensions | Main bar: 23.19 x 2.52 x 6.50 inches / 589 x 64 x 165mm; left/right speakers: 6.3 x 13.27 x 6.5 inches / 160 x 337 x 165mm | 
| Speaker channels | 3.0.2 | 
| Connections | One HDMI input (with eARC), one HDMI output (4K/120Hz), USB service port | 
| Dolby Atmos / DTS:X | Yes/Yes | 
| Sub included | Optional extra | 
| Rear speakers included | No | 
Should I buy the Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8)?
| Sony Bravia Theater Trio (HT-A8) Scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | The system’s three-front-speaker approach enables it to deliver a sound appropriate to really any screen size, even really huge ones. Its processing and audio format support is excellent too. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | Despite the fairly compact size of its three speakers, the Trio package often manages to sound like a premium separates system | 5 / 5 | 
| Design | From the surprisingly compact shape of the center speaker to the gorgeously well-built cylindrical stance of the left and rights, the Theater Trio is an elegantly understated addition to your room. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Setup & usability | The speakers all connected with each other automatically during my tests, and provided you plug the provided mic into your phone and run the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping set up procedure, its speakers are extremely flexible when it comes to where you put them. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Value | The Theater Trio package’s price puts it above the vast majority of regular soundbars — but its sound is a cut above any regular soundbar, too | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You have a very big TV
The Trio’s package of separate center, front left and front right speakers was expressly designed to solve the issue where regular soundbars just don’t create a sound stage big enough to match the size of the pictures made by massive TVs (especially those of 85 inches and more).
You want fantastic movie and music sound quality
The Trio throws off the shackles of some of Sony’s current soundbars, using hi-fi grade speaker designs and up to 24 virtual speakers created by Sony’s amazing 360 Spatial Sound Mapping to craft one of the most powerful but also most refined, balanced and immersive soundstages I’ve heard from a one-box speaker package.
You have an awkwardly shaped room
A key part of the Trio’s 360 Spatial Sound Mapping involves adapting the sound of its real and virtual speakers to your room layout — and this process is so flexible that it can deliver a convincing sound stage no matter how awkward your speaker placement might be.
Don't buy it if...
You can’t afford it
There are some very good soundbars around for much less than the Trio’s $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$2,999 asking price - which rises to nearly $2,750 / £2,700 / AU$4,300 if you add the Rear 9 surround speakers. But if you can afford it, the scale and finesse of the Trio’s sound is a cut above those cheaper soundbar alternatives.
The small sweet spot is a problem
The Trio optimizes the sound stage created by its real and virtual speakers around what turns out to be a rather compact sweet spot. So if you have a big household to cater for, you’ll have to accept that not everyone will get the perfect experience — unless you all huddle up.
You want a sound system that can work as a switch box
The Trio’s limited connectivity prevents you from attaching more than one hard-wired source to it at a time.
Sony Bravia Theatre Trio (HT-A8) review: Also consider
Samsung HW-Q990H
If you can’t quite stretch your finances to accommodate the Sony Trio package, Samsung’s HW-Q990H soundbar system delivers a powerful and detailed full surround sound solution for $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$1,499. The Q990H crafts a remarkably full hemisphere of sound for Dolby Atmos and DTS:X soundtracks, but the Trio’s sound is more refined and flexible — and only requires you to house three speakers. Read our full Samsung HW-Q990H review.
Sennheiser Ambeo Max
Sennheiser’s most powerful soundbar delivers a remarkably large sound stage for a single-bar device, courtesy of the fearsome array of ultra-robust and punchy drivers it squeezes into its uncompromising chassis. This helps it get nearer than any other remotely mainstream single-bar soundbar to supporting really big screens like the Trio does. While it used to cost $2,999.95 / £2,199 / AU$3,999, too, it’s now widely available for $1,699.99 / £1,599 / AU$2,999. It still can’t ultimately match the scale of the Trio, though, due to the latter’s separate left and right speakers.
How I tested the Sony Bravia Theatre Trio (HT-A8)
- I used the Sony Trio as my main living room audio system for 11 days.
- Also tested in a second room with a different size and layout, and with a pair of optional Rear 9 surround speakers.
- Tested with 4K Blu-rays, CDs, streamed audio, and games, using all direct HDMI connection, eARC and wireless connection options
I tested the Trio as my main living room audio system for 11 days overall, as well as using it in a second room with a different layout for two further days. I also moved the left and right speakers (and the optional rears) to all sorts of awkward places to test the flexibility of the 360 Spatial Sound Mapping processing.
During the testing period, I fed the Trio system audio content from a wide range of sources, including movie soundtracks from streaming boxes and 4K Blu-ray players over HDMI; music from a CD player and the various music streaming services the system supports; and game soundtracks from an Xbox Series X. Key movies used were Blade Runner 2049, It Chapter One, Civil War, and Sinners.

In that time he’s reviewed hundreds if not thousands of TVs, projectors and speakers, and spent frankly far too long sitting by himself in a dark room.

articles.title: Souveränes ChatGPT? Mistral Large 4 soll China-Konkurrenz bei Coding- und Cyber-Aufgaben schlagen
articles.text:
Souveränes ChatGPT? Mistral Large 4 soll China-Konkurrenz bei Coding- und Cyber-Aufgaben schlagen
Nach einer dreiwöchigen Preview-Phase hat die französische KI-Firma Mistral AI die Gewichte für ihr neuestes Modell Mistral Large 4 auf Hugging Face zur Verfügung gestellt. Das multimodale Modell wurde auf 3.800 Nvidia-Beschleunigern trainiert und kommt mit einer Billion Parametern. Damit ist das Modell momentan noch zu groß für die Nutzung durch Hobbyist:innen mit Gaming-PCs oder einzelnen Nvidia-KI-Beschleunigern. Seit dem Ausrollen der Vorschauversion an „Mitglieder eines Early-Access-Kundenprogramms und spezialisierte Cybersecurity-Partner“, darunter ASML, Cisco, Crowdstrike, Microsoft und die European Space Agency, habe sich die Qualität des Sprachmodells durch Reinforcement Learning, also durch die „Belohnung“ des Modells bei der Ausgabe erwünschter Ergebnisse und das daraus resultierende Finetuning, nochmal deutlich verbessert.
Mistral galt ein Stück weit abgeschrieben, wenn es um das Rennen um die leistungsfähigsten Open-Weight-Modelle ging. Vor Mistral Large 4 veröffentlichte das KI-Startup das mittelgroße Modell Mistral Medium 3.5. Das wurde zwar als Flaggschiff verkauft. Laut der Analyseplattform Artificial Analysis blieb es in Benchmarks aber teilweise deutlich hinter der Konkurrenz aus China zurück. Auch die Öffnung der eigenen Compute-Infrastruktur für die Konkurrenz deutete an, dass die Nutzung der eigenen Modelle hinter den Erwartungen lag.
Mistral Large 4: Besser als die Konkurrenz von Qwen, Kimi und Co. aber genauso intransparent?
Genau diese Konkurrenz schlägt Mistral Large 4 laut eigener Angabe bei zwei Benchmarks. Auf dem Cybersicherheits-Benchmark CyberGym-E2E liegt es vor der China-Konkurrenz GLM-5.3 und Kimi K3. Beim agentischen Coding-Benchmark Terminal Bench 4.0 zieht es mit GLM-5.3 gleich. Zudem schneidet es mutmaßlich deutlich besser ab als Kimi K3 oder Metas offenes Modell Muse Spark Open. Eine unabhängige Evaluierung von Mistral Large 4 fehlt bislang allerdings. Vor Veröffentlichung der Gewichte lag die Preview-Version von Mistral Large 4 kostentechnisch bei 1,4 US-Dollar für eine Million Input- und 4,2 Dollar für eine Million Output-Tokens. Das ist deutlich günstiger als Kimi K3.1 Pro mit zwei respektive zehn Dollar und auf ungefähr dem selben Niveau wie GLM-5.3 über die offizielle API von Z.ai.
Leistung und Effizienz ist das eine, Vertrauen in generative KI, gerade hinsichtlich aktueller Cyber-Vorfälle rund um KI-Agenten, die von Wissenschaftler:innen zu bedenklichem Verhalten gepromptet werden, das andere. Im Rahmen eines Pressebriefings hat t3n Mistral mit diesem Problem konfrontiert. Auf die Nachfrage, ob die Firma sich vorstellen kann, deswegen statt Open Weight auf voll transparente Open Source zu setzen wie die Konkurrenz von Soofi oder Apertus, weicht Pierre Stock, Wissenschaftsvize des Startups, aus. „Ich denke nicht, dass KI eine derartige Blackbox ist, wie die Leute glauben. Seit es Reasoning-Modelle gibt, wird sichtbar, was die Modelle denken.“ Außerdem nutze man Überwachungs- und Entscheidungsmodelle. Damit wolle man die „Interpretierbarkeit und Transparenz“ seiner größeren Modelle erhöhen. Die Überprüfbarkeit von Reasoning-Schritten könnte allerdings in Zukunft deutlich schwieriger werden.
In den kommenden Wochen will Mistral auch kleinere, sogenannte quantifizierte Versionen von Mistral Large 4 verfügbar machen. Dazu sollen auch Modelle zählen, die auf Laptops oder Gaming-PCs nutzbar sein sollen. Um die Weiterentwicklung seiner Modelle und den Zubau von Rechenkapazität zu finanzieren, hatte die französische Firma erst im September 2026 drei Milliarden Euro frisches Kapital eingesammelt.

articles.title: FCC rebuffs TP-Link again as it attempts to sell Wi-Fi 8 gear in the US — FCC alleges inaccurate documentation and out-of-spec power levels for routers
articles.text:
FCC rebuffs TP-Link again as it attempts to sell Wi-Fi 8 gear in the US — FCC alleges inaccurate documentation and out-of-spec power levels for routers
“The FCC won’t let me be”
TP-Link has been trying everything in its power to gain conditional approval from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). According to a new Bloomberg report, the FCC is citing discrepancies in power levels in TP-Link routers as the latest roadblock on its path to selling new Wi-Fi 8 products stateside.
In letters dated October 15, 2026, the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology made some damning claims about TP-Link's reporting practices. Specifically, the FCC alleged that TP-Link "included false or incorrect information in its applications” related to equipment authorizations for four individual router models (including high-end Archer models).
For a company that truly needs to dot every "i" and cross every "t" when it comes to a Trump administration that is increasingly skeptical of TP-Link's past ties and motives, any perceived missteps are even more magnified. However, in addition to the alleged wonky product information provided to the FCC, perhaps more troubling is that three of the four routers under scrutiny also had higher-than-allowed power usage levels.
In addition to power limits, the FCC's testing regimen for routers includes evaluations of electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), radio frequency (RF) emissions, and national security compliance. The latter has been a big sticking point with the FCC and the U.S. Department of Defense given the proliferation of TP-Link networking gear in civilian and governmental capacities.
We reached out to TP-Link about the FCC’s findings and were provided with the following statement:
"Routine spot checks have been a standard FCC practice across the consumer electronics industry for many years, and individual product test results can occasionally vary.
TP-Link Systems fully supports the FCC’s Office of Engineering and Technology and its role of ensuring that all manufacturers adhere to prescribed specifications for their certified products. We remain fully committed to working collaboratively with the FCC to resolve any technical questions that arise — and if necessary, address any confirmed technical issues as swiftly as possible."
It will likely take a lot more convincing to appease the FCC, which has so far given TP-Link the cold shoulder. And it’s not just the FCC; members of Congress and multiple state attorneys general have filed their grievances with TP-Link over alleged consumer privacy violations and Chinese ties.
For its part, TP-Link has made some significant moves to get in the good graces of the U.S. government, even while competitors like Amazon, Asus, and Netgear have sailed through compliance checks to gain conditional approval to sell wireless products in the U.S. Besides moving its U.S. headquarters to California, the company earlier this month announced a $1 billion joint venture with Key Tronic to manufacture Wi-Fi 8 routers in the U.S.
Brandon Hill is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware. He has written about PC and Mac tech since the late 1990s with bylines at AnandTech, DailyTech, and Hot Hardware. When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

articles.title: Lenovo Launches ThinkVision T34WD-4v Ultrawide Professional Monitor
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
Lenovo Launches ThinkVision T34WD-4v Ultrawide Professional Monitor
Lenovo has added the ThinkVision T34WD-4v monitor to its Product Specifications Reference (PSREF) website. We now have the full specifications of the 34-inch ultrawide curved professional monitor first shown at IFA 2026. The new ThinkVision features a VA panel with 3440 x 1440 resolution, 1500R curvature, and a 48-120 Hz variable refresh rate. The display has 300 nits of brightness, while for response time it can operate in two modes: 4 ms in Extreme mode or 6 ms in Normal mode. As expected from a professional monitor, it covers 99% of both the sRGB and BT.709 color gamuts. The monitor also includes a 5 MP RGB+IR camera, dual microphones, and two 5 W speakers. The connectivity area is generous. Notably, the monitor doubles as a USB-C docking station offering up to 100 W of power delivery. It has three USB-A 3.2 and two USB-C 3.2 ports, plus Gigabit Ethernet. There's also HDMI 2.1 supporting 3440 x 1440 at 120 Hz, and DisplayPort 1.4. 
Additional features include an audio combo jack, a headphone hook, and a fully adjustable stand. Ambient light and time-of-flight sensors are also included. Lenovo initially indicated a December release following the monitor's IFA debut. However, broader global availability may extend into early 2027. The expected starting price for the Lenovo ThinkVision T34WD-4v ultrawide curved monitor is €599.

articles.title: SpaceX AI in talks with Mississippi regulators over data center issues
articles.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI hit with multi-million dollar fine for building Mississippi data centers without the right permits
SpaceXAI faces massive daily fines over unpermitted data center constructions
- Mississippi regulators say three SpaceXAI sites began work without required stormwater permits
- SpaceXAI could face $6.1 million in penalties across three Mississippi sites
- State officials are seeking daily penalties of up to $25,000
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI faces potential penalties reaching $6.1 million after Mississippi regulators identified alleged construction permit violations involving three data center facilities in the state.
State environmental authorities claim construction activities began before the company obtained the necessary stormwater authorization, exposing its subsidiary to substantial financial penalties.
It is now seeking penalties of up to $25,000 daily, with the company's preliminary financial exposure calculated across all three affected facilities.
Three Mississippi data centers face regulatory scrutiny
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality issued the enforcement notice to MZX Tech LLC, a subsidiary responsible for the company's local infrastructure.
The affected facilities include Macrohard and Macroharder, both already operational, while construction continues at a third computing complex known as Minihard.
Although the three facilities support operations around Memphis, Tennessee, their locations across the state boundary place them under Mississippi's environmental regulations.
A fourth computing facility sits within Memphis itself, where the company began developing its artificial intelligence infrastructure during 2024.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The alleged violations were disclosed through a regulatory filing submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission as part of the company's financial reporting.
SpaceXAI confirmed that it is cooperating with state environmental officials and discussing a possible settlement covering the alleged violations at all three locations.
The proposed arrangement would consolidate the regulatory matters into one agreement, although the company has not disclosed any finalized settlement terms.
Separate lawsuit challenges gas turbine operations
Beyond the construction allegations, SpaceXAI faces another legal challenge concerning gas turbines used to generate electricity at its Southaven facility in Mississippi.
The NAACP alleges that the company constructed and operated the power generation installation without securing environmental permits required under federal and state regulations.
The organization is seeking financial penalties and an injunction restricting turbine operations, arguing that the company's activities violated federal air pollution legislation.
Federal government lawyers attempted to dismiss the lawsuit, maintaining that the requested penalties and operational restrictions could threaten economic and national security interests.
However, US District Judge Debra Brown rejected that intervention, determining that federal enforcement responsibilities did not grant unrestricted authority over environmental litigation.
"The EPA’s role as a primary enforcer of the Clean Air Act does not mean that the federal government retains complete control over all Clean Air Act litigation," said Brown.
The decision permits the NAACP's lawsuit to continue without establishing whether the company's turbine operations breached the environmental requirements cited by the organization.
Mississippi has previously penalized developers for construction without stormwater permits, including Complete Oil Field Disposal, which received a $4,200 sanction in August 2024.
In February 2025, JS LLC was fined $10,200 after regulators identified unauthorized construction affecting approximately 10.44 acres.
SpaceXAI has faced separate environmental scrutiny over its Memphis power generation, removing 20 generators and obtaining permits for another 15 following complaints about unauthorized operations.
The company's potential $6.1 million liability across three Mississippi sites remains unresolved, with regulators still discussing a possible settlement.

articles.title: Deux semaines après Gemini 4 Argon, Google frappe déjà un nouveau coup avec Carbon
articles.text:
Des spécialistes de la cyberdéfense recevront cette semaine un accès à Gemini 4 Carbon, le modèle le plus performant de Google selon l’entreprise. Les développeurs et le grand public devront patienter jusqu’à ce que Google termine le réglage de ses garde-fous.
Du côté de Mountain View, on prend les devants, mais on se dépêche. Le 13 octobre, Google ouvrait Gemini 4 Argon aux utilisateurs de l’application Gemini et aux développeurs. Quinze jours plus tard, Google DeepMind dévoile Gemini 4 Carbon, un modèle pensé pour la cyberdéfense, de la recherche de failles jusqu’à leur correctif. D’après Reuters, Google accélère la course contre OpenAI et Anthropic sur le code et la cybersécurité.
88,2 % sur SEC-bench Pro, des scores mesurés sans garde-fous
Pour dénicher des vulnérabilités dans de vrais logiciels, Carbon obtient 88,2 % au test SEC-bench Pro, selon Google. Il décroche 54,8 % lorsqu’il doit exploiter ces failles sur ExploitGym, et 71 % lorsqu’il doit les corriger sur CWE-bench. Google a toutefois mené ces trois évaluations sans garde-fous, alors que les premiers utilisateurs recevront un modèle bridé.
En interne, Carbon produit du code sécurisé avec un taux de réussite plus de deux fois supérieur à celui d’Argon. L’équipe de Chrome a aussi obtenu de lui des correctifs de bonne qualité plus de dix fois plus souvent qu’avec le grand modèle d’un autre laboratoire. Mais bien sûr, fidèle à ses habitudes, Google garde le nom de ce concurrent secret. Notons que tous ces chiffres viennent de Google, et aucun organisme indépendant ne les a encore vérifiés.
L’entreprise ouvre Carbon cette semaine à une partie des défenseurs en cybersécurité, avant d’élargir l’accès à d’autres partenaires de confiance via son programme Fairwind. Google soumet aussi Carbon au dispositif volontaire du gouvernement américain, qui évalue les modèles avant leur sortie.
Moins de tricheries le tarif de lancement d’Argon
Carbon prend la tête de la version 5.0 de l’Intelligence Index d’Artificial Analysis, avec un score de 59. Pendant son entraînement, Google a traqué les raccourcis que prennent certains modèles pour réussir un test sans faire le travail demandé. Sur Terminal-Bench 4.0, Carbon n’a réussi aucune tricherie, et il n’a tenté de tricher que dans 0,4 % des cas. Chez les équipes de Google qui codent avec lui, les alertes graves de désalignement ont diminué de près de 80 %.
Lors des tests d’injection de prompt indirecte de Gray Swan, aucune attaque n’a fonctionné contre Carbon, contre 0,7 % de réussite avec Argon. D’après les tests internes de Google, le modèle avance environ deux fois moins d’affirmations sans preuve que son prédécesseur.
Les clients paieront Carbon au tarif de lancement d’Argon, 2 dollars par million de tokens en entrée et 10 dollars en sortie. Ces prix doubleront à la fin de cette période, à 4 et 20 dollars. Google promet le modèle aux autres utilisateurs « dès que possible », and that's all, folks !

articles.title: Pine Labs sees 6.5x growth in net profit in Q2 FY27
articles.text:
Pine Labs sees 6.5x growth in net profit in Q2 FY27
In its international business, which spans more than 22 markets, revenue from Southeast Asia (SEA) grew by around 40% year-on-year, while its UAE business crossed one lakh daily transactions, the company said.
Fintech company Pine Labs reported a 6.5x rise in net profit to Rs 38.6 crore in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 24% year-on-year to Rs 806 crore.
The fintech company's net profit stood at Rs 6 crore in the same quarter last fiscal, while revenue was Rs 650 crore.
"Q2 was an all-round quarter - growth across acceptance and issuing, 15% of revenues from global markets, and 14% from products launched only in the last two years," said Amrish Rau, CEO, Pine Labs.
According to Pine Labs, it now processes more than 25 million transactions a day across businesses, up from over 22% on a year-on-year basis.
Pine Labs said its online payments business grew by over 45% year-on-year, while gross transaction value (GTV) rose 140%, driven by expansion into agentic commerce, cross-border payments, small and medium businesses (SMBs), and government segments.
In its international business, which spans more than 22 markets, revenue from Southeast Asia (SEA) grew by around 40% year-on-year, while its UAE business crossed one lakh daily transactions, the company said.
Pine Labs also said AI agents now contribute to around 89% of code changes. The company plans to reinvest the resulting efficiency gains into new products, geographies and categories while maintaining a strong EBITDA profile.
According to Pine Labs it is stepping up brand investments to position itself as the default commerce infrastructure for the global south.
"The opportunity set in front of us is widening, not narrowing," said Rau. "A wider set of new products this quarter, 10 lakh soundboxes committed over the medium term, agentic commerce live on a top Indian marketplace, and a UPI monetisation window opening up — this is the time to build.”
