articles.title: Floods, Fires and Blackouts: A Disaster Recovery Plan for a Business With One Server - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Understanding the Stakes for Small Businesses
Disasters strike without warning, and for businesses operating with a single server, the impact can be catastrophic. Floods, fires, and blackouts not only threaten physical infrastructure but also jeopardize critical data and operational continuity. According to a report by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), 40% to 60% of small businesses never reopen after a disaster. This alarming statistic highlights the importance of having a robust disaster recovery plan tailored to businesses with limited IT resources.
For small businesses with only one server, the stakes are even higher. Unlike larger companies with distributed systems and multiple data centers, a single-server setup represents a single point of failure. If that server goes down, the entire business can grind to a halt. This makes it critical to understand the risks and prepare accordingly with a comprehensive disaster recovery plan.
Why a Disaster Recovery Plan is Non-Negotiable
At the core of any disaster recovery strategy lies the ability to restore operations swiftly and efficiently. For a business with one server, downtime translates to total business interruption, loss of customer trust, and potential financial ruin. A disaster recovery plan is a documented, structured approach that ensures a business can recover data, maintain continuity, and resume normal operations after an incident.
The challenge is magnified for small businesses because they often lack the redundancy and resources available to larger enterprises. This makes it essential to adopt best practices and expert guidance to put a resilient plan in place. Leveraging Crumbacher’s disaster recovery insights can provide invaluable perspectives on how to build a plan that minimizes downtime and data loss.
Key Components of a Disaster Recovery Plan for Single-Server Setups
Risk Assessment and Business Impact Analysis
Begin by identifying the most significant threats-be it floods, fires, or power outages-and evaluate how each could disrupt your operations. Conducting a business impact analysis (BIA) helps prioritize which systems and data require the fastest recovery, ensuring resources are allocated effectively. For example, customer databases and financial records are often critical and should be prioritized in recovery efforts.
Data Backup and Offsite Storage
Backing up your data regularly is fundamental. However, backups stored onsite can be equally vulnerable during disasters. Implementing offsite or cloud-based backups ensures your data remains safe even if your physical server is compromised. Statistics show that 60% of small businesses that suffer data loss close within six months, underscoring the critical nature of secure backups.
Offsite backups can be achieved through various means: cloud storage services, physical backup drives kept in a separate location, or even automated backup solutions that sync data to remote servers. The key is to ensure backups are frequent, complete, and easily accessible when needed.
Power Protection and Redundancy
Blackouts can halt server operations instantly. Investing in uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and surge protectors can provide critical power during outages and protect hardware from electrical damage. Additionally, planning for redundant internet connections or alternative communication channels can help maintain connectivity during emergencies.
Power disturbances are a common cause of server failures. According to the U.S. Department of Energy power outages cost businesses over $150 billion annually in lost productivity.
Using a UPS system allows your server to remain operational long enough to perform an orderly shutdown or switch to backup power. For longer outages, businesses might consider generators or cloud-based failover solutions to keep critical systems online.
Clear Recovery Procedures and Roles
Document detailed recovery steps and assign responsibilities to ensure a smooth response when disaster strikes. Knowing who does what, and when, reduces confusion and accelerates recovery times. This includes specifying who is responsible for restoring backups, contacting IT support, communicating with customers, and managing the physical site.
Creating a disaster recovery team, even if small, ensures accountability and faster decision-making. It is also important to keep contact lists updated and ensure that all team members are trained and familiar with the recovery plan.
Testing and Continuous Improvement
Regularly test your disaster recovery plan to identify gaps and improve your response. Simulated drills and reviews help ensure that all stakeholders are prepared and that the plan evolves with changing business needs.
A disaster recovery plan is not something to create once and forget. Periodic testing reveals issues such as incomplete backups, outdated procedures, or personnel changes that impact effectiveness. Incorporating lessons learned from tests builds resilience over time.
Leveraging Expert Support to Strengthen Your Plan
For businesses with limited IT staff or expertise, partnering with external specialists is invaluable. The experts at Endurance IT offer tailored support, combining technical know-how with practical disaster recovery strategies that align with your business requirements. Their expertise can help optimize backup solutions, configure failover mechanisms, and establish recovery protocols that minimize downtime.
Working with experts can also help small businesses stay compliant with industry regulations and adopt best-in-class security measures to protect data integrity during recovery.
Preparing for Environmental Disasters: Floods and Fires
Physical threats like floods and fires require specific precautions. Elevating server equipment off the ground, using fire-resistant cabinets, and securing the server room are practical steps to mitigate damage. Additionally, maintaining an up-to-date inventory of hardware and software assets expedites insurance claims and replacement processes.
Floods can cause severe damage to electrical equipment and lead to data loss. According to the National Flood Insurance Program, floods cause over $3 billion in property damage annually in the U.S.
Fire safety measures include installing smoke detectors, fire suppression systems, and ensuring proper ventilation in server rooms. It is also important to have clear evacuation routes and protocols for protecting data during emergencies.
The Role of Cloud Solutions and Virtualization
Cloud technologies have revolutionized disaster recovery by offering scalable, cost-effective options for data protection and system redundancy. Virtualizing your server environment enables quicker recovery times and greater flexibility, reducing the reliance on physical hardware. Implementing cloud backups or hybrid solutions can provide an additional safety net, ensuring critical business systems remain accessible even if your primary server fails.
Cloud providers typically offer geographically distributed data centers, which means your data is stored in multiple locations, reducing the risk of loss from localized disasters. Additionally, cloud-based disaster recovery as a service (DRaaS) allows businesses to failover to backup environments within minutes.
Virtualization also allows you to create snapshots of your server environment, enabling rapid restoration to a previous state. This is especially useful when recovering from ransomware attacks or system corruption.
The Importance of Communication During a Disaster
Effective communication is often overlooked but is critical during recovery efforts. Establishing a communication plan that includes internal updates, customer notifications, and vendor coordination ensures transparency and helps manage expectations during downtime.
Timely and clear communication helps maintain customer trust and minimizes reputational damage. It also allows employees to understand their roles and reduces confusion during a crisis. Utilizing multiple communication channels-such as email, phone trees, and social media—can increase message reach.
Conclusion: Building Resilience with Proactive Planning
A disaster recovery plan is not just a technical requirement; it’s a business imperative, especially for companies relying on a single server. By assessing risks, implementing robust backups, securing power sources, and involving experts, you can safeguard your business against floods, fires, blackouts, and other disruptions. Remember, the goal is not only to survive a disaster but to emerge stronger and more resilient.
Investing time and resources into your disaster recovery planning today will pay dividends in business continuity and peace of mind tomorrow. With a well-crafted plan in place, your business can face unexpected challenges with confidence and continue to serve your customers without interruption.

articles.title: La huelga de maquinistas paraliza Renfe en Madrid: líneas cerradas y servicios mínimos en duda
articles.text:
Un día después del accidente en Urda (Toledo) que ha provocado la muerte de 69 personas, los maquinistas se han mantenido firmes en su jornada de huelga. Reclamando mayores medidas de seguridad, consideran que hay más motivos que nunca para realizar estos paros. Unos paros que, especialmente en Madrid, han provocado el colapso de algunas líneas.
La huelga. El pasado 16 de octubre, el Sindicato Español de Maquinistas Ferroviarios (SEMAF) convocó una huelga de 24 horas asegurando que "tras registrar la Comisión de Conflictos el pasado 5 de octubre, en la reunión de hoy la conclusión que hemos obtenido es clara: todo sigue igual de paralizado que en el mes de mayo".
Entre las reivindicaciones que se han puesto encima de la mesa, Semaf recalcaba la necesidad de "Trabajar con trenes fiables y seguros: Exigimos soluciones técnicas reales y definitivas a los problemas de seguridad y fiabilidad que arrastramos en el material rodante".
Por lo tanto, han considerado que había más motivos que nunca para parar, después de que un fallo en el sistema LZB y la posterior gestión desde el centro de control de Atocha (conocido como CRC) provocara el conocido accidente grave en Urda (Toledo) con decenas de muertos.
Los paros. Aunque la huelga ha llamado a los paros generalizados en los servicios de la alta velocidad, larga y media distancia y Cercanías, los servicios mínimos obligaban a un gran respaldo.
Renfe señalaba que quedaban del siguiente modo:
- En Cercanías los servicios mínimos se establecen por franjas horarias, siendo del 75% en horario punta, y del 50% durante el resto del día
- En Media Distancia se establece una media del 65% de los servicios habituales
- Alta Velocidad/Larga Distancia se establece una media del 73% de los servicios habituales
- En Mercancías, el porcentaje es del 26% del servicio programado
¿Qué ha pasado? Los paros han seguido adelante pero las afecciones no han sido las mismas en todos los lugares. El Periódico señala que en Cataluña el impacto ha sido inferior al que se esperaba porque los servicios mínimos se han cumplido pero en Rodalies se ha registrado un 25% menos de afluencia a los trenes. La otra cara de la moneda han sido las interminables retenciones de esta mañana en la entrada a Barcelona.
En Madrid, sin embargo, se vive una situación muy diferente. Cercanías ha informado que las líneas C-1, C-3, C4b, C5, C-8a y C-8b han sido suspendidas. Y que el resto de líneas tiene afecciones muy importantes. Esto implica que hay servicios mínimos que no se están cumpliendo porque por las líneas mencionadas no circulan los trenes.
Las posturas. Cuando Renfe anunció los servicios mínimos que se emplearían durante el día de hoy acusaron a Semaf de convocar "una huelga injustificada reivindicando cuestiones que exceden el ámbito competencial de Renfe", asegurando que "se han cumplido de manera íntegra todas las obligaciones asumidas, tal como se ha informado en las diferentes reuniones de seguimiento del acuerdo desarrolladas en abril, mayo y octubre".
Al contrario, desde Semaf contestan que esto no se ha producido y a preguntas de Xataka consideran que el seguimiento de la huelga ha sido un éxito pero rechazan que no se hayan estado cumpliendo servicios mínimos. "No tenemos constancia, puede que algún compañero esté tomando mayores precauciones si lo considera necesario", nos han señalado cuando hemos preguntado a este respecto.

articles.title: Engie prévient ses clients après un vol de données personnelles, attention aux faux conseillers
articles.text:
Dans l'outil commercial des démarcheurs partenaires d'Engie, des pirates ont récupéré les coordonnées et les références de contrat de clients français. Le fournisseur appelle les personnes concernées à se méfier des faux conseillers.
Engie a commencé à prévenir un par un les clients touchés, tous en France. D'après L'Usine Digitale, des inconnus ont consulté leurs nom et prénom, leurs adresses postale et électronique, leur numéro de téléphone, leur identifiant client et leur numéro de contrat. Les courriers consultés par BleepingComputer ajoutent à la liste la référence du point de livraison d'électricité (PDL) ou du point de comptage et d'estimation du gaz (PCE). Aucune donnée bancaire n'a fui, assure Engie, mais ces numéros figurent sur chaque facture et donnent à un faux conseiller l'air d'avoir votre dossier sous les yeux.
L'outil de prospection des partenaires d'Engie piraté
Les pirates ont pioché dans une plateforme externe, utilisée par les partenaires mandatés par Engie pour prospecter et vendre ses offres d'électricité et de gaz. Le système informatique du groupe a été épargné, et les données consultées « se limitent aux coordonnées des clients ainsi qu'à certaines données relatives à leur contrat d'énergie », a précisé le fournisseur à L'Usine Digitale.
Dès qu'il a repéré ces consultations anormales, Engie a coupé les accès concernés et lancé des investigations techniques afin de mesurer l'ampleur de l'incident. Le groupe dit aussi avoir prévenu les autorités, et le RGPD l'oblige à notifier la CNIL dans les 72 heures après la découverte d'une fuite de données personnelles.
Le fournisseur n'a donné ni le nombre de clients concernés ni le nom du partenaire dont l'outil a été piraté, relève JeChange. Lors de la publication de l'article de BleepingComputer, aucun groupe de pirates n'avait affirmé être à l'origine de l'attaque. Cela ressemble presque trait pour trait à l'incident survenu en 2024, quand sa filiale Engie Home Services avait confirmé le vol des nom, prénom et adresse postale de quelques centaines de clients.
Les arnaques possibles avec un PDL et un numéro de contrat
Le PDL et le PCE identifient le compteur d'électricité ou de gaz d'un logement. Ces deux références apparaissent sur chaque facture, et un fournisseur les réclame à chaque souscription de contrat. Muni de ces numéros, un faux conseiller peut annoncer une régularisation de facture ou un remboursement à valider, puis demander un IBAN ou un paiement par carte. Dans son courrier, le fournisseur prévient d'ailleurs que des personnes malveillantes pourraient se présenter en son nom ou au nom de l'un de ses partenaires, selon FrenchBreaches.
Les pirates peuvent aussi imiter le message d'alerte d'Engie sur cette fuite, avec un lien vers une copie de l'espace client conçue pour voler votre mot de passe. Le groupe rappelle qu'il ne demande jamais de mot de passe ni de coordonnées bancaires par message ou par téléphone.
Au moindre doute, mieux vaut raccrocher et rappeler soi-même le service client au numéro inscrit sur une facture ou dans l'espace client, jamais à celui donné par l'interlocuteur. Le numéro qui s'affiche à l'écran ne prouve rien non plus, car les escrocs savent usurper celui d'une entreprise.
Si vous avez communiqué vos coordonnées bancaires à un interlocuteur douteux, prévenez sans attendre votre banque, qui peut bloquer la carte ou surveiller les prélèvements à venir. Vous pouvez aussi porter plainte en cas de préjudice, et la plateforme 17Cyber oriente les victimes vers la police ou la gendarmerie en fonction de leur situation.
Ces fuites touchent une large part des Français. Dans le baromètre réalisé par Ipsos pour Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr en mai 2026, 45 % des 18-75 ans disaient avoir été informés d'une fuite de leurs données en un an, d'après Selectra. Depuis le 1er octobre, la CNIL et la plateforme publient ensemble une liste de gestes à faire, du premier jour jusqu'à un mois après la fuite. Résilier son contrat chez Engie n'effacerait pas pour autant les informations récupérées par les pirates.

articles.title: F5 and Oracle plan to bring F5 web app and API protection to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
F5 and Oracle plan to bring F5 web app and API protection to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
Application security and delivery company F5 Inc. and Oracle Corp. today revealed plans to bring F5’s protection for web applications and application programming interfaces to customers running workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
For now the arrangement rests on a nonbinding memorandum of understanding between the two. Under the plan, F5’s security technology would be integrated directly into OCI.
Oracle and F5 are aiming it at organizations that need to defend critical applications and APIs against sophisticated attacks without specialized security expertise in house. Security, application and platform teams would do that work from inside a cloud environment they already know.
John Maddison, F5’s chief marketing officer, said attacks powered by artificial intelligence “can find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than enterprises can patch them.” Oracle and F5 see AI runtime defense as the answer for cloud teams, he said, because it allows virtual patching that shields exposed systems until the permanent fixes are in place.
Customers need application and API protection that “keeps pace without adding operational complexity,” according to kp Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of global partnerships at Oracle. He said F5’s application security expertise would come into OCI backed by Oracle’s cloud infrastructure and support.
Oracle already has a web application firewall service of its own on OCI. Bots, application-layer distributed denial-of-service attacks and SQL injection are among the threats that product is built to stop. The service can also protect applications hosted on premises or in other clouds. The announcement did not say how F5’s technology would fit alongside Oracle’s firewall.
The two vendors go back a long way. F5 says it has worked with Oracle since 2001, mostly on application delivery for Oracle software such as E-Business Suite and PeopleSoft. Oracle also uses F5 products for some of its own enterprise applications and cloud services.
F5 now groups its delivery and security products, BIG-IP and NGINX among them, under the Application Delivery and Security Platform. The platform’s AI Guardrails and AI Red Team tools formed the F5 side of a partnership with data security company Forcepoint LLC in March. The Oracle announcement came a day after F5 reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $917 million, up 13% from a year earlier.
Neither company gave a date for the OCI integration to become available or named the F5 products it would include. Pricing went unmentioned. A disclaimer in the release adds that the collaboration does not create a partnership or joint venture between F5 and Oracle.

articles.title: Ford's $30K Fathom electric pickup can be used as your home's battery backup without a separate inverter
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Despite discontinuing the F-150 Lightning, Ford isn't abandoning the electric pickup market altogether. The company plans to re-enter the segment in 2027 with the Fathom, a mid-size electric truck expected to cost less than $30,000. It will feature bidirectional charging, allowing it to supply power to homes or external devices and equipment. This capability could turn the truck into a backup power source for households and businesses.
According to Ford, the Fathom's bidirectional charging feature will rely on a built-in inverter, eliminating the need for the expensive 80A wall-mounted unit required by the F-150 Lightning. The inverter will convert power from the truck's battery into AC electricity, supplying up to 10 kW to a home. This would allow the EV to serve as an emergency power source during blackouts.
However, this feature won't be free. Owners will still need to purchase Ford's Home Power Station and second-generation Home Backup Panel to send power back to the grid. That said, the Power Station will cost around 50% less than the $1,310 Charge Station Pro required by the Lightning, while the new backup panel will be 60% cheaper than its predecessor's $5,000 asking price.
Assuming Ford sticks to its pricing estimates, the second-generation backup panel should cost around $2,000. That would put the additional cost of using the Fathom as an emergency home power source at roughly $2,500 to $3,000. While that's still a substantial expense, it's cheaper than comparable solutions currently offered by American automakers.
Ford also announced that it is working with several US and Canadian utility companies to implement its vehicle-to-grid pilot program. The company added that the proposed system complies with existing regulatory standards, including UL 1741 for inverters and related power-conversion equipment, IEEE 1547 for connecting distributed energy resources to the electrical grid, and SAE J3068 for electric vehicle power transfer using a three-phase-capable coupler.
Built on Ford's new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, the Fathom represents the company's next big bet on EVs. Ford has described the truck as its 21st-century "Model T moment," one that could help it compete more effectively against the influx of affordable Chinese EVs. The company has announced a starting price of $28,350, with production expected to begin at its Louisville factory next year.

articles.title: Galaxy Buds 4 com ANC cai para quase metade do preço em oferta • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Buds 4 com ANC cai para quase metade do preço em oferta
Galaxy Buds 4 trazem cancelamento ativo de ruído e áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits; fones sem fio da Samsung recebem desconto de 47% no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre
Os Galaxy Buds 4 estão saindo por R$ 849 no Pix com cupom COMPRAFACIL no Mercado Livre. Os fones de ouvido sem fio da Samsung, com áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits e cancelamento ativo de ruído (ANC), alcançam um desconto de 47% sobre o preço original de R$ 1.599.
Um dos melhores kits de fones wireless da Samsung, os Galaxy Buds 4 contam com o recurso de cancelamento de ruído ativo (ANC), que filtra quase todos os sons externos. O suporte a áudio Hi-Fi (alta fidelidade) de 24 bits garante uma experiência sonora com grande foco nos detalhes.
O conjunto conta com assistentes de Inteligência Artificial (IA) como o Bixby da Samsung, Google Gemini e Perplexity, que oferecem funções por comandos por voz para acionar menus e realizar pesquisas. O Galaxy AI possui um tradutor automático de conversas, mas disponível para uso apenas em gadgets da linha Galaxy.
Outros recursos incluem o Voice Pickup Unit, que torna as chamadas de voz mais nítidas, e o equalizador adaptativo, que ajusta as frequências sonoras com base no formato do canal auditivo do usuário, a fim de personalizar a experiência sonora ao máximo.
As baterias dos Galaxy Buds 4 resistem a até 5 horas de reprodução com o ANC ligado e 6 horas com o recurso desativado. A de 515 mAh presente no estojo de transporte oferece energia extra para uma autonomia total de até 30 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante.

articles.title: Gemini superó los 1.000 millones de usuarios, pero las acciones de Alphabet cayeron cerca de 8% tras sus resultados
articles.text:
La aplicación Gemini de Google llegó a 1.000 millones de usuarios, según informó su empresa matriz Alphabet al presentar sus resultados del tercer trimestre. No obstante, los ingresos y las ganancias quedaron por debajo de lo que esperaban los analistas, y sus acciones cayeron cerca de 8% en las operaciones posteriores al cierre del 28 de octubre.
La empresa facturó USD 127.580 millones, un 25% más que un año antes, según CNBC. Los analistas consultados por LSEG, una firma de datos financieros, esperaban USD 128.220 millones. Es el ritmo de crecimiento más rápido desde 2021, pero no alcanzó la proyección del mercado.
La ganancia por acción fue de USD 2,12, frente a los USD 2,87 del mismo trimestre de 2025. Con el ajuste que usa Wall Street, CNBC la ubica en USD 2,67, contra los USD 3,02 que esperaban los analistas. La utilidad neta cayó a USD 26.170 millones, desde USD 34.980 millones.
El director ejecutivo, Sundar Pichai, definió el período como un “trimestre sólido” en el comunicado de resultados y afirmó que Gemini es “el producto de más rápido crecimiento en la historia de Google”. También dijo que la empresa va camino de registrar medio billón de dólares en ingresos anuales, según Deadline.
Más gasto que efectivo disponible
El dato que más pesó en la reacción del mercado fue el flujo de caja libre, es decir, el efectivo que queda después de pagar las inversiones. Resultó negativo en USD 9.070 millones, frente a los USD 2.700 millones negativos que esperaban los analistas, según CNBC.
El gasto en inversiones, sobre todo centros de datos y chips para inteligencia artificial, sumó USD 51.360 millones en el trimestre, menos que los USD 55.090 millones previstos por los analistas. Aun así, el efectivo que generó el negocio, USD 42.300 millones según BeInCrypto, no alcanzó para cubrirlo.
La ganancia operativa fue de USD 40.580 millones, por debajo de los USD 43.190 millones que esperaba FactSet, otra firma de datos. Las inversiones de Alphabet en acciones de otras empresas también restaron: en el tercer trimestre generaron una pérdida de USD 8.660 millones, tras la ganancia de USD 99.030 millones del segundo, impulsada por sus participaciones en SpaceX y Anthropic.
La nube se duplicó y la búsqueda quedó corta
Los ingresos de Google Cloud más que se duplicaron y llegaron a USD 30.700 millones, por encima de los USD 28.700 millones que esperaban los analistas, con un crecimiento de 103%, según Yahoo Finance.
La búsqueda, el negocio central de Google, facturó USD 63.350 millones, un 12% más, por debajo de los USD 64.960 millones proyectados. Pichai dijo a los analistas que las inversiones en inteligencia artificial impulsaron la tasa más alta de crecimiento de consultas en cinco años, según CNBC.
La publicidad en YouTube creció 9% y alcanzó USD 11.200 millones, según Deadline. La plataforma superó además los 150 millones de suscriptores de YouTube Music y Premium, incluidas las pruebas gratuitas.
Alphabet elevó su previsión de inversiones para este año a un rango de USD 195.000 millones a USD 205.000 millones, y según CNBC el gasto anual superaría los USD 300.000 millones en 2027.
Gemini 4 Carbon, el nuevo modelo de inteligencia artificial de Google
El mismo 28 de octubre, Google lanzó Gemini 4 Carbon, que lidera el índice de Artificial Analysis con 59 puntos, por encima de Claude Opus 5.5 de Anthropic y GPT-6 Astra de OpenAI. Por ahora, el acceso está limitado a un grupo reducido de especialistas en ciberseguridad a través del Programa Fairwind de Google, sin fecha confirmada para su apertura a desarrolladores, empresas o al público general.
Pichai afirmó que supera al modelo Argon, lanzado dos semanas antes, “en casi todos los ámbitos”, según CNBC.
Carbon se destaca en pruebas de seguridad informática y corrección de errores de código, aunque registra más alucinaciones que su predecesor, Argon, en tareas con datos factuales y queda por detrás de algunos rivales en tareas profesionales específicas.

articles.title: Nintendo Switch 2 Exclusives Already Booting on iPhone and PC, Days After First Jailbreak
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
Nintendo Switch 2 Exclusives Already Booting on iPhone and PC, Days After First Jailbreak
Less than a week after the Switch 2's first jailbreak went public, Switch 2 exclusives are already showing up on hardware Nintendo doesn't make. Developer Will Faust posted footage of Mario Kart World running on an iPhone 18 Pro through a private fork of nxnative, a project that runs original Switch games natively on Apple Silicon. That came a day after his macOS demo, which had missing geometry and wrong colors, so many people called it fake. Faust says the iPhone build uses just under 6.5 GB of physical memory thanks to a swap-like, file-backed memory setup. Switch 2 support needed extra work on NVN2, the console's newer graphics API, and Faust has said he won't release the code.
On PC, developer Sheepish got Splatoon Raiders booting in a private build of the Eden emulator. It now reaches character select, though it lags quite a bit, has no VSync, and is missing plenty of features. Sheepish credited AI-assisted development and hinted at a public release later this week. Centro LEAKS also posted that DK Bananza is running on PC, though only an image was shared, and it's unclear who is behind it.For now, these are early demos with nothing public to verify, and they don't show broad Switch 2 compatibility. The jailbreak itself is also tethered, with no kernel exploit or custom firmware yet. Still, the pace is surprising, and a Nintendo response seems likely, given that it sued the team behind the Yuzu emulator and a court recently ordered a Reddit moderator to pay $4.5 million over Switch piracy.
Sources:

articles.title: Bluesky blocks links to leaked DHS employee data as government seeks takedowns | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.
Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collective DDoSecrets were marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outlets broke the news that Homeland Security had been hacked.
TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked data sets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.”
Bluesky did not respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. West Coast business hours about the blocks. A Bluesky spokesperson told Wired that the exposed data violates its community guideline rules, but chose to block the link rather than taking down the posts. (We’ll update if we hear back.)
DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.
“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.
Homeland Security sends takedown notices
Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.
A search site made by journalist, maia arson crimew, no longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” which generally means that the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.
Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.”
CentralNic, which hosts the domain name, did not respond to a request for comment from TechCrunch about the takedown or whether it was instructed to do so by a government demand. ZeroFox also did not respond to a request for comment.
The Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up regarding the takedown notice affecting Icepick’s website.
Crimew also made a locally hosted version of the data, allowing anyone to access it on their own computer.

articles.title: SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that's a problem for America's space agency
articles.text:
For nearly a quarter of a century, Elon Musk and his essential partner at SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, viewed the United States government as El Dorado, the mythical city of gold.
Like machete-wielding treasure hunters, Musk and Shotwell hacked through a tangled jungle filled with lurking carnivores such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin, as well as bean counters and regulators. Over time, against long odds, the pair cleared a path for SpaceX to contracts at NASA and the US military. They sued when things did not go their way. They hollered about unfair playing fields. Most importantly, they delivered quality space products to the US government for less.
And so, after a while, SpaceX found El Dorado and a city of contracts.
Then they started winning everything. So much so that the relationship between the customer and contractor began to change. Slowly at first, but ever more quickly, SpaceX went from needing the US government as an indispensable customer to becoming an indispensable contractor for the nation.
The pendulum has swung so far now that SpaceX seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.
“I guess I am still in denial that there is a divorce pending,” said Lori Garver, a deputy NASA administrator during the Obama White House years who was instrumental in expanding the agency’s use of commercial contracts with companies like SpaceX. “I literally cannot wrap my head around a future yet where SpaceX stops flying Dragon and Falcon. Not yet.”
But the signs point to at least a partial breakup. Consider the following data points:
- SpaceX has told NASA it will stop flying Crew Dragon, the space agency’s only reliable astronaut transportation to the International Space Station, by or before 2030. Shotwell said in September that NASA should rely instead on Boeing for astronaut transportation. “We’re just gonna let them have some business,” she said of Boeing. “They should fly their capsule. The government paid a lot of money for that.” As a result, NASA is investing more in Boeing.
- Ars reported in October that SpaceX had stopped selling commercial launches on the Falcon 9 rocket for missions after the year 2028.
- SpaceX may also still stop flying Falcon 9 for NASA missions. In late October, during a meeting of NASA’s Safety Advisory Panel, Kent Rominger said if the US Deorbit Vehicle (a modified Dragon spacecraft) launches to the International Space Station after 2030, “it may require” a rocket other than the Falcon 9.
- Politico reported last week that SpaceX told the US Space Force it would not bid on three new launch contracts in the late 2020s that would have gone above and beyond its existing commitments to the US military.
- SpaceX previously provided “Rough Order of Magnitude” estimates, or ROMs, for launch costs to US companies building small landers for NASA’s Moon Base as part of the Commercial Lunar Payload Services program. But according to three sources, SpaceX recently told these lunar companies they will not provide launch services.

articles.title: The Canadian legacy of Resident Evil, 30 years later
articles.text:
There are few video game properties as beloved and iconic as Resident Evil. Since its debut way back on the original PlayStation in 1996, Capcom’s survival horror series has left an indelible mark on the medium through its signature mix of haunting atmosphere, tense gunplay, thoughtful resource management systems and ample B-movie charms. With over 200 million copies sold to date, it’s one of gaming’s biggest series, and that success paved the way for numerous high-profile multimedia adaptations, not the least of which being Constantin’s franchise of eight live-action films, including Zach Cregger’s recent eponymous hit.
But despite all of that fame, a lot of people don’t realize just how much of an impact Canadians have had on the Japanese series throughout its entire history. Indeed, from the very first game all the way to its most recent release, actors, directors, models, and other artists hailing from across the Great White North have played pivotal roles in shaping the look, sound, and overall feel of Resident Evil. (That’s to say nothing of the fact that most of the movies were shot in and around Toronto, including multiple from Milla Jovovich’s series and 2021’s oft-forgotten Welcome to Raccoon City, with many Canadian actors featured throughout.)
And so, for the 30th anniversary, we wanted to celebrate Canada’s many contributions to Resident Evil. To do that, we spoke to over a dozen series veterans who worked on everything from the early PS1 games all the way up to the modern photorealistic entries. Along the way, they gave rich insight into the recording and localization processes, the evolution of technology, the vast pool of artistic talent in Canada and much more.
This is the Canadian legacy of Resident Evil.
Wow, what a mansion!
1996’s Resident Evil is one of the most iconic and influential games of all time. It pioneered tense survival horror action. It presented, at the time, incredible 3D graphics. And its setting, the Spencer Mansion, was a masterclass in labyrinthine game design. All of this helped elite S.T.A.R.S. officers Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield’s journey to escape the zombie-filled mansion become an instant classic.
Equally as famous, though, is the voice acting, but not necessarily for the same reasons. In the early days of what would become its biggest series, the company tapped a group of English-speaking expat actors in Japan for both the live-action segments and voice dubbing. But even years later, much of this group would remain in relative obscurity, whether it was due to miscrediting (such as with Jill’s voice, who has often — but never officially — been linked to Alberta actress Una Kavanagh), people not wanting to be associated with the roles, or some having passed away, as was the case of Chris’ actor, Victoria, B.C.-born Scott McCulloch. As a result, this made it difficult to find the right people from this seminal game to include in this feature.
But there is one Canadian who was part of that very first RE who actually openly embraces the project to this day: Pablo Kuntz, who played the villainous S.T.A.R.S. captain Albert Wesker. After graduating from the University of Western Ontario, the Rosemère, Que. native moved to Tokyo at the age of 22 to become an English teacher. However, he soon got bored with that job and tried his hand at modelling and acting, taking on numerous gigs around Tokyo. Along the way, he met Hollywood actor Sergio Alarcon, who was also modelling in Japan, and through him was introduced to a production manager who was casting for a little Capcom game about zombies.
Pablo Kuntz: It was a mixture of wanting to see the world, having a little bit of a glimpse into the culture [from a
childhood friend]. I got a visa, so I could go there legally, and it just seemed like a good fit […] You don’t think too much when you’re like 20. [laughs] You’re like, “Okay, let’s do it, what have I got to lose?” […] Growing up in Quebec, being English first language, I always felt like it was like some sort of handicap. It’s like, if you’re not fluently bilingual, which I’m not […] you learn pretty young that you’re not likely going to get any sort of high position in Quebec if you don’t speak French perfectly. Unless you’re French Canadian, it’s kind of a clique there.
[…] I joined about five or six different modelling agencies [in Tokyo], and I got work right away, pretty much. It was just hustle, hustle, hustle, hustle […] And I remember making friends with this guy named Sergio Alarcon […] Literally at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, I was recording. I remember stealing some line from Q107, actually, when I was doing it, and I put this voice tape together because it was so cheap to rent the studio at that time of the hour, and I gave it to Sergio.
I don’t think they had a pool of 200 people. I really think it was maybe 20, 30 voices. I have no idea the number, exactly, but they knew what I looked like. They knew how old I was. Because Barry [Kjerde] looks like Barry [Burton]. In fact, his name is Barry. He’s Barry! So the Japanese mindset was more like, “Well, if that’s what he looks like, if that’s the height, and then he must sound like that.” They wanted to pair [these attributes]. So when I looked at the picture of Wesker, I was like, “Yeah.” Not that it looked like me, but it wasn’t not me. I started to see [it]. […] It was a small group, and it was hard to get into that voice group. It was tough because they all knew they got paid well, and there wasn’t massive competition. So I was really glad.
While the acting is infamously campy, Kuntz’s recollections of the recording process shed some light on why that came to be.
Kuntz: I remember just being by myself in the recording studio, just one mic. No real direction, that is for sure. I had the mindset of what they needed and what they wanted from TV commercials, which I had done a good year-and-a-half of. A lot of commercials, they’re not long; they’re sometimes eight seconds, and it’s this big emotion, like angry and then sad at the end. You had to overemphasize everything, because when you did that, it translated in a commercial setting. They always said, “More overaction, Pablo, more overaction!” So that was ingrained in us.
That’s just Japan. If you go to Kabuki or you go to see any other live show, they’re always doing that. So we just felt that was the right thing to do. Plus, the dialogue was very obviously just funny translation. Like, why don’t I just say, “Stop, don’t open that door!?” It’s “Stop it!” Why is that “it” there? It’s just totally weird, right? But there was no direction, so it was just, “Stop it, don’t open that door!” And I try to remember that one line why I did it the way I did it. Did I realize that I actually had a couple extra words? “Stop it, don’t open that door!” [laughs] Because the delivery is so corny!
I don’t know what I was thinking. I had the script beforehand, so it wasn’t like I was just going from zero right there. But I didn’t take it that seriously. I’m going to be very honest. I didn’t like read it on, going like, “Okay, I’ve got to get into persona now.” There’s no way. I was just thinking, “Okay, two-day job, I got my lines, see if I can isolate it.” In some situations, I remember doing a couple takes, if it was a long take. You know that last scene in Resident Evil, or close to last scene, where I’m in the hallway and I go [puts on deeper voice] “So, Jill!” That time, I’m kind of getting more warmed up. Because in almost any voice recording, the first few lines are often redone later on. You just get into it, and all of a sudden, “Can we do those first four again? Because it doesn’t sound so good.” But I never had that chance.
[…] It wasn’t like, “Pablo, this time, please….” Nothing like that. It’s nice when a director [does that]. Because in the TV stuff, we often got some direction. “Okay, Pablo, lips a little bit slower this time.” But not [on Resident Evil]. It just felt like one giant experiment. But it was a happy accident. Everything kind of just worked. I think the graphics themselves mimic the voices. They’re all pixelated, and somehow, because the characters are a little bit awkward on screen, the voice being a little bit awkward — it’s somehow a nice marriage there. [laughs] It was so honest.
[…] One person said the reason why your [Wesker] worked […] He didn’t sound necessarily like an evil guy. And I think that’s what was special about Wesker. Because I don’t think I really spent that much time realizing, “Oh shit, I’m actually kind of bad!” [laughs] So that kind of naiveté, the whole thing sort of worked in my favour. There was no hint of me being a bad guy from the onset of Resident Evil. Nobody thought I was a double agent at all […] Because as one person said in the chat, Wesker doesn’t think of himself as being evil. So why do you have to sound evil?
Because it was a brief gig among many, Kuntz never thought much of Resident Evil again and, after a couple of decades, had pretty much forgotten he’d even done it. He would later hold a number of jobs, from building websites for Japanese companies Nissan and Pasona to Unique Japan, his own business that sells certified high-quality Japanese swords. One day, during the COVID-19 pandemic, someone commented on one of his sword videos asking if he was Wesker from the original Resident Evil game, sending him down an internet rabbit hole to rediscover something he had done over 20 years prior. This led him to ultimately embrace the role and the community through interviews, videos and even streamed playthroughs of Resident Evil games with his son on his YouTube channel, Lexonal. But Kuntz admits that he wasn’t always sure if this was the right approach.
Kuntz: My first reaction was like, “Maybe I shouldn’t, because everybody’s making fun of this stuff.” […] I had every reason to just ignore comments and say, “I’m not gonna, what are you talking about?” But there was just a kind of sense of almost taking responsibility. There’s one thing I’ve actually taught my kids, and they know this straight up: if you make a mistake, you fess up to it and don’t run away from that […] That played a role. I think I just said, “Well, I did it!”
Plus, it bothered me a little bit that Sergio was credited. It’s like, “It’s not Sergio!” It still niggles me when I see a video. [laughs] I haven’t seen one in a long time; I think people have come around the fact that it’s me. It’s like, “I could say nothing, and then I’ll live with the fact that it’s always Sergio on here, or just take this time to go and say it’s me.” But I can honestly say I had no idea what that would lead to just by saying it’s me. I really had no clue that people were going to go, “Whoa!” And all of a sudden, I felt this tsunami of interest. I was all of a sudden doing interviews for a while there, Residence of Evil and a few others. But everybody was like, “Yes, we got him! We finally figured out who the guy is!” And some people were still going, “No, no, it’s still Sergio!” And I’m like, “No, it’s not Sergio! Stop with the Sergio crap!” [laughs]
From Tokyo to Toronto
Resident Evil 2 is notable for many reasons. Where the original game focused on the elite S.T.A.R.S. members, this 1998 follow-up stars two scrappy, fresh-faced protagonists: rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield. The sequel also introduced the ingenious “zapping system” in which decisions that players made as one character, such as taking certain guns or defeating specific enemies, would affect how events transpire in another campaign. And if that wasn’t enough, the sequel marked the debut of the classic RE “stalker” enemy that constantly pursues you, realized memorably here with the towering trench-coat-and-fedora-clad Tyrant, affectionately known as Mr. X by fans.
But it wasn’t just the game design that levelled up — so, too, did the voice acting. As it turns out, that was all thanks to a team of marvellous mutants. In the ’90s, X-Men: The Animated Series recorded in Toronto after Fox Kids had great success in the city with Beetlejuice and Dan Hennessey, the late voice director on both shows. Because all of the X-Men vocal talent was already in Toronto, Capcom opted to record X-Men vs. Street Fighter in the city as well. Susan Hart, a local voice director who had already worked with Hennessey on several X-Men episodes, ultimately took on X-Men vs. Street Fighter and, through that, Resident Evil.
Susan Hart (voice director, Resident Evil 2, 3, Code Veronica and many other Capcom games): The scheduler at the studio said, “I’ve got the person for you — just call Susan, she’ll help you.” So when I got the email — “Can you cast this for us?” “Yes.” “Can you produce it?” “Oh, yes!” “Can you voice direct this?” “Of course!” [laughs] It helped because I’d been in the studio before, and I’m comfortable being in the studio, both prior as a performer and being in there working with Dan. It also really helped that I was in casting, so I knew how to direct. I had done many feature films and animated series, so I was very comfortable working with actors. So I knew what a script looked like. I knew the process, and I understood the studio, how that worked, as far as working with the engineer, et cetera, et cetera. So we got started, and I was able to hire a lot of the original cast, and it just kept on coming.
Alyson Court (Claire Redfield, Resident Evil 2, Code Veronica and others, Jubilee in X-Men: The Animated Series): “[Fox] really liked the entire team that they were working with in Toronto, because Dan Hennessey directed Beetlejuice and then went on to direct the X-Men cartoon… They used the same studio, which back then was called Sounds Interchange, and then became D.A.V.E., and then Technicolor. It’s been through a bunch of different names. And it just recently got bulldozed, so that’s very sad. Very similar in a way to Capcom, where they went there for something specific. Beetlejuice was being done there because Nelvana was making it. Nelvana is a Toronto company, but then Fox took it over, and they really liked the team, so they wanted to continue.
And then there’s the fact that the Canadian dollar was lower, and our union fees are cheaper than SAG rates, so it was more economical. And at that time, X-Men and Fox and just the Saturday morning cartoon in terms of superheroes — that was not a thing. It was not popular, and Marvel was in the tank. So doing the X-Men cartoon was a huge leap of faith by the team that put it together and they didn’t really have much of a budget. So economically, I think that played a huge part in the decision to continue in Toronto. And also, the fact that they really loved the talent pool coming off of Beetlejuice. They were like, “No, this is going to be fine.”
They went through several rounds casting for X-Men, and there were a lot of people that were cast in the first place, and then they were replaced. Most of us were replacements, actually — I think after they recorded the initial pilot episode. They were all clearly very passionate about it, and a lot of the replacements were theatre people. They were like, “No, we don’t want people who just have a ton of cartoon experience because that’s not the tone that we’re going for.”
Susan Hart: Toronto has got a plethora of everything. We have film schools. We have theatres. We have improvisational houses. We have so much that the actors can experience and train in all different disciplines. So they’re not just in theatre. They’re also doing some film work. They’re also doing narration. We’ve got Shaw. We’ve got Stratford. We’ve got Soul Pepper. We have production companies from all over the world coming here and shooting. Our actors have got a huge amount of resources to satisfy all their acting itches, and they can perform in a multitude of different disciplines. That is what makes our talent in Toronto, specifically. I know in Vancouver there’s great talent, in Montreal, et cetera, there’s great talent. But right here in Toronto, we’ve got so many platforms for our actors to delve into and grow and become better and better at their craft.
Dawn of the dead
RE2 would be the first of several RE games that were recorded in Toronto. Naturally, this meant that it was a big learning process for all involved. The Canadian and Japanese teams navigated language and cultural barriers. Dealing with the technical limitations of ’90s hardware. Minimal communication about what the project even was. All of that is to say: having this veteran Canadian cast and crew proved invaluable to Capcom.
Susan Hart: They would send out what they needed, cast breakdowns, and so I would do all of that. At that time, when we first started, I think it might have been cassette tapes, not digital audio tapes. We would just do the casting. They’d give me the script. They’d send me the scripts — or sides, pieces of the script — and the character description. And the actors would come in, and they would have the script ahead of time, and I’d audition them, and then we’d send two tapes separately, just in case one got lost. And we sent them via FedEx. So they would get it, they’d listen to it, they’d get back to me if they didn’t hear what they wanted… If they wanted more, I would do it again. And then we would coordinate hours, days, that they would be flying in so I’d book the studio.
The scripts would arrive, but initially, none of the lines were in order. None of the scenes were in order. And initially, the scripts were not allowed out of the studio, so the actors would have to come a day before their booking and sit in the lobby and read the scripts and familiarize themselves with them, just because you didn’t want any of that stuff out there. So we did this for years, and it really was a great system. Initially, we had quite a few people from Capcom come out. I’d say about eight, and there was an interpreter there. And they were just so giving and just so pleased with how organized it was. And the actors coming in were just so kind. There was some broken English going on, but the laughter and the clapping and the camaraderie that was happening — it was really, really nice. And that happened for every game that we did. As the games went on, we started getting to digital audio tapes, less and less people came, and then, for a while, it was just a producer and R&D, probably, that were there at the end of it, when I stopped working there with them.
Alyson Court: They didn’t share really anything about [RE2]. It was the same people that had done the Marvel vs. Capcom game, where I met them to do Jubilee’s voice, but there wasn’t a whole lot beyond that. Even our contracts initially didn’t have the name of the game on them. That was something they did with all of their games. They came here and they came to Toronto and they did a bunch of games, but they were always very secretive on the contracts, which, really, you shouldn’t be. You do have to say what the job is. [laughs]
[…] At the audition, I was told that this character I was reading for, “Think of her as serious, it’s kind of scary, she’s looking for her brother. She doesn’t know anybody, and she’s sort of like Jubilee’s older sister.” [That’s] how it was described to me. “But it’s more adult and serious and that kind of thing.” And what was nice is doing X-Men: The Animated Series definitely gave those of us who had prior animation experience a whole different world to play in in terms of voice acting. Because they didn’t want Saturday morning cartoon characterizations. They didn’t want it for kids, they didn’t want it goofy; they wanted it with some gravitas and serious stories with consequences and people being killed.
They wanted that drama and that level of performance to come through, so I think that’s a huge part of why Capcom chose to sort of set up shop in Toronto for a number of years for so many AAA titles, because they had been introduced to a talent pool. We were all theatre trained, so we had this huge wealth of different mediums behind us and under our belts. So they had a really good talent pool to pull from.
Sally Cahill (Ada Wong, Resident Evil 2, 4 and Darkside Chronicles: It wasn’t so much that there was a lot of secretiveness regarding Resident Evil; there wasn’t a lot of buzz or talk in general. I think perhaps because it was still sort of in development. Things are likely very different today when actors hear there are auditions for Resident Evil! I was attracted to the project because though I had done cartoons and other voiceover work, this was my first major role in a video game. It was different, too; it was intriguing and fun.
[…] I remember meeting the creative team from Capcom at the initial audition and at the recordings. I think it really helped having Susan Hart there. Since there was usually a Japanese interpreter, it was often Susan I could see behind the glass in the recording studio in animated conversation with them. She was very good at communicating back and forth, and then coming on the mic and giving me short, clear direction. Susan Hart was great at that. She left room for our own interpretation as well. Actors love that kind of director.
Alyson Court: It was all very odd. I certainly had never played a game like what we were making, so I didn’t have that conceptually in my brain as to that’s what it could be. And we were pretty isolated during the recordings. We might pass each other, either [Leon actor] Paul [Haddad] and me, or occasionally [Sherry Birkin actor] Lisa [Jai] — I might see them out in the waiting room at the studio. But we were mostly alone in the booth, and there wasn’t a lot of communication because the bulk of the people who came over from Capcom were all from Japan. They spoke Japanese, not English. They had a translator there, but they were very quiet about things. They didn’t like to share information […]
It felt like this impenetrable wall. There was the language barrier, but there was a translator. But it’s just culturally so different, and the idea of sharing information, or why you don’t need to know, or whatnot — it was sort of like, “Why would we need to give information?” Down the road, I think they learned it’s important; you need to give as much information as possible to help [us] understand the nuances. Because for a lot of it, it felt like we were recording the same sections of script over and over again — or certainly the same scenes and dialogue, even though it would have a different scene number. And Paul and I just couldn’t understand what was going on.
[…] I think it got to a point when I would be like, “Hi, so is there a performance note? What is it that you want here?” And they’re like, “Why are you asking this?” I’m like, “Well, because we’ve done this five times already, so clearly you’re not happy with it!” [laughs] “So tell me what you want done differently.” And that was the one time during Resident Evil 2 where they all sort of chit-chatted and they’re like, “Oh no, this is a different scenario.” That was the most I could get out of them, and I was like, “Okay, whatever you say.” And by the time Code Veronica came around, I was like, “Now I get what you mean by ‘different scenario,'” and there was this level of understanding, and we could kind of joke about things and [be] more forthcoming with information.
Sally Cahill: There was nothing to reference it to. We were creating the people we were playing as we were recording with very little background or history. I had to make up my own secrets and ideas about [Ada] — at least that was what it felt like for me, which, looking back now, was actually a great gift.
Susan Hart: There was a process for a lot of the games. We would do the voices first, just the voices, that would go back to Japan. They would do their motion [capture] and their blocking. Then they would figure out, “Oh, we need that voice louder because we’re going to put the enemy further away, or we need that person softer. We need the voice faster.” So then we would come back with those. They would come back with those notes. So we would record the second time — “pickups,” if you want to call them that, or just change of script. And then that would go back, and then they would start working on their animation, and then in the animation, they would find that they were needing more “panic” because they had more explosives, or they needed more “despair” because they had more killings, or the guns were heavier, the equipment was heavier, so they needed more exertion.
So then they would come back a third time, and we would record those. And then a lot of the time, what we would do is they would come back after the game was completely finished, and we would just record the lips, so they would get the proper lip flaps. That happened a little later on, but I liked, initially, how we used our imagination for those things. And we had the creators there, so we used them to get started. And we had borders, of course, but we had a little bit more self-expression. We weren’t tied down to, “Well, it has to be this way because it’s like this and this and this and this in the picture and in the story.” We had a little bit more girth. We had a little bit more room. Not to say how they do it now is worse. It’s not. It’s just a different way of recording. And I liked that format, how we did that.
And then, as the years went on and the games went on, only some of the games did we do lip flaps. Other times they had it down pat. And in different recording systems than what they do in Japan. Like a lot of times, when they’re doing dubbing or records, they just have a big room with all the actors. They’ve got seven or eight microphones set up, and the director’s sitting there, “Go!” and they run up, do their line, they sit down, they run up and do their line and sit down. That’s a different way of doing things. They do that now here for a lot of dubbing jobs where they get the whole crowd in and they just get up for their line, which is good because then you can hear what the other actors are saying and so you can feed off of that. So it worked for everything. It worked for years. The new [way] works as well, so no sadness. [laughs]
Remembering Paul Haddad (1963-2020)
No conversation about the legacy of Resident Evil would be complete without Leon S. Kennedy. With his hunky good looks, lovably corny one-liners and penchant for riotous, over-the-top acrobatics, he’s easily one of gaming’s most beloved heroes. But while American actor Paul Mercier would provide perhaps the most iconic take on Leon in Capcom’s 2005 magnum opus, Resident Evil 4, the man who first gave voice to everyone’s favourite suave, roundhouse-kicking badass was the late British-born Canadian actor Paul Haddad.
He would only portray Leon in the original RE2, but the vulnerability and earnestness that he brought to the rookie cop proved enduringly popular. In his final years, Haddad fully embraced Leon and the Resident Evil community, who fondly remember him to this day. And when he tragically passed away in April 2020 at the age of 56, countless fans paid their respects, including Nick Apostolides, the main Leon actor since 2019’s Resident Evil 2 remake and a lifelong fan of the series. Decades later, Haddad remains a true RE icon.
Alyson Court: I was working with Paul since I was 14, 15. If people go digging through the “Paul Haddad Files,” there’s lots out there. You should look up a TV series called Road to Avonlea, he was on that. Just a beautiful, beautiful young man. We also did a cartoon together called Free Willy, he was the lead in that. [I had] tons of time in the studio working with Paul. Just a gem of a human — just a very, very sweet guy. I think you can hear it in some of the interviews that he did in the last years of his life. There’s that deep appreciation for the Resident Evil fanbase in particular. He was always lovely to work with. And then, when he got throat cancer, that was actually several years before his passing, and he actually went through it and managed to come out the other side. He went through so much because of what a strong, beautiful voice he had, and the idea of that being taken away from you… He went through a lot. But he was always a very kind and generous person to work with.
Sally Cahill: When I was first introduced to Paul Haddad, it was in a dark recording booth with a single light on my script and blackness all around. And then this very intense and amazing voice filled my headphones. It came very naturally for me to work with his Leon because his voice was very committed and compelling. He was always referred to, while I was working in the booth, as “Leon,” as I assume I was likely always “Ada” for him — not “Paul” or “Sally.” And we never met in person. Years later, we did speak on the phone. It was a strangely sweet moment to be chatting as Sally and Paul, but also a little poignant. He was not well then, but I had no idea we would lose him so soon. That’s why Resident Evil 2, besides being the first game I did, will always have a special place in my heart. Because when you play it, Paul is in the room again. And he always will be.
Susan Hart: Paul was very grateful. Paul was very talented. He researched his character, he felt his character. Paul had a real knack for taking the lines and just bringing them to life. And the energy — I will always remember his energy in the booth. I will always remember how grateful he was, and how humble he was, and how he just wanted to keep on learning. And that’s a good actor. When an actor is always open to learning new things, new ways of approaching and listening — those are all good attributes for an actor to have. And Paul had all of those, all of them. That’s what you’re feeling. You’re feeling his insides. You’re feeling that he cared, and that goes a long way with the character. And look where the character is now.
I’ll give you S.T.A.R.S.
Alongside Code Veronica, Capcom was toiling away at its third and final Resident Evil for the original PlayStation. And like Code Veronica, it directly picked up threads from the original game, with Jill and her fellow S.T.A.R.S. members being hunted by a deadly bio-organic weapon (BOW) known as Nemesis. It led to a more action-oriented premise while presenting a stalker enemy that was significantly more frightening than RE2‘s Mr. X. To bring Jill’s harrowing journey to life, Capcom once again looked to both X-Men and its own fighting games, ultimately casting the voice of Jean Grey.
Catherine Disher (Jill Valentine, Resident Evil 3): They were here in Toronto, Capcom, doing the Marvel vs. Capcom fighting games, and they wanted the original voice actors from X-Men on them. But it’s funny, because when you hire an actor for a principal role, and then you give them a secondary role, you get a big discount on the secondary role. And so, instead of hiring more than one female actor at the time on those fighting games, I did Jean, Jill, Psylocke, Spiral… I did Storm because Alison Sealy-Smith wasn’t on it yet. I did a whole bunch of those, and then obviously, not Jill at the very beginning. So that was their first foray in Toronto doing these games, and they stuck around.
And what they said to me [about Resident Evil] was, “Here, listen to this.” And it was the voice actress from the very first Resident Evil. All I heard was a recording of her voice, and they said, “Look, she was a non-professional actor in Japan at the time.” I think she might have even been in high school or something. And so they said, “Can you voice match this? Because we want to shoot it here.” And weirdly enough, I listened to it, and I was like, “Yeah, we sound enough alike. And I’ve done voice matches before. This is no problem.” And so they said, “Great.” And I gave an example, and they were like, “Perfect.”
And so when we started it, I was so aware that they might want an exact voice match that I kept stopping because when I do those kinds of jobs, they have a reference on file, or I make sure they do. And every once in a while, I go, “Hey, can I hear the reference?” And after like the fourth or fifth time, they were like, “You’re fine. Just do whatever you’re doing. That’s great.” So then I stopped worrying about that and just played the part. Because that intrigued me. Those other video games I’d done had all been fighting games, which are mostly grunts or like a few key phrases being thrown out. And this one [RE3] with the diary entries felt like much more of a fully formed character in an interesting situation, so that really appealed to me. And it sort of continued to appeal to me all through the recording. That character, she really felt real, like there was really something to hang on to and play with.
Disher recalls the direction that Hart and Capcom gave her.
Disher: There was a lot of direction given. I mean, yes and no. It’s not like they micromanaged me, but it was more because I had the script with the cues. But you need to know the circumstances of what’s going on. Like, “What am I doing here? Why is this line [here]? What’s going on?” And I forget what the script itself looked like, but that’s informationally what I want to know, and that’s information they can give. So there’s a real give and take there with the voice director. And so in the room, as I recall, we had Susan Hart, we had obviously the engineer, and there was an assistant, and then there were, I think, as many as three, possibly even four, engineers from Japan, game designers, and their translator. So when I had a question, it would always run through the translator to the game designers and then back. And it was a laborious process.
And also, I would do a line, and they were all on the other side of the glass. It was almost like meerkats. They were waiting for the line, and then as soon as I said it, they’d be on their computers like this [taps keyboard]. I was like, “What are they writing? What are they thinking?” And so often you’d do a line and then wait for feedback, and that would take a while to go through. And I remember laughing at one point because I had asked a question about something, or I was waiting for feedback after a line. And keep in mind, we would do take after take after take after take of lines. And also, every time, it almost felt like Groundhog Day because some of the lines were so similar to each other because, of course, it depended on choices that people made in the game.
But I do remember waiting for feedback on a line. They mute you, so I can’t hear what’s going on the other side of the glass in the booth while they talk. And I prefer that. I don’t want to hear anything anyone’s saying about me or my performance. Everything should come through the director, the voice director. So they would mute me, and then I would see the Japanese game designers talking animatedly to their translator, and it would go on for quite a long time.
And then they’d unmute me, and the translator would go, “Faster,” or something, and I’d be like, “Really? Is that all they said to each other?” [laughs] Or maybe he said that to the director, and then Susan would go, “Faster.” And I’m like, “That’s not everything [they] said!” So it was an interesting process, and it took longer because of the translation aspect of it.
I had no visuals. They had no artwork. I had no idea that she was wearing a miniskirt and tube top, fighting zombies. I only found that out when they came back to do some additional dialogue recording later on. I think I was aware that it was titled Resident Evil, but at some points, it was also referred to as 1.9. So there were layers of inscrutability; I wasn’t quite sure what was going on. Interestingly enough, we recorded it in the same studio that we had been recording X-Men, so it was a very familiar studio to me. In fact, we were recording there up until a few months ago. I don’t know if they’ve torn down the building yet at 49 Ontario, but that’s where we did X-Men all those years ago. That’s where they came back and started with X-Men ’97.
[…] I was in there all the time, and they would bring other actors. Like Carlos [Vince Corazza] would come in for two or three days, and Brad [Evan Sabba] would come. People would come in and out, and I got very lonely. I was really excited when they brought other actors in, because it took a long time. I think the fighting games we knocked off pretty quickly, but this, I’m sure, had at least 14 or 15 recording days that we did over the course of a few weeks. So it was a much more involved project, and I did go a bit squirrelly because there’s no window in that studio. And like I said, I didn’t know anything about it, and so I had all these questions about different lines and what the setting was. […] They were all extremely nice, and it was really fun. And I haven’t done another video game like that since, where I was the lead character and had all that stuff to do.
Susan Hart: One thing that was always so fun to do is when we had to do the zombies. Those were like extras. So if we had actors coming in and doing a role and said, “We’ll have a separate role. We’ll have you do a zombie.” It was just always so much fun because they’d have their tongues out and they’d kind of cock their heads and they’d put their arms up. And I just remember having so much fun doing those zombies, doing those little background sounds, background noises when they’re in the market, or when the soldiers were yelling or screaming for their lives…
Doing the layers of directing was a lot of fun. Even when the incidentals came in, which were the smaller characters, and a lot of times, they were more colourful characters. They would be the store owner, or the shop owner, or the driver, or something like that. Even those, I really enjoyed doing, and I took all of those roles as a director seriously, and did something unique with each one of those layers, so that one was just not hanging out, and then you had some drab at the back end. Everybody stood out.
Redfield reunion
One year after Resident Evil 3, Capcom put out Code Veronica, which, at one point, had actually been considered for the next numbered entry instead. In retrospect, that makes a lot of sense, given that the story follows Claire and Chris Redfield as they deal with a viral outbreak in the Southern Ocean and Antarctica and, in the process, come face to face with Wesker. It was also the first Resident Evil game for next-generation hardware, Sega’s Dreamcast, allowing Capcom to feature significantly upgraded visuals including, most famously, a gloriously over-the-top John Woo-inspired opening cinematic.
Alyson Court: I remember after [RE2] came out, I was actually on tour for The Big Comfy Couch, and it was like November, December 1998. A couple of the guys were part of the crew, so they’d travel on the bus, and they had their PlayStations there, and they played their video games. And the one guy was telling me, “You know that Resident Evil is a big deal, right?” I’m like, “Is it? I’m so clueless.” [laughs] He’s like, “Yeah.” I’m like, “Okay.” And so I went and tried to look it up. The late ’90s wasn’t that great for search engines and stuff. And it was my dad that actually found a review of the game where they’re talking about the voice performances and how they were like leaps and bounds better than the first game.
I actually printed that out and took it when Capcom came back in March of 1999 to do Code Veronica. They had me come in and audition again. [laughs] Whether that was absolutely necessary or some of their staff members were just kind of being jokesters, who knows? But they had a full casting session, I guess, because they had to cast some of the other roles. But I had to come in. And on the breakdown, it describes Claire’s character, and it had my name as voice reference. [laughs] And I’m like, “What?” So I printed out the review of the voice performance from Resident Evil 2 and brought it in. I’m like, “Look, I don’t suck! Okay? The people out there are saying we’re really good, so there!” [laughs] And they’re like,”Yeah, okay, whatever.” I was quite tickled to read some of those reviews. I mean, it’s still campy as all get out. But there’s a kind of “chill vibe” camp to it. It’s not this “over-the-top pushed” camp that some stuff has today. It was just naturally campy in places. Now, I find, sometimes things just try too hard to replicate what we managed to just do naturally back then. There’s a bit of a forced vibe now.
[…] When they came back to do Code Veronica, there was a lot more transparency, a lot more information flow, and understanding about, “Okay, so this scene…” And we were much more comfortable with each other by then. So there would be that, “Yes, it feels like the same scene, but this is if Steve didn’t complete the task in the other room, so you guys don’t have the microchip or something.” Just as an example. Or if a different weapon got left behind. So understanding that and having those little bits of information… It might seem like nothing, but let me tell you, when you’re in the booth by yourself, you feel like you’re going crazy because you’re like, “I swear, I recorded this exact same scene like six times! What is going on?”
[Veronica] was a very different experience. First of all, because I now had a certain familiarity and comfort with the environment and what was going on with the property. I had by that point played Resident Evil 2, so I did have an understanding. I got to work with all of the other actors. So any scenes that I had with other characters, we were in the booth together, which was fantastic because a lot of them didn’t understand what we were making. These were theatre people who were like, “Video game is Pac-Man! I don’t understand what’s going on.” And it can be really trippy if you’re there in the booth by yourself and you’re not getting a lot of communication or feedback from the clients. So one of the things, it was actually the producer, Erik Suzuki, who had said he wanted to have me in the booth with all of the other actors because I was basically grounding them. I was their anchor because I’d been through it before, so I could sort of share my battle stories and tips for survival. [laughs]
So it was great. We had a lot of fun working on that. I love working with other actors. There are some people who prefer to be in the booth on their own. For me, ensemble is the way I would always go, if possible. And during those initial recording sessions for Code Veronica, we didn’t get to see the technology. All I knew was that two of the fellas from Japan were from Sega, and they were there because this was for the Dreamcast. And then you had the two guys from Capcom, which were [localization lead] Tom [Takuya Shiraiwa] and Erik, and every now and then they were alternating days between doing Code Veronica and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
