articles.title: Amazon's new Alexa+ Echo devices come to Canada
articles.text:
Amazon has unveiled three new Echo devices powered by Alexa+. These devices include a revamped Echo Dot, an Echo Studio with visual intelligence and a smart clock with Alexa.
Echo Time is the first-ever alarm clock with Alexa for your nightstand. The circular touchscreen offers hundreds of clock faces. It uses a feature called Ominsense and ultrasound sleep sensing to wake you during lighter sleep within a 10-60 minute period before the alarm time, and it’s paired with a sunrise-inspired brightness display. And during the night, the clock face dims, and blue light is reduced.
The Echo Dot is now also a smart home hub. The AZ3 chip powers more on-device AI and can cancel background noise, so Alexa can hear you even in a busy room.
Additionally, it has a redesigned driver that offers 50 per cent more bass than the previous generation. It also connects to hundreds of devices and sports a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender to offer up to 1,000 sq ft of coverage in the eero network.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera features three custom drivers with a high-excursion woofer and Dolby Atmos with immersive 3D sound. It also offers advanced room adaptation and adaptive volume, so it sounds better depending on the room it’s in. It also has a built-in camera system called Sightwise Live, which allows Alexa+ to understand what it’s looking at, such as explaining the rules of a board game or re-ordering food when the shelf is empty.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera costs $329.99.
The Echo Time and Echo Dot offer age-appropriate experiences, including a year of Kids+ with access to Stories with Alexa. There are also built-in privacy controls, with a microphone-off button on Echo Dot and a dedicated button to disable the camera and microphone on Echo Studio. Additionally, the sleep sensing on Echo Time can be turned off in settings or by disabling the microphones.
These three devices are available on October 29.

articles.title: Sam Altman zu Gen Z: Probiert etwas Neues
articles.text:
Neue Arbeitswelt: Wieso Sam Altman von der Gen Z enttäuscht ist
Die KI-Revolution sorgt schon jetzt dafür, dass die Zahl der Stellenangebote für Berufseinsteiger:innen rapide abnimmt – auch in Deutschland, wie eine Analyse des Jobportals Indeed kürzlich gezeigt hat. Vor allem Angehörige der sogenannten Gen Z, also zwischen 1997 und 2012 geborene Personen, fürchten, durch den zunehmenden Einsatz von KI-Tools ersetzt zu werden.
Sam Altman: Anhaltend enttäuscht von Gen Z
Sam Altman will solche Sorgen nicht gelten lassen. Im Sommer 2025 prognostizierte der OpenAI-Chef Uni-Absolvent:innen einen Arbeitsalltag der Zukunft, in dem dank KI „einfach alles besser“ ist – „astronomische Gehälter“ inklusive. Die Gen Z teilt Altmans Begeisterung offenbar nicht, was diesen „anhaltend enttäusche“, wie Fortune berichtet.
In einem Interview mit der Stanford Graduate School of Business erklärte Altman, dass die Studierenden lieber machten, was vor fünf Jahren cool war statt etwas Neues auszuprobieren. Dabei, so der KI-Verfechter, sei genau jetzt die richtige Zeit um neue Wege zu gehen.
KI-Revolution bietet auch Chancen
Es sei vollkommen richtig, dass KI eine große Zahl von Dingen, die heute noch Menschen erledigen, künftig besser, günstiger und schneller mache. Zudem übernehme die KI große Bereiche aktueller Tätigkeiten komplett. Aber: Der Umbruch biete auch Chancen für ambitionierte Arbeitskräfte, so Altman. Dazu müsse man aber bereit sein zu überlegen, welche neuen Geschäftsmodelle sich mithilfe von KI entwickeln ließen.
Die Ausgangslage sei so offen wie nie zuvor. Die KI öffne Unternehmer:innen ein seltenes Zeitfenster, um Bereiche aufzubauen, die noch vor wenigen Jahren schwierig oder gar unmöglich gewesen seien, so Altman. Auf Basis der Technologie, so der OpenAI-Chef, ließen sich Unternehmen entwickeln, die weitaus größer und bedeutender sein könnten als OpenAI selbst.
Karriere in Zeiten des größten Wandels
„Wenn ihr euch jetzt in die Welt hinausbegebt, um an etwas zu arbeiten – dann beginnt ihr eure Karriere vermutlich in einer Zeit des größten Wandels“, gab Altman den Stanford-Studierenden mit auf den Weg. Menschen mit großem Potenzial, Tatendrang, Ideen, einer neuen Sichtweise auf die Dinge sowie neuen Fähigkeiten kämen tendenziell besonders gut zurecht, „wenn der Boden am stärksten bebt“.

articles.title: Denza trae a España el BAO 5: su enorme SUV de 544 CV, hibridación DMO y 835 km de autonomía
articles.text:
El Bao 5, uno de los SUVs más interesantes de Denza, aterriza en España para sumarse al catálogo de SUVs premium disponibles. Se trata del primer SUV de la marca y lo hace con la tecnología de hibridación enchufable DMO con diversas propuestas de motorización y con una autonomía que se dispara hasta los 835 km en autonomía conjunta.
En este sentido, el Denza Bao 5 combina un motor de gasolina turboalimentado de 1,5 litros y dos motores eléctricos, uno delantero y otro trasero, para ofrecer una potencia máxima de 544 CV (400 kW) y 760 Nm de par.
Por separado, el motor de gasolina del Denza Bao 5 desarrolla 150 CV y 240 Nm de par, pero su función principal es suministrar electricidad tanto a la Blade Battery de 31,8 kWh como a los motores eléctricos en el eje delantero y trasero que desarrollan 272 CV y 388 CV respectivamente. Una potencia increíble, teniendo en cuenta que estamos hablando de UN SUV de cinco plazas y 4,9 metros.
Este sistema híbrido supone que el Denza Bao 5 acelere de 0 a 100km/h en tan solo 4,8 segundos en la versión Elegance y en 5,0 segundos en la versión Ultimate. Este SUV de Denza combina un chasis de largueros y travesaños con una serie de sistemas de control propios del DMO.
Además, monta un sistema de suspensión hidráulica inteligente DiSus-P, que analiza constantemente los datos de más de 20 sensores: desde el ángulo de giro del volante y la posición de los pedales del acelerador y del freno, hasta la velocidad y la orientación de las ruedas, e incluso la presión y la temperatura. Cierran el conjunto dos diferenciales electrónicos y un sistema de bloqueo central. Todo ello para ofrecer una enorme versatilidad tanto en caminos como en carretera. Un pack bastante potente para aquellos que quieran un SUV híbrido de gama alta.
Respecto a su interior del Bao 5, el conductor tiene acceso a una instrumentación completamente digital de 12,3 pulgadas y a un Head-Up Display, a la que se suma en la consola central una pantalla táctil de 15,6” (39,6 cm) y una pantalla panorámica para el acompañante, situada justo delante de su asiento. El coche tiene su propio asistente de voz con cuatro zonas distintas de detección y un sistema de audio de alta fidelidad firmado por Devialet y equipado con hasta 18 altavoces en la versión Ultimate.
Sobre el precio, estamos hablando de un SUV premium, por lo que tiene un precio de venta recomendado de 76.290 euros para la versión Elegance y de 86.420 euros para la Ultimate. Esta última incluye una garantía oficial para el vehículo de 6 años o 150.000 km, de 8 años o 150.000 km para el sistema de propulsión y de 8 años o 250.000 km para la Blade Battery. Ambas versiones en una buena selección de colores, tanto exterior como interior.

articles.title: I tried Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro, and touching a MacBook screen feels wonderfully natural
articles.text:
Apple's Touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here, and yes, touching a MacBook screen feels totally and wonderfully natural
Why no M6
Confirming one of Apple's worst-kept secrets, Apple finally unveiled its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro in 14-inch and 16-inch models on Wednesday, October 28, in Los Angeles. The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros. Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon.
Apple CEO John Ternus didn't waste much time on stage, quickly announcing the laptops and running through key innovations like the tandem OLED (PROLED) screens and relatively lightweight (3lbs for the 14-inch model and 4lbs for the 16-inch one) before leaving the stage and directing the assembled group of media, analysts, creators, and Apple execs to an adjacent space where I got my first experience ever with a touchscreen MacBook.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You've been waiting for this
If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display. It feels like I've been waiting my whole life to do this on a MacBook (or at least as long as I've been using MacBooks).
As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this.
For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together. This increases the brightness while maintaining incredibly inky blacks (they're gorgeous). It also allows for a far thinner display panel because you don't need a backlight.
Though there now is a "backlight of a sort. This touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup marks the return of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the display. It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that).
I played mostly with the larger, 16-inch model, which still features the expansive, backlit Magic Keyboard and a huge ForceTouch Trackpad, which honestly is gonna get a little bit less use now that a touchscreen is just inches away.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
A pair of large speaker grills sits on either side of the keyboard, though I couldn't hear them over the din of the demo room. As with previous MacBook Pros, there's still an SD Card slot, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, one USB-4 port, HDMI, and the headphone jack.
In my hands, the 4 lb, 16-inch model felt a tad lighter than previous 16-inch MacBook Pros, though the 14-inch (which might be my preference) felt lightweight at 3lbs.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Touch it, touch it, please say you want to
Let's talk, though, about using the touchscreen.
I tried a 3D design app where I used a couple of fingers to spin a model of a guy in battle armor and then a single finger to paint gold on some of the armor.
I opened Maps and used two fingers to spin the map, then pinch-and-zoom.
I used three fingers to swipe through desktops.
I could use two fingers to grab a window, flip it to one side of the screen, and watch it instantly dock itself as a half-screen app (yes, I've done something very similar on a Surface Pro).
I played touchscreen piano with all my fingers.
At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing. It's obvious. It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired. Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family,
Now, you cannot take the screen and flip it all the way to the back of the laptop (something many touchscreen Windows laptops can do). That might be a shame because I could also use my finger to paint and, though I haven't done it yet, draw.
Speaking of which, there is no indication that the touchscreen MacBook Pro supports the Apple Pencil. Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway.
There is, by the way, a Dynamic Island that's basically copied from the iPhone, but I didn't see it do very much.
As I used the touchscreen MacBook Pro, I was not only reminded of my time with the Microsoft Surface Pro but of my initial weeks and even months with the MacBook after I switched platforms. Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it.
Point is, touch was something I reflexively used on the Surface Pro, and I am now certain I will happily use it on the touchscreen MacBook Pro. You probably will, too.
You will pay for the privilege of touch. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with touch starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / $5,499. Pre-orders are live today, and the laptops ship on November 6.

A 38-year industry veteran and award-winning journalist, Lance has covered technology since PCs were the size of suitcases and “on line” meant “waiting.” He’s a former Lifewire Editor-in-Chief, Mashable Editor-in-Chief, and, before that, Editor in Chief of PCMag.com and Senior Vice President of Content for Ziff Davis, Inc. He also wrote a popular, weekly tech column for Medium called The Upgrade.
Lance Ulanoff makes frequent appearances on national, international, and local news programs including Live with Kelly and Mark, the Today Show, Good Morning America, CNBC, CNN, and the BBC.

articles.title: Toronto-made Curse of Resthaven is a must-play gothic adventure
articles.text:
As a fan of Lil’Guardsman, I’ve been eagerly waiting for the next title from Toronto-based developer Hilltop Studios, Curse of Resthaven. Lil’Guardsman is a wonderful and unique indie title with a lot of great writing and even better visual design, especially character art, so I was always going to pay attention to whatever Hilltop did next.
Plus, I’m friends with the studio’s co-founder and Resthaven’s game director, Scott Christian. We’re both based in Ontario’s capital, and we often see each other at one of the city’s many video game industry-related events and monthly meet-ups.
That’s a disclosure I wanted to get out at the top. While you, reader, are free to think what you want of me reviewing a game from someone I know, it goes against every bone in my being as a critic, a journalist, and an artist, who knows you only really do more harm than good to pull any critical punches. So no need to worry about that in this review.
Curse of Resthaven, like Lil’Guardsman before it, is a feast for players that value strong, unique, and expressive visual and written work. The ways in which Curse of Resthaven weaves its best talents from start to credits (and back to the credits multiple times) is what makes the game so engaging and so difficult to put down.
But it’s not without annoyances and elements that feel either incomplete or like they were pulled back on, for reasons that are almost always more complex than they appear when it comes to indie development. The consequences of those choices remain, as does the rough-edged experience the whole game delivers.
Like a dark version of Groundhog Day
Curse of Resthaven is rough-edged, and I think several of the annoyances I’ve felt across my journey with its protagonist Ambrose and the dutiful purpose that brings him to the titular island of Resthaven in the first place could be fixed in a few patches. That’s where a lot of the observed blemishes lie.
First, Curse of Resthaven begins, like the classic gothic literature whose influence echoes throughout the game, with a letter, or rather the stoppage of them. You play as Ambrose and must investigate the disappearance of his niece Amalia. An upstart gentleman of the Aurelian Empire, Ambrose could’ve been on his way to Parliament but instead pulls political strings to become Governor of Resthaven to find his niece and ensure her safety.
Ambrose ends up on a ship to an island colony that couldn’t look and feel any less like the capital if it tried. Not so much down to how the economy runs or how its residents behave, but because of the insanity that happens every six days, namely the capital ‘G’ Gods rising and destroying the island. But everyone’s back the next day as the whole loop starts anew, like a much more drawn-out and dark version of Groundhog Day.
An engaging story
That might sound like a spoiler, but that cycle is central to the game. On top of searching for Amalia, players must take on the role of Governor along the way. It leads you down an ultimately intertwined path of governing and uncovering the island’s deepest secrets in the search for Amalia, as you venture out on expeditions and interrogate the townspeople of Resthaven.
Solving the mystery of Amalia’s disappearance, of the many mythical and eldritch occurrences and creatures on the island, is the core of the gameplay in Curse of Resthaven. It’s like playing through a really fantastical Midsomer Murders tale with a heavy dose of gothic visuals and vibes, classic adventure-style gameplay, and a splash of roguelike and town-governing-sim mechanics.
The story you uncover (which I absolutely won’t spoil here) as you solve the many mysteries of Resthaven and its people, the voice acting featured across its many characters, the design of each of them and the many areas of Resthaven you get to explore, are all what make Curse of Resthaven so incredibly engaging. I love mystery tales, and even if some of the game’s turns seemed predictable to me, several more were wonderful (and often wonderfully grim) surprises that made it a delight to play through.
Thankfully, that’s true even when you’re experiencing these surprises over and over again, as you progress through multiple six-day loops to the first of the three endings needed to reach the game’s ‘true’ ending. It’s on the whole very well paced, thanks to the permanent upgrades to your ability to both lift the colony’s financial standing and find Amalia that you can unlock at the end of each loop.
Governance has its issues
The governing-the-colony-side of the game can be a little slow to start, but once you get the hang of it, you breeze through most of your interactions with it, as it is ultimately much simpler than the narrative, where all of the game’s actual complexities and juicy, interesting bits lie.
That’s also one of Curse’s larger splotches. The governance is, partly by design in my estimate, never as interesting as speaking to the townspeople or going on expeditions. You collect taxes from the townspeople in the form of playing cards that represent goods like wheat, lumber, sugar, and gold, with each in-town merchant manufacturing various refined and unrefined goods.
Once you’ve made your tax rounds, you then use those cards to trade with the visiting ships in port or to complete expeditions, with both actions aiding towards the goal of getting the colony back on its feet.
Unfortunately, the trading and town governance never really feels properly intertwined with the narrative. It’s more just a way to facilitate access to the cards you collect each day, something to do in between the real meat of the game, and a way to gate and pace out your progress. It’s never entirely obtrusive and doesn’t keep you from interesting story bits for too long, thankfully, but it’s by far the blandest element of the game.
It also doesn’t help that some of my bigger annoyances came from frustrating menu navigation, as I’d often lose my place when cycling through the multiple layers of menus. Though that’s hopefully something that’ll be cleared with a post-launch patch or two.
And while the expeditions are more interesting, they also suffer from a lack of evolution throughout. They’re engaging because you get to see more of the island and interact with some of the game’s more comedic moments while also seeing some of the best works of art across the whole experience. Completing those expeditions, however, by simply bringing the right card with you, playing it once, and then watching the rest of it play out, does get a bit stale before the end.
All of that said, I can’t stress enough how much these complaints only amount to ‘rough edges’ by the time you’ve reached the credits. Curse of Resthaven’s storytelling, art, sound design (the music is an incredibly special element of this game as well) and everything that Hilltop put into telling a strong story is why this game is a must-play. Just don’t expect the most intricate colony-sim mechanics on your way through this gothic horror.
Curse of Resthaven launches on Oct. 29 via Steam for PC/Mac, as well as on Xbox Series X/S, and Playstation 5. It will also eventually come to Nintendo Switch, though the release date hasn’t yet been confirmed.

articles.title: Liam Neeson rompe su silencio tras ser sustituido por Meryl Streep como Aslan en 'Las Crónicas de Narnia'
articles.text:
La nueva película de Narnia: El sobrino del mago, será un reinicio a la franquicia, que esta vez arrancará con el primero de los libros en orden cronológico. Dirigida por Greta Gerwig, será una de las producciones más ambiciosas de Netflix, tanto que llegará a los cines como uno de los grandes estrenos de comienzos de año. Uno de los puntos más comentados ha sido el fichaje de Meryl Streep como Aslan en sustitución de Liam Neeson.
El veterano actor de La Lista de Schindler dio voz al mítico león en las películas de los años 2000. Ahora, sin embargo, la actriz con más nominaciones al Oscar de toda la historia toma el testigo para dotar al personaje de una nueva personalidad. Algo que el mismísimo Liam Neeson no sabía, tal y como ha reconocido en una entrevista concedida a ScreenRant. "Lo siento, esto es nuevo para mí", confiesa sobre la producción de la nueva película de Las Crónicas de Narnia.
"¿Meryl Streep va a hacer de Jesucristo?", comenta sorprendido a continuación. Y es que, recordemos, el león Aslan de Narnia es una representación del Jesús, el hijo de Dios en la religión cristiana. Y lo cierto es que a Liam Neeson la elección de la actriz para el papel le ha parecido fantástica. "Bueno, si vas a convertir a Cristo en mujer, nadie mejor que Meryl", confirma.
En realidad, en Narnia: El sobrino del mago, Aslan no será una leona. Simplemente tendrá la voz de Meryl Streep pero, por lo visto en el primer tráiler, mantendrá el aspecto físico de un león macho. En cualquier caso, el fichaje de Streep para el papel supone un gran golpe sobre la mesa del filme, que se asegura contar con una de las mejores intérpretes de todos los tiempos.
De qué va Narnia: El sobrino del mago
En Las Crónicas de Narnia: El sobrino del mago, al tocar un anillo mágico dos niños son transportados al antiguo mundo de Charn. Allí, por error despiertan a una poderosa y malvada hechicera de su sueño eterno. Sedienta de poder, ella no dudará en destruirlo todo y a todos a su paso. Pero el gran león Aslan hará despertar con su canción una nueva esperanza, un nuevo mundo: Narnia. Un lugar donde todo es posible.
Dirigida por la nominada al Oscar Greta Gerwig (Barbie), la película está protagonizada por David McKenna (El señor de las moscas), Beatrice Campbell (La trama fenicia), Emma Mackey (Sex Education), Carey Mulligan (Una joven prometedora), Ciarán Hinds (Juego de tronos), Daniel Craig (saga James Bond), Meryl Streep (El diablo viste de Prada), Kobna Holdbrook-Smith (Wonka), Denise Gough (Andor) y Susan Wokoma (Enola Holmes).
Narnia: El sobrino del mago se estrena en cines el 12 de febrero de 2027.

articles.title: Operational resilience: InfoScale on protecting live operations - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Why InfoScale wants enterprises to protect live operations, not just servers
Running servers and restored data don’t guarantee that a business can safely operate after a disruption. That gap is pushing enterprises to rethink operational resilience as attackers use AI to scale their campaigns and companies embed automation deep into critical processes.
Many organizations have yet to adjust. As AI raises the stakes for trust and cyber resilience, traditional disaster recovery still protects servers, storage and networks one component at a time, according to Bhooshan Thakar (pictured), senior vice president and general manager of InfoScale at Cloud Software Group Inc.
“The infrastructure survived, but the operational state did not. From the business perspective, the main question becomes: ‘Can the business continue to operate with confidence?'” he said. “Ultimately, resilience is about maintaining the trust in the operational state.”
Thakar spoke with theCUBE’s Krista Case for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why static disaster recovery playbooks break down in dynamic AI environments. (* Disclosure below.)
Operational resilience shifts from recovery to runtime
The pace of change is part of the problem. Enterprises that once ran a planned failover every six months now patch business-critical applications daily or weekly against security threats, Thakar noted. AI is accelerating that cycle, and Cloud Software Group, InfoScale’s parent company, joined Anthropic PBC’s Project Glasswing in June to use the Claude Mythos Preview model for security work.
“In the past, the disruption or downtime was an ‘if, not when’ kind of an event. Today, it is not ‘if,’ it’s ‘always,'” he said. “What I mean by that is you have to always plan for a disruption, whether it’s a planned or an unplanned.”
Public cloud adds a false sense of security. Application owners often assume cloud service providers guarantee their resilience, yet business applications are multitiered stacks whose layers depend on one another. If any layer fails or data is corrupted, the business stops even while infrastructure reports as healthy, according to Thakar.
“If you really look at the fine print, what the CSPs guarantee is resiliency of the cloud, but resiliency in the cloud is your responsibility, meaning an application owner’s responsibility,” he said. “Ultimately, what you’re looking for is whether your business is resilient as opposed to a component of the stack being resilient.”
That view shapes InfoScale’s approach. Rather than acting only after a failure, a resilience platform should run alongside live applications, tracking dependencies, runtime states and data integrity, while real-time replication and immutable checkpoints let teams return to a trusted good state quickly, Thakar explained. He also argued that traditional investments in prevention and recovery leave a gap in resilience.
“If you think about the last decade, our buyers have spent billions of dollars of their budget into two silos: prevention, which is on the security side, and recovery, which is on the backup and infrastructure side,” he said. “If you really think of it, prevention is leaky and recovery is too slow.”
Measurement also needs to change, Thankar noted. Downtime now brings regulatory exposure alongside financial loss and customer churn. Instead of tracking the time to restore a virtual machine, he suggested measuring how long it takes to reach the first validated, clean business transaction after an active disruption, a metric that ties operational resilience to business outcomes.
“Today, when I talk to the [chief information security officers] and [chief information officers] in this context, they’re not asking vendors, ‘How fast can you restore my data after I take an outage?'” I think that is yesterday’s question,” he said. “They are asking, ‘How does your platform guarantee that my mission-critical application or operation keeps running right through an active disruption?'”

articles.title: Windows 11: So richtet ihr euch das Rechtsklickmenü jetzt selbst ein
articles.text:
Windows 11: So kannst du jetzt das Rechtsklickmenü selbst einrichten
Da Microsoft die Funktion schrittweise ausrollt, ist sie nach der Installation des optionalen Updates KB5127936 vom Oktober möglicherweise nicht sofort sichtbar. Sie lässt sich mithilfe des kostenlosen Open-Source-Werkzeugs „ViVeTool“ aber in wenigen Minuten aktivieren – und zwar so.
So bekommt ihr das kostenlose Open-Source-Werkzeug „ViVeTool“
Als erstes müsst ihr „Einstellungen“ > „Windows Update“ öffnen und auf „Nach Updates suchen“ klicken. Falls das Update KB5127936 nicht angezeigt wird, aktiviert die Option „Die neuesten Updates erhalten, sobald sie verfügbar sind“ und sucht erneut. Sobald ihr das Update KB5127936 installiert habt, startet ihr den PC neu. Führt auch den Befehl „winver“ aus, um sicherzustellen, dass ihr Build 26200.9818 oder 26300.9818 verwendet.
Dann klickt ihr im Datei-Explorer mit der rechten Maustaste auf eine beliebige Datei. Wenn ihr unten den Eintrag „Menü anpassen“ seht, habt ihr laut windowslatest.com Glück – in diesem Fall benötigt ihr ViVeTool nicht. Falls die Funktion bei euch, wie wohl bei den meisten Nutzer:innen, noch nicht vorhanden ist, müsst ihr ViVeTool von der offiziellen Github-Seite herunterladen. Entpackt die ZIP-Datei dabei so, dass sich die Datei „ViVeTool.exe“ unter „C:\ViVeTool“ befindet.
Zwei Befehle müssen ausgeführt werden
Klickt dann mit der rechten Maustaste auf die Start-Schaltfläche, öffnet das Terminal als Administrator:in und führt nacheinander die folgenden beiden Befehle aus:
cd C:\ViVeTool
vivetool /enable /id:60813048
Wenn die Meldung „Successfully set feature configuration(s)“ erscheint, könnt ihr den PC neu starten und erneut mit der rechten Maustaste auf eine Datei klicken.
Software-Nostalgie: Kennt ihr diese Programme noch?
Statt 25 Einträgen nur noch acht
Das neue Menü enthält am unteren Rand die Schaltfläche „Menü anpassen“, die direkt zu den Einstellungen unter „Personalisierung > Kontextmenü“ führt. Laut Microsoft ist für die Nutzung der Standardkonfiguration kein weiteres Handeln erforderlich. Wer dennoch das alte Menü im Stil von Windows 10 bevorzugt, kann dies weiterhin aufrufen, indem er beim Rechtsklick auf den Desktop oder eine Datei die Umschalttaste gedrückt hält.
Vor dem Update erschienen laut windowslatest.com bei einem Rechtsklick auf eine Bilddatei unterhalb der Symbole für „Ausschneiden“, „Kopieren“, „Umbenennen“, „Freigeben“ und „Löschen“ 20 weitere Einträge. Diese überladen wirkende Systematik könnt ihr dann beispielsweise so anpassen, dass das neue Standardmenü für eine solche Bilddatei nur noch acht Einträge enthält.

articles.title: Taiwan working on autonomous drone swarms to counter China’s increasingly aggressive grey-zone military tactics — island has already completed flight simulations, now working towards flight trials over maritime areas
articles.text:
Taiwan working on autonomous drone swarms to counter China’s increasingly aggressive grey-zone military tactics — island has already completed flight simulations, now working towards flight trials over maritime areas
Taipei has also received its first shipment of U.S.-made V-BAT drones.
Taiwan’s Ocean Affairs Council is working on an autonomous system that would allow drone fleets to coordinate and execute missions without human intervention in response to "grey-zone" activities carried out by China. According to the South China Morning Post, the council is working with the National Cheng Kung University, which has already completed simultaneous flight simulations of two drone fleets, with each fleet comprising 10 units. This is already the second step of the process, which has shifted from individual aircraft control to the coordination of two drone detachments.
This project is designed to help Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA) to counter Beijing’s grey-zone tactics in the waters surrounding the island nation. There have already been instances of civilian Chinese ships damaging undersea cables that Taipei relies on, with the CGA increasing its defensive patrols around 24 undersea cables and closely monitoring nearly a hundred China-linked boats. Despite that, Chinese “research vessels” continue to loiter over Taiwan-U.S. undersea cables, mimicking the activities of Russian trawlers in the Atlantic.
“The next stage will involve hardware-in-the-loop testing, prototype integration and flight trials over actual maritime areas to assess reliability under different sea and weather conditions,” the council said. The researchers programmed the drones to have a minimum separation of 100 feet in 3D space, and they’re also incorporating leader-follower formation flying and dynamic obstacle avoidance. This should allow them to respond to quickly changing conditions out in the open sea and even deal with unexpected hazards.
More than that, the autonomous system Taipei is working on would let different types of drones coordinate their movements, divide tasks, and plan routes, primarily for maritime surveillance. This is especially important as it would allow them to use different types of drones to accomplish various missions, much like how different air forces use different aircraft types. 
The project is currently focusing on three Western-made drones — the Jump 20, V-BAT, and Flexrotor. In fact, the Ocean Affairs Council just received the V-BAT, a VTOL drone built by U.S. defense firm Shield AI. This unit can take off vertically from the relatively constrained deck space of non-aircraft carrier ships and offers an endurance of over 12 hours for extended missions, making it ideal for the CGA, as it would not need to make major renovations to its ships to accommodate these drones while extending their reach.

articles.title: Why the Office Printer Still Generates So Many Support Calls, and How to Tame It - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Persistent Problem of Office Printers
Despite the rise of digital documentation and paperless workflows, office printers remain a critical component of business operations. Yet, they are notoriously prone to issues that frustrate employees and IT departments alike. From paper jams and connectivity glitches to driver errors and unexpected maintenance alerts, printers continue to be a major source of support calls in many organizations.
The paradox is clear: even with advances in printer technology, the average office printer still generates an estimated 20-25% of all IT support tickets related to hardware malfunctions. According to a 2023 survey by Spiceworks, 22% of IT professionals identified printers as one of the top three hardware devices causing the most support challenges in the workplace. This ongoing issue impacts productivity, delays important document handling, and increases operational costs.
Given that printers are so essential yet so troublesome, it’s no wonder they remain a perennial headache for IT teams. Understanding the root causes behind these frequent support calls is the first step toward taming the problem and restoring workplace efficiency.
Common Causes Behind Printer Support Calls
Printers are complex devices that combine mechanical, electronic, and software components. This complexity creates multiple points of failure. Some of the most frequent reasons for support requests include:
– Paper jams and misfeeds: These mechanical issues can arise from poor quality paper, improper loading, worn rollers, or internal debris.
– Connectivity issues: Wireless or network printers can lose connection due to IP conflicts, expired credentials, router problems, or firewall restrictions.
– Driver and firmware problems: Outdated or incompatible drivers cause print jobs to fail or produce errors.
– Low toner or ink alerts: Unexpected depletion of supplies halts printing until replacements arrive.
– Configuration errors: Incorrect default settings, permissions, or print queue problems can prevent users from printing.
– User errors: Simple mistakes like selecting the wrong printer, printing to an offline device, or misunderstanding printer functions often trigger support calls.
Each of these issues can frustrate end-users and lead them to seek help from IT support teams, diverting resources from higher-value tasks. In fact, a report by IDC found that printer-related issues contribute to roughly 23% of all hardware-related help desk tickets in medium to large enterprises.
Leveraging Expert Help to Streamline Printer Support
One effective way to reduce printer support calls is to partner with specialized service providers who offer quick, reliable assistance. For instance, businesses can benefit from on-demand tech support by OSG, which provides fast response times and expert troubleshooting to resolve printer issues before they impact operations.
With on-demand tech support, companies gain access to technicians who understand the nuances of printer technology and can diagnose problems remotely or onsite. This approach expedites resolution and prevents minor glitches from escalating into major disruptions. By outsourcing printer support, IT departments can focus on strategic initiatives instead of firefighting printer errors.
The Role of Preventative Maintenance
Beyond reactive support, organizations should invest in preventative maintenance and user education to tame printer-related headaches. Regular servicing of printers such as cleaning, replacing worn components, and updating firmware-extends device lifespan and reduces malfunctions.
Preventative maintenance can drastically reduce the frequency of common issues like paper jams and connectivity failures. A 2022 study by Brother International showed that companies that implemented regular printer maintenance saw a 30% decline in support calls related to hardware problems.
Empowering Users Through Training
Additionally, training employees on proper printer use, including how to load paper correctly, clear minor jams, manage print queues, and understand printer status indicators, empowers them to handle small issues independently. This reduces unnecessary support calls and fosters a more efficient workplace culture.
In addition to maintenance, having a reliable local partner can make a significant difference. Companies looking to improve their printer reliability can contact IT Force in Mississauga, where experienced IT professionals can help implement best practices and tailored support solutions.
Data-Driven Insights on Printer Support Impact
The financial and operational toll of printer support calls is notable. A 2022 IDC report revealed that businesses spend an average of $120 per printer annually on support and maintenance, with hidden costs related to lost productivity bringing the total closer to $400 per printer. For enterprises with dozens or hundreds of printers, these expenses quickly accumulate into significant budget items.
Moreover, a study by Brother International found that 65% of employees experience frustration due to printing issues, with delays in printing documents negatively affecting deadlines and customer interactions. Printing delays can lead to missed deadlines, poor customer service, and a general decline in workplace morale.
Understanding these statistics reinforces why tackling printer support calls is vital for business efficiency and employee satisfaction. It also highlights the importance of investing in solutions that reduce downtime and streamline printer management.
Practical Steps to Reduce Printer-Related Support Calls
To minimize printer support tickets, businesses can adopt a multi-faceted strategy:
- Standardize printer models: Limiting the variety of printers in the office simplifies driver management, reduces compatibility issues, and streamlines support processes.
- Implement centralized print management: Using software tools to monitor printer status, toner levels, and usage patterns allows IT to proactively address potential problems before users are affected.
- Automate driver and firmware updates: Ensuring printers are running the latest software decreases errors, enhances security, and improves overall reliability.
- Provide clear user guidelines: Distributing quick reference guides or digital tutorials helps employees troubleshoot basic printer issues, such as clearing paper jams or selecting the correct printer.
- Schedule routine maintenance: Regular checkups by qualified technicians prevent hardware degradation and unexpected failures, extending printer life and reducing support calls.
- Encourage proper printer etiquette: Educate users on batching print jobs, avoiding unnecessary prints, and reporting issues promptly to prevent escalation.
By combining these measures with professional support options, organizations can dramatically decrease the frequency and severity of printer support calls. This integrated approach not only improves printer uptime but also enhances overall IT service quality.
The Future of Office Printing Support
As office technology evolves, so too will the ways businesses manage printer support. Emerging solutions such as AI-driven diagnostics, cloud-based print management platforms, and remote troubleshooting tools are set to further reduce printer downtime and simplify maintenance. These innovations enable predictive maintenance, real-time monitoring, and faster issue resolution.
For example, AI-powered systems can analyze printer usage patterns and detect anomalies before they result in failures, allowing IT teams to intervene proactively. Cloud-based print management also provides centralized control over distributed printer fleets, simplifying updates and access control.
Early adopters of these innovations will enjoy smoother operations, lower IT costs, and enhanced user experience. However, until printers become entirely foolproof, human expertise remains indispensable. Investing in skilled IT support-whether internal or through trusted partners- continues to be a vital part of taming the office printer’s reputation as a frequent troublemaker.
Conclusion
Despite the digital transformation of workplaces, office printers remain a necessary and often troublesome piece of equipment. They generate a significant portion of IT support calls primarily due to mechanical issues, connectivity problems, outdated drivers, and user errors. By understanding these challenges and implementing a combination of preventative maintenance, employee education, and expert support services such as and, businesses can reduce printer-related disruptions.
Reducing printer support calls not only improves productivity but also lowers operational costs and enhances employee satisfaction. With the right strategies and partnerships, companies can finally tame the office printer and transform it from a persistent headache into a dependable workhorse-one that supports rather than hinders daily business operations.

articles.title: Sell first, build second, automate last: A solo founder’s playbook for the AI era
articles.text:
Sell first, build second, automate last: A solo founder’s playbook for the AI era
Hostinger’s Emilis Strimaitis on why founders who build first still fail faster, and the seven-step process that puts customers before code
AI has made building almost effortless. In 2019, Emilis Strimaitis spent nearly a year, and the efforts of a developer agency, on a shopping app that failed. Today, he says, an AI subscription and a weekend would produce the same app, and it would fail just as surely, only 100 times faster.
Speaking at a webinar in association with Yourstory, part of VibeCode 30 at TechSparks 2026, the Head of Product Innovation at Hostinger argued that the steps founders took before AI existed have not gone away. Finding the problem, finding the people who have it and getting them to pay still come first. AI simply changes how fast you can do everything after that.
Why the product is now the cheapest part
If you can build something in a weekend, so can thousands of others. Strimaitis noted that something launched on Monday can have two or three copies by Friday, and one of them will likely be free. Getting attention, he added, has been the real problem all along, long before AI.
The trap is easy to fall into. Founders build with AI, add agents to run the product, then add more agents to run those agents, and still have zero customers. His description: a self-driving car with no roads to drive on.
The audience took part throughout the session, beginning with a live poll on their biggest struggle in launching a digital product or online business. The top answer, at 41%, was being unsure how to sell.
Sell first, build second, automate last
Strimaitis has bootstrapped around 15 businesses over 15 years, generating well over $10 million with no investors. His pattern is consistent. “Every win came from selling first, and every loss came from building it first.”
One small tool, sold before it was built, cost about $100 to develop and earned $29,000. A platform built without proof of demand cost over $40,000 and went nowhere. His rule: use the same tools, the same AI, and the same automations, but in the opposite order.
The seven-step selling machine
First, pick a niche using three checks: can you name the people, can you find them in one place online, and are they already paying for something? AI can help here by turning your skills and interests into a shortlist of ideas.
Next, read the complaints. Search reviews and communities for bad experiences with existing tools. “Somebody else’s one-star reviews are our business plan.” Collect about 50 complaints and check whether they repeat, whether the people complaining actually pay, and whether a better version is possible. An AI tool can group them into top problems in customers’ own words. The rule is not to let AI invent anything.
From there, write 10 promises, or angles, such as faster, cheaper, or done-for-you. Give each one a simple landing page with a title, a description and a button for pre-orders or a waiting list. Then pick one social platform and post daily for 30 days, assuming nobody is watching. Record one long video a week and slice it up.
People who sign up can be invited into a WhatsApp group, but only after they raise their hand. A group of 10 to 20 becomes a research team and a set of beta testers. To borrow an audience, engage genuinely with creators who have roughly 5,000 to 50,000 followers before reaching out.
After 30 days, stop what fails and grow what wins. If people paid, fulfill the first 20 or so orders by hand. Only then build the software, and automate last.
Where human effort still counts
Strimaitis was candid that AI-driven shortcuts can backfire. Cold email is losing effectiveness because everyone now sends AI-personalized messages, so he recommends engaging with 20 to 30 creators by hand instead. On LinkedIn, he said, posts flagged as AI do not rank well. His alternative is to save posts that caught your attention and remake the idea in your own voice.
For attendees using Hostinger’s tools, the session mentioned using AI Builder for landing pages, Hostinger Agent for refining prompts, and e-commerce for quick payment links.
The takeaway is simple. AI is a powerful tool, but demand still has to come first.

articles.text:
Le spécialiste du streaming JustWatch a publié ce mercredi 28 octobre son classement des dix films d’horreur sortis en 2026 les plus populaires sur sa plateforme à l’approche d’Halloween.
À quelques jours d’Halloween, ces données montrent quels films de l’année intéressent le plus les adeptes des marathons d’horreur dans leur salon. De quoi trouver des idées pour la soirée d’Halloween, ce samedi 31 octobre.
Le classement mêle des franchises historiques, comme Scream et Evil Dead, et des films nés et ancrés dans la culture web, comme Backrooms.
Un cru 2026 placé sous le signe de l’angoisse viscérale
L’année 2026 est une grosse année pour le cinéma d’horreur, portée par des films à petit budget devenus des succès en salle, comme Obsession et Backrooms. Du slasher parodique à l’horreur technologique en passant par le thriller psychologique, le catalogue de cette saison couvre presque tous les sous-genres. Voici les dix films du classement, dans l’ordre.
Le top 5 : entre cauchemars psychologiques et pépites virales
- 1. Obsession : en tête du classement, ce thriller psychologique de Curry Barker reprend le vieux principe du vœu qui se retourne contre celui qui l’a fait, sur fond d’amour à sens unique. Tourné pour 750 000 dollars (environ 650 000 €), il a rapporté plus de 500 millions de dollars (environ 430 millions d’euros) dans le monde.
- 2. Backrooms : Kane Parsons adapte sa propre série YouTube, tirée de la légende Internet des Backrooms, ces couloirs jaunes qui ne mènent nulle part. Chiwetel Ejiofor y joue le patron d’un magasin de meubles qui découvre un passage vers ce labyrinthe.
- 3. Hokum : réalisé par Damian McCarthy (Oddity), ce conte macabre envoie Adam Scott, un écrivain en panne, dans un hôtel isolé en Irlande, où il se met à douter de sa santé mentale.
- 4. Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma : derrière son titre volontairement outrancier se cache le nouveau film de Jane Schoenbrun (I Saw the TV Glow), une comédie horrifique distribuée par Mubi. Un hommage sanglant aux slashers des années 1980, plein de gore et de second degré.
- 5. Send Help : Sam Raimi revient à l’horreur avec ce huis clos sur une île, où la lutte pour survivre bascule vite dans la terreur.
De la 6e à la 10e place : franchises cultes et horreur technologique
- 6. Scream 7 : Ghostface reprend du service pour un septième opus devenu le plus gros succès de la saga au box-office. Un jeu de massacre méta, sanglant et diaboliquement drôle.
- 7. Ready or Not 2: Here I Come : la mariée la plus coriace du cinéma d’horreur remet le couvert dans une suite survitaminée qui pousse le concept du jeu de cache-cache mortel encore plus loin.
- 8. Soulm8te : nouveau venu dans l’univers étendu de M3GAN, ce thriller d’horreur technologique explore les dérives mortelles d’une intelligence artificielle érotique et possessive. Prévu pour le cinéma, le film est finalement sorti directement en vidéo à la demande aux États-Unis, avant d’arriver sur Hulu.
- 9. Evil Dead Burn : La saga revient avec son premier film depuis Evil Dead Rise (2023), un volet très brutal, rempli de sang frais et de démons surexcités, par le réalisateur français de Vermines.
- 10. Passenger Ce road movie d’André Øvredal (The Autopsy of Jane Doe) ferme la marche. Un jeune couple qui sillonne les routes en van assiste à un accident mortel, puis se retrouve traqué par une présence démoniaque impossible à semer.

articles.title: Un Tesla Semi brûle tout seul sur une autoroute américaine, et pendant des heures !
articles.text:
Un camion Tesla Semi a pris feu seul aux USA. Et il a vraiment mis le temps pour finalement s'eteindre !
Tesla veut pouvoir compter plus que des voitures dans son catalogue de produit. C'est ainsi que la société a, après de très nombreuses années, finalement lancé la commercialisation en masse de son camion poids lourds électrique Tesla Semi à la rentrée dernière. Une prouesse technologique intèressante, mais qui peut aussi avoir ses mauvais côtés, comme on le voit avec cette histoire qui s'est passée aux États-Unis !
Un Tesla Semi prend feu seul sur la route à San Francisco
Hier, en Californie, un véhicule Tesla Semi prenait feu sur la route I-880. Et ce qui ne serait qu'un petit inconvénient, s'il s'agissait de la plupart des autres véhicules, a cette fois entraîné la fermeture de la route.
L'autoroute I-880 a en effet dû être fermée à la fois au niveau des voies du nord et du sud. Les autorités ont pris cette décision en raison du risque potentiel de fumées chimiques dangereuses qui pouvaient être émises par le camion en flamme - et qui avait brûlé tout seul.
Une batterie en lithium est beaucoup plus difficile à éteindre
Car ici, aucun accident en vue. Les témoins indiquent simplement avoir vu un feu éclater seul dans le Tesla Semi. Pour le moment, Tesla n'a pas encore apporté de commentaires sur ce sujet. Mais il a fallu être patient pour avoir un retour à la normale.
L'ensemble des voies n'a en effet été dégagé qu'au bout d'une dizaine d'heures. Il faut dire que si les voitures électriques ont moins tendance à prendre feu que les thermiques, elles sont aussi sujettes à l'emballement thermique. Ce phénomène est une réaction chimique en chaîne incontrôlable qui fait qu'une cellule ayant chauffé transmet de la chaleur résiduelle à des cellules qui n'avaient pas encore brûlé, alors même que cette même cellule est en train d'être éteinte. Ainsi, pour éviter ce problème, les pompiers doivent effectuer un refroidissement massif, qui consiste souvent à l'utilisation de grosses quantités d'eau des heures durant.
Source : Electrek

articles.title: Auto-Generation Of Properties: Methodology Insertion
articles.text:
Technology is only useful if it improves an existing methodology. Property generation is still refining that goal, but in the long term it could be very useful.
Key Takeaways:
A top-down semiconductor development flow has long been a goal for chip design, and shift left is certainly making that increasingly possible. The problem is that the starting point — the specification — is often incomplete or nonexistent, because the chip industry has been notoriously bad at writing specifications.
There are several ways to insert AI into existing flows. But just because something can be done doesn’t mean it should be. This is one of the big challenges facing AI adoption. Many existing tasks could be done more efficiently using an agentic flow, but it’s not clear whether that is the right thing to do.
This limitation becomes especially apparent when AI starts to help with something that has been woefully inadequate in the past — the creation of good, complete specifications. The big question is whether AI can enable designs, or verification environments, to be automatically derived from a specification. Perhaps a more correct goal is whether AI can help create better specifications. With better specifications, downstream design becomes a lot easier.
“AI can generate a SystemVerilog assertion in seconds,” says Ben Cohen, verification technologist and book author. “Whether that assertion means anything depends entirely on what it was generated from, and in practice that source is rarely a single, clean, natural-language specification. It is just as often an ambiguous paragraph that needs clarifying before it can be trusted.”
Solving this problem should be considered a high priority. “The increasing complexity of modern SoC designs is making AI-assisted artefact generation and verification closure a practical requirement rather than a research option,” says Simon Davidmann, AI and EDA researcher at the University of Southampton. “The verification problem is, in practice, already at the scale where it cannot be addressed without AI assistance. The 5-to-1 ratio of verification engineers to designers in processor development is not a workforce planning anomaly, but a signal that the complexity has outgrown the methods.”
Going from specification to anything is not a reality today. “If we are actually going to make this reality, we need more discipline in terms of writing the spec,” says Ravindra Aneja, director of applications engineering at Synopsys. “If we really want to make it a reality, we have to work on it. As an industry, are we there? No, we are not there. I don’t think we are at a place where, either starting a new design or doing a derivative design, you can say the spec is good enough.”
Are we even thinking about it in the right way? “A prose specification document is not something a formal tool can reason over directly, because formal engines operate on precise, unambiguous, machine-checkable statements, not natural language,” says Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “What AI can help with is narrowing that gap, translating prose into candidate formal statements faster, which is really what deriving properties from specification means in practice. The properties are the formalization of the spec, not a separate step after it. So rather than thinking of it as spec first, then properties, then formal proof, it is more accurate to say the property set is the machine-readable spec, and formal is working on the spec once that translation has happened.”
Sometimes, specifications are purposely ambiguous. “Human designers interpret them with domain knowledge, prior experience, and the ability to ask clarifying questions,” says Southampton’s Davidmann. “AI models receive the specification text and generate output without the ability to flag ambiguity or identify inconsistency. Specification ambiguity is likely a significant contributor to LLM-generated code failures, but the current research literature does not yet systematically characterize how often this is the root cause, as distinct from model capability limits. The next step is developing methods for automated specification analysis that can identify ambiguity before it enters the generation pipeline.”
Should the problem be looked at the other way around? “Rather than having formal work on specs directly, there is a strong argument that modern spec authorship should be formal and machine-readable by construction,” says Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer at Normal Computing. “This is the only way to solve the inherent problems of trust, coverage, and drift. This is structurally impossible using only existing formal methodologies, but is achievable if you can use novel solvers and languages like Lean.”
That can feed the long-term goal. “I want to give a spec to my large language model, and I want it to generate code,” says Paul Graykowski, director of product marketing at Cadence. “But how do you capture the true intent of what a spec is, and make sure that is what you’re using as your single source of truth? There are a lot of things that must be explored, things that existing specifications just take for granted.”
There is probably room for an iterative approach. “When you read RTL, it can give you some abstract information about what your RTL is trying to do,” says Synopsys’ Aneja. “It may not be perfect, but it can give you a good starting point, and then you can modify that spec in an incremental manner. You can go from there. It’s not perfect, but at least it gives you a reasonable starting point.”
Skills migration
One of the supposed advantages of auto-generated properties is that it would reduce the need for specialized verification people. This may not be the case.
“For teams without internal formal expertise, complex AI-generated formal properties can be a boondoggle to review and maintain, and there are well-understood boundaries to the utility of SystemVerilog assertion-based methodologies,” says Normal’s Srinivasan. “The key principle is internal consistency. How can heavily AI-driven design processes leverage formal as both a check against other AI-driven design and verification collateral, but also utilize other collateral as a check against spurious or incorrect formal properties? Users that place stable systems of record and internal consistency at the heart of their processes will be better placed to utilize these systems in a zero-trust fashion.”
Someone still must read each generated SVA property. “They need to judge whether the antecedent is too weak or too tight, whether the consequent captures the actual requirement, whether clocking and reset conditions are handled correctly, and whether the property could pass vacuously,” says Axiomise’s Darbari. “That requires fluency in temporal logic and assertion semantics, as well as deep understanding of micro-architecture. Without that skill, a team has no way to tell a strong property from a weak one that happens to look similar, and they will not know how to interpret a formal tool’s counterexample or a ‘proven’ result correctly either. So the practical requirement is that AI lowers the writing burden but raises the importance of having formal-literate engineers in the loop to interpret and validate the output. Organizations adopting this should budget for that expertise rather than assuming the tooling removes the need for it.”
There are some roles where formal properties may be more beneficial than others. “Formal verification is becoming a more important part of the solution,” says Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “It is particularly strong for architectural compliance — ensuring ISA properties hold for all legal instruction sequences — and for enforcing correctness of hardware protocols in implementation verification. But formal is not a replacement for dynamic verification or system-level validation, especially when full SoC behavior and real workloads are involved. In practice, formal methods play a complementary role, proving deep corner-case correctness, while simulation and emulation establish end-to-end completeness.”
Problem areas
Vacuous assertions are a specific accuracy risk that deserves direct attention. “A vacuous assertion is an SVA that compiles correctly, passes the formal tool, and covers exactly nothing, because it is always true regardless of what the design does,” says Davidmann. “Vacuous assertions are not the same as correct assertions. A model that produces plausible-looking but vacuous SVAs provides false confidence while consuming formal tool capacity. A version of this technology that looks accurate on paper and is genuinely dangerous in practice is the one where the model is confident and wrong, the testbench was also generated by the model, and no one in the loop had the domain knowledge to notice. This is not a hypothetical failure mode. It is a workflow that is easy to construct inadvertently.”
There are significant costs associated with them. “In a formal verification flow, these errors are expensive,” says Cohen. “They consume tool runtime, engineer debug time, and — most critically — erode confidence in the verification results themselves.”
Formal verification involves multiple types of solvers, one of which is satisfiability modulo theories (SMTs). These look at determining whether a mathematical formula is satisfiable. “For agentic systems that put formal tools in the loop, there is a non-trivial cost from SMT solver runs,” says Srinivasan. “In addition, these scale with the complexity of the design and number of properties.”
Getting started
Deciding how to start using properties as part of a methodology is not obvious, and there are several issues that must be considered. There is also no single methodology that has been well tested, and it is likely that every company may need to work out what gives them the best balance of skills, time, and compute commitment, and the highest degree of verification closure.
AI needs to learn how generated properties are going to be used. “There are assertions for simulation and assertion for formal,” says Aneja. “There are techniques where you can write formal friendly properties, and that helps you with scaling in terms of, ‘Can you get a definite answer depending on how you’re writing the property?’ When you’re trying to write these properties, rather than writing a very long property, you want to divide that function into multiple smaller parts. That gives you scalability. Then you’re not getting stuck on a behavior that takes 200 cycles to do anything meaningful because it won’t work in formal.”
“Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a principled solution,” says Cohen. “Rather than relying solely on what an LLM learned during training, a RAG-enhanced system queries a curated knowledge base at generation time — retrieving the specific rules, patterns, and lessons that apply to the task at hand. RAG rules represent years of accumulated application knowledge — rules derived from real projects, real tool behaviors, and real failures. They encode not just what is syntactically correct, but what is verifiably sound; the difference between an assumption that constrains the environment appropriately and one that makes the formal proof space unreachable; between a property that checks the right behavior and one that passes vacuously; between timing diagrams that match the generated code and ones that silently diverge.”
There are stepped approaches that could be tried. “There is an intermediate step called formal test plan, where if you have a perfect spec, it talks about what your design does, not what you want to verify,” says Aneja. “The idea is that with all these LLMs and agents, you have the ability to read text, look at timing diagrams, look at FSM diagrams, other pictures you may have, and then you can extract certain features based on the designs you are doing. And you can train your system to say, is it a CPU design? Is it a GPU design? Is it an AI accelerator? Go one level down, is it a memory controller? Is it an interrupt controller? Is it a bus bridge? Or is it some interconnect across different managers and subordinates? Depending on what that is, it can extract certain features that you may want to test.”
The same considerations go for choosing an LLM. “Domain boundary awareness needs to become a first-class engineering discipline,” says Davidmann. “Before adopting any AI model into a production flow, the right question is not only how accurate the model is, but what it was trained on, what that distribution does not cover, and how close the actual design is to that boundary. Every team deploying these tools should run a deliberate boundary-probing exercise on a representative sample of their most complex and novel design patterns, verifying the outputs independently against what a domain expert would produce. That exercise identifies where the distribution ends and the model uncertainty begins. Without it, deployment is proceeding without the information needed to manage the risk.”
Start small and build confidence. “Pilot on a bounded, well-understood block first, compare the AI output against an existing hand-written property set, and measure the gap before rolling this out broadly,” says Darbari. “Finally, this only works well alongside engineers who already understand formal methods. It is not a way to skip that expertise. It is a way to make expert engineers faster. This is one area where I’m seeing an interesting demand from bigger design houses. Management wants engineers trained in formal so they can drive the entire ecosystem of tools and apply methodology properly.”
It is also important that you consider the domain in which you are working. “Tooling is currently ahead of the governance,” says Davidmann. “Most teams do not yet have a standard for documenting which assertions are human-authored, and which are AI-generated, or what that distinction means for sign-off confidence. In addition, most vendor documentation does not specify the training scope, failure modes, or domain boundaries of the models being deployed. Both gaps need to close before AI-generated content scales into safety-critical designs.”
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Motorola Signature 27 : la date de sortie européenne est officielle, mais son prix s'envolerait — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sur son compte X officiel, Motorola a donné ce jeudi 29 octobre la date de lancement européen de son nouveau haut de gamme. Ce sera le jeudi 5 novembre. Le smartphone avait été dévoilé le 22 septembre au Snapdragon Summit de Qualcomm, avec sa puce et ses appareils photo, mais sans prix ni date de sortie. Dans une semaine, on saura donc combien Motorola en demande. Si le tarif qui circule depuis ce mardi se confirme, la note sera salée, avec 1 594,90 euros pour la version 12 gigaoctets de RAM et 512 gigaoctets de stockage.
Ce prix vient de la fiche produit du revendeur portugais MegaPC, repérée ce mardi 27 octobre par GSMArena. La page montrait le coloris Pantone Coal Smoke, un noir charbon, et indiquait que le téléphone était en rupture de stock, sans date d’expédition. Pour comparer, le premier Motorola Signature, présenté en janvier au CES, avait été annoncé à 999 euros en Europe avec la même mémoire, avant que son prix officiel ne passe à 1 299 euros quelques semaines plus tard. Le Signature 27 coûterait donc près de 600 euros de plus que le prix d’annonce (environ 60 % de hausse), et environ 300 euros de plus que le tarif officiel réévalué (environ 23 %). Motorola n’a confirmé aucun chiffre, et un revendeur peut très bien afficher un prix provisoire avant l’annonce officielle.
    Pour aller plus loin
Quel est le meilleur smartphone à moins de 800 € en 2026 ?
            
Une puce gravée en 2 nanomètres et un zoom de 200 mégapixels
Côté puce, le Signature 27 embarque le Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. C’est le premier SoC de Qualcomm gravé en 2 nanomètres, une finesse qui permet de loger plus de transistors tout en consommant moins. Pour éviter que la puce chauffe et ralentisse sous l’effort, Motorola a prévu un système de refroidissement baptisé ArcticMesh. On y trouve un gel thermique chargé de particules de diamant et une chambre à vapeur 40 % plus grande que sur la génération précédente. Côté photo, le capteur principal est un Sony Lytia 910 de 50 mégapixels. Surtout, le capteur de 200 mégapixels se trouve derrière le téléobjectif périscopique, un zoom dont les lentilles sont couchées dans le châssis pour offrir un grossissement optique de 5x sans épaissir le téléphone.
Motorola promet aussi sept mises à jour majeures d’Android. En revanche, les correctifs de sécurité courent jusqu’à sept ans à partir du lancement mondial, et cette durée varie selon le marché, l’opérateur et le modèle. Le son est réglé par Bang & Olufsen, une première chez Motorola, qui confiait jusqu’ici ce réglage à Bose, y compris sur le premier Signature. Le reste de la fiche technique n’est pas encore officiel : on attend un écran AMOLED LTPO de 6,8 pouces à 165 Hz (une dalle qui fait varier sa fréquence d’affichage pour économiser la batterie), une batterie de 7 000 mAh et un ultra grand-angle de 50 mégapixels. Le premier Signature, que nous avions trouvé bon partout, ou presque, misait surtout sur la finesse, avec moins de 7 millimètres d’épaisseur. Motorola n’a encore donné ni l’épaisseur ni le poids du nouveau modèle.
Le prix français et la date de mise en vente seront connus le 5 novembre. Contrairement au premier Signature, réservé à l’Europe et à d’autres marchés internationaux, le nouveau modèle sortira aussi aux États-Unis, où le site de Motorola annonce une arrivée en novembre. Une édition Swarovski est aussi attendue : en septembre, le code de la page teaser du site européen de Motorola mentionnait déjà un logo « Crystals by Swarovski », comme pour le premier Signature.

articles.title: Anthropic Says Nobody Needs a Mental Model of Claude Code. Practitioners Are Testing That
articles.text:
Anthropic has published how the Claude Code team runs code review now that Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code itself. The claim drawing the most scrutiny is not the percentage but what the team says it no longer needs.
The post, by Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt and Qing Wang, is the companion to Anthropic’s account of replacing git with an in-house system after its monorepo went from roughly 2,500 merged changes a day in May to more than 30,000 in September. Review was the next thing to break. The target is that most pull requests "merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents."
On comprehension, the team is explicit:
Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don’t think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
That passage dominated the Hacker News discussion, where commenter jonahx set out what it trades away:
There is no longer anyone to turn to if this system breaks by, eg, having a critical bug that no one can figure out. No causal model in anyone’s head that can be appealed to, to slowly and methodically debug. The new trust model is: We trust Claude to always understand the system enough to debug anything or make any reasonable change we could want.
He also noted that many large legacy systems already work this way.
One documented case tests the explainer claim on Anthropic’s own repository. In August, Claude Code collaborator Boris Cherny answered a long-running complaint about issue auto-closure in a comment carrying the "Generated with Claude Code" footer. It said issues are closed when they have "had no activity for a while and are missing information needed to reproduce," and that "nothing is triaged solely by counting."
The repository’s issue-lifecycle.ts sets fourteen days to stale and fourteen more to closure, exempting only issues with ten or more upvotes. Developer marcindulak counted more than 6,000 issues labelled as carrying reproduction steps that were closed anyway as "inactive for too long." The remedy the comment offered, commenting to have an issue reopened, is blocked by a workflow that locks closed issues after seven days. That meta-issue is now locked.
The answer that started this issue, and misdiagnosed how issues in this repo are managed, was generated by a world-class model.
The failures the post documents are specific. The first appears only when both sides are machines:
Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.
"One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it," the team writes. Running more rounds by default made things worse, so they capped them. On r/ClaudeCode, commenter ChemicalExcellent463 reported reaching the same control independently, stopping after two failed fixes because repeated failure means the agent’s picture of the code is wrong rather than the line it keeps editing.
The second failure is what those rounds were finding:
When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer’s first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.
What gates a merge is a risk tier picked by a classifier, where "the change sets the tier, not the author." Low risk covers docs, copy, and additive changes behind a flag, and clears with no human approval. Medium risk, including caching, the auto-updater, and system prompts, needs one person. Two rules hold the line: "an agent’s approval never counts as a person’s," and the person who prompted a change "counts as one of the required reviewers."
That boundary drew a question the post does not answer. Reddit commenter Oximy-Naman asked whether low risk covers agent instruction changes shipped as documentation, since those "could change what an agent does without touching application code," and got no reply. The post assigns no tier to CLAUDE.md, the file its own reviewer loads on every review. On compliance, Hacker News commenter gaal_dornick reported that their own SOC 2 reviewer required every change to be seen by a second human before production; the post does not discuss audit requirements.
One control is missing, and the team says so:
We don’t yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.
Not everyone reads this as reckless. Commenter cheema33 argued that large organizations have never had anyone holding a complete model, making this an upgrade on the status quo, and commenter markbao reported spending a few thousand dollars a month on AI review against human review that consumes up to a third of an engineer’s time.
Parts of the system ship publicly. Code Review for Claude Code is generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and the security review runs as an open-source GitHub Action whose README states that it "is not hardened against prompt injection attacks and should only be used to review trusted PRs."

articles.title: Amazon warns engineers just using more AI doesn't make them more productive, says they should avoid tokenmaxxing
articles.text:
Amazon warns engineers just using more AI doesn't make them more productive, says they should avoid tokenmaxxing
Amazon tells engineers to focus on real results
- Amazon urges developers not to blindly focus on AI tool usage
- The era of the "Renaissance Developer" using all kinds of AI is here
- It also urges workers to shun tokenmaxxing, and focus on building a deeper connection with customers
Amazon has told its engineers to look beyond simply using AI to ensure their work gets done, and focus instead on the results of their labor.
In a memo sent to its workforce, the company warned against using “deeply flawed” metrics such as AI token usage or code generation as a measure of team success.
It also cautioned against workers chasing "tokenmaxxing", noting how, "our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI."
The age of the "Renaissance Developer"
The memo, written by Terk Terkowitz, Amazon VP/Distinguished Engineer, Worldwide, and entitled "An update from Amazon engineering leadership on the role of the developer in the age of AI", signaled the apparent beginning of a new era in how the company defines its workers in the age of AI.
This includes the age of the "Renaissance Developer", who is able to blend AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise "to build entirely new things".
"AI is changing the work of software engineering both more quickly and more fundamentally than these previous trends," Terkowitz noted. "What it means to be a software engineer, and what software engineering even is, is changing quickly and durably."
What this means for Amazon's workers is a focus on "on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE (Software Development Engineers) roles".
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This will mean a move away from "deeply flawed" metrics such as token usage or adoption of AI tools, and more focus on the impact on customers, businesses and teams.
The memo urges managers and division heads to make sure that there is "sufficient understanding" among their teams about the benefits AI tools can bring, and told workers to ensure they become "deeply connected" to their customers in order to gain a deeper knowledge of what they really need from Amazon.
"Despite the speed of change, we believe that it is still early. We all need to embrace this change and take the time to learn, or we risk being left behind," Terkowitz concluded.
“We’re just seeing the beginning of AI’s effect on software engineering. While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there’s a lot that’s still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice.”

He has worked as a B2B and B2C tech journalist for over a decade, including at one of the UK's leading national newspapers and fellow Future title ITProPortal. When he's not keeping track of all the latest enterprise and workplace trends, he can most likely be found watching, following or taking part in some kind of sport.
