articles.title: Jennifer Lawrence confirma su regreso a 'Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha': "Fue muy emotivo"
articles.text:
Lo que era un secreto a voces ya se ha confirmado oficialmente. Jennifer Lawrence regresa a la franquicia de Los Juegos del Hambre en su nueva película, Amanecer en la cosecha. La actriz volverá a dar vida a Katniss Everdeen y, además, no estará sola. Tanto Josh Hutcherson como Woody Harrelson también regresan en sus papeles de Peeta Mellark y Haymitch Abernathy.
Aunque Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha será una precuela, Jennifer Lawrence y sus compañeros aparecerán en al menos una escena, probablemente un flashforward que llenará de nostalgia los corazones de los fans de la saga. De hecho, ha sido la propia actriz la que ha confirmado la noticia en el podcast Call Her Daddy.
"Fue increíble. Fue una locura. Era el mismo equipo. El mismo asistente de dirección, con el que he trabajado un millón de veces porque le adoro. Y con Josh [Hutcherson] y Woody [Harrelson]… fue muy emotivo", asegura Jennifer Lawrence sobre su sorprendente regreso a Los Juegos del Hambre.
"Josh y yo no íbamos ni al baño sin estar abrazados. Fue precioso. Y Woody, como era de esperar, se coló por la ventana de mi habitación de hotel sin que nadie le invitara. No sería lo mismo si respetara los límites o utilizara la puerta", bromea también la actriz. Y es que, aunque la noticia de estos especiales regresos ya había trascendido en la prensa hace unos meses, ahora ha sido la propia Lawrence quien se ha encargado de confirmarlo definitivamente.
De qué va Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha
Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha llevará a la pantalla la 50ª edición de los Juegos organizados por el Capitolio. Se trata de una edición especialmente cruel y sangrienta porque el número de tributos de cada distrito será el doble. Por tanto, también habrá el doble de muertos en la arena. Uno de esos tributos será Haymitch Abernathy, quien posteriormente sabemos que será el mentor del Distrito 12 que entrenará y ayudará a Katniss y Peeta a sobrevivir.
En esta precuela se nos presenta a su versión joven, interpretada por Joseph Zada, que deberá mostrar cómo consiguió sobrevivir. El resto del reparto lo componen Ralph Fiennes como el presidente Snow, Jesse Plemons como Plutarch Heavensbee, Glenn Close como Drusilla Sickle, Elle Faning como Effie Trinket, Kieran Culkin como el presentador Caesar Flickerman, Maya Hawke como Wiress, Mckenna Grace como Maysilee Donner o Whitney Peak como Lenore Dove Baird, entre otros.
Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha se estrena en cines el 20 de noviembre.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Carbon, una IA tan potente que por ahora está vetada al público general
articles.text:
Google presentó este miércoles Gemini 4 Carbon, su nuevo modelo de inteligencia artificial, que encabeza con 59 puntos el índice de la firma independiente Artificial Analysis. Por ahora solo lo usará un grupo reducido de especialistas en ciberseguridad; desarrolladores, empresas y público general deberán esperar, sin fecha confirmada.
El anuncio lo firmó Koray Kavukcuoglu, vicepresidente sénior de Google DeepMind y arquitecto jefe de inteligencia artificial de la empresa. Según Google, Carbon lidera tres pruebas públicas de seguridad informática: 88,2% en SEC-bench Pro, que mide la capacidad de encontrar fallas en programas reales; 54,8% en ExploitGym, que comprueba si una falla puede aprovecharse, y 71,0% en CWE-bench, que evalúa si el modelo la corrige.
En el índice de Artificial Analysis, versión 5.0, Carbon supera a Claude Opus 5.5, de Anthropic, con 58 puntos, y a GPT-6 Astra, de OpenAI, con 57, según VentureBeat. Argon, el modelo anterior de Google, obtuvo 50. En la tabla de Google, Carbon logra el mejor resultado en 15 de 17 pruebas.
Argon se presentó el 30 de septiembre para socios de ciberseguridad y se abrió de forma más amplia el 13 de octubre, según VentureBeat. Carbon sigue el mismo camino, 15 días después de esa ampliación. Google no publicó un informe técnico ni la cantidad de parámetros del modelo.
Solo especialistas en ciberseguridad tendrán acceso por ahora
Google dijo que esta semana dará acceso a “un subconjunto de defensores cibernéticos” y que lo ampliará por etapas a más socios de confianza mediante su Programa Fairwind, que tiene más de 650 socios, exige verificación de antecedentes y prohíbe compartir o revender el acceso, según WebProNews, que cita la página del programa.
El resto de los usuarios no tiene plazo. La empresa afirmó que lo ofrecerá a desarrolladores, empresas y consumidores “lo antes posible”, tras reunir comentarios y ajustar las salvaguardas del modelo. También participa en el proceso voluntario del gobierno de Estados Unidos para probar modelos antes de su lanzamiento.
Cuando llegue a los desarrolladores, el precio inicial será de USD 2 por cada millón de tokens de entrada y de USD 10 por cada millón de salida; después subirá a USD 4 y USD 20. Google no precisó cuándo termina ese período introductorio; el de Argon vence el 30 de noviembre.
Las pruebas de seguridad se midieron sin restricciones
Google aclaró que las evaluaciones externas de ciberseguridad se hicieron sin salvaguardas. VentureBeat señaló que, por eso, el anuncio no demuestra que los clientes obtendrán los mismos resultados con las restricciones que acompañen al modelo cuando se comercialice.
La empresa también afirmó que el equipo de Chrome halló que Carbon generó correcciones de mayor calidad con una ventaja superior a 10 veces frente al modelo de otro laboratorio. Google no nombró al rival ni publicó los datos de esa comparación, según VentureBeat.
Las pruebas independientes mostraron matices: Carbon mejora de forma notable sobre Argon en programación y trabajo con conocimiento, pero queda detrás de varios rivales en tareas profesionales y registra más alucinaciones que Argon en una prueba de datos factuales, informó VentureBeat. OpenAI conserva ventaja en una prueba de ingeniería de software y Anthropic en una de uso de la computadora.
Google describió además mejoras en la conducta del modelo: las alertas graves de desvío de conducta bajaron casi 80% en sus equipos internos y, en un banco de pruebas de inyección de instrucciones —ataques que ocultan órdenes en el contenido que lee el modelo—, el índice de éxito de los ataques fue de 0,0%. Todas son mediciones de la propia compañía.
Carbon puede trabajar durante días para encontrar y corregir errores sutiles en grandes bases de código, según observaciones de los equipos internos de Google.

articles.title: SA’s Fynbos Money allows investors to connect portfolios directly to AI - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African investtech startup Fynbos Money is allowing customers to connect their portfolios to ChatGPT, Claude and other AI assistants, helping them ask questions about their investments and receive detailed analysis.
Founded in 2024 by Adrian Hope-Bailie and based in Cape Town, Fynbos Money is a savings and investments platform that consolidates multiple financial products into a single interface. All deposits flow into a central cash account first and then automatically distribute according to a user’s custom rules
The new integration with AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT allows customers to ask questions about their own investments in everyday language and receive analysis based on their actual portfolio information.
Questions such as “Has my money actually grown, or have I just deposited more?”, “What am I actually invested in?” or “What could an extra R500 a month mean over 20 years?” can now be answered using information from their own accounts, giving investors access to insights that have traditionally required specialist financial knowledge.
The launch comes as AI companies push further into financial services. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, recently introduced Claude for Financial Advisors, connecting financial professionals with data and tools used for research, preparation and documentation. Fynbos is taking this shift directly to individual investors, making AI-powered financial analysis accessible to customers using their own investment data.
“Investing has become far more accessible, but access to useful financial insight hasn’t necessarily kept pace,” Hope-Bailie said. “AI has the potential to change that. By giving people the ability to interrogate their own investment information, we can make useful financial insight much more accessible.”
It’s an approach Hope-Bailie calls ‘bring your own intelligence’. Rather than building its own AI assistant, Fynbos allows customers to connect their investments to supported AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, giving them the freedom to use the tools they’re already familiar with.
Customers can choose to connect their Fynbos account to a supported AI assistant, giving it access to read-only information about their accounts, balances and selected funds. The assistant can also use tools developed by Fynbos to perform calculations and projections and access fund information such as performance and fees.
The functionality has been built using Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard that allows AI applications to connect to external tools and data. This means Fynbos customers can use compatible AI assistants rather than being tied to a single provider.
Connecting is entirely optional, and access to the Fynbos account is read-only. AI assistants cannot use the connection to move money, buy or sell investments, switch funds or make any other changes to the account. Any information accessed through a connected AI assistant is subject to that provider’s own privacy, data processing and retention policies.
Fynbos has also launched its first mobile app, responding to one of its most requested customer features. The app introduces biometric login, faster performance and a more responsive mobile experience, while giving Fynbos access to security and usability features not available through its web platform.
“Both developments reflect the direction we want to take Fynbos Money,” said Hope-Bailie. “We want to build technology that makes investing simpler, gives customers greater control and helps them make more informed decisions about their money.”

articles.title: Microsoft just shared Azure's actual revenue in dollars: $33.2 billion | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Microsoft has never disclosed Azure’s quarterly revenue in dollars. It has typically only shared a growth percentage or described revenue dollar milestones in vague ways. But on Wednesday, when it posted another record-breaking quarter, it reported that Azure brought in a healthy $33.2 billion in revenue for the July-September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier.
The disclosure lets investors line up Azure’s performance more directly against Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, whose parent companies already report cloud revenue in dollars every quarter.
Alphabet, which also reported earnings on Wednesday, said Google Cloud brought in $30.7 billion in the same quarter, putting Azure slightly ahead. But Google Cloud, which also includes Google’s Workspace subscriptions, roughly doubled its revenue from a year earlier, growing about twice as fast as Azure, according to TechCrunch’s calculations.
Azure, where businesses rent computing power to run applications, SaaS, and to build and run AI models, is now Microsoft’s largest and fastest-growing product line by the company’s own figures. It accounted for roughly 36% of Microsoft’s $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue.
Azure’s revenue was also about $850 million more than the $32.3 billion analysts expected. Azure’s 48% growth rate also topped the 44% to 45% that Microsoft CFO Amy Hood forecast on the company’s July earnings call.
Azure sits inside Agents and Infra, one of two new business segments Microsoft introduced this quarter. Microsoft previously reported three segments, Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. The new Agents and Infra segment, which groups Azure with Microsoft 365’s cloud business, brought in $76.8 billion, up 25% from a year earlier.
Amazon reports its earnings on Thursday. Analysts also expect its cloud, Amazon Web Services, to grow. It’s been the largest cloud since the beginning of time and no one expects Microsoft to best it right now. But with all of them reporting actual dollars, the race is on.

articles.title: TSMC Could Charge Up to 20% More for CoWoS Packaging Amid AI Crunch
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
TSMC Could Charge Up to 20% More for CoWoS Packaging Amid AI Crunch
TSMC is reportedly considering raising prices for its CoWoS (Chip on Wafer on Substrate) advanced packaging by as much as 20%, according to supply chain sources cited by Taiwan's Commercial Times. Foundries and outsourced packaging firms are apparently weighing another round of 10% to 20% increases, as CoWoS demand has spread beyond AI GPUs to server CPUs and custom ASICs, leaving a growing backlog of unfilled orders. TSMC hasn't confirmed anything yet.
Testing is turning into a bottleneck of its own. Nomura estimates, via Seoul Economic Daily, that NVIDIA's Blackwell takes roughly four times longer than Hopper in final testing, while Rubin could need seven times as long. Packages keep growing too, with TSMC already mass producing CoWoS-L at 5.5 times the reticle limit. Tool lead times have reportedly stretched from three to six months to as long as eight months. TSMC, which usually negotiates for discounts or extra features, apparently placed this year's equipment orders at existing prices instead, which says a lot about how tight things are.Liberty Times also reports that TSMC has finalized plans for 3% to 6% wafer price increases from January 2027, with 2 nm and 3 nm seeing the steepest hikes. Some packaging relief is coming, just not soon. GlobalFoundries reportedly signed a five-year, $2 billion deal to make CoWoS silicon interposers in New York, with volume production expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. At the moment this is mostly a data center problem, since gaming graphics cards don't use CoWoS, though pricier wafers will probably reach consumer chips eventually.

articles.title: Petition seeks 10-minute maximum hold times for Canadian telcos
articles.text:
Amid growing telecom wait times and rising frustration from Canadians, a new petition wants the government to establish customer service access standards like maximum hold times.
A House of Commons petition filed this month asks Parliament to tell the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to “establish a clear, measurable and enforceable customer-service access standard for telecommunications providers.”
The petition also calls for establishing a “maximum 10-minute telephone hold time for customers seeking access to human customer service,” and asks the CRTC to determine how to measure hold times as well as to create “reasonable exceptions” to the rule.
Elsewhere, the petition says the customer service standards should require access to a human representative instead of connecting to automated systems. Specifically, the human representative should be able to start helping with the customer’s concern to prevent unnecessary transfers or further waiting.
Finally, and perhaps most crucially, the petition seeks the creation of “meaningful and proportional consequences for providers that persistently fail.”
At the time of writing, the petition had about 50 signatures. While not many, it’s worth noting the creator also made a similar Change.org petition that received nearly 1,200 signatures. The House of Commons petition closes on Nov. 26, 2026 at 1:03 p.m. ET.
Service standards a partial fix
The idea of customer service standards isn’t exactly new. Other countries have implemented similar rules. Spain, for example, implemented rules requiring telecoms and other large companies to answer customer calls within three minutes 95 per cent of the time.
Similar rules could help address a growing service problem with Canada’s biggest telecoms. It’s increasingly difficult for Canadians to contact their providers, with many reporting multi-hour wait times. When people do eventually get through, they’re often forced to navigate several hurdles like automated systems and transfers. And those who manage to make it to a real person might not even get the help they need, as customer service reps are often incentivized to keep calls short and to sell new products, leading to a lack of help or even reps hanging up on people.
And we can see this growing trend reflected in other places. Canada’s Commission for Complaints for Telecom-Television Services (CCTS), for example, says telecom complaints are up nearly 80 per cent over last year.
However, customer service standards might only address part of the problem. The other issue behind rising complaints is the industry’s incessant cutting and outsourcing of customer service roles. Any customer service standards rules should also address this practice, such as by requiring Canadian-based support workers. Doing so would also benefit Canada’s national security by limiting the amount of telecom information, as well as personal and financial information, that’s shared outside of the country.
Source: Our Commons Via: Reddit, Change.org

articles.title: Rethinking Shift Left In Chip Design
articles.text:
Is it better to do everything earlier in the flow, or should design be more flexible and iterative?
Key Takeaways:
Experts at the Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the good and bad of shifting left amid ongoing changes in how chips are designed, used, and updated throughout the flow, with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise. What follows are excerpts of that conversation.
L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv.
SE: We’ve been talking about shifting left in the design-through-manufacturing flow for more than a decade, but more and more capabilities are being added to improve reliability and yield, and produce silicon faster. What changes are you seeing?
Schirrmeister: We’re now adding digital twins, which are shifting very left.
Berg: That’s correct. And the issue now is working with multi-physics models. Using that data to assemble surrogate models is important. As we go further into different technologies with different materials, you have to go back to the materials science solvers and physics solvers to get models that designers can use. This is happening in areas that are not typically digital design, but as we get down to the CFET level, it’s starting to be used there, as well.
Schirrmeister: There are three changes. Number one, now we have the technical ability with compute, with agents, to shift much further left than we ever hoped we would get to in our lifetimes. The problem there is whether shift left is trustworthy. Is the surrogate model a reliable representation of what’s happening? You can’t have the agent decide that. In the past, for virtual prototyping, you would get a human being who is responsible for ensuring that the model represents what’s happening, and that it’s accurate. That’s number one. So the trust is changing. Number two, you need to trust the shift-left model to be predictive of what you’re doing. Otherwise, you’ll regret you’re shifting left because you’ll need another spin. In a Qualcomm keynote, the speaker talked about the new reasoning gap. He said we used to have a productivity gap, but now we have a reasoning gap. They want engineers to reason about the product and make that product better. But the tools can’t deal with reasoning yet. The third one is the rapid pace of shift-left options. If I get to the point where I can trust the models, then I have new things I can do. At the architectural level, I can decide something and kick off ‘n’ options to try it out if the models are predictive enough.
Darbari: The shift-left discourse started at least 15 years ago. What has changed is AI and the agentic use model. What has not happened yet is the trust element in today’s AI agents. There are all these excellent use models for the agents, which we use and our customers use, to go through the specifications. A lot of discussion has now moved into spec-to-silicon, because people believe you can extract requirements from specification documents — if you have them. But most of the time you don’t have them, and that is one of the problems. Another big change I’m seeing in the work we do with formal verification is that functional verification is now seen as a problem, at the same level as security, functional safety, and power, with all of the hardware feeding into the AI ecosystem, which is the largest investment pool. A lot of companies are investing in PPA analysis on the first day. For example, I know of customers that are taking their designs, even the older generation, and saying, ‘Let an AI agent rewrite it for optimized PPA.’ But how do I know it is correct? Can I prove it to be equivalent to something else? So the big 10 companies in the semiconductor space, which have big budgets and big teams of people, are adopting agentic AI flows, and they’re heavily leaning on whether they can trust it or not trust it. That trust gap is often being solved through early adoption of formal through proofs. The know-how is not necessarily the biggest blocker. It’s mostly whether tools can integrate more seamlessly into the system.
But if you look at what is enabling more shift left, it’s the time spent on debug. When you’re bringing up an architectural analysis and you have a failure, you can feed it to an agent. There’s a lot of data coming out of the agents, and we need to do more work on insights. Are you spending your time wisely? Even if it is correct or incorrect, if a manual review has to happen, that could be a massive blocker in the early phases of adoption of shift left. With agents being adopted earlier, will this lead to better designs with fewer bug escapes? That remains to be seen, and I don’t believe that shift left alone will be able to fix it.
Laviv: Shift left is identifying the bottlenecks in our industry and looking at what you can do in order to pull in work and schedule as much as you can earlier in the design and verification cycle. Nowadays, the agents are leaping forward to help, but everything that happens gets us into bottlenecks — new bottlenecks or old bottlenecks — that we have to solve.
SE: We have so much that has to be looked at and verified concurrently that it becomes a problem to shift that much stuff left, and it gets more complicated with multi-die assemblies and lifecycle management. How do all the pieces go together and stay together?
Schirrmeister: Is shift left even the right thing? Shift left assumes that I have a solid knowledge of what I’m actually going to do, and it assumes I can specify what I want six or nine months or a year from now. Maybe we’re thinking about this wrong. Perhaps what we need is a general direction, and then the ability to make adjustments based on the information we gain as we go toward implementation choices. Shift left implies that you can get to zero in some magic future world by having something spec’d, and you get all the way there. What I hear people doing is different. They say, ‘Okay, I’m building something, and with agentic AI I can now build this model that potentially represents most of it. So now I make the decision, ‘This one is fairly straightforward and it doesn’t need that much effort on an Arm processor, or I can make a RISC-V processor for it.’ Now I reset my spec, which is kind of messed up because I did not have the correct hardware spec, so now I’m making adjustments. The cool part is we are approaching a time when we can shift left to this new refinement. It’s almost like an agile shift left. In an agile way, you make adjustments to your implementation for micro choices that happen later based on what you’re doing now.
SE: That addresses a big problem with these designs, because you don’t know what the workload will be by the time this chip is deployed in the market. This is a more generic approach that focuses on adaptability, right?
Schirrmeister: Exactly, and we didn’t dare do this in the past because this was all sequential. Now it becomes more circular. So there was a product manager who knew the market and said, ‘I’m building this, and then 18 months later you found out it didn’t work.’ Right now you have new data all the time, so there can be this agility in refining what you’re doing.
Darbari: I agree that there are lots of choices in agility and lots of changes, and not everything is known up front, which is the reality in building anything. However, I do not see that things are so fuzzy. If you’re building a new machine learning chip, or a GPU or a CPU, you have some idea of what the derivative design was before. What is the general architecture you’re going to play with? What you don’t know is what the implementation choices are going to be for power, for functionality, and with AI bringing lots of challenges on training or inference. Those are quite novel. So you need to make multiple choices at every step along the way, with or without agents. But agents can help you do that more efficiently. What I don’t know is whether the outcomes of these agile agents can be reconciled very quickly and trusted.
Schirrmeister: You don’t let AI actually make the decision for you, and you don’t trust the AI. You then need to go down into a verified model.
Berg: That’s a really important point. The AI agents don’t replace humans. They are effectively junior engineers, and they need to have their work reviewed by somebody who knows it. The notion that it’s agile, and is growing agile, is very real. There’s this notion that a flow does an inverse design. But what happens if that inverse design could be based on multi-physics solvers. You put together a surrogate model, digital twins, and then you say, ‘Okay, give me a transistor or give me a chip — or even so far as a chip through RTL at this point — that works with these constraints and these things that are going on. And all of a sudden you have an empty set. It’s over-constrained. Now what do you do? This is why the notion that you have to be agile is very valid.
Laviv: If we take the example of the digital flow, you have virtual platforms today, formal, software simulation, emulation, FPGA, and you have engineers and AI engines. You will need to make adjustments. And if you’re designing a CPU, or something that’s tangible, and you can do it better with formal and bring it to the table sooner with a more stable design, then emulation and FPGA can run sooner in the pipeline of doing the verification stuff, and the same thing with simulation. If you have done something to solve the bottlenecks in formal, in simulation, virtual prototyping, or even the flow itself, this would help shift everything left and allow you to make better decisions earlier in the game. That way if you need to change stuff, you can change it.
Darbari: The validation problem is significant. I’m seeing real evidence with some customers, who literally are going back to the drawing board to build a ground-up architecture that can address different phases of their chips being used. So they could build a CPU, a GPU, a machine learning chip, and they really need to scope out whether what they intend to build would cover all kinds of use models. That’s not easy, especially when you bring software into the loop, and the software isn’t what used to run 20 years ago. There is training, inference, power coming into the chain all the way back to the architecture level, and then you’ve got to make these choices.

articles.title: Cyber recovery planning must include storage in the AI era - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Infinidat brings storage into cyber recovery planning
Cyber recovery planning depends on the ability to restore critical data after an attack. As enterprises adopt agentic AI, the systems and information they need to protect are expanding.
That expansion is reshaping how enterprises approach AI trust and cyber resilience. AI models, agents and the software supporting them create additional targets for attackers, according to Eric Herzog (pictured), chief marketing officer of Infinidat Ltd., a Lenovo company.
“We would argue that … anything to do with AI dramatically expands the attack surface,” Herzog said. “Everything you’re doing — the [large language models], the [small language models], that AI software stack you deploy — the cyber criminals are going to go after all of that. Instead of shrinking the attack surface, you’ve actually increased it.”
Herzog spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed cyber recovery planning and why storage belongs in an AI-era cybersecurity strategy. (* Disclosure below.)
Putting storage in cyber recovery planning
Infinidat’s answer is InfiniSafe, a set of cybersecurity capabilities embedded in the company’s InfuzeOS storage operating system. It includes immutable snapshots, logical air-gapping that separates the management plane from the data plane and a fenced forensic environment for examining suspect data. About 90% of the most valuable data at global Fortune 500 companies sits on enterprise storage, which makes that layer a logical place to build defenses, Herzog noted.
“You tell it what you want to do, and the storage then responds to this data center-wide cybersecurity software or the SOC and automatically starts taking action,” Herzog said. “You don’t want to waste a minute if you think you’re having a cyberattack.”
Detection comes next. InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI and machine learning to scan block data, file data and VMware data stores for anomalies, rating each snapshot’s risk as high, medium or low. Some customers scan daily snapshots twice a week, while others use the tool reactively until they reach a known good copy, according to Herzog. Infinidat offers a recovery-time guarantee of one minute or less for immutable snapshots on its InfiniBox platforms.
“That guarantee is an RTO of 1 minute or less no matter how big the dataset size,” Herzog said. “Last July, we did one of our Experts Live events … If you were on that event, you would have seen us recover 9.8 petabytes in 5 seconds.”
Attackers also go after backups and replicas, which is why Infinidat works with data protection companies such as Veeam Software Group GmbH and Commvault Systems Inc., Herzog explained. He pointed to PwC’s latest CEO survey, which ranked cyber as the No. 1 business risk, as a reason to win board-level buy-in.
“What they should do is practically deploy enterprise-wide cyber storage, integrate it with the SOC or the [security incident and event management] or [security orchestration, automation and response] technology so it works together as a team,” Herzog said. “I would argue that from a big enterprise perspective, a cyberattack is a disaster.”

articles.title: Cyberattaque contre les clients Starlink : une campagne de pubs malveillantes vient d'être découverte
articles.text:
Comme le révèle Reuters, des chercheurs de l’entreprise de cybersécurité TrendAI ont découvert que Discover-Tech, une société israélienne de publicité en ligne, enchérissait en masse pour diffuser ses publicités auprès d’utilisateurs de Starlink. L’entreprise a notamment diffusé un nombre conséquent de publicités en Afghanistan, en Libye et en Syrie. Il ne serait donc pas question de simples opérations publicitaires, mais d’une activité qui s’apparente à une surveillance de masse. Dans certains cas, elle serait même parvenue à installer un logiciel espion sur les appareils ciblés. Des institutions européennes seraient également concernées par cette affaire.
Un système publicitaire potentiellement détourné pour suivre des personnes
Pour bien comprendre le mécanisme mobilisé par cette entreprise israélienne, il faut revenir sur le mode de fonctionnement d’un système publicitaire spécifique baptisé Real-Time Bidding (RTB). Il s’agit d’un système d’enchères publicitaires en temps réel. Lorsqu’une personne arrive sur un site, une enchère est organisée en quelques millisecondes pour déterminer quelle publicité sera affichée. Durant ce court laps de temps, certaines données de l’internaute peuvent être transmises aux annonceurs potentiels : adresse IP, caractéristiques de l’appareil, zone géographique approximative…
L’entreprise israélienne Discover-Tech a utilisé ce système, non pas simplement pour simplement diffuser des publicités, mais dans le cadre d’une activité qui pourrait viser à suivre des personnes. Quel élément permet d’aboutir à cette conclusion ? L’entreprise enchérissait en masse pour afficher des publicités dans des pays comme la Syrie, l’Afghanistan, la Libye, le Yémen ou encore le Soudan du Sud. En d’autres termes, des pays sensibles, qui offrent par ailleurs de très faibles revenus publicitaires. Pour TrendAI, ces éléments suggèrent qu’il est question d’une « infrastructure de ciblage et de suivi plutôt qu’une activité publicitaire commerciale ».
À noter que TrendAI n’identifie pas l’entreprise israélienne Discover-Tech dans son rapport, préférant utiliser le nom de code Shadow-Earth-79. Cependant, selon des personnes proches du dossier, il s’agirait bel et bien de cette entreprise. TrendAI aurait anonymisé l’entreprise israélienne par crainte de représailles juridiques.
Des publicités diffusées jusque dans les réseaux d’institutions européennes ?
L’entreprise Discover-Tech aurait donc utilisé des publicités en ligne pour suivre des personnes, mais cela n’est pas tout. Dans certains cas, elle serait également parvenue à installer le logiciel espion Candiru sur certains appareils. Comment cela est-il possible ? Certaines publicités intègrent du code informatique qui s’exécute automatiquement lorsque le navigateur ou l’application affiche la publicité. Le logiciel espion est ainsi installé sur l’appareil, sans aucun clic ni téléchargement.
Toujours selon TrendAI, les publicités de Discover-Tech auraient circulé sur plus de 120 000 sites et 75 000 applications, avec au moins dix millions de publicités diffusées par jour. Plus inquiétant encore, ces publicités auraient été affichées sur des appareils connectés aux réseaux utilisés par l’OTAN, le Pentagone, l’ONU et plusieurs institutions européennes.
Google, Comcast et plusieurs acteurs de la publicité ont aujourd’hui banni Discover-Tech de leurs plateformes. À noter qu’une grande entreprise technologique américaine et une organisation internationale, dont les noms n’ont pas été dévoilés, ont ouvert des enquêtes internes. Nous sommes donc face à une affaire de surveillance de masse particulièrement sérieuse.

articles.title: Police seize Virtualine bulletproof service tied to ransowmare, cybercrime
articles.text:
U.S. law enforcement has seized the primary domain of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting service advertised on cybercrime forums for facilitating illegal activities.
The service also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, and promised to shield customers from legal complaints and requests from law enforcement and other authorities.
The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) confirmed that Virtualine marketed services that permitted “illegal/black hat activities” ranging from phishing, spamming, and carding to port scanning.
The FBI seized the primary domain of the service, virtualine[.net], following an investigation that involved Germany’s Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands’ Politie Midden-Nederland, the U.K.’s National Crime Agency, as well as private partners OverRIPE and Lumen.
Although Virtualine drew an apparent line at child content, authorities say that the operator knowingly hosted an online forum promoting child abuse material and ignored repeated notices from law enforcement, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and a victim’s attorney.
Authorities allege that after legal pressure against the forum increased, Virtualine worked with the administrators to set up a new site.
"Virtualine hosts this new website to this day, and it has already received at least one abuse complaint about sexually explicit images of children found on that website," the DoJ said.
The administrator of the Virtualine rejected the allegation in an open letter to authorities published on a new website, virtualine[.]org, captured by cybersecurity company Silent Push.
The operator said that while claims about the service's illegal activities and customers "deserve a fair investigation," they regarded "sexual exploitation of children as a crime against humanity."
Cybercrime ecosystem
Virtualine also accepted direct Bitcoin payments from customers, helping cybercriminals launder proceeds stolen elsewhere.
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, which provided intelligence support to law enforcement, linked Virtualine’s payment addresses directly to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, scams, and phishing platforms.
“Virtualine accepted direct bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without flagging their funds through hosted exchange compliance programs,” Chainalysis notes.
“Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin,” the blockchain company added.
In a report published today, blockchain intelligence firm TRM said ransomware groups were responsible for 5% of Virtualine’s financial flows, while a Russian drug marketplace made up approximately 44%.
"A large sextortion scheme and a mixer were also major sources of funds," the company said.
TRM says that Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer this year, with transactions indicating a constant financial relationship.
A press release from the Dutch police notes that dozens of physical servers were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline.
Politie also said its investigators recovered data from more than 3,000 Virtualine customers, and follow-up action against them is underway.
According to the authorities in the Netherlands, the illegal platform was facilitating cybercrime operations since at least 2022, including ransomware, botnets, infostealers, phishing, and distribution of child abuse material.
Although the bulletproof hosting provider remains partially online, researchers observed that its network prefixes currently have very low routing visibility, suggesting that much of its infrastructure may no longer be reachable.

articles.title: "It has to touch the lives of people": the Gates Foundation's challenge to Africa's AI builders - TechCabal
articles.text:
Africa’s artificial intelligence developers should measure success by improvements in healthcare, education and incomes rather than the number of products they launch, the Gates Foundation’s Nigeria director told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos.
Uche Amaonwu said AI could widen access to knowledge, services and economic opportunity, but warned that its benefits would depend on deliberate choices about how the technology was developed, financed and deployed.
“For a technology to really be impactful, it has to touch the lives of people,” he said during a keynote address.
His remarks set out a challenge for developers and investors seeking applications for AI across the continent: moving promising tools beyond trials and into the institutions and communities expected to use them.
Amaonwu pointed to the foundation’s Goalkeepers report on AI and equity, released around the UN General Assembly, describing its message as “exciting, but also cautionary”. AI could become “a powerful equaliser”, he said, but that outcome was far from assured.
“If we are not deliberate about how AI is developed and deployed, we could end up widening the very inequalities that we’re actually trying to close.”
The foundation’s approach, he said, starts with three objectives: preventing avoidable maternal and child deaths, protecting the next generation from deadly infectious diseases, and helping hundreds of millions of people escape poverty.
These were “human condition goals”, he said. AI’s value would lie in whether it accelerated progress towards them.
A central part of that effort is the Nigeria AI Scaling Hub, hosted by Lagos Business School in partnership with the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy. Backed by up to $7.5mn from the foundation over three years, the hub aims to expand the use of proven AI tools in health, agriculture and education.
Its focus is the difficult transition from a successful pilot to sustained adoption. A tool that works in a trial still needs infrastructure, institutional support and a viable funding model before it can reach people consistently.
Amaonwu identified four requirements for making that transition.
Developers needed shared infrastructure, including connectivity, trusted data, and systems capable of exchanging information, so that each company did not have to build the same foundations independently.
Tools also needed to reflect Nigerian conditions and languages, earn users’ trust from the outset, and have a clear route to adoption and payment. Identifying who would use a product — and who would finance its continued use — was as important as developing it.
The argument places responsibility beyond technology companies. Governments shape the conditions for adoption through regulation and public systems, while investors determine which businesses receive the capital to expand.
Amaonwu urged the Moonshot audience to return the following year with evidence of practical results like clinics where patients had received care, classrooms where children had caught up, and farmers who had secured better prices for their harvests.
“No one in this room can do all of this alone,” he said. The future worth building was “the one that we must build together”.

articles.title: 6000 €, une autonomie généreuse et un habitacle bien équipé avec 4 places : la Chine lance un nouveau véhicule électrique qui tire encore plus les prix vers le bas
articles.text:
6000 €, une autonomie généreuse et un habitacle bien équipé avec 4 places : la Chine lance un nouveau véhicule électrique qui tire encore plus les prix vers le bas
La guerre des prix se poursuit en Chine et désormais le marché accueille un nouveau véhicule électrique à l’autonomie généreuse pour un prix de départ d’environ 6 000 €. Il s’agit du nouveau Bestune Pony avec cinq portes et quatre places, jusqu’à 328 kilomètres d’autonomie et un habitacle tout équipé. À ce tarif de 6 000 €, beaucoup de petits véhicules électriques vendus en France sont bien plus chers ou beaucoup trop limités.
C’est depuis aujourd’hui que Bestune a lancé la nouvelle version de son Pony en Chine. Rappelons que Bestune est une marque du groupe FAW, qui développe notamment des voitures en Chine dans le cadre de coentreprises avec Volkswagen.
Un véhicule électrique compact à prix attractif
Pour le catalogue, le prix de départ est de 44 900 ¥, soit environ 6 050 €. Pour la version la plus haut de gamme, c’est 54 900 ¥, soit environ 7 400 €. Le constructeur propose aussi une remise de lancement qui fait tomber les prix de 39 900 à 49 900 ¥, soit environ 5 400 à 6 700 €. Pour la version de 328 kilomètres, c’est donc environ 6 000 € après remise.
Précisons toutefois que les 328 kilomètres annoncés par le constructeur sont mesurés selon le cycle chinois CLTC, beaucoup plus généreux que le WLTP en Europe. Selon une estimation chinoise, la conversion ferait passer l’autonomie à 269 kilomètres en se basant sur la norme WLTP. Toutes les versions du véhicule proposent la recharge rapide pour passer de 30 % à 80 % en environ 30 minutes.
Le Bestune Pony mesure 3,35 mètres de long et peut accueillir quatre personnes avec cinq portes. Le coffre propose 265 litres et monte à 1 052 litres quand la banquette est rabattue. Parmi les autres équipements, deux airbags, une caméra de recul, un écran de 7 pouces et le démarrage sans clé.
Pour les finitions supérieures, il y a en plus un écran central de 10,1 pouces, les commandes vocales, une clé Bluetooth et les phares automatiques. On trouve également un contrôle de stabilité, un frein de stationnement électrique et un siège conducteur chauffé pour certaines versions.
Mais alors que vaut ce véhicule par rapport à ce qui est proposé en France en format compact à prix accessible ? Prenons l'exemple de la Citroën Ami fut lancée à 7 990 € avec deux places, 75 kilomètres d’autonomie et une vitesse limitée à 45 km/h.
Mais selon certains, il s’agit d’un véhicule peu fiable en dehors d’un cadre urbain très précis, voire périlleux sur les routes plus rapides. Idem pour l’équipement beaucoup plus simple avec une recharge qui demande près de quatre heures sur une prise adaptée.
Renault a tenté une formule plus ambitieuse avec le Mobilize Duo mais de nouveau, la fiche technique est loin d’être aussi généreuse que celle du Bestune Pony. La version Duo 80 monte à 80 km/h pour un prix de départ de 11 600 €. Renault a finalement abandonné sa production en décembre 2025 face à des "perspectives de rentabilité limitées".
L'Europe n'a pas encore de petites voitures attractives
Les petites voitures européennes peinent encore aujourd’hui à trouver un équilibre entre prix, équipement et autonomie. Mais précisons toutefois que le Bestune Pony joue dans une autre catégorie puisqu’il ne s’agit pas d’un quadricycle comme la Citroën Ami ou le Mobilize Duo. La comparaison tient surtout par rapport au format compact et au prix de départ qui se veut accessible.
Pour être conduit, le Bestune Pony demande donc un permis de conduire puisque son moteur développe 30 kW pour une vitesse maximale de 103 km/h. On ne se trouve donc pas là dans la catégorie française des quadricycles légers accessibles dès 14 ans.
Là où la comparaison peut être un peu plus pertinente, c’est par rapport à la nouvelle Dacia Spring dont la deuxième génération commence à 10 830 € en France après déduction de l’aide maximale, sous réserve d’éligibilité, avec quatre places et jusqu’à 250 kilomètres d’autonomie selon la norme WLTP.
Le Bestune Pony s’attaque à la même clientèle qui vit en ville avec un gabarit bien plus court et un prix accessible, du moins en Chine puisqu’on ne s’attend pas à ce que ce véhicule électrique sorte chez nous. Depuis le lancement du Bestune Pony en mai 2024, ce sont près de 300 000 exemplaires qui ont été écoulés.
Désormais, on trouve au catalogue cette version cinq portes qui cherche à conquérir les jeunes foyers qui cherchent plus d’espace sans passer à une voiture plus chère ou plus volumineuse que l’on retrouve chez d’autres comme BYD ou Xpeng.

articles.title: Dar Blockchain, Hashgraph Association select 18 startups for Web3 incubation programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Dar Blockchain and The Hashgraph Association have selected 18 startups for a new Web3 incubation programme supporting winners of the Hedera Africa Hackathon.
Run in partnership with Tunisian incubator Wiki Startup and investment firm UGFS North Africa, with Softstack as security partner, the programme runs until January 2027. It aims to graduate at least five seed-ready companies by an investor demo day in the week of January 18.
The Hedera Africa Hackathon, which wrapped up in April, drew more than 13,000 developers and 1,300 project submissions. A portion of the hackathon’s prize pool has been set aside to support winners with product development, technical implementation and market validation during the incubation phase.
“Most hackathons stop when the winners are announced. For us, that’s where the real work begins,” said Jaafar Saied, co-founder of Dar Blockchain.
Selected startups will move through four sprints and five jury-audited gates, with 21 workshops, one-on-one expert support and introductions to investors. Teams will also be supported to deploy production-ready products on the Hedera mainnet. The programme targets more than 60 per cent of ventures securing signed letters of intent or launching active pilots by the third milestone gate.
The African startups selected are Nigeria’s GreenAfrica, Beyond Service Game, Upesa, Afiya and Cryptonia CITY; Egypt’s Carboni; South Africa’s Direla; Madagascar’s Nia; Zimbabwe’s RDZ Health; Morocco’s Hedron; and Côte d’Ivoire’s APIx.
They are joined by Effisend X Africa (Mexico), Silsilat Finance (Malaysia), Tedera (Romania), W.A.T.A (Brazil), CryptoMage (India), and US-based KeyRing and Building a Chain of Trust in the Green Power-to-X Market.

articles.title: This open-source keyboard lets you snap keys together in any layout
articles.text:
The takeaway: Custom keyboard builders can swap out switches, keycaps, plates, and firmware these days, but the layout is usually locked in once the PCB is made. Now, a new open-source project called Keybytes is trying to get around that limitation by giving each key its own tiny circuit board and microcontroller. The keys snap together with magnets and connect to a small hub, allowing a keyboard to start out as a single key and grow into pretty much any shape.
The project comes from Nathan Alspaugh, an MIT freshman studying aerospace engineering, who said he has spent around 100 hours working on it since March. When he posted the project to Hacker News this week, he said the idea came from his frustration that nobody sold triangle- or circle-shaped keyboards.
Each key, called a Keybit, consists of a 19.05mm-square circuit board fitted with a Cherry MX switch and an inexpensive CH32V003 RISC-V chip. The neighboring module, whether another key or the hub, receives power and I2C data through spring-loaded pogo pins along all four edges.
The hub, called the Keyword, occupies the same 1u footprint but stacks two PCBs. An STM32WB55 on the upper board handles Bluetooth and stores firmware for every key. Meanwhile, the lower board houses the charging circuitry for an optional LiPo battery and the USB-C port.
Rather than sharing a single bus, each Keybit bit-bangs a separate I2C connection along each of its four sides. Alspaugh explained in the Hacker News thread that this approach reduces parasitic capacitance and allows the software to determine the physical position of each key. In theory, that means a chain of keys could extend indefinitely.
Getting the magnets right took considerably more trial and error. According to his build journal, the first magnetic cases couldn't hold the modules together against the force exerted by the pogo pins. Rather than redesigning the boards to accommodate weaker pins, Alspaugh opted for stronger magnets and printed case after case in resin at a makerspace. The hub's case alone went through 12 iterations. His first working build finally came together on October 24.
Even so, the current demo features just two keys attached to the hub, as Alspaugh is still building additional modules and finishing the firmware. Layout options are also limited to a flat grid for now.
Scaling up would get expensive quickly, too. Alspaugh estimates that a fully assembled, full-size keyboard with two hubs and roughly 110 keys would cost around $900. Almost half that amount would go toward the pogo pins, so he plans to buy and solder them himself if he ever builds one.
Anyone who wants to try the project can find the schematics, case STEP files, and bill of materials on its GitHub page, which is published under an MIT license. The PCB design files are available there, too – something Keychron held back when it opened up its case and plate designs earlier this year.

articles.title: Anatel ordena que clientes de telefonia móvel façam biometria • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Anatel ordena que clientes de telefonia móvel façam biometria
Reconhecimento facial será usado em ativações, troca de chip, portabilidade e mudanças contratuais. Linhas sem cadastro poderão ser suspensas em 2029.
A Anatel tornou obrigatória a validação biométrica para ativar e manter linhas de celular. A nova regra, aprovada pela Superintendência de Planejamento e Regulamentação e divulgada nesta quarta-feira (28/10), vale para pessoas físicas e microempreendedores individuais (MEI) e será implantada gradualmente até o fim de 2028.
Segundo a documentação, o reconhecimento facial será exigido para clientes em novas ativações, portabilidade, troca de chip e alterações cadastrais ou contratuais solicitadas pelo consumidor. Quem já tem uma linha também precisará passar pelo procedimento até 31 de dezembro de 2028. Pessoas jurídicas que não sejam MEI ficam fora da exigência.
O objetivo é dificultar a abertura e a transferência de linhas usando dados falsos ou de terceiros. Uma das fraudes mais conhecidas é o SIM swap, em que criminosos conseguem transferir o número da vítima para outro chip e passam a receber ligações e códigos de autenticação enviados por SMS.
A biometria é mais uma barreira nesse processo. A Anatel já tornou obrigatória a confirmação por SMS nas portabilidades e anunciou o Anatel Protege, ferramenta para impedir a abertura de linhas vinculadas ao CPF do usuário.
O uso de biometria no setor, no entanto, não é novidade. Desde 2021, operadoras já adotam o chamado ID Digital na ativação de algumas linhas pré-pagas, com envio de selfie e documento para validar o cadastro. A nova norma amplia esse tipo de verificação para outras operações.
A norma técnica da Anatel prevê validação do CPF, captura do rosto e uma prova de vida para confirmar que há uma pessoa real diante da câmera. Depois, a imagem será comparada com uma base biométrica já existente, pública ou privada.
Se o reconhecimento não funcionar, haverá alternativas, incluindo nova tentativa, atendimento presencial ou comparação da selfie com a fotografia de um documento oficial.
A Vivo, por exemplo, já utiliza um processo similar em alguns atendimentos. Em solicitações feitas por telefone ou WhatsApp, a operadora pode enviar um SMS com um link para confirmar a identidade. O cliente precisa mostrar o rosto e aguardar alguns segundos pela validação antes que uma alteração de plano, por exemplo, possa prosseguir.
A medida busca dificultar fraudes, mas também cria mais uma situação em que consumidores terão de fornecer dados biométricos para acessar um serviço. As prestadoras também poderão acrescentar outras verificações para identificar fraudes.
A norma determina que a coleta seja limitada ao necessário, exige cumprimento da LGPD e proíbe o compartilhamento irregular com terceiros. Os sistemas também deverão manter registros auditáveis das verificações.

articles.title: Staff Phones on the Company Network: Setting Up Bring Your Own Device Without the Headaches - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Introduction to BYOD in the Modern Workplace
The Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) trend has fundamentally transformed how organizations approach their communications and IT infrastructure. By allowing employees to use personal smartphones and other mobile devices on the company network, businesses can offer greater flexibility and potentially boost workforce productivity. However, this integration also introduces a host of challenges that, if not properly addressed, can lead to security vulnerabilities, compliance issues, and operational inefficiencies. This article explores effective strategies for setting up staff phones on the company network, focusing on how to implement BYOD programs while avoiding the common pitfalls that many organizations face.
Why BYOD Matters for Businesses Today
The adoption of BYOD is no longer an emerging trend; it has become a mainstream practice across industries worldwide. Recent studies indicate that over 70% of employees use their own devices to perform work-related tasks. This shift is driven by several factors, including employee preference for familiar technology, the rise of remote and hybrid work models, and the potential for significant cost savings on company hardware expenditures.
BYOD programs can enable more agile workflows by allowing employees to access corporate resources anytime and anywhere. However, this flexibility can come at a price if not carefully managed. Without appropriate safeguards, personal devices can become entry points for cyberattacks, data leaks, and unauthorized access to sensitive company information. Consequently, businesses must develop robust IT policies and secure network architectures that protect corporate assets while supporting employee mobility.
Starting Strong: Deploying BYOD with Expert Support
Launching a BYOD initiative requires more than just allowing devices on the network; it demands a strategic approach supported by expert guidance. Attentus’s managed IT deployment provides comprehensive solutions that help organizations manage device integration seamlessly. Their services include device onboarding, security policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring to mitigate risks associated with personal devices accessing corporate systems.
Partnering with experienced IT service providers ensures that businesses maintain control over network access and data security without stifling employee flexibility. These experts can also assist in navigating complex compliance requirements, such as GDPR or HIPAA, which may apply depending on the industry or geographic location. By leveraging their expertise, companies can avoid common mistakes that lead to costly data breaches or operational disruptions.
Choosing the Right Provider for Your BYOD Strategy
Selecting a trusted provider like Link High is a critical step toward a successful BYOD rollout. Such providers specialize in offering tailored IT management services that address the unique challenges posed by BYOD environments. These challenges include managing diverse device types and operating systems, enforcing security policies consistently, and ensuring network performance remains optimal despite increased device load.
A capable provider will implement device management platforms, such as Mobile Device Management (MDM) or Enterprise Mobility Management (EMM) solutions, that enable centralized control over personal devices. They can also establish network segmentation practices to isolate BYOD traffic from sensitive corporate resources, reducing the risk of lateral movement by attackers in case of device compromise.
Moreover, providers bring valuable insights into user training and policy development, helping organizations foster a culture of security awareness among employees. This holistic approach ensures that the BYOD program supports business goals without becoming a source of headaches for IT teams.
Key Considerations When Integrating Staff Phones
Before permitting personal devices on the company network, organizations must carefully consider several critical factors to ensure security, compliance, and operational efficiency.
Security and Compliance
Security remains the foremost concern when integrating staff phones into corporate networks. Deploying Mobile Device Management (MDM) solutions is essential to enforce encryption, implement remote wipe capabilities, and control app installations on personal devices. These measures help protect sensitive data in case devices are lost or stolen.
Statistics reveal that 59% of businesses have experienced mobile security incidents linked to BYOD devices. This underscores the importance of rigorous security controls and constant vigilance. Compliance with industry regulations such as GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS also requires careful handling of personal devices accessing protected data.
Network Segmentation
To minimize risk, organizations should separate personal devices from critical business systems through network segmentation. Establishing dedicated VLANs or guest networks specifically for BYOD devices confines potential threats and prevents unauthorized access to sensitive company data.
Network segmentation not only enhances security but also improves performance by managing traffic flow and reducing congestion on core corporate networks. It allows IT teams to apply tailored security policies and monitor BYOD activity more effectively.
Clear Usage Policies
Developing clear, comprehensive usage policies is vital to set employee expectations and responsibilities regarding personal device use on company networks. Policies should outline acceptable use, data privacy guidelines, and consequences for non-compliance.
Effective policies encourage employees to adhere to security best practices, such as using strong passwords, avoiding unsecured Wi-Fi networks, and reporting lost or stolen devices promptly. They also help reduce legal risks by clarifying data ownership and privacy boundaries.
Technical Steps to Enable BYOD on Your Network
Implementing a BYOD program without headaches involves a series of technical best practices designed to secure and optimize network access.
- Inventory and Compatibility Checks: Conduct an audit to understand the types of devices employees intend to use and verify their compatibility with existing network infrastructure. This helps prevent connectivity issues and ensures that security tools support all device platforms.
- Access Controls: Implement strong authentication protocols such as WPA3 for Wi-Fi access, and consider using digital certificates or VPNs to secure connections between personal devices and corporate resources. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds an additional layer of protection against unauthorized access.
- Regular Updates and Monitoring: Continuously monitor device activity on the network to detect anomalies or suspicious behavior. Push security updates and patches promptly to all managed devices to close vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.
- User Training: Educate employees about security risks associated with BYOD and provide guidelines on safe device usage. Training reduces human error, which is often the weakest link in cybersecurity.
Benefits of a Well-Managed BYOD Program
When properly executed, BYOD initiatives can deliver substantial benefits to organizations. A study found that companies with effective BYOD strategies reported a 20% increase in employee productivity and a 15% reduction in IT expenses. This productivity boost is often attributed to employees’ comfort and familiarity with their own devices, which can lead to faster task completion and improved communication.
Additionally, BYOD reduces the need for organizations to invest heavily in purchasing and maintaining hardware, lowering operational costs. It also supports flexible work arrangements, enabling employees to work remotely or on the go without disruption.
However, these benefits are contingent on effective management practices and security controls. Without them, BYOD can become a liability rather than an asset.
Overcoming Common BYOD Challenges
Despite its advantages, BYOD programs can face hurdles that need proactive management.
– Device Diversity: Supporting a wide range of device types, operating systems, and versions can strain IT resources. Standardizing minimum requirements and using cross-platform management tools can alleviate this issue.
– Data Privacy Concerns: Employees may worry about their personal data being accessed or monitored by the company. Transparent policies and privacy-respecting management solutions help build trust.
– Network Performance: Increased device connectivity can lead to bandwidth congestion. Network upgrades and segmentation help maintain performance levels.
– Legal and Compliance Risks: Failure to comply with data protection laws can result in hefty fines. Regular audits and adherence to regulatory frameworks are essential.
Addressing these challenges through strategic planning and expert support ensures that BYOD programs run smoothly and securely.
Conclusion: Balancing Flexibility and Security
The integration of staff phones into the company network via Bring Your Own Device initiatives represents a strategic opportunity to enhance workforce agility and reduce costs. However, successful implementation demands a delicate balance between flexibility and security. Engaging with specialized providers and adopting comprehensive policies are critical steps to ensure smooth deployment and sustained network integrity.
By following best practices such as employing Mobile Device Management solutions, enforcing network segmentation, and providing user training, businesses can mitigate risks associated with personal devices. Moreover, leveraging expert support from trusted partners helps navigate technical complexities and compliance requirements.
Ultimately, a well-managed BYOD program empowers organizations to capitalize on the benefits of employee-owned devices without the headaches-driving productivity, cost savings, and competitive advantage in today’s dynamic business environment.

articles.title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro hands-on: OLED looks great on a Mac
articles.text:
LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It’s not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless.
The first thing I noticed was that it’s lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it’s a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It’s not like it’s in a different general weight class, but it’s a noticeable difference.
The next thing I noticed was the Dynamic Island. Given the larger screen real estate of a laptop, it’s much less dominant on the screen than it is on an iPhone. I do worry about what will happen with fullscreen games, which I wasn’t able to test today. The notch MacBook Pro has an option to maximize apps or games to just below the notch, so it doesn’t cut into the image. I’m curious to test in the full review whether that remains the case with this little cutout.
This is how the Dynamic Island looks when it’s not doing anything…
Samuel Axon
This is how the Dynamic Island looks when it’s not doing anything…
Samuel Axon
…and this is a live activity, expanded by tapping on it. (It’s smaller before you tap on it.)
Samuel Axon
…and this is a live activity, expanded by tapping on it. (It’s smaller before you tap on it.)
Samuel Axon
This is how the Dynamic Island looks when it’s not doing anything…
Samuel Axon
…and this is a live activity, expanded by tapping on it. (It’s smaller before you tap on it.)
Samuel Axon
And lastly, the Apple logo on the back glows again! Some find this tacky, some find it essential. I just think it’s a little bit nostalgic.
The logo glowing on the back of an open 14-inch MacBook Pro.
Credit:
Samuel Axon
The logo glowing on the back of an open 14-inch MacBook Pro.
Credit:
Samuel Axon
Of course, you might make the case that the most notable thing about this laptop is not its weight or the Dynamic Island. For years, people have debated whether Apple should introduce a touchscreen laptop. Steve Jobs was famously against it. A few years ago—there were reports that under Tim Cook and now John Ternus—Apple decided to move ahead with the idea.
I played with it a bit, and it works just about exactly as you expect for a laptop touchscreen.
A few of the things I did with the touchscreen during my brief time with the laptop:
Swiped between desktop spaces with three fingers on the screen
Pinched, zoomed, and scrolled on both images and the Maps app
Dragged windows around and resized them—including a quick flicking gesture that attaches a window to the left or right side of the screen
Dragged files between applications
Launched and closed applications
Drew with my finger in a painting and illustration app
Sketched in colors on a 3D model
Scrubbed through video playback
All of that is nice to have, I guess, but there’s not much you can do with it that you couldn’t already do with trackpad gestures, at least at the OS level; some creative apps, like finger painting on the screen, seemed to offer a bit more.
You can play a musical instrument like a keyboard on the screen with your fingers, but it’s a little awkward, since the laptop does not convert into a tablet mode.
Credit:
Samuel Axon
You can play a musical instrument like a keyboard on the screen with your fingers, but it’s a little awkward, since the laptop does not convert into a tablet mode.
Credit:
Samuel Axon
When the credible reports emerged that the MacBook Pro would get a touchscreen, I imagined a convertible with Apple Pencil support—something you could use as a large iPad or drawing tablet, essentially. That’s not what this is; it only takes the usual laptop shape, and I was told it does not support the Apple Pencil. It’s just a MacBook Pro, in its normal form factor, but you can use your fingers on the screen to do things like drag files around, swipe between desktop spaces, or pinch-to-zoom on maps or images.
But while it’s not about the touchscreen capability for me, I was impressed by the OLED screen itself—and I’m quite the display snob, if I’m being honest. The peak brightness, absolute blacks, well-balanced color, and dynamic range were genuinely remarkable. It’s an enormous upgrade over the MiniLED screen in the previous MacBook Pro.
It took far too long for OLED to come to the MacBook Pro, but unsurprisingly, Apple spared no expense and cut no immediately obvious corners on quality.
I was also happy to see that the cutout near the top of the screen that has replaced the camera notch is what Apple calls a Dynamic Island; it can resize to show live activities and other information on the fly. That’s one of my favorite features on the iPhone, as I’ve been impressed with Apple’s ability to turn something that should be an albatross into an appealing feature.
The 16-inch MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon

Samuel Axon

Samuel Axon

Samuel Axon
