Samuel Axon
Same goes for ports; no changes here.
Samuel Axon
Same goes for ports; no changes here.
Samuel Axon
The keyboard and touchpad are the same as before. (Pictured here on the 16-inch.)
Samuel Axon
Same goes for ports; no changes here.
Samuel Axon
Based on my time with the device and today’s announcement, the screen seems to be the main draw (though it’s nice that it noticeably weighs less, too), but the price is the real barrier. A 16-inch model with an M5 Max, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage is currently priced at $5,799. Sure, that’s a high-end spec, but that’s some serious cash. Much of that is due to the storage and memory; upgrading from 64GB to 128GB adds a whopping $1,600 to that.
Sure, most people don’t need anywhere near that much RAM—but some might for future-proofing for local AI workflows.
I’m looking forward to spending more time with the new MacBook Pro, but for right now, it seems to follow in the lineup’s existing tradition: impressively high-end components like an outstanding OLED panel, but a very steep price to match. No surprises here! Though after well over a decade of speculation and back-and-forth, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that the touchscreen thing actually finally happened.
Samuel Axon is the editorial lead for tech and gaming coverage at Ars Technica. He covers physical and generative AI, large language models, software development, gaming, entertainment, and mixed reality. He has been writing about gaming and technology for nearly two decades at Engadget, PC World, Mashable, Vice, Polygon, Wired, and others. He previously ran a marketing and PR agency in the gaming industry, led editorial for the TV network CBS, and worked on social media marketing strategy for Samsung Mobile at the creative agency SPCSHP. He also is an independent software and game developer for iOS, Windows, and other platforms, and he is a graduate of DePaul University, where he studied interactive media and software development.

articles.title: Beyond AI infrastructure, India’s tech boom rests on the efficient use of power and water
articles.text:
Beyond AI infrastructure, India’s tech boom rests on the efficient use of power and water
At TechSparks 2026, founders of SolarSquare and Boson Whitewater unpack why overcoming perception, pricing gaps, and consumer trust matters far more in climatetech than just building the technology.
India’s technology conversation is increasingly dominated by artificial intelligence, data centres and digital infrastructure, however a more fundamental challenge lies in ensuring that the country has sufficient reliable power and water to sustain its growing cities and industries.
At TechSparks 2026 in a panel discussion titled The Invisible Infrastructure: Rebuilding India’s Energy, Water and Clean Air Systems, Shreya Mishra, Co-founder and CEO of SolarSquare, and Vikas Brahmawar, Founder and Director of Boson Whitewater discussed on how on the significance of scaling these solutions which require more than technological innovation.
Rooftop solar moves beyond a niche market
The residential solar market in India has undergone a significant transformation over the past five years, said Shreya Mishra, Co-founder and CEO of SolarSquare.
Recalling the market, she said that when SolarSquare entered the market, adoption was limited, consumers had little understanding of rooftop solar, and the upfront investment made many households hesitant. The company, however, believed that the economics of distributed power generation and the need for energy security would eventually drive adoption.
“Distributed solar, which is solar on every rooftop, will be the cheapest source of power,” Mishra said.
According to Mishra, it took five years for one lakh homes in India to adopt residential solar when the company began its journey. Today, the country adds that many homes in a single week, so far SolarSquare has powered more than 60,000 homes.
However, the economics alone do not eliminate consumer concerns. Rooftop solar requires a substantial upfront payment, and households may worry about equipment reliability, maintenance costs and whether the system will generate the promised amount of electricity.
For companies in the sector, building trust is therefore as important as making the financial case. Mishra also sees distributed solar as a way to reduce the cost associated with transmitting electricity over long distances. While power may be generated relatively cheaply, transmission and distribution costs can increase the price consumers ultimately pay.
Her argument is that generating electricity closer to where it is consumed can help address that gap.
SolarSquare currently serves both individual households and around 500 housing societies.
Wastewater as an alternative to freshwater
On the other hand, water presents a different challenge. Vikas Brahmawar, who moved from the software industry to work on water reuse, said it took years of effort to build the policy environment needed to support the sector.
“Water, unlike solar, there is a fixed sun which is hitting,” he said, explaining that wastewater treatment must account for changing water quality. The business also needs supportive policies and viable economics to scale.
The need is becoming more pressing as cities and industries compete for increasingly constrained freshwater resources. Groundwater extraction remains a major source of supply, while industrial applications such as data centres, cooling towers, semiconductor manufacturing, electroplating and laundry require significant quantities of water.
Brahmawar said the company had repurposed around 147 crore litres of water over the preceding four years that would otherwise have gone down the drain.
The opportunity is particularly relevant as data centres expand and demand for water-intensive infrastructure rises. Reusing treated wastewater for industrial purposes could help ease pressure on freshwater sources while creating a commercially viable market for recycled water.
But the economics of water supply can be counterintuitive. Brahmawar pointed to Bengaluru’s Cauvery water supply, saying consumers are charged around Rs 7 per kilolitre even though the government spends about Rs 95 per kilolitre to bring the water from a distant river to the city.
The gap, he suggested, illustrates the challenge facing alternative water sources: a solution must compete not only with the availability of freshwater but also with the way existing water systems are priced and subsidised.
Technology is not the biggest hurdle
If rooftop solar has benefited from increasingly visible consumer savings, recycled water faces an additional barrier: public perception.
Brahmawar recounted how the company spent two-and-a-half years speaking to more than 300 apartment complexes about the possibility of using recycled water, including for drinking. The response showed that convincing people to accept treated wastewater can be difficult even when treatment technology is available.
For now, the company is concentrating on industrial applications, where recycled water can replace freshwater without requiring consumers to overcome the same psychological barrier associated with drinking it.
“Technology is the least of the problem,” he said. The bigger obstacles, in his view, are commercial viability, public perception, enforcement and execution on the ground.
Building a broader energy ecosystem
SolarSquare, meanwhile, is looking beyond the installation of rooftop panels. Mishra said the company wants to become a full-stack home energy brand, expanding into batteries, electric-vehicle chargers, home energy monitoring, energy optimisation and smart-grid integration.
The company is also using software to monitor installations and identify problems remotely. Mishra said monitoring data could help detect voltage fluctuations and recurring power outages, allowing the company to identify potential issues and recommend solutions such as battery storage where appropriate.
Such capabilities can improve customer service while reducing the need for physical inspections, she said.
The experiences of SolarSquare and Boson Whitewater highlight two different stages in the development of climate infrastructure. Rooftop solar is benefiting from growing consumer awareness and a clearer financial proposition, while wastewater reuse is still working to overcome pricing, policy and perception barriers.
However, the common challenge for both the companies lies in how to turn a technically viable solution into infrastructure that people and organisations can adopt at scale.

articles.title: Après l'Allemagne, l'Italie réclame une homologation rapide du FSD de Tesla en Europe
articles.text:
Dans une publication sur son compte X ce jeudi 29 octobre 2026, Matteo Salvini, vice-président du Conseil italien et ministre des Infrastructures et des Transports, raconte une conversation « très positive et constructive » avec Elon Musk, le patron de Tesla.
À la sortie de cet échange, il écrit que l’Italie « soutient une approbation rapide par l’UE » du logiciel de Tesla, au nom de « l’innovation et de la sécurité routière ». On a hâte de voir le FSD (dorénavant appelé Tesla Conduite Assistée en Europe) évoluer dans les rues tumultueuses de Rome, réputées pour accueillir un trafic chaotique.
Une Europe qui dit oui, pays par pays
Matteo Salvini est loin d’être le premier ministre européen convaincu après une discussion avec Elon Musk. En France, Philippe Tabarot avait refusé le logiciel en juillet, avant finalement d’annoncer des essais sur route début septembre, à l’issue d’un entretien avec le patron de Tesla. Toutefois, le ministre français n’a pas fait de déclaration élogieuse ni proclamé en public son intention de soutenir l’approbation générale du système. Le 6 octobre, son homologue allemand Steffen Bilger plaidait quant à lui explicitement pour une « homologation rapide » dans toute l’Union européenne.
Certains des pays qui ont dit oui ont posé leurs conditions de sécurité avant le feu vert. Par exemple, la Lettonie a autorisé le FSD ce lundi 26 octobre, mais seulement après avoir fait corriger le logiciel, qui doit rouler moins vite et surveiller davantage le conducteur.
Avec cette dernière nation, ce sont désormais dix pays de l’Union européenne qui ont autorisé le FSD. L’approbation à l’échelle de l’UE, celle que réclament Rome et Berlin, n’a pas encore été accordée et pourrait se décider au 1er décembre, lors de la prochaine réunion du Comité technique des véhicules à moteur (TCMV).

articles.title: Nvidia and Oracle bring Vera CPU instances online in multi-gigawatt deployment
articles.text:
Standalone Nvidia Vera CPUs land in Oracle Cloud's multi-gigawatt deployment — our independent benchmarking of a local server reveals Vera's massive memory bandwidth lead over dual Xeon 6 server
Standalone Vera is generally available on OCI Superclusters now.
Nvidia and Oracle have announced general availability of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Superclusters at Oracle AI World on Tuesday. The announcement comes hot on the heels of Google Cloud announcing general availability for Vera Rubin last week, putting two major hyperscaler feathers in Nvidia’s cap. However, Oracle’s announcement is interesting, specifically calling out standalone Vera instances on OCI Superclusters. We've included a few benchmarks we've performed on a Vera server for a forthcoming review to highlight some of the chip's performance characteristics, but do note that these tests were not conducted on OCI infrastructure.
Neoclouds have been banging the drum of Vera for the past several weeks, with instances under way at Nscale, CoreWeave, and Nebius, among others, so it makes sense to see Vera in the GPU-dominant and AI-focused neoclouds. A standalone deployment at a hyperscaler like Oracle sends a different signal, however.
Although hyperscalers maintain large fleets of hardware, sometimes even renting from the neoclouds, the CPU focus is primarily on x86, with OCI Superclusters otherwise offering the Ampere Altra for an Arm-based instance. It’s Nvidia’s first standalone CPU push into the hyperscale data center, placing Vera alongside the x86 competition regardless of the GPU compute.
Vera is not meant to upend the x86 guard, at least in isolation. Ian Buck, Nvidia’s mind behind CUDA and the face of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure buildout, said in March — when the chip was revealed — that the world couldn’t be served by a single, 88-core SKU. However, Vera is opening the door at hyperscalers like Oracle to expand in future CPU generations.
AMD and Intel maintain the lead when it comes to single-socket density, which is only set to expand in the next generation, as AMD’s upcoming EPYC Venice CPUs can pack up to 512 threads in a single socket. However, Vera offers some distinct advantages due to its topology depending on the workload, many of which are becoming increasingly relevant in the agentic AI era.
Memory bandwidth, for instance, is one of Vera’s strong suits, and that’s not just a marketing claim. Nvidia has said the memory system is capable of 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, but we can see Nvidia’s lead outside of theoretical numbers in our testing below.
Take the industry-standard Stream benchmark as an example. Nvidia’s use of LPDDR5X-9600, along with a monolithic die and distributed mesh for caching, allows it to more than double the bandwidth available on a dual Intel Xeon 6980P system, even when it’s paired with MRDIMMs sporting speeds of 8,800 MT/s. We’re showing triad here, as it’s the most “demanding” of Stream’s operations, but the leads for Vera are similar across add, copy, and scale as well.
This bandwidth is critical for some types of agentic loops, particularly those dealing with large database queries or extensive documentation. You can see the OpenMP “spread” policy offers a massive boost to Vera’s memory bandwidth, as well. Both AMD and Intel maintain centralized memory control and system-level cache, while Vera distributes it in a mesh across the die. The result, at least in OpenMP set properly, is much higher memory bandwidth by binding processes as far away from each other as possible.
Another critical performance vector for agentic AI is Python. The agentic world is expanding, but much of the foundation of the AI software ecosystem is built on Python. Common agentic frameworks like CrewAI and LangGraph are written in Python, and although we’re seeing more frameworks built in languages like Rust and TypeScript, Python performance is still critical to agentic loops.
And, unsurprisingly, it’s an area where Vera is also strong, beating out CPUs that are much more powerful on paper. Popular agentic harnesses are built on Python, but so are many of the applications that also run on Python, including foundational AI libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow.
Nvidia’s focus on agentic AI makes sense given the times we’re living in, but it can miss the forest for the trees. Oracle bringing Vera standalone instances online shifts the focus onto the broader implications of Vera’s entrance into the data center. There are some aspects of performance that characterize agentic AI workloads, but many agent workloads are regular data center workloads in the first place, just under high concurrency.
For instance, SQLite performance is important for any server querying a large database, regardless of its written by logic, a person, or an AI agent. Nvidia’s second-gen Scalable Coherency Fabric (SCF), which we saw at play in Stream, shows up in a real workload here, with these database queries largely bound by data movement across the system.
And that is what makes Vera so interesting in the context of Oracle’s announcement. It’s a CPU built for agentic AI, says Nvidia, but the crosstalk with general data center workloads is strong. It’s not just a CPU to use because you need access to Nvidia’s accelerators. Depending on the workload, it may even be a better choice than the x86 guard.
Ultimately, we have to see how customers of these hyperscalers use (or don’t use) Vera in production. It’s demonstrated its usefulness in agentic AI loops, but it’s also showing early promise in certain general-purpose workloads. Oracle’s standalone deployment is a sign that there’s some demand for Vera that isn't exclusively tied at the hip of a Rubin GPU.
Oracle is approaching cautiously, however, as any hyperscaler should be when bringing up a multi-gigawatt deployment. The company said it will also offer Nvidia’s HGX NVL8, bringing eight Rubin GPUs together in a cluster, connected to a dual, 64-core Intel Xeon 6 host with 4TB of DDR5 memory.
Our testing of Vera shared in this article is part of a larger benchmarking session we had with the chip, and we'll share the technical details of the test setup in our forthcoming review. We’ll be publishing our full results shortly on Tom’s Hardware.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Entrenar grandes modelos exige cada vez más hardware. China responde con un superclúster de 100.000 tarjetas nacionales
articles.text:
Hace unos meses tuvimos ocasión de contar las proezas del Sugon 8000, un superclúster con unas 100.000 tarjetas gráficas, todas ellas diseñadas y fabricadas en China. El sistema se encuentra en Zhengzhou, en la provincia de Henan, y ha sido presentado al público durante la Conferencia Nacional de Computación de Alto Rendimiento de China en Shenzhen, mostrando más detalles de su funcionamiento.
El orgullo de la nación. Construir una máquina de este tamaño significa conseguir que los chips, las redes, el almacenamiento, la refrigeración y el software de programación funcionen juntos, y Sugon afirma que cada una de esas capas proviene de proveedores chinos. Eso importa en un país cuya industria tecnológica ha estado bajo presión de EEUU durante años. Precisamente, según el Registro Federal de EEUU, Sugon fue añadida a la Lista de Entidades en 2019, una lista en la que a las empresas se les restringe la exportación, reexportación y transferencia de tecnología estadounidense sin licencia previa.
En detalle. El clúster es el nodo central de la Internet Nacional de Supercomputación de China, una red nacional que ofrece a universidades, institutos de investigación y empresas acceso remoto a potencia de cálculo. Sugon afirma que el clúster ejecuta más de 13.000 nodos y está cerca de su carga completa, gestionando más de 6.000 tareas a la vez, según las cifras difundidas por los medios estatales chinos.
Los ingenieros del sitio explicaban al medio local Hebccw que el sistema ocupa aproximadamente 2.000 metros cuadrados, pesa alrededor de 1.500 toneladas y contiene unos 1.600 kilómetros de cableado interno.
El problema del calor. Ejecutar 100.000 chips a plena velocidad produce una cantidad enorme de calor. De hecho, según el medio, la producción por hora es comparable a quemar 12 toneladas de carbón. El sobrecalentamiento obliga a los chips a reducir la velocidad y aumenta las tasas de fallos, por lo que Sugon sumerge sus placas en un líquido fluorado no conductor que hierve a unos 50 °C. El calor es disipado posteriormente por un sistema de agua externo.
Según se informa, cada puerto de red transfiere datos a 800 Gb/s, de modo que los chips pueden intercambiar información con la suficiente rapidez para funcionar como una sola máquina.
Lo que ya está haciendo. Sugon afirma haber optimizado más de 300 aplicaciones en más de 30 campos de investigación e industriales, desde nuevos materiales y descubrimiento de fármacos hasta aeroespacial y agricultura. Destacan ejemplos en meteorología, donde en septiembre, la Administración Meteorológica de China y Sugon anunciaron una previsión global del tiempo a 10 días vista y con una resolución de 5 km, generada en aproximadamente una hora en el sistema, según el South China Morning Post. Esto es más preciso que la mayoría de los principales sistemas de previsión de uso habitual.
Otro ejemplo destacado fue el de unos investigadores de la Universidad de Tsinghua, quienes utilizaron el clúster para reconstruir un modelo digital del comportamiento del sedimento y el nivel del agua del río Amarillo, según comparten desde Interesting Engineering.
El superordenador para todo. La empresa presenta el Sugon 8000 como un sistema híbrido, con un comportamiento de superordenador tradicional que prioriza los cálculos de alta precisión para simulaciones científicas, y como un sistema de IA, que sacrifica algo de precisión a cambio de velocidad en procesar enormes conjuntos de datos. Todo en el mismo hardware.

articles.title: Smart TVs spy on you, even when you opt out: study
articles.text:
A new study has shown that your smart TV might be tracking you and what you watch, even when you opt out of tracking.
The study, named Watching the Watchers, was conducted by researchers affiliated with Northeastern University in Boston, Massachusetts.
- Essentially, it examines automatic content recognition (ACR) features, which the study noted are built into most available smart TVs—and whether turning ACR off actually stops TVs from sending whatever is on your screen to providers.
The researchers tested TVs running Tizen OS (Samsung), Roku OS (Roku, TCL), webOS (LG), SmartCast OS (Vizio), Google TV OS (Sony, Hisense, TCL), Fire TV OS, and others like VIDAA and Xumo.
To add some context, here is how ACR works: essentially, the TV takes short audio or video snapshots of what is on screen, and those snapshots (or the digital fingerprints made from them) are then sent to the internet or ACR provider. From there, the provider compares what was sent to a library of known content to determine exactly what you are watching. The data can reveal your viewing habits and can be used for targeted ads or sold to other companies.
Interestingly, the researchers found out that antenna broadcasts were almost always tracked on every analyzed system. On the streaming side, no TV tracked YouTube or Netflix, but free ad-supported streaming platform Tubi was tracked on Tizen OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS.
The researchers also noted that most operating systems tracked their own streaming services, except Fire TV OS and Google TV on Sony.
Outside of antenna and streaming services, the researchers said that devices on HDMI ports were tracked on five screen systems, but not on Roku OS or SmartCast OS. Interestingly, screen mirroring was only tracked on one of the tested brands: VIDAA OS. Even more concerning, Vizio’s SmartCast OS sent ACR-pattern traffic back to its provider, even when the TV sat idle.
The researchers also said turning these features off didn’t always work. After running each scenario more than 30 times across each operating system, only four (webOS, Google TV on Sony, VIDAA OS, and Fire TV OS) were found to actually shut off the feature if the user opted out of ACR. Interestingly, another recent report that dove into LG’s smart TVs found other concerning practices, like capturing data when offline or in standby mode, recording people, scanning Wi-Fi networks, and more.
Samsung’s built-in streaming service still showed ACR-consistent traffic, and the same thing happened with Vizio, where traffic was sent to its Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint.
If you own a smart TV, Watching the Watchers also shared some tips for what to do if you don’t like being spied on. Turning ACR off is the first step, especially if you have a TV that actually lets you turn it off. Further, you can disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device that doesn’t use ACR. Finally, for those using TVs that don’t respect the ACR toggle, the researchers also shared a blocklist that you can use to prevent the TV from communicating with the ACR endpoints.
Source: Watching the Watchers

articles.title: Kylian Mbappé: qué pasó con el futbolista del Real Madrid, qué estudios tiene y más preguntas trend de Google
articles.text:
Kylian Mbappé volvió a ser noticia mundial, pero no por un gol ni por un título. Un comentario informal sobre un meme que usaba su rostro junto al de Mao Tse-tung desató una crisis diplomática con China, obligó a Javier Tebas a disculparse en nombre de LaLiga y terminó con el propio futbolista pidiendo perdón públicamente.
En paralelo, su nombre domina las búsquedas de Google por otros motivos: su formación académica, su lugar entre los mejores del mundo y su relación con la actriz Ester Expósito.
Qué pasó con Kylian Mbappé
Todo comenzó con una frase que Mbappé pronunció de manera casi informal. “Con el meme que más me he reído es con ese en el que usan mi cara creo que con un dictador chino. Lo utilizo mucho con mis amigos en línea”, dijo el delantero, en referencia a una imagen que suele compartir con su círculo cercano sobre Mao Tse-tung, uno de los mayores genocidas del siglo XX.
La palabra elegida por el francés, dictador, resultó ser el punto de quiebre. El régimen de Beijing considera ese término inaceptable cuando se aplica a la figura de Mao, y la respuesta no tardó en llegar.
China suspendió las emisiones de LaLiga en su territorio y ordenó a corporaciones locales cancelar los contratos millonarios que mantenían con Mbappé. El régimen de Xi Jinping instruyó además a la cadena estatal CCTV borrar al delantero de sus transmisiones y rescindir los acuerdos televisivos vigentes.
La magnitud de la respuesta encendió las alarmas en el negocio del fútbol, un ámbito que suele izar banderas en defensa de los derechos humanos. Javier Tebas, presidente de LaLiga, salió de inmediato a pedir disculpas en nombre del fútbol español. “No podemos permitir que unas declaraciones individuales empañen la relación”, afirmó el dirigente.
La postura de Tebas dejó al delantero del Real Madrid sin margen de maniobra. Mbappé terminó disculpándose a través de un comunicado: “Tengo un profundo respeto por el pueblo chino y su historia, estoy sinceramente arrepentido”, escribió.
Qué estudios tiene Kylian Mbappé
Entre las preguntas que más se repiten en los buscadores sobre el delantero del Real Madrid aparece su formación académica. Mbappé concentró su desarrollo juvenil en academias deportivas, lo que marcó el rumbo de su educación desde una edad temprana.
Su recorrido futbolístico arrancó en el AS Bondy y continuó en el INF Clairefontaine, la academia de la Federación Francesa de Fútbol dedicada a jóvenes talentos. En 2013 se incorporó al centro de formación del AS Mónaco, donde terminó de formarse antes de debutar como profesional.
En el plano escolar, Mbappé cursó la secundaria y obtuvo el Baccalauréat, el equivalente al bachillerato francés, en la especialidad de Ciencias y Tecnologías de la Gestión y Administración (STMG). El futbolista no cuenta con estudios ni títulos universitarios.
¿Es Mbappé el mejor jugador del mundo?
Otra de las búsquedas frecuentes vinculadas al atacante francés tiene que ver con su ubicación dentro de la jerarquía mundial del fútbol. Definir si Mbappé es “el mejor del mundo” responde a un criterio subjetivo que varía según cada aficionado o periodista, aunque su pertenencia a la élite absoluta del fútbol actual no admite discusión.
A fecha de octubre de 2026, varios hitos recientes respaldan ese estatus. En la edición 2026 del Balón de Oro, Mbappé terminó en el segundo lugar de las votaciones, por detrás del delantero inglés Harry Kane.
A mediados de octubre también fue distinguido por la revista francesa Onze Mondial con el premio Onze d’Or al mejor jugador de la temporada 2025-26. El reconocimiento llegó con el 48,2% de los votos de los lectores, por encima de João Neves y Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.
Quién es la pareja de Kylian Mbappé
La vida personal del futbolista también concentra buena parte del interés en los motores de búsqueda. A fecha de finales de 2026, la pareja de Kylian Mbappé es la actriz española Ester Expósito.
La relación salió a la luz a principios de este año. Ambos procuraron mantener su vínculo en privado, aunque el romance se hizo público y notorio durante el verano de Italia, especialmente después de que se los viera de vacaciones juntos en Cerdeña.
La presencia constante de Expósito en los estadios, donde acompañó a Mbappé durante el Mundial de 2026, terminó de confirmar la relación ante la opinión pública.

articles.title: « Il tournera sur PC portable » : Mistral nous confirme un Large 4 allégé — Frandroid
articles.text:
Mistral a publié ce jeudi 29 octobre les poids de Large 4, son modèle le plus puissant, qui rattrape les meilleurs modèles ouverts chinois en code. Ses poids sont téléchargeables par tous, mais le faire tourner demande du matériel de centre de données, hors de portée d’un particulier.
La promesse de Mistral
Lors d’un briefing presse organisé ce mercredi 28 octobre, nous avons demandé à Mistral quand arriveraient des versions plus petites, de quelle taille, et si l’une d’elles tournerait sur un ordinateur portable ou un PC de jeu. Réponse de Pierre Stock, vice-président chargé de la science chez Mistral : « Ça va arriver bientôt, dans le mois qui vient. Il y aura une famille de modèles, et l’un d’eux pourra tourner sur un ordinateur portable, c’est certain. »
La logique, selon Mistral : des gros modèles pour les tâches difficiles, à un certain coût, et des petits modèles pour les tâches plus simples, « bien plus rapides et bien moins chers ». Ce que demandent ses clients, assure l’entreprise.
Pour un particulier, l’intérêt d’un modèle qui tourne en local tient en deux points : il fonctionne sans connexion, et les données ne quittent pas la machine. Mistral avance le même argument pour Large 4 auprès des entreprises, qui peuvent l’héberger sur leurs propres serveurs et garder leurs données chez elles.
Pourquoi Large 4 ne tournera pas chez vous
Large 4 compte 1 000 milliards de paramètres. Même compressé en 4 bits (version dite quantifiée), il pèse environ 690 Go et exige, selon Mistral, quatre GPU Nvidia B200 ou B300. Ce matériel ne se trouve que dans des centres de données.
Pour comparer, un MacBook Pro M5 démarre à 16 Go de mémoire unifiée, et la version M5 Max plafonne à 128 Go, le maximum proposé par Apple sur un portable. Même quatre Nvidia DGX Spark reliés entre eux, le maximum prévu par Nvidia, ne suffiraient pas : avec 128 Go chacun, ils plafonnent à 512 Go, autant qu’un Mac Studio M5 Ultra dans sa version la plus dotée.
Plus tôt dans le briefing, Pierre Stock avait pourtant présenté cette version quantifiée comme capable de tourner « sur une machine assez petite ». Interrogé ensuite sur le matériel nécessaire, Mistral a cité ces mêmes quatre B200 ou B300. Petite, donc, à l’échelle d’un centre de données, où le modèle complet occupe un serveur entier.
Un modèle distillé, c’est quoi ?
La distillation consiste à entraîner un petit modèle à imiter les réponses d’un gros. Le petit coûte bien moins cher à faire tourner et répond plus vite, mais il perd une partie des capacités de son aîné.
Mistral revendique cette méthode. « Nous commençons toujours par un gros modèle, parce que les petits sont entraînés à partir du gros », explique Pierre Stock. L’entreprise pratique déjà la distillation sur mesure pour des entreprises clientes.
Le futur modèle pour portable sera donc de la même famille que Large 4, mais il n’aura pas son niveau. Mistral n’a donné aucun chiffre sur l’écart attendu.
Ce que Mistral n’a pas dit
Sur le contenu de cette promesse, Mistral est resté vague. Mistral n’a donné ni la taille du modèle, ni de date ferme au-delà de « dans le mois », ni aucun résultat de test. Le communiqué publié ce jeudi n’en dit pas plus : il ne mentionne ni famille de petits modèles ni version pour portable, et annonce seulement « d’autres modèles de cette génération dans les mois à venir ».
Surtout, l’entreprise n’a pas précisé ce qu’elle entend par « portable ». Un modèle qui exige un MacBook Pro à 128 Go de mémoire unifiée ne promet pas la même chose qu’un modèle qui tourne sur un portable ordinaire à 16 Go. Dans le premier cas, le modèle visera les développeurs et les passionnés équipés ; dans le second, tout le monde. Microsoft, par exemple, présente son MAI Code 1.1 Flash comme un modèle local, mais réclame 75 Go de RAM.
    Pour aller plus loin
J’ai remplacé ChatGPT par une IA chinoise gratuite : 11h de vol sans Internet avec un PC Nvidia RTX Spark
            
Ce que Mistral propose déjà
Mistral a déjà des modèles qui tournent sur un portable : les Ministral 3, publiés en décembre 2025 aux côtés de Large 3, en versions de 3, 8 et 14 milliards de paramètres et sous licence Apache 2.0. Le plus gros tient dans moins de 24 Go de mémoire une fois quantifié, selon Mistral, et toute la gamme a été obtenue par distillation d’un modèle parent, la méthode annoncée pour la future famille. Avant eux, Mistral Small 3.1 tournait déjà sur un ordinateur dès mars 2025.
Medium 3.5, sorti en avril, joue en revanche dans une autre catégorie : avec ses 128 milliards de paramètres, il ne tient sur une seule carte graphique de 96 Go qu’une fois compressé en 4 bits, un format de station de travail.
    Pour aller plus loin
Quel mini PC choisir pour l’IA ? Notre sélection 2026
            
La nouveauté serait donc un petit modèle issu d’une génération qui joue désormais dans la même catégorie que les meilleurs modèles ouverts chinois en code. On peut citer Qwen 3.8 27B, ou le nouveau Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B de Nvidia capables de tenir dans moins de 32 Go de VRAM.
Rendez-vous dans un mois, donc. À la sortie, il faudra regarder quatre choses : la taille du modèle, la mémoire qu’il exige, sa licence, et un test de code indépendant qui le compare à Large 4. articles.title: Cloudera expands its AI ecosystem with partnerships and packaged blueprints - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cloudera expands its AI ecosystem with partnerships and packaged blueprints
Cloudera Inc. Tuesday announced an expansion of its enterprise artificial intelligence ecosystem, introducing preconfigured AI applications built with Nvidia Corp. technology and expanding partnerships with Neo4j Inc. and Mistral AI SAS.
Cloudera said the initiatives are intended to help enterprises move AI projects into production while maintaining control over their data, infrastructure and deployment costs. Announced at the company’s Evolve26 conference in New York, the offerings reinforce Cloudera’s strategy of bringing AI processing to enterprise data rather than requiring organizations to move sensitive information into centralized cloud environments.
“We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives,” Wim Stoop, Cloudera’s senior director of product marketing, said in an interview at the conference.
The centerpiece of the announcements is Cloudera Blueprints, a portfolio of ready-to-deploy AI packages that combine Nvidia’s AI reference workflows with Cloudera’s data management, security and governance capabilities.
Built using Nvidia Agent Toolkit and deployed through the Cloudera AI development platform, the blueprints are intended to reduce the integration work involved in turning experimental AI applications into production systems.
The initial portfolio includes applications for financial transaction analysis, automated clinical documentation, telecommunications network configuration and synthetic video detection. They incorporate technologies including Nvidia NIM microservices, Nemotron models and graphics processing unit-accelerated data processing.
Stoop said enterprises increasingly understand AI’s potential but struggle with the operational and financial implications of deployment.
“The biggest challenge for a lot of organizations seems to be how to go from a pilot to something that actually operates in production without incurring horrific costs,” he said.
Cloudera also announced an expansion of its Enterprise AI Ecosystem, adding Neo4j’s graph technology to help AI agents understand relationships among enterprise data.
Neo4j’s knowledge graphs provide semantic context that can help agents connect information about customers, transactions, products and business processes. Combined with Cloudera’s governed data infrastructure, the technology is intended to support AI systems that can reason about enterprise information and take actions.
The expanded ecosystem also includes partnerships with Mistral AI and Vast Data Inc., giving customers additional options for AI models and infrastructure.
Cloudera executives said the Mistral relationship is particularly important to its sovereign AI strategy, which emphasizes customer control over data, models and infrastructure.
Organizations increasingly want the flexibility to use open-weight models within their own environments instead of relying exclusively on externally hosted proprietary systems, Stoop said. “Our partnership with Mistral is a great example of that,” he added, citing the ability to deploy models locally and customize them with proprietary enterprise information.
That flexibility matters in Europe, where data privacy requirements, geopolitical concerns and regulations are pushing companies to examine where AI workloads run and who controls them. However, Stoop cautioned that sovereign AI goes beyond keeping data within national boundaries. Organizations must also establish control over model execution, data lineage, infrastructure and operational processes.
Cloudera said its approach preserves deployment flexibility across public clouds, private clouds, on-premises infrastructure and edge environments, allowing customers to choose configurations that match their requirements.
Stoop said flexibility could also help organizations manage the economics of AI inference, where computing costs can grow substantially as applications scale. The goal isn’t to move every workload into a sovereign environment, but to let organizations choose the most appropriate deployment model, he said. “It’s important for organizations to have that flexibility to be able to choose the right infrastructure for the right job,” he said.
Cloudera is betting that combining reusable AI applications, broader technology partnerships and consistent governance across environments will help enterprises overcome the technical and economic barriers separating AI experimentation from production.

articles.title: Bosch veut vendre son usine de Vendôme, ses salariés répondent avec une grève illimitée
articles.text:
Les salariés de l’usine Bosch de Vendôme, dans le Loir-et-Cher, sont en grève illimitée depuis mardi. Lors d’un référendum, 60 % des votants ont demandé l’arrêt de la vente du site, faute de repreneur jugé fiable.
Une grève illimitée a débuté le mardi 27 octobre 2026 à l’usine Bosch de Vendôme, dans le Loir-et-Cher, où une majorité de salariés a cessé le travail. Le mouvement fait suite à un référendum interne, lors duquel 60 % des 198 votants ont réclamé l’arrêt de la vente du site, qui produit notamment des colonnes de direction (la pièce qui relie le volant au reste du système de direction), engagée par l’équipementier automobile allemand en juin 2025. En cause, des repreneurs que les syndicats jugent insuffisamment fiables, rapporte France 3 Centre-Val de Loire.
Les salariés de l’usine de Vendôme lancent une grève illimitée pour bloquer la vente de leur site
Le lundi 26 octobre fut mouvementé du côté de Vendôme, où les salariés ont été consultés par référendum sur l'avenir de leur site. Sur les 198 votants, une grande partie a réclamé l'arrêt du processus de vente. Un résultat nourri à la fois par l'usure et l'agacement. Les salariés disent être « menés en bateau » depuis des mois par une direction qui ne leur inspire plus confiance. Dès mardi, la majorité d'entre eux s'est mise en grève illimitée, un mouvement que les syndicats jugent tenable.
Le fond du problème, ce sont les candidats au rachat. Benoît Freudenreich (CFDT) et Patrick Pigoreau (CGT) assurent qu'ils n'étaient pas opposés à l'idée d'un repreneur au départ. Mais une fois les dossiers étudiés avec l'aide d'un cabinet d'expertise, le constat fut amer. Les garanties sur l'emploi ne sont pas toujours au rendez-vous, ou se résument à de belles promesses.
Le couperet est tombé la semaine dernière, avec la visite d'un nouveau repreneur. D'après les syndicats, elle aurait eu lieu à la demande du géant Stellantis, le client qui pèse le plus lourd dans la production du site. Sans retour à leur demande de plan de relance, les salariés ont d'abord débrayé, c'est-à-dire cessé le travail pour une courte durée. Bosch France dément d'ailleurs que Stellantis soit à l'origine de cette visite. Selon l'entreprise, le candidat avait simplement besoin de revenir sur place avant de retravailler son projet de relance.
Bosch maintient le cap jusqu'au verdict de décembre
La direction, elle, n'entend pas céder si facilement. Elle rappelle que 40 % des votants ne souhaitent pas arrêter la vente et que tout le monde n'a pas voté, à commencer par les intérimaires. Les syndicats écartent cet argument, puisque selon eux, ces intérimaires ne font pas vraiment partie de l'entreprise, car rattachés à une agence d'intérim. Bosch dit respecter le droit de grève, mais prévient qu'un mouvement prolongé pourrait fragiliser la confiance des clients et des repreneurs potentiels.
Selon Bosch France, les discussions sont pourtant en bonne voie. Les projets des différents candidats seront présentés le 3 décembre, et une décision sur la reprise est attendue une grosse dizaine de jours plus tard, le 15 décembre. D'un côté, on a donc une direction décidée à mener la vente à son terme. De l'autre, une majorité de votants qui refuse de signer un chèque en blanc. Les semaines à venir s'annoncent tendues.
Le site de Vendôme est assez symptomatique de ce que subit l'entreprise. Bousculé par une électrification plus lente que prévu et par la montée des concurrents chinois, le premier équipementier automobile mondial réduit peu à peu ses effectifs et revoit son organisation. Il a par exemple annoncé l'an dernier quelque 13 000 suppressions de postes d'ici 2030, en majorité en Allemagne. Le 22 octobre, il a ajouté la transformation de sa branche Mobility allemande et de trois unités de services en filiales distinctes, une réorganisation qui touchera pas moins de 62 500 salariés outre-Rhin à partir d'août 2027.

articles.title: Galaxy Watch und Ring erkennen Schlafapnoe jetzt genauer
articles.text:
Auch für einige ältere Smartwatches: Samsung bringt neue KI-Gesundheitsfunktion
Allein in Deutschland sollen laut AOK etwa drei Prozent der Frauen und fünf Prozent der Männer an sogenannter obstruktiver Schlafapnoe leiden. Die nächtlichen Atemaussetzer sorgen für Müdigkeit und Konzentrationsstörungen am Tag. Bei Betroffenen steigt aber auch das Risiko für Folgeerkrankungen wie Diabetes Typ-2, Herzinfarkt oder Depressionen.
Samsung: KI-Update für Schlafapnoe-Funktion
Smartwatches von Samsung verfügen seit dem Start der Galaxy Watch 4 über eine Funktion zur Erkennung von Schlafapnoe. Seit Juni 2025 ist die Schlafapnoe-Funktion auch in Deutschland verfügbar. Bisher ließ sich so aber lediglich erkennen, ob eine Person in der Nacht Atemaussetzer hat. Mit dem aktuellen Update geht Samsung jetzt einen Schritt weiter.
Wie das Unternehmen mitteilt, nutzt die erweiterte Schlafapnoe-Funktion auf Galaxy-Geräten wie Watch und Ring einen KI-Algorithmus. Damit sollen sich die Atemstörungen in drei Schweregrade einteilen lassen: leicht, gelegentlich und häufig. Dazu sind mindestens zwei nächtliche Messeinheiten innerhalb von zehn Tagen notwendig, in denen Ring oder Uhr jeweils fünf Stunden getragen werden.
Start auf Smartwatches in Südkorea
Nach einer Freigabe durch die Gesundheitsbehörde FDA in den USA im Juli 2026 hat Samsung jetzt auch die Genehmigung der südkoreanischen Behörde für Lebensmittel- und Arzneimittelsicherheit erhalten. Entsprechend will Samsung das Update der Schlafapnoe-Funktion schon im November 2026 für Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Galaxy Watch 9 und Galaxy Ring in Südkorea ausspielen.
Die USA könnten innerhalb kurzer Zeit folgen, wie Androidpolice schreibt. Für einen möglichen Europa-Start der KI-gestützten Schlafapnoe-Funktion für Samsung-Smartwatches gibt es derweil bisher keinen offiziellen Termin. Die CE-Freigabe der europäischen Behörden steht noch aus.
Ältere Geräte bis Galaxy Watch 7 folgen
Ebenfalls unklar ist, wann Samsung die Funktion für ältere Modelle freischaltet. Dabei soll es sich um Galaxy Watch Ultra, Galaxy Watch 8 und Galaxy Watch 7 handeln. Auf noch älteren Smartwatches soll laut Samsung zumindest die bisherige Schlafapnoe-Funktion verfügbar bleiben.

articles.title: Bank of America tells customers to stop sharing banking passwords with AI agents — agentic payments are becoming a major thorn in the side of banking
articles.text:
Bank of America tells customers to stop sharing banking passwords with AI agents — agentic payments are becoming a major thorn in the side of banking
Stop giving out your financial information
- Stop giving out your username and password to your AI assistant, Bank of America warned customers
- AI agents are now capable of making agentic purchases, but that doesn't mean they should
- Customers are being locked out of accounts thanks to erroneous purchases made by AI agents
Bank of America has requested that customers do not share their usernames and passwords with anyone, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”
As agentic AI assistants have exploded in popularity, so too has the trend of having personal AI assistants make payments on a customer’s behalf. But that has led to a regulatory headache for banking providers.
AI agents ingest everything you tell them, including highly sensitive information which can be regurgitated if there is a security flaw.
Stop giving your banking details to bots
There is an obvious pro to having an AI agent make a purchase on your behalf: if something drops in price or suddenly becomes available after being out of stock, the agent can purchase it so you don’t miss out.
But these payments can sometimes be flagged as unauthorized by financial institutions, leading to customers being locked out of their accounts. Or an agent could purchase something you didn’t want it to, putting some customers into a battle with the bank to try and get the money back.
In these cases, the onus is largely on the customer. Had the AI agent not had your banking details, the purchase wouldn’t have been made.
AI firms have been praising the helpfulness of AI agents in helping organize a busy life, or help regain financial stability through analyzing spending and finances. But there is such a thing as giving too much detail on your life. As we’ve discussed before, even organizing meetings or scheduling your day can have disastrous consequences.

articles.title: Datadog Builds a Specialist AI Model for SRE Investigations
articles.text:
Datadog has released Scout, a model trained to investigate production problems. It runs inside Bits Investigation, the company's AI SRE product, where it can pick up an alert, look through telemetry and suggest what caused the problem. Datadog engineers and a small number of customers are using it in a closed preview.
Most of the work described in the announcement concerns cost. An investigation may require many model calls as Bits tries a query, studies the result and decides what to check next. General-purpose models can do this, but Datadog says the bill makes it difficult to run them against every alert. The authors of the announcement want Bits to begin work while an engineer is still responding to the page.
"Our goal is for Bits to serve as an always-on first responder, gathering evidence and identifying likely causes before an engineer steps in."
Othmane Abou-Amal, Ben Cohen, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ameet Talwalkar, Omri Sass and Daniel Shan
On Datadog's AlertEval benchmark, Scout medium received a similar score to GPT-6.1 Sol high and Claude Opus 5.5 high. Its estimated inference cost was between three and eight times lower. At the xhigh setting, Datadog says Scout matched Claude Fable 5.1 xhigh for one quarter of the cost. No prices are published, so these figures are relative to the cost of a Scout medium investigation.
AlertEval uses real alerts, archived telemetry and explanations written by Datadog engineers. An LLM judge compares Scout's account with an expert account, rewarding matches at both the immediate and underlying cause level. Contradictions and claims without evidence lose marks. The resulting score runs from zero to 100, but Datadog warns that it is not a percentage of incidents solved.
Scout is based on GLM-5.3 Flash. Datadog post-trained the model with reinforcement learning, using incident simulations made from patterns found in historical cases. The simulations contain an alert, telemetry that can be queried and a known cause. They do not contain customer data, according to the company. Scout practises with tools modelled on the ones in Bits, including searches across logs, metrics and traces, as well as code, deployment and feature flag inspection.
"Its training rewards finding the cause and supporting its conclusions with evidence."
Othmane Abou-Amal, Ben Cohen, Afshin Rostamizadeh, Ameet Talwalkar, Omri Sass and Daniel Shan
The technical report gives a useful account of what went wrong during training. A reward based on the final answer prompted Scout to make fewer claims and stop investigating early. That made it less likely to be penalised, without making it a better investigator. The team changed the reward to take account of correctness, exploration and supporting evidence. They also removed tools from some training runs, or shortened the time available, to stop the model learning one fixed route through an incident.
Datadog ran a second evaluation on SREGym, a public set of 90 faults. Scout resolved 71 cases at medium effort, 79 at high and 80 at xhigh. GPT-6.1 Sol xhigh completed 82. Datadog carried out these tests itself, including the runs for newer comparison models, so independent results would be useful.
Scout arrives as observability suppliers work out how much of an incident an agent should handle. AWS DevOps Agent combines telemetry from several monitoring products with source code, deployment records and runbooks. AWS is joining information across tools, whereas Datadog is training a cheaper model for repeated use inside its own product.
Honeycomb's Canvas Agent is closer to the way many engineers investigate by hand. It opens a shared Canvas when an alert fires or an SLO burns, runs queries, tests ideas and leaves the evidence visible for an engineer to examine. Teams can capture familiar debugging procedures as Canvas Skills. Honeycomb also provides an MCP server, which allows external agents to query its telemetry. Honeycomb has not announced a dedicated SRE model; its focus is on the query engine and the record of how the investigation progressed.
Splunk and New Relic have gone further into the repair stage. Splunk AI SRE groups alerts and produces a probable cause with an evidence chain. A connected Claude agent can prepare a code change in a sandbox and open a pull request. New Relic's SRE Agent brings runbooks, incident reviews and previous resolutions into its analysis, while Autopilot can suggest remedial action. Both keep an approval step before a production change.
A ClickHouse study reported by InfoQ found that general-purpose models could produce summaries, but needed human guidance to find root causes consistently. Instacart takes a similar approach with Blueberry: agents collect context before an engineer assesses the proposed cause in Slack.
The benchmark evidence for Scout remains largely Datadog's own. In a response to the launch, the independent AI news account AGTP pointed out that AlertEval has not been independently tested. It also asked for an audit trail showing which evidence Scout considered and discarded. Honeycomb's visible Canvas and Splunk's evidence chain indicate that other vendors see the same requirement. A short answer may help during an incident, but engineers also need to see how the model reached it.
Datadog has not given a date for general availability. The company plans to add more types of failure to its simulations and eventually allow Bits to carry out repairs. The preview stops before that point: Scout investigates, gives its diagnosis and proposes recovery actions, while an engineer remains responsible for the change.

articles.title: Cisco Open Sources Quarry to Catch AI Agent Attacks Hidden in Harmless Steps
articles.text:
Detecting an AI agent attack isn’t simply finding multiple small needles scattered in a large haystack; it is recognizing whether and for what purpose the needles are connected.
Traditional security controls evaluate single actions to classify whether an intent is bad or benign. This approach fails on AI agent activity when the bad intent only emerges over a series of benign actions. It only becomes apparent if and when the overall sequence of actions is viewed or actioned.
Fraud detection is an example. A bank analyzes each purchase on its own. That’s largely how traditional security operates. Fraud detection, however, needs to see patterns of apparently benign single purchases across multiple purchases, possibly in multiple locations with unlikely timing (potentially employing agent capability). “Agent security needs the same combination of pattern detection and evidence, applied to the steps an agent takes rather than to purchases,” writes Cisco in announcing the open sourcing of its Project Quarry.
Cisco describes Quarry as a neurosymbolic rule language, combining machine learning judgment with rule-based checks. “It covers single-turn and multi-turn large language model (LLM) conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs.”
Each defined rule draws on neural evidence from ML classifiers and LLM judges, and symbolic rules that check exact conditions, sequences, string matches, and tool relationships. It is designed to provide a shared policy layer rather than be a replacement for every detector or every enforcement control.
Quarry can be used to provide runtime guardrails on agents, post-hoc rule set security analytics, and incident response. It integrates with Cisco’s existing Integrated AI Security & Safety Framework. It expands the framework from describing AI risk toward detecting it in agent activity, and is positioned as the policy and evaluation layer for the framework. The framework defines AI risks while Quarry provides detection of the risks in agent activity – the framework categories also offer a roadmap for the further development of new rules.
Quarry’s detection purpose is to identify suspicious patterns that span individual permitted actions. Such patterns may only become suspicious over a period of time. In 2025, Claude Code was used by bad actors in two campaigns: one against around 30 organizations, and a second against Mexican government institutions. The former attack was split into small routine-looking tasks that told the existing defense it was part of new defense testing. It looked like an authorized pentest from its parts, but the true intent (theft of data) only became apparent when the requests came together in the right sequence.
It is the ability of AI to separate an attack into multiple individually benign steps that defeats traditional defenses and requires this new form of neurosymbolic threat detection. But it is not a ‘write once and move on’ requirement. Attackers are constantly developing new approaches to their attacks. So, whenever a new attack technique is recognized, defenders must respond immediately by writing a new Quarry rule that can be used by all organizations everywhere.
But writing new rules by hand does not scale against the attackers’ use of AI to develop new malicious agents. “We want agents, as well as security and AI engineers, to be able to write Quarry rules,” declares Cisco. A Quarry Plugin allows a coding agent to compose, compile, and refine rules from a plain-English description of an organization’s risk, and then test those rules against real conversations. A rule that passes in a coding agent should behave the same way at runtime.
By open sourcing the project, the traditional cybersecurity asymmetry of attack and defense (multiple attackers against individual defenders) is equalized (multiple global attackers now face multiple global defenders). Allowing the use of AI for development also balances the speed advantage that bad actors have enjoyed in AI-assisted attacks.
“The open-source project,” says Cisco, “gives practitioners a working foundation for detection engineering.” The Quarry starter pack includes:
- a readable DSL for conversations, tool use, and event relationships;
- an evaluation runtime with configurable safety and resource limits, which compiles each rule when it loads;
- a command-line scanner for individual traces, directories, and datasets;
- a Python SDK for application integration;
- optional configured model operations for semantic signals;
- the Quarry plugin for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents;
- rule metadata, examples, documentation, and message-format guidance; and
- a workflow for validating rules against positive and benign datasets.
Project Quarry is intended to become a common, open standard for expressing and sharing detections for AI-agent attacks, much as Snort, YARA, and Sigma became standards in other areas of cybersecurity. “Hugging Face reconstructed roughly 17,600 agent actions after the fact,” says Cisco. “Our aim with Project Quarry is to help defenders recognize sequences like that one while they are still in progress, and to preserve the evidence behind each finding for the people who have to act on it.”

articles.title: Police are pulling people over because license plate cameras say their travel patterns look "suspicious"
articles.text:
In context: Communities across the US have pushed back against the deployment of AI-powered automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) because of concerns about mass surveillance. Reports over the past year or so illustrate how authorities have used data from these devices to conduct traffic stops based on nothing more than "suspicious" travel patterns.
The ACLU recently outlined a pattern of police traffic stops based solely on data from Flock cameras and other license plate readers. The reports go back to at least 2025 and show how closely authorities can track the movements of most motorists.
In one case from late 2025, a woman only understood the extent of the surveillance when an officer demonstrated the software following a traffic stop. As she traveled through several states on a road trip to Florida, a self-identified FBI agent ran her license plate through a database and stopped her simply because she was from another state and her recent travels seemed unusual compared to the information the ALPR network had on her.
Although the account did not specifically mention Flock, the agent likely used a database built by Flock or another company that has installed ALPRs in thousands of communities nationwide. The AI-powered cameras automatically input passing cars' license plates (not always accurately) into nationwide databases that authorities can search without warrants.
The technology lets officers theoretically track the movements of any vehicle that has driven past ALPRs. In some cases, authorities can track associations between different vehicles and mobile devices to build and link profiles. While supporters claim the cameras can help solve crimes, find missing persons, and combat illicit trafficking, multiple incidents have raised concerns over police conduct.
Dozens of officers have been caught using the cameras to stalk ex-partners. Even in routine police work, traffic stops based on ALPR data raise questions about whether driving patterns amount to probable cause.
In another 2025 case, police stopped a man simply because he drove back and forth between his home in Wisconsin and Michigan. Because marijuana is legal in Michigan, authorities suspected that anyone driving in and out of the state might be trafficking it to parts of the country where it remains illegal.
Earlier this year, an Oklahoma judge called a similar stop unconstitutional indiscriminate mass surveillance, even though it led to the seizure of 91 pounds of meth. In response to such incidents, a Florida representative recently introduced a bill to require warrants to search ALPR databases. However, other politicians want to ban the technology outright.

articles.title: Google expands AI Search ads globally as core ad growth slows | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google is bringing ads in its AI-powered Search experiences to international markets, betting that generative AI can open up new revenue opportunities even as growth in its core search advertising business slows.
The announcement came Wednesday during Alphabet’s third-quarter earnings call, as the company reported $127.6 billion in revenue, up 25% year over year. But Search advertising growth continued to decelerate, and Alphabet shares fell 8% following the results.
Google Search revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, down from 17% growth in the second quarter and 19% in the first quarter. The slowdown puts added pressure on Google to turn its expanding AI features into a meaningful source of advertising revenue.
“We are now scaling high-quality ads within AI overviews in AI mode to more users and queries,” Philipp Schindler, Google’s chief business officer, said during the call with investors. “This includes taking our monetization footprint global for the first time. Today, we’re announcing the expansion of ads in AI mode into international markets alongside multi-turn ads and AI mode in the U.S.”
Google says early results suggest the formats are working. Click-through rates for sponsored product listings in AI Mode are already comparable to those for organic listings, according to Schindler. The company’s user research also indicates that people find the ads relevant.
The move builds on Google’s May announcement of new Gemini-powered ad formats, including conversational discovery ads that respond to users’ questions and sponsored recommendations integrated into AI-generated answers.
Google CEO Sundar Pichai also said that Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years, though he did not disclose the exact growth rate. He credited AI features with changing how people use Search, including prompting longer and more complex queries.
Queries in AI Mode are three times longer on average than traditional searches, Pichai said, while one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images, or documents. Google has also surpassed 50 billion visual searches per month.
“[Search] is bringing the benefits of AI to more people than any other product in the world,” Pichai told investors. “People are using our AI features more, searching in entirely new ways. Their queries are longer, personalized, and multimodal.”
Alphabet’s Google Services division, which includes Search, generated $96.3 billion in revenue, up 11% year over year. Google Cloud revenue surged 103% to $30.7 billion.
The results follow a busy quarter for Google, including the release of Gemini 4 Argon, the growth of the Gemini app to 1 billion monthly users, and the launch of its Pixel 11 lineup.

articles.title: SK hynix Expects Memory Demand to Outpace Supply Through 2030
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
SK hynix Expects Memory Demand to Outpace Supply Through 2030
SK hynix reported its latest Q3 2026 quarterly results with a record $78.129 billion in net revenue. However, the company also shared a market outlook, highlighting its long-term supply agreements and plans for expansion with new fab capacity and facilities under construction. For the consumer market, the outlook is grim as SK hynix expects memory demand to continue outpacing supply through 2030. The main supply constraint is the complexity of leading-edge semiconductor nodes and the lengthy lead times for fab construction, which take years to translate into regular mass production volumes.
Despite sustained demand, pricing is also on an upward trajectory, with the average selling price of memory modules in Q3 increasing by over 20% compared to Q2. This is concerning, as it suggests that the prices of consumer electronics devices might jump by more than 20% once memory inventory is depleted. Although SK hynix expects a decrease in PC and smartphone shipments, this will be offset by a strong rollout of AI data centers. About 14 major customers, including most hyperscalers, have signed 5-year long-term agreements, which will account for over 50% of total capacity sold for 2027 and 2028.SK hynix expects its DRAM business to continue aggressively adopting the 1c nm node. As a reminder, DRAM nodes differ from conventional logic nodes. DRAM manufacturers use variations of 10 nm, scaling them with more EUV layers or advanced features. For SK hynix, the currently dominant 1b node is around 12-13 nm in actual design and involves about 4 layers of EUV patterning, while the most advanced 1c node shrinks to 11-12 nm with 5-6 layers of EUV. SK hynix will use the 1c node to manufacture HBM4E, LPDDR6, and DDR5 memory. For the older 1b node, SK hynix produces DDR5, LPDDR5X, HBM3E, and HBM4.
In the HBM segment, Q4 is expected to see HBM4 surpass HBM3E in shipment and revenue share, and negotiations for 2027 HBM have been finalized. Finally, for NAND, the majority of production output is now 321-layer NAND Flash, and SK hynix continues to work on HBF solutions.

articles.title: Solink raises more than $100 million USD to help physical stores keep an eye on their business | BetaKit
articles.text:
Ottawa-based surveillance tech company Solink has raised more than $100 million USD ($140 million CAD) in a new strategic investment round to solidify itself as a global leader in what it sees as an emerging industry: AI vision intelligence.
The company announced the round, led by Toronto-based private equity firm Vertu Capital, on Thursday morning. In an interview, Solink CEO Michael Matta did not disclose how much Solink raised, but said it “may be a small rounding error” from the announced $100 million USD.
“That’s really the focus of this investment: continuing to position around where we see the puck going.”
Michael Matta, Solink
The round consisted of a mix of primary and secondary capital. More than 90 percent of the proceeds are headed to Solink’s balance sheet, and the remainder are going through employee and investor stock sales. Existing investor Goldman Sachs reinvested in Solink through the new round, citing “strong customer adoption and an ambitious product vision,” while new investors Golub Growth and Comcast Ventures also participated.
The new capital will help solidify Solink’s evolution from a cloud-connected surveillance platform for restaurants and retailers into a provider of AI-powered business intelligence for the physical world, Matta explained to BetaKit.
“The physical world is a lot more chaotic than the digital world,” Matta said. “Things don’t repeat in a certain cadence, and so that reasoning layer of being able to understand the physical world, and what the intent and context is, is really important today.”
Essentially, Matta is saying that, while data gathering is easy for an online retailer, brick-and-mortar stores are comparatively helpless. Solink helps store security teams manage and keyword search their thousands of hours of footage, but Matta also sees potential in helping those businesses extract value from the other “99 percent” of unseen surveillance footage by using AI. This includes identifying store factors, like missing products or long lines, that resulted in missed sales.
“You can go into hundreds of rabbit holes as to why we are not optimizing our physical space or the priorities that we have as a business,” Matta said. “Solink wants to be that sidekick to operators and to owners to be able to help them execute.”
Surveillance tech backlash
Solink is equipping more retailers’ surveillance cameras with its AI-powered toolkit amidst a wave of public backlash surrounding surveillance technologies, from protests against Flock cameras to the outcry against surveillance tech in billboards and M&M vending machines. That tech is also lucrative; the global AI surveillance market is expected to grow from $4 billion USD to nearly $11 billion USD by 2032. When asked how public sentiment has affected Solink, Matta stressed that the company is running a “very different business.” He explained that Solink doesn’t install any of its own cameras, only bolstering cameras that are already recording a business’ premises, and does not provide biometric data.
“The way I like to think of it is, it’s not the actor; [Solink is capturing] the actions that are happening, and being able to understand at scale what is taking place,” Matta said, adding that Solink’s tech is not identifying individuals. “It has less to do [with] us creating a viral product that’s selling anonymized information, or anything like that.”
A Solink spokesperson later added that surveillance data is confined to the business owner, and that their data doesn’t get shared with anyone, not even police, unless there is a warrant and consent from the business owner.
Data intelligence for the physical world
The last time Solink raised money was in 2023, when it secured $60 million USD in Series C funding to help take its surveillance software global. When the company expanded its Ottawa headquarters just over a year ago, Matta told BetaKit that Solink was not looking to raise any more capital, and that it still had “a lot of liquidity” from the 2023 financing.
This week, Matta said the new raise wasn’t driven by a need for liquidity; rather, Solink wants to invest in the shift from data intelligence being a strictly digital affair to a physical one.
“Today, I believe we’re operating in a trillion-dollar TAM.”
Michael Matta, Solink
“I believe in the next two to three years we’re going to continue to see that level of AI and intelligence penetrate our physical world,” Matta said. “We just wanted to be the leaders in that space, and that’s really the focus of this investment: continuing to position around where we see the puck going.”
Solink has already experienced rapid growth in recent years. Matta did not provide specific revenue numbers, but said Solink has been “scaling revenue pretty aggressively,” increasing between 40 and 50 percent year after year. On Wednesday, Solink placed 10th on Deloitte’s 2026 Enterprise–Industry Leaders list, sporting a 241-percent revenue growth rate over the past four years.
The company says its platform is in more than 35,000 customer locations (nearly double since 2023) and 500,000 cameras in 65 countries, ingesting more than 750 million hours of video every month. Its customers include stores like Gap, JYSK, Domino’s, Moose Knuckles, and Tim Hortons.
RELATED: Solink expands Ottawa headquarters as it targets 1,000 employees by 2030
To entrench its place in the market, Solink will use the new funding to execute on an AI roadmap, renew its go-to-market efforts, and explore “growth through strategic opportunities.” Solink’s AI roadmap includes an upcoming hardware launch that will provide a way for its customers to host its AI agents on premises, rather than run on an external data centre, Matta said. On the go-to-market side, an “important” reselling partnership with new investor Comcast also opens up an avenue for Solink to reach the US telecom giant’s restaurant and retailer partners.
While the physical security and security guard industries are hundred-billion-dollar businesses on their own, Matta said he believes those industries will increasingly shift their spend away from people and towards technology in the coming years. And that’s just the security side. With Solink looking to provide store managers more value from their surveillance footage than just stopping ne’er-do-wells, Matta sees his company well positioned to be a “global business that just happens to be based in Canada.”
“We used to operate in a $70 billion TAM [total addressable market],” Matta said. “Today, I believe we’re operating in a trillion-dollar TAM.”
Feature image courtesy Alex Riehl for BetaKit.

articles.title: Tus mensajes de Discord podrían aparecer en Google si no haces este ajuste
articles.text:
Discord implementará un cambio que podría poner en riesgo la privacidad de sus usuarios. La plataforma anunció que parte del contenido publicado en sus servidores públicos comenzará a ser visible en los buscadores web, incluyendo tus mensajes. Si piensas publicar en alguno de ellos, tus conversaciones podrían aparecer en Google a menos que realices un ajuste.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, Discord intentará recuperar el papel de los viejos foros de la web, esos lugares en donde las personas publicaban y comentaban sobre algún tema en específico. La popularidad de la plataforma terminó por enterrar esa práctica, migrando las conversaciones a lugares cerrados en los que necesitabas una invitación para mirar el contenido. Ahora Discord quiere abrirse al mundo y robarle un pedazo de mercado a Reddit, que domina en las búsquedas.
La novedad afecta solamente a los Canales Descubribles, que son comunidades públicas con al menos 1.000 miembros y que aparecen en el sistema de descubrimiento de Discord. Según la empresa, estos espacios recibirán una mayor presencia en la web para que cualquier usuario encuentre respuestas a preguntas sin necesidad de navegar dentro de la aplicación. Todos los servidores contarán con una página pública en internet, que mostrará información sobre la comunidad y resúmenes automáticos de las conversaciones de los canales públicos.
Las páginas públicas se mostrarán a partir del 16 de noviembre de 2026, aunque semanas después la medida se extenderá a los mensajes. Discord confirmó que mostrará mensajes de canales públicos en los resultados de búsqueda de la web a mediados de diciembre de 2026. La compañía afirma que hay miles de respuestas útiles dentro de sus comunidades, las cuales permanecen ocultas para quienes buscan información en internet.
Cómo evitar que tus mensajes de Discord aparezcan en las búsquedas de Google
La decisión ya prendió las alertas entre los defensores de la privacidad, aunque la compañía dejó claro que no hay nada que temer. Los mensajes no incluirán nombre de usuario ni la fotografía de perfil de la persona que lo escribió y solo se considerarán aquellos que se hayan publicado antes del 16 de noviembre. Aquellos enviados antes de la entrada en vigor de esta función no se indexarán en los motores de búsqueda.
Si eres usuario de Discord y no deseas que tus publicaciones se muestren en Google, existe un modo de evitarlo. Solo basta entrar en los ajustes de tu cuenta y elegir la opción Datos y Privacidad, ubicada en el menú lateral. Ahí encontrarás una opción llamada "Mostrar el contenido de mis mensajes de los canales descubribles en la web", la cual tendrás que deshabilitar. Aprovechando que te encuentras en esa sección, también puedes desactivar el resto de funciones que aprovechan tus datos para que Discord te espíe y muestre contenido patrocinado.
Una vez que deshabilites la función, los mensajes que publiques en los canales públicos no aparecerán en Google. Es probable que las conversaciones publicadas mientras la opción estaba activa permanezcan visibles si ya se indexaron por el buscador, siempre y cuando el administrador no las haya eliminado manualmente.
Por último, los administradores tendrán la última palabra sobre el contenido de sus comunidades, ya que podrán elegir qué canales participan en la indexación o desactivar la exposición del servidor.

articles.title: Elle utilise l’IA pour contester ses impôts : le tribunal la sanctionne avec une amende
articles.text:
Le 4 décembre 2025, Marie-Line X a introduit une requête pour contester un redressement fiscal datant de 2023. Autant dire que cette requête n’a pas été bien reçue. En fait, le tribunal administratif de Rennes (Ille-et-Vilaine) lui a infligé une amende de 500 euros pour recours abusif, comme le rapporte Franceinfo. Parmi tous les éléments qui ont abouti à cette amende, le tribunal a constaté « une requête manifestement écrite à l’aide d’un outil d’intelligence artificielle ».
Une amende de 500 euros pour recours abusif
Pourquoi le tribunal a-t-il infligé à Marie-Line X une amende de 500 euros ? Tout d’abord, la contribuable bretonne avait déjà déposé une requête similaire, qui avait été rejetée. Ensuite, elle a saisi le tribunal administratif de Rennes sans avoir préalablement adressé de réclamation à l’administration fiscale, une démarche obligatoire dans ce type de litige. Marie-Line X assure de son côté être « de bonne foi », avoir « suivi les indications écrites » du Service des impôts des entreprises (SIE) et n’avoir « jamais été informée d’une dette en 2023 jusqu’à la notification ». Enfin, et non des moindres, le tribunal a relevé un manque de précision dans ses arguments.
Concernant ce dernier point, le magistrat explique : « les moyens de la requête – laquelle a au demeurant été manifestement écrite à l’aide d’un outil d’intelligence artificielle – ne sont pas assortis des précisions les plus élémentaires permettant au juge d’en apprécier la portée et le bien-fondé ».
Le recours à l’IA pointé du doigt par le tribunal
Le tribunal administratif de Rennes semble avoir été quelque peu agacé par le fait que Marie-Line X ait eu recours à l’intelligence artificielle pour élaborer sa requête, et ce principalement pour deux raisons. D’une part, le recours à l’IA entraînerait une multiplication notable des requêtes judiciaires. La juridiction explique à ce titre : « Dans un contexte marqué par une hausse particulièrement forte du nombre de requêtes (…) devant tous les tribunaux administratifs depuis deux ans, on constate l’usage de plus en plus décomplexé des outils d’intelligence artificielle pour générer des “requêtes” ».
D’autre part, l’IA générerait des requêtes creuses, qui manquent de détails. La juridiction explique qu’ « aux yeux de bien des justiciables, les requêtes “fabriquées par l’IA” ont toutes les apparences de leur côté : un vocabulaire juridique y est employé et le propos paraît structuré ». Cependant : « aux yeux du professionnel du droit, ces requêtes ont souvent un vilain défaut : elles sont creuses et fourmillent de références fallacieuses ».
En fin de compte, le tribunal administratif de Rennes a principalement sanctionné le caractère abusif de la requête de Marie-Line X, et le recours à l’intelligence artificielle ne l’a clairement pas aidé dans cette affaire. Il semble que la juridiction veuille aussi lancer un avertissement pour limiter le nombre de requêtes élaborées à l’aide de l’IA. La présidence du tribunal invite d’ailleurs les justiciables bretons à « utiliser avec tact, discernement et mesure » les outils d’intelligence artificielle. Prudence donc la prochaine fois que vous devrez élaborer ce type de requête, même si, rappelons-le, le recours à l’IA n’est pas le seul élément qui a mené à une amende dans cette affaire.
