articles.title: Bluebulb has launched a treasury management platform to help African businesses oversee cash, currencies, and international payments from a single dashboard, as the fintech seeks to expand beyond moving money.
articles.text:
Bluebulb has launched a treasury management platform to help African businesses oversee cash, currencies, and international payments from a single dashboard, as the fintech seeks to expand beyond moving money.
The company introduced Orbita at Moonshot by TechCabal 2026 in Lagos, targeting finance teams that rely on multiple banking portals and spreadsheets to track funds across accounts and markets.
The platform combines multi-currency wallets, cross-border payments, payment tracking, and treasury analytics. Bluebulb said it would help businesses monitor liquidity and cash flow while reducing their dependence on disconnected financial systems.
The launch addresses an operational challenge for companies expanding internationally: establishing where their money sits, which payments remain outstanding, and how much cash is available to meet approaching obligations.
Paying suppliers in different countries can require finance teams to reconcile information across banks, currencies and payment networks. That fragmentation can make it harder to assess a company’s financial position or respond quickly to funding needs.
“Africa is not short of ambitious businesses. What we need is financial infrastructure that can match that ambition,” Ola Daramola, Bluebulb’s chief executive and co-founder, said ahead of the event.
Daramola said the company wanted to move beyond payments by giving businesses greater visibility and control over their finances as they compete internationally.
Orbita is intended to bring those functions together. Alongside initiating and tracking payments, finance teams can use the platform to monitor balances across currencies and analyse cash movements, according to Bluebulb.
The distinction is significant for businesses operating across several markets. A completed payment shows that money has moved; treasury management provides a broader view of available funds, upcoming commitments and exposure to currency movements.
Bluebulb’s proposition rests on making that information easier to consolidate and act on. For customers, the test will be whether a single platform can replace enough manual reconciliation and fragmented reporting to make managing international operations simpler.

articles.title: Discord to let search engines index public server messages
articles.text:
Discord will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation.
The goal is to surface useful information to the wider internet community instead of keeping it buried in Discord conversations.
“Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you’re looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord,” the messaging platform explains.
The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers, publicly listed communities with at least 1,000 members. The platform says it hosts approximately 63,000 such servers.
This decision excludes private servers, direct messages between users, and group announcements on servers that don’t meet the requirements.
According to the company's schedule, the rollout will happen in two stages:
- On November 16, every Discoverable Server will get a public Server Web Page which will display automatically generated summaries of active conversations from that date onward.
- Starting mid-December, every eligible message posted on Discoverable Servers will appear on the Server Web Page and may be indexed by web search engines.
Server Web Pages will be automatically created on November 16 if admins haven’t created them by then, and the only way to avoid them is to change the server type to private before the cutoff date.
Discord has been piloting Community Messages and Server Web Pages in the NBA 2K, Rust, and Dead by Daylight gaming groups.
The December rollout will be gradual, and Discord says messages posted before the release date will be excluded.
Channel administrators can choose to exclude individual channels or turn off all channel content sharing entirely using controls available under Server Settings > Web Presence.
Community members can also control if their messages appear on the Server Web Page through User Settings > Data and Privacy. However, changing that setting only affects future messages, and past messages that became public cannot be retracted.
If admins and users leave the settings at their defaults, their content will automatically be included in the new sharing scheme.
However, message sharing will stay off by default in all EU countries, the UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea. In those places, members must explicitly enable it in their privacy settings.
Underage users are automatically excluded and cannot activate the feature until they turn 18.

articles.title: IA faz preço de chips disparar e tira poder de barganha histórico da Apple
articles.text:
A disparada dos preços das memórias flash, impulsionada pela demanda de empresas de inteligência artificial, mudou a relação entre a Apple e seus fornecedores. Após anos pressionando fabricantes por descontos, a empresa enfrenta custos maiores e menor poder de negociação.
Segundo a TechInsights, os preços dessas memórias quintuplicaram no último ano, fortalecendo a posição comercial da Kioxia e de outras fabricantes.
Demanda por IA muda o mercado
Durante anos, a Apple foi a maior compradora mundial de memórias flash, chips usados para armazenar fotos, músicas e aplicativos. Seu volume de compras permitia exigir preços baixos e condições contratuais favoráveis.
Dois anos atrás, a empresa comprava quase o dobro da quantidade adquirida em conjunto por Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Google, segundo estimativas da TechInsights. Agora, essas quatro empresas compram, juntas, o dobro da participação da Apple no mercado.
Em 2026, Meta, Microsoft e Amazon assinaram contratos de fornecimento de longo prazo com a Kioxia, aceitando preços mais altos. Os acordos também protegem os lucros da fabricante caso o mercado mude.
A memória flash representa uma parcela menor do custo de construção de um data center do que da fabricação de um iPhone. As regras contábeis também permitem distribuir esses custos ao longo de vários anos, o que ajuda a explicar por que as empresas de IA conseguem pagar mais pelos componentes.
A TechInsights estima que a Apple gastará US$ 25 bilhões (cerca de R$ 131,25 bilhões) com memórias flash em 2026, ante US$ 6 bilhões (R$ 31,5 bilhões) em 2025, para adquirir aproximadamente a mesma quantidade.
Custos maiores pressionam as margens
A alta surpreendeu a Apple, apesar dos alertas anteriores de analistas, segundo pessoas familiarizadas com as práticas de compras da empresa ouvidas pelo The Wall Street Journal.
Em 2023, o preço da memória flash chegou a cinco centavos de dólar por gigabyte. Com a demanda do setor de IA, ultrapassou 30 centavos, uma alta superior a 500% em relação àquele patamar.
O encarecimento afeta diretamente a rentabilidade das versões com mais armazenamento. No iPhone 17 Pro, a Apple cobrava US$ 200 adicionais pela versão de 512 GB em comparação com o modelo básico de 256 GB. Na época, a memória extra custava US$ 15 à empresa. Esse valor subiu para US$ 66.
Segundo a análise do The Wall Street Journal, a Apple obteve, em média, mais de US$ 0,80 de lucro bruto por dólar cobrado pelo armazenamento adicional em iPhones e iPads desde o lançamento desses produtos até 2025.
A pressão sobre os custos também coincide com aumentos nos preços dos produtos. Nos últimos meses, a Apple reajustou quase toda a sua linha, com alta média de 13% nos iPhones, incluindo modelos antigos que normalmente ficam mais baratos com a chegada de novas versões.
Walt Coon, analista da TechInsights, resumiu a mudança de posição dos fornecedores: “A Apple historicamente negociou de forma muito dura com os fornecedores de memória. E não falta satisfação entre os fornecedores agora que o equilíbrio de poder está mudando”.
Uma relação marcada por disputas
A relação entre a Apple e seus fornecedores começou a ganhar força em 2001, quando engenheiros da Toshiba apresentaram à empresa um disco rígido de 1,8 polegada e 5 GB. A Apple adquiriu direitos exclusivos sobre o componente, que se tornou parte central do iPod.
Em 2005, a empresa passou a usar memória flash no iPod Nano e antecipou US$ 1,25 bilhão para garantir o fornecimento até 2010. O lançamento do iPhone, em 2007, ampliou seu poder de compra e reforçou uma estratégia de negociação baseada em preços baixos, auditorias nas contas dos fabricantes e contratos que buscavam assegurar condições comerciais iguais ou melhores que as oferecidas a outros clientes.
Em 2023, quando a queda na demanda por dispositivos derrubou os preços das memórias, a Bernstein Research estimou perdas operacionais de US$ 19 bilhões para o setor. No mesmo ano, a Apple obteve US$ 14 bilhões em lucro bruto com a venda de armazenamento adicional. Agora, a expansão da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial elevou a demanda e os preços dos componentes, fortalecendo os fabricantes nas negociações. A empresa que durante anos usou seu poder de compra para impor condições enfrenta um mercado em que garantir o fornecimento exige aceitar custos mais altos.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: 40 millions de voitures en France : voici les départements qui boudent l’électrique et polluent le plus en thermique
articles.text:
40 millions de voitures en France : voici les départements qui boudent l’électrique et polluent le plus en thermique
Au 1er janvier 2026, le parc automobile français avait atteint 40 millions de voitures. Malgré l’essor de l’électrique, les Français roulent moins et conservent leurs vieux véhicules thermiques. Voici les chiffres à retenir.
La France vient de franchir un cap symbolique. Au 1er janvier 2026, 40 millions de voitures particulières circulaient sur le territoire, soit une hausse de 0,4 % sur un an selon les derniers chiffres du Service des données et études statistiques (SDES). Malgré un recul de 5,2 % des ventes de voitures neuves en 2025, le parc roulant croît car les ménages prolongent la durée d’usage de leurs modèles thermiques face à la flambée des prix du neuf, creusant un fossé majeur entre les régions. Les motorisations électriques peinent quant à elles à s’imposer dans le paysage routier réel.
La Creuse et l’Indre en tête des départements qui résistent à la transition électrique
L’analyse des vignettes Crit’Air illustre parfaitement cette fracture territoriale en termes de pollution. À l’échelle nationale, les véhicules classés Crit’Air 1 dominent désormais à 38,0 % (+ 2,3 points), suivis par les Crit’Air 2 à 34,2 %. Pourtant, 24,3 % du parc français reste composé de modèles Crit’Air 3 ou plus, contre 26,5 % un an plus tôt.
Au cœur de la diagonale du vide, les motorisations anciennes et polluantes résistent d’ailleurs le plus : la Creuse arrive en tête, suivie par l’Indre et l’Ariège, avec plus de 36 % de véhicules classés Crit’Air 3 ou au-delà. À l’inverse, Paris, les Hauts-de-Seine, la Haute-Savoie et les territoires d’outre-mer concentrent les flottes les plus récentes et cumulent les plus fortes parts de vignettes Crit’Air 0, 1 et 2.
Sur le plan des motorisations, les modèles exclusivement thermiques (essence et diesel) représentent encore 86,1 % du parc roulant. “Les voitures diesel restent prédominantes, mais elles représentent désormais moins de la moitié du parc de voitures en circulation (46,1 %)”, précise l’étude. En face, les motorisations électriques plafonnent à 3,5 % du parc total (malgré près de 20 % de parts de marché sur le neuf en 2025 grâce au bonus écologique et au leasing social), devancées par les hybrides non rechargeables à 7,4 % et suivies des hybrides rechargeables à 2,0 %.
Preuve que les automobilistes privilégient une transition douce, l’hybride essence simple progresse fortement pour atteindre 7,0 % du parc, contre 5,3 % début 2025.
Un parc automobile français vieillissant et qui roule moins
Ce maintien des motorisations traditionnelles s’accompagne d’un vieillissement généralisé du parc, avec un âge moyen de 11,8 ans par véhicule, contre 11,4 ans au 1er janvier 2025. Les voitures envoyées à la casse atteignent même 20,0 ans en moyenne (19,4 ans pour le diesel et 21,5 ans pour l’essence), après avoir parcouru quelque 212 000 kilomètres, et jusqu’à 239 000 kilomètres pour les blocs gazole.
Enfin, les Français utilisent de moins en moins leur voiture : avec une baisse de 1,0 % à 11 600 kilomètres en 2025, “le kilométrage annuel moyen, qui avait fortement reculé en 2020 au cœur de la pandémie de Covid-19 (-18,4 %), reste en 2025 inférieur de 7,3 % au niveau observé en 2019, avant la crise, et s’inscrit dans la tendance baissière observée depuis plusieurs années (-10,0 % depuis 2011)”. Une tendance qui devrait se confirmer pour l’année 2026, notamment à cause de la hausse des prix de l’essence.

articles.title: Amazon anuncia os novos Echo Dot, Echo Time e Echo Studio; veja preços • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Amazon anuncia os novos Echo Dot, Echo Time e Echo Studio; veja preços
Amazon Echo Time é destaque por funcionar como um despertador inteligente. Todos foram anunciados para o mercado brasileiro.
A Amazon atualizou a linha Echo com três dispositivos. Estamos falando dos novos Echo Dot, Echo Time e Echo Studio com Câmera. Todos são compatíveis com a Alexa, obviamente, sendo também capazes de funcionar com a Alexa+.
As novidades foram anunciadas para vários países, incluindo o Brasil. Por aqui, os preços começam em R$ 819.
O Echo Dot continua sendo um alto-falante portátil e com corpo arredondado. Mas, agora, o gadget pode funcionar como um “hub de casa inteligente”, que não depende de um aparelho externo para gerenciar outros dispositivos inteligentes do lar. Para quem prioriza o aspecto sonoro, a novidade está na acústica aprimorada para permitir que o alto-falante reproduza graves 50% mais intensos.
O Echo Time não é uma atualização, mas um dispositivo novo. Na primeira olhada, ele remete a um Echo Dot, só que com tela. A sua principal função é atuar como um despertador inteligente. Nesse sentido, o destaque fica para a tecnologia Omnisense, que monitora parâmetros específicos para despertar o usuário em momentos de sono leve. A tela fica mais escura à noite e aumenta o brilho gradualmente conforme o nascer do Sol.
O Echo Studio já existia, mas, agora, traz câmera integrada, como o nome deixa claro. O componente tem sensor de 13 megapixels e traz o recurso Visão Inteligente, que “permite que a Alexa+ veja e entenda o que está à sua frente e ajude em tempo real”, segundo a Amazon. Outro destaque é a função Live View (Vídeo ao Vivo), que monitora a casa na sua ausência. Quanto ao aspecto sonoro, um dos atributos é a tecnologia Áudio Espacial Imersivo.
No Brasil, o novo Echo Dot e o Echo Time já estão em pré-venda no site da Amazon, embora o lançamento oficial esteja previsto somente para 11 de novembro de 2026. Já o Echo Studio com Câmera chegará “em breve”, de acordo com a companhia.

articles.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
articles.text:
It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year. Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon, Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon. This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.
Gemini 4 Carbon reportedly makes big gains in cybersecurity applications. Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon. Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models. Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena, now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts. Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon. The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it. Its new model also beats GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1 in almost every test. Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests. The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.

articles.title: Milliarden für KI, enttäuschende Umsätze: Alphabet gerät unter Druck
articles.text:
Milliarden für KI, enttäuschende Umsätze: Alphabet gerät unter Druck
Die Google-Mutter Alphabet hat im dritten Quartal ihren Umsatz zweistellig gesteigert, enttäuschte aber trotzdem die Erwartungen der Anleger. Der Umsatz kletterte um 25 Prozent auf 127,6 Milliarden Dollar, blieb jedoch hinter den Prognosen der Analysten zurück.
Besonders die Werbeeinnahmen aus der Suchmaschine und verwandten Bereichen, die etwa die Hälfte des Gesamtumsatzes ausmachen, enttäuschten. Sie stiegen um zwölf Prozent auf 63,4 Milliarden Dollar, während Analysten mit rund 65 Milliarden gerechnet hatten. Auch die Werbeeinnahmen von YouTube lagen mit 11,2 Milliarden Dollar unter den Erwartungen.
Hohe KI-Investitionen belasten
Alphabet integriert immer mehr KI-Funktionen in Produkte wie die Suchmaschine, YouTube und Gmail. Doch diese Neuerungen schlagen sich bislang nicht in höheren Umsätzen nieder, die die hohen Investitionen rechtfertigen könnten. Laut Bloomberg erklärte Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler in einer Telefonkonferenz, dass der KI-Modus in der Google-Suche die Ergebnisse aktuell sogar belastet, weil die Suchanfragen bisher weniger Möglichkeiten zur Monetarisierung bieten.
Getragen wird das Geschäft vor allem von der Cloud-Sparte, deren Umsatz um 103 Prozent auf 30,7 Milliarden Dollar stieg und damit die Prognosen von rund 29 Milliarden übertraf.
Zum zweiten Mal in Folge verzeichnete Alphabet einen negativen freien Cashflow. Die Barmittel nach Abzug der Investitionen sanken auf minus 9,1 Milliarden Dollar. Gleichzeitig steigen die Kosten für den KI-Ausbau. Im vergangenen Quartal flossen 51,4 Milliarden Dollar in Rechenzentren und andere Ressourcen. Für das Gesamtjahr plant Alphabet sogar Investitionen von bis zu 205 Milliarden Dollar, um die Rechenleistung für KI-Anwendungen von Kunden und Mitarbeitern abzusichern.
Der bereinigte Gewinn lag bei 26,2 Milliarden Dollar, was 2,12 Dollar je Aktie entspricht – deutlich weniger als die 2,87 Dollar im Vorjahr. Zudem belastete ein Bewertungsverlust von 8,7 Milliarden Dollar auf Beteiligungen, vor allem an Elon Musks Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX, das Ergebnis. Im Vorquartal hatten Buchgewinne aus SpaceX und Anthropic das Ergebnis noch nach oben verzerrt.
Microsoft überzeugt
Die schwachen Alphabet-Zahlen schüren die Sorge, dass KI-getriebene Tech-Konzerne ihre hohen Investitionen nicht in entsprechende Gewinne ummünzen können. Die Aktie verlor nachbörslich 9,97 Prozent und fiel auf 292,50 US-Dollar.
Auch Banken reagieren offenbar vorsichtiger. Laut dem „Wall Street Journal“ musste Broadcom trotz zugesicherter Sicherheiten höhere Zinsen akzeptieren, um Anthropic noch vor der Vorlage der IPO-Unterlagen eine Chip-Finanzierung über 63 Milliarden Dollar zu ermöglichen.
Andere Tech-Unternehmen stehen bei der Veröffentlichung ihrer Zahlen ebenfalls unter Beobachtung. Einen Lichtblick lieferte gerade Microsoft: Der Konzern übertraf die Erwartungen bei Umsatz und Gewinn: der Quartalsumsatz stieg um 19 Prozent auf 92,3 Milliarden Dollar, der operative Gewinn legte um 20 Prozent auf 45,9 Milliarden Dollar zu. Wachstumstreiber war die Cloud-Sparte Azure, die um 48 Prozent auf 33,17 Milliarden Dollar zulegte.

articles.title: Adobe, Veeam, Juniper Networks Patch Critical Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Adobe, Veeam, and Juniper Networks have released patches for over three dozen vulnerabilities across their products, including multiple critical-severity code execution flaws.
This week, Adobe fixed 12 vulnerabilities in Campaign Classic, Connect, Creative Cloud, and Substance 3D Painter.
The Campaign Classic update resolves eight critical-severity bugs, including code/command injection, incorrect authorization, and XSS issues.
Successful exploitation could lead to arbitrary code execution, security feature bypass, and privilege escalation, Adobe warns in a priority 2 advisory.
Another critical-severity defect leading to arbitrary code execution was addressed in Adobe Connect for desktop and mobile.
The security updates for Creative Cloud and Substance 3D Painter resolve high- and medium-severity security holes leading to code execution, privilege escalation, and memory leaks.
Adobe says it is not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.
Veeam rolled out fixes for nine security defects in Backup for Microsoft 365, Backup & Replication, Veeam ONE, and Veeam Agent for Linux.
In Backup for Microsoft 365, Veeam fixed four flaws, including a critical issue that could have allowed attackers to read/write configuration data cross-tenant and achieve remote code execution.
It also resolved a critical-severity bug in Backup & Replication that could have allowed unauthenticated attackers to bypass authorization.
Veeam’s updates also resolved high- and medium-severity weaknesses leading to REST API authentication bypass, arbitrary file read or write, local privilege escalation, and multi-factor authentication bypass.
The company makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild.
Juniper Networks patched 18 vulnerabilities in Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor, including two critical-severity flaws leading to unauthenticated arbitrary command execution and privilege escalation.
High-severity flaws leading to arbitrary file read/write/deletion, code execution, privilege escalation, command execution, information disclosure, and denial-of-service (DoS) were also resolved.
Juniper Networks discovered the bugs internally and is not aware of any of them being exploited in the wild.
In a separate advisory covering the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, the company noted that CVE-2026-109618 affects Junos OS, but not in an exploitable way. It also investigated roughly a dozen other products and found none to be vulnerable.

articles.title: AI Raises The Bar For Tomorrow’s Engineers
articles.text:
Universities are redesigning curricula and assessments around judgment, validation, and technical depth.
Key Takeaways:
Today’s science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) students will be entering the workforce at a pivotal moment. They grew up on iPads, attended high school classes on Zoom during the COVID pandemic, and are navigating college amid an AI revolution. Now, with generative and agentic tools able to accelerate many tasks, a burning question remains: How can universities adapt to this new era and help students harness AI’s advantages without weakening the foundational knowledge and judgment they will need as engineers?
Academic institutions are working to help students get the most out of AI tools while ensuring the next generation of engineers doesn’t cut corners on foundational knowledge. One trend is universities placing greater emphasis on critical-thinking tasks so students don’t swallow GenAI slop in totality. Just as large language models need guardrails, universities are developing tests and quizzes to ensure students learn properly and to minimize cheating. [See Table of University Approaches below.]
“We are seeing people who skate through or miss something fundamental that was important for a particular job, and they have to go back and relearn it,” said Alexandra Werth, assistant professor in biomedical engineering at Cornell University. “Higher ed is in trouble if we don’t work hard to make sure that doesn’t happen. I just went to an American Society of Engineering Education conference, where there were thousands of engineering educators, and this was what everyone wanted to talk about and figure out because this is what makes education relevant. People are trying a lot of different things, and we’re still in a weird place where AI technology is constantly changing. Saying, ‘This is the right approach,’ or ‘This is the wrong approach,’ is still in flux.”
Students are adopting AI tools faster than industry and academia can determine the right balance. “Everybody’s kind of struggling with it, to be honest,” said Matthew Ozalas, master application development engineer, scientist at Keysight. “I’ve talked to professors and heard a lot of different perspectives across the gamut. Some professors are saying, ‘No technology in my class — just blue books back to the old days.’ Others say, ‘Use whatever you want, but you have a time limit.’ I’ve been really impressed with how AI-savvy young people are. At the same time, there’s this idea about how much they need to know in the engineering field. People have asked, ‘Do they even need to know everything anymore? Can’t they just ask their large language model?'”
That means validation of AI responses is key. “The biggest shift we’re seeing is that next-generation engineers need to be good at defining problems, providing the right context to AI, validating its output, and understanding tradeoffs,” said William Wang, founder and CEO of ChipAgents. “Engineering judgment has become even more important, not less, because engineers are now responsible for validating AI-generated work, recognizing incorrect assumptions, and knowing when deeper investigation is required.”
That uncertainty only raises the stakes for mastering the fundamentals, especially when AI can produce answers that sound convincing but are wrong. “From an industry perspective, it is strongly recommended that universities should teach students how to combine fundamentals with AI-assisted workflows,” said Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at Arteris. “Specify the problem clearly, generate alternatives, validate assumptions, test results, and document decisions. The graduates who will stand out are not those who use AI, but those who can use it safely, critically, and productively.”
Students also must be able to defend their findings orally, without AI help. “Graduates need soft skills tailored for a generation who have grown up on screens,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “In industry, engineers have to explain their reasoning on the spot — in design reviews, with customers, and when something goes wrong. Clear, confident verbal communication matters more in the AI era because it shows thinking that AI can’t produce for you. Universities should make it a deliberate part of the curriculum.”
In short, students still need the knowledge and judgment to evaluate what an LLM tells them.
Experience makes the risks clear. “If you work with AI and you’re experienced, you can see how confidently it gives you completely wrong answers or will hallucinate its way through,” said Ozalas. “It’s the balancing act that we have to strike. I can imagine it’s really hard right now to be a student or a young person trying to get into this.”
One professor, who spoke on condition he not be named, pointed to a potentially more disturbing issue. “AI is a resource that has been helping facilitate student research and learning over the past several years,” he said. “However, over this period, I have observed an overall decline in student retention and performance in the same type of curriculum, suggesting that the benefits of AI may be outweighed by increased reliance on this tool. The overall trend has appeared to be that students are having decreasing attention spans as AI becomes more integrated into education and knowledge transfer.”
Another professor, speaking on condition of anonymity, declined to discuss students’ use of AI. Her reason: “Because then I’ll be bitter.”
Universities must address such concerns. “It is essential for university curricula to target GenAI weaknesses,” said Tamara Popovic, educational developer for IT and electrical engineering at ETH Zurich. “One of the biggest challenges we face is what’s called the illusion of competence. When a student prompts an LLM to explain a concept like heterojunction formation, the tool generates a beautifully structured, highly confident response. The student reads it, feels an immediate sense of clarity, and mistakes that passive clarity for actual mastery. They skip the difficult mental strain required to truly internalize the physics behind the phenomena. To break that illusion of competence, we started to design learning activities that target the specific cognitive blind spots of GenAI, namely, complex spatial relationships and non-standard visual abstractions.”
For example, the university introduced exercises based on multi-variable graphic shifting. “We present a standard plot, like a MOSFET C-V curve, but introduce a unique physical anomaly,” said Popovic. “Text-based LLMs, for now, cannot accurately map these multi-layered physical transformations onto new visual representations without making fatal logical leaps. Forcing students to navigate these visual-spatial shifts ensures they are relying on their own internal mental models rather than an external algorithm.”
If AI can mimic understanding, universities must decide how to teach the real thing.
Developing curricula in the AI era
Universities are figuring out how to allow AI tools while preserving academic rigor and integrity.
“Faculty is uncomfortable,” said Stanley Chan, professor of electrical and computer engineering and director of engineering AI education at Purdue University. “It’s the first time that we are navigating this path, and I tell administration and faculty members that we don’t have a crystal ball.”
The Purdue board recently approved a plan to integrate more AI into each successive year of a four-year degree. “We have to make the transformation because otherwise we will be outpaced by AI,” said Chan. “It’s a matter of time that higher education will be fundamentally reshaped because a new technology is here.”
To avoid loss of learning, professors have to ask students tough questions, and students need to learn how to ask AI tough questions, noted Chan. “Why are you doing this? Can you give me the evidence? Can you show me that this is working? Have you considered other design options? Why is this design done in this way, and have you thought about approaching the problem in another way? Maybe you should think about the other direction.”
Syllabi also need to strike the right balance. “There is that question of how to even write a good syllabus nowadays,” said David Janes, professor of electrical and computer engineering and the director of the semiconductor degrees program at Purdue. “In your syllabus you need to define what is and is not appropriate use of AI, and the answer is usually that you can’t use AI. If you use AI, you are still responsible for verifying and checking it. You are responsible for independently learning and understanding these concepts.”
Fig. 1: A student and professor working in Purdue University’s Birck Nanotechnology Center. Source: Purdue
Given this complex semiconductor work, AI fluency must be grounded in engineering fundamentals, whether students are tackling network-on-chip congestion or semiconductor test.
“AI can propose a fabric configuration in seconds, but knowing whether it will hold up under real traffic patterns, achieve physical implementation, and survive routing and other tradeoffs requires that underlying domain depth,” noted Nandan Nayampally, chief commercial officer at Baya Systems. “That combination — AI plus real expertise — is where you get the actual productivity boost, not from AI alone. Without the fundamentals to validate it, AI-driven design accelerates disasters as fast as it accelerates progress.”
For semiconductor testing, students need deep, domain-specific knowledge that takes time to develop, observed Ryan Moran, head of talent acquisition at the Center of Excellence at Teradyne. “Universities that treat AI literacy as complementary to rigorous foundational training are producing the graduates we most want to hire. The more forward-thinking programs are redesigning assignments so that AI tool use is assumed. New graduates who arrive having used tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or similar assistants can produce working code drafts faster than earlier cohorts. The challenge is to maintain technical knowledge to both understand and verify what the code actually does.”
Foundational skills and deep disciplines such as physics and mathematics bring many job opportunities. “You can go very deep in linear algebra or calculus,” said Pradheepa Raman, chief people officer at GlobalFoundries. “If you go into the linear algebra side, you become a data scientist or AI engineer. If you go into the calculus side, you can become a quant in financial institutions. These old types of deep skills are in many curricula to help students become deep experts. I would prioritize that first because it’s hard for companies to teach students unless you have the basics.”
Ideally, graduates will know both science and AI. “The strongest candidates are those who know how to use AI as a productivity tool while also demonstrating solid engineering judgment, a problem-solving mindset, and a strong grasp of first principles,” said Gabriela Cruz Thompson, director of university research collaboration at Intel. “In other words, we are not looking for graduates who simply know how to prompt an AI model. We’re looking for graduates who understand the underlying science and engineering well enough to know when an AI-generated answer is correct, incomplete, or wrong.”
Producing those graduates requires assessments that reveal genuine understanding, not merely polished AI output.
AI-proof assessments
While students can enter prompts for just about anything, from emails and job applications all the way to semiconductor designs, the most valuable new skill is not prompt writing by itself. “It is the ability to use AI as an engineering assistant while maintaining technical ownership of the result,” Arteris’ Nightingale said. “The challenge for universities is to move beyond policing AI use and toward teaching responsible, verifiable engineering with AI in the loop.”
However, no universal silver bullet can prevent students from using AI to cheat. Assessments must be AI-proof, and professors need teaching assistants to help them adapt the curriculum course by course, Purdue’s Chan noted. “We need to ask the question, ‘Can AI solve all the homework problems by itself?’ If the answer is yes, then the class itself has to be rethought. Otherwise, no matter how many countermeasures you put in, it’s going to be ineffective.”
That need for course-by-course redesign is widely shared. “AI can now answer most of the questions we used to set in exams and coursework, and universities are under pressure to make assessments AI-proof,” said Axiomise’s Darbari. “That isn’t only an assessment problem. It changes how students learn and what they are equipped with when they graduate. The risk is that we produce graduates who can get answers but can’t stand behind them.”
At the same time, students must still memorize some math and physics. “Some of the higher-level concepts they have to learn by heart,” said Chan. “We still want to keep some of the paper and pencil exams so that when they go to the design stage, they will know what questions to ask. That cannot come in a day.”
Creative assessments are also key, and some faculty hold in-class competitions. “There is an engineering design goal such as building a robot, and then there are targets, and you see who performs better,” he said. “You cannot cheat by just using AI. The robot has to physically run on the road.”
Students lose out if they take shortcuts. “At the Bachelor level, mastering a course such as semiconductor devices requires a massive amount of mental effort,” said ETH Zurich’s Popovic. “When students use generative AI as a cognitive shortcut, they bypass the very struggle that builds deep engineering intuition.”
Students using AI to cheat is not viewed differently from students copying others’ code or written work. Purdue has used plagiarism checkers on graduate theses for quite some time to ensure students write their own work and cite appropriate sources, Purdue’s Janes says. “It’s a very parallel thing with AI, though we would go about it differently if it’s an engineering analysis than writing. We all struggle with the same problem.”
Physics cannot be traded for AI. “When engineers don’t know physics, they don’t know reality,” Keysight’s Ozalas said. “It’s the same with coding. If you don’t know coding and you just prompt everything, you lose the connection with the real world, and that’s a concern.”
Ultimately, traditional tests may still be best for fundamental knowledge. “Then provide more workshops, more projects, more labs, but definitely allow them to use the AI tools,” said GF’s Raman. “If you don’t, it’s like saying, ‘Hey, I have all these tools, but I want you to go the traditional way even though it will take enormous time.’ Time is also of the essence. They can learn more if they are allowed to use the tools.”
All the company’s summer interns had access to AI tools, Raman noted. “They were amazing using these tokens. They were happy to get access and build things. It was awesome to see.”
Given the direction the industry is heading, denying students access to AI tools is pointless, even though the industry still hasn’t decided on the best approach to manage access. “From the AI perspective, you do need to build AI,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Everything will have AI built in as a technology eventually, so you need AI security specialists to make sure that they build secure solutions for AI. AI tools might change the job landscape, but I don’t think positions will go away. It’s just that they’re going to change in their nature. To keep up with the technology, you’ll have to use AI tools and rely on AI assistance. I’ve heard from academia that there is a need for having specialized skill sets.” However, she added that the exact nature of these skills is still evolving.
This also means students need both hard knowledge and soft communication skills. “The graduates who do well in the AI era will be the ones who can use the tools, defend their reasoning, and communicate it clearly in the moment,” said Darbari. “Universities that build all of that into their curriculum will produce the engineers the semiconductor industry most needs.”
Darbari’s tips for universities:
The pace and depth of change in university curricula vary considerably across institutions. Both academia and industry benefit from open discussions about navigating the AI era.
| University | Directive | Hard skills | Soft skills | Innovations | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cornell | Each discipline needs to wrestle with what AI literacy means to them. | Math; mathematical graphical intuition; programming; prompting; weigh up pros/cons of various AI algos (see biomedical examples). | Critical thinking; professional behavior; how to email and find contacts; human networking to get past AI bots on resumes; lifelong learning skills. | Completely oral exams; small quizzes in class; flipping the class with recorded lectures and in-person workshops. | 
| ETH Zurich | Does not integrate AI into its formal degree curriculum; focuses on building a profound physical understanding of underlying phenomena, preserving the integrity of the learning process. | Understand abstract concepts such as carrier transport and quantum tunnelling taught in physics courses; connect concepts to real-world electronic devices. | Critical evaluation; treat AI not as an authority, but as a flawed draft that requires expert auditing. | Classroom activities where they flip the script by providing students with AI-generated solutions to complex problems, then task them with identifying structural flaws, false assumptions, and hallucinations in the text. | 
| Georgia Tech | Per its AI policy and guidance, encourages responsible, ethical use of AI to support teaching and learning; instructors encouraged to establish clear expectations for AI use and help students develop skills to use AI responsibly, ethically, and effectively. | Strong engineering fundamentals and AI competency; focus on defining problems; evaluating and validating AI-generated results; integrating information from multiple sources; how to use AI tools effectively; when to trust AI vs. when to question outputs. | Deeper learning, critical thinking, and responsible AI use; accountability for own understanding and work; exercise sound engineering judgment; communicate and collaborate effectively across multidisciplinary teams; critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and professional judgment central to engineering practice. | In the school of ECE, developed SMART Tutor, a course-specific AI tutor that combines RAG with principles of self-regulated learning; guides students through the problem-solving process; encourages them to develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills. | 
| Purdue | Every graduate will need to have AI competency; each college and department determines what that means; each year to have progressively more AI integration; students must get the fundamentals right, per industry stakeholders. | Physics, math; fundamentals of AI technology; statistical thinking, probabilistic reasoning to make sense of data; algorithmic reasoning; programming; data analysis; Python for data science class to look at data and programming together; verification. | Human perspectives, creativity, originality, and ability to make judgment; understanding how AI works and what it can and can’t do; utilizing AI in projects; how to be a manager of AI; building intuition and knowledge to keep moving forward without AI doing everything for them. | Launched summer bootcamp for graduating class, including how to do an interview in the AI era according to recent grads; how to prepare a portfolio or resume; 4+1 program for extra training; semiconductor degrees program, advised by a 40- member semiconductor degrees leadership board; semiconductor career fair. |

articles.title: Virgin Galactic Apeiron : le nouveau vaisseau coûte 750 000 dollars, mais va-t-il dans l'espace ?
articles.text:
Vous vous souvenez de Virgin Galactic, la société de tourisme spatial lancée par Richard Branson en 2004 ? Ses clients n’ont plus volé depuis le 8 juin 2024 et la retraite de son avion-fusée VSS Unity. L’engin a toutefois repris l’air le 27 mai 2026, pour des vols planés destinés à entraîner les pilotes de la prochaine génération d’appareils.
L’entreprise a présenté le successeur du VSS Unity ce mercredi 28 octobre. Son nom ? Apeiron. Il s’agit d’un terme provenant du grec ancien, qui signifie « sans limites », et qui a été retenu à la suite d’un vote ouvert au public. Le même jour, l’avion-fusée a bouclé son premier trajet, qui consistait à quitter son usine pour rejoindre sa base.
On parle bien ici de trajet et non de vol. En effet, l’Apeiron a voyagé en tant que passager, accroché sous Eve, l’avion porteur de la société. C’était un voyage relativement court, puisqu’à peine 450 kilomètres séparent l’usine de Mesa (Arizona) et Spaceport America (Nouveau-Mexique). Virgin Galactic a partagé plusieurs contenus liés à ce déplacement sur X.
Pas d’emballement pour autant : avant d’embarquer le moindre client, Virgin Galactic doit encore valider le logiciel d’avionique, c’est-à-dire l’électronique de pilotage, puis boucler ses essais en vol.
L’entreprise vise désormais un premier vol commercial au début du deuxième trimestre 2027. Le second vaisseau doit suivre fin du deuxième trimestre ou début du troisième. Ce calendrier a déjà glissé deux fois : au printemps, Virgin Galactic visait encore le quatrième trimestre 2026, puis elle a repoussé ses débuts à février 2027 en août.
Spatial, selon la définition américaine
Les guillemets du titre ont leur raison d’être : comme Unity, Apeiron est largué en altitude par Eve, puis allume son moteur-fusée pour un saut suborbital de quelques minutes, sans jamais se mettre en orbite. Lors de son dernier vol propulsé, le 8 juin 2024, Unity a culminé à 87,5 kilomètres d’altitude.
Cette altitude dépasse le seuil de 80 kilomètres retenu par la FAA, l’aviation civile américaine, et par Virgin Galactic, pour dire que le vaisseau est « entré » dans l’espace. En revanche, elle reste sous la ligne de Kármán, placée à 100 kilomètres, la référence mondiale qu’utilise aussi Blue Origin, le concurrent fondé par Jeff Bezos.
Hé oui, selon la définition retenue pour déterminer le « début » de l’espace, les passagers d’Unity sont allés dans l’espace… ou pas.
Ce n’est pas un sujet tout à fait anodin, surtout lorsque le billet s’est vendu 750 000 dollars (environ 670 000 euros) à la réouverture des ventes en avril 2026, contre 600 000 dollars (environ 535 000 euros) auparavant. Cela étant, les 50 places de cette vague sont toutes parties, et Virgin Galactic a annoncé en août que la suivante serait plus chère.
Ces 10 à 20 kilomètres manquants n’ont donc pas refroidi les acheteurs. Il faut dire qu’ils n’ont guère d’autre choix : Blue Origin, dont la capsule New Shepard dépasse bien les 100 kilomètres, a suspendu ses vols touristiques fin janvier 2026, pour au moins deux ans.

articles.title: Poussé par l'IA, Fujifilm va multiplier par cinq sa production... de bandes magnétiques
articles.text:
On les croyait reléguées aux archives de l’informatique. Pourtant, les bandes magnétiques connaissent un regain d’intérêt spectaculaire grâce à l’intelligence artificielle. Au point que Fujifilm prévoit d’investir 57 millions d’euros pour multiplier par cinq ses capacités de production d’ici à 2028.
Qui aurait imaginé que l’intelligence artificielle, avec ses GPU surpuissants et ses centres de données dernier cri, remettrait au goût du jour les bonnes vieilles bandes magnétiques ? C’est pourtant ce qui se passe chez Fujifilm, qui s’apprête à réaliser son plus gros investissement dans cette technologie depuis une vingtaine d'années.
Selon le quotidien économique japonais Nikkei, le groupe prévoit de consacrer 10 milliards de yens, soit environ 57 millions d’euros, à l’agrandissement de son usine d’Odawara, près de Tokyo. L’objectif est de multiplier par cinq sa capacité de production par rapport à l’exercice 2025, mesurée en volume de données stockables, d’ici à l’exercice 2028.
Des cartouches capables de stocker jusqu’à 100 To
Fujifilm n’a jamais vraiment abandonné les bandes magnétiques. Engagé dans la recherche sur les bandes magnétiques depuis 1954, le fabricant japonais a simplement vu leur utilisation évoluer, des enregistrements audiovisuels vers la sauvegarde et l’archivage professionnels.
Aujourd'hui, ses cartouches LTO-10 peuvent contenir 40 To de données sans compression, et jusqu’à 100 To avec compression (2,5:1, selon la nature des données stockées). Une capacité considérable pour un support aussi compact, qui trouve naturellement sa place dans les gigantesques infrastructures informatiques.
Car si l’IA a besoin de mémoire vive et de SSD rapides pour fonctionner, elle génère et exploite également d’immenses quantités de données qu’il faut conserver pendant des années. Et toutes ne nécessitent pas d’être accessibles instantanément.
Pourquoi la bande magnétique peut battre les disques durs
Les bandes magnétiques conservent un avantage de poids face aux supports de stockage modernes : leur coût. Selon Nikkei, conserver des données sur bande peut revenir jusqu’à quatre fois moins cher que sur disque dur, dans certaines configurations d'archivage.
Elles consomment également très peu d’électricité une fois stockées, puisqu’une cartouche n’a pas besoin de rester alimentée. Mieux encore, elle peut être retirée de son lecteur et conservée hors réseau, ce qui offre une protection supplémentaire contre les ransomwares.
Le revers est connu. Contrairement aux SSD ou aux disques durs, la bande magnétique impose un accès séquentiel aux données. Retrouver un fichier précis peut donc prendre beaucoup plus de temps. Mais pour les données rarement consultées, les fameuses cold data, cet inconvénient pèse finalement assez peu face aux économies réalisées.
Fujifilm n’est pas le seul à profiter de cet appétit pour les données. Kioxia et Sandisk prévoient également d’investir massivement dans la mémoire flash, alors que Toshiba cherche à augmenter sa production de disques durs, tout comme Seagate et Western Digital qui planchent sur la densité des plateaux de leurs HDD. Avec la gourmandise de l’IA en mémoire et capacité de stockage, il n’y a plus de petites économies…
Source : Nikkei via Computerbase

articles.title: MediaMarkt liquida hoy consolas portátiles (con unidades limitadas) en su outlet: PS Portal y Nintendo Switch, a precios top
articles.text:
En apenas unos días entramos en noviembre, el mes con las mejores ofertas del año gracias a campañas de rebajas tan potentes como el 11 del 11, el Black Friday o el Cyber Monday. Una ocasión perfecta para comprar, por ejemplo, alguna de las actuales consolas portátiles a los precios más bajos posibles. Algo más crítico en 2026, un año en el que no dejamos de ver subidas y más subidas de PVP.
Sin embargo, no hace falta que esperemos a entonces para conseguir buenos precios en consolas Nintendo Switch, Switch Lite o PS Portal: el outlet de MediaMarkt está liquidando hoy unas pocas unidades de todas ellas y las tiene desde 173,40 euros.
Ofertas ideales para adelantar algunas compras navideñas
MediaMarkt también vende en su popular outlet de eBay, además de en sus tiendas físicas y online. Un lugar donde pone a la venta, habitualmente, dispositivos que provienen de exposición o devoluciones. Pero a veces, también aparece algún chollo en estado nuevo y a estrenar. En todos los casos, con precios muy buenos. Y, eso sí, con pocas unidades disponibles.
Ahora, como decimos, el outlet de MediaMarkt tiene rebajadas varias consolas portátiles de Nintendo y Sony en diferentes estados:
- Nintendo Switch por 173,40 euros, en estado "usado"
- Nintendo Switch Lite por 182,15 euros, en estado "de exposición"
- PS Portal por 224,90 euros, en estado "nuevo"
Nintendo Switch y Switch Lite siguen siendo dos excelentes videoconsolas portátiles a día de hoy, incluso con Switch 2 en el mercado desde hace algo más de un año, gracias a un enorme catálogo de títulos (algunos tan potentes como 'Zelda Breath of the Wild' o 'Super Mario Odyssey').
PlayStation Portal, por su parte, permite el juego en la nube sin necesidad de contar con una PS5 desde hace algunas actualizaciones (mediante suscripción). Una consola con una genial pantalla 1080p de 8 pulgadas con la que disfrutar de casi 3.000 títulos vía streaming con una genial experiencia.

articles.title: Amazon despidió a unos 250 empleados de su área de dispositivos tras semanas de lanzamientos
articles.text:
Amazon despidió el miércoles 28 de octubre a hasta 250 empleados de su unidad de dispositivos y servicios, la que fabrica los Kindle, las tabletas y los altavoces Echo. Los recortes llegan después de semanas de lanzamientos de productos, según informó la agencia Reuters, y la empresa los confirmó.
Una persona al tanto del asunto dijo a Reuters que los recortes afectaron a no más de 250 puestos, principalmente en desarrollo de software. Amazon no precisó el número ni las áreas.
“Tomamos la difícil decisión de eliminar un pequeño número de puestos”, afirmó un portavoz de la empresa tras la consulta de la agencia. Agregó que los despidos ayudarán a “operar con más eficiencia” y a alinear la estructura con la hoja de ruta de productos.
Como es habitual en Amazon, los trabajadores se enteraron por mensajes de texto y correos electrónicos enviados temprano. Reuters vio uno firmado por Cherie Robinson, vicepresidenta de Recursos Humanos de dispositivos y servicios, que hablaba de una “revisión a fondo de nuestra estructura”.
Un mes de anuncios de hardware
El mismo miércoles, Amazon presentó cinco dispositivos con Alexa, su asistente de voz. El Echo Time es un reloj despertador que cuesta USD 199,99 y, según la empresa, puede despertar al usuario en una fase de sueño ligero, dentro de una ventana de 10 a 60 minutos antes de la hora programada.
El Alexa Photo Frame es un marco digital con pantalla táctil de 10 pulgadas que parte de USD 199,99 y toma las fotos de Amazon Photos. Incluye 90 días de Alexa+, la versión del asistente con inteligencia artificial que Amazon ofrece con la suscripción Prime.
La línea suma un Echo Show 16, una pantalla inteligente de 16 pulgadas con Fire TV integrado, un Echo Dot rediseñado y un Echo Studio con cámara. Según The Verge, Alexa+ está disponible para todos en Estados Unidos desde febrero.
Dos semanas antes, el 8 de octubre, Amazon había presentado tres tabletas Alexa que reemplazan a la línea Fire y permiten descargar aplicaciones de Google Play. La Tablet 8 parte de USD 230, la Tablet 11 de USD 330 y la Tablet 12 Pro cuesta USD 500, según Engadget.
Las tabletas salieron a la venta el 14 de octubre en Estados Unidos, México y Canadá, y el 19 de octubre en varios países de Europa, según TechCrunch.
Engadget registró además nuevos Kindle, equipos de Ring y un Fire TV Stick 4K. Amazon no hizo un evento único, sino presentaciones escalonadas durante semanas. Panos Panay, jefe de dispositivos de Amazon, dijo a Engadget que el año pasado solo dos productos recibieron atención.
Otro recorte de Amazon en 2026
A comienzos de este mes, Amazon ya había eliminado cerca de 1.000 puestos en su división principal de comercio minorista, según Reuters.
Según un comunicado de la compañía, en enero de 2026 Amazon había despedido a 16.000 empleados corporativos en todo el mundo como parte de una reorganización interna iniciada en octubre de 2025. El plan buscaba simplificar la estructura, reducir la burocracia y acelerar la adopción de la inteligencia artificial en sus operaciones.
Esa ronda se sumó a un ajuste previo que había afectado a cerca de 14.000 puestos administrativos y de gestión, con lo cual el plan completo apuntaba a eliminar unos 30.000 empleos corporativos, equivalentes al 10% de la plantilla global. Las áreas más golpeadas fueron AWS, la unidad de computación en la nube, y Prime Video, además de Recursos Humanos y otras funciones centrales. Los recortes no alcanzaron a los trabajadores de centros logísticos ni de almacenes.
El nuevo ajuste de octubre ocurre un día antes de que la compañía publique sus resultados del tercer trimestre, tras el cierre de la bolsa del jueves 29 de octubre.

articles.title: Mistral Large 4 rattrape les meilleures IA chinoises en code, et tout le monde peut le télécharger — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le 6 octobre, Mistral présentait la préversion de Large 4, son grand retour face aux laboratoires chinois. Trois jours plus tard, les tests indépendants la montraient en retrait sur le code et les tâches d’agent. Mistral promettait alors les poids du modèle pour la fin du mois : ils sont publiés ce jeudi 29 octobre.
Ce qu’on peut télécharger
Depuis ce jeudi, les poids de Large 4 sont publiés sur Hugging Face, la plateforme de partage de modèles que Nvidia a annoncé racheter en septembre. Les poids, c’est le modèle lui-même, que chacun peut récupérer et faire tourner sur sa propre infrastructure. Une version quantifiée, compressée pour réduire la mémoire nécessaire, est publiée en même temps.
Le modèle, que Mistral surnomme « Chonk », compte 1 000 milliards de paramètres au total. Comme la plupart des grands modèles actuels, il n’en active qu’une partie pour chaque mot généré : 52 milliards. Il est multimodal : il comprend les images qu’on lui soumet, mais ne répond qu’en texte et en code.
Ce qui a changé en trois semaines
Le progrès le plus net porte sur le code agentique : l’IA n’écrit pas seulement du code, elle enchaîne seule des commandes dans un terminal pour mener une tâche à bout. Sur Terminal-Bench 4.0, le test de référence de cet exercice, Large 4 passe de 28 % pour la préversion à 41 %, selon les graphiques présentés à la presse.
GLM-5.3, le meilleur modèle ouvert chinois du graphique, est à 40 %, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash à 31 % et Kimi K3 à 21 %. Mistral en tire deux titres : premier modèle ouvert au monde en code agentique sur l’indice d’Artificial Analysis, et meilleur modèle ouvert conçu en Occident.
L’autre progrès porte sur la sobriété. Selon Mistral, Large 4 consomme 47 % de jetons en moins par tâche que GLM-5.3 sur l’indice de code agentique, et 50 % de moins que la préversion sur Terminal-Bench. Or une IA se facture au jeton. Le 9 octobre, Artificial Analysis relevait justement que la préversion était particulièrement bavarde : 200 millions de jetons consommés sur ses tests, contre une médiane de 81 millions.
Mistral a aussi ajouté deux modes de raisonnement plus courts, « low » et « medium », au mode « high », à la demande des entreprises qui ont testé le modèle, pour choisir combien de temps il réfléchit avant de répondre. Le mode « high » consomme désormais 50 % de jetons en moins.
Ce qui s’est passé en coulisses
Comment progresser autant en trois semaines ? Par l’apprentissage par renforcement, la dernière étape de l’entraînement. Mistral soumet au modèle des problèmes de code et de cybersécurité générés en interne, de plus en plus difficiles, le récompense quand il trouve la solution et le pénalise quand il échoue.
Mistral compare l’exercice à celui d’un étudiant à qui l’on donnerait des examens « de plus en plus durs ». Cette phase s’est déroulée sur les serveurs de Mistral en France, avec « seulement 10 mégawatts ». Dans le communiqué, l’entreprise assure que les gains se poursuivent « sans signe de saturation » pour le moment.
Mistral insiste sur la modestie de ses moyens. Le modèle a été entraîné sur 3 800 GPU Nvidia Grace Blackwell, dans les centres de données européens de l’entreprise. Cette puissance de calcul a été financée par la série B de Mistral. Les 3 milliards d’euros levés en septembre serviront surtout à acheter de nouveaux serveurs.
« D’autres laboratoires ont levé des centaines de milliards pour développer des capacités équivalentes ; en trois ans, Mistral a levé environ 6 milliards de dollars », précise Arthur Mensch, PDG et cofondateur.
La cybersécurité comme argument de vente
Mistral met en avant un second domaine : la cyberdéfense. Sur CyberGym-E2E, un test qui consiste à reproduire une vraie faille dans un logiciel libre, puis à la corriger, Large 4 obtient 79 %, à égalité avec MiMo-V2.6-Pro de Xiaomi. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash est à 76 %, Kimi K3 à 58 %.
Corentin Petit, vice-président chargé des solutions, dont les équipes déploient les modèles chez les clients, vend un outil de cyberdéfense installé sur place, « que personne ne peut couper » contrairement aux modèles fermés. Il cite des entreprises qui automatisent déjà les tests d’intrusion ou la recherche de failles dans leur code. Selon le communiqué, des partenaires spécialisés en cybersécurité ont testé le modèle avant sa publication.
Sur ce test, Claude Opus 5.5 d’Anthropic et GPT-6 Astra d’OpenAI obtiennent un score proche de zéro, parce qu’ils refusent la tâche. L’écart avec les modèles américains reflète donc en partie leurs garde-fous. Quels garde-fous équipent les poids publiés par Mistral ? Pendant le briefing, Pierre Stock a seulement affirmé que le modèle avait été entraîné avec des garde-fous « dès le départ », sans les détailler.
La question se pose d’autant plus que Mistral distinguait deux variantes pendant la préversion : la version ouverte au public était davantage bridée en cybersécurité, tandis qu’une variante moins restreinte, aux fonctions cyber étendues, était réservée à des entreprises de sécurité, des partenaires et des agences gouvernementales sélectionnés jusqu’à la publication des poids.
Où se situe vraiment Large 4
Face aux modèles ouverts chinois, Large 4 fait jeu égal : 41 contre 40 en code avec GLM-5.3, 79 contre 79 en cyber avec MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Le 6 octobre, Guillaume Lample, cofondateur de Mistral, situait la préversion « au niveau des meilleurs Chinois d’il y a un mois ou deux ». Le retard est donc comblé, du moins sur ces deux tests.
Pierre Stock en fait un argument face aux laboratoires chinois : rien ne garantit, selon lui, qu’ils continueront à publier les poids de leurs modèles, alors que Mistral « s’engage » à le faire pour les siens. L’entreprise héberge pourtant elle-même GLM sur ses serveurs depuis septembre.
Face aux modèles fermés américains, l’écart reste grand. Opus 5.5 et GPT-6 Astra se situent entre 59 et 65 % sur Terminal-Bench, selon les mesures d’Artificial Analysis et de Vals.ai relevées le 9 octobre. Ils ne figurent pas sur le graphique de code de Mistral. Et Google a encore relevé la barre ce mercredi avec Gemini 4 Carbon.
Pour placer Large 4 parmi les autres modèles, voir le classement des modèles ouverts de QUELLE IA, son classement en code et la fiche de Large 4, ainsi que notre guide pour lire les benchmarks sans se faire avoir.
Prix, matériel et disponibilité
Installer Large 4 chez soi suppose un serveur de centre de données : il faut quatre GPU Nvidia B200 ou B300 pour faire tourner la version quantifiée, qui pèse environ 690 Go en 4 bits. Les particuliers devront attendre une version plus légère, que Mistral promet d’ici un mois.
Le prix n’a été donné ni pendant le briefing ni dans le communiqué. Pour repère, la préversion était affichée à 1,36 dollar (environ 1,22 euro HT) en entrée et 4,18 dollars (environ 3,75 euros HT) en sortie par million de jetons, avec une remise de 50 % pendant ses deux premières semaines. L’argument de Mistral : à prix égal au jeton avec GLM-5.3, consommer moitié moins de jetons revient moins cher.
Large 4 est disponible sur Hugging Face, par l’API de Mistral et, selon le communiqué, pour « certains utilisateurs » de Vibe, l’assistant de Mistral (ex-Le Chat), dont il devait devenir le modèle par défaut.
Quant aux entreprises qui l’ont testé, Mistral parle de « gouvernements et d’entreprises » sans les nommer, pas plus dans le communiqué que pendant le briefing. L’entreprise cite des usages : transformer un plan en 2D en modèle 3D dans un logiciel de CAO, analyser des documents financiers, ou repérer des feux de forêt sur des images satellite. Le 6 octobre, elle revendiquait plus de 125 grands clients, dont Airbus, ASML et HSBC.
Le même jour, Ecosia annonçait pourtant dans un entretien à Politico abandonner Mistral, cinq mois après l’avoir choisi pour remplacer OpenAI. Son fondateur, Christian Kroll, se disait « déçu de la qualité » et jugeait le laboratoire français en retard d’un an. Le moteur de recherche berlinois utilise désormais des modèles ouverts, dont les chinois Qwen, GLM et Kimi. Ecosia s’appuyait toutefois sur Mistral Small 3.2 et Small 4, des modèles intermédiaires.
Mistral promet désormais d’accélérer : itérer vite sur la même base, pour être « à la cadence de la frontière », selon Pierre Stock. Large 4 ouvre une nouvelle génération de modèles, après Voxtral 3 pour la voix, et d’autres doivent suivre dans les prochains mois. Sur ses propres graphiques, l’entreprise a nettement progressé en trois semaines.

articles.title: Palit says the Galax factory isn't closing, despite a report blaming Nvidia chip shortages
articles.text:
What just happened? For the second time this year, the Galax graphics card brand has been forced to deny that it's in trouble. This time, brand owner Palit confirmed that its Galax factory wasn't closing down due to Nvidia not supplying enough RTX 5000 chips, something that had been rumored.
Palit's official statement says it is aware of recent reports and speculation regarding Galax's business operations. It adds that the brand continues to operate as usual, no manufacturing facilities have been shut down, and Galax products remain available in both domestic and international markets.
The statement also notes that Galax and Palit share the same manufacturing facilities, with production and business operations continuing as normal.
The rumors stemmed from an "exclusive" news report by a Spanish outlet, which claimed industry sources had confirmed Palit was closing the Galax factory as Nvidia couldn't provide enough RTX 5000 chips to keep it running.
 – 포시포시 (@harukaze5719) October 28, 2026
This would have been an especially surprising turn of events, given that Galax launched the GeForce RTX 5080 HOF Extreme - the world's first RTX 5080 with two 16-pin connectors - only last week.
It's easy to understand why people might have believed this report. There have long been rumors that Nvidia is prioritizing the GB202 chip used in the RTX 5090 for the more lucrative RTX Pro Blackwell-based models. It had even been claimed that the flagship was being discontinued, though Nvidia denied it.
Then there's the whole Palit/Galax situation. In April, Galax was rumored to be doing an EVGA and shutting down entirely. However, Palit, which has owned Galax since 2007, confirmed that it was undergoing a restructuring that brought Galax's operations directly under Palit Group headquarters in Taiwan, sparking the rumors.
The company said at the time that it would continue to develop, produce, and support the Galax, KFA2, and HOF brands to strengthen its presence in the discrete GPU market.
Ultimately, the rumor was just another effect of the AI-driven memory chip crisis that has pushed the price of graphics cards to astronomical levels. The RTX 5090, for example, is hard to find for less than $9,000 these days – and we complained when it arrived with a $2,000 MSRP.

articles.title: The Complexity Between The Bits
articles.text:
What biological reasoning can teach us about verifying silicon systems.
By Vidya Chandran Darbari and Ashish Darbari
A recent conversation about carbon intelligence and silicon intelligence stayed with me. What interested me was not which one wins, but the complexity we take on as we ask silicon to sense, interpret, decide and act.
My work as an experimental structural biologist taught me to ask what a structure could explain, and what it could not. Solving a molecular structure was not the same as explaining the behaviour of the system to which it belonged. The next question was always about mechanism: what happens when the parts interact? That question shaped my perspective as a deep generalist in life sciences, connecting molecular mechanisms, biological networks and system behaviour.
Now, as Chief Strategy and Operations Officer at Axiomise, I return to that question in a different setting.
A chip is not a cell. But investigating biological complexity can sharpen how we investigate engineered systems—provided the comparison changes a question we ask, an observation we make or an obligation we verify. Otherwise, it remains an interesting analogy.
In life sciences, a protein interaction map is where questions begin. A connection identifies a possible interaction; it does not establish when that interaction matters. Concentration, localization, binding affinity, feedback and timing influence the outcome.
The same messenger can stimulate or suppress an immune response depending on the receptor and the receiving cell’s state. The molecule has not become inconsistent. Our description was incomplete without its context.
Silicon engineers already understand dependencies. The useful transfer is not simply to think in networks, but to distinguish connectivity from the conditions under which connected components produce a particular behaviour.
A link can transport packets correctly, a controller can enter its power states correctly, and an interconnect can arbitrate correctly under its assumptions. Their combination can still violate a requirement if those assumptions cease to hold.
The engineering consequence is to make context explicit: which neighbouring states, available resources and event orderings does each guarantee depend on? Those conditions belong in verification, not just in integration notes.
Our senses make context tangible. Combining cues helps only when their timing supports treating them as evidence of the same event. More signals do not automatically resolve ambiguity.
Consider an illustrative edge controller combining camera and distance-sensor data. Both measurements could be accurately encoded, transported without corruption and individually plausible. If they describe different moments but are treated as simultaneous, the fused estimate can represent a situation that never existed.
The bits arrive intact while the interpretation is wrong.
The biological perspective directs attention to the signal’s relationship with the state in which it is received. The engineering response is concrete: timestamp association, freshness, allowable skew and missing observations belong in the requirements.
Similar questions arise during reset, link retraining and power transitions. What happens to a transaction accepted before the transition? Which state survives recovery? When can a receiver safely treat new data as valid?
An interface is a relationship over time, not merely a set of wires. Verification must capture that relationship, particularly when the resulting interpretation controls an action.
It is tempting to describe biology as grey and silicon as black and white. That contrast obscures more than it explains.
Biological models can combine continuous quantities, discrete events, deterministic equations and stochastic processes. These are separate distinctions. A graded response need not be random.
A digital block can have a uniquely defined next state for a given state and input while leaving a system question unresolved: which input sequences and environmental behaviours must we consider? Formal verification can examine behaviours admitted by a model under stated assumptions. That is not physical randomness.
Beneath the abstraction sits physics. Metastability is not digital logic becoming analog because an architecture grew complicated. It is physical behaviour the design must accommodate.
The differences matter because a physical measurement, statistical association and logical proof answer different questions. Learning from biology should make us more precise about where uncertainty resides—not less demanding about correctness.
My life-sciences training made me wary of assuming that a symptom identifies its cause.
Consider an illustrative chiplet system, not a customer incident. A transaction times out. A power controller has gated a clock before outstanding traffic drained. It will restore the clock after receiving a wake request, but that request is queued behind the stalled traffic.
Each side waits for the other. The timeout is the symptom; the mechanism is a circular dependency. Extending the timeout would not remove it.
Other mechanisms could produce the same symptom: a lost credit, inconsistent reset state or starvation. Reproducing a trace does not distinguish those explanations.
Here, experimental reasoning suggests a useful question: which intervention would separate the hypotheses? What happens if the clock remains running? What if wake delivery is independent of normal traffic? Does the failure persist when downstream service changes?
These are familiar verification activities. Their explanatory purpose matters: choose an investigation because its outcome challenges a mechanism, not merely because it produces another passing run.
A counterexample also needs interpretation. It may expose a defect, an unrealistic environment or behaviour introduced by abstraction. A passing result needs equal scrutiny: did the assumptions exclude the situation we needed to examine?
Life sciences investigates activity at different levels: genome sequence, gene expression, protein machinery and metabolism. These measurements are not interchangeable. Discrepancies can reveal regulation, compensation or an incomplete explanation.
There is no exact mapping from these layers to a chip. The transferable principle is to connect evidence across levels rather than expect one measurement to explain everything.
RTL and configuration describe one view. Workload activity, transaction traces and physical telemetry provide others. Imagine a workload increasing power demand, a thermal policy reducing frequency and a controller approaching its deadline. Neither the transaction trace nor the temperature reading alone establishes whether the complete sequence was permitted.
I see an opportunity for tools that organize observations around shared events and competing explanations. AI-assisted analysis could help propose relationships, but correlation should lead to a testable hypothesis, not be labeled a root cause.
Observability should follow the same reasoning. For the clock-gating example, we need to relate outstanding traffic, clock decisions, wake generation and wake delivery. More logs are not necessarily better evidence if those relationships remain invisible.
Once we understand a mechanism, we should not leave it in a debug report.
What must prevent the circular dependency? Must traffic drain before clock gating? Must wake delivery remain independent? What happens if the normal sequence is interrupted?
These questions turn explanation into architectural obligations. This is the connection I see between biological reasoning and formal-first engineering: one directs attention towards context and competing mechanisms; the other helps express and check precise requirements in a design model.
At Axiomise, formal-first means asking those questions while the architecture can still change. Credits must not be lost or double-counted. Ordering must be preserved where required. Reset and recovery must restore compatible endpoint states.
Progress needs its own argument. Nothing being corrupted does not establish that an accepted request eventually completes. Service and fairness assumptions must be justified by the architecture.
Local proofs need the same treatment. If one component assumes a neighbour responds, where is that response established? Individually successful checks cannot establish a system claim when their assumptions are incompatible or circular.
Formal-first is not formal-only. Simulation, emulation, physical analysis and system validation contribute different evidence. The task is to connect them around identifiable questions.
If a failure mechanism crosses power management, traffic control and recovery, preventing it cannot depend solely on each team completing local checks.
Someone must own the cross-system obligation: what must remain true, which components contribute, which assumptions are required and which changes trigger reassessment. A revised power policy should reopen the progress argument if it changes its conditions.
This does not diminish specialist expertise. It gives the relationships between specialisms the same standing as the components they produce.
Other fields will not hand silicon engineering a ready-made solution. They can help us recognize incomplete descriptions and design better investigations. Biology’s contribution is not permission to accept ambiguity, but a discipline for challenging explanations.
Looking back at structural biology, I recognize the temptation to let a beautifully resolved model feel like the end of the investigation. The important question was what it helped explain—and what should follow.
The bits can be binary. Our understanding of the system is not automatically complete.
Ashish Darbari is the founder and CEO of Axiomise.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Data discovery and classification anchors AI governance - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI gets keys to unmapped data: theCUBE’s AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit day-two kickoff analysis
Data discovery and classification are becoming important considerations as enterprises bring AI into their operations. Security teams need to understand what information is available to AI systems and how access is governed.
Data discovery and classification are becoming important considerations as enterprises bring AI into their operations. Security teams need to understand what information is available to AI systems and how access is governed. Turning AI trust and cyber resilience principles into practical controls presents a challenge for organizations, according to Jon Oltsik (pictured, right), principal analyst in residence at SiliconANGLE and theCUBE.
“A policy is a policy,” he said. “You write a policy down, you put it on a piece of paper, you educate people. But then when it comes to policy enforcement, that becomes much more difficult. That’s where your controls have to be in place.”
Oltsik and theCUBE Research’s Krista Case (left) provided a day-two kickoff analysis at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed turning AI policy into enforceable controls, starting with data hygiene. (* Disclosure below.)
Data discovery and classification as AI’s first line of defense
A central concern for chief information security officers is controlling AI inside their own organizations. But none of it is entirely new since organizations have long used role-based access control and least privilege to protect regulated data, Oltsik noted.
“Now we have to adjust it to a very dynamic, non-deterministic world of AI, and we have to do that at a pace that keeps up with the scale and speed of AI,” Oltsik said. “None of that is easy.”
How much autonomy to grant agents depends on each organization’s risk tolerance.
The European Commission has issued draft guidance on classifying high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act, according to Oltsik. Agents that touch sensitive data or act autonomously still warrant human oversight, much as early intrusion prevention tools once did.
“What we have to do is ease into those decisions, understand what actions agents or models are taking and then, over time, develop a comfort level,” he said.
Enterprises should get the basics right, starting with data discovery and classification, identity and access management and audits of overly permissive accounts, including those held by agents, Oltsik noted. Security leaders also need to participate in decisions about how the business adopts AI.
“The security team can’t be the division of ‘no,’ or the [chief information security officer] cannot be Dr. No,” he said. “How do you do that? How do you make sure that you go into AI with business objectives and business goals, but the right type of risk management and risk mitigation?”
