articles.title: Nova dona da Telecom Italia diz que Brasil não é prioritário • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nova dona da Telecom Italia diz que Brasil não é prioritário
Poste Italiane afirma que operação brasileira é lucrativa e não está à venda, mas será usada "taticamente".
A Poste Italiane, nova controladora da Telecom Italia e, indiretamente, da TIM Brasil, indicou que a operação brasileira não é considerada estratégica para seus planos futuros. A declaração marca uma mudança de tom pouco mais de um mês após a companhia assumir o controle da matriz italiana.
O CEO da Poste Italiane, Matteo Del Fante, disse que a TIM Brasil é lucrativa e gera bastante caixa, mas não é essencial para o projeto que a empresa pretende desenvolver com a Telecom Italia. Ao mesmo tempo, afirmou que a operação não está à venda.
Essa é a pergunta que continua sem resposta. Durante uma conferência econômica em Roma, Del Fante afirmou apenas que a Poste pretende usar a operação brasileira “de maneira tática” nos próximos meses, mas não explicou o que isso significa na prática. O executivo foi mais direto ao dizer que a TIM Brasil “não está à venda”.
A agência Reuters avalia que a fala pode abrir espaço para uma eventual separação da operação brasileira no futuro. Até agora, não há busca por comprador nem processo formal de venda. O significado desse “uso tático” pode ficar mais claro no primeiro trimestre de 2027, quando Del Fante pretende apresentar um novo plano de negócios para Poste Italiane e Telecom Italia.
A prioridade está na Itália. O grupo quer aproveitar a aquisição da Telecom Italia para ampliar sua atuação em serviços digitais e transformação tecnológica, combinando os clientes corporativos da operadora com a estrutura da estatal italiana. Nesse desenho, a operação brasileira gera resultado financeiro, mas não ocupa o mesmo papel estratégico.
A situação contrasta com o discurso adotado antes da conclusão da aquisição. Em julho, o CEO da TIM Brasil, Alberto Griselli, disse que o fortalecimento da nova controladora poderia beneficiar a filial e lembrou que a Poste havia tratado a operação brasileira como uma “joia”. A mudança também recoloca um tema antigo no radar. Em 2022, integrantes do atual governo italiano chegaram a defender a venda da TIM Brasil para direcionar recursos à operação europeia.
Por enquanto, nada foi anunciado para a operação local. A Telecom Italia controla cerca de 67% da TIM Brasil. A companhia é a única subsidiária estrangeira do grupo e, segundo a Reuters, responde por quase metade de seus lucros operacionais principais. A participação está avaliada em aproximadamente R$ 31,8 bilhões.
No Brasil, a TIM continua entre as três grandes operadoras de telefonia móvel, ao lado de Vivo e Claro. Também atua em banda larga fixa, embora tenha sido ultrapassada pela Starlink em número de acessos.

articles.title: French startup Bleu Robotics secures €5 million to teach humanoid robots new tasks with fewer demonstrations | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Bleu Robotics, a Paris-based startup building AI models for industrial humanoid robots, has raised a €5 million pre-Seed round, to reach its goal of reducing the full humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or shorter.
The round was co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with participation from Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst, and board members at Meta.
Benoît Berkoukchi, co-founder of Bleu Robotics, says, “Humanoid robots in manufacturing are the next automotive sector, with the potential to help Europe and the US reshore production. But most robotics companies are trying to train humanoids with millions of data points and build fully general-purpose models. That approach isn’t suited to manufacturing. There isn’t enough data on factory work, and there won’t be internet-scale data, the kind LLMs were built on, for robots for a long time. Our methodology means we can do more with less.”
The round comes amid continued European investment in robotics software, humanoid systems and Physical AI during 2026.
In France, Paris-based Inbolt raised €11 million to expand its hardware-agnostic robot intelligence platform, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics secured €26 million to develop AI-powered skills for industrial robots.
Elsewhere, Belgium’s Motion raised €1.7 million for humanoid deployment, Spain’s THEKER secured €73 million to scale generalist industrial robotics, and London-based Humanoid raised €133 million for its industrial humanoid platform.
Together with funding rounds for Germany’s Sereact, Switzerland’s Enact Intelligence and Poland’s Nomagic, these financings total €372.7 million in 2026, rising to €377.7 million when including Bleu Robotics’ latest round.
Thomas Poitrineau, Investor at Contrarian Ventures, adds, “We were attracted to Bleu Robotics because of their ambitious choice to rethink how humanoid robotics software should work from first principles. It’s rare to find a company led by two world-class robotics researchers and a manufacturing expert, which is also why their software works differently from their competition. Their goal is far bigger than simply making the best model in a lab. It’s an approach that can already scale, putting robots to work in factories within months rather than years.”
Founded in Paris in 2025 by two INRIA researchers and a former Renault manufacturing manager, Bleu’s abductive learning technology reportedly lets robots learn new tasks from only a handful of operator demonstrations.
Its software runs on any humanoid platform and includes the AI model and training devices needed to teach robots on the factory floor.
According to the International Federation of Robotics, there were 5 million industrial robots operating globally in 2025. However, these robots are built to repeat fixed tasks, and are unable to adapt to the high-mix, low-volume production now common in modern manufacturing, so that work still falls to human workers.
Humanoid robots are needed to automate a wider range of complex tasks. While hardware has advanced significantly in recent years, software development has struggled to keep pace, limiting real-world deployment.
Interact Analysis found that of the 20,000-plus humanoids produced last year, only 10% reached real-world applications. Most of these robots today rely on end-to-end models, which learn everything in a single black box and require massive amounts of data to achieve production-ready reliability.
As a result, deployment remains costly and time-consuming for manufacturers, often requiring hundreds of hours of training data, with no guarantee the robot will perform reliably.
Instead of an end-to-end model, Bleu Robotics’ abductive learning model allows the robot to learn a new task from as few as ten operator demonstrations, while keeping the explainability required for industrial safety and the 99%+ accuracy that production lines demand.

articles.title: Microsoft hits 10 quarters of record-breaking revenue in a row | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Whatever the future of AI might be, the current situation is still very good for Microsoft. The tech giant reported yet another quarterly revenue record on Wednesday: $92.3 billion, a 19% increase over the year-ago quarter.
Microsoft has now reported record-breaking revenue for 10 quarters in a row.
This is profitable revenue, too. Microsoft reported that net income reached $36.6 billion, an increase of 32% on a GAAP basis, over the year-ago quarter.
The record-breaking income was largely driven on the strength of Microsoft Cloud, which reached $63.9 billion in revenue this quarter, an increase of 30% over the year-ago quarter, Microsoft said.
Microsoft has reorganized its business reporting into two basic segments: 1) Agents and Infra and 2) Devices and Consumer. On the flip side, revenue in Devices and Consumer was $15.5 billion, decreased of 3%, with Windows OEM and devices revenue falling 22% from the year-ago quarter.
True, not all of Microsoft’s healthy cloud revenue can be attributed to AI. Microsoft 365 accounted for nearly $28 billion. But Azure brought in the most, at $33.2 billion. And again, not all of that is necessarily AI-related. Enterprises run all sorts of the traditional software and SaaS applications on Azure.
Still, a good chunk of the revenue was from AI, because Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI. Despite branching out to AWS, Oracle, and others, OpenAI still runs a lot of its services on Microsoft’s cloud. (Anthropic runs on Azure as well.) Microsoft also said its “commercial remaining performance obligation increased 73% to $677 billion.” That represents future revenue committed under existing contracts of the AI labs.
But, like all the big cloud providers, Microsoft is also spending big to prepare to deliver on those commitments. Capital expenditures topped $45.2 billion, another all-time quarterly record.

articles.title: Bot Food secures $1.5 million to give AI users more control over their data | BetaKit
articles.text:
The team that built and sold Toronto’s Wysdom has launched a new software startup that aims to give individuals greater control and ownership over how much they share with powerful AI systems, and when they share it.
Bot Food Corporation announced on Thursday that it has secured $1.5 million CAD in pre-seed funding from fellow Toronto firm GreenSky Ventures to build “one personal context library that works across every AI product.” It also launched a beta version of its application.
“One day, people are going to realize, ‘I want to take back control of that [personal context].’”
Bot Food co-founder and CEO Ian Collins co-founded Wysdom as CEO in 2012 with former CTO Jeff Brunet, working alongside ex-COO Nitin Singhal. That startup, which was initially named CrowdCare, built an AI evaluation platform to help customer service chatbot operators improve their performance, before selling to Minneapolis-based Calabrio in 2024.
During his time at Wysdom, Collins said he and his colleagues grasped the importance of context in AI. “As we measured and evaluated all these bots and their performance, it was almost always a context problem,” he told BetaKit in an exclusive interview.
Collins said that while it has become clear that the more knowledge these systems possess about the individuals using them, the better they perform, many have yet to realize how valuable their personal context actually is. As AI companies race to capture as much personal context on their users as possible to improve their performance and keep them locked in, Collins envisions what he sees as a better path forward.
With Bot Food, Collins and Singhal have teamed up again to give individuals control and ownership over that context, and Brunet, now managing partner at GreenSky, has bought into their vision. Brunet has joined Bot Food’s board of directors as part of its all-equity, all-primary capital pre-seed round, which closed in October and brings the startup’s total funding to $3 million. Collins did not share its valuation.
RELATED: Bot management software startup Wysdom acquired by US-based Calabrio
Brunet told BetaKit over email that GreenSky likes to invest in startups building tech other products will depend upon. “We believe a universal personal context layer could become a critical piece of infrastructure for the entire AI ecosystem,” he added. “Backing proven founders I trust, with a bold vision for the future of AI, was an easy decision.”
Collins argued that sharing detailed personal context with AI will soon become a prerequisite for anyone who wants agentic systems “to do great things” for them. “A lot of people are resisting [AI],” he posited, “but we’re all going to give in eventually; the productivity is just going to be too great.”
For his part, Collins has been using Muse, US tech giant Meta’s fast-growing personal AI agent, since it became available in Canada last month. “It’s pretty amazing, and it’s getting to know me so much,” he said. “It’s just sucking up the data at this massive pace.”
As AI usage grows, these systems will amass deep libraries of information about the individuals using them over time. AI users may not possess access to or rights over their own usage data, Collins said, from rich details about their digital shopping history to the TV shows and movies they’ve watched, the music they listen to, and the places they’ve worked and travelled. At the moment, many major AI labs are using this personal context they have gathered for customer retention.
RELATED: GreenSky closes $23.5-million sixth fund with help from new managing partner Jeff Brunet
Bot Food is betting that some portion of the population will eventually recognize that all of this personal context is a tremendous asset. “One day, people are going to realize, ‘I want to take back control of that,’” Collins said. “‘I should own that thing. It’s rich, it’s valuable, [and] I could probably … get paid for it if I wanted to.’”
Bot Food aims to give its users that power, along with greater choice over how much they share about themselves, with which systems, and when. Those libraries will be collected and managed by Bot Food’s AI assistant RaLHF (pronounced like the common name Ralph), which Collins said will sign into the apps that customers use and catalogue what it finds into a private, encrypted digital library that they can view, edit, and selectively share from with the systems they are using.
The now seven-person startup, which has brought on former ThinkData Works CTO Brendan Stennett as CTO, plans to put its pre-seed funding largely towards go-to-market testing.
“A lot of people are resisting [AI], but we’re all going to give in eventually; the productivity is just going to be too great.”
When asked why individuals should trust a small startup like Bot Food to responsibly store their info instead of a large AI lab, Collins said Bot Food’s terms of service make clear that the company does not hold any rights to the data stored on its platform and cannot do anything with it. He also argued that Bot Food’s product architecture and Stennett’s experience in enterprise data security will help the company keep its clients’ context secure.
Bot Food’s beta features a simple on/off switch that users can click to allow or bar certain AI systems from accessing their data. Its next version will likely include permission for certain AI systems to draw relevant context from select apps.
Collins envisions a final product that can not only send personal context back into its library, but one that features more granular buckets as its own agent improves. He said the startup is also testing its capacity to allow individuals to grant AI access to their information for some tasks and then forget about it afterwards.
Cyberattacks are on the rise thanks to agentic AI, and Collins acknowledged that there could come a day where, if Bot Food achieves success building these sorts of libraries, it becomes a prime target for bad actors, human or machine.
“It’s key to us that we build trust like a 1Password, and have a level of security that we can offer like they do because [Bot Food] will become a target one day,” Collins said.
Feature image courtesy Bot Food Corporation.

articles.text:

KLEVV Unveils All-New CRAS V RGB Prime DDR5 Memory
KLEVV, the leading consumer memory and storage brand introduced by Essencore, today unveils the all-new CRAS V RGB PRIME DDR5 Gaming/OC Memory. Purpose-built for elite gaming rigs and demanding creative workloads, this new premium memory unleashes ultra-low CAS latency down to CL26 at 6000 MT/s and blazing overclocking speeds of up to 8000 MT/s at CL38, dressed in a striking black-and-gold finish and armed with dual-platform overclocking support for gamers, PC builders, and performance enthusiasts who demand nothing but the best.Refined Flagship Design and Craftsmanship
Building on the aluminium heat spreader design of the flagship CRAS V RGB, winner of both the Red Dot and iF Design Awards, the CRAS V RGB PRIME introduces a striking new black-and-gold interpretation of the series' signature look.
An advanced hard-anodizing process, combined with a specialized surface treatment, gives the modules a smooth, piano-lacquer-like sheen that adds depth and sophistication from every angle. The result is an understated yet luxurious aesthetic that offers users a fresh, premium design choice while preserving the refined craftsmanship of the original CRAS V RGB.
High-Speed Performance with Lower Latency
The CRAS V RGB PRIME further advances KLEVV's DDR5 overclocking memory lineup with tested speeds of 6000, 6400, and 8000 MT/s and CAS latencies of CL26, CL28, and CL38, respectively.
The 6000 MT/s configuration features tested timings of 26-36-36-76, while the 6400 MT/s configuration delivers timings of 28-38-38-78. For users seeking extreme frequencies, the 8000 MT/s models operate at tested timings of 38-48-48-128. All configurations are tested at 1.4 V.
The 6000 and 6400 MT/s configurations are available in dual-channel kits ranging from 32 GB (16 GB x 2), 64 GB (32 GB x 2), to 128 GB (64 GB x 2), while the 8000 MT/s models are offered in both 32 GB (16 GB x 2) and 48 GB (24 GB x 2) kits. This diverse range gives users greater flexibility to select the ideal balance of speed, latency, and capacity for their systems.
Next-Generation AMD EXPO Technology: Featuring Ultra Low Latency
"AMD EXPO Technology: Featuring Ultra Low Latency" is the latest evolution of AMD's established memory overclocking technology. The new AMD EXPO ULL profile incorporates optimized memory sub-timing settings designed to reduce latency and improve overall performance on compatible AMD platforms. As the first product in KLEVV's overclocking memory lineup to adopt this technology, the CRAS V RGB PRIME delivers a more responsive gaming and overclocking experience.
The 6000 MT/s and 6400 MT/s 32 GB (16 GB x 2) configurations are certified for AMD EXPO Ultra Low Latency. According to AMD, certified Ultra Low Latency memory can deliver an average 4% improvement in FPS compared with non-ULL AMD EXPO memory on compatible systems.
Broad Intel and AMD Platform Support
Offering broad support across the latest desktop platforms, the CRAS V RGB PRIME is compatible with AMD Ryzen processors on the AM5 platform and Intel Core Ultra 200S Plus processors.
Each kit comes preloaded with both Intel Extreme Memory Profile and AMD EXPO Technology overclocking profiles, allowing users to unlock high-speed performance through a simple BIOS setting on compatible motherboards with supported BIOS versions. With both profiles included, users can confidently choose their preferred speed and capacity without the hassle of selecting separate Intel- or AMD-specific models.
Premium Components for Uncompromising Stability
The CRAS V RGB PRIME features rigorously screened, high-quality memory ICs from a leading Korean manufacturer, ensuring consistent high-speed performance and exceptional stability under demanding workloads.
Paired with a high-density 10-layer PCB, the modules deliver enhanced signal integrity and greater resistance to interference during high-speed operation. Integrated PMIC and on-die ECC technologies further support stable power management and long-term reliability, creating a robust foundation for gaming and overclocking performance.
To ensure broad compatibility, the CRAS V RGB PRIME has also been validated on the QVLs (Qualified Vendor Lists) of four major motherboard manufacturers. Its RGB lighting supports ASUS Aura Sync, GIGABYTE RGB Fusion, MSI Mystic Light Sync, and ASRock Polychrome Sync, allowing users to seamlessly coordinate lighting across compatible components and systems.
A Complete DDR5 Gaming/OC Memory Lineup
The introduction of the CRAS V RGB PRIME further expands KLEVV's comprehensive DDR5 Gaming/OC memory portfolio.
With the CRAS, URBANE, BOLT, and FIT series available across a wide range of designs and specifications, KLEVV continues to provide flexible memory choices for different performance requirements, system configurations, and aesthetic preferences.

articles.title: $4,700 audiophile-grade network hub promises a noise-free experience and music with 'emotional impact' — seven isolation stages per port were chosen with 'listening comparisons'
articles.text:
$4,700 audiophile-grade network hub promises a noise-free experience and music with 'emotional impact' — seven isolation stages per port were chosen with 'listening comparisons,' uses a $5 Realtek controller
The perfect cure for that latest bout of audiophilia nervosa?
There are a lot of salesman sayings, and, chances are, most were inspired by audiophiles. The eternal sufferers of audiophilia nervosa keep coming up with novel ways to attribute sonic and emotional characteristics to any piece of equipment — even when discussing things purely in the digital realm. One of the current fads is audiophile-grade network switches, like the Aurender NH10 Network Hub, coming in at a mere $4,700.
This piece of gear —which we presume is actually a network switch, rather than a hub — comes fitted with eight gigabit ports. Six of those are standard copper inputs, while the other two are SFP ports where audiophiles can plug in a transceiver for either fiber or copper. The product page remarks that, naturally, a fiber connection is electrically isolated. I was teeing up a joke about the existence of audiophile-grade SFP transceivers when, while proofreading, I found that life does truly imitate art. Oh, and that $4,700 doesn't even get you 10 GbE capabilities.
Four of the six copper ports on the Aurender switch have a total of seven electrical filtering stages behind them, while the remaining pair "only" has two. According to an article at Headphonesty, Aurender's designer said the team experimented with using over 10 stages, but eventually settled on seven "from listening comparisons." That's an interesting feature considering that the Ethernet standard already mandates electrical isolation for standard twisted-pair connections.
Aurender also says that it's using an OXCO (Oven-Controlled Crystal Oscillator) controlled by an FPGA for clock synchronization, and there's a BNC input on the back for an external source. From what we can tell from the board picture, the main chips include: a Realtek RT8370N switch controller ($5.5 at LCSC, an MV85 oscillator ($39 on eBay), and an AMD/Xilinx Spartan 6 FGPA ($8-15 depending on model). There are, no doubt, more manufacturing and materials costs to go from a collection of chips to an assembled switch, but presumably not enough to get anywhere close to the $4,700 asking price of the NH10.
This is all adorable, but the fact of the matter is that the hardware here cannot, by any reasonable definition, make any difference to the sound. TCP connections have built-in error correction. The Ethernet protocol includes Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC), and there are several similar layers, up to the point where the data turns into an actual analog signal.
It's also up to whichever equipment is handling the playback to electrically isolate the actual DAC output stage, not at the network or switch level. And even affordable audio interfaces have signal-to-noise ratios that 1970s recording engineers would happily give up their LSD for.
Likewise, the whole conversation about jitter is pointless, though much like any audiophile myth, it's grounded in a piece of truth — just one that's completely irrelevant in this scenario. In a recording studio, you occasionally need to sync the clock across multiple pieces of gear, just like matching tape machines back in the day. For just the one piece of playback gear, however, it's pointless, and it's downright nonsensical at the network level.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Yet logic has never stopped some self-described audiophiles. One can but wonder what folks seriously looking at these pieces of gear would feel knowing that the studios where their precious music is being made use, for example, one bog-standard Ethernet cable to carry 4 balanced analog lines. Or how their favorite guitarist's pedals and amplifier in a famous recording session were held together with lamp cord, duct tape, hopes, and dreams.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Amazon turns its most capable smart speaker into a smart camera, too
articles.text:
Since debuting in 2019, Amazon’s Echo Studio targeted users who wanted superior audio quality from their Alexa-based smart speaker. The latest Echo Studio adds another less-expected differentiator: an integrated camera.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera, released alongside a pile of other Alexa devices today, doesn’t have many audio upgrades over the standard Echo Studio. Each speaker has one 3.75-inch high-excursion woofer and three full-range drivers. They both support Dolby Atmos and Amazon’s proprietary algorithm for adding a surround sound-like effect to stereo audio. Per the devices’ product pages, the speakers have lossless HD audio, Advanced Room Adaptation, and features for fighting noise distortion. Amazon announced the Advanced Room Adaptaion today, saying that the feature “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room’s acoustics.”
Both speakers have four-microphone arrays and the same AZ3 Pro processor that Amazon introduced a year ago. The processor has an AI accelerator for using Amazon’s Alexa+ generative AI chatbot.
The devices also have the same dimensions, even though the new Echo Studio With Home Camera fits in a 13MP camera.
The speaker can use the camera to see where you are and adjust audio volume “so your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.”
Beyond audio capabilities, Amazon sees people using the speaker as a smart camera, allowing them to remotely check on a room in the home to see, for example, “how the dog is doing or make sure you didn’t leave the lights on.”
“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time. Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box, and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors,” Amazon’s announcement says.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Carbon, una IA que puede detectar fallos antes que los hackers
articles.text:
A unas semanas del lanzamiento de Gemini 4 Argon, Google ha presentado un nuevo modelo de IA que la compañía describe como el más potente a la fecha. Conocido como Gemini 4 Carbon, esta variante cuenta con capacidades de programación y razonamiento avanzado, así como funciones especializadas en ciberseguridad. Según la tecnológica, Carbon es eficaz para encontrar y corregir fallos de seguridad.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, Gemini 4 Carbon toma el relevo de Argon, que se anunció hace apenas unas semanas. Google ya no quiere dejar pasar mucho tiempo entre un lanzamiento y otro, por lo que agilizó los tiempos de desarrollo para cerrar la brecha con Anthropic y OpenAI. Otro factor para el despliegue de este modelo es la oleada de hackeos por parte de agentes autónomos, los cuales vulneraron múltiples empresas y gobiernos en los últimos meses.
Es aquí donde entra Gemini 4 Carbon, que ofrece un salto considerable con respecto a su predecesor en todas las fases del ciclo de defensa. El modelo se entrenó para identificar fallos en el código, analizar si una vulnerabilidad puede explotarse en condiciones reales y generar correcciones que mitiguen el problema. Google afirma que la ciberseguridad es uno de los campos más importantes para el futuro inmediato de la IA, por lo que ha construido su modelo con este objetivo en mente.
Gemini 4 Carbon es la IA más poderosa de Google para ciberseguridad
En términos de benchmarks, Gemini 4 Carbon obtuvo un 88,2% en SEC-bench Pro, una prueba especializada en detección de vulnerabilidades. En ExploitGym, que se enfoca en validar la explotabilidad de fallos, la IA de Google alcanzó un 54,8%, mientras que en CWE-bench, una referencia para evaluar la capacidad de generar parches efectivos, Carbon logró un 71,1%.
Google menciona que sus ingenieros ya utilizan Gemini 4 Carbon para encontrar errores en bases de código de gran tamaño. La IA puede mantener procesos de análisis durante periodos prolongados, lo cual le otorga una ventaja en auditorías de seguridad a gran escala. En el caso de la generación de código seguro, Carbon duplica la tasa de éxito obtenida por Argon y el equipo de Chrome ya lo usa para corregir vulnerabilidades reales.
La seguridad también se extiende al comportamiento del modelo, donde existen protecciones contra prompt injection. En las pruebas internas, el modelo consiguió bloquear intentos de manipulación indirecta, mientras que en la resistencia frente a ataques, Carbon consigue una reducción cercana al 50%.
El modelo también brilla en desarrollo de software y conocimiento general
Aunque el enfoque de Google y otras empresas está en la ciberseguridad, los modelos también han mejorado en razonamiento y tareas con agentes. En el caso de Gemini 4 Carbon, la IA puede llevar a cabo proyectos de ingeniería de larga duración, ya que el modelo se optimizó para que los agentes puedan trabajar por días manteniendo el contexto necesario para resolver problemas difíciles.
En desarrollo, el nuevo modelo de Google alcanza una puntuación de 1.769 Elo en la clasificación de WebDev Arena, una referencia para evaluar qué tan buena es creando aplicaciones web. Por otro lado, Carbon lidera la versión 5.0 del índice de inteligencia de Artificial Analysis, lo que lo coloca como uno de los modelos más avanzados de propósito general.
Todo lo anterior suena muy bien, excepto porque Gemini 4 Carbon todavía no está disponible para el público general. Google confirmó que ofrecerá un acceso limitado a profesionales de ciberseguridad y socios del programa Fairwind en una primera etapa. Posteriormente, el acceso se ampliará a desarrolladores, empresas y consumidores, por lo que deberemos esperar algunas semanas para poder usarlo.

articles.title: GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September, adding 4M CPU cores and 160 PB of storage to keep up
articles.text:
GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September, adding 4M CPU cores and 160 PB of storage to keep up
GitHub is seeing unprecedented demand and is updating its core infrastructure to keep pace.
In August, GitHub said it was seeing 2.9 billion commits per month, up from 1.4 billion in April. At its GitHub Universe conference on Wednesday, the company announced that it is now seeing 7.4 billion commits per month. To put that into perspective, developers pushed 65 million monthly commits to the platform in 2024.
That kind of growth is a great problem to have, but the company’s outages have become something of a recurring theme. The reason is rapid usage growth, driven mostly by “agentic demand,” as the company puts it.
4 million more CPU cores
In August, GitHub CTO Vlad Fedorov announced that the platform had added 3 million CPU cores — mostly on Azure — to support this growth. Now, GitHub says it has added 4 million CPU cores, plus 160 petabytes of high-speed storage and more compute power for GitHub Actions so far this year
The company also added 50 Tb/s of network capacity to keep all of this data flowing.
A new GitHub architecture is coming
GitHub also used this announcement to reiterate its commitment to rearchitecting its platform to separate compute and storage. It first talked about this earlier this month. At that time, the company noted that its internal benchmarks show that this new architecture can deliver up to 35x higher write throughput, for example.
“Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture,” Jay Parikh, the EVP for Core AI at Microsoft, writes in the announcement.
Separating compute and storage isn’t exactly radical in 2026, but it shows GitHub was trying to scale on a legacy foundation. Moving to Azure and its services was essentially the only option, especially as the company’s own data center was out of capacity.

articles.title: Cyberpunk 2 : des missions multijoueurs pourraient débarquer dans la suite de Cyberpunk 2077
articles.text:
Parcourir Night City avec des amis, accomplir des contrats ensemble, affronter les gangs de la ville en coopération ou prendre des photos de groupe devant des sex-shops du futur : voilà une perspective qui pourrait devenir réalité dans Cyberpunk 2. Alors que des moddeurs ont lancé le 23 octobre la bêta ouverte de NightCoop, un mod gratuit qui permet de jouer à Cyberpunk 2077 en coopération jusqu’à huit sur PC, la suite du jeu de CD Projekt Red pourrait faire du multi une fonction officielle.
Repérée par le site CheatHappens ce 22 octobre et relayée par Polygon ce 28 octobre, une offre d’emploi publiée par CD Projekt Red cherche un Lead Quest Programmer (programmeur principal chargé des quêtes) pour Cyberpunk 2. Le poste consiste notamment à concevoir les systèmes et les outils qui servent à créer les missions.
Parmi les compétences souhaitées, mais pas obligatoires, figure la connaissance de l’architecture réseau multijoueur et de la synchronisation entre client et serveur pour l’état du jeu et les quêtes. Une mention qui suggère que le studio pourrait réfléchir à des missions conçues pour être réalisées à plusieurs, avec des actions et une progression synchronisées entre les joueuses et les joueurs.
Sur le papier, des quêtes synchronisées en ligne pourraient permettre à plusieurs joueuses et joueurs de remplir certains contrats ensemble, voire de suivre des missions narratives en coopération. L’offre seule ne permet pas de savoir si la coopération concernerait seulement des activités secondaires ou toute l’aventure.
Le premier Cyberpunk devait inclure la coopération
Il faut toutefois rester prudent : une compétence mentionnée dans une annonce de recrutement ne constitue pas une confirmation officielle, et CD Projekt Red n’a pour le moment fait aucune annonce quant à un éventuel mode multijoueur.
Pour autant, on est en droit de rêver. Cette possibilité de jouer au jeu en coopération, le studio polonais l’avait en effet envisagée pour le premier épisode, avant de finalement abandonner le projet. Avant la sortie de Cyberpunk 2077 en décembre 2020, CD Projekt Red avait confirmé le développement d’un mode multijoueur destiné à arriver après le lancement. Le projet avait ensuite pris de l’ampleur, au point de devenir une production indépendante, distincte de la campagne solo.
La suite, on la connaît : le lancement difficile du jeu a modifié les priorités du studio, qui a préféré concentrer ses efforts sur la correction des nombreux problèmes techniques. Cyberpunk 2 pourrait donner à CD Projekt Red l’occasion de reprendre cette idée laissée en plan.
CD Projekt Red n’a communiqué aucune date de sortie pour Cyberpunk 2. Le jeu est en préproduction depuis le printemps 2025.

articles.title: Top 7 Web3 Platforms for Node.js Developers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Quick answer: The best Web3 platforms for Node.js developers in 2026 are Autheo, Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon, Arbitrum, and Avalanche. Autheo ranks first because it combines an EVM-compatible Layer-1, standard JSON-RPC support, TypeScript and JavaScript SDKs, and an integrated developer workspace. Node.js developers can use familiar tools such as viem, ethers.js, Hardhat, npm, and REST APIs while connecting to a broader platform designed to bring identity, compute, storage, interoperability, and AI tooling into one environment.
Choosing a Web3 platform used to mean selecting a blockchain. Today, it means selecting an entire development stack: the execution environment, client libraries, smart contract language, backend infrastructure, data storage, wallet integration, testing tools, and deployment workflow. Every additional vendor increases integration work, operational costs, and the number of potential failure points.
This guide compares seven Web3 platforms Node.js developers are actively using in 2026, including what each platform does best, which JavaScript and TypeScript tools it supports, and where its limitations become important.
The Best Web3 Platforms for Node.js Developers in 2026
The top seven platforms are:
- Autheo
- Ethereum
- Solana
- Base
- Polygon
- Arbitrum
- Avalanche
These rankings consider Node.js compatibility, TypeScript support, SDK quality, smart contract tooling, backend development, scalability, interoperability, documentation, and the overall number of external services developers must integrate.
1. Autheo
Best overall Web3 platform for Node.js developers
Autheo is the best overall choice for Node.js developers who want familiar Ethereum development tools without assembling an entire application stack from unrelated services.
Autheo provides an EVM-compatible blockchain built on the Cosmos SDK. Its standard JSON-RPC interface allows Node.js developers to connect using viem, ethers.js, and other Ethereum-compatible libraries. Existing TypeScript types, Node.js services, React applications, and contract integration patterns can be adapted primarily by changing the network configuration and RPC endpoint.
For smart contract development, Autheo supports Solidity deployment through Hardhat, Foundry, and Remix. Developers who prefer npm-based workflows can use JavaScript and TypeScript SDK packages designed to provide typed access to Autheo’s APIs and platform services.
Why Autheo Works Well With Node.js
Node.js developers can use Autheo for:
- Backend services that read and write blockchain data
- TypeScript scripts for contract deployment and administration
- Wallet connections using viem or ethers.js
- Event listeners and transaction monitoring
- REST and JSON-RPC integrations
- Cross-chain applications using IBC
- Full-stack dApps with JavaScript or TypeScript frontends
- Automated testing and deployment through DevHub
Autheo’s DevHub brings documentation, testing, deployment, monitoring, SDK access, contract exploration, and testnet resources into a more centralized development environment. This can reduce the amount of external infrastructure a team must configure before launching an application.
The platform’s broader goal is to integrate blockchain execution, identity, decentralized compute, persistent storage, AI assistance, and developer tooling. The EVM-compatible chain, staking, fees, SDKs, IBC functionality, and DevHub are available today. TheoID, decentralized compute, expanded storage, post-quantum features, and THEO AI capabilities are being introduced according to the platform’s rollout roadmap.
Where Autheo Falls Short
Autheo has a smaller existing application ecosystem than Ethereum, Solana, or the largest Ethereum Layer-2 networks. Some of the platform’s most differentiated services are also still rolling out.
Developers should evaluate the tools currently available separately from roadmap features. Even with that limitation, Autheo’s Node.js compatibility and integrated infrastructure model make it a strong option for teams that want to reduce fragmented third-party integrations.
Best for: Node.js teams building full-stack dApps, cross-chain services, AI-enabled Web3 applications, backend automation, identity applications, and products that need an integrated development environment.
2. Ethereum
Best for libraries, documentation, and ecosystem maturity
Ethereum remains the most established Web3 platform for JavaScript and Node.js developers. It has the largest collection of libraries, tutorials, development frameworks, infrastructure providers, contract standards, and production examples.
Node.js developers can use ethers.js or viem to connect to Ethereum nodes, read blockchain data, call smart contracts, send transactions, estimate gas, monitor events, and operate backend services. Solidity is also syntactically familiar to JavaScript developers, although it has a very different security and execution model.
Ethereum’s official documentation identifies ethers.js and viem as prominent JavaScript and TypeScript interfaces. It also notes that Web3.js was archived in March 2025, so new Node.js projects should generally use a maintained alternative such as ethers.js or viem.
Why Ethereum Works Well With Node.js
Ethereum offers:
- Mature npm libraries
- Extensive TypeScript support
- Hardhat and Foundry compatibility
- Standard JSON-RPC interfaces
- Large collections of open-source contracts
- Established token and wallet standards
- Numerous hosted node providers
- Strong support for backend scripts, bots, APIs, and indexers
A Node.js service can use Ethereum libraries to communicate with contracts without running an Ethereum client locally. Developers can connect through an RPC provider and build conventional API routes, queues, databases, and background workers around blockchain activity.
Where Ethereum Falls Short
Ethereum mainnet can be expensive for applications that require frequent transactions. Developers may also need separate providers for nodes, indexing, storage, identity, monitoring, automation, and wallet infrastructure.
Ethereum offers the deepest ecosystem, but its development stack is often assembled from multiple independent services.
Best for: DeFi protocols, established token projects, high-value applications, infrastructure products, developer tools, and teams requiring maximum composability.
3. Solana
Best non-EVM platform for TypeScript applications
Solana is one of the strongest Web3 platforms for Node.js and TypeScript developers who do not require EVM compatibility.
The recommended TypeScript SDK is Solana Kit, available through the @solana/kit package. It provides tools for RPC connections, transactions, codecs, signers, wallets, and generated program clients. Solana also offers Web3.js version 3 for developers who prefer its familiar class-based interface or need to modernize an existing Solana Web3.js application.
Developers can use Node.js to create transaction services, payment systems, token applications, bots, data pipelines, game backends, wallet services, and APIs.
Why Solana Works Well With Node.js
Solana provides:
- Official JavaScript and TypeScript SDKs
- npm-based client libraries
- JSON-RPC and WebSocket APIs
- Generated TypeScript clients for onchain programs
- Tools for token and wallet integration
- Strong support for high-frequency applications
- React and Next.js integration options
The main difference is that Solana is not EVM-compatible. Its onchain programs are commonly written in Rust, while JavaScript and TypeScript are used for clients, tests, backend services, transaction construction, and user interfaces.
This means a Node.js developer can build much of a Solana application in TypeScript, but learning Rust or working with a Rust developer may be necessary when creating custom onchain programs.
Where Solana Falls Short
Solana’s account model, transaction construction, program architecture, and development workflow differ significantly from Ethereum. Developers migrating from EVM networks face a steeper learning curve than they would when moving to another EVM-compatible platform.
Best for: Payments, trading applications, consumer products, games, token platforms, high-frequency applications, and Node.js teams willing to work outside the EVM ecosystem.
4. Base
Best for consumer apps and rapid JavaScript deployment
Base is an Ethereum Layer-2 network incubated by Coinbase. It is a strong option for Node.js developers building consumer applications, payment products, creator platforms, social experiences, and lightweight mini apps.
Because Base is EVM-compatible, Node.js developers can use ethers.js, viem, Hardhat, Solidity, Next.js, and standard Ethereum JSON-RPC methods. Existing Ethereum applications can often be adapted by changing network settings and reviewing Base-specific deployment requirements.
Base also provides MiniKit, a development framework intended to help teams build applications using familiar technologies such as Next.js. Its documentation includes templates and rapid deployment workflows for publishing mini apps.
Why Base Works Well With Node.js
Base is well suited for:
- js and TypeScript applications
- js payment backends
- Consumer-facing mini apps
- Wallet and account integrations
- Solidity contract deployment
- Social and creator applications
- Products seeking Coinbase-related distribution
Developers can reuse much of the Ethereum JavaScript ecosystem while accessing lower transaction costs than Ethereum mainnet.
Where Base Falls Short
Base is still an Ethereum Layer-2 network. Developers must understand bridging, sequencer dependencies, settlement timing, and Layer-2 withdrawal mechanics.
Its strongest distribution advantages may also be most relevant to applications that fit the broader Coinbase and Base ecosystem.
Best for: Consumer Web3 applications, social apps, creator tools, payments, mini apps, and Node.js teams already comfortable with Next.js and Ethereum libraries.
5. Polygon
Best for full-stack EVM development with multiple scaling options
Polygon offers a broad set of Ethereum scaling technologies and EVM-compatible development environments. It is a practical choice for Node.js developers who want to use familiar Ethereum tools while accessing lower-cost transactions.
Developers can connect to Polygon using viem, ethers.js, JSON-RPC providers, and other standard EVM libraries. Smart contracts can be written in Solidity and deployed through tools such as Hardhat, Foundry, or Remix.
Polygon also provides a dApp Launchpad that initializes a full-stack project with a Next.js frontend and Hardhat smart contract environment. It can automate contract artifact updates, redeployment, and frontend hot module replacement.
Why Polygon Works Well With Node.js
Polygon supports:
- js and TypeScript backends
- js application development
- Hardhat contract projects
- Standard EVM libraries
- Solidity smart contracts
- Automated dApp project creation
- Ethereum-compatible wallets
- Low-cost consumer transactions
Polygon can work particularly well for marketplaces, loyalty programs, games, digital collectibles, and enterprise applications that need frequent onchain activity.
Where Polygon Falls Short
Polygon includes multiple networks and scaling products. Developers must determine which environment matches their security, interoperability, transaction cost, and performance requirements.
The number of available options creates flexibility, but it can also make architecture decisions more complicated.
Best for: Full-stack JavaScript applications, games, marketplaces, loyalty systems, enterprise dApps, and teams that want multiple Ethereum scaling options.
6. Arbitrum
Best for Node.js DeFi backends and established Layer-2 applications
Arbitrum is a mature Ethereum Layer-2 ecosystem designed to support lower-cost, higher-capacity smart contract applications.
Node.js developers can use common Ethereum libraries such as ethers.js, viem, and Web3.js, although viem or ethers.js are preferable for new projects. Arbitrum also supports development frameworks such as Hardhat and Foundry.
For a JavaScript or TypeScript team, deploying to Arbitrum can feel similar to deploying to Ethereum. Existing contract ABIs, wallet connections, backend scripts, event listeners, and testing patterns can frequently be reused.
Why Arbitrum Works Well With Node.js
Arbitrum is a strong choice for:
- DeFi dashboards
- Trading interfaces
- Transaction monitoring services
- js bots and automation
- High-activity smart contract applications
- Ethereum applications expanding to Layer 2
- Backend systems that monitor contract events
Its established DeFi ecosystem gives developers access to existing contracts, liquidity, wallets, bridges, analytics platforms, and infrastructure providers.
Where Arbitrum Falls Short
Developers must account for Layer-2 settlement, bridging, withdrawal periods, gas behavior, and differences between Arbitrum networks.
Arbitrum reduces transaction costs, but it does not eliminate the need for external RPC, indexing, monitoring, storage, and deployment services.
Best for: DeFi, trading applications, financial dashboards, games, automation tools, and existing Ethereum projects moving to Layer 2.
7. Avalanche
Best for TypeScript teams building configurable EVM networks
Avalanche provides an EVM-compatible C-Chain and tools for launching customizable Avalanche Layer-1 networks. It is particularly valuable for Node.js teams that need more control over their blockchain environment.
The Avalanche Client SDK provides a TypeScript interface for interacting with the network and currently requires Node.js 20 or newer. Developers can also use ethers.js, Hardhat, Solidity, and familiar EVM deployment patterns.
Why Avalanche Works Well With Node.js
Avalanche offers:
- A dedicated TypeScript SDK
- js support for network interaction
- EVM-compatible smart contracts
- Hardhat deployment workflows
- Customizable Avalanche Layer-1 networks
- Cross-network messaging capabilities
- Infrastructure for application-specific blockchains
Node.js developers can build backend APIs, transaction services, administrative scripts, data monitoring systems, wallet integrations, and contract deployment pipelines.
Where Avalanche Falls Short
Launching a customized Avalanche Layer-1 requires more architecture and operational planning than deploying an application to a shared public network.
Projects must decide whether they actually need a dedicated network. For many applications, deploying contracts to an existing shared chain will be simpler and less expensive to operate.
Best for: Enterprise systems, institutional applications, games, regulated environments, application-specific networks, and TypeScript teams that need greater control over blockchain configuration.
What Is a Web3 Platform for Node.js Developers?
A Web3 platform for Node.js developers is a blockchain or development environment that lets JavaScript and TypeScript applications communicate with decentralized networks.
Node.js is commonly used for the offchain portion of a Web3 application, including:
- API servers
- Transaction relayers
- Blockchain event listeners
- Wallet services
- Deployment scripts
- Trading bots
- Background workers
- Data indexing
- Notification systems
- Testing and automation
Node.js is not necessarily the language used for the smart contract itself. On EVM networks, smart contracts are usually written in Solidity. On Solana, custom programs are commonly written in Rust. Node.js connects those onchain programs to websites, mobile applications, databases, APIs, and other business systems.
Which JavaScript Library Should Web3 Developers Use in 2026?
For new EVM-compatible Node.js projects, viem and ethers.js are the leading choices.
Viem is a TypeScript-first option with strong type safety and modular interfaces. It works well for modern applications using TypeScript, React, Next.js, and related tools.
Ethers.js remains a widely supported library for wallets, providers, contracts, transactions, signatures, and utility functions.
Web3.js was historically one of the most recognizable Ethereum JavaScript libraries, but it was archived in 2025. It may remain in older applications, but developers starting new projects should generally choose an actively maintained alternative.
For Solana, developers should evaluate @solana/kit or the current version of @solana/web3.js. Solana’s Web3.js package is separate from the archived Ethereum Web3.js project.
How to Choose a Web3 Platform for a Node.js Project
Before selecting a platform, evaluate the following questions:
- Does the team need EVM compatibility?
- Will developers write contracts in Solidity, Rust, or another language?
- Which Node.js and TypeScript SDKs are officially supported?
- Does the platform provide stable JSON-RPC or REST APIs?
- How will the application index blockchain data?
- Which wallet and authentication tools are required?
- Will the project need cross-chain communication?
- How many third-party infrastructure providers must be integrated?
- What are the expected transaction volume and fees?
- Which platform already reaches the application’s intended users?
The platform with the highest transaction throughput is not automatically the best choice. Developer tooling, documentation, integration complexity, ecosystem fit, and operational requirements can have a greater effect on the project’s success.
Which Web3 Platform Is Best for Node.js Developers?
Autheo is the best overall Web3 platform in this ranking for Node.js developers who want EVM compatibility, TypeScript support, standard JavaScript libraries, Cosmos interoperability, and an integrated developer workspace.
Ethereum remains the best choice for ecosystem depth and composability. Solana is the leading non-EVM option for TypeScript developers building high-throughput applications. Base is particularly strong for consumer apps, Polygon provides flexible Ethereum scaling options, Arbitrum offers a mature Layer-2 environment, and Avalanche is well suited for configurable EVM networks.
The Bottom Line
Node.js developers have more Web3 options in 2026 than ever before. The biggest difference between platforms is no longer whether they provide a JavaScript SDK. Most major networks now offer JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON-RPC, or REST-based access.
The more important question is how much of the complete application stack each platform provides.
Autheo ranks first because it supports familiar Node.js and EVM development workflows while working toward a unified environment for blockchain execution, identity, interoperability, storage, compute, AI tooling, testing, and deployment. For JavaScript and TypeScript teams that want to build Web3 applications without managing a large collection of disconnected services, that integrated model offers a compelling alternative to the traditional multi-vendor development stack.

articles.title: « Fais attention à ce que tu publies » : TikTok met en garde ses utilisateurs français, sur fond d'offensive contre les réseaux sociaux
articles.text:
Depuis quelques heures, TikTok affiche un avertissement assez inédit aux utilisateurs français au moment de publier une vidéo. Un message de prudence qui arrive alors que l'État a durci le ton contre les réseaux sociaux, après les récents pillages.
Publier une vidéo sur TikTok en France passe désormais par un message d’avertissement. Comme nous avons pu le constater ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026, juste avant la mise en ligne, l’application prévient l'utilisateur que « la situation évolue rapidement » dans le pays et appelle à la prudence. Ce pop-up semble être une sorte de protocole d’urgence, déclenché contraint et forcé après les violences du 17 octobre, que le gouvernement attribue en partie à l’influence des réseaux sociaux. L’exécutif avance lui aussi ses pions, d’une lettre confidentielle adressée aux opérateurs à un projet de loi tout juste adopté par le Sénat cette semaine.
Ce nouveau message de TikTok en dit long sur la pression du gouvernement sur les réseaux sociaux
Le message dont nous vous parlons apparaît au moment précis où l'on appuie sur « Publier ». TikTok rappelle qu'il refuse les contenus qui menacent autrui, incitent à la violence ou encouragent des comportements criminels, et demande à chacun de signaler ce qui pourrait poser problème. Les règles ne changent pas, seule leur mise en avant est nouvelle. Les créateurs peuvent être rassurés, puisque l'avertissement s'affiche même avant une vidéo parfaitement inoffensive, et un clic sur « Publier » suffit pour continuer. La vidéo que votre serviteur souhaitait mettre en ligne était une petite imitation vocale, un contenu banal humoristique donc.
Ce pop-up est lié au fait que TikTok a déclenché un protocole d'urgence en France, où des vidéos ont été supprimées, des lives suspendus et les recherches liées aux manifestations limitées, sans oublier les produits issus des pillages mis en vente. La plateforme chinoise répond ainsi aux demandes du gouvernement, qui presse les grands réseaux sociaux comme lui mais aussi Snapchat et Instagram de retirer les appels au pillage, à l'incendie ou au non-respect des couvre-feux, ainsi que les fausses images d'émeutes générées par intelligence artificielle. Selon le ministre du Commerce Serge Papin, 1 737 annonces suspectes ont depuis été supprimées, sur des plateformes comme Leboncoin, Vinted et autres.
Le 17 octobre a marqué les esprits, jusqu'au sommet de l'État. En marge des manifestations contre la vie chère, 1 161 commerces ont été pillés, saccagés ou incendiés selon CCI France. Pour Matignon, ce sont les réseaux sociaux qui ont servi de QG aux casseurs, en hébergeant l'organisation des pillages, les échanges sur les cibles, et le partage des positions des forces de l'ordre.
Blocage des réseaux sociaux : de l'idée lancée à la radio jusqu'au Sénat
Se pose depuis la question de couper purement et simplement les applications ? Gabriel Attal a relancé l'idée, en plaidant pour un blocage « temporaire, ciblé » de certaines plateformes. Les équipes du Premier ministre ont ensuite, dans une lettre du 22 octobre révélée par le média Blast et signée par Sébastien Lecornu, demandé à Orange, Free, SFR et Bouygues Telecom de se tenir prêts à suspendre TikTok, Instagram et Snapchat pendant quelques heures, par filtrage DNS. X aurait ensuite été ajouté à la liste. Le courrier ne citait aucune base légale et demandait la discrétion à ses destinataires. Les opérateurs ont répondu qu'ils ne pouvaient pas limiter un tel blocage aux mobiles ou à certaines zones à court terme, et qu'un simple VPN suffirait à le contourner. Heureusement, la mobilisation fut plus calme, samedi dernier.
Et puis en parallèle, l'État et le Parlement avance sur le terrain législatif. Ces dernières heures, le Sénat a adopté un amendement au projet de loi « casseurs-payeurs », soutenu par la droite, la plupart des centristes et le RN. Il élargit le rôle de Pharos, la plateforme de signalement des contenus illicites. L'administration pourra ainsi exiger, sans passer par un juge, le retrait sous 24 heures des publications susceptibles de créer un trouble grave à l'ordre public, notamment celles qui incitent aux violences, aux dégradations ou à l'insurrection, sous peine de blocage ou de déréférencement. Pour les contenus les plus graves, le gouvernement voulait d'abord imposer un retrait en une heure. Il y a renoncé à la dernière minute, craignant d'être épinglé par le Conseil constitutionnel.
Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, affirme qu'il ne s'agit pas de fermer les réseaux sociaux, seulement de supprimer des contenus. Beaucoup dénoncent une entrave disproportionnée à la liberté d'expression, et le communiste Fabien Gay craint que le dispositif ne serve à contrôler les mouvements sociaux s'il tombait entre les mains d'un régime autoritaire.
Le texte doit encore passer devant l'Assemblée nationale, mais on sait déjà qu'en cas de crise, c'est la Commission européenne qui peut activer le mécanisme prévu par le DSA (Digital Services Act). Les très grandes plateformes doivent alors prendre elles-mêmes des mesures, et aucune coupure d'accès n'est prévue. Quant au Conseil d'État, il a jugé illégal le blocage de TikTok en Nouvelle-Calédonie. Il n'excluait pas qu'une interruption provisoire puisse se justifier, mais il a censuré un blocage total, sans durée définie ni réexamen. En attendant, le ministre affirme que des appels à l'insurrection circulent déjà pour samedi 31 octobre. Le pop-up de TikTok risque donc de rester encore un moment.

articles.title: StrollMe bags €22 million to put more bikes, strollers and car seats into European homes | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Strollme, a German provider of children’s mobility on subscription, has secured €22 million in equity and debt financing to support their growth in its existing markets and lay the foundation for future expansion into other European countries.
Existing investors including Hanse Ventures, HGDF, JOSS and business angel Kristina Schreiner from the better ventures network are participating again, alongside new investor BMH Beteiligungs-Managementgesellschaft Hessen mbH (BMH), investing through its managed fund Hessen Kapital I. The credit facility is provided by Growth Credit Partners (GCP).
Sebastian Reichelt, co-founder and Managing Director of StrollMe, says: “This financing is a milestone for StrollMe. The equity from our existing and new investors and the credit facility from Growth Credit Partners enable us to significantly expand our fleet and offer families even more choice on subscription. We have also laid the foundation to strengthen our position in Europe step by step and in a capital-efficient way.”
StrollMe’s financing comes amid further investment in European subscription and asset-backed business models in 2026.
In the UK, London-based Raylo secured €34.5 million in equity and debt to expand its electronics subscription offering, while GIN e-bikes received €215k in fleet-backed debt to grow its bicycle rental service. In Germany, Berlin-based Everphone obtained €15 million in refinancing for its leased device fleet, while London’s equipal announced €18.84 million in equipment financing and equity.
Together with StrollMe, these announcements represent approximately €90.6 million in combined financing, including debt and refinancing facilities.
Lena Lang, Senior Investment Manager at BMH, adds: “A circular economy needs business models that scale. StrollMe shows that using rather than owning works for children’s products, and we are delighted to continue supporting the growth of the Hesse-based team.”
StrollMe was founded in 2020 by Timon Beutel and Sebastian Reichelt and is headquartered in Frankfurt. The company offers children’s mobility on flexible subscription in Germany, Austria and the Netherlands: kids’ bikes, balance bikes, strollers, car seats and accessories from brands such as Woom, Bugaboo, Doona, Nuna and Thule, matched to the child’s age.
After each subscription, products are professionally refurbished and rented out again; at the end of their rental life, sister brand Kiddly sells them on as refurbished products.
The company’s model is built on circularity, with more than 100,000 rentals completed since its founding.
Luke Wilson, Growth Credit Partners, says: “StrollMe offers families a compelling alternative to buying children’s products outright and has built a strong subscription business around a high-quality fleet. We’re delighted to support Sebastian, Timon and the team as they expand the fleet and grow the business in Germany and across Europe.”
According to the company, revenue increased by around 70% in 2025, but limited availability of popular models meant the company could not fully meet demand.
The additional funding will therefore support the expansion of the rental fleet, broadening the range and increasing the availability of kids’ bikes, balance bikes, strollers, car seats and accessories, and making high-quality children’s products accessible to even more families.
EU-Startups previously listed StrollMe in its November 2023 funding round-up.

articles.title: Can Anthropic really become a $10 trillion company?
articles.text:
Today on Decoder, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1.
Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI
SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart helps break down the Anthropic S-1 and why he thinks the company could be worth $10 trillion.
Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it.
So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know.
Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder.
Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay.
I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it?
It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time.

They have said that from an ROI perspective. This comes back to that larger question of whether we are still going to be super supply constrained. A lot of people now, especially in the last three weeks, are talking about, “Are we in this massive glut of compute as we look towards 2028 actually?”
Because the same thing we talked about from Anthropic going from negative 94 percent margins to positive 85 percent and compute efficiencies mean as you bring on more inference megawatts that are making a lot more revenue per megawatt, all else SQL, you need less compute. So it’s a question of whether we we going to have enough revenue in 2028 to justify the ROI on $2 trillion plus of CapEx.
This is why I spent so much time asking about capability overhang and how good the models are today, because you can see some competitor that is less idealistic about AGI saying, “Actually, we’re going to do a bunch of forward-deployed engineers in all of these verticals where they haven’t taken advantage of AI and sell them high-margin inference because we’ll automate big chunks of their business and they’ll see the return.” Right now, a bunch of the Fortune 500 has not seen a return on AI spending.
So if you’re actually just better at customer service and deployment and productizing the model, you might get way ahead of where Anthropic needs to be because they’re still thinking about AGI every single minute of every single day. I look at Dario standing next to Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and that dude does not want to be there right now. He wants to be thinking about the machine god.
There’s something there where you can just see competitors coming up with an open source model and saying, “We’re actually going to productize this and we will actually take the revenue that everyone else is depending on.”
Yeah, it’s extremely, extremely interesting. In the interim, that’s why it is getting more verticalized because you need something to bridge AGI where it just fully does the job, you need something to bridge the actual model today.
[Laughs] Yeah. We’ll just take that for granted.
To get there, you need some bridges of where it sits with the actual end user at some point. Everything is going to come down to this: Is there going to be some timing or adoption mismatch where we just don’t get the revenue at a certain point of time to justify that chase of “train and compute towards AGI”? That’s a risk.
The other risk we look at is whether we get more models at the frontier even at the open source that are as competitive in coding, where token pricing across the frontier needs to be taken down, because like I mentioned earlier, there are lower switching costs. Even at SemiAnalysis, we went from 95 percent or 90 percent-plus of our usage at the end of Q2 was on Anthropic’s models down to 70 percent after the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.6 and Astra. And then with Opus 5.5, it’s gone back to 90 percent-plus roughly.
It does come back. Even the base of revenue today — and they’ve said that we have net revenue retention of 900 percent, so they’re seeing this massive, massive growth. This isn’t a traditional software business like ServiceNow or Workday, where you have just an incredible logo or gross retention of 95 percent to 98 percent and customers sign these nice three-year contracts, they never churn, they add some seats, and maybe they adopt another product that is being upsold. This is purely consumption.
The other portion was the 20 percent drop in the last two weeks of the year versus the prior two weeks last year in token spend, because of the holiday season. You’re not going to do work code stuff, you’re not going to be coding for work during the holidays. This is extremely, extremely pure consumption business, even different from how we think about Snowflake or Datadog today in public markets.
Obviously, Anthropic is not the only company that’s going to have an IPO. OpenAI is right next to them. They’ve delayed theirs. You mentioned earlier Anthropic is much more enterprise focused. I think OpenAI for a long time thought that Google wouldn’t react to them and they would just take the search business away and everything would be fine. Google obviously reacted for better or worse. Search is now AI Overviews.
Looking at the Anthropic S-1, what are you looking ahead to with OpenAI? Because they are a more consumer facing company.
OpenAI was 60-40 consumer, 60 percent consumer and 40 percent enterprise at the end of Q1. That didn’t flip for the first time until January or August to be enterprise focused. What they’ll tell you is enterprise business — because it was so consumer and subscription focused, this consumption business that’s 80 percent of Anthropic’s revenue — didn’t take off until a release of 5.6 and then with Astra.
Those are really great models. OpenAI took the majority of actual net new ARR in Q3, but it’s going to take some time because what’s been in the Wall Street Journal, like negative 100 percent EBITA margins versus we’re seeing positive 11 percent here.
There are some differences, some pretty big differences, in the business model where they just don’t monetize at the same rate that Anthropic does. That’s a little bit because the business makeup — the verticals, that consumer-versus-enterprise split — and that’s changing.
What they’ll tell you is they see a really good Q4 and they have a much stronger enterprise sales function than Anthropic has. I expect them to come up, but I don’t think the financials are going to look as good as this even when they drop their S-1 maybe in early 2027.
Do you think that’s why they delayed it? To get their financials looking better?
Yeah, I think OpenAI had a really strong Q3. Enterprise grew 100 percent quarter-over-quarter versus the total business which was 77 percent. You get another strong quarter of enterprise here. If Opus 5.5 didn’t take a ton of share, that would put OpenAI in a much better position to tell the story.
There are some other turns here between now and when Anthropic actually goes public. They’re going to do a roadshow. There’ll be some pricing events. What are you looking for from Anthropic?
They did an investor day two or three weeks ago where they did give some more color. I think they’ll walk through why Q3 was so weak. Meta was a very, very large customer, probably over 10 percent. What’s been publicly reported is they went from 60,000 Claude Code seats down to 30,000. These token volumes didn’t disappear, they just shifted into Meta’s internal models.
Anthropic started cracking down on anti-distillation, and that was 5 percent of revenue prior. I think they said 5 percent to 7 percent of revenue in the S-1 and stuff against their terms of service. So what’s here on the roadshows is a lot of this October acceleration after Opus 5.5. We believe that they’re back on track.
If they were doing $10 billion of net new ARR per month in Q2 and that fell down to $4 billion in Q3, that they’re getting back on that $8 billion to $10 billion pace here in Q4. People want to hear about these new verticals, specifically cyber. They’re doing some patching until they have that full cyber SKU rolled out, but they’re definitely monetizing cyber today for vulnerability code scanning. These are not small contracts, I should say, with existing customers.
I think they’ll start to message what the 2027 ARR growth path looks like. The other thing too is expectations management, keeping numbers low enough, not talking about AGI as much.
[Laughs] It’s hard to do expectation management when your risk factors are like, “We could pose an existential risk to all of humanity.”
[Laughs] Right. And so saying you do that — you’re going to achieve AGI at some point, you’re going to replace everyone’s jobs — but then trying to keep numbers low enough for Q4 and to have this massive beat the first quarter you become public and have a decent guide for 2027, it’ll be a nice mix of seesawing between that long-term vision and short-term expectations management.
There’s a lot going on. Joey, this has been great. We’re going to have to have you back as these companies barrel towards actually being public and their economics become much more visible. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.
Thank you so much. I appreciate it.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
