articles.title: Investable.Africa launches platform to connect African startups with investors - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African startup funding platform Investable.Africa has launched in open beta, giving founders access to a database of more than 4,000 investing firms and investors free access to deal flow from all 54 African countries.
Investable.Africa grew out of a WhatsApp group founder Craig McLeod – who also runs online store builder BoxCommerce – has run for the past decade as both a venture capitalist and a founder. The group brings African founders and VCs together with three aims – increasing funding into Africa, eliminating bad term sheets, and helping founders build the networks they need.
“For 10 years I’ve watched great African founders struggle to reach the right investors, and sign terms they didn’t need to accept,” said McLeod. “The group showed what happens when founders and investors talk openly. Investable.Africa takes that to every founder on the continent, not just the ones who already have the right phone numbers.”
The platform allows founders to build a profile covering their problem, solution, traction, team and current round, with every profile checked by the Investable.Africa team before going live. Founders can upload a pitch deck, which only approved investors can open, and a data room, with founders deciding who sees which folders.
Founders can search the investor database by stage, cheque size, sector, lead or follow, ownership target, founder focus and location, with each firm’s partners and contact routes listed. The database is built from public lists, which are credited openly. Founders can also connect Claude, ChatGPT or another AI assistant to the database to shortlist firms that fit their round and draft personalised outreach for review.
Founders can see who has viewed their profile, opened their deck or read a file, post updates to investors following them, and receive messages from investors addressed to the whole founding team.
Investors use the platform for free, and are vetted before they can see full profiles and decks. They can filter startups by region, country, sector, stage, round type and raise size, or view only companies currently raising. A deal flow overview brings together matching startups, open access requests, data rooms and updates, while investors can request data rooms with a short note explaining their interest and follow startups to receive founder updates by email.
Investors can also list their own firm in the database, and can buy vouchers to sponsor a founder’s listing for a year, with credit as the sponsor.
Founders can build a profile for free, with a listing costing US$99 a month or US$299 per year. Investable.Africa takes no share of any raise and does not handle investment money.

articles.title: Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks using 'Silent Train' framework
articles.text:
Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including for zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems.
The framework has been dubbed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation, and refreshes it continuously.
Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, the threat research division of communications company Lumen, have been tracking Silent Train for three years and confirmed that Volt Typhoon exploited at least four zero-day vulnerabilities in attacks targeting edge and management infrastructure.
Targets include telecommunication firms, government agencies, defense contractors, educational institutes, utilities/critical infrastructure, satellite service providers, IT firms, MSPs, transportation, aviation, and emergency services.
Black Lotus Labs’ observations indicate the most targeted regions are California, Texas, and Hawaii, suggesting a focus on Indo-Pacific matters.
Volt Typhoon previously targeted U.S. critical infrastructure, including communications, energy, transportation, and water systems, with CISA warning that it seeks to establish access for potential disruption during a future crisis or conflict.
According to the researchers, Silent Train's deployment was partly fueled by the FBI's disruption of KV-Botnet, a botnet that Volt Typhoon used to evade detection when attacking critical infrastructure in the US.
Silent Train relay network
Silent Train is practically a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices that Volt Typhoon uses to hide the origin of its attacks.
The operators route their activity through VPS infrastructure outside the United States, then pass it through hacked devices such as routers that act as intermediate relays before launching attacks.
Black Lotus Labs says Intelbras modems served as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices acted as hops in the U.S.
The threat actor's use of Silent Train involves exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, exfiltrating data, and maintaining persistent remote access to compromised systems.
By monitoring Silent Train activity, the researchers were able to observe zero-day exploits for the following products:
- CVE-2026-16812 – VeloCloudOrchestrator
- CVE-2026-20127 – Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN
- CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 – N-able N-central
- CVE-2024-39717 – Versa Director
- Quest KACE (suspected zero-day)
Compromising these platforms gives threat actors broad administrative control, enabling credential theft, remote access, and reach into downstream customers without the “noisy” lateral movement that might trigger detection.
“To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node,” Black Lotus Labs explains in a report today.
“This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and “live off the land” utilities.”
After the session ends, typically in under 8 hours, the threat actors remove all their tooling, keys, and configuration files from the disposable relays.
By early 2025, researchers noticed that the framework become hybrid, using disposable relays alongside compromised enterprise systems thaat were retained between one and three months.
Black Lotus Labs believes Silent Train was reserved for high-value targets and careful, hands-on operations conducted on China Standard Time (CST) timezone. The use of zero-days against those targets further strengthens the assumption.
The researchers recommend strengthening security around centralized management systems, restricting internet access to administrative interfaces, rapidly patching vulnerabilities, and centralizing logs with longer retention.
They also advise monitoring for unusual administrative activity, reviewing trusted connections that could expose customer or partner networks, and following CISA and NCSC guidance on Volt Typhoon.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Paula, española trabajando en Holanda: “Puedo decir que ahorro entre 800 y 1.100 euros todos los meses”
articles.text:
Paula, una ciudadana española que lleva cerca de dos años viviendo en Holanda, ahorra “entre 800 el mes que menos gano y 1.000 o 1.100 el mes que más gano”, pagando un alquiler de unos 2.000 euros al mes, agua y electricidad incluidos, de los que su parte es de 1.000 euros. “Sí que es verdad que es caro”, admite; la dificultad para encontrar alojamiento se debe a que, en sus palabras, “La demanda aquí en Holanda es muy grande y hay muy poca oferta”, lo que hace que los precios estén, a su juicio, “un poco desorbitados”.
El seguro es obligatorio en el país de residencia y de trabajo y cuesta 142 euros al mes; se le abonan unos 129 euros del Estado, por lo que, según sus cálculos, los gastos personales de Paula ascienden a unos 11 o 12 euros al mes: la ayuda se determina en función de los ingresos de cada persona.
Su otro gasto regular es el gimnasio, con 38 euros, y la línea telefónica con datos ilimitados a cambio de una promoción para menores de 30 años, con 25 euros. Paula y su novio (con quien comparte vivienda) tienen una cuenta conjunta en la que ingresan 150 euros cada uno para la compra, pero su gasto medio en comida (tanto de ella como del novio) es de 300-350 euros al mes.
Se desplazan en un coche compartido que funciona con gas, pero consume gasolina, un gasto de 80 euros al mes, de los que se le reembolsa parte a Paula por kilómetros recorridos por su empresa. También destina entre 300 y 350 euros al mes al ocio, a lo que suma suscripciones como Netflix, Prime o Spotify. Le sobra algo de dinero, concretamente lo que no gasta de su cuenta bancaria, y ahorra 180-190 euros al mes en una cuenta de inversión. En el mejor de los casos, Paula puede ahorrar unos 1.200 euros al mes con estos dos tipos de cuenta.
Aunque Paula no menciona sus ingresos (lo que dificulta el cálculo de ahorro en función de los gastos), la suma del alquiler (1.000 euros para Paula), el seguro (11 o 12 euros, una vez descontada la ayuda), el gimnasio (38 euros), el móvil (25 euros), la mitad de los gastos de comida (150 euros; aunque más bien la mitad de 300-350 euros, ya que ella y su novio gastan esa cantidad entre los dos), la gasolina (80 euros, de los que su empresa se encarga de parte) y el ocio (300-350 euros) asciende a entre 1.600 y 1.700 euros al mes (si los 80 euros de combustible son solo los de Paula) o más (si se incluyen los de su novio). Sin duda, ahorra según sus posibilidades, restándole la suma mencionada anteriormente a su salario.
Cómo funciona la ayuda sanitaria
La prestación social parece ser la zorgtoeslag y, según la Agencia de Impuestos de los Países Bajos (Belastingdienst), en 2026 se puede acceder a ella con un ingreso anual de hasta 40.857 euros para una persona sin pareja a efectos de la prestación, y de hasta 51.142 euros entre los dos para una pareja a efectos de la prestación. El patrimonio del beneficiario a 1 de enero también está sujeto a un máximo, y asciende a 146.011 euros en el primer caso y a 184.633 euros en el segundo.
Sus pagos se reducen a medida que aumentan los ingresos. Por ejemplo, con un ingreso computable de hasta 29.500 euros en el caso de una única persona, o conjunto en el caso de dos personas, durante el año 2026, según la tabla oficial, la prestación asciende a 129 euros al mes, y a 246 euros al mes para dos personas (no 129 euros por persona). La cantidad de la prestación no depende de la prima del seguro.
Según la información facilitada por Paula, a ella se le reconoce una subvención de unos 129 euros al mes; no especifica si el Gobierno considera que ella y su novio forman parte o no de una unidad familiar a efectos del cálculo de la ayuda.
El procedimiento de solicitud es único, a través de internet y con el DigiD (identificación oficial neerlandesa); una vez concedida, se sigue cobrando cada año siempre que se cumplan las condiciones. Para ello, hay que cumplir los requisitos, entre los que se incluyen la contratación de un seguro de asistencia sanitaria básico en los Países Bajos y disponer de la nacionalidad neerlandesa o de un permiso de residencia otorgado por el Gobierno neerlandés; Paula, ciudadana española, dice que la recibe; la página web del Gobierno neerlandés no especifica cómo se concede a los ciudadanos de la UE.
Lo que no entra en sus cuentas
En las cuentas de Paula no figuran dos cuestiones más: en primer lugar, el plazo para contratar el seguro básico en caso de trabajar para un empleador neerlandés y pagar allí el impuesto sobre el salario (lo cual no se menciona expresamente), que es de cuatro meses; quien espera demasiado se arriesga a una multa, y mientras no se asegure, la atención corre por su cuenta.
También hay que tener en cuenta la franquicia que los asegurados deben sufragar antes de que el seguro cubra la atención; se trata de un pago estándar de 385 euros (en 2026) por persona de 18 años o más. Quedan fuera de la franquicia, entre otras cosas, las visitas al médico de cabecera y la enfermería a domicilio.
El coste de una vivienda en alquiler es de media un 4,4 % más alto en julio de 2026 que un año antes, con un aumento del 4,5 % en la vivienda libre y del 3,8 % en los contratos existentes sin cambio de inquilino (según el CBS, la Oficina de Estadística de Holanda). Se trata de un porcentaje inferior al registrado en este tipo de operaciones en los años anteriores: 4,9 % en 2025 y un 5,4 % en 2024.
Para situar este aumento porcentual en perspectiva, el Observatorio de Emancipación del Consejo de la Juventud de España, basándose en datos de mediados de 2024, indica que el alquiler mediano de una vivienda libre era de 1.072 euros al mes, lo que suponía el 102,3 % del salario mediano neto de una persona joven asalariada que quisiera vivir sola.
El artículo de Genbeta relacionado con esto incluía la información sobre la evolución de los sueldos frente al alquiler para los representantes de la Generación Z.
La última actualización de la información sobre el seguro y la ayuda sanitaria neerlandesa tuvo lugar el 15 de septiembre de 2026 con la publicación de los presupuestos de los Países Bajos para 2027.
Por el momento, el Gobierno neerlandés prevé que la prima media aumente en 12,50 euros, hasta situarse en 169 euros al mes en 2027; el importe máximo de la ayuda para el seguro en el caso de una persona sin pareja a efectos de la ayuda será de 140 euros, y la franquicia ascenderá a 400 euros; es decir, habrá una subida de 11 euros en la ayuda máxima frente a un aumento de 12,50 euros en la prima media del seguro; los costes individuales dependerán de la aseguradora en cada caso concreto, por lo que la situación de Paula en 2027 estará sujeta a los cambios.

articles.title: Journées Stars E.Leclerc : Fonctionnement, Avantages et Astuces — Frandroid
articles.text:
Que ce soit pour remplacer son smartphone, trouver un nouveau PC ou faire des centaines d’euros d’économies sur un téléviseur, le site d’E.Leclerc est devenu en quelques années un incontournable des sites marchands français pour acheter des produits high-tech.
Il faut dire que l’enseigne E.Leclerc propose régulièrement des opérations ponctuelles qui permettent de faire de belles économies. Parmi elles, les Journées Stars se distinguent par leur durée très courte et leurs avantages réservés aux porteurs de la carte de fidélité E.Leclerc. Mais il faut encore savoir quand regarder et quels produits sont concernés.
Qu’est-ce que les Journées Stars E.Leclerc ?
Les Journées Stars E.Leclerc sont des opérations promotionnelles de courte durée, consacrées à une marque ou à une catégorie de produits (smartphone, téléviseur, électroménager, etc.). Principalement proposées sur le site E.Leclerc, elles fonctionnent sur le principe d’une vente flash : les avantages sont accessibles pendant un à deux jours seulement et peuvent tomber également le weekend.
Leur particularité tient aussi à la sélection des produits. Une opération peut mettre à l’honneur une gamme d’une marque précise, comme Apple, Samsung ou Acer. Une autre peut concerner une catégorie entière, par exemple les téléviseurs, les smartphones ou l’électroménager, avec plusieurs marques représentées.
| Type de Journée Star | Produits concernés | Exemples de marques ou de catégories | 
| Une opération dédiée à une marque | Une sélection de produits ou une gamme de cette marque | Apple, Samsung ou Acer | 
| Une opération dédiée à une catégorie | Une sélection de produits de plusieurs marques | Téléviseurs, smartphones ou électroménager | 
En 2026, E.Leclerc a par exemple organisé une Journée Star TV le dimanche 1er mars, avec 30 % en Tickets E.Leclerc sur une sélection de téléviseurs, puis une Journée star JBL le samedi 6 juin, avec 30 % en Tickets sur une sélection d’enceintes Bluetooth. Ces deux opérations ne duraient que 24 heures.
E.Leclerc annonce parfois en avance des Journées Stars sur sa page Facebook ou dans les médias. Vous pouvez alors repérer les produits concernés, comparer leurs caractéristiques et vérifier leur prix avant le lancement. Il suffit ensuite d’acheter pendant les dates indiquées pour bénéficier de l’avantage.
Quels sont les avantages exclusifs des promotions Journées Stars E.Leclerc ?
Les Journées Stars permettent de récupérer jusqu’à 20 % du montant de vos achats éligibles en Tickets E.Leclerc, et parfois jusqu’à 30 % ou 34 % sur certaines opérations ou marques. Sur un smartphone, un PC ou un téléviseur, cela peut représenter plusieurs dizaines, voire plusieurs centaines d’euros à utiliser pour vos prochains achats.
Les Tickets E.Leclerc sont des euros crédités sur votre carte de fidélité après l’achat, sous forme de remise différée. Pour un téléviseur à 500 euros avec 20 % en Tickets E.Leclerc, vous payez donc 500 euros et recevez 100 euros sur votre cagnotte.
Voici ce que vous récupérez pour un achat éligible de 500 euros :
| Avantage en Tickets E.Leclerc | Montant payé à l’achat | Montant crédité sur votre carte | 
| 20 % | 500 € | 100 € | 
| 30 % | 500 € | 150 € | 
| 34 % | 500 € | 170 € | 
Exemples de calcul, selon le taux proposé et sous réserve des conditions et plafonds de l’opération.
Pour comparer cette offre à celle d’un autre marchand en ligne, tenez compte du prix payé et de l’utilisation que vous ferez de la cagnotte. Si vous faites régulièrement vos courses chez E.Leclerc, les Tickets pourront servir à régler une partie de ces dépenses (comme vos courses hebdomadaires par exemple).
Certaines Journées Stars proposent aussi des remises immédiates réservées aux porteurs de la carte E.Leclerc. La réduction est alors directement déduite du montant à payer : vous profitez de l’économie dès l’achat, sans attendre de dépenser des Tickets lors d’une prochaine commande. À titre d’exemple, un produit à 500 euros bénéficiant de 20 % de remise immédiate vous revient à 400 euros au moment du paiement. Le type d’avantage et les produits concernés sont précisés dans les conditions de chaque opération.
Autre point pratique : selon l’opération et les produits concernés, les offres sont accessibles en ligne, au Drive ou dans les magasins participants. Les produits éligibles au Click & Collect peuvent être retirés gratuitement sous deux heures, dans les magasins proposant ce service, pour une commande passée pendant les horaires d’ouverture et au moins deux heures avant la fermeture.
Carte E.Leclerc et Tickets : comment fonctionne la cagnotte ?
La carte E.Leclerc est obligatoire pour bénéficier des offres en Tickets des Journées Stars. Cette carte est 100 % gratuite et disponible immédiatement.
La carte est réservée aux personnes de plus de 15 ans, avec une seule carte par personne, selon les conditions générales d’E.Leclerc.
Vous pouvez la créer sur le site E.Leclerc, dans l’application Mon E.Leclerc ou à l’accueil d’un magasin. Pour un achat en ligne, pensez à associer votre carte à votre compte en ligne.
Les Tickets E.Leclerc sont des bons d’achat en euros qui s’ajoutent à votre cagnotte de fidélité. Vous payez le prix affiché du produit, puis vous utilisez le montant cagnotté pour régler de futurs achats. L’argent n’est donc pas remboursé sur votre compte bancaire.
Les Tickets sont utilisables dès le lendemain de leur obtention, dans l’ensemble des centres E.Leclerc participant au programme de fidélité, au Drive et sur le site E.Leclerc. Vous pouvez les dépenser pour vos courses ou un autre produit : leur utilisation n’est pas limitée à la catégorie qui vous a permis de les obtenir. Les carburants sont toutefois exclus.
| Question | Fonctionnement | 
| Faut-il une carte E.Leclerc ? | Oui, elle est gratuite et disponible immédiatement. | 
| Avec une offre en Tickets, le prix baisse-t-il au moment de l’achat ? | Non, l’avantage en Tickets est crédité sur votre cagnotte. | 
| Quand peut-on utiliser les Tickets ? | Dès le lendemain de leur obtention. | 
| Où peut-on les dépenser ? | Dans les centres E.Leclerc participants, au Drive et sur le site E.Leclerc. | 
| Pour quels achats ? | Tous les produits, hors carburants, sans obligation de racheter dans la même catégorie. | 
Quelles conditions pour profiter des Journées Stars E.Leclerc ?
Les Journées Stars sont réservées aux achats pour votre consommation personnelle. E.Leclerc limite également le nombre maximal de produits qu’il est possible d’acheter par foyer.
Selon l’opération, le plafond peut notamment être fixé à 5 ou 15 articles identiques. La limite est toujours indiquée dans les conditions de l’offre.
Les Tickets E.Leclerc des Journées Stars ne se cumulent pas avec une autre promotion sur les mêmes produits. Vous ne pouvez donc pas additionner deux avantages pour augmenter le montant crédité sur votre carte.
Avant l’achat, consultez les conditions de l’opération et votre espace fidélité. Certaines offres nécessitent une activation : dans l’application Mon E.Leclerc, elles se trouvent dans la rubrique « Avantages », puis « Bons à activer ».
Sur le site, vous pouvez les ajouter à votre carte depuis la rubrique « Mes bons de réduction » de votre compte. Cette activation concerne les offres qui la demandent ; elle n’est pas systématique pour toutes les Journées Stars.
| Point à vérifier | Ce qu’il faut retenir | 
| Produits concernés | Vérifiez que la référence choisie fait partie de la sélection éligible. | 
| Quantité autorisée | Respectez le plafond par foyer indiqué pour l’opération. | 
| Cumul des promotions | L’avantage Journées Stars E.Leclerc ne s’ajoute pas à une autre promotion sur les mêmes produits. |

articles.title: Payer sans déverrouiller son smartphone ? Google Wallet prépare une nouveauté pour aller plus vite
articles.text:
Payer avec son smartphone est très pratique, mais cela demande quelques préalables, comme le fait de vérifier son identité avec votre empreinte digitale ou un code par exemple avant de valider une transaction. Cette validation reste alors active quelques minutes seulement avant d’expirer. Mais Google Wallet pourrait changer cela pour coller à un système proche de ce qui existe déjà dans l’application pour valider les paiements de titres de transport en commun.
De nouveaux indices dans le code de l’application
C’est dans les paramètres de la version 26.42.1003171897 de l’application Wallet que l’on retrouve une option baptisée « Tap to Pay » (« Payer d’un simple geste »), qui fonctionne notamment grâce au NFC. Actuellement, il est déjà possible de désactiver cette option pour les réseaux de transport en commun pris en charge, ce qui permet de valider un trajet sans déverrouiller son appareil. L’arrivée potentielle de cette option pour les paiements de tous les jours offrirait donc un fonctionnement similaire.
Dans l’onglet « Sécurité », « Tap to Pay » apparaît désormais à côté du paiement de titres de transport en commun. – Source : Android Authority
Bien qu’elle soit visible dans le code en dessous de la mention « Indiquez si vous souhaitez valider votre identité lorsque vous utilisez vos éléments stockés dans Wallet », cette option n’est pas encore opérationnelle. En sélectionnant l’option « Tap to pay », l’application se ferme brutalement à cause d’un bug, ce qui rend pour l’instant impossible l’accès aux éventuels réglages ou détails prévus par Google.
La question de la sécurité
Supprimer l’obligation de déverrouiller son smartphone pour régler des achats pose forcément des questions sur la protection des données et la sécurité de vos comptes bancaires. Si un tiers venait à s’emparer du téléphone, l’absence de vérification préalable vous exposerait immédiatement à des risques de paiements frauduleux.
À lire : Google Wallet change complètement l’affichage de vos cartes de paiement, voici à quoi ça ressemble
L’analyse du code ne permet pas encore de savoir si Google prévoit d’ajouter des garde-fous spécifiques pour encadrer cette nouveauté. Dans la mesure où il s’agit d’une option trouvée dans le code, mais pas encore activée, impossible de savoir si Google se décidera à la déployer ou non et dans quelles conditions. En attendant, dites-nous si vous seriez prêt ou non à sacrifier de la sécurité contre de la praticité.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.
Source : Android Authority

articles.title: De Mercredi à From, les 10 meilleures séries à regarder pour Halloween 2026
articles.text:
De Mercredi à From, les 10 meilleures séries à regarder pour Halloween 2026
À la recherche d'une ou plusieurs séries effrayantes à regarder en attendant Halloween ? Les Numériques vous a trouvé 10 séries horrifiques à ne pas manquer en streaming.
Halloween approche à grands pas et vous avez peut-être envie de regarder des séries horrifiques en plus de vous faire peur devant des films du même genre. Cela tombe bien car Les Numériques a fait le tour des plateformes de streaming pour vous proposer une sélection de séries d'épouvante parfaites pour la saison qui donne la chair de poule.
De fictions franchement flippantes comme Ça : bienvenue à Derry et From à des séries plus gentillement effrayantes comme Mercredi et Les nouvelles aventures de Sabrina, voici 10 fictions sérielles pour vous préparer à la fête du 31 octobre à retrouver sur Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, HBO Max et Paramount+ (dont l'offre est accessible via Canal+).
Ça : bienvenue à Derry (HBO Max)
Ça : Bienvenue à Derry
HBO Max
- Date de sortie
- 27/10/2025
- Genre
- Epouvante-horreur
- Durée
- 60 min
- Episodes
- 9
Des événements étranges se déroulent dans la ville de Derry dans les années 1960, liés au clown Grippe-Sou, un personnage mystérieux qui hante les lieux.
Ça : Bienvenue à Derry se base sur le roman Ça de Stephen King pour étendre son univers et la vision mise en place par Andy Muschietti dans ses deux films Ça. Résultat ? Une série absolument terrifiante et magistrale, un petit bijou horrifique du petit écran racontant une histoire captivante, soutenue par des protagonistes attachants, une mythologie fascinante et une mise en scène aussi glaçante que poignante. Tant pis si ça fait peur, on ne veut plus quitter Derry.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
The Haunting of Bly Manor (Netflix)
Dans l'Angleterre des années 1980, après la mort tragique d'une jeune fille au pair, Henry Wingrave engage une gouvernante américaine inexpérimentée pour s'occuper de sa nièce et de son neveu. Ces deux orphelins résident à Bly Manor avec le responsable du domaine Owen, la gardienne Jamie, et l'intendante Mrs Grose. Mais le manoir regorge de faux-semblants, et des siècles de sombres secrets n'attendent que d'être exhumés au fil de cette terrifiante romance gothique sur l'amour et le deuil. Car à Bly Manor, les morts ne sont pas tous des disparus...
Ce drame gothique inspiré de plusieurs histoires surnaturelles emblématiques d'Henry James est le deuxième volet de l'anthologie The Haunting de Mike Flanagan. Portée par une distribution épatante, des décors inquiétants et un récit captivant, cette série sait émouvoir autant que donner la chair de poule.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Widow's Bay (Apple TV)
Le maire d'une ville de Nouvelle-Angleterre souhaite en faire une destination touristique, malgré les avertissements sur le fait qu'elle est maudite.
Vous aimez l'horreur, les intrigues pleines de mystère et l'humour noir ? Alors vous serez comblés par cette série portée par un Matthew Rhys (The Americans) en grande forme. Sur fond de petite île à l'atmosphère inquiétante, Widow's Bay déroule une histoire prenante, soutenue par une mise en scène experte et des performances irréprochables de la part de l'ensemble de la distribution.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Entretien avec un vampire (Paramount+)
En 2022, le vampire Louis de Pointe du Lac raconte son histoire au célèbre journaliste Daniel Molloy. En 1910 à La Nouvelle-Orléans, Louis et Lestat forment une famille vampirique à laquelle vient s'ajouter Claudia, la novice adolescente.
Entretien avec un vampire est l’une des meilleures séries de ces dernières années et a su s’approprier Les Chroniques des vampires d'Anne Rice pour en faire une version plus sensuelle et contemporaine que l'adaptation cinématographique de 1994 avec Tom Cruise et Brad Pitt. De la distribution à l’écriture, en passant par la mise en scène, la cinématographie et les costumes, tout est soigneusement calibré pour proposer au spectateur une histoire gothique délicieusement addictive, portée par les performances impeccables de Sam Reid et Jacob Anderson.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Chair de poule (Disney+)
Cinq lycéens se lancent dans une terrible enquête pleine de rebondissements afin de cerner les circonstances du décès tragique, trente ans plus tôt, d’un adolescent, et découvrent au passage les lourds secrets de leurs parents.
Avec cette série, Disney+ modernise les histoires cultes de R.L. Stine et propose une fiction horrifique à la Stranger Things, avec une bande d'ados confrontée à des forces surnaturelles. Chair de poule mélange humour, drame et épouvante pour donner lieu à une histoire rythmée qui ouvre la porte au genre de l'horreur pour ceux qui ne s'y aventurent pas souvent.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Les nouvelles aventures de Sabrina (Netflix)
La magie se mêle au trouble alors que Sabrina, demi-humaine demi-sorcière, navigue entre deux mondes, sa vie d'ado mortelle et son héritage familial, l'Église de la Nuit.
Cette production Netflix réinvente la sitcom culte des années 1990 pour en faire une série bien plus sombre et tournée vers l'occulte, le macabre et l'épouvante. Sur fond d'histoire sur le passage à l'âge adulte, la série brille par son atmosphère inquiétante, son casting épatant (Kiernan Shipka, Miranda Otto, Lucy Davis...) pour offrir aux spectateurs un mélange de série pour ados, surnaturel et frissons.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Penny Dreadful (Prime Video)
Londres, 1891, une menace quasi invisible massacre la population. Vanessa Ives, une jeune femme aux pouvoirs puissants et hypnotiques, rencontre et propose à Ethan Chandler, un homme rebelle et violent, de s'allier à elle ainsi qu'à Sir Malcolm Murray, un homme riche d'un certain âge aux ressources intarissables, pour combattre cette nouvelle menace.
Laissez-vous séduire par cette série gothique à souhait qui a eu droit à trois saisons entre 2014 et 2016. Portée par Eva Green, Timothy Dalton et Josh Hartnett, cette série entre fantastique, épouvante et drame met en scène des personnages phares de la littérature du 19e siècle pour raconter une histoire aussi macabre que poétique. Des décors aux costumes en passant par la distribution, tout sort son plus grand jeu pour donner vie à une fiction sans pareille.
- Regardez une bande-annonce de la série :
From (Paramount+)
L'histoire d'une ville effrayante au milieu des États-Unis où toute personne qui y entre se retrouve piégée. Les habitants de la bourgade essaient de maintenir les choses aussi normales que possible tout en cherchant un moyen de s'échapper, car la nuit venue ils sont terrorisés par des monstres meurtriers.
Créée par John Griffin (Le Cratère, La Quatrième Dimension) et produite par des anciens de Lost, cette série d'horreur et de science-fiction plaira aux spectateurs qui aiment les personnalités fortes coincées dans une situation impossible. La série captive grâce à une histoire et des personnages fascinants tout en donnant des sueurs froides avec des créatures cauchemardesques.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
Mercredi (Netflix)
La série suit les aventures de Mercredi Addams, désormais étudiante à la Nevermore Academy. Alors qu’elle apprend à dompter ses nouveaux pouvoirs psychiques, la jeune fille doit aussi déjouer une série de meurtres monstrueux qui terrorisent la ville et résoudre le mystère auquel ont été mêlés ses parents il y a 25 ans, le tout en tentant péniblement de nouer de nouvelles relations au sein de Nevermore.
Mercredi propose une histoire palpitante et bardée de rebondissements. Une série généreuse et délicieusement macabre qui saura plaire à tout le monde, de l’ado rebelle à ses parents déboussolés, en passant par l’adepte d’énigmes rondement ficelées. Un tour de force pour une famille Addams dont on a définitivement envie de faire partie.
- Regardez la bande-annonce de la série :
American Horror Story (Disney+)
Maisons hantées, asiles, sorcières, hôtels maudits ou sectes : la série change d’époque, de décor et de personnages à chaque nouvelle intrigue, tout en conservant certains visages familiers au casting. Les histoires mêlent surnaturel, violence, croyances, crimes et traumatismes profondément ancrés dans la société américaine. Certaines saisons finissent aussi par se répondre ou partager des personnages, dessinant peu à peu un univers commun derrière cette anthologie. Chaque chapitre explore ainsi une nouvelle forme de peur, souvent inspirée autant par les monstres que par les êtres humains.
Créé par Ryan Murphy, le showrunner et scénariste derrière les séries Dahmer, Glee et Ratched, American Horror Story est LE programme parfait pour les fans de frissons et d'horreur. Chacune de ses saisons possède sa thématique propre, de la maison hantée au cirque, en passant par l'apocalypse et l'asile, et joue avec brio de son ambiance glauque et de sa tension pour vous river à votre siège. Une série culte à rattraper ou revoir sans modération.
- Regardez une bande-annonce de la série :

articles.title: Wrangling Telemetry at Scale: A Guide to Self-Hosted Observability
articles.text:
Transcript
Colin Douch: Do you ever feel a looming threat of complexity? I feel as I've developed in my infrastructure life, I've developed the ability to almost smell it. It feels like even in simple systems, we're always fighting this uphill battle against this ever-encroaching demon. It's so easy to make something complex, and sometimes that complexity is out of necessity. Our world is complex, so our systems must sometimes also be complex. Sometimes it's out of false necessity. I thought it needed to be complex, or perhaps these days my AI thought it needed to be complex. Sometimes it's out of organic growth. Something started simple and became more complex over time. Sometimes it's just out of a lack of care. No matter what, we live in a world of complexity. For those of us who have to build, run, and operate these complex systems, tough luck, like that's our collective punishment for sins in a previous life.
There's a few escape hatches that sneaky folks like us like to run to when we try and escape that complexity beast. We can scoff and decide to rewrite it. Surely if we rewrite it, then all of the complexity will fall away and reveal the soft underbelly of a simple system that does all the things the complex one did with none of the complexity. Or we might try to ignore it, put it in a box, shield it from solar rays and funny looks, and try not to think about it. Or if we have to touch it, we might fob it off onto whoever is unlucky enough to be our next hire. Increasingly with distributed systems, our old methods don't work. These things become too large to rewrite, too complex to throw in a corner, and so scary that if you gave them to a new hire, they might just run away.
In those scenarios, when we have to stop running and actually have to start to tame the complexity that has been wrought upon us, we have to turn to observability. I often get asked by engineers, because I do have some experience in this field, should I run my own observability stack? My answer is, no. You don't need that hassle. In fact, I think you should put as much effort as you can possibly muster into fighting the urge to do so. You see, it's that complexity demon again. He's invading your mind. As soon as I say that, I often get a Datadog bill or a Splunk bill thrown in my face. Can people stop doing that? I have so many paper cuts on my face. How many folks out there spend at least part of your day trying to tame a Datadog or a Splunk bill? That's crazy that that's something that people have to do.
Doesn't the thought of just chucking Prometheus and Grafana on a $10 a month VPS sound so alluring? No. Back, complexity demon. There is a reason that even in the face of those monumental bills, I will say, do not run your own thing. I will recommend that you stick with a provider. That doesn't mean not changing a provider. You can certainly do better than Datadog and Splunk these days. Please, unless you need to, buy your way out of this problem, you'll save yourself so many gray hairs and so much alcoholism.
There will come a time when your life starts to go downhill where you do need to start doing things for yourself. That billing thing is a real problem. It does get exponentially worse as your telemetry volumes get bigger and you outgrow your providers, or perhaps auditors are coming around asking tricky questions like, why do we shovel so much data to this random third party? Or maybe you've decided your BI folks need a feature that you don't have the clout with your SaaS provider to build for you. Or maybe that complexity demon has finally just sapped your will to live. As complexity starts to consume the systems we run, so too does it consume our observability itself. That's what I want to talk about today. How can we run our own observability stack? What does that look like? What are the tradeoffs? How can we weave a bunch of disparate tooling together into one debugging canvas?
Background
I'm Colin Douch. I, at the moment, am a site reliability engineer at DuckDuckGo. Before that, I created and then co-led the observability team at Cloudflare. Before that, I was a founding member of the SRE team at Xero doing cloud accounting stuff, doing basically the same observability work. Before that, I was doing observability work in the real-world mining sector. DuckDuckGo in particular has been a real trip, because DuckDuckGo still uses Carbon, and Graphite, and Icinga 1, not Icinga 2. Using that to provide observability into a massive Perl monolith has been a challenge, to say the least. All that being said, I have quite a bit of experience building self-hosted observability systems. Today, I want to share that, what I've learned and how people can better build, maintain, and monitor the complexity that seems to have become inevitable these days. Whatever the reason, and there are a myriad, you need to be prepared for the baggage that building your own observability system comes with.
Be prepared to dedicate at least two to three engineers, that's at least to run it. Spend more time and money than you ever thought you would need to. Spend more time in GitHub Issue pages than you ever have in your entire life. Put in an amount of effort that would make you wistfully look at your Datadog bill like you're hoping your ex will take you back.
What Does a Self-Hosted Observability Stack Look Like?
What does a self-hosted observability stack even look like? For most people who haven't been indoctrinated into the all you need is tracing crowd, it's going to look like the three pillars. We're talking systems for metrics, logs, traces, but crucially, ways to tie them together. Observability is not about the data you're storing. It's about how you can move between that data to find what you want. That's the hardest part of building it yourself because there aren't any great open-source tools that allow you to do that, at least by default. No matter what, we're going to need telemetry storage. Let's talk about that. We can start with metrics.
Metrics
If I asked you, what should I use to store my metrics, what answers would I get? I imagine some of you are rolling your eyes and saying, Prometheus, obviously. The more well-researched or newer to the game might say, VictoriaMetrics smugly, and then put on a top hat and a monocle, and show how efficient it is, before laughing and cackling at the Prometheus people. The older folks might suddenly grow another wrinkle and say, Graphite, or RRD, or Carbon. In this instance, I think the Prometheus folks are right, but not for the reason you think. Don't get me wrong. As a time series database, VictoriaMetrics is just better. It just is. If you need a strict what you put in is what you get out type of database, VictoriaMetrics is lossy in that way, so maybe not. In terms of efficiency, in terms of scalability, in terms of ease of running, VictoriaMetrics is what we want.
That's just if you want metrics. We want observability. Prometheus has one feature that VictoriaMetrics refused to implement, exemplars. Exemplars are what allow us to start stitching together metrics into our other types of telemetry. You have to enable them in Prometheus with a feature flag at the moment. They are included in the OpenMetrics spec, the attempt to formalize the Prometheus text exposition. Hopefully that will change soon and everyone will be able to enjoy them. What exemplars allow you to do is attach a second labelset to your metric. The special thing is that that labelset can change but still be attached to that same metric, which allows you to provide an exemplar. For example, let's say we have this nice little error metric. He's running along, all good, no errors. Then suddenly, no, he's fallen over. No, we've got an error. This is standard monitoring. We know this.
Something went wrong, but we don't know what. We just got an error. If we're exporting traces or logs with a correlation ID, we can add that to the error metric as an exemplar. This trace ID is an example of a request that triggered this increase in the error metric. Now we have something to go on. We can start to move between systems. Grafana even has the ability to show these in graphs alongside the metrics themselves, which allows you to one-click jump from your graph that went wrong to traces that tell you why. If you go with Prometheus, eventually you're going to start hitting scaling issues. This is where the VictoriaMetrics folks like to jump back at me and get all smug and point out that VictoriaMetrics has a clustering which allows it to horizontally scale. Prometheus just doesn't. It doesn't horizontally scale at all, really.
It was built with this natural tree structure in mind, like one Prometheus server or a pair of them for redundancy for a set of servers. If you run out of space, you vertically scale or you shard it and split your metrics across different servers. Neither of which are particularly good solutions. Scaling up, you start to hit scaling issues, especially if you're on a cloud provider, pretty quickly. Sharding requires a huge amount of manual effort, especially when there's no natural boundary to shard on, because you then have to create another federated instance to share metrics. It becomes a huge mess.
It begs the question, how do you scale this thing? There are a few dimensions to consider. The number of active time series, which is the number of time series that have had a sample in the last two hours, and your retention, which starts to bound your CPU for queries and things like that. For your active time series, Prometheus buffers the last two hours' worth of metrics in memory, which is known as the head chunk before it's finalized to disk. Unfortunately, that's just Prometheus's design. There's not much you can do about it. At Cloudflare, we found that for each time series in that head chunk, it takes about 4 kilobytes, so use that for your capacity planning. What makes this a little bit easier and solves the retention issue as well is long-term storage systems. You can probably name a few: Thanos, Mimir, Cortex. They all serve to solve the retention problem in different ways.
Mimir and Cortex, through Prometheus's remote write system, directly writing metrics to a receiver service, which removes the need for that head chunk, and then writes them to blob storage. If you are running into head chunk issues, go there. Thanos, on the other hand, because it can only upload completed blocks, which are finalized every two hours, it relies on having to pull directly from the sidecars that run next to each Prometheus instance before it can run a computation, which tends to make highly distributed environments quite difficult with Thanos. There are a couple of tips here that I think, in the general case, make Thanos shine over Mimir and Cortex. The first is the distributed query engine. Usually, when Thanos does a query, it fetches data from all the sidecars and centralizes it and then runs the query over that data, which, if you're querying over a large number of data centers, is disastrous.
It's way too much data. If you use the distributed query engine with that flag there, it pushes that computation down into the sidecars, which then send partial results back and those get combined centrally, which, if you have the architecture to require it, a more distributed system rather than one or two data centers, this unlocks the ability to horizontally scale your Prometheus query layer, which is pretty great when it's for free. The other is the Parquet storage engine. One thing that's really frustrating about the Prometheus world is that Prometheus people tend to be very protective of Prometheus. I remember at PromCon, I think in 2017, 2018, when Alexander first announced VictoriaMetrics, and Brian Brazil and a couple of other maintainers threw together a very quick lightning talk that basically amounted to, no. So too today, because Thanos has a new neat little experiment they're running, rewriting Prometheus blocks into Parquet.
If you use it, the benchmarks are incredibly impressive. They take you to basically the performance of VictoriaMetrics, but without any of the micro-optimizations that VictoriaMetrics does, which is quite exciting. You can have a look at it there. It's just an experiment at the moment, but I'm hoping that maybe that will start to get pulled into Prometheus itself, maybe in Prometheus 3.
Logs
Enough about metrics. They're boring. They're so retro. What we want is logs. We want observability, these things. To me, logs are the most fun part of an observability stack. They're ubiquitous, and they're simple. Just about everyone has done a hello world, which is a log, albeit a terrible one. At the same time, a lot of people get logging wrong. Lots of companies will try and tell you, logs are bad, you should do tracing. There is some merit to that. There's that complexity demon raising his head again, because I can call println, or I can import 10 megs of OTel libs and use their convoluted APIs. I would argue that in most cases, if you can get away with logs, do logs. Here's how you do them right. For starters, as you get more and more loglines, finding things becomes harder and harder. Things like Elasticsearch excel at full text search, which makes this work.
Elasticsearch is commonly used for this sort of thing. Full text search is slow, and even with the indexing that Elasticsearch does, especially if you want to start introducing regexes and wildcards, it starts to fall down. The simplest example I can give is searching for user records. Let's say we're logging a user ID, and we want to search for user 20. This pattern is very common in nginx logs, for example, older things that don't structure logs. Let's search for it. Because we're doing full text search, we also get user 202 and 2070. We can chuck in some anchors and search for breaks between words, but then we start to hit other issues. What if other call sites structure the data differently and it starts to get messy? No, plain-text logs, they suck. What you want is structured logging. People equate structured logging with JSON, and that's what it boils down to these days.
Really, the difference is in the storage engine, rather than how that structure is ultimately produced. You need a storage that allows storing and indexing on those structured fields, ideally with support for dynamic schemas, so you don't have to define up front what your data looks like. Elasticsearch, again, was the go-to for this for a long time. Dynamic field support in Elasticsearch just sucks. You can only have a certain number of dynamic fields in your index before ingestion just stops, and you have to bump the limit in your YAML file. If you bump the limit too high, the performance of your Elasticsearch server just tanks.
I haven't used it, but from what I've heard, OpenSearch, Amazon's fork of Elasticsearch from when things started to go weird with their licensing, does this a bit better. There are more specialized log storage things that seem to fit the bill. The first real competitor to come out was Loki from Grafana, which flips the storage model on its head. Instead of storing one big indexed stream, like a standard database, Loki stores logs in individual streams with stream labels. If you're not a big fan of the whole cattle not pets thing, you could have a stream for Node, or Node and services, like a couple. Crucially, that's all the indexing you get with Loki. If you want a field to be indexed, you have to say that at ingest time, which basically brings us back to that full text search problem. Anything you didn't say you wanted to be indexed goes back into that full text search, which means that you either have to know what you want to search for ahead of time or suffer the penalty of full text search.
That's not very observability of you, Grafana. VictoriaLogs, on the other hand, does not have that limitation. It's a full columnar database like its metrics counterpart. If you're starting from scratch or looking to move, VictoriaMetrics would be my recommendation. Of course, you could just go with a dedicated columnar database, like inserting logs directly into ClickHouse and using SQL to query them, or a gateway like Quesma. Those tend to be a lot higher maintenance in my experience. If you're not already running one, it's not worth starting just to run your logging system. Cloudflare got away with this by having a whole dedicated ClickHouse team to run the stack for us. Not everyone has that luxury or the ability to poach half of ClickHouse Inc. Remember the complexity demon? You really do need a columnar database with support for dynamic indexing. The reason for that is inherent in observability itself. We don't know what we don't know. Having to decide ahead of time what fields to index just doesn't work when we start to look at those unknown problems.
Speaking of observability, how can we actually start using logs to answer those questions? We have to think about the usability of our data. A lot of time, logs are sprinkled around. We're like a chef, just sprinkling them in wherever you need one. That leads to this annoying situation where for a single error, you have a bunch of disparate logs that are all unordered and all just strewn about, like old clothes you can't be bothered to put away. What we really need is a way to tie all of those logs together into one event, which is where canonical logging comes in. I think Stripe came up with this idea originally. It's a really simple idea that bridges the way between logging and tracing. Instead of doing this, where we have a bunch of individual log calls, we instead collect all our fields into a context block as we go through a function.
Then at the end, or in Go's case in a defer func, we emit it as one thing. Instead of having a bunch of disparate logs, we have one log per block of work. With one logline, there's no chasing through different streams to try and find what you need. It's all just there in one event. Generally, we do this at the handle level. If your service is an HTTP microservice, or in some sort of logic or top-level function, like a processing function, if not. You can even be super fancy and generate a UUID and add it in. Look, we've got a correlation ID that we can add to our exemplars. Between structured logging into a proper columnar database and canonical logging, we have a pretty good way to debug individual services, which might be enough if that's your architecture. Remember that complexity demon? Fight it off as much as you can.
Tracing
If you must, and we're here to talk about distributed systems after all, we need to talk about how we can debug across multiple systems that all talk to each other. We need to talk about tracing, which is what we're all here for. This is the debugging distributed systems track after all. I hope I've made a case that you can actually get pretty far with metrics, with exemplars, and canonical logs. As with so much here, keep fighting that complexity demon. Tracing explodes your complexity. Suddenly, you have to decide what tracing libraries to use. You have to worry about how you're going to export your data and in what format and what context format you're going to use, and how that gets serialized and deserialized between your systems and your RPC. There's a little secret here, one that tracing advocates don't want to tell you. Tracing is only tracing if it comes from the distributed tracing region of San Francisco.
Anything else is just sparkling logs, because that's really what they are, just logs with a little bit of structure dictated on top of them, rather than being arbitrarily freeform. Take a structured log, add a random ID, we'll call it a span ID, shall we say. Add a couple of passed in IDs, one that represents the request, we'll call that maybe a trace ID. We'll generate another one that we take in, and we'll call that the parent span ID. We've got a span. We collect a bunch of those spans together based on that top-level request ID, and we've got a trace. Why is tracing important? It's because of those parent-child relationships. It's a simple idea, but a pretty crucial one. Logs come in and get ordered by time, but on computers, time is weird and flexible and sometimes goes backwards, which is a crazy thing that time can do.
There's no real guarantee that a log coming in was actually produced before another log that came in later. The idea of a parent span ID strips that causal relationship there and models what we actually want. This function called this other function, rather than having to infer that based on temporal information. Having that alongside the wide context is tremendously useful in debugging, especially when you can communicate those IDs over a network between services, and stitch together spans from all over the place where those time issues become infinitely worse.
Because tracing has become this hot buzzword, there are so many tools that have popped up to try and be the one to take, process, and store your traces, which brings me to OpenTelemetry, or OTel. OTel, the spec, and the associated libraries attempt to try and mask over that complexity demon that is inherent in tracing. The OTel libraries make sane default choices for you so that if your entire stack is using them, they just work masking over a lot of those choices. Useful if you're just getting into tracing and you don't really care, or if you're instrumenting multiple different services in multiple languages and want to make sure that you've made the same decisions in each one. It's worth mentioning as an aside, OTel also has a spec for metrics and logs, but there's a reason I haven't mentioned them until now. I would recommend you don't use them.
Remember that complexity demon? Don't make things any more complicated than they need to be. The OTel project attempting to ingratiate themselves into existing open-source communities like Prometheus has caused quite a stir because they're completely ignoring what exists and just trying to dictate a spec. I highly recommend looking at the Prometheus mailing list for all the OTel discussions, if you need a dose of cortisol in your system, because it's quite a read. I would recommend the OTel libs for tracing. They're the most stable of the telemetry types, and the complexity they introduce becomes worth it because tracing is so useful. There are older alternatives out there. You can instrument with Jaeger or Zipkin, but both of which are older and being deprecated or are deprecated in favor of the OTel format. OTel is really your only choice here.
It's all well and good exporting a bunch of data. A lot of people just import OpenTelemetry, chuck in a bunch of auto-instrumentations and call it a day, but we're doing observability and observability isn't about collecting a bunch of data. We actually care about being able to use that data to solve problems. We want to store it and we want to care about what that storage can provide us in terms of useful queries and links to other systems. Yet again, we have a few options here, mostly Jaeger or Tempo. In the past, I would have recommended Jaeger as the original, but I think Tempo starts to tip it over because it starts to provide those observability features. Jaeger has made some impressive strides here. The new monitoring page in Jaeger, which I'd recommend you upgrade to, provides RED metrics for free from your tracing data. When it actually comes down to getting actionable insights out of your data, Tempo wins every day.
It actually has a bunch of features that make it quite useful. Things like TraceQL is tremendously powerful for searching through your spans. The ability to generate metrics from your traces is fantastic to enable those cross-telemetry bridges. The main problem I have with it is that it uses its own storage engine. From what I've seen, that doesn't scale well beyond a few tens of thousands of traces per second. Maybe that's just a me problem. Jaeger on the other hand, can scale as you go, which is why we went for it at Cloudflare. It's storage system agnostic, so you can start with Elasticsearch and then graduate to ClickHouse if necessary. Which provides a much nicer scaling path, but at the cost of losing out on a bunch of features, a lot of which we ended up implementing in our own private fork as much as I wanted to open source them.
Which is really frustrating because that's the point of tracing, collecting large amounts of data and then being able to sift through it. I really think there's an opportunity here for Jaeger to improve or a new system to blossom, because the lack of a fully featured scalable tracing system is probably one of the biggest downsides of the open-source observability world. The VictoriaMetrics folks are cooking up VictoriaTraces, which might be a solution here. It uses the same columnar DB as their logs offering, so provides that necessary wide event storage, but it's a little too new and untested for me to consider at the moment. Even though the point is to collect large numbers of wide events, you can't collect everything, at least not without bankrupting yourself.
We should probably talk about sampling. There are two types of sampling we can consider here. One easy, one more complex, head sampling and tail sampling respectively. Head sampling is a no-brainer. Probabilistically determine whether or not we should keep a span or a trace. Where this gets messy is when we then try and reason about our traces afterwards. For example, if we're only keeping 10% of our spans, we have to remember to multiply every stat we generate from those by 10. If we then change that ratio, we have to remember when we changed that ratio and apply different multipliers at different times. The hack here, if you're doing head sampling is to embed the sampling rate into your spans itself, so your query engine at query time can do that multiplication in line, which is quite useful. In a proper columnar database, because those numbers don't change very often, they compress to basically nothing.
Tail sampling is where things get interesting and messy, to the point that I would actually recommend against tail sampling, unless you are starting to get into the types of issues that head sampling causes. Tail sampling adds a little bit more logic to the flipper coin and choose whether you accept a span or not. Instead, we put an if statement in the mix. If it's an error, sample it at this rate. If it's not an error, sample it at a different rate. Useful if your errors are being drowned out by the noise of all your successes, which is a nice problem. There's that complexity demon again. Tail sampling requires you to have somewhere to buffer a trace because you don't know until all the spans come in whether or not something is an error. It requires you to have that resource usage that comes with buffering things and complexity and hard decisions, like how long to buffer for, which there is no real answer to because it entirely depends on where all your spans are coming from, and how to shard your traces so that all the spans from one trace end up on the right nodes so you can make the decision with all the data is a giant mess. Generally, if you are trying to host your own tracing system, I would recommend against it unless you are hitting tens of thousands of spans per second level. If you are considering it though, all of those sampling decisions we just talked about have to happen somewhere and that somewhere is a telemetry pipeline.
One of the most annoying things about modern observability in general is that because it pushes you to higher cardinalities and higher rates of data, that implies higher processing, and that processing has to happen somewhere. Generally, it means you're running a collector of some kind that takes your telemetry, runs logic over it, transforms them, drops them, that sort of thing. In the old world of logs and metrics, we can get away with just shipping things to the backend. Not so much these days unless you want your budgets to run away from you. You need some sort of processor. Again, a few options here. OTel itself provides one, the OTel Collector written in Go. Grafana Alloy is similarly based off of the OTel Collector. Vector recently acquired by Datadog, so take what you will from that, but written in Rust. Again, it starts to get messy. I love the OTel project.
It's a great effort. The idea of standardizing all of your telemetry formats so you can move between providers is a noble one even if it doesn't work in practice. The OTel Collector is a bit of a mess. That's speaking as a contributor to it. Because it's run by the CNCF, there's a certain amount of bureaucracy involved. Because it's run by unpaid volunteers, even minor changes can take weeks. If you want timely changes, that requires you to fork internally and run your own builds of a collector. It's a real pain point if you actually want to manage one. I'm not sure, at least until the components start to get a bit more stabilized that I can recommend running it. You've got a lot of data, lots of it. Data isn't observability, like a warehouse full of unlabeled boxes isn't a library. A Grafana instance full of graphs that no one understands isn't a debugging tool.
UI - Tying It All Together
The last thing we need is something to tie it all together. Something that we can actually use to solve problems. Generally, that comes in the form of a UI, because fortunately AIs and APIs haven't taken over the world quite yet. Again, Grafana may seem like the optimal choice here, or perhaps the only choice, save for those individual UIs out there. I would present you with another, Perses. It's a CNCF project that is designed to try and be a bit more of a user friendly and open-source friendly version of Grafana. Grafana in particular has the annoying problem of being owned by a company, which unfortunately in our capitalist society means they have to make money, which I mean, fair dues, no problem with that. I acknowledge the realities of our society. In pursuit of less, they end up locking a bunch of features behind paying them money.
Features that are really useful for making a better observability system, like usage tracking on certain dashboards or proper data source permissions. Even when folks try and contribute those features open source upstream, they get shut down. It's a bit disappointing. On the other hand, Perses provides all those features along with a few others, like better support for automated dashboards and things like ephemeral dashboards, dashboards that disappear after a certain amount of time. Because I think that's actually something a lot of people get wrong with dashboarding in particular. I've seen Grafana instances with thousands of built-up dashboards, copies of copies of copies of minor things changed. Because Grafana locks down those features behind its paywall, then most self-hosting people are not going to pay. You can never be quite sure whether a dashboard is safe to delete. I think there's an interesting distinction to be made in your dashboarding about two different use cases.
You have your BI dashboards. The ones that tell product folks things that keep the business going. How many users are there? Your click-through rate for things. Even your SLOs are a BI dashboard to some extent. These tend to be much longer lasting because business metrics don't really change that much. Then you have debugging dashboards. These display things like service metrics, specific drill-downs on known failure modes, things like that. I hate these because they tend to just stick around despite the fact that when you're debugging a problem, it tends to be different each time. If they're not, that's another question to ask yourself. Why are you getting the same problem over and over again? I would encourage you if you're running a dashboarding solution to go and tag each of your dashboards with one of these two labels and then audit your debugging dashboards for deletion.
It'll make it so much easier to use, which brings me back to Perses. Ephemeral dashboards automate that whole process for you. No manual cleanup required. They can get automatically deleted after a certain amount of time. They can even be automatically created by your alerting tool via webhooks specifically for any firing alert. Once you've got everything flowing together, we have to have to start thinking about how all this data weaves together into a cohesive structure. That all stems from our correlation IDs or trace IDs, if you're doing tracing. You see, by embedding those into our metrics with exemplars into our canonical logs as a context field and into our traces, we start to get this neat flow where our telemetry data merges together. This becomes a typical flow. Your alert fires, you have a metric spike. You picked Prometheus, so you have an exemplar on that metric, a trace ID attached to an example request that triggered it.
You click through to Tempo or Jaeger, you're now in a trace. You can see exactly what service in your distributed system starts behaving. You can see what downstream calls it caused. Because you've instrumented canonical logs, each span has a corresponding single logline. If you put enough context into them, because we all love high context as we should, you can see exactly what failed where.
What About the Future?
What about the future? Because observability stacks do have one thing, multiple separate tools do kind of suck even though you can make them better by weaving them together. There's a lot of duplication when you have multiple different systems, because what you really have is metrics, logs, and traces. It's the same data with different granularities. Your logs are basically subsets of your traces, and your metrics are just counts and aggregations over them as well. Effectively, if your traces are good enough for the wide enough context, you don't actually need to generate the others in your application because you can synthesize them in your observability tool. It means that one instrumentation of your wide events just gives you the rest of the telemetry. There are starting to be tools that do this well. SigNoz for one does an ok job at being an all-in-one solution, although it suffers from the problem of doing everything fine and nothing great.
Your pipelining tools are starting to develop these features as well with OTel Collectors connector format, and vectors log to metric function to do similar. I think the key thing here is that logs and metrics aren't going away. They're just changing. I do see a future where in the open-source world, not just the SaaS world, you only have to instrument your applications once with these wide high-context events. From those, all your other types of telemetry are derived. Metrics for graphing and alerting, logging for debugging and tracing for locating problems, all just the one original source of data where the three pillars aren't gone, but they're instead pushed up the stack. In doing so all work in harmony on one grand observability canvas.
Questions and Answers
Liz Fong-Jones: You said that the state of open-source tracing tools is less mature than the other signals. Why do you think that is? What can people do to solve that problem?
Colin Douch: There's a lot of aspects to a good tracing tool and a lot of open-source projects do some of the things required. Open-source contributions are always welcome. The CNCF Jaeger project is tremendous. Please go contribute, if you're welcome to it. The other upcoming things like HyperDX from ClickHouse and things like that are also worth keeping an eye on because they are up and coming.
Liz Fong-Jones: I noticed you didn't mention the word AI anywhere in this talk. What thoughts might you have about how can AI help us build or run these telemetry systems?
Colin Douch: I have a lot of thoughts around, especially like SRE workloads and AI because what it amounts to for AI observability at the moment is chucking a bunch of traces into a context window and hoping that something gets spat out the other end. There's work to do in distilling information before it hits an AI agent. AI agents are very useful at summarizing information, but especially with wide high context events, that context window gets burned very quickly. There needs to be some intermediate layer that helps in the meantime.
Liz Fong-Jones: You're saying that I shouldn't just shove an MCP server directly on top of the logging API and have it spit out 500 kilobytes of logs?
Colin Douch: You're welcome to try, but I'd love to know how much hallucination is there.

articles.title: Instagram monetizará videos largos: “exploramos opciones para que los creadores reciban pago”, afirma director de la app
articles.text:
Adam Mosseri, director de Instagram, reaccionó a los videos de larga duración que la plataforma comenzó a probar y afirmó que exploran opciones de pago para quienes produzcan ese tipo de contenidos.
“Entendemos que la economía es muy importante, y estamos explorando múltiples opciones para ayudar a los creadores de videos de formato largo a recibir pago”, señaló en Threads.
La iniciativa se vincula con Features, la nueva función con la que Instagram permitirá publicar videos horizontales de hasta 90 minutos.
Por ahora, la herramienta está en fase de prueba y solo está disponible para un grupo de creadores de contenido en Estados Unidos. Mosseri advirtió que el despliegue será gradual. “Esto va a tomar tiempo para que esté bien, pero estamos emocionados y comprometidos”, explicó.
Además, indicó que las características todavía no fueron lanzadas por completo y que la compañía amplía lentamente el acceso mientras recopila comentarios.
Cómo funciona el nuevo formato de video en Instagram
Features está diseñada para que los usuarios puedan pasar de clips breves a contenidos extensos sin salir de Instagram.
Los Reels funcionarán como adelantos: si un creador vincula un video corto con una producción completa, quienes encuentren ese fragmento podrán pulsarlo y continuar la reproducción.
El formato apunta a contenidos como entrevistas, episodios de pódcast y videopodcast, que requieren más tiempo de reproducción.
Hasta ahora, muchos creadores usaban Instagram para compartir extractos y dirigir a su audiencia hacia otras plataformas para ver el material completo.
La prueba inicial se desarrolla en dispositivos móviles. Según la información difundida sobre la función, Instagram prevé llevar posteriormente la experiencia a pantallas grandes mediante una aplicación para televisores, aunque todavía no informó una fecha ni los dispositivos compatibles.
Cómo reaccionaron los usuarios al nuevo formato de video de Instagram
Los usuarios reaccionaron con reservas al nuevo formato de videos largos de hasta 90 minutos que Instagram comenzó a probar. Algunos cuestionaron que la plataforma se aleje de su función original como red social para compartir fotografías entre amigos.
“¿No podemos recuperar el viejo Instagram, cuando era una aplicación para compartir fotos con amigos? ¿Y cuando mis amigos realmente veían mis publicaciones?”, escribió uno de los usuarios en respuesta a la novedad.
Otros señalaron que Instagram debería priorizar la monetización de quienes ya producen contenido breve. “Con todo respeto, si no van a monetizar como YouTube, deberían seguir siendo una plataforma de formato corto, porque eso es lo que hacen bien”, comentó un usuario.
La posibilidad de que Instagram explore formas de pago para los creadores de videos largos también generó críticas. “¿Qué tal si primero les pagan a los creadores de formato corto?”, planteó otro usuario.
Qué otras nuevas funciones hay en Instagram
Además de Features, Instagram ha incorporado herramientas para modificar la experiencia de consumo y creación de contenidos.
Una de ellas es Your Algorithm, que permite revisar y ajustar los temas que la plataforma utiliza para recomendar publicaciones en el feed, Reels y Explorar. La función ofrece mayor control sobre los intereses que influyen en las sugerencias.
Para los creadores, Instagram reforzó Edits, su aplicación de edición similar a CapCut, con opciones para crear carruseles, organizar proyectos y aplicar efectos. También sumó herramientas para reemplazar el audio de publicaciones ya difundidas y editar miniaturas después de publicar un video.
Otra novedad es Instants (o Instantáneas), una opción para compartir fotos temporales y sin edición con Amigos cercanos o seguidores recíprocos.
La plataforma además amplió las etiquetas para perfiles generados con inteligencia artificial y las normas de originalidad para fotos y carruseles, con el objetivo de priorizar contenidos propios en las recomendaciones de usuarios que los descubren.

articles.title: Amazon confirma “crediário” no Brasil; pagamento chega a 12 parcelas • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Amazon confirma “crediário” no Brasil; pagamento chega a 12 parcelas
Nova modalidade oferecida pelo e-commerce pode ser acessada pelo aplicativo. Usuários podem ativar diretamente no aplicativo.
A Amazon confirmou ao Tecnoblog que começou a oferecer um novo parcelamento sem cartão diretamente no aplicativo. O e-commerce se junta a concorrentes como Mercado Livre e Shopee, que já liberam uma espécie de “crediário” para realização de compras. A modalidade está em fase de implementação e pode não aparecer para todos os consumidores.
O Amazon Crédito é apresentado diretamente no site e app da Amazon. Apenas titulares podem solicitá-lo e a operação passa por análise de crédito. A documentação da Amazon indica a cobrança de taxas e de juros, mas os detalhes só são apresentados diretamente ao cliente final.
No fim das contas, trata-se de um empréstimo. Um exemplo fornecido pela Amazon cita o crédito de R$ 100 em 5 meses, com parcelas de R$ 27,74, totalizando R$ 138,70 com os juros. O Custo Efetivo Total (CET) fica em 12% ao mês. A Amazon nos explicou que a modalidade chegará em etapas, e recomendou que os interessados chequem periodicamente se a opção está disponível.
O Amazon Crédito é uma alternativa às compras no cartão de crédito. A ideia é aumentar o leque de opções para adquirir produtos, a exemplo do que já acontece em apps concorrentes. A Shopee, por exemplo, tem o SParcelado.
A ativação do Amazon Crédito pode ser feita da seguinte maneira:
O limite de crédito e a quantidade de parcelas mudam de acordo com o cliente. Nem todos terão direito às 12 vezes num primeiro momento. Isso pode mudar conforme o uso e o pagamento em dia.
O Tecnoblog apurou que o Amazon Crédito não é operado pela Amazon. Na realidade, o consumidor assina o compromisso financeiro com a Celcoin Sociedade de Crédito Direto, que está inscrita sob o CNPJ 48.632.754/0001-90. Esta instituição financeira tem autorização do Banco Central.
Há alguns requisitos básicos para os titulares que desejarem o Amazon Crédito. Segundo a empresa, é necessário ter idade entre 21 e 75 anos, renda mensal de pelo menos R$ 1.500 e documentação válida, assim como endereço no Brasil. Todos os clientes com conta ativa na Amazon podem pedir o Amazon Crédito. Além do cadastro, é necessário passar por uma análise de crédito antes de começar a usar.
Depois de aprovado, o “crediário” é exibido na Amazon. Não é possível utilizá-lo para empréstimos ou compras em outros sites, por exemplo. Uma vez ativo, basta selecionar a modalidade nas opções de pagamento.

articles.title: Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV
articles.text:
“Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about.
Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030. It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the GMC Sierra EV, and of course the divisive Hummer EVs. And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category.
So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. Yes, you did read that right, it does weigh 4 tons. And yes, the electric Escalade does weigh a third more than the last gas-powered one we tested.
The Escalade IQ holds its own among the medium-duty trucks.

Jonathan Gitlin
Since the loss of the EV tax credit, the Escalade IQ has been a harder sell.
