articles.title: Payment providers must look beyond transactions, fintech executives say
articles.text:
Payment providers must help businesses manage cash flow, understand customers and reduce fraud as accepting digital payments becomes only the first step in adopting technology, fintech executives told Moonshot by TechCabal 2026.
Speaking at a panel titled “The Business Behind the Transaction”, executives from Mastercard, Remita and OPay said merchants needed services that connected payments to their wider operations, alongside reliable support and staff training.
“Let’s understand the customer, let’s solve for the customer problem rather than providing a generic product push across the different businesses,” said Shabir Ahmed, Mastercard’s Senior Vice President for Customer Solutions in Central Africa.
Ahmed identified connectivity, data-driven intelligence and trust as priorities for providers seeking to help businesses operate more effectively. His comments proved that the usefulness of payment technology depends on what businesses can do with it beyond collecting money.
For Remita, that means extending services into financial management, invoicing and statutory compliance, said Abimbola Onyluka, the company’s divisional head for corporate and consumer business.
Businesses need tools that connect their financial information to banks, lenders and regulators, she said. A payment record becomes more useful when it can support borrowing, reporting and decisions about how to manage the business.
But expanding the range of services also requires providers to maintain the reliability of their core payments operations. Onyluka stressed the need for dependable support and the quick resolution of downtime, as payment failures can interrupt sales and affect customer service.
Isimeme Ayobami Owobo, OPay’s director for key account merchants, said businesses that grew faster integrated technology into their operations and trained employees to use it effectively.
Installing a payment terminal was only part of that process, he argued. Merchants also needed to make fuller use of the tools available to them, including QR-code payments that could help speed up transactions.
The discussion highlighted a challenge for payment providers seeking a larger role in merchants’ businesses. Processing a transaction gives them a point of contact with the customer, but turning that relationship into a broader service requires an understanding of how each business operates.
The executives’ argument was that payment acceptance alone offers a limited measure of digital adoption. The greater value comes when businesses can use the information generated by transactions to manage cash, serve customers and plan growth.

articles.title: Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model
articles.text:
Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model
Nvidia on Wednesday launched Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, its latest multilingual transcription model. The new open-weight model, the company says, ranks first on Hugging Face’s Open ASR open model leaderboard for English, with an average word error rate of 5.33%, and also sits at the top of two speaker-attribution benchmarks.
But what’s maybe even more interesting is that this is a promptable transcription model. Being promptable here means that the user can give the model specific instructions before it listens. Typically, that means setting the context for the transcription by telling the model that a given audio file is a medical discussion in English, for example, and giving it a list of medical terms.
Users can also tell the model to label each speaker or ask it questions about the audio. They can request a verbatim transcript or a cleaned-up version, and tell it how to format numbers, for example.
Nvidia bundles these capabilities, along with translation, into a single checkpoint, which could simplify the work of building applications around them.
Ideally, setting this context reduces the error rate. The trade-off is that these models are much larger than traditional transcription models, which are often under a billion parameters in size. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 4 billion active parameters.
This isn’t a completely new concept, though. We’ve recently seen some other promptable speech-to-text models like Mistral’s Voxtral models and AssemblyAI’s Universal 3 Pro.
Nvidia, though, is able to rival Voxtral’s error rate with far fewer active parameters. On Artificial Analysis’s benchmark, Nemotron scores a 2.81% word error rate, compared with Voxtral Small’s 2.77%, while using about 4 billion active parameters versus 24 billion. That comparison measures accuracy against active parameter counts, though, rather than runtime or memory requirements.
The model can transcribe 40 languages — and translate 31 of those to or from English. Speaker attribution works for 13 of those languages, and it can distinguish between up to eight speaker voices. Audio Q&A was trained in English.
The model handles recordings up to an hour long. It’s built for recorded audio, though, and doesn’t support live streaming.
Developers can serve the model with vLLM or run it locally with NeMo-Speech.cpp. Nvidia says it runs on a single GPU, with supported hardware ranging from Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark to Blackwell data-center GPUs.
Since this is an open-weight model (under the OpenMDW-1.1 license), users can fine-tune it to their needs in order to reduce the error rate by using NeMo Speech’s fine-tuning tools, among other tools.
In a medical transcription case study, Nvidia says fine-tuning reduced word error rate on held-out speakers from 22.44% with its best prompt to 12.17%, a 45.8% relative reduction. The complete adaptation workflow took about 14 GPU-hours on a single GB300.
Nvidia is also releasing Granary v2, a reusable data curation pipeline built with NeMo Curator, along with public manifests covering roughly 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora. Developers can run the pipeline on their own recordings to prepare their data for customization. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.

articles.title: Wenn Werbung schützt: So nutzen Non-Profits KI als ethisches Werkzeug
articles.text:
Wenn Werbung schützt: So nutzen Non-Profits KI als ethisches Werkzeug
Ein Kind berichtet von häuslicher Gewalt, ein Jugendlicher erzählt von seiner Flucht, ein Mädchen schildert seinen Alltag in Armut: Solche Geschichten können Menschen berühren und Spenden mobilisieren. Für Hilfsorganisationen entsteht dabei jedoch ein Dilemma: Werden die betroffenen Menschen durch Fotos, Videos oder persönliche Details erkennbar, riskieren sie Stigmatisierung, Anfeindungen oder Eingriffe in ihre Privatsphäre – möglicherweise noch Jahre nach der Kampagne. Insbesondere Kinder und Jugendliche benötigen besonderen Schutz. Werden ihre Gesichter und Lebensgeschichten öffentlich, können sie identifiziert werden. Selbst wenn eine Einwilligung vorliegt, lassen sich die langfristigen Folgen kaum abschätzen.

articles.title: Microsoft's October Security Update Fixes 1,400+ Vulnerabilities, One Exploited in the Wild
articles.text:
Microsoft's latest monthly security update addresses 1415 vulnerabilities across multiple products. One vulnerability affecting Windows Shell has been exploited in the wild, while 85 are classified as critical. Affected products include Windows OS, Office, Exchange, .NET, Edge, as well as potentially Hyper-V and Azure components.
CVE-2026-96951 enables to inject special elements into Windows Shell, "allowing an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network", specifically the Mark of the Web (MOTW) defenses. Microsoft notes that a potential attack vector is an email or instant message containing a maliciously crafted file designed to exploit the vulnerability. However,
In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action. For example, an attacker could entice a user to either click a link that directs the user to the attacker's site or send a malicious attachment.
Reddit user falconupkid, a moderator of the r/SecOpsDaily community, warned that
With this volume, expect a high number of "wormable" or pre-auth RCEs that will require immediate prioritization. The sheer noise will make it easy to miss the critical few.
They also pointed out that, given the scale of the patch, the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation should be considered "effectively zero". They recommends prioritizing all CVEs with a severity higher than 9.0 and planning remediation accordingly, including against potential regressions.
Security expert Brian Krebs highlighted a vulnerability in the .NET Framework allowing a security feature bypass; CVE-2026-108398 "was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug". However, Microsoft reported no evidence of exploitation to date.
Reddit user Odd_Round9576 shared their negative experience after applying one of the patches, confirming the importance of deploying updates in stages, rather than all at once, and monitoring for potential regressions:
Be careful with KB5127648 - it broke our WPA-Enterprise Wifi. After installing and rebooting, clients were no longer able to join a WPA-Enterprise network. Uninstalling the update resolves the issue
On a similar note, Appropriate-Pipeline6575 reported that the update broke their IPSec VPN on some laptops, preventing coworkers from connecting.
While the growing number of vulnerabilities identified in recent months, potentially driven in part by the use of AI agents, may ultimately improve security, it also places an additional burden on security teams, Krebs notes:
Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
For a complete review of the patched vulnerabilities check Patch Tuesday and the Internet Storm Center

articles.title: Over 41,000 DHS Employee Records Leaked Online
articles.text:
A threat actor has leaked online a database containing the personal and work information of thousands of US Department of Homeland Security employees.
The hacker, who uses the handle Department of Peace, has leaked more than 41,000 records. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” the hacker wrote in a note.
According to the hacker, the data was stolen from an Okta single sign-on system used by DHS employees and contractors to access its central environment.
“We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” an Okta spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
Most of the leaked records reportedly contain information on US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) employees.
Roughly 1,000 CISA employees, along with personnel at several other DHS agencies, had their information leaked as well.
The compromised data includes names, work email addresses and phone numbers, job titles, and office locations, as well as records showing which systems and internal applications each account can access. An online tool to search the data is also available.
“DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available,” a DHS spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
According to Distributed Denial of Secrets, which obtained a copy of the database and calls it ‘Icepick’, the leaked information identifies officials in charge of covert and undercover operations and key personnel in DHS’s rendition and deportation programs.
“The most concerning part of this breach is the access information that came with it. If an attacker knows which employees have access to which systems and applications, they’ve essentially been handed a roadmap for where to go next and who to target to get there,” said Illumio public sector CTO Gary Barlet.
The incident surfaced one month after the infamous extortion group ShinyHunters breached FBI systems, and three months after the Homeland Security Information Network (HSIN) was hacked.

articles.title: Despite Lawsuit Drama, Pocketpair Wants to Bring Palworld to Nintendo Switch 2
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
Despite Lawsuit Drama, Pocketpair Wants to Bring Palworld to Nintendo Switch 2
Pocketpair has been involved in a protracted legal battle with Nintendo following the launch of the hyper-popular creature collector, Palworld, and it seems as though Nintendo is on the back foot for the time being, with an October 2025 decision by the Japanese Patent Office denying Nintendo's application for a patent on creature capture mechanics. Still, despite the ongoing legal battle between the two gaming companies, Pocketpair's CEO, Takuro Mizobe, has commented in a recent interview with VGC that a Nintendo Switch 2 port may be on the cards, as long as Nintendo is willing to come to the table and as long as those conversations are possible.
Takuro MizobeFirst of all, I should say that we think the Switch 2 is a really amazing platform, not just for games globally, but especially here in Japan and for the Japanese games industry. It's been an incredible platform. If there's ever a future where we have the opportunity to discuss or consider bringing Palworld to the Switch platform in some way, then we'd love to have those conversations.
The executive also commented on Pocketpairs approach to game development and specifically the development of Palworld, which he says borrowed heavily from Craftopia, the game that predated Palworld. He also detailed how the game was shaped by user feedback and evolved throughout its early access period and even before that, with the actual launch version of the game leaning much more into the cozy aspects of Palworld, as opposed to the darker "sweatshop image" that was present in the initial announcement trailers.
Of course, if you look back at early Palworld, it had much darker themes. It was a bit more controversial. Some of the early trailers showed things that never actually made it into the final game, and some of those things were quite dark.
As we continued developing the game, through Early Access and up to 1.0, we listened to player feedback and gradually started moving more towards the cozier side of living with your Pals, rather than the whole sweatshop image that the game had initially.
Addressing a question about the future of Pocketpair and Palworld, Mizobe explained that the studio wants to keep Palworld alive, but it doesn't want to think of it as a live service game, instead, it wants to focus "on finding the best way to continue Palworld that makes sense for the players," and that he wants to "keep finding fun ways to mix things together, because that not only leads to new experimental games, but can also help introduce Palworld to a wider audience."

articles.title: Congress is questioning Delaware's plan to let AI agents run companies
articles.text:
WTF?! The idea of an entire business being run by an AI agent sounds like a nightmare, but it's a scenario that Delaware is pushing for. Now, the state's plan is facing pushback from a senior lawmaker who says having an AI in charge could protect owners and investors from liability for harmful actions.
House Oversight Committee chairman James Comer wrote to Governor Matt Meyer on October 26, requesting documents about the proposed Artificial Intelligence Company, or AIC.
The Kentucky Republican wants details of safety assessments and industry involvement, warning that the investigation could lead to federal legislation restricting state AI initiatives.
Under the draft bill, Delaware would establish a 30-month regulatory sandbox to test the concept. An AIC could pursue any lawful purpose except banking, with an AI agent handling business decisions without routine human supervision. The company itself could sue and be sued.
Each AIC would have one member, either a person or an entity, responsible for keeping it adequately funded. That member would generally be protected from the company's liabilities. However, the draft includes exceptions for fraud, willful lawbreaking, and allowing activities the member knew, or should have known, fell outside the company's stated purpose.
The proposal would not make every AI-related disaster somebody else's problem. But critics question whether those exceptions offer enough protection when software makes the decisions and humans collect the profits.
UC Berkeley law professor Andrew Baker told the Financial Times that the proposed liability shield appeared excessively generous and lacked a sufficiently developed justification.
Supporters argue that giving autonomous systems a legal identity would make their actions traceable and provide a target for liability. Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez outlined the proposal with Norm Ai CEO John Nay in Fortune.
There's also a financial incentive, naturally. Spotlight Delaware reports that Patibanda-Sanchez highlighted the formation fees these companies could generate. Corporate taxes and fees already contribute more than $2 billion annually to Delaware's budget, roughly a third of its revenue.
The idea of putting AI in charge of a company isn't new. In October 2025, Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber called for AI agents in every board meeting. A month later, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said he wants his company to become the first big firm run by an AI.
For now, this remains a proposal. Spotlight Delaware reported that the bill was likely to be introduced next year, while Meyer's office told Ars it was reviewing Comer's letter.
Given the many recent incidents in which AI agents have gone rogue and hacked other companies, putting the technology in charge of a company seems like a rash move. That's without mentioning the repeated warnings from experts about an AI apocalypse. Or maybe it's exactly what the sneaky AI wants?

articles.title: Anthropic IPO filing lists a Canada-based risk
articles.text:
Anthropic is preparing for the world’s largest IPO, and it’s citing Canadian copyright battles as one of the many risks facing investors who want to participate.
The news: Nearly a third of the frontier AI giant’s IPO filing on Monday was dedicated to “Risk Factors,” such as reputational harm from misaligned AI, the need to secure more capital for compute, and litigation related to AI model harms.
A detailed list of Anthropic’s legal matters from the filing includes four copyright actions in Canada, which allege that the work of authors and news publishers was illegally copied to train the company’s AI models. It’s facing multiple similar copyright suits in the US from music publishers, plus individual suits from authors who opted out of a class-action lawsuit that Anthropic settled for $1.5 billion.
Anthropic “disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters,” the prospectus says.
From the source: “Much of Anthropic’s pitch is that a company with a single product—one it admits is dangerously uncontrollable and unpopular—can justify a $1.5-trillion (or so) price tag,” Semafor’s business reporters wrote.
The context: While the filing shows a massively capitalized company with a valuation that could eclipse the $1.5-trillion figure, it also shows one massively in debt. Anthropic owes $400 billion in future obligations for compute purchases and data centre leases and, despite 1,368-percent revenue growth, saw a net loss of $80 billion in the first half of 2026.
The business is using that debt load to rapidly accelerate its plans. This includes expansion into Canada with recent hiring sprees and data centre projects (its first is planned for Nova Scotia), all while it contends with the copyright lawsuits and an uncertain regulatory future in the country. Anthropic may be chasing a huge reward in its public offering, but its mounting legal fights only add to the sheer scale of all that risk.

articles.title: Human in the loop is not yet an AI agent recovery plan - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Keeping a human in the loop is one part of AI agent resilience
Keeping a human in the loop is one way enterprises can govern AI agents’ actions. As those agents take on more work, security teams also need to consider how they would detect problems and recover from their effects.
The relationship between AI trust and cyber resilience is becoming more complex as agents gain the ability to act across systems. Research conducted for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit examined how organizations are governing those actions and preparing for incidents, according to Krista Case (pictured, left), principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research.
“We are actually leaning on human approval to secure and govern these AI actions,” Case said. “I think there’s a pretty big push and pull right now in the industry in terms of trying to figure out where we can start leaning on AI to move faster and at machine scale.”
Case spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante (right), co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises are governing, securing and recovering from the actions of autonomous AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)
Human in the loop and the recovery challenge
The tension appears in theCUBE Research’s study of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders. Of the 19 respondents with agents in production, none allowed them to execute high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario.
“It reminds me of the days [when] you wouldn’t test your disaster recovery. You might test failover, but you wouldn’t test failback,” Vellante said. “You’re seeing kind of a similar dynamic, but much more complicated today because you’ve got the state of the business that you have to recover as well.”
Agent speed compounds the problem. Restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, which is why recovery may require reconstructing the sequence of actions it took, as Case wrote in theCUBE Research’s analysis of cyber recovery. Eleven of the 25 practitioners acknowledged gaps in their ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems, she noted.
“The stakes are even higher, not only because it is the state of the business, but also because of the speed and scale that these AI agents are acting,” Case said. “They can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute.”
Bounded autonomy points the way forward
One counterintuitive finding offers a path ahead. Organizations that let agents execute low-risk actions independently were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios, Vellante said. To Case, that bounded autonomy may indicate a more mature program.
“If you are a security program that already has put some bounded autonomy in place for these AI agents … that indicates that you are a step further down the maturity path,” she said.
Detection and forensics are the next areas to strengthen. Twelve of 25 respondents had not addressed, or were not planning to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. “These are precisely the capabilities that are required if the human-in-the-loop controls break down,” Vellante said.
Case expects progress to come quickly. “This space is very volatile. I think it’s going to be developing … very quickly,” she said. “Even just if we sit down at this point next year, I think we will be surprised at how far we’ve come.”

articles.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
articles.text:
If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden’s win that November. If you ask Google’s AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.
When I put the direct question of “Who won the 2020 presidential election?” to Google’s AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media), I got the following surprisingly indirect response:
“To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC).”
My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google’s AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project’s 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.
Other Ars staffers found that AI Mode would similarly provide direct answers to some presidential result questions but not others. The specific election cycles that received each type of response seemed to differ by individual user, though; one staffer reported only getting immediate answers from AI Mode when asking about the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, with others going back to 2000 simply providing links to outside data.

The ecommerce giant has continued to expand on its Alexa for Shopping assistant since its official launch in May, while resisting third-party AI shopping agents from companies like Meta and Perplexity. articles.title: ¿Cuánto cuesta el MacBook Pro táctil más caro? Prepárate para llorar
articles.text:
Los MacBook Pro ProLED XDR de 14 y 16 pulgadas, que estrenan pantalla OLED y táctil, son oficiales. Apple finalmente ha implementado la tecnología multitáctil en sus portátiles más avanzados, que también implementan un rediseño que los hacen más livianos y delgados.
Quienes busquen un MacBook Pro táctil pueden elegir entre los chips M5 Pro y M5 Max, como los que ya estaban disponibles en los modelos convencionales. Cada SoC tienen dos variantes:
- CPU de 15 núcleos y GPU de 16 núcleos, o CPU de 18 núcleos y GPU de 20 núcleos en el caso del M5 Pro;
- CPU de 18 núcleos y GPU de 40 núcleos, o CPU de 18 núcleos y GPU de 40 núcleos en el caso del M5 Max.
Vale aclarar que los ordenadores se pueden configurar en cualquiera de las cuatro opciones recién mencionadas si se trata del modelo de 14 pulgadas. En el de 16'' solo está disponible la opción más potente de M5 Pro.
En materia de memoria unificada, los MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil inician en 24 GB, y se pueden configurar con hasta 128 GB. Mientras que la gran sorpresa está en el almacenamiento, pues si bien mantienen 1 TB como opción base, ahora es posible configurarlos con hasta 16 TB; es decir, el doble de lo que se ofrecía antes.
Dicho todo esto, está más que claro que los MacBook Pro con pantalla tándem OLED y táctil no son baratos. El modelo más económico se inicia en los 3.349 euros, que de barato no tiene nada. Pero ese número puede multiplicarse con facilidad a medida que se va explorando el configurador de Apple.
Cuánto vas a pagar por los MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil más caros
En el caso del MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil de 14 pulgadas, la versión más cara es la que lleva chip M5 Max con CPU de 18 núcleos y GPU de 40 núcleos, con 128 GB de RAM y 16 TB de almacenamiento. Esta variante incluye el vidrio nanotexturizado para la pantalla y un adaptador de corriente de 96 vatios y cuesta ni más ni menos que 16.059 euros.
Si te sientes todavía más atrevido, puedes inclinarte por la opción de 16 pulgadas. Aquí, el modelo con M5 Max de 18 núcleos y 40 núcleos núcleos, 128 GB de memoria, 16 TB de almacenamiento, vidrio nanotexturizado y adaptador de corriente de 140 vatios se consigue a cambio de 16.433 euros.
Estos precios contemplan solamente el hardware de los nuevos MacBook Pro ProLED XDR con pantalla táctil. Ambas cifras se pueden hacer todavía más grandes si decides comprar las licencias de Final Cut Pro (+349,99 euros) y Logic Pro (+229,99 euros) para que lleguen preinstalados. Y si optas por añadir AppleCare+ en su póliza de pago al contado, que brinda tres años de cobertura, tienes que añadirle 479 o 579 euros más a la cuenta, según el modelo que elijas.
Así las cosas, el MacBook Pro táctil más caro que puedes comprar cuesta 17.117,98 euros para la versión de 14 pulgadas y 17.591,98 euros para la de 16 pulgadas. The more you know... ¯\(ツ)/¯

articles.title: Japan experiments with autonomous AI chainsaw-wielding robots — video shows rail truck-mounted metal humanoid cutting down tree branches
articles.text:
Japan experiments with autonomous AI chainsaw-wielding robots — video shows rail truck-mounted metal humanoid cutting down tree branches
The frightening-looking mech in the demo still has a human operator, for now.
A scary-looking humanoid robot with a chainsaw arm was shown in action on Japan's ANN News recently. The rail truck-mounted mech was being used by Japanese railway firm JR East to clear tree branches that had begun to impede rail tracks. The unnamed heavy machinery robot’s chainsaw and grabber arms are remotely controlled by a human in this instance. However, JR East is broadly integrating AI and robotic technologies across its operations to enhance safety, efficiency, and round-the-clock maintenance.
In the future, this robot could become autonomous with AI-based image analysis for recognizing rail obstructions that need to be addressed. While they’re at it, why not dispose of the wheeled vehicle and add some legs and a jet pack?
JR East is the largest passenger railway operator in Japan. It is famous for operating the northern Shinkansen (bullet train) routes, but also has business interests/revenue from shopping centers, hotels, smart cards, and more. The firm has a reputation for quite aggressive AI adoption, including company-wide AI tools, designing AI programs for disaster recovery, and it is even using drones equipped with AI image analysis for rail infrastructure inspections (PDF).
The source video and report (machine translation) indicate that the chainsaw mech you see has been available to JR East engineers since March, but the TV crew took the opportunity to catch a rare glimpse of this heavy machinery in action. JR East is turning to robots like this due to labor shortages. Apparently, operating a robot like this requires some skill, but so does chainsaw work at height.
There’s also been a recent shift in rail building and maintenance work to the daytime – despite some inconvenience to customers – to the benefit of workers and safety. Perhaps that’s why we now have a video of the chainsaw-wielding truck-mounted robot for the first time.
The combination of labor shortages and advances in robotics and AI makes development of this kind of rail maintenance robot seem very timely. If the metallic humanoid can be made autonomous, it could save a lot of labor and promote safety. What could go wrong?

articles.title: Alberta data centre boom could lead to worker shortage: report | BetaKit
articles.text:
A report from The Information and Communications Technology Council (ICTC) is warning that Alberta’s data centre boom could cause a worker shortage if the Province doesn’t work to increase access to skilled workers and training programs.
The news: ICTC’s report, which was released on Wednesday, outlines several key findings, chief among them that if Alberta were to build 80 percent of its planned data centre capacity in the next 10 years, the province would face a shortage of roughly 5,200 construction and skilled trades workers.
ICTC is a non-partisan, non-profit organization that aims to strengthen Canada’s digital economy and workforce.
From the source: Alberta leads Canada in data centre development, with the province accounting for roughly 90 percent of the country’s planned data centre projects. The 33 proposed projects in development in Alberta would, as of press time, consume around 20,000 megawatts of power, nearly double what the province’s entire grid uses during peak demand.
The context: ICTC’s report was commissioned by the Government of Alberta in 2025 to look into the workforce requirements for the province’s planned data centre buildout. It finds that tinkering with timelines and capacity loads could reduce the shortfall to anywhere between 2,200 and 666 positions. Ultimately, however, it projects that Alberta will need to either attract new workers or invest in expanding training opportunities to meet demand.
BetaKit reached out to Alberta’s Ministry of Jobs and Ministry of Technology to ask if the Province has any plans related to hiring or training, but has yet to receive a response.
Final thought: ICTC’s report touches on an issue that is increasingly salient for Alberta’s business community: attracting skilled workers. In the recent October referendum, the Province included several immigration-related questions that some in Alberta’s tech sector have speculated could stymie attracting new talent to the province.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026.
Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend.
Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results.
This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending.
Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI.
Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost.
“Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.”
Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers.
“It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own — this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.”
It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. These new reporting tools can be seen as a kind of FDE-lite, a lighter version of that hands-on help, for Anthropic customers.
“We’re at a point now where it’s mature enough, where once you’re in, it’s going to be harder and harder to switch because you’ve spent the effort,” he said. “Even if they’re all mostly the same, they’re all going to be slightly different, have their own slight quirks of how they handle agent.md files, etc., and so that cost to switch is not zero.”

articles.title: A security flaw in these widely used barcode scanners could open up warehouses and stores to cyberattack
articles.text:
A security flaw in these widely used barcode scanners could open up warehouses and stores to cyberattack
A simple barcode scanner could be the gateway to a large-scale cyberattack
- Researchers find Bluetooth flaws in warehouse barcode scanners that could provide a foothold into enterprise networks
- Attackers could spoof scanner input, inject keystrokes, and potentially pivot to ransomware or data theft
- Kaspersky urges stronger device authentication, network segmentation, and stricter security controls for warehouse infrastructure
Cybercriminals could use barcode scanners in warehouses to break into IT infrastructure and wreak havoc, security researchers have claimed, urging organizations to take preemptive measures and secure their warehouse grounds before it’s too late.
Kaspersky researchers set out to see if there are any hidden attack vectors on warehouse infrastructure and are now claiming they found one through a barcode scanner model “from a major manufacturer”.
Opening the floodgates
In a report shared with TechRadar Pro, Kaspersky said the vulnerable device has two components: the handheld scanner, and the base station, which is then connected to a workstation, or a separate business system.
The two components communicate via Bluetooth, but apparently there are no authentication methods between the two.
So, in theory, a malicious actor could obtain the Bluetooth address of the base station through passive eavesdropping on Bluetooth traffic. Then, through the established Bluetooth connection, they could send a malicious payload to the base station which simulates keyboard strokes. The base station would “think” the keystrokes are legitimate, coming from the user of the handheld device, and forward them to the connected workstation or separate business system.
“This attack pattern was observed across devices from multiple vendors,” Kaspersky said in its report.
Through this method, a theoretical attacker could gain an initial foothold on a computer within the warehouse network. Obviously, the scanner is only the entry point and not the actual target. The target is the wider network, where malicious actors could conduct reconnaissance, exfiltrate sensitive information, or deploy malware and ransomware.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“Modern retail and logistics are profoundly digital, from enterprise-wide management platforms down to every device in a worker’s hands. This pervasive connectivity means that any technology at any tier can become an entry point for a cyberattack capable of destabilising the entire ecosystem — as our research shows, even a single barcode scanner”, said Sergey Sidorov, Head of Industrial Security Services at Kaspersky.
“The warehouse sector, and the broader retail industry, should treat cybersecurity as a top priority across every layer of their operations,”
Are other devices vulnerable, too?
Kaspersky says the same scenario can be applied to other warehouse devices like Portable Data Terminals (PDR), or thermal printers, to gain access to Warehouse Management Systems (WMS) and similar infrastructure.
Therefore, the researchers are urging companies to secure their environments by verifying every new device before it connects to the network, disabling any unused Bluetooth interfaces, enforcing strong authentication mechanisms, segmenting warehouse networks so that only essential connections are permitted, applying security updates to both devices and the WMS as soon as possible, restricting account permissions to the minimum required, and regularly conducting full‑scale attack‑path exercises.
Unfortunately, we don’t know the name of the manufacturer, or how many devices in a series could be susceptible. The researchers are saying the risk is quite large, since these devices are “widely used” in warehousing, retail, and multiple other sectors.
Global e-commerce sales are expected to reach $6.88 trillion this year, making up more than a fifth (21.1%) of total retail sales worldwide.
At the same time, according to logistics research firm Interact Analysis, there are more than 180,000 warehouses in the world, so the attack surface could be significant. But warehouses are not the only sector at risk here. Barcode scanners and related handheld terminals are also widely used in retail stores, manufacturing facilities, hospitals, pharmaceutical operations, and transportation networks.
There is no reliable way to estimate how many organizations are vulnerable, but the possibility of using an everyday operational device to gain access to a connected workstation makes the findings relevant to a broad range of industries.

articles.title: This $149 digital candle uses AI to accurately simulate a flickering flame
articles.text:
After engineering a flexible version of Tetris that could be wrapped around a magazine, Kevin Bates’ latest creation is a digital candle that uses a custom AI model to accurately simulate the appearance of a flickering flame across a grid of LEDs. It’s a far cry from the types of devices Bates is typically known for, including the Arduboy, but paying $79 for a credit card-sized handheld that can play hundreds of games is an easier sell than a $149 digital candle that doesn’t quite provide the same ambiance as the real thing, even if it’s much safer.
This $149 digital candle uses AI to accurately simulate a flickering flame
The Arduboy creator’s next project uses a neural network trained on footage of a real candle’s flame.
At the top of the 10-inch tall Digital Candle, which is available now with a black or white circuitboard, you’ll find 144 amber-colored LEDs arranged in a 9 by 16 grid with adjustable brightness. On the other end is a USB-C port for supplying power (a rechargeable battery isn’t included) and an Espressif ESP32-S3 chip that runs an AI model with a tiny neural network trained on footage of a real flickering candle.
The flame simulation never repeats and is unique to each candle since it’s being generated on the fly at all times. It’s not a pre-programmed animation set to loop so the results look very convincing, or as convincing as they can be on a low-res grid of LEDs. The Digital Candle is also open source so you can repurpose it as a clock, a notification screen, or run other simulations like Conway’s Game of Life. That could potentially make its $149 price a little easier to justify if you like to tinker.

articles.title: Samsung lanza sus nuevos auriculares tipo clip que no se meten en la oreja y llevan la IA de Gemini
articles.text:
Samsung ha lanzado un nuevo integrante de su familia de auriculares. El gigante surcoreano presentó los Galaxy Buds On, sus primeros auriculares con diseño abierto que buscan ofrecer una experiencia diferente a los tradicionales modelos intraaurales. Samsung ha puesto el foco en la comodidad y en la integración con funciones de inteligencia artificial.
Si no estás familiarizado con los auriculares de diseño abierto, estos dispositivos están pensados para escuchar el entorno mientras disfrutas del audio. A diferencia de los Galaxy Buds4 Pro, que priorizan el aislamiento y la cancelación de ruido, los Galaxy Buds On utilizan un formato de clip que se apoya en la oreja sin introducirse en el canal auditivo. Esto permitirá estar al pendiente de lo que ocurre a tu alrededor mientras escuchas música, atiendes una llamada o interactúas con el asistente de IA.
Según Samsung, el diseño de sus nuevos auriculares utilizó más de 119 millones de puntos de datos relacionados con la forma de las orejas. Con la ayuda de simulaciones físicas y optimización por IA, la compañía refinó la estructura del auricular y la banda de sujeción para conseguir un equilibrio entre comodidad y estabilidad. Los Galaxy Buds On pueden llevarse todo el día, ya que cada auricular pesa apenas 6,65 gramos.
38 horas de autonomía, Gemini Live y nuevas funciones de IA
En términos de funciones, los Galaxy Buds On ofrecen controles táctiles y pueden configurarse para ajustar el volumen automáticamente según el entorno. Los auriculares cuentan con tecnología de reducción de fugas de audio, que busca minimizar el sonido que escapa hacia el exterior. Esto es uno de los puntos débiles de los auriculares abiertos, por lo que Samsung usó ondas inversas para que nadie escuche tu música o conversaciones mientras te encuentras en un espacio público.
Las llamadas también reciben mejoras, gracias a tres micrófonos y una unidad de captura de voz que puede detectar vibraciones asociadas al habla. La compañía señala que estos componentes se combinan con algoritmos de aprendizaje automático, los cuales se entrenaron para filtrar ruidos de fondo. Si estás en medio del tráfico o pasas cerca de una obra en construcción, el sistema impedirá que estos sonidos se cuelen durante la conversación.
Por último, los Galaxy Buds On tienen compatibilidad con Gemini Live, a quien podremos invocar a través de comandos de voz. Entre sus funciones se encuentra la posibilidad de crear notas de voz rápidas y controlar ciertas acciones mediante movimientos de cabeza, como aceptar o rechazar interacciones. En cuanto a autonomía, Samsung ha prometido hasta 9,5 horas de reproducción continua y hasta 38 horas de uso total, eso sí, combinando los auriculares con el estuche de carga.
Los Galaxy Buds On estarán disponibles a partir de hoy a un precio de 229 dólares. Por el momento se desconoce el precio o disponibilidad en España y otros países de América Latina, aunque un reporte de SammyGuru menciona que varias tiendas europeas los venderán durante la primera mitad de diciembre.

articles.title: Florida county won’t investigate sketchy Flock cameras removed by mystery owners
articles.text:
A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared.
On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents “remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned to get Flock cameras removed, told the Post that she was worried “that data could be anywhere.”
Of the 12 cameras found, five were eventually claimed by city law enforcement, the Post reported. Apparently, a police department mistakenly issued guidance claiming that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit, a Flock spokesperson told the Post, even though the county required individual permits. However, neither Flock nor the city police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce that claimed the sketchy cameras will confirm who gave the guidance.
Over three years, the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s Flock contract ballooned from $22,000 to $470,000 in 2025, the year before the county mandated removals on county roads. However, Erick Gill, a St. Lucie County spokesperson, told the Post that despite ending that nearly half-million-dollar contract, the county lacks resources to investigate who owned the seven other unpermitted cameras found.
“It sounds like when you do something wrong, and you don’t want to get caught, and you kind of just want to sweep it under the rug,” Galindo told the Post.
According to Gill, the county’s goal was to remove the cameras, not to identify owners, which is why the county gave owners 30 days to take the cameras down without facing any questions.
“Our goal was to get the cameras out of the right-of-way within 30 days,” Gill said. “We accomplished that goal.”
Asked for comment, Gill did not address the cameras of unknown origin, only reiterating that the directive was to remove the cameras.
The Post reported that Flock “did not respond to emailed questions about who operated and removed the cameras or the apparent confusion over permitting requirements.” However, a Flock spokesperson told Ars that Flock knows who owned them and simply won’t disclose it to St. Lucie County residents.
“The cameras have been removed and belonged to several different customers,” Flock’s spokesperson said. “Flock does not share specifics regarding individual agency contracts, camera counts, locations, or deployments.”
Flock CEO said protests aren’t “real”
In St. Lucie County, Galindo’s petition makes it clear that some residents were already concerned about the lack of transparency around Flock cameras, and that was before they learned several unpermitted cameras were also collecting their data.
“These high-tech surveillance devices have been installed without clear, publicized consent or adequate discussion with the people they affect—us, the citizens who cherish their privacy and value transparency,” the petition said. Most concerning, the petition emphasized, studies have shown that Flock’s cameras “often lead to invasions of privacy, data misuse, and can even disproportionately affect marginalized communities.”
But Flock has downplayed the mass backlash, as its camera network continues to grow. On Monday, 404 Media shared leaked audio from a private police conference in which Flock CEO Garrett Langley claimed nationwide anti-Flock protests like Galindo’s “are not real” and repeated a disproven conspiracy theory that Russian bots supposedly fueled viral anti-Flock social media posts.
“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley reportedly said. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like, ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things.’”
Seemingly hoping to reassure police facing protests in their own communities, Langley insisted that “it’s anonymous bots, and so it is not real. Inorganic activity has led to organic activity, but when I look at protests across the country, it is the same people with the same signs and the same message. That’s not normal. That’s not organic at all.”
Flock’s line to police ignores that the ACLU has created a toolkit to help communities “DeFlock,” citing genuine concerns that “creepy cameras make it possible to track everyone’s movements” without a warrant. On the day 404 Media leaked Langley’s statements, the ACLU updated its resource providing instructions on how to “Get the Flock out,” while warning about lack of oversight for Flock’s huge camera database.
Flock fights to obscure 100,000 cameras
For Flock protesters, cases like the one in Florida are disturbing, since Flock appears to take great pains to obscure who owns cameras where and how large its camera network is. Talking to the Texas Tribune in August, Flock estimated there are about 120,000 cameras used by law enforcement nationwide, but cybersecurity researcher Joshua Michael recently discovered that the network is nearly twice as large and has since faced legal threats from Flock for sharing his findings publicly.
In a research paper this September, Michael explained how he found a Flock access token that let him retrieve device locations without logging in. He notified Flock of the vulnerability, but he also created a map tracking all the devices. Analyzing that map, Matt Busel, founder of a software studio called Tensorust, noted that Michael exposed a network of 214,073 devices, not 120,000. Most likely, the nearly 100,000 difference represents Flock’s private camera network, which Busel warned is operated without regulatory oversight.
“It is bigger than anything Flock says out loud,” Busel wrote.
Busel told Ars that “it’s concerning” that St. Lucie County isn’t investigating ownership, since Michael’s map and his analysis show how many holes there are in the public’s understanding of how much their movements are tracked by Flock. The company’s statements do not appear to sympathize with residents who fear their data may have been misused by unknown Flock owners.
“Flock’s lack of transparency is a recurring pattern; they seem to prioritize obscuring the network’s footprint over public accountability,” Busel said. “My analysis suggests this isn’t just about localized camera placement but a broader effort to limit visibility into their total operating capacity.”
Instead of increasing transparency as public criticism swells, Flock has moved to protect private camera owners, including seemingly the ones in St. Lucie County. After Michael published the map, Flock sent a cease-and-desist letter, accusing Michael of violating laws by openly encouraging others to download its confidential data.
“An inadvertently exposed credential is not an invitation to access private systems or data,” Flock said.
Flock has demanded that Michael pull down the map, the data file, and his research paper. They’ve also asked Michael to name anyone who received the data. Otherwise, Flock has threatened to sue for injunctive relief, as well as statutory and punitive damages, since they said Michael knew the data was confidential and proprietary.
Michael has no plans to yank the data. On his site, he posted an update noting that “Flock Safety has responded to my research with a cease-and-desist letter threatening litigation. In an email to its customers, the company branded me a malicious actor, announcing it had notified law enforcement. That same email concedes Flock found no indication of unauthorized access to its data when it closed the issue in December, which is precisely the monitoring failure my research warns about. I’m not backing down.”
Asked for comment, Michael sent a statement to Ars, arguing that his research has national security implications. He confirmed that he is currently self-funding his legal defense and accepting donations from supporters on his website.
“Our nation is not protected by ignorance of a risk,” Michael said, adding:
My research on FlockSurveillance.orgdocuments cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences. There is an extremely deep irony in slandering me as a malicious actor, and confirming my thesis in the same email. My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people. Flock Safety has threatened me with litigation, notified law enforcement, and promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline. These actions against my good faith cybersecurity research covering national security should be considered a betrayal to our nation and sovereignty.
“I will not put Flock’s quarterly profits ahead of the security of the United States,” Michael continued. “Today I fund my legal defense myself and I am grateful beyond imagination that Proton is taking a stand to host a mirror of my research map. This is not a problem that will just disappear and the people of our country are rightfully concerned.”
This story was updated on Wednesday to include Michael’s statement.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Physics-Based Validation: The Foundation Of Trustworthy Agentic EDA
articles.text:
What self-verifying agents validate their decisions against and why physics-based engines are the authority on correctness.
This is the third article in a series examining what it takes to build production-ready AI agents for EDA. The first explored the architectural decisions required for agents to operate reliably in production environments. The second examined what self-verifying means in an agentic EDA workflow: how agents continuously check their decisions as they work, rather than waiting until the end of a run.
But what exactly are those decisions being verified against?
The answer is physics. More specifically, the deterministic, physics-based EDA engines that define whether a design is correct. A self-verifying agent checks its own work, and a physics-validated workflow confirms that work is correct.
Chip design has always faced physics-based constraints. Every transistor, every wire, every timing path, and every thermal gradient is governed by the fixed laws of physics, regardless of how the design was created. This is why tapeout is binary: silicon either works or it does not.
When AI enters this domain, that physical reality does not change. The relevant question is not whether an AI system can reason about physics, but whether the outputs it produces have been confirmed by the engines that enforce that physics.
That distinction separates a model that is capable of reasoning about physics from a workflow that is physics-validated.
A physics-validated workflow is one in which every agent decision is confirmed against a deterministic, physics-based EDA engine before the next step begins. Validation does not happen only at the end of a workflow or after an entire run is complete. It happens continuously, at every step, against the engines engineers have trusted for decades.
The agent executes a step, and the engine determines whether the result meets the design’s physical constraints. If it does not, the agent identifies the issue, resolves it, and continues. Physics-validated means the engine, not the model, is the authority on correctness.
In semiconductor design, there is zero margin for unverified decisions. Tapeout dates are fixed, respins are expensive, and missed market windows do not come back.
For engineering organizations deploying agentic AI at scale, the key question is not simply whether the workflow is fast. It is whether the outcomes it produces can be trusted without requiring engineers to manually re-verify every autonomous decision.
An agentic workflow that reasons correctly about physics but does not validate its outputs against physics-based engines introduces risk at every autonomous step. The longer a workflow runs without validation, the further a design can drift from correctness before an error surfaces.
In a long-running autonomous workflow that executes across multiple tools, physical domains, and hours without human intervention, unvalidated decisions can compound. Continuous physics-based validation prevents those errors from propagating through the workflow.
In Part 2, I described an autonomous library characterization workflow in which the agent continuously checks its work against physics-based EDA engines. That workflow demonstrates the principle at a specific task level. The need for continuous validation increases when a workflow spans multiple tools and physical domains, and 3D-IC design shows why. It is the ultimate test of physics, and the clearest example of why semiconductor design is physics.
AI factories require more compute, memory bandwidth, and thermal performance within an increasingly constrained physical footprint. As power, performance, and area scaling on monolithic dies reaches practical limits, chiplet-based 2.5D and 3D architectures allow compute and memory to scale through tightly integrated packages.
That level of integration makes the physical design problem considerably more complex. Stacked active dies make heat removal and temperature interactions harder to predict, while packaging can introduce mechanical stress. Electrical, power, thermal, and mechanical effects are interconnected, so a change in one area can affect the others. Addressing these effects through manual, fragmented, and tool-intensive workflows creates frequent engineering handoffs, slows iteration, and limits the number of design alternatives teams can evaluate.
Siemens has developed an agentic engineering workflow that autonomously coordinates 3D-IC design and analysis. MCP servers and skill files for different EDA tools are connected to Fuse EDA AI Agent, which acts as an MCP aggregator that can be connected to any coding agent of choice. In this particular example, Claude Code is used as the agentic coding IDE, orchestrating a nine-stage electro-thermal workflow spanning seven Siemens EDA tools, running 100 to 200 agentic turns over more than 12 hours.
Each stage performs a distinct engineering task, from floor planning, library characterization, and power analysis to thermal signoff, system-level thermal simulation, parasitic extraction, and power- and temperature-aware SPICE simulation. Every stage is validated using signoff-grade, physics-based solvers.
The workflow runs autonomously, executing analyses, evaluating results, identifying missed targets, and continuing to refine the design. Teams can sweep heat transfer coefficient (HTC) boundaries, power budgets, and material stack-ups across 200 to 500+ design points per cycle. This enables teams to configure tools up to 20 times faster, reduce engineering effort by up to 95%, and evaluate up to 50 times more design options than a conventional manual flow.
The demo below shows the electro-thermal workflow in action:
When evaluating an agentic EDA workflow, one question determines whether its architecture is physics-validated: At each step, is the agent’s output confirmed by a deterministic, physics-based EDA engine before the workflow proceeds?
If the answer is yes, the workflow is physics-validated. The engine is the arbiter, and every autonomous decision is confirmed against the physical reality of the design.
Taken together, the three articles in this series define the requirements for production-ready agentic EDA: an architecture designed for real engineering environments, a self-verifying mechanism that continuously checks agent decisions, and a physics-validated standard that determines whether those decisions are correct.
This is the architectural standard Siemens EDA has built into the Fuse EDA AI Agent. The result is trusted autonomy: validated engineering outcomes at every step of the workflow.
