articles.title: Nos données personnelles sont partout : Bitdefender Premium Security veut limiter les risques
articles.text:
Les données personnelles circulent bien au-delà de nos publications sur les réseaux sociaux. Mises bout à bout, elles intéressent de près les cybercriminels. Voici les risques à connaître et les réflexes à adopter pour protéger votre vie privée en ligne.
Partager des informations personnelles en ligne ne se limite pas à publier des photos de vacances sur les réseaux sociaux. Cette exposition prend des formes multiples, parfois moins visibles et auxquelles on prête moins attention.
Nos traces numériques en disent trop
Une adresse postale transmise pour obtenir une carte de fidélité. Un numéro de téléphone pour réserver une table au restaurant. Une simulation de crédit ou d’assurance. Des données physiques ou intimes renseignées sur une application de rencontre. Sans oublier les cookies et autres traceurs qui enregistrent, en coulisses, une partie de nos activités en ligne.
Prises individuellement, ces données peuvent sembler anodines, mais une fois croisées, elles prennent une tout autre dimension. Pièce après pièce, elles forment en réalité le puzzle de nos vies : nos goûts, nos habitudes de consommation, certains traits de notre personnalité et même des éléments de notre situation économique.
Sans céder à la psychose, l’enjeu est important, il est crucial de reprendre la maîtrise de nos données personnelles. Savoir quelles informations nous divulguons, à qui, dans quel but et avec quelles conséquences.
Quels sont les risques concrètement ?
Ce qu’il faut bien comprendre, c’est que les risques ne sont ni uniformes ni systématiques. Ils varient selon les données partagées, en fonction des fuites (qui sont de plus en plus importantes et massives), mais aussi selon le profil de chaque personne.
Cyberharcèlement, arnaques et usurpation d’identité
Pour un enfant ou un adolescent, l’un des risques majeurs est le cyberharcèlement, avec les conséquences que l’on connaît : stress, perte de confiance, honte et repli sur soi pour échapper au regard des autres. À un âge où l’identité se construit et où le besoin d’appartenance est fort, ces violences peuvent devenir un véritable poids psychologique.
Chez les adultes, les risques sont souvent liés aux arnaques et à l’usurpation d’identité. Entre l’intelligence artificielle et l’accumulation de données personnelles, les escrocs peuvent concevoir des pièges toujours plus crédibles. Profession, date de naissance, lieu de résidence, adresse e-mail … une fois le profil établi, ils peuvent se faire passer pour un proche, un employeur ou un organisme officiel, usurper une identité ou manipuler une victime pour lui soutirer de l’argent.
Quand le virtuel rattrape le réel
Parfois, la frontière entre le monde virtuel et le monde réel s’efface.
Partager son parcours de course à pied en temps réel peut faciliter le repérage et exposer à des risques de harcèlement. Publier une photo devant une maison facilement identifiable peut également révéler son adresse et, dans certaines circonstances, faciliter un cambriolage.
Ce ne sont que quelques exemples parmi tant d’autres, mais tous rappellent que les conséquences peuvent être destructrices.
Comment protéger ses données et éviter de devenir une cible ?
Une fois que l’on a pris conscience de cette réalité, reste à savoir comment agir. Il y a des habitudes à faire évoluer, des réflexes à changer et des outils à utiliser pour accompagner cette démarche.
Faire le tri dans ce que l’on partage
Il n’est pas toujours nécessaire de communiquer son nom de famille pour obtenir une simple carte de fidélité ni de renseigner sa date de naissance complète lorsque celle-ci n’est pas indispensable.
Sur les réseaux sociaux, mieux vaut également éviter de publier sa position ou ses trajets en temps réel. De même, utiliser plusieurs adresses e-mail qui ne dévoilent ni son nom ni son prénom peut s’avérer très utile.
Verrouiller ses comptes
Les risques de piratage sont nombreux, et plus vous multipliez les comptes en ligne, plus vous augmentez les points d’entrée pour les cybercriminels.
À défaut de combler toutes les failles présentes en ligne, vous pouvez limiter les risques en utilisant un mot de passe différent pour chaque compte.
Un gestionnaire de mots de passe comme celui inclus dans Bitdefender Premium Security facilite cela. Il génère des mots de passe robustes, les conserve dans un espace chiffré et remplit automatiquement les formulaires.
Par ailleurs, un outil de détection des violations de données est aussi disponible. Il donne accès à une liste des organisations ayant exposé vos informations, afin de mieux agir.
Sécuriser ses connexions
La présence d’un VPN dans l’offre Bitdefender Premium Security apporte un haut niveau de confidentialité en ligne, il bloque aussi des publicités indésirables et limite l’exposition depuis les réseaux publics.
Parallèlement, à cela la protection contre les virus, ransomwares et logiciels espions agit en temps réel sur Windows, macOS, iOS et Android.
Accompagner les plus jeunes
Si le dialogue et la pédagogie restent essentiels avec les plus jeunes, notamment pour leur expliquer ce qu’ils peuvent publier en ligne et pourquoi Internet n’oublie rien, la suite Bitdefender Premium Security intègre également des outils de contrôle parental. Ils permettent de compléter cette démarche en encadrant les usages de vos enfants.
Se protéger contre les arnaques
Avec l’essor de l’IA, les arnaques en ligne ne ciblent plus uniquement les personnes les plus vulnérables. Le mieux est donc de prendre quelques précautions avant de tomber dans le piège.
Le dispositif Scam Protection Pro, intégré dans la suite Bitdefender Premium Security, est intéressant car il couvre de nombreux aspects.
Il est capable de sécuriser les e-mails, les SMS et les conversations en ligne. Si un message ou un lien vous paraît suspect, vous pouvez le soumettre à un assistant IA pour obtenir un avis et savoir plus facilement à quoi vous en tenir. Quant à Scam Radar, il vous alerte sur les arnaques en cours près de chez vous.
Bitdefender Premium Security en promo (-50 %)
En ce moment, Bitdefender Premium Security est proposé en réduction à 55 €, donc une ristourne de 50 %.
Avec un seul abonnement, vous pouvez protéger jusqu’à 5 appareils. Un choix clairement convaincant compte tenu des outils proposés et des enjeux.

articles.title: Apple tiene nueva versión del MacBook Pro y ahora es táctil: hasta 24 horas de batería
articles.text:
Apple presentó una nueva versión del MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil, hasta 24 horas de batería y una tecnología OLED en tándem llamada PROLED XDR. La computadora estará disponible en modelos de 14 y 16 pulgadas, incorpora los chips M5 Pro y M5 Max y suma cambios en diseño, conectividad, audio y herramientas basadas en inteligencia artificial.
La llegada de funciones táctiles representa un cambio en la línea profesional de Apple. Hasta ahora, la Mac se había apoyado en el teclado, el trackpad y accesorios externos como principales vías de interacción. Con este modelo, los usuarios podrán desplazarse, ampliar imágenes, mover archivos y utilizar aplicaciones creativas directamente sobre la pantalla.
La pantalla PROLED XDR incorpora tecnología OLED en tándem
El nuevo MacBook Pro estrena la pantalla PROLED XDR, basada en dos capas de píxeles autoiluminados. Apple indica que esta tecnología alcanza hasta 2.000 nits de brillo máximo tanto en contenido HDR como SDR, con una relación de contraste de 10.000.000:1.
La compañía señala que el panel busca ofrecer negros profundos, mayor detalle en las zonas oscuras y reflejos más intensos sin los halos que pueden aparecer en otros sistemas de iluminación. La frecuencia de actualización variable llega hasta 120 Hz mediante ProMotion y puede bajar hasta 10 Hz para reducir el consumo energético.
La pantalla incluye compatibilidad con los espacios de color P3 y Adobe RGB, una característica dirigida a fotógrafos, diseñadores, coloristas y editores de video. También ofrece una cobertura superior al 80% de Rec. 2020 para la edición de contenido HDR.
El equipo contará con una opción de nanotextura para reducir reflejos y deslumbramientos en lugares con iluminación intensa. Según Apple, el panel se calibra en fábrica para mantener precisión en luminancia, punto blanco y gama cromática.
El MacBook Pro permite tocar, arrastrar y dibujar en la pantalla
Las capacidades táctiles llegan por primera vez a la línea MacBook Pro. La pantalla responde a gestos como desplazarse por páginas, pellizcar para ampliar fotografías, arrastrar elementos entre ventanas y tocar dos veces para maximizar una aplicación.
El sensor táctil está integrado en el panel, sin una capa externa superpuesta. Apple sostiene que este sistema reduce la latencia y hace que la interacción se sienta más directa. Una bisagra rediseñada busca aportar estabilidad cuando el usuario toca la pantalla.
Los diseñadores podrán utilizar la pantalla como lienzo, los músicos tocar instrumentos virtuales y los desarrolladores probar gestos para aplicaciones de iPhone y iPad. La interacción táctil convivirá con los atajos de teclado y los gestos del trackpad.
La empresa indica que macOS traducirá automáticamente los toques en clics para muchas aplicaciones existentes. También se mencionan herramientas compatibles como Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Shapr3D y djay Pro.
La Isla Dinámica se integra en la computadora
Otra de las novedades es la llegada de la Isla Dinámica a la Mac. Este espacio funcionará como acceso a Spotlight, Actividades en Vivo y Siri AI. Desde allí, el usuario podrá consultar información, responder llamadas, controlar música o revisar actualizaciones en tiempo real.
La computadora ejecutará macOS 27 Golden Gate, que incorpora Apple Intelligence y una nueva versión de Siri AI. Según Apple, el asistente podrá utilizar contexto personal para buscar información en mensajes, correos y fotografías, además de realizar tareas entre aplicaciones.
M5 Pro y M5 Max apuntan a flujos de trabajo exigentes
La nueva MacBook Pro incluirá los chips M5 Pro y M5 Max, con hasta 128 GB de memoria unificada y hasta 16 TB de almacenamiento. Apple enfoca estas configuraciones en edición de video ProRes 8K, modelado y animación 3D, composición musical, programación y ejecución local de modelos de lenguaje.
El sistema incorpora tres puertos Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, lector de tarjetas SDXC, MagSafe y conector para audífonos. El modelo con M5 Pro puede conectar hasta tres pantallas externas y la versión M5 Max, hasta cuatro. También suma Wi‑Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 y carga rápida hasta el 50% en 30 minutos.
El modelo de 14 pulgadas pesa 1,36 kilogramos y el de 16 pulgadas, 1,81 kilogramos. Apple abrirá las reservas el 28 de octubre y prevé que los equipos estén disponibles desde el viernes 6 de noviembre.
La incorporación de una pantalla táctil modifica la relación histórica entre la Mac y sus usuarios. Apple mantiene el teclado y el trackpad como herramientas centrales, pero añade una interacción más directa para creación, edición y consulta de contenido. El resultado dependerá de si las aplicaciones profesionales adoptan esos gestos como parte habitual de sus procesos.

articles.title: Pieterjan Bouten’s Entourage closes €100 million second fund after surpassing €75 million target in two weeks | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Entourage, the London-based early-stage VC firm founded by Showpad co-founder and former CEO Pieterjan Bouten, today announced the close of its €100 million second fund, just over two years after launching its first fund in 2024.
Entourage Fund II has been backed entirely by entrepreneurs, family offices and private investors, including founders behind Aikido, TechWolf and Collibra. It has surpassed its original €75 million target in just 2 weeks and has secured over €100 million in commitments before being capped at €100 million. 
“When we launched Entourage two years ago, we had a simple ambition: to back the next generation of legendary founders. We wrote the first cheques into companies like Aikido, Conveo and Lexroom. What these founders have achieved in such a short time has only strengthened our conviction in our founder-first approach. With Fund II, we’re doubling down,” said Pieterjan (PJ) Bouten, Founder and General Partner of Entourage.
Founded in 2024 by Bouten, Entourage claims to bring a founder’s mindset and an operator’s experience to venture capital. It backs “exceptional founders” at the pre-Seed and Seed stages and invests across sectors, including AI, enterprise software, robotics, and DeepTech.
Bouten co-founded and scaled Showpad into a global software company generating more than €89.84 million ($100 million) in annual recurring revenue. He then became an active angel investor before launching Entourage.
In this episode of The EU-Startups Podcast, Bouten reflects on his journey from co-founding In the Pocket and scaling Showpad to now building and funding the next generation of B2B SaaS companies through Entourage Studio and Entourage Capital.
According to him, this experience helped forge Entourage’s approach: build conviction, invest early and keep founders firmly in the driver’s seat.
The firm states that it extends its founder-first philosophy to governance as well, and therefore rarely takes board seats despite leading or co-leading most of its investment rounds.
Bouten said, “Most VCs destroy value in early-stage boardrooms. Too few have built a company at scale. After more than a decade as a founder and CEO, and investments in over 60 companies, I’ve seen investors slow founders down with misplaced advice and operational interference. Great founders don’t need babysitting. They need trust, challenge when it counts and perspective at pivotal moments. That’s why we rarely take board seats, even when we lead a round.”
He also highlighted that the firm’s investor base reflects that philosophy. “Many of our investors have built companies themselves. They know what it takes. That creates a powerful alignment between the people funding Entourage and the founders we back,” he added. 
Since launching in 2024, Entourage reported that it has backed some of Europe’s fastest-growing technology companies, including Aikido Security, which reached unicorn status earlier this year; Conveo, which recently raised a €44.92 million ($50 million) Series A; and Lexroom, which reached €30 million in annual recurring revenue in just 24 months.
“Entourage was among the first investors in all three, backing their founders before major international venture capital firms arrived – often before a product launch or the first euro of Revenue,” the firm mentioned in the press release. 
Fund II will back around 25 companies at the pre-Seed and Seed stages across Europe and beyond, with initial cheques of €1 million to €5 million and “ample” capacity for follow-on investments.
Entourage states that it seeks “driven, ambitious founders building their life’s work.” It argues that while the first fund focused primarily on software, Fund II will broaden its focus to include AI and enterprise software, robotics, physical AI, and DeepTech.
The London-based VC firm also builds companies through Entourage Studio, its venture-building arm. Alongside Fund II, Entourage has expanded its investment team around partners Pieterjan Bouten, Evert Beeckman and Maarten Mortier. It has added three investors—Erwan Gardelle, Sixtine Riescher, and Illja Schiller—opened a London office and established a presence in Paris.

articles.title: New iPad mini preorders are live — I'm rounding up the best deals and offers from Apple, Best Buy, Amazon, and more
articles.text:
New iPad mini preorders are live — where to find the best deals, trade-in offers and freebies with Apple's latest tablet
Preorders start now ahead of a November 6 launch
A brand-new iPad Mini is on the way — and preorders have started. If Apple's latest little tablet is on your shopping list and you're looking for the best place to pick one up, I've gathered together where you can buy one right here, including some of the best preorder deals and trade-in offers.
Announced earlier this week, the eighth-generation iPad mini is a much bigger upgrade than we expected. Headline new features include a sharper, brighter, and more vibrant 8.5-inch OLED Super Retina XDR screen, a powerful A20 Pro chip, improved audio, and IP67 water and dust resistance thanks to the new aluminum design.
All those upgrades do come at a more considerable cost, though, as the iPad mini starts at $699 / £699 / AU$1,099 for the standard WiFi version with 128GB of storage. That's $200 / £200 / AU$300 more than the launch price of the previous iPad mini. There are also 256GB and 512GB versions available if you want more room for files and applications.
With that increase in price, it's more important than ever to find a good deal if you want to preorder the new iPad Mini. Here are the best ones I've found so far from retailers, networks, and mobile operators — and I'll continue adding any new offers when I spot them.
iPad mini preorders in the US
Apple Store: from $699 — or lease from $14.99 a month with Apple Upgrade
The Apple Store is naturally one of the first places to check for new iPad Mini preorders. Without any special discounts, the tablet is simply available to buy from $699. However, if you have a device to trade in, you can get a discount of up to $915. You can also make use of the Apple Upgrade service to lease your iPad Mini from as little as $14.99 a month for 36 months.

Amazon: preorder now from $699
Amazon has added the latest mini to its iPad lineup. Unsurprisingly, there are no discounts available on any models at this point, although Apple tech has sometimes been given a small discount at the retailer ahead of launch in the past. I'll keep an eye out for any offers.
Read moreRead less▼

Best Buy now has the new iPad Mini available for preorder, and as expected, it's got one of the strongest offers from the big retailers. On top of a discount of up to $300 when you trade in an existing iPad, you also get a $50 Best Buy gift card with your order. Not bad to put towards some accessories, or something from the retailer's upcoming Black Friday sale.

We'll have to see if that's repeated ahead of launch.

Specialist electronics retailer B&H Photo has the new iPad mini ready to order before the tablets go out for shipping by November 8. However, there's no sign of anything like that right now, so full price it is.

iPad mini preorders in the UK

If you have an existing device you want to trade in, then you can save up to £840, too. That's likely one of the highest trade-in discounts we'll see.

articles.title: Paystack looks beyond payments as it enters its second decade
articles.text:
Paystack will look beyond payment acceptance to address more of businesses’ financial needs as it enters its second decade, co-founder and chief executive Shola Akinlade said at Moonshot 2026 in Lagos.
Akinlade described how the Nigerian fintech’s payments infrastructure had supported businesses across other sectors, arguing that its next phase would build on the same premise: enabling entrepreneurs to concentrate on their products.
The discussion traced Paystack’s development from a company helping Nigerian merchants collect payments online to a broader financial services group with operations across several African markets.
“I feel very qualified to talk about ambition because a lot of my ambitions over the last 10 years have been realised,” he said. “If you know anything about the Paystack story, we had a simple ambition to build to help merchants accept payments in Nigeria and then probably Africa.”
Akinlade used PiggyVest, the Nigerian savings platform, to illustrate how the infrastructure Paystack developed had enabled businesses beyond its original ambitions.
He recalled how the founders approached Paystack with an idea to automatically debit users’ accounts so they could save money regularly. Paystack already had the infrastructure to support the idea, even though building a savings business was not its own ambition.
“The most exciting thing about that story is that I didn’t do anything. The founders built the business; they took the risk,” he said. “The only thing we had to do was focus on building our infrastructure.”
The experience, he added, showed why infrastructure businesses could have an influence beyond the services they directly offered.
“That’s what really gets exciting about building infrastructure because you don’t know what people are going to build on it.”
Akinlade said that influence also extended to former employees who had gone on to establish companies of their own. He cited Douglas Kendyson, founder of Selar, which helps creators sell digital products; Femi Aluko and Olumide Ojo, co-founders of food delivery company Chowdeck; and Abdulhamid Hassan, co-founder of financial infrastructure provider Mono.
“One of the things I have learned in the last 10 years is that ambition is contagious,” he said. “When you achieve the ambition, every other person you engage with, the ambition continues to go round.”
Amandine Lobelle, the company’s chief operating office, outlined the company’s geographical expansion, saying Paystack had grown its footprint across Ghana, Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire and South Africa, while securing regulatory licences for Egypt and Rwanda.
The discussion comes as Paystack broadens its corporate structure and product offering. In January, it announced The Stack Group, a parent company encompassing Paystack, consumer payments app Zap, Paystack Microfinance Bank and venture studio TSG Labs.
Akinlade said the company was expanding its view of the problems it could solve as customers’ needs developed beyond collecting payments.

articles.title: Chrome Opens Trial for the Email Verification API: Letting Sites Verify Without Sending Emails
articles.text:
Google has opened a Chrome origin trial for the Email Verification API, a WICG proposal that lets a browser confirm a visitor owns the email address they typed, without sending a single message. The trial began in Chrome 150 on desktop, with Gmail taking part as the first participating provider.
The idea replaces the familiar one-time code or magic link. Today a user enters an email, leaves for their inbox, copies a code, and returns, a context switch that often loses them. The proposal uses a three-party model where the browser sits between the site (the "verifier") and the mailbox provider (the "issuer"). If the user is already signed in to their provider, the browser quietly fetches a signed token and drops it into the form, and the server validates that token on submission. Google notes the issuer never learns which site made the request.
For developers the front end implementation is fairly straightforward. The email field needs an autocomplete hint, plus a hidden input carrying a session-bound nonce:
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="hidden" name="token" nonce={nonce} autocomplete="email-verification-token">
The heavier work sits on the server side, where the token's signature is checked against the provider's keys. Resend's Phil Nash, who wrote a walkthrough of the flow, published an npm package and a Next.js example to handle that parsing and validation.
On Hacker News a developer said there is "literally no worse context switch" than hopping to an inbox mid sign-up, and that email verification had cost them "dozens, maybe hundreds" of registrations they never finished. Another pointed out that verification mail is frequently blocked or filtered to spam, with no visible difference between delayed and lost messages, so removing it is a genuine win.
One commenter argued the privacy claim is thin:
Make everything what works complicated.
There is no advantage.
"User privacy is enhanced as the issuer does not learn which web application is making the request as the request is mediated by the browser." Every web application nowadays send you a welcome, onboarding, reminder after the verification. (No user privacy enhancement)
So we get a new process that solves nothing, but makes everything complicated. (And complicated helps the big and hurt the little in th long run)
Not verified but feels like a Google draft that closes the web.
Another called the issuer's blindness to the requesting site a "functional liability" rather than a feature. Developers who rely on per-recipient addresses, such as name+site@example.com, noted the flow still forces a fallback whenever the provider cannot attest those aliases. Others likened it to FedCM, folding identity primitives into the browser as password managers once did.
Outside Chrome with a signed-in Gmail account, sites drop back to the classic confirmation email, and the established syntax, MX, and SMTP checking services still cover the addresses this API cannot.
Teams already testing should track breaking changes. Chrome's October update added Android and third-party origin trials in Chrome 154, renamed the Sec-Fetch-Dest issuance value to email-verification, and from Chrome 156 returns the email exactly as submitted. The verifier and issuer guides track the current contract.
The Email Verification API remains an experimental proposal, best used today as a progressive enhancement while the WICG gathers feedback from sites, providers, and users.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raphael Gruber, Jan Rothörl, Simon M. Fröhlich, Maarten A. Brems, Fabian Kammerbauer, Maria-Andromachi Syskaki, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Sachin Krishnia, Asle Sudbø, Peter Virnau, Mathias Kläui. Real-time observation of topological defect dynamics mediating two-dimensional skyrmion lattice melting. Nature Nanotechnology, 2025; 20 (10): 1405 DOI: 10.1038/s41565-025-01977-2

articles.title: Rockstar Game Workers Union Announces Union Vote Aligned with GTA VI Launch
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
Rockstar Game Workers Union Announces Union Vote Aligned with GTA VI Launch
Aside from the GTA VI hype, Rockstar has been in the news quite frequently of late, relating to a new union forming at its UK offices. That union, which started taking shape in early 2026 following what it called unfair firings, has now officially started coming to fruition, as recognition of the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union will officially be put to an employee vote from November 12 to 26, according to a new announcement by the union on Bluesky. 
According to the union's social media page, the vote seeks to officially ratify the recognition deal agreed to by management and workers across union meetings that have taken place over the last few months, and it would "give workers a say over issues including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies." The union vote will coincide with the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which appears to have been a deliberate publicity move by the union, and it will take place via an anonymous online vote.The Rockstar Game Workers Union isn't the only new union agreement to pop up in the light of the layoffs that have plagued the gaming industry of late, with a recent Blizzard workers union agreement addressing sought-after protections against generative AI and layoffs as well as a need for remote work. The newly formed United Videogame Workers Union also launched in mid-2025 due to fears relating to AI and layoffs.

articles.title: Discord will make some channels and messages searchable on Google
articles.text:
In context: Discord is widely considered a relatively private communication channel compared to the open web. However, in a bid to revive the usefulness of forums, the company will start making some messages more public in the coming weeks. Server admins should now start seeing new controls to determine which chatrooms and messages can eventually appear in Google search results.
Answers posted after mid-December to questions in discoverable Discord servers can appear in search results on the open web. Usernames and avatars won't appear next to the messages, and admins can already opt out of the new policy.
Most Discord servers will remain relatively private, inaccessible to search engines and anyone without an invite. However, users can already enter certain large servers, called Discoverable servers, without an invite, and Discord aims to make information from and about these servers more visible.
Discoverable servers must have more than 1,000 members, be more than eight weeks old, and meet certain safety and privacy requirements. Discord's website already hosts links to some Discoverable servers, along with brief descriptions of them.
All discoverable servers will have web-accessible description pages starting November 16 unless admins opt out. Admins can limit public access to certain channels, but Discord will automatically generate default descriptions for discoverable servers if admins haven't written their own or adjusted the relevant settings by the deadline. The new controls can be found in Server Settings > Web Presence.
Furthermore, answers to questions posted in public channels will appear in server web pages and search results starting mid-December – if admins and users don't opt out. Channels where messages can go public will be labeled. The new system applies only to questions and answers posted after mid-December, and usernames and avatars will be hidden.
Users can opt out now by heading to User Settings > Data and Privacy. If users change their visibility settings after posting public messages, those messages will still appear on the web and in search results unless deleted. However, new messages will remain private.
The change aims to make troubleshooting solutions and other helpful advice more widely available. Although public forums still exist, many users complain that troubleshooting threads and other informative discussions have migrated to private Discord servers, making them harder to access and putting them at risk if the servers close.

articles.title: NanoTess delivers wound-care treatment to Ukraine’s front lines | BetaKit
articles.text:
A made-in-Calgary treatment for wound and burn care is now treating soldiers on the front lines of the war in Ukraine.
The news: NanoTess, a Calgary biotech startup, announced at the CAN Health Network Annual Conference on Wednesday that its flagship product, NanoSALV Catalytic, is being used to treat wounds sustained by soldiers and civilians in Ukraine. The company claims NanoSALV, a topical gel that uses tiny, catalytic particles to accelerate healing, has reached more than 6,000 soldiers and civilians impacted by the war.
From the source: “Effective medical treatment in active conflict zones and during recovery is critical to our soldiers. Burns require urgent care, and complex blast wounds, typically sustained in drone strikes, are easily contaminated by debris and can quickly become infected,” Dr. Vasyl Voronets, a military surgeon working in Ukraine’s eastern front, said in a press release. “In a conflict where medical access can never be taken for granted, this support matters deeply to our soldiers and to the people we serve.”
The context: To deliver NanoSALV to the often remote and dangerous regions along the Ukrainian frontlines, NanoTess is partnering with Calgary-based charity Medical Mercy Canada, as well as the Public Health Centre of Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military’s Medical Forces Sustainment Group East. Much of the deployment is occurring via drone delivery, the company said.
Since being authorized by Health Canada in 2022, NanoSALV has gone on to be used in more than 2,500 hospitals and health facilities; it’s also available in 14,000 pharmacies. In 2023, the company received support from the CAN Health Network, a federally funded organization that connects health-tech companies with healthcare providers to launch commercialization.
Final thought: Ukraine and Canada have deepened cooperation. In September, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky signed a 100-year declaration to collaborate on defence innovation. Amid that collaboration, as well as Canada’s larger defence expansion, dual-use technology from the private sector has been prioritized. NanoTess has expanded toward dual-use capability, participating in the Department of National Defence’s (DND) Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security program, and receiving support from the DND to build out its manufacturing.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of NanoTess

articles.title: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming 'vulnpocalypse' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched. According to researchers who found the bugs, this is only the beginning, as AI changes how quickly novel vulnerabilities can be uncovered and exploited.
On this episode of TechCrunch’sEquity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Tomer Schwartz, CTO of Exposure Management & AppSec at Google-owned Wiz, who was part of the scramble — alongside OpenAI, research group Calif, and the PHP team — to fix the bugs. On the show, Schwartz and Bellan get into what the race looked like from the inside, how early-stage startups can build with security in mind, and why patching by hand won’t scale.
Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

articles.title: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.text:
LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.)
Apple’s demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration.
The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it’s taking for that weren’t yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors.
Beyond that, the design is largely similar to the existing one, but there are a few notable differences. First, it’s much lighter. Apple said when announcing it that the 14-inch model is just 3 pounds, down around half a pound from the previous model, depending on configuration.

articles.title: The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
articles.text:
The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability.
In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.
Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming.
—James Temple
This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries
Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.
The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.
Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise.
—Alexander C. Kaufman
This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.

articles.title: Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
articles.text:
The Anthropic S-1 seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it’s in the business of selling IT contracts, Anthropic has just offered a handy solution: Doing a bunch of things that look like you’re trying to build the machine god is the only way to avoid going bankrupt.
Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed?
Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed?
Forget about the machine god for a minute. At least in my read of the S-1, it seems like Anthropic is pinning the future of its company to dramatic growth; it has to, in order to meet its fixed costs. You don’t have to be an AI skeptic to lift an eyebrow at these numbers. But if you are skeptical that dramatic recursive self-improvement is possible — in the way the business plan seems to require — this doesn’t look like a good investment.
Let’s start with the good news for Anthropic fans. The company’s revenue grew fourteen times to $16.3 billion between the first half of 2026 and the first half of 2025. There’s an $80 billion loss, but it’s largely an accounting thing that isn’t relevant to the underlying business. If we remove that, and some other charges, including employee compensation, we’re looking at $1.62 billion in adjusted income in the first half of 2026. I’ve asked before if AI can make enough money to pay for itself, and the answer from Anthropic’s S-1 appears to be, at least for this company, at least right now, yes.
Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals
Anthropic was considerably more disciplined than OpenAI or Elon Musk, and it seems to be paying off. (Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals. Better luck next time, Elon!) The company has never released an AI image generator, an AI TikTok clone, or an AI waifu. Instead, it specialized in tasks like coding and cybersecurity, staying laser-focused on the thing it is easiest for a computer to do: more computer. And it focused on the enterprise market, which is less fickle than consumers. Its net revenue retention is 900 percent. Pretty good! That revenue isn’t consumers, either. About three-quarters of customers in the first half of 2026 are spending at least $100,000 a year.
On the other hand, Anthropic is under intense competitive pressure — from both other frontier labs and open-source models. The other frontier labs are all rushing for the cutting edge, too. Claude Opus 5.5 currently sits atop the Epoch Capabilities Index, but that leaderboard changes frequently. And for anyone who doesn’t care that their software is four months behind, there are the open-source ones.
What’s more, Anthropic has a disadvantage against a rival like Google. It doesn’t have multiple paths to revenue — and Google does. Google can also wrap its AI into other products businesses already use. Remember when Microsoft Teams ate Slack? It wasn’t because Teams was the better product; Microsoft just had better distribution, since Teams was bundled with other programs companies were already paying for. Having the best model matters more for cybersecurity — one area Anthropic is targeting for growth — than for instant messaging software, but it’s hard to compete on distribution.
There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic
And also, revenue comes in spurts, usually after a new model is released. Between the competition and growth in use after each novel model, Anthropic can never stop training, and it has to do so more efficiently than its much larger competition.
So one important question is: Can Anthropic continue to provide the results we see in the S-1?
There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic. Sure, there’s a convenient blank on its purchase commitments and lease agreements on page 64, and another kicky little blank on the amounts it’s expecting to spend before December 31st, 2030, on page 137. However, we know the commitments run through 2045.
Fortunately, there’s a “Commitments and contingencies” section that can help us out a little. There’s a fixed minimum of non-cancelable purchase commitments that total $265.6 billion, with terms between one and 20 years. The company has lease agreements “primarily related to compute and infrastructure capacity” that haven’t yet commenced of $321.4 billion, as of the unaudited June 30th figures. After that, Anthropic entered new compute and infrastructure agreements totaling about $245 billion, again with terms between one and 20 years. There’s some other transactions that haven’t yet been finalized, which Anthropic estimates as costing $125 billion to $150 billion. There are also other compute commitments that are variable.
“The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage.”
If I add all that up, I’m looking at a minimum of around $850 billion of commitments over the next 20 years, which will rise to about a trillion dollars if the transactions that haven’t been finalized are added in at the current estimated cost. And that’s assuming I’m not missing anything, which I may very well be.
So to meet those commitments, Anthropic’s growth must continue at breakneck speed. Anthropic doesn’t give us a payment schedule for its future commitments, but analyst Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook models it at about $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, which means $188 billion in revenue to keep the current ratio of cost to compute stable. “Growth is not optional for this company,” he writes. “The contracts assume it.”
Compute and infrastructure (and a few other items) associated with customers cost $2.3 billion in the first half of this year. Model development (and a few other items) was significantly more expensive; Anthropic spent $9.7 billion on it. But Anthropic simultaneously got more efficient — spending less money on compute to bring in each dollar of revenue, according to Rolfes.
Everyone in cybersecurity has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic
Is that a long-standing trend? Hard to say. We don’t have the third quarter numbers in front of us. “The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage and they didn’t have enough compute so they are able to charge more for what they had,” says Brendan Burke, an analyst at Futurum Group.
As enterprise software, it makes sense for Anthropic to target companies’ IT budgets. Conveniently, cybersecurity is a place where you will absolutely get your shit rekt if you are not constantly up to date — everyone there has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic. Of course, AI is part of the problem; hackers can use it to brute-force stuff they couldn’t do before. Plus, the products themselves are also causing headaches thanks to a partner’s sloppy fuck-up of security protocols around AI agents.
Frontier labs need high-margin products to avoid a race to the bottom on token pricing, notes Burke. That made something else stand out to me: Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs by 40 percent over Opus 5. Now, Anthropic says that lower cost means more usage, which lets the company preserve its margins. If you assume that cost reduction happens every time a new model is released, pretty soon you wind up with tasks at a fraction of the price.
Claude is already building Claude under human direction
This isn’t necessarily an insurmountable problem, in part because increased efficiency doesn’t always slash margins, says Gil Luria, an analyst with DA Davidson. Amazon Web Services and other cloud providers ”have become far more efficient every year and reduce their prices every year and they have had steady growth and rising margins,” he says.
But the pressure for growth is pretty undeniable. That’s where recursive self-improvement, with minimal or no supervision, comes in. “More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.” Based on the general rhetoric Anthropic has about the apocalypse or whatever, it expects to hit dramatic recursive self-improvement, maybe soon.
Claude is already building Claude under human direction. In its risk factors, Anthropic warns that it’s locked in to that approach. That comes with a clear tradeoff, since using AI to develop more AI “may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures.” If I am reading that right, Anthropic is saying that its business relies on building new models so fast, using work it may not fully understand, that it is essentially forced, for business reasons, to do stuff that may be risky to everyone. Which is why we’ve got a bunch of weird stuff about the existential hazards of “catastrophic” harm and the development of “forms of sentience” in the risk factors.
Is dramatic recursive self-improvement that escapes the bounds of human supervision possible? Dunno. But if it isn’t, that makes it much harder for Anthropic to meet its existing compute commitments and turn a profit.

articles.title: El MacBook Pro estrena pantalla táctil y OLED: Apple rompe su gran tabú
articles.text:
Más de 16 años después del recordado discurso de Steve Jobs explicando por qué las pantallas táctiles en los ordenadores portátiles no funcionaban, Apple rompió su gran tabú. "Las superficies táctiles no quieren estar en vertical. [...] No funcionan, son terribles ergonómicamente", dijo el cofundador y exCEO de la compañía en octubre de 2010, y a partir de hoy sus sucesores lo van a poner a prueba con el nuevo MacBook Pro OLED con pantalla táctil.
Apple acaba de completar su semana de lanzamientos con el estreno del MacBook Pro de por primera vez con pantalla táctil como método de entrada. Este cambio llega de la mano de la adopción de paneles OLED, lo que garantiza negros más profundos y optimizaciones en materia de brillo, contraste y colores más vívidos.
Puede parecer que Apple ha dado el brazo a torcer con la inclusión de una pantalla táctil en los MacBook Pro OLED, tras años de negarse a hacerlo. Sin embargo, se ha dado el gusto de hacerlo a su manera. Es que, más allá de las posibilidades que desbloquea poder controlar el ordenador con los dedos, la realidad es que los de Cupertino mantienen el teclado y el ratón como los métodos de input principales. Los comandos táctiles para interactuar con macOS se presentan como un complemento y no como un reemplazo de los elementos ya convencionales.
Nuevo MacBook Pro OLED con pantalla táctil, disponible en 14 y 16 pulgadas
Con el nuevo MacBook Pro OLED, Apple no solo da el salto a una pantalla táctil, sino que traer un cambio muy esperado. La empresa finalmente se despide del notch e introduce la Isla Dinámica, que brinda un funcionamiento idéntico al que vemos en el iPhone.
El MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil incorpora un panel tándem OLED que Apple llama ProLED XDR. Este presume de un brillo pico de 2.000 nits (HDR), tasa de refresco de 120 Hz y una relación de contraste de 10.000.000:1. Al igual que con los modelos convencionales, los de Cupertino ofrecen su nuevo portátil en dos tamaños: 14 y 16 pulgadas. Vale mencionar que, en realidad, las pantallas miden 14,2 y 16,3 pulgadas, respectivamente.
Apple ha dotado a sus portátiles con un diseño renovado que les da bordes de pantalla más delgados y los hace más ligeros. El MacBook Pro táctil de 14 pulgadas pesa 1,38 kilos, mientras que la versión de 16'' queda en 1,84 kilos. Como comparación, los modelos con pantalla convencional pesan 1,6 y 2,1 kilos, respectivamente. El dato curioso de estos portátiles es que traen de regreso un ícono de los Mac de antaño: el logo de la cubierta que se ilumina.
Los MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil son también un poco más delgados. Es por ello que los de Cupertino han implementado un nuevo sistema de refrigeración que ayuda alejar el aire caliente de la pantalla, sin necesidad de sacrificar rendimiento.
Chips M5 Pro y Max, y hasta 128 GB de memoria y 16 TB de almacenamiento
En su modo de hacer las cosas "a lo Apple", los de la manzana prometen desterrar uno de los problemas más complejos de los portátiles con pantalla táctil: los sacudones que da la pantalla al pulsarla. Es por ello que han diseñado una bisagra especialmente pensada para minimizar ese movimiento que puede resultar tan molesto. A esto se suma una estabilización avanzada de vídeo para evitar que la imagen se sacuda cuando se usa el input táctil en una vídeollamada.
El portátil llega impulsado por los chips M5 Pro y M5 Max ya disponibles en los modelos sin panel táctil, así que no hay sorpresas en tal sentido. En materia de RAM y almacenamiento, el MacBook Pro táctil de 14 pulgadas se inicia en 24 GB y 1 TB, mientras que el modelo de 16 pulgadas se puede configurar con hasta 128 GB de memoria unificada y 16 TB de espacio interno.
En materia de conectividad y puertos, el MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil soporta WiFi 7, Bluetooth 6 y Thread gracias al chip N1 de Apple. Llega con tres puertos Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, un lector de tarjetas SD, conector de 3,5 milímetros para auriculares y MagSafe 3. En materia de autonomía, promete hasta 24 horas de uso y soporta carga rápida, pudiendo recuperar el 50 % de la batería en 30 minutos.
Disponibilidad y precio de los MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil
Apple ha abierto las reservas de los MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil, que comenzarán a llegar a los compradores el 6 de noviembre. Los portátiles estarán disponibles en los dos colores tradicionales: negro espacial y plata.
Como puedes imaginar, los MacBook Pro ProLED XDR no serán nada baratos. El modelo de 14 pulgadas con M5 Pro se inicia en 3.349 euros, mientras que la variante del mismo tamaño con M5 Max comienza en 5.249 euros. En tanto que el modelo de 16 pulgadas tiene precios iniciales de 3.949 euros (M5 Pro) y 5.649 euros (M5 Max).

articles.title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act Reaches Chip And IP Suppliers
articles.text:
Determining which products may fall within the CRA’s scope and what information may need to be provided to customers.
Many of today’s electronic products connect to networks and other devices to communicate, exchange data, coordinate tasks, and receive software updates. These connections make everyday work-life tasks incredibly convenient. However, this convenience also comes with risks. Weaknesses in these products can give cyberattacks a way into trusted devices. Responding to an attack takes time and money. Even worse, reputational damage can last long after the incident. To help reduce these risks, the European Union (EU) established common cybersecurity requirements that set a baseline for product development.
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), adopted in October 2024, establishes the requirements framework. Companies supplying digital products to the EU market must consider the CRA, whether they sell directly or supply components for a customer’s finished product. The rules apply regardless of where a company is based or where development takes place.
The regulation applies to semiconductors sold separately. Manufacturers must exercise due diligence when incorporating third-party components into their products. Semiconductor intellectual property (IP) suppliers may need to provide security evaluation results and explain the assumptions for secure use.
The CRA addresses widespread product vulnerabilities, inconsistent security updates, and insufficient information for secure use. The CRA’s mandatory reporting phase took effect in September 2026. When manufacturers learn that a vulnerability in their product is being actively exploited, or that a severe incident has affected its security, an early warning must be submitted. A more detailed notification follows, with a final report explaining the findings and corrective measures. Manufacturers submit these notifications through the CRA’s Single Reporting Platform.
The CRA also lists semiconductor products such as microprocessors, microcontrollers, ASICs, and FPGAs according to core functionality, including security-related functions. The applicable category and obligations depend on the product and how it is placed on the market. Chip and IP companies need to understand which CRA responsibilities apply to their products and what information they may need to provide to customers. That determination can be challenging because commitments vary with the product’s classification. Figure 1 illustrates how suppliers may provide security evidence to support CRA reporting.
Fig. 1: Illustrative supply chain showing how component information and security evidence may move between suppliers and the product manufacturer in support of its EU CRA documentation. (Source: Arteris, Inc.)
To help companies prepare, Arteris developed the EU CRA Hardware Readiness Guide. It provides a checklist to help companies assess which products may fall within the CRA’s scope, identify who is responsible for each product, and determine what information customers may request. It also helps identify where classification, responsibility, processes, or security documentation may need further work. The guide distinguishes design-stage security evidence from a completed conformity assessment. The results can support a manufacturer’s compliance work, but it does not cover all of the manufacturer’s CRA duties.
For the security assessment, the checklist asks companies to identify assets such as keys, configuration, and debug state. Companies can also define protection boundaries and document where those assets can and cannot travel. A design that performs its specified functions does not, by itself, show that sensitive assets remain protected.
Suppliers can use the readiness guide to organize information and security evidence that may support customers as they prepare their technical documentation. Annex VII of the CRA lists what manufacturers must provide in their technical documentation. It includes cybersecurity risk assessments, relevant design and development information, and supporting evidence, where applicable. Dated, repeatable evaluations can help document the design examined, describe what was covered, and note any limitations. The guide also recommends mapping evaluation findings to named hardware weakness classes. The CRA sets security outcomes but does not mandate a specific evaluation method.
The Arteris checklist helps companies organize their preparation. In addition, Cycuity, an Arteris brand, offers Radix for hardware security verification, helping developers generate traceable security evidence. It translates security requirements into rules that can be checked in existing simulation and emulation flows. Radix-S checks those rules during simulation, and Radix-M carries them into emulation, allowing system-level analysis.
The software tracks designated assets, such as cryptographic keys and configuration data, through a design to identify flows that violate defined rules. It can also help assess whether Root of Trust features work as intended. Findings help companies locate potential weaknesses, measure security coverage, and identify areas for further testing.
December 11, 2027, marks the next major deadline. The CRA’s broader cybersecurity, conformity assessment, and documentation requirements take effect. CE marking will also be required, which declares that the product conforms to applicable EU requirements.
Before the full requirements take effect, hardware and IP suppliers can work with customers to identify which product versions are intended for the EU market. Early identification gives both sides time to align program schedules and plan necessary work while designs are still in development.
Arteris can help companies make sense of the CRA’s requirements and consider how they apply to hardware and IP products. The EU CRA Hardware Readiness Guide offers a practical starting point, and Arteris teams can help companies work through questions as they prepare.

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.text:
We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
Right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools. Here’s what we need to do instead.
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.
The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.
AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.
No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.
Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

Surveillance towers, increasingly powered by AI, promised faster responses to crossings. Our investigation of deaths near the towers found they are failing to deliver.
