articles.title: Apple: Dieser neue Mac Studio kostet mehr als ein Neuwagen
articles.text:
Apple: Dieser neue Mac Studio kostet mehr als ein Neuwagen
Mitte Oktober hatte Meta sein neues lokales KI-Modell Muse Spark Open vorgestellt. Das sei für Apple-Silicon-Prozessoren optimiert. Damit waren jedoch weder ein Macbook Air mit M3-Chip, noch ein Pro-Modell mit M4-Max-Prozessor gemeint. Wer das Modell nutzen will, braucht gleich zwei Mac Studio in einer Konfiguration, die Apple jetzt anbietet. Und die hat es in sich. Technisch, aber auch preislich.
Allein der Arbeitsspeicher kostet 17.000 Euro
Die Rede ist von der Variante mit 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher, die Apple für Ende Oktober versprochen hatte und nun tatsächlich im Online-Store verkauft. Wer seinen Mac mit derart viel RAM ausstatten will, hat dabei allerdings wenig Auswahlmöglichkeiten. Denn in der „günstigen“ Konfiguration mit M5-Max-Chip ab 2.999 Euro lässt sich der Arbeitsspeicher gar nicht aufrüsten. Er bleibt auf 36 Gigabyte beschränkt.
Klickt ihr im Konfigurator auf die 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher, zeigt euch das Formularfeld an, dass ihr schon zum voll ausgestatteten M5‑Ultra-Prozessor mit 36 Rechen- und 80 Grafik-Kernen greifen müsst. Nur diese Variante unterstützt derart viel RAM. Allein das Upgrade auf diesen Chip kostet euch 5.030 Euro zusätzlich. Hinzu käme dann noch der Sprung von 96 auf 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher. Allein dafür zahlt ihr noch einmal 17.050 Euro extra.
Wollt ihr dann noch den SSD-Speicher maximal ausreizen, zahlt ihr für das Upgrade von ein auf 16 Terabyte noch einmal 8.250 Euro extra. Insgesamt landet man so bei 33.329 Euro. Zum Vergleich: Ein kompaktes E-Auto wie der Citroën ëC3 kostet in der Basisvariante neu direkt beim Hersteller 20.140 Euro.
Für KI und Kreative
Natürlich ist ein Mac Studio in dieser Konfiguration kein Gerät für den Alltag im Homeoffice. Apple richtet sich an Kreative wie Filmemacher:innen, die mit einem solchen Computer hochauflösendes 8K-Material bearbeiten. Als weitere Zielgruppen nennt Apple selbst Datenwissenschaftler:innen, die auf solchen Maschinen KI-Modelle trainieren.
Außerdem eigne sich der Mac eben zum Ausführen lokaler KI-Agenten wie jenem von Meta. Dafür braucht man, wie gesagt, allerdings gleich zwei dieser voll ausgestatteten Mac Studios.

articles.title: How Next-Generation Mobile Processors Are Revolutionizing Smartphone Hardware and Graphics - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Gaming phones are getting ridiculously powerful. We’re well past the point where mobile gaming only means simple games designed to pass ten minutes while you’re waiting for something.
Newzoo expects 3.1 billion people to play mobile games in 2026, with the market generating $121.1 billion. Console gaming is forecast at $46.9 billion for the year, so mobile isn’t exactly the smaller side of gaming anymore.
Below, we’ll explore how gaming phones are closing the gap with consoles.
Advanced, Powerful Hardware and Graphics Potential
Current gaming phones have everything needed for demanding games, from processors to cooling systems.
The REDMAGIC 11 Pro, for example, uses Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 with an active cooling system and a 144Hz display. Testing by Android Authority found the chipset could comfortably run Call of Duty Mobile at 120fps, something we couldn’t have imagined even five years ago, and Genshin Impact held around 60fps at maximum settings.
Heat is still sometimes a bit of a limitation because you’re putting all that hardware inside something that fits in your pocket. But that’s also why gaming phones are investing more in vapor chambers, fans, and other cooling methods.
Remote For Cloud Gaming and Streaming, With More Options Than Ever Before
DEvelopers have identified the high potential of mobile gaming, and the market is now brimming with titles that have been optimized for the small screen. It’s not all about the app store downloads, either. Leading sites utilize advanced PWA technologies to offer smooth, high quality experiences without a single download needing to take place. True versatility vs apps that need to be added to a phone via a WiFi connection.
But the phone doesn’t always need to run the game, either. Xbox Cloud Gaming lets players stream supported console games directly to phones and tablets. Xbox Remote Play can also stream games installed on your own console, with progress carrying across devices.
GeForce NOW takes the same idea further on supported Android phones. NVIDIA currently supports streaming at up to 1440p and 120fps, although that level needs a compatible device, Ultimate membership, and at least a 35Mbps connection. Add a proper controller that can connect via Bluetooth, and we’re nowhere near what traditional mobile gaming was not so long ago.
Remember that cloud gaming is only as good as your connection, and bad Wi-Fi can ruin the illusion quickly.
Engagement Levels Competing With Consoles
Sensor Tower recorded around 221 billion hours of mobile gaming playtime during the first half of 2026.
Then you’ve got the 3.1 billion mobile players Newzoo expects this year. Mobile and console habits are still different, so not everyone will spend a 6-hour gaming session on their phone as they might on a console. But developers have an enormous audience that’s willing to spend a lot of time with mobile games.
Gaming phones are being built for those people rather than your parents occasionally playing Candy Crush on the bus or the sofa.
Cross-Platform Releases on Mobile and Console
Warframe launched globally on Android in February 2026. It’s not a small mobile spin-off. The Android release uses the same content build as the main game and supports cross-platform progression, letting players use the same account across mobile, PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch, and PC.
Fortnite, Genshin Impact, and other major games already work across mobile and console ecosystems. Players are getting used to starting something on one device and continuing somewhere else rather than choosing one platform and staying there.
Gaming phones still have obvious disadvantages compared with consoles, such as smaller screens or batteries that run down, but the gap is definitely shrinking. It’ll be interesting to see how close the two become over the next ten years.

articles.title: Falha no Telegram para Android permitia invasão ao atender chamada
articles.text:
Uma falha no Telegram para Android permitia que invasores executassem código no celular da vítima após ela atender uma chamada de voz. Descoberta pela empresa de segurança NebuSec, a vulnerabilidade foi corrigida na versão 12.10.4 do aplicativo.
O problema afetava versões entre 8.6.2 e 12.10.3, dentro do período de março de 2022 a setembro de 2026. Para se proteger, os usuários devem verificar se estão com a versão corrigida ou uma mais recente.
Como funcionava a vulnerabilidade
O erro estava no processamento de mensagens usadas para configurar e informar o estado das chamadas. Quando uma delas não continha todos os campos esperados, o código acessava indevidamente uma área da memória do aparelho.
A NebuSec demonstrou a execução de código em uma chamada privada atendida em um celular com processador ARM64. No vídeo divulgado pela empresa, o Telegram fecha, a tela inicial do aparelho aparece e exibe a mensagem “HACKED BY NEBUSEC” (“invadido pela NebuSec”, em tradução livre).
Entre as características e limitações identificadas pela empresa estão:
- O ataque exigia apenas uma conta comum no Telegram.
- A falha foi confirmada em chamadas privadas em aparelhos com processadores ARM64.
- Não havia evidências de impacto direto nos aplicativos para iOS, computador ou nas chamadas em grupo.
Como verificar a atualização
Para conferir a versão instalada, o usuário deve abrir as configurações do Telegram e consultar o número exibido na parte inferior da página. A versão 12.10.4 corrige a falha.
Embora os aplicativos compartilhem uma biblioteca utilizada nas chamadas de voz e vídeo, a correção já havia sido incorporada aos códigos das versões para iPhone e computador antes de chegar ao Android.
Em 29 de outubro, a vulnerabilidade ainda não tinha um identificador CVE, utilizado para catalogar falhas de segurança. O The Hacker News informou que questionou o Telegram e a NebuSec sobre o uso da vulnerabilidade em ataques reais e sobre o alcance do código executado no aparelho.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Nigeria’s securities exchange urges founders to list on local bourse
articles.text: Nigeria’s securities regulator has urged local founders to look closer to home for capital, arguing that crowdfunding and debt markets can offer a route to an eventual stock market listing. Emomotimi Agama, director-general of the Securities and Exchange Commission, told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos on Wednesday that founders could start by raising money from people who already trusted them, then use instruments such as commercial paper to test investor appetite. Debt could also help entrepreneurs fund growth without surrendering equity, he said. But he warned against using short-term bank loans to finance long-term ambitions. “That’s a mismatch that will drown you.” “The problem that a lot of people have is that they are shy of speaking to the regulator or even financial advisers,” Agama said. “Once we understand your constraints, we are also able to tell you exactly how to go about it and what you need to do to raise capital.” The SEC wants the local market to absorb more of the money founders now chase overseas. On October 19, Vice President Kashim Shettima unveiled the Nigerian Capital Market Master Plan 2.0 , a 10-year roadmap targeting ₦750 trillion ($549 billion) in market capitalisation by 2036. Agama said the market has already grown from ₦55 trillion ($40.3 billion) in 2024 to more than ₦162 trillion ($118.6 billion). He pointed to the Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO, which closed on October 27 after an SEC-approved extension, saying investors from 54 African countries subscribed. Digital asset firms got a blunter message. In January, the SEC raised the minimum capital for crypto exchanges and custodians to ₦2 billion ($1.46 million) from ₦500 million ($366,000), with a compliance deadline of June 30, 2027. Agama said capital requirements test whether a company can carry out its business, and he urged young founders to pool resources with partners. “You cannot be a cockroach and decide to wrestle with elephants,” he said. Licensing has also moved slowly. An audience member from the Virtual Asset Service Providers Association asked why no crypto platform is fully licensed, more than two years after the SEC launched its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme (ARIP) in June 2024. Quidax and Busha received provisional licences that August and are still awaiting full approval . Agama said the SEC has charged ARIP firms no fees while it studies the risks in their businesses, and that it cannot act alone because other regulators share the space. “If you are not an investor, then you must be a victim,” he said, meaning anyone who invests in an unregulated business. For founders building stablecoin or tokenisation products, the lesson is to engage early. Agama said the SEC oversees digital asset activity outside payments, while the Central Bank of Nigeria handles payments. Firms that fall under SEC rules and stay away are in violation, he said, and “ignorance of the law is not an excuse.”

articles.title: Cisco SD-WAN Zero-Day Exploitation Tied to Volt Typhoon’s ‘Silent Train’ Network
articles.text:
A threat actor whose infrastructure overlaps with a covert network used by China’s Volt Typhoon exploited a critical Cisco SD-WAN vulnerability to deploy malware designed to harvest encryption keys, Cisco Talos reported on Wednesday.
The same day, Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs published research on that network, Silent Train, which Volt Typhoon used to target US organizations, including in a zero-day campaign exploiting the same Cisco flaw.
The vulnerability, CVE-2026-20127, has a CVSS score of 10 and was disclosed in February 2026. Without needing credentials, attackers can exploit it remotely to get past the peering authentication of SD-WAN controller components and obtain admin rights. Cisco warns that this access can be leveraged to alter the SD-WAN network’s configuration.
Attackers planted KeyDrift malware on SD-WAN controllers
Talos attributes the attacks to UAT-11473, which it describes as a highly sophisticated APT targeting space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research. Talos calls the activity historical but has not said when the attacks occurred.
According to Talos, the malware framework, named KeyDrift, was designed to give its operators persistent access to the SD-WAN controllers and to automatically siphon off keying material. It is injected into legitimate control-plane processes, giving it access to control traffic after it has been decrypted.
Its main module, PolyFlame, works as a backdoor and can also relay commands to other hosts as an intermediate command-and-control (C2) node. A second module, LittleFilch, collects keying material that Talos believes includes keys protecting data-plane traffic.
Talos assessed with high confidence that UAT-11473’s infrastructure “overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s ‘Silent Train’ covert access network.” It does not say the two are the same group.
Volt Typhoon used Silent Train in several zero-day campaigns
Black Lotus Labs has monitored Silent Train since late 2023. The network routes the attackers’ traffic through chains of hacked small office routers, IoT devices and enterprise systems that are frequently replaced, and the operators clean up after each session.
Lumen’s monitoring led to hundreds of victim notifications. It also helped uncover at least four confirmed zero-day campaigns targeting Versa Director, N-able N-central, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, and VeloCloud Orchestrator, plus a likely zero-day campaign against Quest KACE.
According to Lumen, Volt Typhoon was exploiting CVE-2026-20127 by late 2025 and kept doing so long after Cisco’s disclosure. The group focuses on management platforms and other control-plane systems that offer broad access across an organization.
“Every zero-day campaign through Silent Train targeted this kind of platform,” Lumen noted.
Victims include telecoms firms, government entities, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communications providers, MSPs, universities with military ties, and critical infrastructure operators. Hawaii, California and Texas were targeted the most.
Lumen says the victimology points to an attempt to secure footholds in systems that would matter most during a geopolitical crisis, particularly one involving the Indo-Pacific region. However, Black Lotus Labs researcher Mike Horka told journalist Kim Zetter that the hackers have also exfiltrated documents on military operations and network structures, and he believes the activity combines pre-positioning and espionage.
Lumen’s report does not mention KeyDrift or UAT-11473.

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
Story Source:
Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan, Seigo Tarucha. Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2

articles.title: Buckle up for more body-swapping hijinks in Jumanji: Open World trailer
articles.text:
Let’s face it, the mid-December box office will be dominated by Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three, but for those seeking fun holiday family fare, Jumanji: Open World opens the very next week on Christmas Day. Sony Pictures just released a new trailer for director Jake Kasdan’s sequel to his 2019 hit, Jumanji: The Next Level, teasing the usual wacky hijinks with a twist that calls back to the original 1995 film.
As previously reported, Kasdan gave the franchise a welcome major overhaul with the release of 2017’s Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle, updating the original board game into a vintage video game and giving us a hugely entertaining action-adventure. Welcome to the Jungle racked up over $960 million at the global box office and spawned the equally successful 2019 sequel Jumanji: The Next Level.
A third film was always in the cards: The Next Level featured a tantalizing mid-credits scene in which a heater repairman (Lamorne Morris) visits Spencer Gilpin’s (Alex Wolff’s) house, sees the broken video game console, and inadvertently triggers the game. The COVID-19 pandemic paused the third film’s development, but things picked up again in 2024, and here we are. Per the official synopsis:
This Christmas, Dwayne Johnson, Kevin Hart, Jack Black, and Karen Gillan are reunited in Jumanji: Open World, the hilarious final installment of the globally beloved action-adventure trilogy. Our heroes have escaped the perilous jungles of Jumanji before, but this time Jumanji breaks free of its console, unleashing its chaos into our world.
Star Dwayne Johnson—who plays in-game avatar Dr. Xander “Smolder” Bravestone—let slip in 2019 that The Next Level‘s in-game villain, Jurgen the Brutal (Rory McCann), was actually the avatar of another unknown real-world player.

articles.title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime, a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched.
Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it.
A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image.
This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository, and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough.
What you get without building anything
The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. The tag this sample pulls, public.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/ray:train-ml-cuda-v1.1, replaces a build that would otherwise look like this:
| Layer | What you would otherwise build and keep aligned | In the Ray Train DLC | 
| Distributed runtime | Ray with the dashboard and job server, at a version KubeRay supports | Ray 2.58.0 with Train, Tune and Data | 
| Framework | PyTorch compiled for your CUDA version | PyTorch 2.13.0, torchvision 0.28.0 | 
| GPU runtime | CUDA, cuDNN and NCCL releases that agree with each other | CUDA 13.0.2, cuDNN, NCCL 2.29.7 | 
| Networking | EFA installer, libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl, built against that NCCL | EFA latest, AWS OFI NCCL plugin, GDRCopy | 
| Training libraries | DeepSpeed, flash-attn and Transformer Engine compiled for your CUDA | DeepSpeed, flash-attn, Transformer Engine, PyTorch Lightning, Hugging Face libraries | 
| Diagnostics | NCCL tests built from source | all_reduce_perf already on the path | 
The networking row is the one most teams would least like to own. A mismatch there doesn’t produce an error. NCCL drops to TCP sockets, and the job runs to completion at a fraction of the speed. In the DLC, those libraries are built and tested together, and AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests, which are exactly the paths this sample uses.
A few more properties remove work that you would otherwise do per cluster:
- No registry setup – The image is public, so nodes pull it without credentials and nothing is built or pushed on the way.
- No driver matching – On startup the entrypoint checks the host’s NVIDIA driver and, if it is older than the image’s CUDA, turns on the bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries automatically.
- No head-versus-worker images – The image has no fixed role. Whatever starts the container supplies the ray start command, so one tag serves every pod.
- No separate inference image family – Ray Train shares the ray ECR repository with the Ray Serve DLC and Ray LLM DLCs, under the train-ml tag prefix.
Configure it, don’t rebuild it
Everything that differs between one training job and the next is set around the image. The sample uses each of these mechanisms:
| What you control | How you set it | In this sample | 
| Head or worker role | KubeRay rayStartParams per pod group | Same DLC_IMAGE for both. Head runs with num-gpus: "0" | 
| GPUs and EFA per pod | Kubernetes resource requests | nvidia.com/gpu: 4, vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 1 | 
| Network transport | Environment variables on the pod or the job | FI_PROVIDER, NCCL_NET_PLUGIN, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_DEBUG | 
| Extra Python packages | Ray runtime_env at submit time | Any package a job needs, installed at submit time | 
| Image version | Versioned or digest-pinned tag in DLC_IMAGE | train-ml-cuda-v1.1 | 
| Cluster shape | Variables in scripts/ env.sh | Instance type, node count, GPUs per node, Region, AZ | 
| Training job | Arguments to train.py | Model, steps, sequence length, batch size | 
Packages per job. The image ships the HuggingFace training stack, so this sample’s job needs nothing added. When an experiment does need a library the image does not carry, Ray installs it for that job at submit time through runtime_env and the image is unchanged. No new image, no new tag.
Transport per job. The image defaults to FI_PROVIDER=efa, and its NCCL configuration excludes the loopback and Docker bridge interfaces. On EKS you point NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME at the pod’s eth0. The sample sets all four networking variables in the manifest anyway, so the behavior is visible in one file and doesn’t depend on image defaults. Because these are plain environment variables, a single job can override them through its runtime_env.
Versions you choose. The sample pins train-ml-cuda-v1.1, the current minor release, so a cluster is reproducible from one run to the next. The vX.Y tags move with security rebuilds. The fully qualified vX.Y.Z tags stay frozen at the original release build, so pin a digest when you need a byte-identical run. The same image is also available from private ECR URIs.
How the cluster is laid out
All nodes sit in private subnets of one virtual private cloud (VPC) and reach the internet only through a NAT Gateway, which is how every node pulls the DLC from Amazon ECR Public and how workers download model weights from Hugging Face. One m7i.xlarge forms the system node group, hosting kube-system add-ons, the KubeRay operator and the Ray head. The head runs the job server on port 8265 and Ray’s control store on 6379, and it advertises no GPUs, so no training work lands on it. Jobs are submitted from inside the head pod with kubectl exec, through the EKS API, so port 8265 is never exposed outside the cluster.
Training runs on two g6.12xlarge instances, each with four NVIDIA L4 GPUs, 48 vCPUs, 192 GiB of memory, 40 Gbps of networking and one EFA interface. Each runs one Ray worker pod that claims all four GPUs and the EFA interface, and Ray Train places four workers in each pod: ranks 0–3 on one instance, 4–7 on the other. Because EFA traffic doesn’t cross Availability Zones, the scripts place both instances in a single zone that has been checked to offer g6.12xlarge.
What Ray Train does inside the container
The DLC provides the stack. Ray Train provides the part that would otherwise be launcher code. Multi-node PyTorch normally means starting a process per GPU on every host and giving each one its rank, the world size and a rendezvous address. With Ray Train you write the training loop as a function and pass it to TorchTrainer with a ScalingConfig. Ray starts one worker per GPU wherever the cluster has GPUs, forms the torch.distributed process group, and runs your function on each worker.
This sample asks Ray Train for FSDP, which splits the model’s weights, gradients and optimizer state across all eight GPUs rather than copying them to each one. Qwen2.5-1.5B in bfloat16 needs about 12 GB for those four tensors. Sharded eight ways, each L4 GPU holds roughly 1.5 GB. The price is communication: FSDP gathers each layer’s weights before using it and reduce-scatters gradients afterwards, so the whole model crosses between ranks on every step. Between the two instances, that traffic is what the DLC’s EFA stack carries.
Prerequisites
You must have the following in place before you start:
- Tools: AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 signed in to the target account, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, and envsubst from GNU gettext.
- Quota: 96 vCPUs of G-family On-Demand capacity for the two g6.12xlarge instances, in an AWS Region where at least one zone offers them. If you already hold an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the instances, set CAPACITY_RESERVATION_ID instead. The scripts launch the node group into it and skip the capacity search.
- Budget: about $9.50 an hour while the GPU instances are up, covering both instances, the EKS control plane and the NAT Gateway.
A quick way to confirm that the CLI is pointed at the account that you expect:
The training code: One function and a trainer
code/train.py is the whole job, and it contains nothing specific to the container, the cluster or the network. Ray runs train_func once per GPU. It asks Ray for its rank, loads the model, hands it to prepare_model for FSDP, and runs an ordinary PyTorch loop:
code/train.py — the per-GPU function (abridged)
The driver joins the running cluster, counts its GPUs and starts the trainer. Because the worker count comes from the cluster, the same script runs unchanged on one node or many:
code/train.py — the driver (abridged)
The batches are random token IDs so that the run depends on nothing but the cluster. The sample is judged on whether real FSDP collectives crossed both nodes and the job completed. For a real fine-tune, replace the random tensor with a Ray Data or DataLoader pipeline. Nothing else in the function changes.
The manifest: The only place the DLC is configured
manifest/raycluster.yaml is where the image meets the cluster, and it is short because the image needs so little. The head’s only special setting is NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void, which stops the container runtime’s NVIDIA hook from failing on a node that has no GPU. The worker group holds everything else:
manifest/raycluster.yaml — worker group (abridged)
Read it as three decisions.
Which image: ${DLC_IMAGE}, unmodified, for both head and workers.
Which hardware: four GPUs and the node’s single EFA interface per pod. Requesting vpc.amazonaws.com/efa is what makes the EFA device plugin mount the interface into the container. Without it, NCCL can’t see EFA and falls back to sockets.
Which transport: four environment variables, so nothing is left to auto-detection.
Two smaller details keep a multi-node job stable. First, requests should equal limits, which places the workers in Kubernetes’ Guaranteed Quality of Service (QoS) class. This matters because a single throttled or evicted rank stalls the other seven. Second, num-gpus is derived from the same variable as the GPU request, so Ray’s view of capacity always matches Kubernetes’.
Bringing it up: One command for the infrastructure, then the job
Configuration lives in one place, scripts/env.sh: cluster name, Region, Kubernetes version, node types and counts, the image, pinned versions of KubeRay and both device plugins, and the training parameters. Export any of them to change it for a run. All five scripts are idempotent and safe to re-run. deploy_cluster.sh, deploy_node_group.sh, and deploy_ray_train_job.sh each prompt before creating or touching cluster resources. install_gpu_plugins.sh and install_kuberay.sh are reconcilers and run straight through.
./deploy_all.sh – Finds where the capacity actually is, then builds the infrastructure there.
g6.12xlarge capacity shifts between Regions and Availability Zones day to day, so this is the starting point rather than a Region guessed up front in env.sh. It first runs find_gpu_capacity.sh, which checks, per candidate Region: whether g6.12xlarge is offered in each Availability Zone, whether the account’s On-Demand G/VT-family vCPU quota has room for the requested node count, and the EC2 Spot placement score as a capacity signal. With --probe, which deploy_all.sh passes by default, it gets a definitive answer by creating and immediately canceling a real Capacity Reservation in each candidate zone. It then shows the plan and asks once:
Answering y runs, in order, deploy_cluster.sh, deploy_node_group.sh, install_gpu_plugins.sh, and install_kuberay.sh in the recommended Region, each skipping its own repeat confirmation because this one already asked (-y skips this prompt too, and --plan shows the plan without creating anything). If the GPU node group can’t launch in the best zone, the script removes it and tries the next zone the probe confirmed. GPU_AZ is also cross-checked against the cluster’s actual private subnets, not only where g6.12xlarge happens to be offered, so the GPU node group can’t end up pinned to an Availability Zone the cluster has no subnet in. The chosen Region and zone are saved to scripts/.placement.env, which every other script reads, so later commands target the same place without re-exporting anything. Together the four steps take 20 to 30 minutes on a fresh Region. An existing cluster or node group is detected and reused.
deploy_cluster.sh creates the EKS control plane, VPC, OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, core add-ons, and the m7i.xlarge system node group, choosing subnets in zones that actually offer g6.12xlarge. deploy_node_group.sh adds the two g6.12xlarge instances with EFA turned on, labeled role=gpu-worker and nvidia.com/gpu.present=true. The second label is one that teams often overlook. Without it, the NVIDIA device plugin chart’s DaemonSet runs on zero nodes, with no error pointing at the cause. install_gpu_plugins.sh makes sure both device plugins are present. Recent eksctl bundles them into an EFA-enabled node group, so on a fresh cluster it finds them and skips. Otherwise it installs them at pinned chart versions. Either way it verifies nvidia.com/gpu and vpc.amazonaws.com/efa are allocatable on every GPU node rather than trusting a successful Helm release. install_kuberay.sh installs the KubeRay operator onto the system node, keeping it off the GPU instances.
What deploy_all.sh does not do by default is run the training job. That stays a separate step you can re-run as often as you like, because it is a real job run rather than infrastructure, and a failed job then never sends you back through cluster setup. Pass --train to chain it:
./deploy_ray_train_job.sh — the RayCluster, the job, and the checks.
Renders the manifest with envsubst and applies it. It then re-reads each GPU node’s allocatable resources before waiting on any pod: if a device plugin didn’t come up, you get a clear error here rather than a pod that sits in Pending until a timeout. Once the head is Ready and both workers are Ready, it copies code/ onto the head and, through kubectl exec, submits from inside it:
The submit call streams logs from all eight ranks and returns when the job does. The script then inspects which transport NCCL used and exits with an error if the job failed or EFA wasn’t in the path, which also makes it usable as a continuous integration (CI) gate. ./deploy_ray_train_job.sh status prints the RayCluster state, which instance hosts each pod, and GPU capacity. A correctly provisioned cluster looks like this:
Adapting it to your workload
Because the image is used as published and the job learns its scale from the cluster, most changes touch exactly one file:
| You want to change | Where | No changes needed to | 
| The model | MODEL_ID | Code, manifest, image | 
| Steps, sequence length, batch size | STEPS, SEQ_LEN, BATCH_SIZE | Code, manifest, image | 
| The training loop itself | Body of train_func | Trainer, manifest, image, scripts | 
| An additional Python package | --runtime-env-json pip list | Image | 
| A pinned DLC release | DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag | Everything else | 
| The GPU instance family | GPU_NODE_TYPE, GPUS_PER_NODE | Code, image | 
| How many GPU instances | GPU_NODE_COUNT, plus replicas, minReplicas and maxReplicas in the manifest | Code (it counts the GPUs) | 
| Region or zone | REGION, optionally GPU_AZ | Everything else | 
Variables in the table live in env.sh unless stated otherwise. When switching instance families, GPUS_PER_NODE has to match the hardware, and the family needs EFA support plus a place on the EFA device plugin’s list of allowed instance types. The plugin version pinned here is known to include g6.12xlarge. Moving to p5 or another GPUDirect-capable family needs no change to the image or the training code.
Tearing it down
The GPU instances are the expensive part, at around $9.50 an hour together with the control plane and NAT Gateway. Remove things in the opposite order to how they were created:
Where to go next
Two instances and eight GPUs ran a sharded fine-tune on EKS with a container nobody built. The Ray Train DLC supplied a tested stack from CUDA through EFA. KubeRay started it as head and workers from one tag. Ray Train placed the workers and formed the process group. Everything that varied, from hardware to transport to Python packages, was set from outside the image. The EFA path the image ships engaged with four environment variables and doubled throughput over TCP on unchanged code.
Natural next moves:
- Replace the random batches with a real dataset, and checkpoint to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon FSx for Lustre.
- Pin DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag for reproducible runs.
- Turn on FailureConfig so long runs survive a lost instance.
- Move to a larger model on a GPUDirect RDMA family such as p5. The image and code stay the same.

articles.title: Nvidia releases all-in-one adaptable Nemotron 3.5 audio transcription and translation model - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Nvidia releases all-in-one adaptable Nemotron 3.5 audio transcription and translation model
Nvidia Corp. today released a leaderboard-winning open artificial intelligence model for multilingual audio transcription and translation, along with an open data pipeline for fine-tuning Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe.
Traditional transcription AI models follow a workflow that detects speech, transcribes it, identifies and labels different speakers, then answers questions about the transcription. Transcribe does all of this in a single model pass and is capable of digesting and answering questions about 100 hours of audio, in 40 languages and can label up to eight speakers.
It’s an open-weight, 30-billion parameter mixture-of-experts model with 4 billion active parameters. That means it can fit on reasonably small hardware, though more powerful hardware lets it transcribe faster.
For its size, Transcribe punches way above its weight and it can run anywhere from the edge to the data center depending on compression. The model runs on a single Nvidia graphics processing unit, from a Jetson AGX Thor, an edge computer robot brain, or DGX Spark, a desktop AI supercomputer, all the way to a Blackwell data-center GPU. Nvidia said a Blackwell Server Edition GPU with NVFP4 precision and one-quarter model compression processes 100 hours of audio in under three minutes.
According to the company, Transcribe hits a high accuracy benchmark for getting words right, with 30.8% error rates out of the box, which can be reduced to 20.8% with careful prompting. Fine-tuned for specialized work, for example, on the Eka Care Indian medical speech benchmark, the model hit 11.8% word error rate, a substantial reduction.
Users can guide transcription analysis or ask questions with prompts. The same checkpoint can turn a recording into different outputs with separate prompts.
For example, a user could instruct the model with, “Transcribe the recording and label each speaker,” or “Translate this audio into English,” or “What decisions were made in this meeting?” or some combination. Users can also provide the model with important jargon or dialogue to help it better understand the conversation before transcribing, improving accuracy.
To build the model, Nvidia extended Granary v1 into Granary v2, the company’s massive open-source public multilingual speech AI dataset. Built with Nvidia NeMo Curator, v2 expands significantly on the previous generation of Granary. The public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in Granary v1. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.
Granary v2 generates three transcripts for each recording in clean verbatim styles that can be requested from Transcribe with a prompt. One provides everything, including “ums” and “ahs.” Another reduces full wording to figures, such as spelling out numbers as symbols. A third eliminates filler words.
All that lets developers adapt transcription from different languages using the pipeline data into readable formats and fine-tune model outputs.
Transcribe is available as a Hugging Face demo, where developers can download a checkpoint and adapt it for domain expertise with fine-tuning.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Freiburg’s VUSE XR raises €1.2 million to bring AI-powered mixed reality training to enterprises | EU-Startups
articles.text:
VUSE XR, a Freiburg-based startup developing enterprise software for mixed reality training, today announced the closing of a €1.2 million pre-Seed financing round.
The round was led by IACD, a Düsseldorf-based business angel network, with additional participation from individual business angels.
“From an investor’s perspective, VUSE XR brings together everything we look for at this stage: an exceptional team, defensible AI-driven technology, and strong commercial traction. The company has demonstrated its ability to turn a technically demanding product into a scalable software business with considerable growth potential, further accelerated by continuous AI-powered feature enrichment,” said Markus Roithmeier, IACD member and Chairman of the VUSE XR Advisory Board.
Founded in November 2023 by cousins Niclas Matthias and Dr. Paul Matthias, VUSE XR develops the VUSE XR Hub, an enterprise software platform that enables industrial and life sciences companies to create, manage and deploy immersive mixed reality training for complex products and processes.
While mixed reality hardware has matured rapidly, producing the training content to run on it has remained expensive and difficult to scale; VUSE XR is addressing this problem. The startup replaces the traditional model of costly, agency-led custom mixed reality projects with a standardised, AI-assisted workflow that allows companies to build, update and distribute training content themselves, across products and locations.
The biggest selling point here is the ease with which VUSE XR helps enterprises to create mixed reality training content. The VUSE XR Hub works by converting existing CAD models, engineering data and product documentation into photorealistic 3D models, which users can then arrange into interactive training sequences using AI-assisted tools or drag-and-drop functionality.
“Mixed reality hardware is advancing rapidly, but creating mixed reality training content remains the biggest barrier to broader enterprise adoption. The VUSE XR Hub removes this bottleneck, enabling companies to unlock significant business value from mixed reality,” said Niclas Matthias, co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of VUSE XR.
Once the content is created, training can be delivered via a web browser, mobile devices, or fully immersive XR headsets such as Meta Quest. The results are tracked centrally, and content can be updated and redeployed across an organisation at any time.
The company already counts some of the major names in the industrial and life sciences space as its customers. Its customer base includes ZEISS, Hologic, Badenova, Scheidt & Bachmann, WITRON, University Medical Centre Hamburg-Eppendorf (UKE) and Sartorius. VUSE XR has won the smartXautomation Award 2025, the AI Champions Award 2025 from the German state of Baden-Württemberg, and the pitch competition at Black Forest Space 2026.
Andreas Goss, IACD member and former Chief Executive Officer of thyssenkrupp Steel, said, “Effective training is critical to productivity, knowledge transfer and the safe operation of increasingly complex products and processes. The technology developed by VUSE XR has the potential to fundamentally change how companies deliver training, making it more accessible and scalable across products and locations.”
Alongside the funding, VUSE XR is strengthening its commercial leadership team with two senior appointments: Jan Hendrik Degner, who joins as Chief Commercial Officer, bringing experience from J.P. Morgan and CEWE Group, and Robert Günther, whose background includes senior positions at Meta and Unity, takes the role of Vice President of Sales and Service Delivery.
The startup says it will use the pre-Seed capital to advance its enterprise mixed reality training platform VUSE XR Hub, expand its AI-assisted creation capabilities and accelerate commercial growth. “With this funding and our expanded commercial team, we are ready to build VUSE XR into the category leader in enterprise mixed reality training,” Matthias added.

articles.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
articles.text:
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
A powerful feedback loop could drive more warming than predicted.
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.
A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.
None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.
A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.
At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.
So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.
Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

articles.title: Apple launches its new touchscreen MacBook Pro | TechCrunch
articles.text:
After years of resisting, Apple today launched a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starting at $2,899. The release comes nearly 10 years after the company first tried integrating touchscreens on its laptops, with its Touch Bar on a MacBook Pro, which it later went on to remove.
The new MacBook Pro more fully embraces the touchscreen, offering a new PROLED XDR Display in both 14-inch and 16-inch screen sizes. The device is powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options to choose from, along with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. The display has 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
To make the new MacBook easy to use, Apple designed a hinge that stabilizes the screen when users touch it. This also helps to stabilize the camera when you are on a video call and trying to access content on the display.
In addition, the screen will include a Dynamic Island-style cutout instead of the notch that’s present on most of the current MacBooks. Plus, the new MacBook features a six-speaker array with a new woofer design for better sound.
The 14-inch Pro weighs 3.0 pounds (1.38 kg), and the 16-inch Pro weighs 4.0 pounds (1.82 kg) — lighter than its non-touch predecessors.
Both feature three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. Users can hook up three external displays on the M5 Pro variant and up to four displays on the M5 Max variant.
The Touchscreen MacBook Pro 14-inch starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch version starts at $3,399.
Consumers can place a preorder for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro from October 30, and the device will be available starting November 6.
The new Touchscreen MacBook marks two marquee product launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also introduced the company’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, in September. Various Apple executives, including Steve Jobs and Tim Cook, have scoffed at the idea of a touchscreen Mac in the past. Jobs famously called the idea “ergonomically terrible” at one point. However, rumors of the company working on such a variant started circulating nearly three years before today’s introduction.
The launch follows yesterday’s unveiling of a new standard MacBook Pro with the M6 chip in 14-inch size starting from $1,999.

articles.title: SK hynix Announces 3Q26 Financial Results
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
SK hynix Announces 3Q26 Financial Results
SK hynix Inc. announced today that it has recorded 104.6155 trillion won in revenues, 83.3338 trillion won in operating profit (with an operating margin of 80%), and 39.7756 trillion won in net profit (with a net margin of 38%) in the third quarter. In a market environment in which prices of key products have risen on the back of growing demand for AI memory, the company once again posted all-time-high quarterly results in both revenue and operating profit, underpinned by the competitiveness of its high-value-added products. In particular, revenue exceeded 100 trillion won for the first time in the company's history. Revenue and operating profit increased by 32% and 38%, from the previous quarter, respectively.
By product, DRAM results were driven by a significant increase in sales of server DDR5 while HBM4 shipments began in earnest. In NAND, sales of 321-layer TLC eSSD expanded, and high-value-added products for data centers continued to grow across the board. The company's financial structure has also become significantly concrete. At the end of the third quarter, cash and cash equivalents stood at 114.5 trillion won, up 26.5 trillion won from the end of the previous quarter, while borrowings decreased by 2.8 trillion won to 15.8 trillion won. As a result, net cash increased to 98.7 trillion won.Memory supply shortage to persist through 2030
SK hynix analyzed that a virtuous cycle has taken hold in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue generation in areas such as software development, customer service, and search lead to greater AI adoption, which in turn drives increased investment in infrastructure. It also projected that, as the drivers of AI investment move beyond the early stage, when a small number of companies accounted for most of it, and broaden to include general enterprises and nation-level initiatives, the global AI data center infrastructure market will continue to grow steadily.
The company likewise expects the memory market to sustain its growth, led in the short term by enterprise and personal AI and, over the mid-to-long term, by physical AI such as autonomous driving and robotics.
The company assessed that supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.
Expanding production capacity and strengthening product competitiveness to achieve a further step up in growth next year
Building on these favorable conditions, the company plans to accelerate the expansion of production capacity and the strengthening of product competitiveness in order to sustain the current growth momentum, and to scale up revenue and profit one step further next year.
First, the company plans to rapidly increase the portion of its 10 nm-class 6th generation (1c) process technology and expand sales of DDR5 and LPDDR5 SOCAMM for AI servers, thereby further strengthening its DRAM portfolio centered on high-value-added products.
To respond to surging HBM demand, the company will ramp up M15X to maximum capacity by the end of the year to increase HBM4 production. Accordingly, the company expects HBM4 to surpass HBM3E in both shipment volume and revenue in the fourth quarter and to establish itself as a mainstream product.
In NAND, the company will raise the ratio of its 321-layer process to more than half of its domestic production capacity in the fourth quarter, and thereby increase the supply of high-performance, high-capacity eSSD. Over the mid-to-long term, the company intends to develop NAND into a core solution that enhances the throughput and economic efficiency of AI services, based on HBF and system optimization technologies.
Long-term agreements secured for more than 50% of 2027~2028 production capacity and the company to drastically expand investment next year
To improve mid-to-long term demand visibility and solidify its growth foundation, SK hynix is expanding long-term agreements (LTAs) with customers. The company has currently signed LTAs with 14 major customers, including leading global cloud service providers (CSPs), and is also proactively discussing with a number of customers the possibility of extending the contract terms, which are typically five years.
The LTA volume secured to date corresponds to more than 50% of total production capacity for 2027 and 2028. In particular, by introducing a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers, the company has established a structure that secures stable profitability while allowing flexible responses to market changes.
Backed by the demand visibility, the company is also moving to expand its production capabilities. Next year, with the Yongin Phase 1 entering full-scale operation and domestic and overseas infrastructure investment gaining momentum, investment is expected to increase significantly. The company nevertheless plans to adjust the scale and timing of its investment flexibly, after carefully weighing customer demand, product competitiveness, profitability and investment efficiency.
Most of the gains from the Kioxia investment to be shared with shareholders, with approximately 100 trillion won in shareholder returns to be executed this year
As previously indicated in August, SK hynix announced its additional shareholder return plan. For fiscal year 2026, the company will pursue shareholder returns totaling approximately 100 trillion won, comprising cash dividends of 30 trillion won or more and share repurchases and cancellations of 60 trillion won or more in total, including the 40 trillion won announced in August. Through this, the company intends to fulfill its commitment to return 50% or more of free cash flow (FCF). Of this, the 40 trillion won share repurchase announced in August was completed last week, and the shares will be cancelled shortly.
The company also set out its principles: the dividend amount will be determined on the basis of operating results; if significant investment gains arise, they will be returned additionally through special dividends; and share repurchases will continue every quarter.
At today's meeting, the Board of Directors resolved on a third-quarter cash dividend of 14 trillion won and a share repurchase of 20 trillion won. Of the shares to be repurchased, 10 trillion won, earmarked for shareholder returns, will be cancelled in full, while the remaining approximately 10 trillion won will be used for employee compensation and is not included in the shareholder return total.
The third-quarter dividend is 20,000 won per share, consisting of a 10,000-won dividend reflecting improved earnings and a 10,000 won special dividend that shares the gains from the Kioxia investment. The company has decided to return to shareholders most of the gains realized from its Kioxia investment this year.
SK hynix emphasized that it will deliver stable results based on robust memory demand growth and technological competitiveness and the company will consistently share financial achievements with our shareholders.
