articles.title: 10 dispositivos y accesorios que puedes conectar en el puerto USB del celular, más allá del cargador
articles.text:
El puerto USB-C de un teléfono tiene funciones que van mucho más allá de la carga de batería. Teclados, discos externos, cámaras y hasta redes por cable pueden pasar por ese mismo conector y mejorar el uso del celular.
La razón está en el propio diseño del USB-C: a diferencia de conectores anteriores, no se limita a transmitir electricidad, sino también datos, audio y video, e incluso puede alimentar otros dispositivos. Esa versatilidad explica por qué un mismo puerto admite usos tan distintos entre sí.
Dispositivos que se pueden conectar al puerto USB del celular
- Periféricos: teclados, ratones y mandos
Casi cualquier teclado o mouse USB puede conectarse a un teléfono mediante el cable o adaptador correcto.
Los mandos de videojuegos siguen la misma lógica. El DualSense de PlayStation se conecta de forma directa gracias a su propio puerto USB-C, mientras que soluciones como el Backbone Pro sujetan el teléfono y permiten jugar con carga simultánea si se usa un hub con esa función. La limitación habitual es que, sin un accesorio adicional, no se puede cargar el equipo y usar el mando al mismo tiempo.
Los hubs USB-C amplían estas posibilidades al sumar varios puertos en un mismo cable. Prácticamente cualquier hub funciona con un teléfono, y los modelos con paso de energía permiten cargar el equipo mientras se usan otros periféricos conectados.
- Almacenamiento externo y lectores de tarjetas
Los teléfonos pueden leer y escribir en unidades externas como pendrives, discos duros y unidades de estado sólido, siempre que el dispositivo use un sistema de archivos compatible, entre ellos exFAT o FAT32. Las particiones en NTFS, propias de Windows, no son reconocidas.
Algunos modelos de iPhone permiten además grabar video en 4K a altas tasas de bits directamente sobre una unidad SSD conectada por USB-C, siempre que el cable admita velocidades de transferencia de 10Gbit/s y la unidad alcance los 220MB/s o 440MB/s según la resolución elegida. Para creadores de contenido y periodistas, esto evita depender del almacenamiento interno del equipo.
Los lectores de tarjetas SD y microSD funcionan de forma similar y suelen venir integrados en muchos hubs. El teléfono reconoce la tarjeta en cuanto detecta contenido en ella, y permite tanto gestionar archivos como importar fotografías directamente a la galería.
Las cámaras digitales también pueden conectarse como si fueran una unidad de almacenamiento más. En pruebas con una cámara Sony, el equipo debió adaptarse de micro USB a USB-C y mantenerse encendido para que el teléfono lo reconociera como dispositivo de transferencia.
- Pantallas externas y proyección de video
Muchos teléfonos pueden enviar su señal de pantalla a monitores, televisores o proyectores mediante un cable o adaptador compatible, gracias a una función que transporta video por el mismo puerto de carga. En la mayoría de los casos, el dispositivo detecta la conexión y comienza a reflejar la pantalla de forma automática.
El resultado no reemplaza a un escritorio completo: el teléfono suele mostrar una réplica vertical de lo que aparece en su pantalla, salvo en modelos que incorporan un modo de escritorio, como el de Samsung, capaz de abrir varias ventanas y redimensionar aplicaciones como si fuera una computadora.
- Auriculares, DAC y micrófonos
La desaparición de la entrada de 3,5 milímetros impulsó el uso de adaptadores con conversor digital-analógico, o DAC, que mejoran la calidad de sonido respecto a los componentes internos del teléfono. También existen auriculares y audífonos USB que se conectan de forma directa, sin necesidad de adaptador.
Los micrófonos USB siguen un comportamiento similar. En pruebas con un modelo Samson conectado mediante un adaptador a USB-C, el dispositivo fue reconocido de inmediato y el sistema ofreció activarlo como entrada de audio principal.
- Conexión a internet y carga entre dispositivos
Un adaptador USB-C a Ethernet permite conectar el teléfono a una red por cable, con menor latencia e interferencias que el Wi-Fi. En una prueba, el equipo mantuvo la navegación incluso en modo avión, y el sistema priorizó automáticamente la conexión por cable sobre la inalámbrica.
Por último, el mismo puerto permite la carga inversa: el teléfono puede ceder energía a auriculares inalámbricos, relojes inteligentes u otro celular compatible. No está pensada para una carga completa, ya que agota rápido la batería propia, pero resulta útil para sumar minutos de autonomía a un accesorio sin enchufe cerca.

Image Source: TechCabal Grey has spent six years helping Africans get paid from abroad. Now it wants to become the place where payday begins. What happened? Yesterday at Moonshot by TechCabal, Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payments company, launched Paycheck , a salary product for professionals earning in dollars, pounds and euros. Users can receive and organise salary payments, while qualifying customers get higher savings rates, larger transaction limits and priority support. The launch comes as Grey crosses three million users and nearly $5 billion in processed payments. Its payment volume has also grown 170% year on year. Explain like I’m new here: Grey did not start out trying to manage salaries. Idorenyin Obong and Femi Aghedo launched the company in 2020 as Aboki Africa, helping Nigerians exchange foreign currency in domiciliary accounts. The founders soon realised receiving the money was itself a bigger problem. In 2021, they pivoted to virtual dollar, pound, and euro accounts for remote workers and freelancers. Grey joined Y Combinator in 2022 and raised a $2 million seed round later that year. It had about 100,000 users in 2022 and crossed one million in 2024. Today, it operates across dozens of markets and is also pushing into business payments. Between the lines: Receiving foreign payments is no longer enough of a moat. Grey competes with Raenest, Cleva, Afriex, and others offering versions of the same multi-currency account. Paycheck changes the relationship. If a salary lands in Grey every month, the company gets the first chance to handle what happens next: saving, converting currencies, sending money, or paying bills. The customer also has one less reason to move that income immediately to another financial app. Zoom out: Grey Business, launched in February, has already processed nearly $100 million. Now Paycheck is attacking the consumer side of the same problem. Grey built its first growth phase around helping people receive money; Obong said it is targeting between 10 million and 20 million users. Getting to that milestone may depend on giving them reasons to leave the money there. Upgrade your business today Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay . Fintech Mastercard and Interswitch bring Google Pay to Nigeria Kari Tukur, Country Manager, West Africa, Mastercard. Image source: Kari Tukur on LinkedIn If you’re in Nigeria and used to making transfers or paying with your credit card, you’ll start seeing less of that. What happened? Mastercard, the global payments giant, and Interswitch, a Nigerian payments infrastructure provider, have partnered to bring Google Pay to eligible Mastercard cardholders in Nigeria. The service lets customers add supported bank cards to Google Wallet and use an Android phone to make contactless payments at compatible point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. Explain like I’m new here: Nigeria has been trying to get people to make contactless payments for a while. In 2015, Unified Payments launched PayAttitude, which used NFC tags to enable contactless payments. Access Bank has experimented with tap-to-phone payments, while Touch and Pay Technologies’ Cowry card has made contactless payments a familiar part of Lagos public transport. CashAfrica also recently partnered with Chicken Republic to introduce mobile tap-to-pay across more than 350 outlets. Mastercard’spartnership lets users add an existing bank card to Google Wallet and turn the phone already in their hand into a tap-to-pay device. How it works: Your bank still holds the money, and Mastercard still sits behind the payment. Google Wallet stores a digital version of the card, while Mastercard’s tokenisation technology replaces the card number with a unique digital credential when you pay. When you tap, the merchant does not receive your physical card details as it would from a traditional card transaction. The rollout includes eligible Mastercard cards issued by banks including FirstBank, GTBank, UBA and Zenith Bank. Why this matters: Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) recorded ₦284.9 trillion ($212 billion) in instant-payment transactions in Q1 2025, while the country had 5.9 million deployed PoS terminals by March. PoS transaction values reached ₦10.51 trillion ($7.8 billion) in the same quarter. However, Nigerians are already comfortable with transfers, so tap-to-pay needs to offer something better than being another way to do the same thing. The harder part is getting enough merchants to accept contactless payments and enough Nigerians to change their payment behaviour. More value with Mycoverai You already have a great product. articles.title: Attackers Exploit Second Cisco Firewall VPN Zero-Day Since August
articles.text:
Cisco on Wednesday released fixes for an exploited vulnerability affecting its Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software.
Tracked as CVE-2026-76418 and assigned a CVSS score of 8.6, the bug resides in the Remote Access SSL VPN service. Attackers can exploit it remotely, without authenticating, to force the device to restart unexpectedly and disrupt its availability.
Cisco attributes the issue to logic errors affecting tunnel groups configured with secondary authentication. Exploitation involves a malicious request sent while connecting to the SSL VPN.
“A successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path,” Cisco noted.
For an attack to work, the firewall must be running an unpatched release, have its SSL VPN login service reachable, and use secondary authentication in an affected tunnel group. The company’s cloud-delivered firewall and management offerings, Secure Access, and the Secure Firewall Management Center are not vulnerable.
Cisco’s product security team learned in October that the flaw was being exploited in the wild. No information has been shared about the attacks or the threat actors behind them.
The vulnerability came to light during a Cisco TAC support case, and the company credited Eric Fernald with finding it.
No workarounds are available. Depending on the default tunnel group’s settings, customers can reduce their exposure by turning off the tunnel group list or removing secondary authentication. Cisco cautioned that dropping secondary authentication makes remote access VPN less secure, and it recommends upgrading instead.
This is the second ASA and FTD zero-day exploited for DoS attacks in recent months. In August, Cisco released fixes for CVE-2026-20349, an HTTP request processing flaw that also lets unauthenticated attackers remotely trigger a reload through the Remote Access SSL VPN service.
Cisco did not disclose details on those attacks either. It’s unclear whether both flaws were exploited by the same threat actor.

articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.text:
MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.
- Share:
A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.
The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.
By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.
In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.
"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "
A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle
The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.
Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.
"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."
The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.
From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot
The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.
For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.
When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.
The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.
"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."
For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.
They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.
The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.
To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.
"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."
Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot
Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.
The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.
This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.
The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.
By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.
Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.
The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.
The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.
How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim
With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.
The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.
Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.
"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."
To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.
As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.
Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.
The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.
"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."
The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Jennifer Chu. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maheera Bawa, Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, Seanbiron Johnson, Ritu Raman. 2D Skeletal Muscle Thin Film Actuators Enhance Efficiency of Biohybrid Robots. Advanced Functional Materials, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/adfm.78065

articles.title: Building an Offline-First AI Coding Tutor for Low-End Android Phones
Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3
As quality assurance (QA) automation adoption grows inside an organization, a new problem appears that has nothing to do with writing tests. A platform team stands up test automation, then a second team wants to join, then a dozen more. Soon hundreds of test cases belong to different products and squads, and everyone can see everyone else’s tests. No one can answer a basic question at a glance: is this application’s test coverage healthy right now? Test authoring stops being the bottleneck. Organizing tests and controlling who can touch them becomes the work.
A second, related question follows close behind: who owns this application and its tests, and who is accountable when coverage slips? Without a clear owner, health problems have no one to land on.
In the first post, we introduced QA Studio, a reference solution built with Amazon Nova Act. Teams use it to define tests in natural language and run them through AI-powered visual navigation. In the second post, we added test suites and a CLI for batch regression testing in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. In this post, we cover two capabilities that help QA Studio scale across an organization. The first, applications, organizes tests and reports health metrics. The second, team-based user management, controls who can see and change what.
Organizing tests with applications
An application in QA Studio represents the system under test: a website, a web app, a service front end. It’s the container that gives a collection of tests, a home, and an owner. Use cases (the individual tests from Part 1) and test suites (the regression collections from Part 2) belong to an application, and they inherit its ownership. Instead of one flat list of every test in the deployment, each team works inside the applications they own.
Creating an application takes a name, a base URL, and an optional set of environments such as development, staging, and production. From the application page, teams create new use cases directly in context, add existing ones, and group them into test suites. This is also where QA Studio reports on the health of the tests it runs.
Understanding application health with metrics
Tests produce results. Understanding those results over time is what tells a team whether the development lifecycle for an application is healthy, not only whether a single build is ready for release. QA Studio records the outcome of every execution as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by application and by environment. It turns these metrics into a health view on the application page.
The top of the page answers the immediate question with three figures: the pass rate over the selected window, the total number of executions, and the current failure count. Alongside them, QA Studio computes a health score of 0–100. The score starts from the pass rate and subtracts a penalty for flaky tests. That way, an application whose tests pass but flip between pass and fail doesn’t present a falsely perfect picture. A team scanning a portfolio of applications can tell the stable ones from the ones that need attention without opening each result.
The metrics tab moves from the current snapshot to trends. Teams choose a 7-day window with hourly granularity or a 30-day window with daily granularity, and QA Studio charts executions, successes, failures, and average duration across that period. Because the underlying metrics carry an environment dimension, teams filter the view to a single environment. For example, they can compare how staging behaves against production for the same set of tests.
Two views target the tests that cost teams the most time. The flaky tests view ranks use cases by how often they flipped between passing and failing over the last seven days. This surfaces the intermittent failures that erode trust in a suite before they turn into a production miss. The recent failures view lists the latest failed executions for quick triage. Each one links back to the Amazon Nova Act trajectory logs and session recordings described in Part 1. That way, moving from “this test is failing” to “here is exactly what the agent saw” takes one click.
Controlling access with teams and roles
Metrics tell a team how their applications are doing. Team-based user management decides which applications are theirs in the first place. QA Studio organizes access around teams, and an application belongs to exactly one team. Members of that team work with its applications. Everyone else doesn’t see them.
Every team member holds one of five roles, and each role includes the permissions of the ones below it:
- Admin: Studio-wide access to every team, application, and user, including creating teams and assigning applications. Admin is a studio-wide role rather than a per-team assignment.
- Team Lead: Manages their own team members and creates applications for the team.
- Editor: Creates and edits use cases and test suites within the team’s applications.
- Executor: Runs use cases and suites but doesn’t modify them.
- Viewer: Read-only access to the team’s applications and results.
Because roles are cumulative, a Team Lead has everything an Editor has, and so on down to Viewer. Access to a use case or a test suite follows the application that contains it. If a member can work with the application, they can work with its tests, bounded by their role. This keeps permission management at the application level instead of on thousands of individual tests.
An administrator sees the whole studio. The Users page lists every account with its team and role in one place. An admin can tell who holds Team Lead on which team and who carries Studio-wide Administrator rights. In the reference deployment shown here, four users span two teams: two Team Leads, one Viewer, and one Studio-wide Administrator. The Teams page rolls the same data up by team, showing each team’s member count and application count side by side. An admin can see which teams are expanding before opening any one of them.
The same membership data, rolled up by team, appears on the Teams page.
Switching from teams to applications, the studio-wide Applications list shows every application across all teams.
Sharing applications between teams
Teams rarely work in complete isolation. A platform team might own an application that a feature team needs to run against, without handing over the ability to change it. QA Studio supports this with shared access: the owning team grants another team access to an application at a view, execute, or full level.
Shared access follows a ceiling rule. A user’s effective permission on a shared application is the lower of their own role and the level of the grant. A Viewer who is given full access to a shared application remains view-only, because their role is the ceiling. This way, an owning team can share widely without granting more than a recipient’s role allows.
What a team lead sees
A team lead works inside a single team rather than the whole studio. Opening My Team presents four tabs that cover everything the lead controls: Members, Applications, Use Cases, and Shared Access. The Members tab lists the people on the team. The lead can change any member’s role inline or add a new one, so day-to-day access management stays with the person closest to the work. In the AWS Team shown here, the lead manages two members, one Team Lead and one Viewer.
The Applications tab shows only the applications the team owns, each with its test-case count and last-run time. This keeps the lead focused on their own surface rather than the full studio inventory. The Shared Access tab is where cross-team sharing becomes concrete. Here the AWS Team has granted the AMZN Team view access to an application, and the lead can grant, revoke, or change the level of that access. Because the grant was view level, an AMZN Team Editor still sees the shared application read-only: the ceiling rule from the previous section, applied in practice.
The same Team Lead’s Shared Access tab records which other teams can reach the team’s applications, and at what level.
How it works
QA Studio builds team-based access control and metrics on the same serverless foundation described in the earlier posts, adding a few AWS services to the mix:
- Amazon Cognito: Each team maps to a set of Cognito groups, one per role. An AWS Lambda authorizer resolves a caller’s groups into API scopes and team context on every request.
- Amazon DynamoDB: Teams, memberships, application ownership, and cross-team share grants are stored in the existing single-table design.
- Amazon CloudWatch: Every execution emits custom metrics in the QAStudio/Executions namespace, dimensioned by application and environment. The metrics API reads them back to build the health view and trend charts.
- AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway: The backend enforces access at two layers: the scope a caller’s role grants, and a resource check that confirms the caller’s team owns or has been shared with the application.
Because access is derived from Cognito group membership, the OAuth client credentials flow from Part 2 fits the same model. A CI pipeline authenticates as a machine identity with the scopes it needs and no more.
Getting started
Applications, metrics, and team-based access control are part of the QA Studio reference solution, which you deploy in your own AWS account with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). All test data, results, and metrics stay within your account boundaries. After deploying, an administrator creates teams, assigns members and roles, and assigns applications to teams. Each team’s health metrics begin populating as their tests run.
For deployment instructions and configuration details, see the QA Studio GitHub repository and its documentation.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how QA Studio scales agentic QA automation from individual tests to an organization. Applications give every team a home for their use cases and test suites. They report health through pass rate, trend charts, a flaky-adjusted health score, and failure triage built on Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Team-based user management, backed by Amazon Cognito, keeps each team working within the applications they own, with cross-team sharing bounded by a clear ceiling rule.
These capabilities build on the natural language test authoring from Part 1 and the suites and CI/CD integration from Part 2. Together, they help QA automation grow across many teams without losing visibility or control. To try it in your own environment, deploy the reference solution from the QA Studio GitHub repository, create your first team and application, and run a few use cases to watch the metrics take shape. To learn more about the agent behind it, see the Amazon Nova Act product page.

articles.title: A new report accuses Microsoft of using 10 "dark patterns" to keep you on Edge
articles.text:
A hot potato: It's no secret that when it comes to pushing its Edge browser onto users, Microsoft isn't afraid to play dirty. There have been numerous stories about the aggressive tactics the company uses, and other browser makers aren't happy about it. Now, a new report dives into the "dark patterns" Microsoft adopts to get more people onto Edge.
The Browser Choice Alliance (BCA), a group of browser makers advocating fair competition and freedom to choose a browser, commissioned the report, which was produced by the Behavioural Insights Team (BIT).
The report maps any harm to users from Microsoft's PC browser choice practices, focusing on dark patterns that are used by the company.
For those unfamiliar, dark patterns are designs that steer people into choices they wouldn't otherwise make, such as hiding a decline button or making cancellation difficult.
BIT identified 10 dark patterns that it said make it harder to choose a browser other than Edge or subvert a user's choice of an alternative browser after that decision has already been made. These are:
1. Pushing Edge ads when you search for rival browsers: Banners try to talk you out of downloading another browser and steer you back to Edge.
2. Making the switch incomplete: Setting another browser as your default still leaves files like PDFs assigned to Edge, requiring more changes.
3. Restricting alternatives through Windows S mode: Users have to leave the restricted mode before they can install competing browsers.
4. Ignoring your choice in Windows Search: Web results open in Edge even when you've chosen another default browser.
5. Sending Widgets and lock-screen links to Edge: These parts of Windows bypass your preferred browser, too.
6. Forcing News and Interests links into Edge: Clicking stories in Windows 10's news feed opens Microsoft's browser instead of your chosen one.
7. Giving Outlook and Teams separate browser settings: Links can open in Edge unless you change settings inside those apps as well.
8. Blocking tools that help you avoid Edge: Microsoft has blocked workarounds that redirect Edge-only links to your preferred browser.
9. Pulling another browser's tabs into Edge: The report describes tabs from competing browsers reopening in Edge when you sign in.
10. Pushing you back toward Edge after updates: "Recommended settings" prompts make accepting Microsoft's browser settings easier than keeping your own.
BIT also identified practices that make Edge seem easier to use and safer than rival browsers, potentially without supporting evidence, including blocking its removal and showing strong safety warnings when users leave S mode.
Source: StatCounter Global Stats - Browser Market Share
The report concludes that Microsoft's tactics work together to make switching away from Edge harder and sticking with another browser more frustrating. It says this undermines user choice, wastes time and particularly affects people without a strong browser preference.
European users face fewer barriers, but the problems haven't disappeared. In 2025, Microsoft said it had stopped nagging users in the European Economic Area to set Edge as their default browser as part of its compliance with the Digital Markets Act.
This isn't the first time BCA has called out Microsoft over Edge. It sent a letter to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in June demanding it stop burying rival browsers.

articles.title: Dell connects AI trust to proving data recovery - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell ties AI trust to the ability to recover clean data
AI trust is becoming as much a recovery problem as a security one. As agents touch more enterprise data and attackers use frontier models to find weak spots faster, simply holding a copy of the data no longer proves a business can bounce back.
That shift is pulling data protection out of the back office and into core infrastructure design. Dell Technologies Inc. has been expanding its cyber recovery offerings as enterprises confront those risks, according to Simon Jelley (pictured), vice president of product management at Dell.
“The reality is, within the trusted AI adoption, it requires more than just protecting the actual model itself,” he said. “You have to assume that ultimately, in this software-connected world, anything that’s software-connected, there’s a potential for that threat boundary. You have to ultimately have resilience built into the architecture itself.”
Jelley spoke with theCUBE’s Christophe Bertrand for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why proving recoverability now matters more than keeping a backup. (* Disclosure below.)
Building AI trust into the recovery architecture
Two forces are driving the change. AI raises both the value and the volume of enterprise data, while frontier models let attackers chain low-severity vulnerabilities into a working attack path. That means treating resilience as part of how the business operates, according to Jelley.
“The efficacy of the data itself is one element, but the other is you’ve got to really build in resiliency as a business process,” he said. “Resiliency is just built into the architecture and the business process you’re delivering overall.”
Dell uses a vault to keep a copy of data off the production network and outside the identity privileges that govern primary systems, according to Jelley. The company argues that immutability alone isn’t isolation.
“We’ve worked with thousands of organizations to bring vaults into play. Some don’t use that intelligence layer. And interestingly, we found that they have recovered data that had time bomb threats within them,” he said. “It’s not just important to isolate your data and say, ‘Great, I have a recovery copy.’ How do you know that recovery copy is ultimately clean? That’s really critical when you’re ultimately trying to stand back up your business.”

articles.title: Ubisoft Ends Major Content Support for Black Flag Resynced With Update 1.0.8
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
Ubisoft Ends Major Content Support for Black Flag Resynced With Update 1.0.8
Ubisoft is wrapping up major content support for Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced with Title Update 1.0.8, which went live on October 27 across all platforms. The main draw is the New Game+ mode Ubisoft promised back in July and confirmed last week. It lets players restart Edward Kenway's campaign while keeping almost everything, including unlocked weapons, outfits, the Jackdaw's upgrades and pets, and the Kenway fleet. Quest items, recruited officers, and captured forts do reset, though. Difficulty climbs with each run, as Elite Soldiers appear more often and max rank ships start patrolling the seas, up to New Game+++++. 
Players after a tougher fight get Nightmare Mode, where enemies deal 1.8x damage, parry timing is tighter, and the one-shot kill safety net is switched off. Stealth gets harsher too, with faster detection and enemies hearing anything quicker than a walk. A new currency called Escudos, earned from challenges and from chests that were already looted, unlocks outfits and items exclusive to the mode. The patch also restores hidden blade, unarmed, single sword, and gunblade takedown animations from the 2013 original, and Ubisoft has hidden new community chests without offering any hints.Black Flag Resynced beat Ubisoft's full-year sales target within two weeks of its July 9 launch, so ending major content support after less than four months is a little surprising. The download weighs 15.5 GB on Xbox Series X|S and 4.5 GB on PS5, while PC players are looking at somewhere between 2.1 GB and 4.3 GB, apparently depending on the storefront. Smaller quality-of-life patches will continue over the coming months. 
Source:
				Ubisoft

articles.title: Auriga Partners reaches €80 million interim close for second fund dedicated to cybersecurity | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Auriga Partners, a Paris-based asset management firm specialising in venture capital and innovation investment, has announced an €80 million interim close for Auriga Cyber Ventures II, its second fund dedicated exclusively to cybersecurity.
Auriga Cyber Ventures II is backed by Bpifrance through the French National Seed Fund No. 3, managed on behalf of the French State as part of the France 2030 investment plan. It also benefits from the support of the European Union under the InvestEU fund, through the European Investment Fund (EIF), as well as an Equity Guarantee managed by Bpifrance’s Investor Partnerships and Guarantees team.
“Given the economic, industrial and sovereignty challenges posed by cybersecurity, Europe must equip itself to develop global leaders. We have a particularly dynamic pool of talent, technologies and startups, but they need both substantial capital and specialised support to realise their potential,” said Geoffroy Rosset, Managing Partner, Auriga Partners.
Founded in 1998 by Jacques Chatain, Bernard Daugeras, and Patrick Bamas, Auriga Partners calls itself a pioneer in venture capital in France. Since its inception, it has backed more than 150 companies, including Neolane, Nexthink, Wallix, Vade and Vestiaire Collective. The latter two investments enabled Auriga to distribute more than €500 million to its investors over the 2025-26 period alone.
The firm’s cybersecurity approach is built on the expertise of a network of industry founders, including Jean-Noël de Galzain, founder of Wallix; Georges Lotigier, founder of Vade; Thierry Rouquet, founder of Sentryo, which was acquired by Cisco; and Édouard de Rémur, co-founder of Oodrive and Virtual Browser.
“Our community of experts and entrepreneurs, which we continuously strive to expand, provides startups with more than just capital. It brings collective intelligence, combining in-depth market knowledge, privileged access to industry decision-makers, support for business development and expertise in international expansion. In cybersecurity, the ability to provide hands-on support is just as critical as funding,” said William Lecat, Managing Partner, Auriga Partners.
Auriga Partners’ second dedicated fund for cybersecurity firms comes amidst the escalating urgency around digital security. With more than 30 billion connected devices globally, a cyberattack occurs every 39 seconds, and the global cost of cybercrime is estimated at $10.5 trillion in 2025, equivalent to the world’s third-largest economy.
The Auriga Cyber Ventures II fund has a target of €100 million and a hard cap of €120 million, and it builds on the success of Auriga’s first €55 million cybersecurity vehicle launched in 2022. The fund primarily targets early-stage European startups, from pre-Seed to Series A, with investment tickets ranging from €500,000 to €5 million.
It will take minority equity stakes and plans to allocate roughly half its capital to follow-on investments in its most promising portfolio companies. The fund aims to back around 30 startups, with a focus on two high-priority segments: artificial intelligence security (protecting AI models, data and emerging applications) and identity and data protection, which addresses increasingly sophisticated fraud and digital access proliferation.
Since 2022, Auriga says its teams have analysed more than 2,000 European cybersecurity startups, and it has already deployed capital from the new fund into four startups: Finovox (document fraud prevention), Fleuret (AI-powered automated penetration testing), Mankind’s (AI systems auditing and compliance), and Nextident (AI agent security). It plans two to three further investments before the end of 2026.
Over the past five years, the firm has backed 30 European companies spanning the full cybersecurity value chain, including Tenancy, Patrowl, Emproof, Cytix and Mindflow. Auriga Partners has already established what it describes as Europe’s largest dedicated cybersecurity startup portfolio, and with Auriga Cyber Ventures II, the firm plans to build on that portfolio.

articles.title: Wealthsimple announces $425-million Series F at $13.8-billion valuation | BetaKit
articles.text:
Toronto FinTech firm Wealthsimple has agreed to up to $425-million CAD in Series F financing from existing investors at a $13.8-billion post-money valuation—up from $10 billion a year ago.
Wealthsimple revealed the round late Tuesday. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC is leading with support from Power Corporation of Canada, Power subsidiary IGM Financial, US-based Iconiq, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, and Montréal’s Inovia Capital.
“This is an exciting vote of confidence in what we’re building at Wealthsimple from a group of globally respected technology investors.”
It will include $300 million in fresh equity funding. Wealthsimple plans to use this primary capital to accelerate its product roadmap and bolster its technology infrastructure. The round will also feature a secondary offering through which those investors will buy $125 million worth of shares from Wealthsimple employees. When reached by BetaKit, Wealthsimple declined to share more detail regarding the secondary offering or when the round might close.
“This is an exciting vote of confidence in what we’re building at Wealthsimple from a group of globally respected technology investors,” Wealthsimple co-founder and CEO Michael Katchen told BetaKit over email.
Despite strong demand, Katchen said the company saw no need to bring on new backers at this time.
“Since co-leading last year’s round, our conviction in Wealthsimple’s ability to become Canada’s leading financial services platform has only grown,” Vinay Yarlagadda, managing director of GIC’s Technology Investment Group, said in a statement.
Wealthsimple launched in 2014 as a robo-adviser. Since then, the company has broadened its investment capabilities and moved into other areas of money management, like banking, wooing wealthier clients and more sophisticated traders as part of its quest to build “a full-service financial solution” for Canadians, as it targets $1 trillion in assets under administration (AUA) by 2034.
During the last quarter, Wealthsimple said new chequing accounts outpaced new investing accounts for the first time.
This round comes one year after Wealthsimple announced a $750-million Series E financing round consisting of $550 million in primary and $200 million in secondary capital at a $10 billion valuation. That was double the $5 billion the company had been valued at in 2024.
RELATED: Wealthsimple hits $10-billion valuation in new round backed by Dragoneer, GIC, CPP Investments
Wealthsimple has since launched more than 50 new investing, spending, chequing, and business products. The company also claims it has remained profitable and seen its total AUA soar from $100 billion to more than $169 billion. As of the end of September, more than four million Canadians (up from three million in 2025) and 30,000 businesses were using the company’s platform. The company also claimed that a quarter of Canadians aged 18 to 40, and one in nine Canadians between the ages of 41 and 55, are using Wealthsimple.
“Today, people can live their whole financial lives on Wealthsimple, and we’re seeing more and more Canadians choose us,” Katchen said.
As it competes with Canada’s big banks, Wealthsimple currently has no plans to seek a banking license of its own.
Wealthsimple plans to reveal what else it has built and plans to develop at its product showcase next week on Nov. 5.
“There’s still a lot of opportunity to improve access to financial products and make financial services in Canada more competitive,” Katchen added. “We started with low-cost investing, and today, serve more than four million Canadians across a full suite of financial products. We have big ambitions, and there’s still work to be done to make financial services more accessible and affordable for Canadians.”
This Series F also advances Wealthsimple’s status as one of Canada’s most valuable private tech companies, appearing to put it below only Toronto AI firm Cohere, which is joining forces with Germany’s Aleph Alpha at a reported $27-billion valuation.
UPDATE (10/28/26): This story has been updated to include additional information and commentary shared by Wealthsimple.
Disclosure: Wealthsimple vice-president of payments strategy and chief compliance officer, Hanna Zaidi, sits on BetaKit’s board of directors.
Feature image courtesy Wealthsimple.

articles.title: DoorDash is acquiring Instacart for $17 billion
articles.text:
DoorDash has announced that it’s buying Instacart in a deal valued at approximately $17 billion. The acquisition will give DoorDash a bigger presence in online grocery delivery thanks to Instacart’s established grocery marketplace and retailer partnerships, with Instacart CEO Chris Rogers saying the deal will make “online grocery more seamless and affordable” for millions of households.
DoorDash is acquiring Instacart for $17 billion
The deal could help DoorDash’s grocery business compete against Amazon and Walmart.
DoorDash says the acquisition will give Instacart users acces to more than 50,000 additional stores, and allow DashPass and Instacart Plus members to “pay one membership fee instead of two.” The deal is expected to close “in the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028,” subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. When finalized, DoorDash says it will preserve Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app, so the services will remain separate instead of being merged into a single platform.
In its post-close commitments, DoorDash said local grocers won’t be limited by platform exclusivity, and will be free to work with either delivery service. Instacart shoppers will also retain flexibility around their working hours and which orders to accept, and will be able to choose whether to take on DoorDash orders or just stick with shopping for Instacart.
DoorDash, which started as a restaurant courier service, already has its own grocery delivery business, but that faces ongoing competition from Instacart, Uber, Walmart, and Amazon. DoorDash is also incentivized to diversify further because its rivals have been stepping into the food delivery territory it’s best known for, with Uber acquiring Postmates and Delivery Hero.
Here’s what DoorDash said regarding increasing competition:
“Most grocery shopping still happens in stores, but more people are buying groceries and everyday goods online. They expect fast, affordable delivery and an easy way to order. The biggest online retailers and grocers are racing ahead, building their own delivery fleets, warehouses, membership programs, and AI shopping assistants. A grocer or retailer running on thin margins cannot build all of that alone, and with AI, the playing field risks being tilted even further away from local commerce.”
Rumors around the deal started circulating last week after The Information reported that Instacart was in talks with rival platforms Uber and DoorDash regarding a potential sale. By Monday, The Wall Street Journal reported that DoorDash was in “advanced talks” with Instacart, and that a deal could be reached “as soon as this week.” That proved to be accurate, though finalization will take much longer — giving stockholders and regulators time to voice their feelings about the acquisition.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the announcement. “Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

articles.title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
articles.text:
The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.
In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.
The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.
Gayen said the study combined six independent datasets to track changes in the Southern Ocean from 2004 to 2024. The data came from Argo floats, which drift through the ocean and periodically descend to different depths to measure water properties such as density and salinity, then resurface to transmit the readings. A 2025 study also detected increasing surface salinity linked to declining sea ice, he added.
Antarctic sea ice reached its highest extent in the satellite record in 2014 and suddenly dropped to a record low just two years later. The sea ice remained well below the 2014 extent and reached another low point in 2023, when it measured about 1 million square miles below the 1981 to 2010 average, with an area of ice about four times the size of Texas gone. As the ice dwindles, there’s less freshwater available during the melt season, making the Antarctic Intermediate Water saltier.
Changes to the density, thickness and salinity of the layer influence how heat moves between the surface of the ocean and deeper waters, which “could affect how the ocean stores and redistributes heat,” Gayen said. More monitoring is needed to track the changes, he added, because impacts are potentially “knocking on your door” within five years.

articles.title: Xreal Aura is a new wired headset powered by Android XR | TechCrunch
articles.text:
At the Android Dev Summit on Wednesday, Google’s smart glasses partner Xreal launched its new Xreal Aura wired smart glasses, powered by the Android XR and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite platforms. The companies had teased the glasses earlier in the year at Google’s I/O developer conference.
As Meta expands its push into smart glasses, competitors like Apple and Google are keen to release their own devices. Much like it did with Android smartphones, Google is relying on an assortment of partners, including Samsung and Xreal, to bring devices powered by its Android XR platform to consumers.
The new Xreal Aura smart glasses are tethered to a smartphone-like device for processing power, rather than handling all the computing themselves. The glasses then display the content in the wearer’s field of view.
The device’s design, meanwhile, is closer to Meta’s smart glasses than Apple’s Vision Pro, which is a larger headset.
Xreal Aura uses Sony’s Micro-OLED display with 1200p resolution at 120 Hz and a 95-degree field of view — screen specs that put the glasses above the Ray-Ban Meta Display on paper. However, Xreal’s smart glasses are heavier at 95 grams compared to Meta’s 69 grams, and you have to carry the puck.
At launch, the Aura supports many popular Google Play apps and games along with specific XR experiences, including the NBA App for Android XR; Nevatars; Fallout: Factions; Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars; the NASCAR XR App; and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s “The Nutcracker.”
Users can opt to plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into the Xreal Aura via USB-C to make it an augmented display. The device can also allow for various entertainment and productivity use cases by spinning up a multimonitor setup or a big virtual screen.
For audio, the Xreal Aura uses Bose’s tech to power its sound while watching videos or listening to music.
Given that the new smart glasses are powered by Android XR, Gemini is available to users as a Q&A assistant and can help them understand on-screen context.
The Xreal Aura is available to order starting today in the United States, Canada, Japan, and
South Korea. The 12GB + 256GB version costs $1,279 with a limited launch price of $1,099 through December, and the 16GB + 512GB version is priced at $1,499 with a launch price of $1,299 through December. The company said it will start shipping by mid-November.
In May, Xreal CEO Chi Xu told TechCrunch that building a smart glass business is hard and everyone is losing money. He also said that the Aura glasses will have a wide range of use cases, and the industry has reached an inflection point of having the right hardware, software, and design smart glasses to reach scale.
“You need all the key pieces ready — you need the hardware ready, the operating system needs to be ready, and then you need a great user interface,” Xu said at that time.

articles.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
articles.text:
Sponsored
Creating AI value with enterprise context
How establishing a company brain can support more accurate, cost-effective AI and autonomous agents.
In association withAtlan
Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.
An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.
Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.
“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”
The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.
This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
