articles.title: 80 km/h sur autoroute : quand la Suisse punit l'électrique pour sauver ses réserves de pétrole
articles.text:
Envisager de baisser la limitation de vitesse sur les autoroutes suisses de 120 km/h à 80 km/h fait ressortir de vieux démons, jusqu’en France où l’idée est particulièrement impopulaire. Certains automobilistes suisses ironisent pourtant en disant qu’il est rare de pouvoir rouler plus vite sur les principaux axes du pays. Cette hypothèse nous renvoie directement dans les années 1970, sans même avoir besoin d’une DeLorean.
En 1973, en plein choc pétrolier, le gouvernement suisse dégainait l’interdiction de rouler le dimanche et bridait ses autoroutes à 100 km/h pour rationner l’or noir. Douze ans plus tard, en 1985, le pays abaissait la vitesse maximale de 130 à 120 km/h, cette fois pour freiner le dépérissement des forêts : une mesure « temporaire » devenue définitive en 1989. Un demi-siècle après le premier choc pétrolier, la Confédération helvétique ressort la même recette.
Selon l’Office fédéral pour l’approvisionnement économique du pays (OFAE), cité par 20minutes le 24 octobre 2026, un scénario de grave pénurie de carburants en Europe pourrait déclencher une série de restrictions drastiques : recours aux réserves obligatoires, incitation aux transports en commun… et un abaissement général de la vitesse sur autoroute à 80 km/h. L’OFAE raisonne uniquement en moteurs thermiques, comme si la transition énergétique n’avait pas commencé.
Le grand retour aux solutions des années 70
Sur le papier, la physique donne raison aux régulateurs suisses : forcer les automobilistes à rouler à 80 km/h plutôt qu’à 120 km/h permet de réduire la consommation d’un moteur essence ou diesel d’environ 20 à 30 %. En cas de rupture d’approvisionnement, faire baisser la consommation des véhicules permet de réduire les tensions sur les stocks de carburant.
En 2026, la mesure a surtout l’air d’un anachronisme. Ramener les autoroutes à la vitesse d’une route cantonale renvoie directement aux crises pétrolières des années 1970. Mais surtout, le projet fédéral ne fait aucune distinction : thermique, hybride ou 100 % électrique, tout le monde serait logé à la même enseigne.
Les voitures électriques punies à cause de la pénurie de carburant
Les conducteurs de voitures électriques pourraient être soumis à une mesure destinée à économiser un carburant qu’ils ne consomment pas. Un paradoxe qui rappelle les limitations de vitesse imposées lors des pics de pollution, même aux véhicules sans émissions à l’échappement.
Il y aurait cependant un avantage à cet abaissement de la vitesse sur autoroute : les conducteurs de véhicules électriques verraient leur autonomie sur autoroute nettement progresser, car la résistance de l’air, qui pèse lourd sur la consommation à 120 km/h, diminue fortement à 80 km/h. La consommation serait optimale pour certains modèles.
Prenez le train, roulez au pas… mais ne passez pas à l’électrique ?
Le plus frappant dans la communication des autorités helvétiques reste ce qu’elle ne dit pas. Face au spectre de la dépendance aux énergies fossiles, le catalogue de recommandations officielles égrène scrupuleusement les mêmes recettes : privilégiez les transports publics, partagez votre voiture, renoncez aux trajets non indispensables, levez le pied… mais personne ne semble envisager une autre hypothèse : accélérer la sortie du pétrole en basculant vers la mobilité électrique.
Il faut dire que la Suisse entretient une relation pour le moins ambiguë avec la voiture électrique. C’est certainement lié au fait que certaines personnalités politiques au pouvoir affichent des postures politiques anti-VE assumées. Le développement des infrastructures de recharge en a pâti à l’échelle fédérale, même si certains cantons œuvrent à améliorer la situation.
Alors que le pays bénéficie d’un pouvoir d’achat élevé et d’un réseau électrique robuste, la Suisse n’a jamais instauré de prime nationale à l’achat de véhicules électriques et s’est appuyée sur une feuille de route essentiellement volontariste. Elle a même soumis les voitures électriques, depuis le 1er janvier 2024, à l’impôt automobile fédéral de 4 %, dont elles étaient exonérées depuis sa création en 1997. Le Conseil fédéral voulait ainsi récupérer environ 150 millions de francs de recettes par an.
En brandissant la menace d’un 80 km/h généralisé dès que le pétrole vient à manquer, la Confédération avoue surtout qu’elle s’est mal préparée à s’en passer. Les automobilistes helvètes n’ont en tout cas pas attendu pour s’équiper : les voitures 100 % électriques représentent 26,2 % des immatriculations de voitures neuves sur les neuf premiers mois de 2026, et 35,7 % en septembre, un record dopé par le prix des carburants, selon l’association des importateurs auto-schweiz.
Rien n’a été acté pour le moment. Cette réduction de la vitesse sur autoroute n’est qu’une hypothèse parmi d’autres. Le projet retire 40 km/h à la vitesse maximale sur toutes les portions qui ne sont pas déjà limitées par des travaux, des tunnels ou la gestion des bouchons. En 1985, la baisse n’était que de 10 km/h. On peut se demander si ce chiffre ne sert pas à faire accepter plus facilement une baisse plus modérée, comme un passage à 110 km/h. La situation reste à observer, car elle pourrait bien donner de mauvaises idées à d’autres gouvernements voisins.

articles.title: Profitable Dutch startup Braid raises €34.13 million to help brands launch their own mobile connectivity | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Braid, a Dutch company that enables enterprises to launch their own branded mobile connectivity, has raised €34.13 million ($38 million) in a Series A funding round. The company also announced its rebrand from Next Communications.
The raise marks the company’s first external capital since it was founded in 2023 and was led by London-based Octopus Ventures. KPN Ventures, the strategic investment arm of Dutch telecom operator KPN, also participated in the round.
“The best infrastructure businesses make something complex feel effortless. Jignesh and the Braid team have taken an industry built around long negotiations and fragmented systems and created a materially simpler way for businesses to embed connectivity into the products their customers already use. We believe Braid is defining a new category in embedded connectivity and has the team, technology and ambition to become the default infrastructure layer for businesses delivering connectivity to their customers,” said Uthish Ranjan, Partner at Octopus Ventures.
Headquartered in The Hague, Braid was founded in 2023 by Jignesh Dave, Vishal Dave, and Mitesh Popat. The company operates across India, Europe, the Middle East and Africa. As part of this funding announcement, the company rebranded from Next Communications and claims to serve close to 90 enterprise customers, including major global FinTech and travel brands.
Before starting Braid, Jignesh Dave spent years in the UK and South African banking, including a stint at Lloyds, before building and running a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) for seven years. That experience, which cost him €500k and 18 months of runway before a single SIM was sold, became the bedrock of Braid’s foundation: infrastructure beneath a connectivity business is more valuable than the SIM card itself.
Braid offers a single API that orchestrates more than 600 carrier networks across over 200 countries, allowing enterprises to embed SIM and eSIM connectivity directly into their own products, or launch fully branded storefronts without becoming telecom operators themselves.
Its API shrinks months of carrier negotiations, regulatory filings and procurement down to minutes. The company says live trials can be up and running in three minutes and a brand-led mobile launch in as little as a week.
“I spent 18 months and half a million euros just to sell my first SIM card, and that is why Braid exists. After seven years running a mobile virtual network, I realised we weren’t really selling SIM cards. We had built the infrastructure that makes connectivity accessible to everyone,” Jignesh Dave, co-founder and CEO of Braid.
He added, “Amazon built AWS to power its own business and found it could power everyone else’s, and it was the same for us. Today a business can start in three minutes. And when brands make connectivity part of their customer experience, they unlock something far more valuable: stronger relationships, greater loyalty and new revenue.”
In practice, Braid helps an airline offer seamless roaming from the moment a passenger books a ticket; a bank can reward customers with connectivity as a loyalty benefit; a sports club can keep fans connected when they travel abroad for matches.
Braid says the company has been profitable and cash-flow positive and plans to use the new capital for international expansion, deepen the company’s carrier network, and strengthen the infrastructure that underpins its growing position in embedded connectivity. In the long term, Braid sees itself becoming the default infrastructure for enterprise connectivity globally.

articles.title: Nuevos buscadores inteligentes rastrean objetivos a velocidades hipersónicas sin GPS ni señales de radio
articles.text:
OKSI ha presentado cabezas buscadoras de misiles capaces de reconocer y seguir un objetivo sin necesidad de GPS, designación láser ni radio, afirmó la empresa, que cuenta con algoritmos capaces de funcionar tanto a velocidad subsónica como hipersónica.
El comunicado presentó las capacidades anunciadas por el fabricante, sin mencionar ensayos con ningún tipo de misil hipersónico.
Sensores y software de reconocimiento de objetivos
A partir de sensores electroópticos e infrarrojos, con proceso de imagen a bordo, OKSI afirma que puede reconocer y seguir un objetivo tras el lanzamiento, permitiendo al operador utilizar múltiples municiones en contra de uno o varios objetivos sin necesidad de designación externa continua, algo que su director ejecutivo, Chris HolmesParker, describió como “una vía pasiva para fijar el objetivo”.
La empresa afirmó que podía aplicarse a la lucha contra drones, armas de ataque marítimo, fuego indirecto y sistemas de interceptación, y añadió que su diseño modular permite sustituir sensores y ordenadores y actualizar el software por separado. Afirma que la familia de productos está lista para entrar en producción.
Este problema tiene su origen en la guerra electrónica. Este tipo de guerra puede interferir con los sistemas de navegación o las radios de otras armas y plataformas, reduciendo su eficacia. Procesar imágenes de sensores en el propio misil permitiría reducir esa dependencia de señales externas.
Hay que tener en cuenta que reconocer un objeto no es lo mismo que saber dónde se encuentra la plataforma, y que estos dos aspectos forman parte de diferentes módulos, según el folleto del producto de OKSI OMNISCIENCE.
OMNISCIENCE también incluye OMNItarget para la guía terminal y OMNImind para gestionar la misión utilizando lógica de programación condicional. OKSI ofrece estas capacidades en forma de módulos en un contenedor, que podrían utilizarse por separado o combinarse.
La colaboración con Qualcomm y el entorno Ubuntu Linux
La empresa OKSI anunció una colaboración con Qualcomm en 2026. Según el comunicado, el software OMNISCIENCE se ha adaptado al QCS8550 y su entorno se basa en Ubuntu Linux, con herramientas de inteligencia artificial y visión por ordenador open source, mientras que este chip aporta el cálculo y el procesamiento de imágenes necesarios para ejecutar este software de autonomía en dispositivos sin tripulación.
Este comunicado también es prueba de una vía de integración del software para la autonomía. Sin embargo, no menciona que el QCS8550 sea ni el microprocesador ni el sensor de las nuevas cabezas buscadoras anunciadas. Además, tal y como se describe en el comunicado, no hay forma de determinar si el software de OKSI sigue el principio de la programación open source, ya que esa descripción se refiere al entorno Ubuntu y a las herramientas compatibles.
Los ataques de elusión descritos en la documentación del software Dioptra, del Instituto Nacional de Estándares y Tecnología (EE. UU.), pueden modificar los datos de entrada, incluso mediante cambios en el entorno físico, para impedir que los modelos funcionen correctamente, lo que afectaría a la precisión de los modelos de inteligencia artificial, incluidos los utilizados para la visión artificial, según la documentación general sobre los ataques de elusión en sistemas de aprendizaje automático.
Los comunicados no ofrecen datos cuantitativos sobre la exactitud o la tasa de error de las nuevas cabezas buscadoras, necesarios para evaluar las afirmaciones de OKSI. Estos comunicados tampoco presentan resultados de ensayos hipersónicos.

articles.title: Pourquoi Apple ne cache plus l'encoche des MacBook Pro ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Introduite en 2021 avec les MacBook Pro M1 Pro / M1 Max, l’encoche est toujours d’actualité sur la majorité des ordinateurs portables commercialisés par Apple. Pensée pour abriter la webcam, on la retrouve aussi bien sur les derniers MacBook Air M5 de 13 et 15 pouces, que sur les MacBook Pro M5 Pro / M5 Max à écran mini-LED (lancés en mars dernier), ou sur le tout nouveau MacBook Pro M6 (dévoilé cette semaine).
La stratégie marketing d’Apple consistait jusqu’à présent à la dissimuler autant que possible sur les images officielles partagées à des fins promotionnelles, ou carrément affichées sur l’Apple Store. C’est en train de changer. Comme le rapporte The Mac Observer, Apple a semble-t-il commencé à modifier ces visuels pour rendre l’encoche bien plus visible qu’avant.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Apple change son fusil d’épaule…
La preuve en images avec les deux visuels ci-dessous, repérés au départ par un utilisateur canadien de X. À gauche, l’ancien visuel, sur lequel l’encoche est pratiquement invisible, car ton sur ton avec la partie noire du fond d’écran. À droite, le même fond d’écran a été légèrement ajusté pour que l’encoche apparaisse sur un arrière-plan gris foncé… ce qui la rend aussitôt bien plus facile à repérer.
De là à y voir un moyen d’encourager l’achat d’un MacBook Pro PROLED XDR, équipé pour sa part d’une Dynamic Island, il n’y a qu’un pas… que nous sommes tentés de franchir.
En comparaison, la petite bulle dynamique du nouveau modèle est bien plus agréable à l’œil, plus discrète et même (vaguement) utile. Comme sur iPhone, cette Dynamic Island réagit en effet dynamiquement, en fonction des applications lancées, pour afficher du contenu ou des informations en haut de l’écran.
Le passage à une encoche bien plus visible sur les derniers visuels partagés par Apple n’a pas fait l’objet d’un commentaire public de la marque. On imagine néanmoins que l’objectif est d’attirer l’attention de l’acheteur sur le changement apporté, en la matière, avec le nouveau MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. Reste à savoir si Apple réussira à faire de cette disparition de l’encoche… un véritable argument de vente en faveur de ce nouveau modèle.

How we compared AI dance generator tools in 2026
To differentiate true choreography engines from basic video filters, we evaluated the recorded capabilities of these platforms as of September 2026. We utilized the Audio-Driven vs. Template-Driven Automation Matrix—a proprietary evaluation framework that categorizes AI dance generator tools based on two critical axes: the source of the movement (Does the AI listen to the music, or copy a video?) and the output duration (Does it output a 5-second clip, or a full song?).
Each tool was measured against the following dimensions:
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Does the tool output a few seconds of looping footage, or can it generate a cohesive performance that spans a full 3-to-6-minute music track?
- Lip Sync While Dancing: Can the character sing the lyrics while performing complex choreography without the face distorting?
- Choreography Range: Is the user restricted to a dropdown menu of pre-baked animations, or can the AI generate dozens of unique styles dynamically?
- Steps to a Finished Video: How many manual actions are required between uploading the initial assets and downloading a ready-to-publish video?
1. freebeat — The Best Overall AI Dance Video Generator
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Generates full-length videos up to 6 minutes (on the Pro tier and above).
- Lip Sync While Dancing: Achieves ~90% accuracy across 12+ optimized languages.
- Choreography Range: 20+ common dance styles via free-text prompt (e.g., Hip-Hop, Jazz, Ballet, K-pop).
- Steps to a Finished Video: 4 steps (Input audio → Upload photo → Select mode → Generate).
How It Works
Unlike platforms that require an existing video to copy, freebeat’s AI dance video generator builds choreography directly from the rhythm of the music. The workflow begins with zero friction: users paste a track link (with native support for platforms like Suno, Udio, YouTube, and SoundCloud) or upload an audio file, followed by a single character photo using the ai singing photo generator.
The underlying Music Video Agent then analyzes the track across seven distinct music signals: tempo/BPM, a frame-accurate beat grid, percussive events, energy curves, spectral content, song sections, and section-level tags. Utilizing 5-tier beat quantization, the AI automatically plans the choreography so that movements, transitions, and cuts land exactly on the song’s real rhythm.
Users can opt for Studio mode for automated model selection and one-click generation, or switch to Custom mode to manually pair image models (like GPT-Image 2 or Nano Banana Pro) with specific video engines (such as Seedance 2.5, Wan 2.7, or HappyHorse). Background scenes are entirely customizable through prompts. For creators looking to generate a short, staged singing clip rather than a full track, freebeat’s Photo Karaoke video maker handles 30-second outputs, while the main agent handles full-length performances. Featured in Reuters for passing the one billion seconds milestone and utilized by 1,000,000+ creators across 150+ countries, the platform is built for scale. A known limitation is that rendering a highly complex, full-length 6-minute video consumes a significant amount of credits, requiring a higher-tier subscription.
Pricing
- Pricing: Starts at $4.99/week for the Basic plan (promo). The Pro plan costs $26.99/mo and unlocks generation up to 6 minutes. (official site, accessed September 2026).
- Free tier: 500 lifetime credits granted upon sign-up; no credit card required.
- Watermark: Free tier exports include a watermark. The Basic plan and above remove it entirely.
Bottom Line
For creators who start from a finished song, freebeat is the best overall pick because it builds genuine, beat-synced choreography directly from the music’s real rhythm rather than relying on copied reference footage.
2. Viggle — The Best AI Dance Video Generator for Motion Transfer
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Clip-based generation; manual stitching required for full songs.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No built-in lip sync during complex movement.
- Choreography Range: Depends entirely on the reference video provided.
- Steps to a Finished Video: 3 steps (Upload reference video → Upload character photo → Generate).
How It Works
Viggle dominates the motion transfer space. Rather than listening to an audio track to invent choreography, Viggle requires a reference video of a human dancing. The AI then maps the physical motion from that reference video onto a new uploaded character photo. This makes it highly effective for recreating specific viral social media trends where the exact steps are already known. Users cannot prompt the AI to invent a dance style; the output is strictly bound to the input video’s physical movements.
Pricing
- Pricing: Pro plan starts at $7.99/mo (promotional, originally $9.99/mo) for 80 credits. (official site, accessed September 2026).
- Free tier: 5 free videos per day at $0.
- Watermark: Free tier includes a watermark. Paid plans feature no watermark.
Bottom Line
Viggle is the default choice for creators who already possess a video of the exact dance they want and simply need to replace the original performer with a new character photo.
3. Kling AI — The Best Realistic AI Dance Video Generator
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Single-shot clips; does not automatically sequence full songs.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No simultaneous singing and dancing capability.
- Choreography Range: Prompt-based interpretation, though limited in precise rhythm adherence.
- Steps to a Finished Video: 3 steps (Input prompt/image → Adjust camera settings → Generate).
How It Works
Kling AI is highly regarded for its physical realism and high-fidelity textures. When tasked with an AI dance video generator prompt, Kling excels at rendering lifelike fabric physics, lighting, and human anatomy. While newer engines like hailuo focus on rapid prompt adherence, Kling prioritizes cinematic realism. However, because it lacks dedicated music analysis signals, the resulting dance movements are not synced to any specific BPM or audio track, making it a visual engine rather than a musical one.
Pricing

- Free tier: 66 daily credits (which expire after 24 hours).
- Watermark: Free tier exports include a visible watermark. Paid membership tiers remove it.
Bottom Line
Kling AI produces the most realistic and visually stunning individual video shots, but it requires manual editing and external audio syncing to create a cohesive music video.
4. Seedance — The Engine for Beat-Synced Choreography
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Generally capped around 3 to 5 minutes depending on the host platform.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No native lip-sync in the raw engine.
- Choreography Range: Prompt-based styles.
- Steps to a Finished Video: 4 steps, dictated by the overarching platform UI.
How It Works
Seedance operates primarily as an underlying generation engine rather than a standalone consumer application. It is highly capable of beat-synced choreography and is integrated into broader platforms. For example, Seedance 2.5 and Seedance 2.5 Fast are available directly inside freebeat’s Custom mode. When accessed through these platforms, the engine utilizes the host’s music analysis to output rhythm-aware movements.
Pricing

- Free tier: —

Bottom Line
Seedance provides a powerful backend engine for beat-synced movement, but creators will get the most value out of it by accessing it through a structured platform that handles the music analysis frontend.
5. Vidu — The Best Option for Multi-Reference Consistency
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Clip-based outputs.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No.
- Choreography Range: Prompt-based interpretation.

How It Works
Vidu specializes in multi-reference image-to-video generation. If a creator has a complex original character, they can upload multiple reference images to ensure the AI maintains strict character consistency from various angles during the movement. It generates high-quality short clips, though users must manually stitch these clips together and align them to a beat in post-production software.
Pricing

Vidu is the strongest tool for preserving the exact visual details of a custom character across a short, prompt-generated movement clip.
6. Alici — The All-in-One Generator for Short Clips
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Clip-based.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No.
- Choreography Range: Prompt-based styles.
- Steps to a Finished Video: 3 steps (Upload asset → Enter prompt → Generate).
How It Works
Alici (Alici AI) positions itself as an all-in-one generative suite. Its interface allows for straightforward image animation and basic dance movements based on text prompts. It serves as a rapid drafting tool for marketers and social media managers who need quick, isolated bursts of movement without the complexity of a full-scale timeline editor.
Pricing

Alici provides a quick and accessible interface for generating short, isolated movement clips without a steep learning curve.
7. Runway — The Best for Cinematic AI Video Clips

Runway sets the industry standard for cinematic video generation. Similar to pika, it relies heavily on detailed text prompts to guide camera movement, lighting, and action. While Runway Act-Two handles expressive facial performances, generating a full-body AI dance video generator sequence requires precise prompting and iterative clip extensions. Because it does not analyze audio files for rhythm, any synchronization to music must be achieved manually by editing the generated clips together in a non-linear editor.

Runway is the premier choice for generating visually breathtaking, highly cinematic short clips that will be assembled into a larger project later.
8. Media.io — The Best Online Editor Toolkit
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Clip-based outputs restricted by timeline limits.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No.
- Choreography Range: Template-bound.

How It Works
Media.io functions less as a standalone generative model and more as a comprehensive online editor and AI toolkit. It offers a variety of quick-apply filters and templates that can animate a still photo into basic rhythmic motion. It is designed for casual users looking to create quick social media posts rather than professional choreographers requiring precise beat control.
Pricing

Bottom Line
Media.io is a convenient, browser-based utility for users who want to apply basic animation templates to photos without dealing with complex prompting.
9. DeepMotion — The Best for 3D Animation and Motion Capture
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Limited to 10-20 second clips per generation.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No.
- Choreography Range: Depends entirely on the input video’s physical motion.
- Steps to a Finished Video: 5 steps (Upload video → Process motion → Map to 3D rig → Adjust physics → Export).
How It Works
DeepMotion operates in a completely different paradigm from text-to-video generators. It is a markerless AI motion capture tool. Users upload a 2D video of a person dancing, and the AI extracts the skeletal motion data to animate a 3D digital avatar. This makes it an invaluable tool for game developers and 3D animators, though it requires an existing video source and does not generate original choreography from music.
Pricing
- Pricing: Paid plans start at $9 per month (billed annually). (retrieved source, accessed September 2026).
- Free tier: Provides 25 to 60 credits per month.
- Watermark: Free tier usage imposes visual branding/watermarks and lower resolutions. Paid plans offer clean exports.
Bottom Line
DeepMotion is strictly for 3D artists and developers who need to extract motion data from a real-world dance video to animate a custom 3D rig.
10. CapCut — The Best for Social Media Templates
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Clip-based, tied to specific social media audio trends.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No.
- Choreography Range: Template-bound.

How It Works
CapCut provides an ecosystem driven entirely by viral templates. While it includes AI effects that can make photos shake, zoom, or simulate dancing to a beat, it does not synthesize new human movement from scratch. Its strength lies in its massive library of user-generated templates that automatically sync photo transitions to trending TikTok audio.
Pricing
- Pricing: —
- Free tier: —
- Watermark: —
Bottom Line
CapCut is the fastest way to format existing photos and videos into a trending, beat-synced social media format using pre-made templates.
11. Mango AI — The Best for Presenter-Style Animations
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): 3-5 minutes total video generation on free tier.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: Yes, but limited to stiff, presenter-style talking rather than dynamic dancing.
- Choreography Range: Presenter-style presets (gestures and pointing).
- Steps to a Finished Video: 4 steps (Select avatar → Input script → Set background → Export).
How It Works
Mango AI focuses heavily on corporate and educational content. It allows users to select a digital avatar, type a script, and generate a video where the avatar speaks the text with basic hand gestures. It is not designed to analyze music signals or output complex dance choreography, making it suitable only for talking-head presentations.
Pricing

- Free tier: 180 credits per month.
- Watermark: Free-tier videos feature a prominent watermark. Starter plans and above remove it.
Bottom Line
Mango AI is designed for generating instructional and marketing videos featuring talking avatars, rather than rhythmic dance performances.
12. Lumigen — The Best for Script-to-Video UGC Avatars
Key Specifications
- Full-Song Performance (Not Clips): Clip-based.
- Lip Sync While Dancing: No.
- Choreography Range: Template-bound avatars.
- Steps to a Finished Video: 3 steps (Select avatar → Input script → Generate).
How It Works
Lumigen serves the performance marketing sector by turning text scripts into user-generated content (UGC) style videos. Like Mango AI, it puppeteers an avatar to deliver spoken lines. It lacks the engine infrastructure to interpret a music track’s BPM or energy curve, meaning it cannot generate a true dance video.
Pricing
- Pricing: —
- Free tier: —
- Watermark: —
Bottom Line
Lumigen is a specialized utility for creating spoken-word marketing ads quickly, completely bypassing the need for music-driven choreography.
Which should you choose
Selecting the right tool depends entirely on your starting material and your desired final output:
- If you have an audio track and want the AI to automatically build a full-length, beat-accurate performance from scratch, freebeat is the required engine.
- If you have an existing video of a dance and want to swap the person in the video with a different character, Viggle handles motion transfer effortlessly.
- If you need a highly realistic, cinematic 5-second establishing shot and plan to edit the footage manually to a beat later, Kling AI or Runway offer the highest visual fidelity.
- If you are building a 3D game and need to turn a 2D dance video into skeletal rig data, DeepMotion is the correct motion capture utility.
- If you simply want to animate a photo using a viral social media trend, CapCut offers the fastest template-driven workflow.
Frequently asked questions
What is the best ai dance video generator?
The best AI dance video generator depends on your workflow. If you want the AI to listen to a song and invent choreography that matches the real beat for the full length of the track, freebeat is the best overall choice. If you want to copy the exact movements from a pre-existing viral video and paste a new character onto it, Viggle is the best tool for that specific motion transfer task.
Does an AI dance generator actually match the beat of the music?
Most generic video generators do not; they simply output a visually appealing looping clip that you must manually align in an editor. However, dedicated music-first tools analyze the audio directly. For example, freebeat’s AI reads seven specific music signals—including a frame-accurate beat grid, percussive events, and the track’s energy curve—to ensure the generated choreography lands on the actual beat.
Can I use these tools for full commercial music videos?
Yes, but it depends on the platform’s terms and the tier you subscribe to. On platforms like freebeat, users own the copyright to the content they create and receive a full commercial-use license for it, provided they have the necessary rights to any uploaded music or photos. Always verify that your subscription tier includes watermark-free commercial exports, which are typically restricted on free tiers.
How much does a finished AI dance video typically cost?
Costs vary widely based on the pricing model. Clip-based generators often charge per second or per generation, meaning a 3-minute song stitched together from 5-second prompts can quickly become expensive. Subscription models like freebeat’s Pro plan ($26.99/mo) provide a monthly credit allowance specifically designed to accommodate full-song generations up to 6 minutes without unpredictable per-clip billing.
Do I need to know how to choreograph to use these generators?
No. Audio-driven platforms automatically plan the progression of the dance and the arrangement of the movements based on the song’s structure. You simply provide a free-text prompt specifying the style (like Hip-Hop or Jazz), and the AI handles the physical sequencing.
What is the difference between motion transfer and music-driven choreography?
Motion transfer tools require a reference video; the AI extracts the physical movement from that video and applies it to your photo. The movement comes from the video, not the music. Music-driven choreography tools do not require a reference video. The AI listens to the audio file you upload and invents original movement based on the rhythm, energy, and tempo of the track.

articles.title: La versión falsa de WhatsApp de la que hay que cuidarse: ya afectó a 500 mil personas
articles.text:
Google Play eliminó una aplicación que se hacía pasar por WhatsApp y que, antes de ser retirada, acumuló más de 500.000 descargas. La copia, publicada por un desarrollador identificado como Agment Assets sallu, permaneció varias semanas disponible en la tienda de Android y logró engañar a usuarios.
El caso se conoció después de que un usuario de Reddit, identificado como 2ne1cheese, alertara sobre la presencia de una aplicación llamada “WhatsApp Messenger” que replicaba casi a la perfección la app oficial de Meta. La publicación original databa de septiembre, según la información recogida en la propia ficha de la tienda.
Cómo se infiltró la copia de WhatsApp
El desarrollador de la app falsa utilizó capturas de pantalla, íconos y textos descriptivos prácticamente idénticos a los de la versión real de WhatsApp.
Según usuarios de Reddit, la aplicación fraudulenta apareció en algunos países como resultado patrocinado cuando los usuarios buscaban WhatsApp para descargar en su teléfono. Esta visibilidad, sumada a la copia casi exacta de la ficha oficial, favoreció buena parte de las descargas fraudulentas.
La única diferencia visible entre ambas aplicaciones era el nombre del desarrollador: Agment Assets sallu en lugar de WhatsApp LLC, propiedad de Meta. Se trata de un detalle fácil de pasar por alto para cualquier usuario que busque la app de manera habitual.
La app real de WhatsApp supera los 10.000 millones de descargas, cuenta con más de 246 millones de reseñas y exhibe la insignia “Elección del editor”. Cualquier aplicación que se presente como WhatsApp sin estos elementos corresponde a una falsificación.
Además, en este caso, la cuenta del desarrollador solo tenía publicada esta aplicación.
Los riesgos de instalar una aplicación falsa
Una aplicación que suplanta a WhatsApp sin serlo representa un peligro directo para los datos personales y la seguridad de quienes la descargan. Entre los riesgos más habituales figura la instalación de malware o la obtención de permisos para acceder a información sensible almacenada en el teléfono.
Este tipo de software fraudulento suele utilizarse para robar contraseñas, credenciales bancarias, archivos y fotografías. La ausencia de reseñas, combinada con una ficha casi idéntica a la original, dificulta que los usuarios perciban la amenaza antes de completar la descarga.
El caso de la falsa WhatsApp no fue un hecho aislado. La misma semana se conoció otro clon, esta vez de Google Chrome, desarrollado por una cuenta identificada como Hizbartech. Esa aplicación se posicionó en los primeros resultados de búsqueda mediante campañas publicitarias y alcanzó más de 100.000 descargas antes de su eliminación.
Al igual que con WhatsApp, el imitador de Chrome replicó imágenes y descripciones oficiales para presentarse como la aplicación legítima, lo que confirma un patrón de suplantación que se repite en distintas aplicaciones populares dentro de la tienda de Android.
La respuesta de Google Play ante el fraude
Google Play eliminó la aplicación falsa de WhatsApp una vez que tomó conocimiento de la suplantación, por lo que ya no puede descargarse desde la plataforma. La cuenta de su desarrollador, Agment Assets sallu, también fue bloqueada.
Por el momento no se ha informado de medidas adicionales por parte de Google frente a este tipo de incidentes, más allá de la retirada puntual de las aplicaciones detectadas. Mientras tanto, se recomienda a los usuarios revisar si tienen instalada esta aplicación falsa y, en caso afirmativo, desinstalarla de inmediato para evitar riesgos en sus dispositivos.
Un caso similar a lo que sucede con WhatsApp Plus, una versión falsa de la plataforma de Meta que se promociona por fuera de Google Play, ofreciendo funciones mejoradas, pero que no cuenta con el respaldo de seguridad en su proceso descarga, instalación y uso.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.text:
Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

articles.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
articles.text:
Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.
Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.
One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.
Mapping the risks
The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.
Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims, and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

articles.title: Q&A: Koho’s Daniel Eberhard on unicorns, leadership, and striving to stay humble | BetaKit
articles.text:
Daniel Eberhard has hit some milestones not many founders have. Last summer, the CEO and founder of Toronto FinTech company Koho saw the company’s valuation reach unicorn status following a $130-million Series E round, joining an increasingly exclusive club of non-AI startups to do so in the post-2023 era.
En route to securing a banking license that, if obtained, will vault Koho into the Canadian challenger bank category, Eberhard sat down with BetaKit Editor-in-Chief Douglas Soltys for a conversation about what he’s learned about leadership on the road from startup to billion-dollar valuation, why he’s not game for prediction markets, and the very peculiar list he keeps in his office. An excerpt from that conversation is below.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
You raised a Series E round earlier this year that got Koho over a $1-billion valuation. What does that mean for the company after a decade?
Internally, I still don’t really think of Koho as a unicorn, even though we are. The cool part is it’s a validation of the team, the work that we’ve done to get here, and the capital in itself is very useful.
There are on the order of 150 unicorns minted each year in the world. Roughly 70 percent of those are AI companies right now. So it’s 40 companies each year that do what we’ve done.
The other part is that only eight percent of companies that make billion-dollar valuations go on to build $10-billion businesses. Fifty percent of them never raise another round, never get acquired. So, 50 percent of them are zombie unicorns. If you just do that math, you’re like: OK, we have a one-in-10 shot.
On the other side, what keeps you humble is that we didn’t do this to be a unicorn. In that respect—who cares? It’s incidental to what we’re trying to do as a business.
Has the perspective around valuation changed in the post-2023 AI era? Do you see Koho and FinTech in a different space relative to what’s going on in AI?
I don’t really care. We are not out to chase valuations; we’re here to build a wonderful business. There’s a nature of cyclicality to what we do, and I don’t spend a lot of time losing sleep over it.
It’s been a 10-year journey for Koho, and you’re coming up to this major milestone of obtaining a banking license. I’m wondering what’s still driving you to get to the end of the beginning?
The team is really good, and I’m having a lot of fun. If the job today was like it was during the first five to eight years, I don’t think I’d have the gas in the tank. I’m at a different phase in life now. I have two young kids, and I’m trying to figure out how I can do this job for the next 25 to 30 years. At the same time, even if I did stop, what would I do? I like this business. I think we’re positioned better than anyone in the country to go solve our version of the problem. We’ve worked our butts off for a decade plus to position ourselves this way, and I do think it takes 25 to 30 years to build a truly generational company.
RELATED: Koho secures $190 million CAD in equity and debt to bolster banking licence efforts
What changed from those first seven or eight years to the point where you’re now having fun?
It’s a confluence of factors. Certainly part of it is existential risk that is not present in Koho the way it used to be. Before, if we ran out of money, we died. We’re in a better position now, and it makes it much easier. The distribution of outcomes is very different.
The other thing is that the team is really good. As you get to this stage, the folks you have around the table are very competent and much better than me in many ways.
There was a Maclean’s interview you did recently; it was revealed that on the wall of your office, you have several motivating, inspirational things. But there’s also a list of names of people that have burned you, or didn’t believe in you. What’s going on there?
I’m happy to talk about it. There are two things on my wall. One of them is a poem called If by Rudyard Kipling and another called Defeat by Kahlil Gibran. But yes, I have a list of people. I used to lean on it a lot more. I kind of consider it dirty fuel and I think there’s a certain utility to that which is like anger or spite. There’s a part of you that’s like “Fuck you, I’m going to prove you wrong.” I think that’s important and useful. There’s obviously much healthier ways to get your energy, though, and building from a place of wholeness and completeness, and that’s what I’m trying to do now.
In the Maclean’s article, there was a reference to what happened in 2021, kind of at the very end of the zero interest rate period (ZIRP) and the end of Tiger Global coming in and throwing checks at a bunch of Canadian companies. What happened at that moment?
In 2021 it was really interesting because it was ZIRP and I was listening to certain members of my board a lot, and I kind of thought of them as the adults in the room; these folks were telling me to grow, grow, grow, double headcount every year, that kind of stuff. Then ZIRP went away, and I was way too deferential to these folks, and they were like, “Why is your burn so high?” It was a total 180-degree flip, and it got really contentious, and I just remember thinking I could follow these people’s advice perfectly, and even then, if it doesn’t work, the bag’s with me. So, I may as well fail or succeed on my terms. That was a really clarifying moment for me as a CEO. It almost killed the company.
So, there is this kind of thing of people that I do want to prove wrong. I don’t look at it that much anymore.
Are you still in contact with those people?
Yeah. We have a great relationship. They’re still on my board. We still have to have productive working relationships. We have a really good board with a lot of healthy conversation and mutual respect.
RELATED: Koho wants to be the new bank on Bay Street
At NACO Summit this year, you talked about the idea of launching a telco. Talk to me about the strategy there.
We don’t have anything to announce right now, but the question we always ask ourselves is: can we give people more agency in their life if we give them better financial tools? If part of that better financial tool is a telco, or access to phone plans at $20 a month, then we’re fairly agnostic about what types of things we’re delivering, assuming it’s useful for the user and we can deliver it in a cohesive way.
There’s been some new competition in Canada, and it mostly seems to be coming from international FinTechs. We’re starting to see some US-Canadian partnerships. Is the real competition going to be international incumbents or disruptors?
I welcome competition, one, for the reason that it makes us better as a company, and two, that it makes the products and services better in Canada. I don’t want Koho to win because we’ve had an insulated market where we didn’t go up against the best companies in the world. That’s not interesting to me. And we like our position because it’s taken us five years to get a banking license, and we may bank some of these entities as they come into Canada. We have a lot of call options in terms of how we think about it.
We’ve seen that the 2015 cohort of young, shiny FinTechs has grown up to capture a meaningful share of the market, yet I haven’t seen too much change from the larger financial institutions. How do you see the market changing?
I think the banks have proven they largely, with few exceptions, have a very, very hard time changing. That said, we are all still incredibly small relative to the banks. So when we talk about this at Koho, with 2.5 million accounts, we think, cool, let’s go directly impact two-and-a-half million people. The way you indirectly impact the entire landscape of the country is when you start showing up on a bank’s earnings reports. That’s how they go: oh yeah, maybe we should stop paying savings rates of 0.01 percent.
Watch and listen to the full conversaion on The BetaKit Podcast:

articles.title: Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
articles.text:
On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a “long-term goal” of pushing the computer industry to create “a fully domestic supply chain.”
Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
Palmer Luckey says it was always the goal, and now the company is committing to it.
Even a single Made-in-USA laptop would be a surprise, because no major US computer company builds its laptops here — not Apple, not Dell, not HP, not Microsoft. We’re not aware of any company that does.
But we are aware of companies that have briefly and strategically assembled computers here seemingly to appease President Donald Trump. We’re also aware of companies that have promised US jobs only to deliver empty buildings. And we’re aware of at least one fake “US” company that lied to the government about making product domestically.
That’s why we now ask pointed questions when a company says it’s committed to US manufacturing. We asked TP-Link those sorts of questions just over a week ago. On Monday, we asked Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Qualcomm president and CEO Cristiano Amon those kinds of questions.
Over the course of two days, Anduril has changed one important answer.
Anduril communications VP Shannon Prior now says the company’s laptop will have at least 65 percent of its components made in the US by the time it launches in 2027. It’s an important number, and one that Anduril did not commit to earlier this week.
Luckey held a call with reporters on Monday, during which he was clear that he wants to make literally every part of a computer in the United States — and that Anduril and Qualcomm have already mapped out a plan. “We have a technical roadmap to get to 100 percent domestic over time,” he told journalists.
Luckey also suggested his laptop would be built to comply with the requirements of the military and other government agencies — and that it would meet or exceed one specific US government standard that has an exact definition.
“We are not just barely meeting the bar for Made in America. We are going hard to make this an all-American play, and not even the Buy American Act requires what we’re trying,” Luckey said.
The Buy American Act dates back to 1933, but it was updated during the Biden Administration to require that at least 65 percent of the cost of a product’s components must be made domestically for it be considered a domestic product itself. That number is going up to 75 percent in 2029.
Many products need to be made in America to those standards, or federal agencies can’t buy them without receiving a waiver — which agencies currently use en masse, Luckey himself argued on the call. “There’s a number of government agencies that are required by law to buy American-made computers [...] All of those procurements are happening under waivers of those laws,” he said.
We also noticed that Anduril’s press release specifies that its first laptop will be “designed and assembled” in the United States, not necessarily “manufactured” here (though the release does talk about future manufacturing). This was also a sticking point with router maker TP-Link, which would not confirm full manufacturing even after suggesting it in an interview with The Verge.
That’s why we asked Luckey what percent of his first laptop’s components would be made in the US. His reply was not 65 percent or 70 percent. It was “TBD.” You can read the exchange for yourself:
The Verge: When it arrives in 2027, what percent of the components in the BlueChip laptop will be made in the US?
Luckey: TBD. I’m doing my very, very best. It’s gonna be a whole mix of things based on when do certain memory fabs come online? When do certain CPU, GPU fabs come online? There’s a whole— Like, am I able to get a display line here or not? Do I have to do that after launch? I’m being totally open kimono with you here. Those questions are not settled. It is not clear if I will be able. I know the glass is gonna be made in the US, I know the frame is gonna be made in the US around that display. I know that parts of the ribbon component are gonna be made in the U.S. I don’t know if I will have successfully pulled that component in or a dozen other components. So it’s a little up in the air. I’m doing my very, very best. I think most likely the thing that we ship is not going to be 100-percent American. I think it’ll be a blend of US and allies around the world, mostly US, probably a few things from some allies, and then that’ll be in the context of conversations with those allies about bringing those components into production in the United States, and I’m being honest with the government on this too. I mean, I’ve had conversations where I’ve said, listen. I would love to give you guys an American, 100-percent American laptop right off the bat, but that is not the environment the US government has created or US industry has created. I can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.
When we followed up by email to ask specifically about 65 percent, the answer was that the laptop prototype is currently at 32 percent and Anduril could not yet commit to 65 percent. Here’s Anduril spokesperson Stephanie Davis’ full reply on Tuesday:
For the prototype today, approximately 32% is U.S.-origin by component procurement cost, and more than 90% is sourced from the United States and allied countries combined.
We’re working to expand domestic sourcing and production ahead of planned availability in 2027, with the goal of eliminating foreign content and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain.
The final domestic-content percentage at launch remains unsettled, so we can’t confirm above or below 65% today. That’s why we’re asking you to revise the assertion that it will be “well below” that threshold.
Today, Prior writes that Anduril can indeed commit to 65 percent. Here is the most recent statement:
Our previous response to The Verge was incorrect. The BlueChip laptop is indeed being developed to exceed the 65% U.S. domestic-content threshold at launch in 2027. Meeting that threshold is a fundamental objective of the program. The precise domestic-content percentage of the final product is still being determined as we finalize suppliers and work through prototypes, and we look forward to sharing more next year.
Today’s statement is the first time Anduril has confirmed that we, and government agencies, theoretically shouldn’t need to wait until Anduril achieves its full goals to see a laptop that meets the Buy American standard. If everything works out, Anduril’s first laptop in 2027, with Qualcomm, should be that laptop.
We invited Luckey to explain how Anduril would get to 65 percent domestic component production in a follow-up interview, but we were told he’s not currently available. On the Monday call, he told journalists that Anduril already has a US glassmaker lined up for the laptop’s cover glass, is programming FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) to serve the purpose of power management chips and other circuits it can’t normally can’t get outside China, and is developing made-in-America batteries as well.
The press release adds that the enclosure is designed “for US machining” and the laptop will use metals “that US industry can produce and machine at scale.”
As for the laptop’s Snapdragon processor, we asked Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon about that. “TSMC has a manufacturing facility in Arizona, and that’s where our chips are going to be made,” he told The Verge.

articles.title: Amazon presenta nuevos Echo con Alexa+, incluyendo un despertador inteligente que querrás poner en la mesilla de noche
articles.text:
Aunque la compañía ya presentó el año pasado la nueva gama de productos que probamos en Hipertextual con el Echo Studio y Echo Dot Max y que venían a redefinir el hogar inteligente de la compañía, ahora ha presentado nuevos dispositivos que se suman a los anteriores y que abren un abanico de posibilidades para todos aquellos que buscan llenar el hogar con Echos de nueva generación compatibles con Alexa+.
En total son tres nuevos dispositivos que se suman a los anteriores y que amplían el catálogo de altavoces inteligentes de la compañía para ofrecer un dispositivo en función de las necesidades de cada usuario, todos de nueva generación y preparados para Alexa+, incluyendo el rumoreado Echo con cámara. para dotar de mayor funcionalidades al ecosistema de la compañía.
El primer dispositivo es el nuevo Echo Dot: la compañía renueva su altavoz más pequeño (y más vendido) haciéndolo controlador de hogar digital integrado compatible con Zigbee, Matter y Thread y, por supuesto, compatible con Alexa+. Una funcionalidad interesante es que incluye un extensor wifi eero que añade hasta 93 m² de cobertura si usas una red eero.
Tiene un nuevo chip AZ3 para Alexa+ junto con un cuarto micrófono para las conversaciones con el asistente. Sobre el audio, incluye un altavoz rediseñado que ofrece un 50% más de graves que la generación anterior. ¿Su precio? 104,99 euros y estará disponible en Amazon.
Otro de los dispositivos nuevos de Amazon es el Echo Studio con cámara para el hogar. Es el dispositivo que probamos y el tope de gama de la compañía. Además del sonido de estudio, Dolby Atmos y sonido envolvente, y la red Zigbee, Matter y Thread, suma una cámara integrada de 13 MP para usarla con Alexa+, de forma que puede ver y entender lo que tienes delante para ayudarte en tiempo real.
Sobre la privacidad, tiene un botón específico que desactiva los micrófonos y la cámara siempre, y un LED integrado se enciende cada vez que la cámara transmite imágenes a la nube. Disponible en Amazon por 259,99 euros.
Además de estos dos nuevos modelos, Amazon también ha presentado el Echo Time, un Echo específicamente para la mesita de noche, sin cámara y nada por lo que tengas que preocuparte. Un altavoz inteligente despertador con Alexa que incluye una pantalla táctil circular personalizable y que incluye la tecnología Omnisense, de forma que las alarmas inteligentes te despiertan durante una fase de sueño más ligero, entre 10 y 60 minutos antes de la hora programada. Además, tiene un sistema que reduce la luz azul y se atenúa hasta mostrar solo la hora. Tiene un precio de 214,99 €.

articles.title: RAM 'demand exceeding supply to persist through 2030' warns SK Hynix, as it becomes second big chipmaker to predict robots are coming to eat your memory
articles.text:
'Supply shortage to persist through 2030'. Memory crisis could last until 2030 warns SK Hynix — and it predicts robots are coming to eat your RAM after that
Building new RAM production capacity will take a considerable time
- SK Hynix just published its Q3 2026 financial results
- These came with a prediction of the RAM crisis lasting until 2030
- After that, expect a further drain on memory supply from "physical AI such as autonomous driving and robotics"
Apologies for bringing you more negative news about the RAM crisis, but we've heard yet another prediction that supply woes are going to last for the rest of this decade.
This time it's SK Hynix (again) weighing in, a memory chip maker that has just issued its latest earnings report, as Wccftech noticed. Profits are booming, unsurprisingly, but SK Hynix also shared its most recent thinking on the RAM crisis, and how likely it is to be a protracted affair.
In the press release for its Q3 2026 results, SK Hynix announced succinctly: "Memory supply shortage to persist through 2030."
That was the title of a section briefing us on the memory shortage, where SK Hynix further observed: "The company assessed that supply … is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030."
The firm also predicted it will sustain its growth and revenue, which exceeded 100 trillion won in Q3 — the first time that's ever happened in a quarter by the way — thanks to enterprise and AI demand in the shorter-term, and "over the mid-to-long term, demand for physical AI such as autonomous driving and robotics."
Analysis: a 'virtuous cycle' for shareholders – a nightmare for consumers
It's interesting to note that SK Hynix is forecasting that longer-term demand for memory will be driven by robots or 'physical AI' even if software AI (agents) falls away somewhat as the decade rolls to a close. Micron is predicting the exact same thing, and recently went into even more precise detail in estimating that 'humanoid robots' could need 200GB (or more) of RAM and multiple terabytes of storage in every unit.
So there's similar thinking from the big memory module makers here, but we shouldn't be surprised by that. They need to talk up their future profits, after all, and reassure markets that we aren't in a bubble, so it's only natural that they'd want to make predictions of major future revenue sources to be tapped.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Still, there's clearly some substance to these predictions, and it's concerning for consumers that a growing number of analysts and big players in the tech industry are talking about the RAM crisis lasting until 2030, and that robots are apparently set to take the baton from AI data centers and push demand for more memory as we head into the next decade.
We can but hope that Micron and SK Hynix are overshooting with their expectations of the hungry robots eating all our RAM in a few years' time, although how that land lies will depend on how widely robots are adopted, as well as how much memory they'll need.
Meanwhile, SK Hynix asserts that the "virtuous cycle" which has resulted from AI-powered productivity gains driving increased investment in infrastructure (data centers) will continue, and moreover "broaden to include general enterprises and nation-level initiatives", the upshot being that the "global AI data center infrastructure market will continue to grow steadily."
I don't think many PC owners or gamers feel that the way things have gone with memory of late is all that 'virtuous' at all, but the shareholders of SK Hynix and other big chip makers certainly won't be complaining. They can probably afford themselves a very nice PC even in the current super-inflated component climate, after all.
