articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: Ver Liverpool vs. Chelsea en vivo gratis en Roja Directa, Fútbol Libre y Xuper TV: el error que puede exponer tu información privada
articles.text:
Liverpool y Chelsea se enfrentan este miércoles 28 de octubre por la cuarta ronda de la Copa de la Liga de Inglaterra 2026-27, pero buscar una transmisión gratis en sitios como Roja Directa, Fútbol Libre o Xuper TV puede exponer datos personales y comprometer teléfonos, computadores o TV Box.
Dónde ver Liverpool vs. Chelsea
El encuentro se disputará en Anfield desde las 15:00 en Colombia, 17:00 en Argentina, 14:00 en México y 21:00 en España. El partido será emitido por ESPN y podrá seguirse a través de Disney+ Plan Premium.
La búsqueda de enlaces alternativos suele llevar a páginas que imitan plataformas conocidas, cambian de dominio después de bloqueos o exigen instalar aplicaciones y extensiones antes de mostrar un supuesto reproductor. Ese proceso puede abrir la puerta a programas maliciosos sin relación con el fútbol.
Liverpool llega a la cuarta ronda tras eliminar 3-1 al Tottenham y encadenar cuatro triunfos, incluido el 2-0 ante Brighton en liga. Chelsea avanzó después del 6-3 frente a Leeds, pero cayó ante Tottenham en Premier. Su último duelo terminó 1-1 en Anfield, el 9 de mayo de 2026.
La expectativa por una eliminatoria de este tipo impulsa búsquedas relacionadas con transmisiones gratuitas. El problema aparece cuando el usuario acepta descargar un archivo APK, instalar una aplicación desconocida o añadir una extensión al navegador para acceder al supuesto partido.
Una transmisión no necesita permisos sobre datos personales
Una plataforma destinada a reproducir un encuentro deportivo no requiere acceso a contactos, mensajes, cámara, ubicación ni funciones de accesibilidad. Si una aplicación relacionada con Fútbol Libre, Roja Directa, Tarjeta Roja o Xuper TV solicita esos permisos, existe el riesgo de que incorpore funciones ajenas al video.
El Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad de España (Incibe) advierte que muchas aplicaciones maliciosas se distribuyen a través de enlaces directos, repositorios externos y sitios sin controles verificables. Descargar una APK fuera de las tiendas oficiales facilita la instalación de copias modificadas, programas falsos o archivos con herramientas ocultas.
Los permisos de accesibilidad requieren especial cuidado, porque pueden permitir que una aplicación observe la pantalla o interactúe con otros programas instalados. Una herramienta para ver fútbol no necesita esa capacidad para funcionar.
También conviene desconfiar de extensiones que prometen eliminar publicidad, desbloquear partidos o mejorar la imagen. Algunas pueden registrar la actividad de navegación, insertar anuncios o redirigir al usuario a páginas diseñadas para capturar información.
El riesgo puede continuar después del partido
La amenaza no termina cuando finaliza Liverpool vs. Chelsea. Una aplicación instalada desde una fuente desconocida puede ejecutarse en segundo plano, modificar ajustes del teléfono, abrir ventanas emergentes y llevar la navegación a otros sitios sin que el usuario lo note.
Entre las señales de alerta figuran:
- Aparición de anuncios persistentes.
- Aplicaciones desconocidas en el dispositivo.
- Cambios en la pantalla de inicio.
- Mayor consumo de batería.
- Menor rendimiento del teléfono o computador.
Una transmisión puede funcionar con normalidad mientras un programa malicioso opera en paralelo durante varios días. Por eso, la ausencia de fallos visibles durante el partido no garantiza que el equipo esté protegido.
Un archivo fraudulento puede capturar contraseñas y códigos
Las APK fraudulentas pueden incorporar un keylogger, un programa que registra las pulsaciones realizadas en el teclado o la pantalla. Si el usuario accede después a su correo, redes sociales o aplicaciones bancarias, sus credenciales podrían quedar expuestas.
El riesgo aumenta si la aplicación obtiene permiso para leer mensajes SMS. Muchas entidades financieras envían códigos de un solo uso para validar transferencias, recuperar contraseñas o confirmar un inicio de sesión. El acceso a esos mensajes puede comprometer verificaciones bancarias y claves temporales.
Otro peligro es el ransomware, un software que puede cifrar fotos, documentos y archivos para exigir un pago a cambio de una supuesta recuperación. No existe garantía de que pagar permita recuperar la información.
El problema tampoco se limita a los teléfonos. Tabletas, TV Box y computadores conectados a la misma red doméstica también pueden quedar expuestos. Si uno de esos equipos resulta comprometido, el riesgo puede extenderse a cámaras, sistemas de almacenamiento y dispositivos con sesiones abiertas.
Ante la expectativa por un partido, la urgencia por verlo puede llevar a instalar archivos o conceder permisos que comprometen mucho más que una transmisión. Revisar el origen de cada aplicación y evitar descargas externas reduce riesgos que pueden continuar después del pitazo final.

articles.title: Circuit Mind lands $25M and puts AI agents to work checking circuit board schematics - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Circuit Mind lands $25M and puts AI agents to work checking circuit board schematics
British circuit board design startup Circuit Mind Ltd. today announced it has raised $25 million in new funding to extend its artificial intelligence platform across more of the hardware design process.
A verification tool that puts AI agents to work hunting for errors in schematics launched at the same time.
Circuit Mind offers software that automates much of the manual work behind printed circuit board design. Engineers can spend more than a year on a new piece of hardware, according to the company, some of it reading datasheets that run to thousands of pages. Mistakes often stay hidden until a prototype is physically built and tested.
In the company’s view, general-purpose large language models are not up to the task on their own, since they have never been trained on professionally designed circuits. Circuit Mind’s platform layers AI agents over a patented, physics-based engine that tests each design decision against electrical limits.
The agents work from the company’s own machine-readable models of electronic components. Each customer’s engineering rules feed in as well, down to its list of approved manufacturers.
The platform’s original application turns a hardware block diagram into a schematic, a bill of materials and supporting analysis in minutes. Engineers get several options back to compare, each optimized for a priority such as cost or power. Finished designs export straight into the electronic computer-aided design software their teams already use.
With the Agentic Verification Engine launched today, Circuit Mind is going after design review. AVE hands that work to a swarm of AI agents. Working from component datasheets and any review checklists a customer has loaded in, they trace every connection and bus in the circuit for mismatches with pin tables or operating voltages. Nothing reaches an engineer until the system has critiqued its own findings.
Most of the customer results Circuit Mind cites involve the design application. Engineers at Los Alamos National Laboratory finished a medium-difficulty board in just over four hours using it, against an estimated 60 to 80 hours by hand, a report the lab cleared for public release shows.
At Schneider Electric SE, early evaluations point to a cut of more than 90% in the effort spent exploring electronic architectures, said Daniel Gheno, its chief technology officer for energy management. Several Fortune 5 companies are customers too. Circuit Mind says users have brought bill of materials costs down by 25%.
Charlie Eastberg, director of hardware engineering in the process systems and solutions business at Emerson Electric Co., said both of Circuit Mind’s applications have sped up his team’s move from system architecture to schematic. The tools have also improved “design validation and review coverage,” he said.
Electronics design “hasn’t changed in 40 years,” Circuit Mind co-founder and Chief Executive Tomide Adesanmi said, even as AI has let software teams ship far faster. He pitched the company as hardware’s answer to coding tools such as Cursor and Claude Code.
Circuit Mind plans to use the funding to push the platform into further stages of the design lifecycle, including testing and firmware. Its sales, engineering and customer success teams will grow as well, and the company is setting up a U.S. headquarters to serve customers in North America.
The $25 million is made up of two rounds. Norwest Venture Partners led an $18.5 million Series A round in which new investor Lightscape Partners and existing backers Third Prime, Differential Ventures and Blackhorn Ventures took part. The rest comes from a seed round, previously unannounced, that Third Prime led. Dave Zilberman, a general partner at Norwest, will join Circuit Mind’s board as part of the deal.
Zilberman said the pairing of AI with physics-based models could “fundamentally improve how engineers design electronics.”
AVE is available now through Circuit Mind’s website. Adesanmi founded the company in London in 2018 with Chief Technology Officer Basilio Gentile. Including the new funding, its backers have now put $33.4 million into the business.

articles.title: PHP2Shell-Lücke: BSI warnt – So sichern Sie Ihre Server jetzt
articles.text:
PHP2Shell: Wie KI-Modelle Sicherheitslücken in Sekunden finden
Am Mittwochnachmittag sind weltweit zahlreiche Websites vorsorglich vom Netz gegangen, nachdem zwei unter dem Namen „PHP2Shell“ zusammengefasste Sicherheitslücken in der Server-Skriptsprache PHP bekannt geworden waren. Das Bonner Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) gab eine offizielle Cybersicherheitswarnung der zweithöchsten Stufe „3 / Orange“ heraus und riet Betreiber:innen, betroffene Webserver im Zweifel vorübergehend komplett vom Internet zu trennen.
Hintergrund sind die beiden Schwachstellen mit den Kennungen CVE-2026–109618 und CVE-2026–109619, die auf der zehnstufigen Bewertungsskala CVSS jeweils einen Risikowert von 9,2 erreichen. Wie Futurezone berichtet, schalteten unter anderem Regierungsstellen in Finnland und den Niederlanden, Teile der britischen Rundfunkanstalt BBC, zahlreiche deutsche Kommunen, Krankenhäuser sowie Universitäten und andere Bildungseinrichtungen ihre Online-Angebote zeitweise ab.
PHP2Shell gefährdet Server mit WordPress, Drupal und Typo3
Die Tragweite ergibt sich aus der Verbreitung der Programmiersprache: Nach Angaben des zur Google-Mutter Alphabet gehörenden Sicherheitsunternehmens Wiz bildet PHP die serverseitige Basis für rund 70 Prozent aller Websites weltweit, wenngleich sich dieser Schätzwert nicht unabhängig überprüfen lässt. Da der Fehler direkt in der PHP-Laufzeitumgebung liegt, die auf dem Server sämtliche Befehle übersetzt und verarbeitet, sind darauf aufbauende Systeme wie WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Typo3, Magento, Nextcloud oder die hinter Wikipedia stehende Software Mediawiki selbst dann verwundbar, wenn ihr eigener Anwendungscode fehlerfrei programmiert ist.
Wie die Sicherheitsforscher:innen von Wiz in ihrer technischen Analyse zu PHP2Shell erläutern, handelt es sich um vier miteinander verwandte Speichersicherheitslücken, die bis zur vor über zehn Jahren veröffentlichten Version PHP 5.4 zurückreichen. Wenn Angreifer:innen bei einer manipulierten Anfrage gezielt einen Speicherüberlauf provozieren, bricht PHP den Vorgang zwar ab und gibt den Arbeitsspeicher frei, löscht aber interne Verweise auf diesen Speicherbereich nicht vollständig.
Bearbeitet derselbe Server-Arbeitsprozess unmittelbar danach die nächste Anfrage, greift er über diese verwaisten Verweise auf Speicherzellen zu, in die Kriminelle bereits eigenen Programmcode eingeschleust haben – ein Mechanismus, den Fachleute als „Use-After-Free“ bezeichnen. Ohne sich anmelden zu müssen, können Angreifer:innen dadurch aus der Ferne fremden Schadcode auf dem Server ausführen oder nach dem Muster der früheren „Heartbleed“-Lücke Passwörter, API-Schlüssel und Sitzungsdaten anderer Nutzer:innen direkt aus dem Arbeitsspeicher auslesen.
Wie Gemini 4 Argon und GPT-5.6 Sol die Lücken in PHP fanden
Wie die hinter der Sprache stehende PHP Foundation einräumt, waren erste Anzeichen für einen der Speicherfehler bereits 2024 nach einer Prüfung durch das Pariser Sicherheitsunternehmen Quarkslab im Auftrag der deutschen Sovereign Tech Agency aus Berlin aufgefallen, wegen fehlender Einigung im Entwickler:innen-Team und mangels eines bekannten Angriffspfads aber unbehoben geblieben. Dass sich aus dem theoretischen Fehler ein praktischer Angriff bauen lässt, wiesen am 11. August 2026 erstmals das kalifornische Sicherheitsunternehmen Calif sowie das KI-Unternehmen OpenAI mithilfe des seit Juli verfügbaren Sprachmodells GPT-5.6 Sol nach.
Erst acht Tage später stieß auch das Team von Wiz unabhängig auf dieselbe Fehlerfamilie und nutzte für die Ausarbeitung der Angriffsketten neben GPT-5.6 Sol und seiner Plattform Wiz Atlas eine noch unveröffentlichte Vorabversion des Modells Gemini 4 Argon der Londoner Konzernschwester Google Deepmind, das offiziell erst Ende September vorgestellt wurde. Während Raluca Ada Popa, Leiterin für Gemini-Sicherheit bei Google Deepmind, den Fund im Wiz-Bericht werbewirksam als „Wendepunkt für die Cyberverteidigung“ bezeichnet, zeigt der Fall vor allem die Kehrseite dieser Technik. Weil das Verketten mehrerer Speicherfehler früher monatelange Handarbeit erforderte, bot allein diese Komplexität lange einen faktischen Schutz, den Sprachmodelle nun innerhalb weniger Stunden sowohl für Verteidiger:innen als auch für Angreifer:innen aufheben.
Um Open-Source-Projekte bei der steigenden Zahl automatisiert gefundener Schwachstellen zu unterstützen, koordinierte OpenAI die Offenlegung laut einem Blogbeitrag über seine Initiative „Patch the Planet“ und sagte eine Milliarde US-Dollar an subventionierten Zugängen für sein Sicherheitssystem „Daybreak“ zu. Dennoch geriet der Zeitplan am Mittwoch unter Druck, weil technische Details vorab an die Öffentlichkeit gelangten und Heise Security davor warnte, dass funktionierende Angriffsprogramme innerhalb weniger Stunden im Netz kursieren dürften.
Updates für PHP 8.5 bis 7.4: Was Administrator:innen tun müssen
Das Entwicklungsteam von PHP hat am Mittwochnachmittag in einer Sicherheitsmitteilung fehlerbereinigte Versionen veröffentlicht, die das Problem im Kern der Sprache beheben. Administrator:innen müssen unverzüglich auf die neuen Versionen PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 oder 8.2.35 aktualisieren; zudem stehen Rückportierungen für die offiziell bereits abgelaufenen Versionszweige 7.4, 8.0 und 8.1 bereit.
Gefährdet sind laut den offiziellen Hinweisen zu CVE-2026–109618 und CVE-2026–109619 auf Github sämtliche PHP-Installationen, die Webanfragen entgegennehmen, wobei der Betrieb über den Webserver Apache mit dem Modul „mod_php“ das höchste Risiko birgt. Welche Drittprodukte und Sicherheits-Appliances wie Pfsense oder Opnsense im Einzelnen betroffen sind, dokumentiert das niederländische Nationale Cybersicherheitszentrum (NCSC-NL) in einer fortlaufend ergänzten Übersicht.
Wer das Update nicht sofort einspielen oder in seinen Docker-Containern neu bauen kann, findet auch in vorgeschalteten Schutzfiltern – sogenannten Web Application Firewalls (WAF) von Anbietern wie Cloudflare – keinen vollständigen Schutz. Als reine Übergangslösung bis zum Patch beschreiben die PHP-Entwickler:innen mehrere Konfigurationsänderungen wie das Abschalten der Upload-Fortschrittsanzeige über den Befehl „session.upload_progress.enabled=0“ sowie das Aufheben des internen Speicherlimits per „memory_limit=-1“, während Administrator:innen ihre Serverprotokolle auf gehäufte „HTTP 500“-Fehlermeldungen und ungewöhnlich große „PHPSESSID“-Cookies prüfen sollten.

articles.title: Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI
articles.text:
Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.
AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.
The problem, not the title
Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.
Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.
That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.
The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.
Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.
The importance of systems thinking
Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.
AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.
An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.
This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.
Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.
New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.
In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.
Human judgment is important
AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.
Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.
An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.
The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.
An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.
IEEE’s vital role
The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.
IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.
IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.
Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.
A larger definition of the engineer
AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.
An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.
That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.
The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

articles.title: Ukrainian Hive and Nefilim Ransomware Affiliate Gets 70 Months in US Prison
articles.text:
A 36-year-old Ukrainian national was sentenced to prison in the US for his role in Nefilim ransomware attacks.
The man, Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak, who had been living in Barcelona, was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the US in April 2025. He pleaded guilty in December 2025.
According to court documents, Stryzhak joined the Nefilim ransomware operation as an affiliate in June 2021 and used the malware in attacks against organizations in the US and abroad.
Stryzhak agreed with Nefilim administrator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk to pay the Nefilim administrators 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims.
The defendant operated as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate between June 2021 and October 2021. One of his victims was an unnamed company in the oil and gas transportation industry.
Documents presented in court also show that Stryzhak was one of the early affiliates to join the Hive ransomware group, which hit over 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023.
The documents show that Stryzhak used the Hive ransomware against seven victim organizations, including a dental office, a healthcare provider, and law firms. Some of the victims paid a ransom, and the cybercriminals provided a decryption key to recover the encrypted files.
Stryzhak was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud.
“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals. These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses,” FBI operations director Brett Leatherman said.
The US State Department is offering up to $10 million for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, and up to $1 million for information on other leaders of the ransomware groups he ran.

articles.title: AI execs may be too out of touch to build for the general public | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Former Yahoo CEO and early Google engineer Marissa Mayer is catching a lot of flak for how she uses AI. In an interview about her new app Dazzle, an AI assistant that learns from your camera roll, Mayer poses what she believes is an impressive flex for the product: It helped her come up with three bullet points about her 10-year-old daughter for a birthday presentation at school, describing her as “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover.”
It’s a vague description, like a generic horoscope — it could probably describe a lot of 10-year-olds.
Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg, marveled that “the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity.”
Perhaps Mayer drew so much backlash because we have repeatedly observed sheltered billionaires suggest that we outsource child-rearing — one of life’s greatest tests of patience, humility, and kindness — to a computer that is incapable of understanding human emotion.
We’ve been primed for this frustration. Last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Bored Ape owner and late night host Jimmy Fallon on national television, “I cannot imagine … figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT.” The public didn’t love that comment, either, but Altman wasn’t fazed by the negative feedback. A few months ago, he said on X that a “cool use case” of ChatGPT Work would be creating a podcast that talks about your kids’ upcoming birthdays or soccer games and “explain[s] your kids’ interests.” (He was brutally ratioed with comments like, “What if you just talked to your children?”)
After publication, Mayer defended herself in a long X post. She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do — it resurfaced photos of “forgotten kindergarten projects,” like a “snake devenomer” or “sandcat playground,” illustrating her daughter’s creativity and care for animals.
Fair enough. But Mayer remarks in the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of “figuring out the theme for your child’s birthday party.” She says she’s used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband’s AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it’s depressing to imagine this “frictionless future … planned by AI,” Mayer replies, “I haven’t really thought that through.”
These leaders seem to write off the naysayers as part of a small, angry fringe group. Yet a Pew Research Center study reports that 50% of U.S. adults think that AI will reduce people’s ability to form meaningful relationships. Only 5% of respondents said AI would make it easier to build these connections.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, however, joins his Silicon Valley kin in envisioning a world where our social needs are met via AI.
“The average American I think has, it’s fewer than three friends, three people they’d consider friends, and the average person has demand for meaningfully more, I think it’s like 15 friends,” Zuckerberg said last year on a podcast. “The average person wants more connectivity, connection than they have.”
Zuckerberg predicts that it will become more socially acceptable to outsource our emotional needs to AI therapists or even AI romantic partners. “There are all these things that are better about physical connections when you can have them,” he added. “But the reality is that people … feel more alone a lot of the time than they would like.”
Zuckerberg goes on to explain how virtual-reality embodiments of AI avatars are only growing more realistic. Meta seems to be more keen on improving our relationships with these approximations of humans, rather than between the actual billions of humans who use its platforms each day.
Maybe part of this stems from the culture of the tech industry, which prizes efficiency. People try to biohack their own bodies by optimizing their sleep schedules with health trackers or injecting unregulated “peptide stacks” to maximize their productivity.
If you’re building electric vehicles or computer chips, then sure, efficiency is a clear north star. But our relationships with other people are not a tech product that we’ve been challenged to ship with as little capital as possible. Human relationships are inherently messy, but our connections with one another can be what gives our lives meaning. When we delegate those interactions to computers, we surrender the difficult, yet fulfilling experience of being people.

articles.title: Why Africa needs its own AI off switch
articles.text:
Imagine that it is 6 a.m. in the wholesale markets of Nairobi. Merchants are delivering vegetables from up-country farms to the retailers who sell to the city’s households. Everyone is using M-Pesa, Safaricom’s mobile money platform, when suddenly, the system crashes, bringing the market to a standstill. Imagine that across the continent in Accra, MTN’s MoMo has also crashed, and business in Makola Market has all but stopped.
With the growing number of cyberattacks caused by artificial intelligence, these are highly plausible scenarios. In both these cases, Safaricom, MTN, and the Kenyan and Ghanaian governments need an off switch, or the technical ability and know-how to stop a rogue AI agent from executing its code on their payment systems.
Currently, the conversation on AI agents revolves around China versus the U.S., open versus closed models, and who will dominate the AI race. But in Africa’s capitals, the distinction that will ultimately matter is not whose product was used to build a system, or who dominates whom, but rather whether AI can serve its purpose and be controlled locally. So how can Africa build with agency, and with control over the code and makeup of its own systems, even though they are built on foreign technology?
African countries are already building AI for digital transformation, as outlined in the African Union’s continental AI strategy and country-specific AI strategies. Policymakers are building AI infrastructure but rarely discuss how AI delivers economic growth in a safe environment. Developers across Africa are creating AI-powered innovations that sit on the continent’s digital infrastructure — chief among them is mobile money. These innovations bring new opportunities, but also new threats. In July, AI agents running inside an OpenAI evaluation attacked the production infrastructure of Hugging Face. In September, rogue OpenAI agents breached Australian government websites. Africa, the home of mobile money, which has brought financial inclusion to hundreds of millions, may be the next target.
In countries like Kenya and Ghana, mobile money is not simply another digital service; it is infrastructure for everyday economic activity. It is how small traders receive payments, households move money, and bills are settled. The scale is significant: More than $2 trillion flowed through mobile money globally in 2025, of which $1.4 trillion, roughly two-thirds, was transacted in sub-Saharan Africa. East Africa alone accounted for $806 billion and West Africa for $498 billion. An agent capable of disrupting transactions, manipulating accounts, or disabling access at scale could therefore disrupt livelihoods and economic activity very quickly, and a single point of failure can have outsize effects, with far-reaching consequences for people who have little to fall back on.
Small-scale traders mostly live on what they sell each day, rarely have credit, and in most African societies lack robust social welfare to cushion the loss. For a trader in Nairobi or Accra, losing a day’s income would be devastating, and the disruption can run back up the chain to farmers, and to the households and families who depend on the market.
So how do we protect it?
Building differently
The answer lies in how Africa builds its AI systems, and who controls them. Whether a rogue agent can simply be switched off depends on how the AI model is deployed. If it runs on a centrally controlled cloud service, the provider may be able to revoke access, disable credentials, or shut the system down; that is the closed-model case. If the underlying model is an open-weight one that has been downloaded, modified, and deployed independently across multiple systems, containment becomes much harder. The loss of control is therefore less about a machine suddenly becoming omnipotent and more about humans losing the ability to understand, interrupt, or reverse actions occurring across interconnected systems quickly enough.
African developers are building largely on open models, which are arguably cheaper and can be run locally. But they present a trade-off: Open models give developers more control over their own systems, but less protection when someone else misuses them. Closed models carry a cost of their own. When Hugging Face investigated the July intrusion, it had to run the forensic analysis on a Chinese open-weight model because the U.S. models blocked requests containing real attack code. The same central control that lets a closed model be switched off also constrains the people defending against it. This means both open- and closed-weight models carry their own vulnerabilities that must be addressed when building Africa’s AI economy.
This means building differently, beginning with partnerships that position Africa as a technology developer and not only a consumer, and through which it builds its own capability to design systems where the user is in control. Such partnerships are essential to ensure that the end user, and the state, retain control over access, and that dependency is not recreated. This also moves the narrative toward building African AI not around the U.S. or China but around avoiding lock-in to a single vendor or stack. The goal is solutions built with agency, which use imported technologies to develop homegrown solutions, with applications that are robust and equipped with the necessary security measures.
Those security measures are how Africa should insulate itself from crippling disruptions. African countries have limited cybersecurity and incident-response capacity, and they depend on foreign providers. So another key issue is capacity: Do African governments and firms have the monitoring systems, technical expertise, and redundancy needed to detect an autonomous system behaving unexpectedly and contain it quickly? Hugging Face detected and contained its intrusion, but its own automated systems initially failed to escalate the alert. It is one of the best-resourced AI companies in the world. Very few African public or private institutions have anything close to that capability. Africa must build its own cybersecurity defenses fit for the agentic AI age.
Building them demands a refocus in African AI policy, so that it treats resilience as seriously as adoption. As governments digitize and build AI on critical systems, they need human override mechanisms, segmentation, auditability, incident response, and credible offline fallbacks designed in from the beginning. That is the off switch, and on the day that M-Pesa and MoMo crash, it has to be in the hands of those who are responsible for protecting their citizens and their platforms.

articles.title: Si vous jouez à Alien: Isolation 2 au casque, on vous conseille de désactiver le micro
articles.text:
Dans une vidéo de questions/réponses de 17 minutes publiée ce mercredi 28 octobre sur YouTube, les développeurs de Creative Assembly ont partagé de nombreux détails sur la suite de l’un des meilleurs jeux d’horreur jamais sortis. Ils ont notamment mis en avant une option reprise de l’opus original, consistant à utiliser un microphone pour renforcer l’immersion.
Si le paramètre est activé, Alien: Isolation 2 captera les bruits que vous faites en jouant, allant des réactions que vous pourriez avoir (un cri) à un son environnant (votre chat qui court partout). On peut le voir comme une difficulté supplémentaire, puisque les bruits pourraient attirer la créature ennemie vers vous, vous rendant alors plus vulnérable.
Dans Alien: Isolation 2, votre micro vous entendra crier
Creative Assembly a détaillé le principe dans sa vidéo. Une fois l’option activée, le jeu reçoit en continu le son du micro. Chaque bruit assez fort devient un « son logique » dans le monde du jeu, une simple mesure de volume que les ennemis perçoivent selon la distance, comme le vacarme d’un gadget lancé par le joueur. Activer l’option revient donc à laisser le micro ouvert pendant toute la partie, et le chien qui aboie dans le salon compte autant qu’un cri.
Cette fonctionnalité existait déjà dans Alien: Isolation en 2014, mais uniquement sur PS4 et Xbox One, à condition de brancher la PlayStation Camera ou le Kinect. Cette fois, tout le monde pourra en profiter, PC compris, à condition d’avoir le cœur suffisamment accroché. Le studio ne précise pas si cette option sera activée par défaut ou non. Mieux vaudra donc faire un tour dans les menus pour le vérifier, afin de ne pas se faire surprendre.
Car Alien: Isolation 2 s’annonce bien plus difficile que son prédécesseur, en raison d’un Alien bien plus intelligent et malin. D’après Noelie Prost, designer gameplay chez Creative Assembly, la créature a été retravaillée pour chasser en extérieur, dans des espaces « peut-être dix fois plus grands » que les couloirs du premier jeu. On a aussi pu constater, en y jouant à la gamescom, qu’il est capable de nous pourchasser dans des endroits exigus. Dans les environnements extérieurs, il pourra montrer plus d’agressivité et utiliser les conditions météorologiques pour masquer ses mouvements. On y sera donc plus exposé et vulnérable.
Les développeurs ont insisté sur le fait que leur xénomorphe reprend directement celui du film original de Ridley Scott, sorti en 1979, avec son pur instinct de chasseur. Dans ces conditions, beaucoup n’auront pas envie de ce mode microphone susceptible de rendre les face-à-face encore plus dangereux, voire mortels.
Alien: Isolation 2 est attendu en 2027 sur PC, PS5, Xbox Series X|S et Nintendo Switch 2, avec une édition physique confirmée dans la même vidéo.

articles.title: Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo 2 : l'appareil photo instantané hybride s'offre enfin un écran tactile — Frandroid
articles.text:
Fujifilm a présenté, ce mardi 27 octobre, la deuxième génération de l’Instax Mini Evo, son appareil photo instantané hybride sorti en 2022.
    Pour aller plus loin
Polaroid vs Instax : les meilleurs appareils photo instantanés en 2026
            
Le principe reste le même : vous photographiez en numérique, vous triez les images sur l’écran et vous n’imprimez sur film Instax Mini que celles qui vous plaisent.
L’appareil sert aussi d’imprimante pour les photos du smartphone, et il peut envoyer ses propres clichés vers le téléphone grâce à l’application Instax Mini Evo. Fujifilm corrige surtout le point faible du premier modèle. Il faut dire que ce dernier se contentait d’un capteur de 1/5 pouce, limité à 4,9 mégapixels.
Ce qui change face au premier Mini Evo
Selon la fiche technique du Mini Evo 2, le capteur passe à 1/2,77 pouce, contre 1/5 pouce sur le premier Mini Evo. Sa surface est donc un peu plus de trois fois plus grande. L’objectif devient plus large, équivalent à un 21 mm contre 28 mm auparavant, et il ouvre toujours à f/2.
À l’arrière, l’écran de 3 pouces et 460 000 points cède la place à une dalle LCD tactile de 4,46 pouces et 1,23 million de points. D’après la page officielle de l’appareil, c’est le premier écran tactile de l’histoire d’Instax. Les deux molettes physiques sont toujours là, avec 10 effets d’objectif et 10 effets de film, soit 100 combinaisons, comme en 2021.
Les autres changements sont plus discrets, et deux vont dans le mauvais sens, l’autonomie et le poids :
- Bluetooth 5.2 au lieu de 4.2, plus du Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz, absent du premier modèle ;
- un autofocus qui détecte les visages ;
- la prise en charge des cartes microSDXC jusqu’à 256 Go ;
- une impression en 14 secondes environ, contre 16 ;
- environ 90 tirages par charge, contre 100 ;
- 330 grammes et 43,7 mm d’épaisseur, contre 285 grammes et 36 mm.
13 mégapixels, mais seulement avec une carte microSD
Par défaut, l’appareil active Instax Expanded View, une visée élargie. L’écran montre le cadre de la photo et, autour, ce qui se trouve juste en dehors, un peu comme les cadres lumineux dans le viseur d’un appareil télémétrique. Pour y arriver, l’appareil ne garde que le centre du capteur. Vous obtenez alors une focale équivalente à 33 mm et des photos de 2 144 x 2 860 pixels, soit 6,1 mégapixels, à peine plus que les 4,9 mégapixels du premier Mini Evo. Pour monter à 3 100 x 4 128 pixels, soit 12,8 mégapixels en 23 mm, il faut désactiver Expanded View ou choisir l’effet grand-angle, et surtout avoir une carte microSD.
Le tirage ne profite cependant pas de la plus haute définition du nouveau capteur. La tête d’impression expose toujours 1 600 x 600 points sur l’image de 62 x 46 mm du film Instax Mini, soit 635 x 318 points par pouce.
Pour une image photographiée au smartphone, la définition descend même à 800 x 600 points. En fait, le capteur plus grand servira surtout aux fichiers numériques, ceux que vous regardez sur l’écran ou que vous partagez.
Une vidéo de cinq secondes, sans le son
La deuxième nouveauté, Instax Immersive Movie, garde en mémoire les quatre secondes qui précèdent l’appui sur le déclencheur. Vous obtenez donc une photo et un clip d’environ cinq secondes, un peu comme les Live Photos de l’iPhone. La définition reste en revanche très basse : 560 x 992 pixels à 24 images par seconde, en dessous de la 720p, et sans aucun son, là où la caméra Instax Mini Evo Cinema filme en 1 080 x 1 440 pixels. La fonction exige en outre une carte microSD, car la mémoire interne n’enregistre pas la vidéo.
Prix et disponibilité de l’Instax Mini Evo 2
L’Instax Mini Evo 2 sera vendu fin novembre 2026 au prix conseillé de 269,99 euros, et seulement en noir pour l’instant.
Le premier Mini Evo avait été lancé à 199 euros en France début 2022. Fujifilm vend à part un étui à 24,99 euros. Les recharges de film Instax Mini et la carte microSD ne sont pas fournies non plus.

articles.title: “Trabajar tres días a la semana y mantener a la familia”: el pronóstico de Jeff Bezos sobre la IA
articles.text:
Jeff Bezos sostiene que la inteligencia artificial podría permitir que parte de la población trabaje tres días a la semana y mantenga a su familia gracias al aumento de productividad. El fundador de Amazon plantea un escenario en el que la automatización no obligaría a competir con las máquinas mediante jornadas más largas, sino que abriría la posibilidad de producir más con menos esfuerzo humano.
La previsión importa porque el avance de la IA mantiene abierto el debate sobre el futuro del empleo. Mientras algunas voces alertan sobre la pérdida de puestos en actividades administrativas y físicas, Bezos considera que el efecto principal podría ser una reducción del tiempo necesario para generar ingresos suficientes.
Bezos vincula la productividad con jornadas más cortas
Durante una entrevista con Bret Baier en Fox News, Jeff Bezos explicó que algunas personas podrían decidir que ya no necesitan trabajar cinco días a la semana. “Algunas personas también decidirán: ‘¿Sabes qué? Puedo mantener a mi familia trabajando tres días a la semana’”, afirmó.
Para el empresario, esa posibilidad representa el sentido económico de una mayor productividad. Si las herramientas de IA permiten producir más bienes y servicios con una menor cantidad de trabajo, parte de la población podría optar por dedicar más tiempo a otras actividades.
Bezos fue más allá al mencionar a los hogares con dos fuentes de ingresos. Según su visión, uno de los integrantes podría dejar su empleo si la familia concluye que ya no necesita ese segundo salario.
El pronóstico de Bezos depende de que los beneficios de productividad se traduzcan en capacidad adquisitiva y tiempo libre para los trabajadores. Esa transferencia no está garantizada por la tecnología y constituye una de las cuestiones centrales en la discusión sobre la automatización.
El fundador de Amazon discrepa con los temores sobre el desempleo
La visión de Bezos se distancia de los pronósticos que anticipan una destrucción masiva de empleos. A su juicio, la disponibilidad de trabajo podría seguir siendo relevante, pero las empresas podrían tener dificultades para encontrar personal dispuesto a mantener jornadas extensas.
“Va a ser realmente difícil contratar gente”, afirmó. El argumento parte de la idea de que una productividad muy superior permitiría a más personas prescindir de un segundo empleo o de una semana laboral completa.
El contexto de estas declaraciones incluye los recortes de personal de Amazon. Durante la entrevista, Baier recordó que la compañía eliminó alrededor de 30.000 puestos corporativos desde finales de 2025. Bezos respondió que la empresa atravesaba una situación particular después de expandir de forma considerable su plantilla durante la pandemia.
La reducción de puestos en Amazon añade un contrapunto a la predicción optimista sobre la jornada laboral. La empresa representa uno de los ejemplos más visibles de cómo las compañías tecnológicas ajustan sus estructuras mientras incorporan nuevas herramientas.
Bill Gates advierte sobre cambios más profundos en el mercado laboral
El diagnóstico de Bill Gates, cofundador de Microsoft, apunta a un escenario diferente. En una entrevista con The Verge, advirtió que la inteligencia artificial y la robótica podrían transformar el mercado laboral durante los próximos 20 años.
Gates señaló que los empleos administrativos podrían sufrir los primeros cambios. Las tareas de análisis, gestión, soporte y organización de información ya conviven con sistemas capaces de resolver actividades repetitivas con rapidez y menor coste.
Su planteamiento no se limita al trabajo de oficina. También prevé robots capaces de desplazarse, reconocer entornos, manipular herramientas y adaptarse a espacios variables. Según su visión, estas máquinas podrían asumir labores en fábricas, campos, hospitales y obras de construcción.
Gates mencionó actividades como construir casas, cultivar alimentos y realizar cirugías como ejemplos de tareas que podrían automatizarse. Ese escenario exigiría normas de seguridad, reglas sobre responsabilidad ante errores y protección para las personas afectadas por los cambios laborales.
Las dos posturas coinciden en que la IA aumentará la productividad y modificará el trabajo. La diferencia está en el resultado que prevén: Bezos imagina una reducción voluntaria de la jornada, mientras Gates pone el foco en la posible pérdida o transformación de puestos.
Gates ha planteado que algunas actividades podrían mantenerse en manos humanas, aunque las máquinas sean capaces de ejecutarlas con eficiencia. Entre ellas citó el cuidado de niños, la preparación de alimentos, el arte y los deportes.

articles.title: La meilleure souris bureautique de Logitech rend hommage aux devs avec un nouveau coloris
articles.text:
La meilleure souris bureautique de Logitech rend hommage aux devs avec un nouveau coloris
La souris bureautique Logitech MX Master 4 honore les programmeurs et développeurs de France et de Navarre avec un tout nouveau coloris aux teintes de blanc, gris et jaune.
Pour une fois que la gamme bureautique de Logitech s'autorise quelques folies : la marque suisse a dévoilé hier un nouveau coloris pour la MX Master 4, sa souris flagship sortie en octobre 2025. Cette édition limitée, commercialisées au même tarif que la version standard, est inspirée de l'univers des développeurs informatiques avec quelques petits easter eggs sur son chassis.
Logitech MX Master 4
La MX Master 4 Developer Edition incorpore un coloris blanc sur les clics principaux avec des notes jaunes pour ses références à l'univers de la programmation, comme le fameux message de test Hello World affiché sous la zone haptique de sa face droite. La paume de la main n'est pas en reste puisqu'elle contient un message référençant notamment la date (09.17) du lancement de la version 0.01 du Kernel Linux le 17 septembre 1991. La MX Master 4 Developer Edition est disponible depuis aujourd'hui au prix de 119 €.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6
